| 2026-10-09 | **ADD-UNITS REDESIGN BUILT UNDER THE PO GO OF THIS DATE (`CR-176-BRC10`, `DEF-MET-10035`) — NINE JUDGMENTS OF OURS, NONE PUT TO THE PO (law 13).** **(1) THE UNITS LIST'S BAR vs `DEF-TEN-5840`.** The 2026-09-19 fix made the selection bar show whenever the list had rows so *Select all {n}* was reachable; today's ruling says *"the selection bar shows only once a unit is ticked (no '0 unit(s) selected')"*. The newer ruling wins and the older one's purpose survives: one tick brings the bar and *Select all 3412* with it, so 3,412 units are one tick and one press away, never 3,412 ticks. Two static tests that asserted the bar at zero now assert its absence and a DOM test ticks one row and finds *Select all 3412* over a page of one row. **(2) THE DEFAULT LABEL IS `Unit {seq}`, NOT `{seq}`** (superseding CR-089 E4's plain-case default). The approved drawing labels the run *Unit 2 to Unit 4* and the ruling's own worked figure (*"Unit 1, Unit 2, Unit 3 are taken. Use 6"*) only works if the run's labels are *Unit N*; the seeded tenant's buildings hold *Unit 1*, *Unit 2*, so `{seq}` made labels (`1`, `2`) that never clashed with them and the screen said *"Unit 1 is taken"* about a label it was not going to write. The row creating the new version is listed and worded against its partner's stored `before`, so it reads *Rate: 2.00% → 6.00%*; the partner row is not listed (History and the plan Audit tab alike). **(4) A PLAN'S AUDIT TAB FOLLOWS THE TAX'S CHAIN:** a plan binds the tax ROW it was attached to, and a new rate is a new row in the same chain (`chain_id`) — matched now, or the row carrying the new rate was never the plan's. Its *Changes underneath* rows say the change in History's words (*Tax · City Utility Franchise Fee 2% — Rate: 2.00% → 6.00%*), never only *Edited*. **(5) THE VERSIONS TABLE IS THE OVERVIEW TAB'S Version · Dates · Status TABLE** (the plan page has no separate Versions tab); it gains a fourth column *Change* in History's words (*Minimum bill: $10.00 → $12.00*). **(6) THE MARK, AND HOW IT IS DECIDED:** a copy `_publish` writes from now on carries `terms_recorded: true`; a correction's copy carries its terms in `version_terms`; any other copy counts as recording its terms only where its four terms equal the version row's own term columns — the pre-fix copies held the replaced version's columns, so v2 at $12.00 holding $10.00 fails it while every v1 and a v2 that moved no term pass. Where this copy or the one before it fails, the cell reads *Terms not recorded* (3 words, B14 rule 33 fact) and no change is claimed; nothing on disk is rewritten. | 2026-10-08 | **SECURITY-SETTINGS LANE — SEVEN JUDGMENTS MADE BUILDING THE PO'S "MAKE THE SECURITY TAB TRUE" RULING (`DEF-IDN-10022`/`10023`/`10024`, 2.562.0).** The ruling is the row below; these are the places it left a choice, each decided rather than asked (law 13). **(1) Expiry's clock starts at `password_changed_at`, and where that is empty, at the day the login was created (`users.created_at`).** Treating an empty date as "never expires" would exempt exactly the oldest passwords; the creation day is the earliest the password can have been set, so it errs towards asking. Worked: 90-day policy, password changed 91 days ago → the sign-in lands on *Set your password*; 89 days ago → the dashboard; a seeded login with no change date created 91 days ago → *Set your password*. **(2) "Older than" is strict: day 90 is still good, day 91 is expired.** **(3) Expiry is enforced at a SUCCESSFUL sign-in only**, by raising the existing `must_change_password` — no new screen, no new gate — and a wrong password still counts towards the lockout and says nothing about expiry. A temporary password is never re-flagged (it has its own 7-day clock); a temporary password is told apart from an expired one by `temp_password_expires_at`, which only a temporary one carries. **And a "Keep me signed in" renewal is refused once the password has expired**, because a renewal is a sign-in nobody typed: without it an expired password would ride a 30-day trusted session past its expiry. The forced change after expiry is audited as `auth.password_changed`, not `auth.password_reset` — the person chose the old password. **(4) Password history is a TABLE (`password_history`, `identity/0010`, RLS ENABLE + FORCE in the `NULLIF` form), not a JSON column on `users`**: append-and-prune, its own timestamp, the same RLS block as every tenant table (hard rule 1). It holds Django hasher strings only. **"The last 5 passwords are blocked" means the CURRENT password and the FIVE before it are refused; the sixth-oldest is allowed again** (Priya: Meadow → wind1 … wind6; wind6 and wind1–wind5 refused, Meadow allowed). Pruned to 5 rows per user on every write. **(5) Which paths check it:** `change_password` on BOTH its paths (ordinary and forced). A temporary-password RESET records the password it replaces, so the forced change that follows cannot go straight back to it; the temporary password itself never takes a slot. Owner provisioning does NOT check it — it creates a login that has no previous password, so there is nothing to repeat. The customer portal's own passwords are not this tab's and are untouched. **(6) The idle clock: ONE mechanism, in `07-frontend/src/api/client.ts` — every request sent while nobody has pressed, typed, scrolled or touched the page for a minute carries `X-Background-Refresh: 1`, and `identity/auth.py` authenticates it in full and does not slide `last_seen_at`.** Chosen over tagging each `refetchInterval` query because there are five kinds of poll today (TanStack `refetchInterval` on the bill run and three import screens, `pollJob`, and two plain `setInterval`s in the field app) and a per-query tag is exactly what the next poll forgets (law 2). A minute is a quarter of the shortest idle limit a utility can pick (15 min), so it cannot hold a session open on its own. Worked: 30-minute policy, the bill run polling every 30 s with nobody there → signed out at minute 31; the same page with a click at minute 20 → good until minute 50. Trusting the header is safe in the only direction it can be abused: sending it can only expire a session SOONER. CORS now grants it (`x-background-refresh`), or every cross-origin poll would fail at preflight. **(7) DevOps check for Allowed addresses is a read-only `manage.py client_ip_check`**, which runs the same `client_ip` every request runs: it prints `TRUSTED_PROXY_COUNT`, the address the server recorded for the newest sign-ins, and with `--remote-addr`/`--xff` what a given load-balancer line resolves to. The allowlist logic is unchanged. | security-settings lane (AI), under the PO ruling of 2026-10-08 | `06-backend/apps/identity/services.py` · `auth.py` · `models.py` · `migrations/0010_def_idn_10023_password_history.py` · `management/commands/client_ip_check.py` · `07-frontend/src/api/client.ts` · `tests/test_def_idn_security_settings_true.py` · `BR-IDN-020/025/026` · `09-infra/02-aws-runbook.md` r7 |

| 2026-10-07 | **CR-174-BRC10 (LANE JUDGMENTS) — US PAYMENTS (PRIME): THE BUILD'S OWN EIGHT DECISIONS, NONE PUT TO THE PO (law 13), EACH WITH ITS FIGURE.** Built on the PO's D1–D4 (the row below that starts *"PO RULINGS — US PAYMENTS (PRIME)"*). **J1 — A FOURTH PAYMENT ORIGIN, `agent`.** D3 says US Payments money must not enter `/partner/v1/receipts` or the New World file and the filter (`origin = webhook`) must not change. The three existing words mean *a person keyed it* (`entry`), *it arrived over a wire* (`webhook`) and *it came in a file or a batch* (`import`); `webhook` is true of US Payments and is exactly what the feed selects, and the other two are false. So `payments/0049` widens `ck_payments_origin` to a fourth word, `agent` — *a payment agent took it on the utility's behalf and told us*, labelled **Payment agent** — which the feed excludes by construction. Worked: Rosa's **$150.00** kiosk payment is `origin = agent`; `collectable(origin="webhook")` returns 0 rows for it (test `test_us_payments_money_never_enters_the_new_world_receipts`). **J2 — THE NACHA CODE GETS ITS OWN COLUMN, AND THE REASON IS CHOSEN FROM IT.** `payments.return_code` on the reversing row (CHECK: only on a reversing row). Reason: `R01` and `R09` (insufficient / uncollected funds) → `nsf`, which counts toward cash-only exactly as a bounced cheque does; every other code, and a return with none → `bank_chargeback`. The two staff reasons are never chosen by a machine. **J3 — CHANNEL AND MACHINE ARE COLUMNS, NOT A PARSE OF THEIR JSON.** `payments.channel` (`kiosk·csr·web·ivr·other`, an unknown word → `other`) and `payments.terminal` (`4471`), written at INSERT; the raw message keeps them whole on `payment_webhook_events.body` too. The payment page reads columns rather than a partner's field names. **J4 — CLEARED ON ARRIVAL.** `record_payment` leaves a payment with no clearing date `processing` and unallocated — exactly the *"still shows $147.85"* the PO ruled against in D1 — so a US Payments payment is cleared on its business date and allocates at once. **J5 — A RETURN THAT OVERTAKES ITS PAYMENT ANSWERS `503`.** Not `500` (not our fault), not `400` (not their mistake): *come back shortly*. Nothing is kept, so the identical resend is a first delivery. **J6 — THE SYSTEM ADMIN IS TOLD ON THE THIRD SUCH REFUSAL, ONCE.** A return overtaking its payment is a race the first resend normally wins; the third refusal for the same `paymentId` means it is not a race. Counted from the connector's own run rows (`request_key = <paymentId>|return`), so nothing else is written. D2's residue — a payment for an account that has gone — alerts at once: landed, nothing posted, the landing row says `account_not_found`, answer `200`. **J7 — THE TENDER VOCABULARY IS REUSED, AND THAT READS THE 2026-09-16 *"no mapping at connector level"* THROUGH D1 RATHER THAN IGNORING IT.** A payment posted inside the call needs its method resolved inside the call; Runbooks is not built and the vocabulary is the one built mechanism. `OTHER` is the fallback (*"unknown → OTHER, never refuse"*) and the connector cannot be switched on until it is mapped (refused: *"Map OTHER first, then switch on."*); on switching on, CASH→cash, CHECK→check, ACHCHECK/ACHSAVINGS→ach, CREDIT/DEBIT/GOOGLEPAY/APPLEPAY→card are applied where the utility has those codes — nothing is created. **J8 — THE LANDING ROW AND THE MONEY ARE ONE TRANSACTION.** A post that fails after the row is written would otherwise answer the resend `409` over money never posted. | 2026-10-06 | **`DEF-BIL-9751` BUILT — WHICH READ COUNTS A PROCESSING DEPOSIT, CALLER BY CALLER (lane MVI-DEPOSIT-9751, `CR-171-BRC10` §26; maintenance; law 13, none put to the PO — the ruling above settles the first bill, and what follows are our judgments on its blast radius).** (1) **THE FIRST BILL COUNTS IT.** `credit.deposit_payments_for_account` (billing's only reader, through `payments_seam.deposit_paid_for_account` → `first_bill.deposit_line_for` and the one-time preview's `_move_in_charges`) now reads `deposit_release.deposit_counted_paid`: every deposit-purpose payment, cleared OR processing, net of returns and releases. It is NOT narrowed to payments the move-in wizard wrote: a deposit line exists only on a first bill, so the deposit money that can meet it is the money taken when service starts, and the ruling's reason (*"what the customer actually did at the counter"*; a bounce is handled by the existing process) holds for any tender and any door. (2) **A RELEASE DOES NOT.** `deposit_still_held` — what a cancelled move-in releases to credit and then REFUNDS — still draws on cleared money only. Counting a cheque in the drawer as paid for a bill puts nobody's money at risk (if it bounces the deposit is owed again); counting it for a refund would pay out money the utility may never receive. (3) **A VOIDED CHEQUE IS NEITHER (`DEF-PAY-9782`, filed here).** `cheques.void_cheque` moves a processing cheque to `failed` and writes no reversing row, and `deposit_still_held` excluded only `processing`, so a voided $150.00 deposit cheque still read as HELD and a cancel could have refunded it. Both reads now exclude `failed`. Cancel (an original `cancelled` + its −amount `cancelled` row) and Reverse (a −amount `reversed` row, same purpose) already net themselves out. (4) **THE MOVE'S BILLING TAB IS UNCHANGED.** *Deposit taken* stays the cleared register (`accounts.deposit_on_file`), *$150.00 not cleared yet* stays (`DEF-CUS-9755`, a true fact the ruling did not change), and *Still to collect* already read **$0.00** — so the tab and the first bill now agree: nothing owed on either. No string moved. (5) **"OWED AGAIN" IS PROVED THROUGH THE EXISTING PATHS ONLY:** a processing cheque cancelled → the first bill's deposit line is $150.00 again; a cleared cheque reversed NSF → $150.00 again; a voided cheque → $150.00 again and held $0.00. **Not built, stated:** once the first bill has ISSUED without a deposit line, a later bounce leaves the deposit owed on the move's Billing tab (*Still to collect* returns to the full figure) but no later bill carries a deposit line — the deposit line is a first-bill line (BR-BIL-012), and adding one elsewhere would be the new path the ruling forbids. **Worked (the PO's figure):** the church pays **$325.00** by cheque at move-in ($300.00 deposit + $25.00 connection); its first bill carries no $300.00 deposit line; if the cheque bounces, the $300.00 is owed again. Stated instead: a window booked from a screen before `2.519.1` reads early by the utility's UTC offset (5 h in summer, 6 h in winter on US Central) and is re-booked once. (2) **"Unscheduled" means NO VISIT WINDOW, not "no deadline" (`DEF-WRK-9693`).** Every job carries a deadline (`BR-WRK-018` stamps one from the priority), so "no date" can only mean no booked visit. | 2026-10-04 | **CR-168 ROUND 6 · SRV-5 — TELL PEOPLE AND PRINT: TWELVE JUDGMENTS OF OURS BUILDING RULING 3 (lane SRV-5, law 13; none put to the PO; `2.517.0`).** Ruling 3 (23 Sep): *"Notification reaches the consumer and the back office, and work orders print"* — four consumer kinds, three back-office kinds. (1) **The four consumer words map to four catalogue events**: booked → `appointment_window`, moved → `visit_moved` (NEW), on the way → `technician_on_the_way`, done → `completion_receipt`; all ride the `appointment` kind (`OQ-WRK-1495`: never `notice`, no print floor). (2) **When each fires**: booked on the FIRST assign/schedule that leaves a job with a customer holding a time; moved on a later one that changes the window — once per NEW window (moving it to the same window twice tells the customer once), and a job never told *booked* is told *booked* rather than that it moved from a time nobody gave them; on the way on each `depart`; done when the office ACCEPTS a job whose outcome is *passed* — never at the field close (`WM-47`: nothing is final until a person accepts) and never for a failed job. Worked, in the walk: WO-0050 assigned to R. Patel 08:00–12:00 → *Visit* email + text queued; Patel sets off → text; Dana accepts → email; four rows, nothing twice. (3) **Channels are the CUSTOMER's election ∩ the utility's switch**: `accounts.paperless` → email, `.sms_reminders` → text, the same read billing uses; a customer who chose neither gets nothing and the act says `visit_message_no_channel_elected`. (4) **One queue call per channel**, because one call pins one template and an email body is the wrong text message; four new templates seeded (`service_visit_moved`, `sms_visit_booked`, `sms_visit_moved`, `sms_technician_on_the_way`). (5) **Text messages are WRITTEN UNADDRESSED today** (`recipient_not_resolvable`): customers' read holds no MOBILE number and refuses to guess one from a landline — the row stands and says why; the gap is the platform's, not this lane's. (6) **`edit.notify_reschedule` now goes through the same path** — it queued an `in_app` row with NO template for a CUSTOMER (an inbox they do not have, rendered from nothing). (7) **The three back-office kinds are catalogue events with their own switches** (`work_job_at_risk`, `work_job_declined`, `work_job_blocked`, in-app, `staff_field_work`), fire on EVERY job from the act — no Work rule row — and each is a FAILURE under `BR-NOT-021`: whoever sent the job out + every System Admin, no *Also tell* (that narrowing is for a rule's escalations only). *Blocked* is a job put on hold (it cannot go ahead; the hold reason says why), once per hold. (8) **At risk needs the utility's at-risk window**: the hourly sweep tells the office once per PROMISE when an open job comes within `work_settings.at_risk_window_hours`; with no window set there is no *before* and nothing is sent — a passed promise is the rule's *Past due* escalation, and the first sweep after `2.517.0` must not flood a utility with one notice per overdue job. (9) **A utility seeded before `2.517.0` keeps booked / on the way / done OFF** (stored when they were drawn and refused) until a supervisor switches them on — SRV-4's `sla_breach` precedent; `visit_moved` and the office kinds read the catalogue default (on). Its four new templates arrive by the next `seed_notice_templates` (`manage.py seed_demo --tenant`), the way `staff_field_work` did. (10) **Printing reuses the product's ONE PDF writer**: billing publishes its page engine unchanged as `apps/billing/page_print.py` (B14 rule 43 — one writer; B1 — no reach into `documents.py`'s underscore names), Work calls it through `billing_seam.page_engine()`; the bill's bytes do not move. (11) **On demand, not stored**: §7.3 sketched *"rendered through the tenancy document store"*; an open job's sheet changes with every dispatch, so a stored copy is stale by the next move, and the final document of an accepted job already has its home (`WorkOrderReport`). Deterministic — the same job printed twice is the same bytes. (12) **What paper carries**: the premises' address walked (hard rule 8), the customer read live, the visit in the utility's zone, safety and tasks as boxes to tick, readings with their units, parts, a sign-off; NO database id in the bytes (B14 rule 31, tested). A day pack is a technician's or a crew's OPEN jobs whose window (else due time) falls on the day, in order, a cover list then one sheet each; an empty day prints *No open jobs on this day.* The door is **Print** on every shape of the order (first, the destructive action still last) and **Print day…** on a technician's page with a date (today by default); a crew's pack is served (`?crew=`) and has no screen door yet. | lane SRV-5 (our judgment; PO not asked — law 13) | `CR-168-BRC10` §24 · `06-backend/tests/test_cr168_srv5_messages.py` · `test_cr168_srv5_print.py` · `DEF-NOT-9666` |

A WARNED reading (`high`, `low`, `zero`, `vacant_unit` …) IS validated, because BR-MET-129 posts it (*"we can give the warning, but we cannot reject the reading"*) and BR-MET-022 says *"flags never block billing by themselves"*. Using billing's own list makes *validated* here and *billable* there one set. **(3) *HIGHEST* IS THE REGISTER VALUE**, then consumption, then the later-written row; an estimate (no dial, BR-MET-028) ranks below any actual. | 2026-10-04 | **TECHNICIAN SYNC DESIGN — THE PO DELEGATED IT WITH ONE HARD RULE: NO DATA RECORD IS EVER DROPPED, EITHER WAY (`CR-168-BRC10` §F; our design, recorded).** PO, verbatim: *"in case you have better way to manage sync - both ways, notification both ways, and large number of data records + images coming from phone or tab - then im okay with that approach also - we cant drop data record in sync process both ways"*. **Our design, built on what exists** (`offlineStore.ts` outbox, `sync.py` per-item keys, `push.py`), keeping every earlier ruling of today (paging both ways, link created with the record and handed to the async upload, never reject a photo, shared device, accurate location, accept held while photos upload): **(1) Acknowledged outbox.** Every capture is written to the device's durable store first, with its own id, technician, capture time and location. It leaves the device ONLY when the server has acknowledged that exact item; "sent" is never enough. **(2) Server never refuses field data for a STATE reason.** A job cancelled, reassigned or already accepted while the phone was offline still has its items STORED and flagged *Needs review* for the office. This supersedes the instruction given to lane FIELD-FIX earlier today to refuse an item from a technician who is not the assignee: it is stored and flagged instead. Only a non-technician or a foreign-tenant caller is refused, because that is not field data. A malformed item is stored as received and flagged, never discarded. **(3) Server → phone by change feed.** The phone asks for *everything changed since my cursor*, paged, including removals (a job reassigned away). It never re-downloads whole lists, and the cursor is per technician, so the shared device never mixes logins. **(4) Images.** The link is created with the record; the upload is a background queue with retry and back-off. The server checks the bytes' hash against what the phone declared, so a half-sent image is asked for again, never stored broken. A link still empty after 24 hours is listed for the office; it is never deleted. **(5) Notifications both ways.** Server → phone: a push is only a *wake up and sync* signal carrying no data, so a lost push loses nothing; the next sync or app open catches up. Phone → office: the office is told when a job closes, when its photos are complete (Accept unlocks), and when anything is flagged *Needs review*. **(6) Always counted.** The phone always shows *N waiting to send* (`BR-WRK-036`'s marker extended). Every sync writes a receipt, and a per-device report compares items captured with items acknowledged, so a gap is visible rather than silent. | PO (chat), design ours | `CR-168-BRC10` §F · `BR-WRK-036`, `042`, `047` |

a unit gate blocks its unit, a whole-build gate every unit of its service; a build with no gate order has nothing that blocks. **(d)** open to-dos are listed on the warning and never block (`BR-MET-114`). **(e)** notes are `connection_todos` rows with `kind='note'` (`metering/0065`), not `account_notes`: a single-family build has no account to hang one on; The tenant's own required-document checklist (`BR-CUS-095`) is keyed on the JOB a request becomes, which a clerk decides after reading it, so at the portal there is nothing to key it on. At Send each requirement becomes one of `BR-CUS-095`'s designed types (`photo_id` → *proof of identity*, `proof_of_address` → *proof of address or occupancy*; none → *other*), so the clerk's checklist and the applicant's file meet on the request. It is held on the draft in the applicant's own words (like `address_as_given` — never a home; `G85` passes) and read through `customers.portal_seam.application_mailing_address`, the shape `application_tax_id` set; `services._carry_request_decisions` — which BOTH request account doors (master, move-in) already run — adds it as the account's ONE `kind='mailing'` row **only where the clerk's payload says nothing about addresses** (both wizards omit the key when empty, so an empty list from a clerk is an answer and is obeyed). It is US-format, the staff side's own rule: the kit's state list and `12345`/`12345-6789`; an unticked box with no street, city, state or ZIP holds Continue and is refused at Send naming step 3. **(4) THE DASH MEANT "NOT WORKED OUT YET"** — reproduced at 77 Nowhere Lane: an address the utility does not hold carries `if_you_apply: null`, so both lines drew `—` (the PO's screenshot). It now reads *We will tell you* on both; a held address whose plan has no deposit reads *No deposit* (`money.nothing()`); a real figure, `$0.00` included, prints as the figure. The dash survives only while the availability read is in flight. **(5) FOOTER** — `WizardFooter` (Back left, commit right, DOM order Back → commit) on seven screens; start-service step 2 has no Back because step 1 is another route that mints a new draft, so its Continue still sits right; `BR-CWP-109` minted; `09-component-inventory.md` §5's *"commit first"* superseded in place. **(6) VERSION** — `components/BuildVersion.tsx` re-exports `package.json`'s version (the staff frame now imports it from there too), drawn *Version 2.456.1* in `neutral-700` at the foot of both portal frames — on the holding page too, for the staff frame's reason (a screenshot of a switched-off portal is a defect report). **(7) TWO REDS DATED, NOT CAUSED:** `test_be11_openapi.py::tc02` was red from `5ac17a0e9` and `89f8cd698` (2026-10-02, three guest document doors never listed) — listed now with the fourth; it stays red on `get /api/reports/delivery/{token}`, unlisted since `639bffa2a` (2026-09-27), not this lane's to rule. `G103` was red on five start-service holds since `DEF-CWP-4877`; all six now have rows. | AI lane (portal start-service) | `DEF-CWP-9162`…`9167`; `BR-CWP-109`; portal `0013` (review ledger) |

(4) **the sweep runs at 03:47 UTC**, one task per utility on the default queue, the shape of `identity.session_cleanup`; a row is stamped `deleted`, never removed, so run history keeps it as *expired*; | 2026-10-02 | **A READING PARTWAY THROUGH THE PERIOD NO LONGER CUTS THE BILL OFF AT IT — `DEF-BIL-9016` FIXED (PO standing instruction *"if you find the bugs fix it"*; coordinator 2026-10-02).** Metering stores each reading as measured from the one before it; billing took the period's quantity from the newest reading alone. With seasons the 1 Oct reading still cuts: 200 × $0.12 + 100 × $0.10 = **$34.00** (was $10.00). **Three calls, ours under law 13:** (1) the chain is walked by DIAL — a reading's predecessor is the newest earlier billable reading on the same meter and register whose dial equals its prior — so an estimate a later reading measured across is never counted twice, and a reading on another meter ends the chain; (2) **a reading dated the period's first day is the OPENING DIAL and is not counted** — metering stamps a reading at 00:00 of its date, so its own usage belongs to the period before (the same reading of a date as the season-change-day ruling); (3) a predecessor that is flagged, has no quantity, carries another unit, or WRAPPED (its dial went backwards) ends the chain, which is the old answer for that case rather than a new refusal — so a wrap is still the clerk's to accept through the anchor's rollover suggestion (PO 2026-09-30, changes rows 45–46; `test_def_bil_5270_tc5d` unchanged). When **10 bills IN A ROW** fail with the same unexpected fault — named by the innermost cause's class (`issue.fault_signature`: `psycopg…UndefinedColumn`, not the message, which carries each bill's own number) — the pass raises `IssuePassStopped` and the batch stops the Send. The Send screen shows *Send stopped — a system fault. Unsent bills are untouched. Press Send once it is fixed.* in place of the generic line. A false stop costs a pause and a Send press; the missed stop cost 22,640 false *not sent* rows. Counted per batch, so with four batches running at most ~40 bills are tried before all have stopped; a batch with fewer than ten drafts left cannot trip and files breaks as before. **Why only the Send:** `issue_run`'s default (`None`) never stops, so the inline release and every other caller keep B11's one-break-per-bill exactly. **Why the class and not a list of 'system' exceptions:** a `ProgrammingError`/`OperationalError` on ONE bill can be that bill's (a deadlock, a statement timeout), and a `RuntimeError` on every bill can be the system's (a freeze step skipped) — repetition decides, not the type. **Proved:** `tests/test_def_bil_8747_send_circuit_breaker.py`, 8 cases, on SQLite AND PostgreSQL 16 (a real failing statement inside the per-bill savepoint, law 14): 7 drafts, limit 3 → stopped after 3 attempts, 0 breaks, release not completed; pressed again → 7 issued once, 1 journal and 1 audit row each, numbers unchanged and unique, release completed once. | 2026-10-01 | 🧭 **SEND AT SCALE — THE SEND IN BATCHES OF 500 UNDER A COORDINATOR, AN INDEX ON THE BILL LINE'S ID, AND A DEAD WORKER'S SEND HANDED BACK BY THE SEND SCREEN; SEVEN JUDGMENTS TAKEN HERE RATHER THAN ASKED (law 13; `DEF-BIL-8708`, `8726`, `8710`, `8743`, `8745`; `2.424.0`, `2.426.0`, `2.428.2`).** **(1) THE INDEX IS `invoice_lines (id)`, NOT `(tenant_id, id)`.** The ORM's update names `id` only; the tenant predicate is RLS's and exists only under a non-bypass role, so `(id)` serves every role and `(tenant_id, id)` would walk the index again under a superuser, a maintenance script or the test database. pressing Send again does the same. **(7) AT COMPLETION EVERY OPEN SEND BREAK WHOSE BILL IS NO LONGER A DRAFT IS CLOSED `issued`** (`DEF-BIL-8746`) — a batch killed between issuing and filing loses its pass's answer, so the bills are asked. **MEASURED (40,008 bills, `sbh_send40k`, PostgreSQL 16, RLS enforced, real Celery, 4 slots):** 1.9 → **4.0** bills a second with no index, one batch at a time; **5.7** with the index; **11.2 and 10.9–12.4** with two batches — **about an hour for 40,008 instead of 5.8 hours**; four kills each handed back by the screen in 16–19 s; 40,008 issued once, no number twice, journals balanced at $7,371,531.12. **NOT DECIDED HERE:** `DEF-BIL-8747` — a fault of the deployment (code ahead of its database) broke 22,640 bills one by one rather than stopping the Send; | 2026-10-01 | 🧭 **SIGN OFF AT 40,000 — THE WHOLE-RUN SUMMARY IS READ IN ONE BATCH PER MODULE AND SAVED ON THE RUN UNDER A KEY OF EVERY ROW IT IS BUILT FROM, REBUILT THE MOMENT ANY OF THEM IS WRITTEN; FOUR JUDGMENTS TAKEN HERE RATHER THAN ASKED (law 13; `DEF-BIL-8696`, `8697`, `8694`, `8720`).** **(1) BATCHING ALONE DOES NOT MEET S2, SO THE ANSWER IS SAVED.** Every seam Sign off asked per account is now asked once for the run, with the run's accounts handed over as a SUBQUERY rather than as bound ids (40,000 ids as parameters cost ~30 µs of Python each — 7 s for one read before PostgreSQL saw it). That took the read from **327 s to ~10 s at 40,008 bills** (load ~7) — still five times S2's 2 s, because it must still read every bill, line, check row and payment of the run. So the built summary is SAVED on `bill_runs.sign_off_snapshot` (billing `0038`) with a key of every row it reads, built at the end of every Calculate, and served only while the key is unchanged: **0.5–0.8 s at 40,008**. This is the shape the PO ruled for the Check itself (OQ-843 re-ruled 2026-09-30, option C: *"Save results, and automatically re-check an account when its plan, reading, meter or payment changes"*), not a cache that can go stale: a read never serves a copy built before any row it depends on was written. **(2) STALE MEANS A ROW IT READS WAS WRITTEN — MEASURED BY POSTGRESQL'S ROW VERSIONS, NOT BY `updated_at`.** The key is, per set of rows, the count and the SUM of `xmin` (`core/row_versions.py`): an insert, an update (a queryset `.update()` that never touches `updated_at` included) or a delete each move it; a SUM rather than a max so a long transaction committing after the key was read still moves it. The sets: billing — the run's own columns, every bill of the run and of its accounts, its lines, check rows, findings, decisions, standing answers, Pending-billing rows, release, its accounts' credit notes and level-pay status; payments — its accounts' payments, refunds, plans, instalments and the allocations by or against them; customers — its accounts and opening buckets; metering — the cycle and the utility's routes, service points, units and premises. Each module computes its own part (B1). So a re-Calculate and a decision change each rebuild it (the two the brief named), and so does a payment posted while the run waits, which the bills would count at Send. **NOT KEYED, stated so nobody reads it as covered:** the tenancy catalogues (service codes, account types, areas). **(3) THE GET THAT FINDS THE KEY MOVED BUILDS, SAVES AND SERVES IN THAT REQUEST** (~10 s at 40,000, inside the 60 s worker) rather than serving the old copy marked stale — a clerk never signs off a figure the bills would not print. Off PostgreSQL nothing is saved and every read builds, as before. **(4) THE PLAN ARITHMETIC IS STATED ONCE MORE, IN `open_balance.plan_not_yet_due`, AND `issue._plan_not_yet_due` STILL HOLDS ITS OWN SIX LINES** — the Send lane holds `issue.py` today, so it moves onto the shared function in a later change; `tests/test_d8696_signoff_batched.py` asserts Sign off and the stamped bill agree to the cent ($107.00 on the $62 + $45 plan bill, **$688.42** over five shapes), and on the J72 world sent through Send the four Sign off totals equal the sum of the seven bills' stamps exactly (**$563.83**, where the old Sign off read $675.78 — `DEF-BIL-8720`). **ALSO:** the staleness sweep before every Check read now asks metering and payments what changed since the run's oldest check for the whole utility (no id list) and reads back only the saved rows those changes can touch (5.7 s → 0.16 s at 40,015, load ~7); the Ready list binds whichever of its two id lists is shorter (2.06 s → 0.41 s). Figures unchanged, compared key by key: 40,191 at 40,008 (sent), 192 at 10,008, 152 on J72 — the only differences the new `plan_not_yet_due` and, on J72's one plan account, the Amount due `DEF-BIL-8720` moves on purpose. **FOUND, NOT FIXED:** once a run is sent Sign off reads every money figure as unanswered (`DEF-BIL-8727`). | Sign off at scale lane (claude) | `06-backend/apps/billing/signoff.py` · `core/row_versions.py` · `apps/billing/migrations/0038_d8696_sign_off_snapshot.py` · `check_staleness.py` · `check_store.ready_accounts` · `release.current_position_bills` · `10-scripts/d8696_signoff_parity.py` · `19-check-cost-measured.md` §12 |

| 2026-10-01 | **A FLAT CHARGE-CODE AMOUNT IS STORED AS ONE *ALL SIZES* ROW IN `charge_code_amounts`, SO FLAT AND SIZED PRICES SHARE ONE DATED, LOGICALLY-KILLED HISTORY AND A PAST BILL READS THE PRICE IN FORCE ON ITS DATES (PO 2026-10-01, option A).** Problem put to the PO: a flat amount lives in `charges.amount` and an edit overwrites it, so a catch-up bill for September created in December would price at December's amount; PO verbatim: *"so we have one proble in case of flat amount in charge code - we dont have a history to refer - so if any pas bill ot be created whn chanrge code is flat amount - in that case historical price/amount cannot be picked - how we can handle this - with out chaging the structure"*. Three options shown — (A) flat amount as an *All sizes* row; (B) rebuild past prices from `rate_change_log` (written only when the code is in use, carries the save date not the start date); (C) copy from the account's last sent bill line (nothing to copy for a new account or a missed month). **PO chose A, verbatim quoting the row: *"this is good - A · Flat amount as an \"All sizes\" row (recommended) BASE-S $9.00 is stored as one row in charge_code_amounts with size \"All sizes\". An edit closes that row and adds a new one, the same as for sizes. The old field on the charge code is no longer written; today's values move into rows once. No new table. The existing price table gets the dates and killed mark that logical kill already needs. Nothing. A past bill reads the row in force on its dates."*** **RULED:** (1) no new table; `charge_code_amounts` gains effective-from, effective-to and the killed mark (the logical-kill ruling of the same day); (2) a flat amount is one row whose size is the reserved value *All sizes* (per class where priced by class); (3) `charges.amount` is no longer written, and every existing flat amount is moved into an *All sizes* row once, by migration; (4) billing picks the row in force on the bill period's dates, and a period crossing a change is split by days. | 2026-10-01 | 🧭 **B28 BUILT — THE CHECK RUNS IN PARALLEL BATCHES OF 500 UNDER ONE COORDINATOR; SIX JUDGMENTS THE TWO 2026-09-30 RULINGS DID NOT SPELL OUT, TAKEN HERE RATHER THAN ASKED (law 13; changes row 55, plan B28, `2.418.0`).** **(1) THE COORDINATOR DOES NOT WAIT FOR ITS BATCHES.** The Check job plans, dispatches up to the cap and returns (`core.jobs.HANDED_OFF`); its record stays `running`, and the LAST batch to finish counts the totals and succeeds it. A coordinator that waited would hold a worker slot for the whole Check — with the repo's 2 slots, two utilities starting a Check at once would each hold one slot waiting for batches that can never start. **(2) THE CAP COUNTS EVERY QUEUED OR RUNNING BATCH OF THE UTILITY, ACROSS ALL ITS RUNS,** decided under a PostgreSQL advisory lock keyed on the utility, so two utilities never wait for each other's lock and one utility's second run waits for a slot rather than doubling its share. Worked: 8 workers → cap 4; a 40,000-account Check holds 4 batches, a second run in the same utility waits, another utility's run starts its own 4 at once. **(3) THE CAP IS TWO PLATFORM SETTINGS,** `BILLING_WORKERS` (the slots infrastructure runs, default 2 as `docker-compose.yml` runs) and `BILLING_CHECK_BATCHES_PER_UTILITY` (0 = derive half, never fewer than 1), because the code cannot see how many workers infrastructure scaled to. **(4) A WHOLE-RUN BATCH IS AN ACCOUNT-NUMBER RANGE, NOT A LIST OF IDS** — 80 ranges fit in a few kilobytes of the job record, the database does the comparison so collation cannot open a gap, and an account added mid-Check falls into exactly one batch; a re-check of NAMED accounts carries its ids. **(5) PROGRESS IS THE NUMBER OF ACCOUNTS THIS CHECK HAS SAVED, COUNTED IN THE DATABASE,** so batches finishing out of order still read *n of N*; resume per batch skips exactly those saved rows, so a finished batch delivered again writes nothing. **(6) A RE-CHECK OF ONLY SOME CATEGORIES (DEF-BIL-8286) IS NOT BATCHED** — it re-checks the accounts one fix touched, in one pass as before. **NOT WIDENED, NOT CLOSED:** `DEF-BIL-8600` (partial re-check path, untouched) and `DEF-BIL-8601` (needs the database's snapshot boundary) — each batch still stamps its accounts with its own read time, exactly as one chunk of the single pass did. **MEASURED (40,015 accounts, real PostgreSQL 16, RLS enforced, real Celery):** before, one process 8.0 min; after, 4 slots · cap 2, 9.1 min — no gain ON THIS MACHINE, whose four cores other lanes held at load 5.6; 81 batches, never more than 2 at once, every account saved once, the run audit PASS. | 2026-09-30 | 🧭 **BULK BILL RUN CHECK ENGINE BUILT (plan B7, B8, B9/DB1, B10–B13, B15–B17, B21; A3–A6) — AND SEVEN JUDGMENTS THE RULINGS DID NOT SPELL OUT, TAKEN HERE RATHER THAN ASKED (law 13).** Built to the day's rulings (*"dont stop at first problem"*; OQ-843 re-ruled option C; the alternatives table; *"NO CHECK FIXES ANYTHING BY ITSELF"*; the four kinds; the seven tag buckets). **Judgments:** (1) **The change feed is POLLING, not events** — the repo has no signal, outbox or event bus between modules and cross-module writes are forbidden, so billing asks three new read-only *changed since* seams (metering `units_changed_since` — unit row incl. its plan, readings, meters; rating `plans_changed_since`; payments `bill_run_checks.accounts_changed_since`) and re-checks only accounts whose fact moved AFTER their own `checked_at`: on every findings GET of an open run, and from a beat entry every 60 s. Up to **50** stale accounts re-check inside the request (137 ms each measured ≈ 7 s), more go to the billing queue. Measured on the test fixture: re-checking the **6** accounts whose plan was published took **0.47 s** against **0.61 s** for the whole 8-account run — the saving grows with the run (137 ms/account). (2) **An unanswered Check decision keeps the account out of the calculate pass without writing anything** (`decisions.DECISION_NEEDED`), because *"Nothing is applied to a bill without a clerk's click"*; it is not put in Pending billing (that queue is for a HOLD a clerk chose). (3) **A disputed reading stays out of the run in every legacy list** (BR-MET-024's hold) while the Check shows it as a DECISION tag: both ratified answers keep it off this run's bills today (*Bill on an estimate* needs an estimate the Check cannot take — filed). (4) **Choices whose money application is not built are recorded and HOLD** at a named boundary (the `extra_charge`/`apply` precedent) — built: accept the meter's unit, accept a register rollover the meter's own digits prove, bill with multiplier 1, bill the other services, whole period at the period-end price, split at the change, and the payment choices that leave this bill as gathered; everything else is filed as `DEF-BIL-8243`. (5) **When an account's readings are refused, the plan and tariff checks still run on metering's own un-anchored figures as a PROBE** — gathered with no readings, R3 reported a false *"no meter"* blocker; the probe is never billed. (6) **A mid-period price or plan change is a decision even when the split prices cleanly** (the table: *"whole period at the PERIOD-END price"* suggested, split the alternative) — a bulk-run account on a split is therefore held until answered, where it used to bill split automatically. (7) **The legacy `GET …/findings` still recomputes** (S31.2, unchanged); the new Check reads the SAVED rows at `…/check/findings`. **B16 🔒:** the bulk run's rate version is the one in force at the PERIOD END (`selectors.prepared_for` → `prepare_run(price_date=period_end)`), the bill date stays the documents' date — worked in a test: $3.25 to Jun 30, $3.50 from Jul 1, period ends Jun 30, bill date Jul 1 → **$3.25**. But while every web task migrated on boot, a task **could not physically serve a schema older than its code** — and that invariant was held by an implementation detail, never by a check. The day the detail moved, the guarantee went with it, no test and no gate could see it, and the product was down within hours. ⚠ **AND THE ENTRYPOINT PREDICTED IT, IN PROSE, ON THE DAY IT WAS WRITTEN** — *"a rollout that skips it starts tasks against an older schema, and the symptom is a column-not-found error from a view rather than anything that names the deploy"*. That is hard-won law 1 with nothing left to infer: **a comment claiming a guarantee is not the guarantee.** The assumption it named was to be honoured by a pipeline that **does not exist** — every workflow in `.github/workflows/` is `.disabled`, and `docker-release.sh` has exactly two callers, `make release` and a human runbook step. ⚠ **THE DECISION: THE WEB TASK REFUSES TO BOOT ON A PENDING MIGRATION, AND DOES NOT WARN.** The criterion is the entrypoint's own, already stated above its RLS block — `ALLOWED_HOSTS` warns because localhost-under-production is legitimate; the RLS check refuses because *"serving is strictly worse than not serving"*. **It is strictly worse here too, and more visibly**: a booted task answers 500 to every request that reads a new column while its probe answers 200, so the balancer keeps a useless task in rotation and nothing in any log names the deploy; a refusing task fails the ROLLOUT instead, and under a rolling deploy **the previous task definition goes on serving customers**. ⚠ **THE OTHER SIDE WAS ARGUED AND IS A REAL RISK, NOT A FORMALITY:** *pending* is not *needed*. A migration that adds a column no code reads yet is harmless, and nothing can tell the two apart — Django knows a migration is unapplied, not whether this build reads what it adds. The moment that bites is **not** the deploy but an unrelated task replacement — a spot interruption, an AZ event, a 9am scale-out — where a refusal takes capacity off a site that was working. **So the resolution is hard-won law 3's rather than a cleverer test: refuse by default, and let an operator who KNOWS the migration is forward-compatible type `SBH_ALLOW_PENDING_MIGRATIONS=1`**, which boots and prints every assumed migration on every boot so it cannot be left in a task definition quietly. ⚠ **THREE STATES, BECAUSE `manage.py migrate --check` CAN ONLY EXPRESS TWO — MEASURED, NOT ASSUMED.** On PostgreSQL 16, 2026-09-28: schema at tip → **exit 0**; `identity` rolled back to `0005` → **exit 1**; `DATABASE_URL` on a closed port → **exit 1**; `DATABASE_URL` naming a database that does not exist → **exit 1**. **Exit 1 means "pending" OR "I could not ask"**, so a boot guard written as `migrate --check || exit 1` would crash-loop the whole service through a thirty-second RDS failover. `06-backend/core/schema_guard.py` therefore returns `CURRENT` / `PENDING` / `UNREACHABLE`, and on `UNREACHABLE` it **warns and boots** — a process that cannot reach the database fails every request whatever its schema, and one that refused would be gone when the database came back. That third state is `rls_guard`'s own shape and exists for the same reason: *we could not tell* must never render as either answer. ⚠ **`/api/health` IS DELIBERATELY NOT MADE DEEPER, AND THAT IS THE SECOND DECISION.** It answered 200 all the way through the outage, which reads like the bug and is not it: `core/health.py` is a LIVENESS probe and `tests/test_health.py::test_health_answers_with_the_database_unreachable` pins it there, because a probe that queries the database turns a slow database into no service at all and manufactures the outage it exists to report. **The answer to "the probe said healthy while every sign-in 500'd" is that the process answering the probe must not exist when the schema is wrong** — so the guard is at BOOT and the probe is untouched. Measured after the fix on the same stale clone: the entrypoint exits **1** naming `identity.0006`, `identity.0007` and `identity.0008` and the recovery command, and `GET /api/health` answers nothing at all because nothing is bound. After `docker-release.sh` applied the three, the guard printed `0 unapplied migrations` and the same sign-in call answered **401 `AUTH-001`** instead of 500. ⚠ **WHAT REMAINS A HUMAN STEP, SAID PLAINLY RATHER THAN IMPLIED:** nothing in this repository runs `docker-release.sh` automatically and this change does not create a pipeline. `make up` runs `make release`; a host that runs `docker compose up -d --build` directly, or restarts only the backend, does not — **and that is the exact path that took production down.** What changed is that the path now FAILS LOUDLY at the only place the repo can reach it: the container refuses, names the three migrations and prints `make release`. `G136` holds the four halves together (the entrypoint does not migrate · it calls the guard before `exec gunicorn` · `docker-release.sh` migrates · the runbook names the recovery) and reads EXECUTABLE lines only, because the prose that predicted this outage was itself a comment. | lane INF-SCHEMA (Eng), maintenance track `12-governance/22-product-maintenance-process.md` | `12-governance/10-defect-log.csv` `DEF-INF-7683` · `06-backend/core/schema_guard.py` · `06-backend/docker-entrypoint.sh` · `06-backend/docker-release.sh` · `06-backend/tests/test_def_inf_7683_schema_guard.py` · `10-scripts/gates/g136_release_step_cannot_be_skipped.py` · `09-infra/02-aws-runbook.md` §H6 and §12 · CHANGELOG `2.391.1` · supersedes nothing in `CR-144-BRC07` H4, whose three reasons stand · CLAUDE.md hard-won laws 1, 2, 3, 7 |

AFTER, the same three dates answer `9581.530000 / 30`, `0 / 0` and `0 / 0`, and a ladder inside the tenant's own history moves: `2026-08-02` **16223.53 / 45**, `2026-08-15` **16106.56 / 44**, `2026-09-02` **31968.22 / 46**, `2026-09-30` **9581.53 / 30**. **THE JUDGMENT, RECORDED RATHER THAN ASKED (law 13 — no signed rule is reversed and no ❄️ B4/B5 figure moves):** a position at a date is built from **bills ISSUED by that date** (`invoices.issued_at`, which `billing/migrations/0002` FREEZES once set, so it cannot be back-dated) and **money POSTED by that date** (`payments.posted_at`, `BR-PAY-021`'s posting clock, which `BR-REP-001` already puts this report on). The clearing date still drives nothing. Both comparisons are on the DAY (`__date__lte`), so a payment taken at 16:20 on the closing day is inside the closing day. **TODAY'S FIGURES DO NOT MOVE** — every bill issued and every payment posted before `as_of` means the as-at set IS the open set, which is exactly what the old read always returned, and the sample tenant's `2026-09-30` row is byte-identical either side. **A SECOND FIGURE IMPROVED WITHOUT BEING ASKED TO:** `BR-REP-008`'s tie-out reads the ledger's AR control AT `as_of` already, so the two sides were being struck at different dates; the gap at `2026-08-31` falls from **6,920.26** (9,581.53 against 16,501.35) to **200.26** (16,301.09 against 16,501.35). **WHAT IT STILL CANNOT DO, WITH ITS NUMBER (`DEF-PAY-7020`, filed):** a bill that is `void` or `corrected` TODAY but was live at `as_of` cannot be restored, because `invoices` carries `issued_at` and **no `voided_at` and no `corrected_at`** — nothing records the day a live bill stopped being live. The read counts them and publishes `retired_bills_cannot_be_restored_to_a_past_date` with the count rather than understating silently (hard-won law 7: a blind spot with no number beside it is indistinguishable from an empty one). `corrected` is in principle reconstructible — the replacement carries `corrects_invoice_id` and its own `issued_at` — but that needs a new billing publication and is deliberately NOT done here; `DEF-PAY-7020` carries it. ⚠⚠ **AND THE ENGINE IS NOW AHEAD OF THE SCREEN — UNFILED FOR WANT OF AN ID, REPORTED TO THE COORDINATOR THE SAME HOUR.** `GET /reports/ar_aging` takes any `as_of`, and **the Aging view cannot ask for one**: `07-frontend/src/features/ledger/RevenueArPage.tsx:1678-1679` builds `agingParams` from `period.start`/`period.end` — the tenant's CURRENT accounting period — while the screen's own period control (`DEF-LED-6719`, landed 2026-09-27) sets `windowFrom`/`windowTo` and is rendered only inside the Revenue-by-service panel, which the Aging view does not show. `AgingView.agingConfig` offers **band and service and nothing else**, although p035's FILTER CRITERIA table names **five** criteria and `as_of` is the first of them. So a finance officer still cannot type a past month-end on the screen. That is hard-won law 2's mirror — a fixed engine behind a control that does not exist — and it needs a `DEF-LED-` id from a ledger block; this lane holds `DEF-PAY-7020–7029` only and deliberately did not take *the next free number*. **PENDING PROPAGATION, AND IT IS A FENCED FILE THIS LANE MAY NOT WRITE:** `06-backend/apps/reports/dashboard_tab.py` lines ~569–590 still describe `DEF-PAY-6940` as live and quote the old identical figures; the Reports lane owns that file and must amend it. The departure is recorded in `04-docs/05-modules/05-assets/conformance/CR-143-BRC07-size-column-departure.md` and in the page's own header, rather than left to be found as drift. ⚠ **THE COLUMN WAS NEVER THE MISSING PART — THE PRINTABLE VALUE WAS.** `Asset.size_class` has existed since `BR-AST-500` and the list read has served it since then, as a bare `service_size_classes.code` (`W-58`, `FL-2`). B14 rule 32 keeps an internal code out of clerk-facing copy, so the registry has had the fact and no permission to draw it. The list now serves `size_class_name` beside it — the TENANT's own name for the code, `Water 5/8"` — which is also the only one of the two that carries a UNIT, as CLAUDE.md hard rule 3 asks of any dimension on screen. **The customer portal settled the identical question one module along on 2026-09-11 (`DEF-CWP-4848`, *"the size class as a person reads it, not the code"*) and the reasoning is reused rather than re-argued.** ⚠ **WHY IT MATTERS AND NOT JUST WHY IT IS TIDY, IN THE FIGURE PUT TO THE PO:** a capacity service's size class PICKS the base charge and the count multiplies it — one 6" fire line is **$60.00** a month and one 2" line is **$12.00** — so a clerk auditing a bill run against this list was being asked to check an arithmetic whose FIRST INPUT the list did not show, one asset at a time. **THE FIVE JUDGMENTS, since the drawing speaks to none of them:** (1) the NAME, never the code; (2) names read from the TENANT's own rows **including RETIRED ones**, because `BR-AST-500` says a retired size must not vanish from a record that already priced with it — filtering to active would blank the column on exactly the rows a clerk audits; (3) a code the tenant's list cannot NAME draws the dash rather than falling back to the code, which would be the breach; (4) the empty cell is the registry's own em dash — the detail screen's honest 12-word sentence *"Not recorded — a rate ladder that prices by size cannot price this meter"* is right on a Fact and is 12 words in every row of a 50-row page here, which B14 rule 33 caps at six; (5) placed between `SERVICE` and `MULT.` on Meters because the base charge resolves *service → account type → size class* (`BR-RAT-108`, R3) and those two facts belong together, and on **Behind the meter** between `METER` and `EXPORT CAPACITY` because a fire line is a behind-the-meter asset and that is where the size IS the price. **Sub-meters gets NOTHING**: `offersConnectionSize` refuses a size on a sub-meter, so the column could only ever draw a dash for ever — hard-won law 2's mirror. ⚠ **ONE CONSEQUENCE RECORDED AND NOT FIXED:** a clerk with a saved `table.S49.columns` preference gets the column HIDDEN until they tick it, because `columnsFromPreference` keeps only the keys the stored preference names. That is the shared kit's behaviour on all 54 lists and changing it is the risk the PO ruled out of an Assets pass on 2026-09-12 (*"It's the right fix and it touches 54 lists at once"*). ⚠ **AND ONE DEFECT FOUND AND DELIBERATELY NOT FIXED HERE — `DEF-AST-7100`:** `AssetDetailPage.tsx` prints the bare code `W-58` in its own Connection size Fact, the same rule-32 question, on a different screen. Filed rather than fixed in a commit about the registry. **No `OQ` minted (law 13).** No migration, no new catalogue key, no new component: `assets.col.sizeClass` = *Connection size* already exists in all eleven languages and is already the label on the edit form, the add wizard and the detail Fact — one pair of words for one fact. | PO + lane AST-SIZE | `12-governance/change-requests/CR-143-BRC07-size-column-on-the-asset-registry.md` · `04-docs/05-modules/05-assets/conformance/CR-143-BRC07-size-column-departure.md` · `07-frontend/src/features/assets/AssetSizeColumn.dom.test.tsx` |

So a customer read *we cannot work this out* on `CWP-052` over a bill of **$19.75**, and every account on that schedule was counted UNPRICED by the rate-change impact analysis. **The other direction is worse and was also measured:** with the named code scoped to `commercial` and the account residential, the bill REFUSED by name while the portal quoted **$8.00** — a figure nobody will ever be billed, on a customer's own screen, with nothing visibly wrong anywhere. **THE FIX IS THE BINDING TRAVELLING, AND IT IS THREE HOPS.** `rating.seams.base_charge_for` gains an optional `named_code`, passed UNCONDITIONALLY to `selectors.base_charge_from_charge_code` — never degraded, the posture `billing.gather._base_charge_code_for` already takes, because dropping it prices the INFERRED code under a schedule naming another. Both call sites hand down their own version's binding: the impact analysis off the two projections it already holds (each side its OWN, so a filing that MOVES the base between codes is priced rather than reported as costing nothing), and the portal off `selectors.named_base_charge_code`, a NEW single narrowing so a fourth hand-written `version.base_charge_code.code if …` cannot disagree with the three that exist. ⚠ **AND THE THING THAT WAS ACTUALLY WRONG WAS BIGGER THAN THE BRIEF — `DEF-RAT-7000`, FOUND ONLY BY REPRODUCING.** On the PLAINEST configuration there is — ONE base code, nothing named, nothing scoped — both doors answered `{'wired': True, 'amount': None, 'refusal': 'TypeError'}`. `seams.base_charge_for` resolves a PRIVATE function in billing by name and passed it `code_label=`, which `gather._base_charge_for` LOST on 2026-09-24 in `2b5c1b4c6` (`DEF-CUS-6550`, cutting a 63-word refusal to ten under B14 rule 33 — correctly; the parameter had stopped being read). The seam's `except Exception` then reported the broken call as an ordinary refusal named `TypeError`. **Every tenant with an `is_base` charge code was affected, which is every tenant this product provisions**, so for three days the portal's standing charge and the WHOLE rate-change impact analysis answered *we cannot work this out* over bills that were being produced normally. `tsc`, every gate and the whole suite were green: the nine red cases in `test_br_rat_091_rate_change_impact.py` were read as an impact fault (`DEF-RAT-6980`) rather than as this. **The `except Exception` is KEPT** — it carries billing's named refusal back rather than swallowing it and it did its job; what it cannot do is tell a REFUSAL from a BROKEN CALL, so the durable repair is the test, which now exercises the seam on a configuration where the code ANSWERS. **MEASURED, BOTH DIRECTIONS.** New suite `test_def_rat_6960_one_base_on_all_three_surfaces.py`: **8 failed at the pinned tip `8cf7e6868`, 8 passed after**, and with `test_def_rat_5782` beside it **17 passed**. Neighbourhood re-run with the three files restored BYTE-FOR-BYTE from the tip and then restored again: **tip 17 failed / 45 passed → after 16 failed / 46 passed**. The single difference is `test_br_rat_091__silver_creeks_OWN_water_filing_reads_5_28_pct_not_6_pct`, which this change turns GREEN — one of `DEF-RAT-6980`'s 28. **Nothing else moved in either direction.** ⚠ **THE POSTGRESQL RUN DID NOT FINISH AND IS RECORDED AS A GAP:** 8 errors in 18m43s, every one `psycopg.errors.DiskFull — No space left on device`, with the container at **98%** and twenty sibling test databases holding 865 MB. Not retried, because a second attempt could have filled the disk under five working lanes. Nothing here catches a database error or continues past one, so law 14's trap cannot apply — which is why the change is safe without it and is not a substitute for it. `10-scripts/03-golden-verify.py` **33 PASS, 0 FAIL** and the engine golden suite **23 passed, 1 xfailed**, both unchanged; no golden test was added or removed, so `G64`'s engine-verified record stays at **14 of 61** and no ❄️ FROZEN figure moved. ⚠ **A THIRD FINDING, FILED AND NOT FIXED — `DEF-CWP-7001`.** The eight red cases in `test_us_cwp_062_stop_or_restart.py` are NOT the seam: `apps/portal/sample_data.py` seeds the demo plan's `trash` base at **`$8.00`** while its charge code `BASE-TRASH-PORTAL` says **`$9.00`**, so `gather._base_charge_for` refuses the migration artefact by name and `standing_charge_monthly`'s one-refusal-refuses-all rule kills the whole figure. `water` and `sewer` agree; only `trash` diverges, by `$1.00`. Both figures were introduced together in `08a8d08df` (2026-09-16) and the TypeError above has been masking the real refusal since the 24th. It is a FIXTURE question about what a demo utility looks like, not a pricing one, and fixing it inside this task would have widened scope past what is reviewable. ⚠ **`DEF-RAT-6961` WAS OFFERED AND DELIBERATELY LEFT.** `services._guard_bound_base_charge_code` condition 3 admits a code whose `service_id IS NULL` — *the spec's "Any"*, and exactly what `resolution.resolve_charge_codes` admits — while `selectors.base_charge_from_charge_code` filters `service__code=service_code` and can never return one. They are listed in `tests/test_be11_openapi.py` in `CREDENTIALLED_BUT_PUBLISHED_AS_PUBLIC`, **apart from the genuinely-public list rather than inside it**, because writing a credentialled door into a constant named *needing no credential* is the same lie one layer further in. Respelling eighty-nine ids across every register, docstring, commit message and rule citation is the mass shared-file rewrite hard-won law 11 exists to prevent — the same reasoning that kept `OQ-291` from becoming `OQ-00291` under the five-digit ruling of 2026-08-31. **WHY THE SUFFIX ALONE IS NOT ENOUGH, WHICH IS THE WHOLE ENGINEERING CONTENT OF THIS ROW.** Two branches can both reach for ninety and produce `CR-090-BRC01` and `CR-090-BRC02` — two different changes, both called ninety. **The STRING is unique and the NUMBER is not**, and the number is what a person says out loud, writes in a commit subject and cites from a business rule, so *"CR-90"* would name two different changes with no way to tell which. Worse, **git cannot see it**: one file per CR means the two branches touch two DIFFERENT files, and the index row in `11-change-requests.md` is an append, so both sides merge cleanly, no conflict is raised and nothing goes red. The collision is invisible to the merge and visible only to a reader. **THE EXCHANGE IS RECORDED BECAUSE THE ANSWER WAS A RE-AFFIRMATION AND NOT A FIRST ANSWER.** The engineer raised exactly those costs and offered the alternative; **the PO reaffirmed the suffix twice** — *"No - I said I want Suffix"*, then *"Ensure you assing branch Suffix to CR number"* — so it is ruled, and it is not to be re-asked (law 13). **The resolution was therefore not "a suffix INSTEAD of a guarantee" but "the suffix AND a guarantee":** the suffix is kept exactly as ruled, as PROVENANCE, and a disjoint number block per branch plus a duplicate-NUMBER check are added underneath it. **THREE LAYERS, AND ONLY THE LAST ONE ENSURES ANYTHING.** ⓵ **Before a branch starts** — its block and its branch code go into `14-id-reservations.md`: `BRC01` = `CR-090`–`094`, branch `claude/hi-0jmv62`; `BRC02` = `095`–`099` and `BRC03` = `100`–`104` are UNCLAIMED, and a block is claimed by writing a branch name into its row, never by taking the numbers quietly. Two branches drawing from disjoint blocks cannot reach for the same number. ⓶ **At push time** — `10-scripts/allocate.py cr --verify <n>` re-asks **every fetched `origin` ref** rather than this checkout, because a sibling working in its own worktree has its rows in none of the places a listing can see until it pushes; caught here, renumbering costs two files. ⚠ **It CANNOT reserve and does not claim to** — nothing writes to the remote, so two branches calling it in the same second still get one answer. Sewer volume is also ESTIMATED from the water meter rather than measured, which makes a fine-grained ladder a false precision. Bellaire, Texas prints `$4.52` across 0–5,000 and 20,001+ alike, which is the shape recommended. **(c) ⚠ THE RETURN-TO-SEWER FACTOR — THE ENGINEERING BRIEF'S UNDERSTANDING IS CONFIRMED, ONE NUMBER IS TIGHTENED, AND THE COMMONEST RESIDENTIAL PRACTICE TURNS OUT NOT TO BE A PERCENTAGE AT ALL.** **Confirmed:** real municipal factors are in the eighties and nineties. **San Francisco Public Utilities Commission** applies **90% for single-family residential, 95% for multifamily and 90% for all other users**; **Chula Vista, California** applies **90% residential, 90% commercial, 84% mobile home, 79% multifamily**. **Tightened:** the brief said 80–95% with a lower figure used to allow for outdoor watering; what was actually found is **79–95%, clustering hard on 90%, and NEITHER of those two utilities discounts residential for irrigation** — SF charges households the same 90% it charges everyone, and Chula Vista's LOWEST factor is for multifamily, which has the least irrigation of any class. **So the irrigation allowance, where it exists, is not made by lowering the factor.** ⚠ **IT IS MADE BY CHOOSING WHICH MONTHS TO MEASURE, AND THAT IS THE PRACTICE THE BRIEF ASKED ABOUT: WINTER-QUARTER AVERAGING, AND IT IS AT LEAST AS COMMON AS ANY FACTOR.** The winter-quarter average is each account's own water use in January–March of a prior year, carried for the whole following year, on the reasoning that summer water goes on lawns, cars and pools and never enters the sewer. It is in use at **Los Angeles DWP, Fairfax County (Virginia), Phoenix (City Code 28-35, *"determination of sewage discharge volume"*), Bristol (Connecticut), Maple Grove (Minnesota) and Laramie (Wyoming)**, and **the City of Paris, Texas bills 100% of metered water on a flat winter average** — i.e. no factor at all, the allowance made entirely by the choice of months. Some cap at *winter average × 1.3 or actual consumption, whichever is lower*. **IF THE PO WANTS THE PHYSICALLY HONEST ANSWER, WINTER-QUARTER AVERAGING IS IT — but it is a DIFFERENT MECHANISM, not a different number:** it needs a stored winter average per account and a rule for a new account with no winter history, where a factor needs one figure on a tariff. **That difference is why it is reported rather than recommended: it is a bigger change than `CR-081` currently describes, and only the PO can say whether it is wanted.** ⚠ **AND THE FINDING THAT MATTERS MOST IS THE INTERACTION, BECAUSE THE TWO KNOBS MULTIPLY AND EACH LOOKS REASONABLE ALONE.** What a customer pays is `factor × rate`. At **40% × `$5.00`** the effective charge is **`$2.00` per thousand gallons of METERED WATER**, against a municipal market that effectively charges **`$4.50`–`$9.00`** for the same thing (those utilities bill sewer on 90–100% of the water). **So keeping 40% and taking a market rate leaves the seeded sewer bill at roughly a THIRD of what a real customer pays** — which is lawful and may be exactly what is wanted for a demo, but should be a choice rather than an accident. **THREE COHERENT PACKAGES, so the PO can pick one rather than two numbers:** **A — keep 40%, rate `$5.00`.** Amounts stay near today's; the `40%` is NOT a return-to-sewer factor and no document may describe it as one. **B — physical factor 90%, rate `$2.25`.** The factor then means what it says and the money barely moves (`WE-1` `$16.20` against today's `$15.80`), but `$2.25` is below every municipal rate found. **C — market-realistic: factor 90%, rate `$5.00`.** `WE-1` becomes **`$36.00`** a month, which IS what a municipal sewer customer pays on 8 kgal — and it more than doubles every one of the six frozen figures. **THE SIX RECOMPUTED AT THE RECOMMENDED `$5.00` ON THE `40%` BASIS (package A), all six because a signature covers only what was shown:** `WE-1`/`GT-17` 8 kgal → 3.2 kgal → **`$16.00`** (today `$15.80`, **+`$0.20`**) · `WE-4`/`GT-20` 12 → 4.8 → **`$24.00`** (today `$24.96`, **−`$0.96`**) · `WE-9`/`GT-25` 6 → 2.4 → **`$12.00`** (today `$10.60`, **+`$1.40`**) · `WE-10`/`GT-26` Jan–Mar 6 → 2.4 → **`$12.00`** (today `$10.60`, **+`$1.40`**) · `WE-10` Apr–Jun on tariff v4 6 → 2.4 → **`$12.00`** (today `$11.24`, **+`$0.76`**) · `WE-12` 3.1 → 1.24 → **`$6.20`** (today `$4.96`, **+`$1.24`**). **Across the five worked examples that is `$82.20` against `$78.16` today, `+$4.04`** — and note the direction is not uniform: residential rises and commercial falls, exactly as `CR-081` predicted, because commercial water is flat `$5.20`/kgal against residential's `$4.9375` average. **Under package C the same six become `$36.00` · `$54.00` · `$27.00` · `$27.00` · `$27.00` · `$13.95`.** ⚠ **NOTHING WAS SEEDED AND NO SEWER CODE WAS TOUCHED.** `CR-081` remains HELD at step 2; | 2026-09-07 | 🔕 **A MESSAGE THAT WILL NOT BE SENT MUST SAY SO ON SCREEN — PO ruling, and it is a general rule about SILENCE rather than a notifications feature.** PO verbatim: *"in such cases - we ahve to let user know that email will not be sent or message - SMS, Notification etc will not be send since it is disabled - so that theya re aware otherwise they will think it is working"*. **THE PRINCIPLE: a disabled channel is a DECISION THE PRODUCT MADE, and the person who caused the action is entitled to know it was made.** Today a clerk issues a bill or closes an account, the screen reports success, and whether an email actually left is invisible — so *"it worked"* and *"it was silently dropped"* look identical, which is the exact shape this repository keeps paying for (hard-won law 2's mirror: a control that appears live and is not; `G32` reporting **0 unresolved** over **21 live refusals that reach a clerk as silence**; a Usage screen that could never show a tip because *"nothing today"* was also the right answer on a quiet day). ⚠ **THE RULING WAS PROMPTED BY A CLAIM OF MINE THAT WAS WRONG, AND THE RULING SURVIVES THE CORRECTION — BOTH FACTS ARE RECORDED SO NOBODY BUILDS ON THE BAD HALF.** I told the PO that *"sixteen of the eighteen callers omit the event key … including the bill itself"*. **The bill part is FALSE.** `apps/billing/delivery_seam.py:919` does `event_key = event_for_bill(invoice)` on **every** bill — deriving which event it is from `invoices.corrects_invoice_id`, the correction chain's own link — and reads the tenant's switches through `rule_service.channel_switches`, at a measured cost of two SELECTs per bill and no write, asserted by `tests/test_cr048_b2_billing_fires_its_events.py`. **So unticking *"Bill ready — email"* DOES stop that email.** ⚠ **HOW THE WRONG NUMBER WAS PRODUCED IS THE LESSON: I grepped for the literal `event_key=` within eighteen lines of each `queue_document(` call. Billing assigns it to a VARIABLE first, so the search could not see it. I counted a SPELLING and reported it as a BEHAVIOUR** — law 7's *reporting zero over a scope it silently excludes*, committed by the lane that has spent the day warning others about it. **No corrected count is stated here**, because the honest one cannot come from another grep: it needs each caller asked whether a switch actually reaches it. **WHAT THE RULING REQUIRES, and three things must not be got wrong.** (1) **THE PRINT FLOOR MEANS "NO EMAIL" IS NOT "NOTHING HAPPENED".** `BR-BIL-036` (the PO's own closure of `OQ-091`) makes print the floor: **every bill is printed whatever else is switched off**, and the floor is applied inside notifications so no writer can forget it. A message reading *"nothing was sent"* on a bill would therefore be a NEW false statement replacing the old silent one. **Say what DID go and what did not.** (2) **NAME THE CHANNEL AND THE REASON, not a generic refusal** — the good existing sentences do this (*"closing an account does not send this"*), and B14 rule 33 caps a refusal at five or six words while rule 32 sets a description budget, so this is a short specific line and not a paragraph. (3) **IT MUST BE DERIVED, EXACTLY AS THE `used_by` RULING OF THE SAME EVENING REQUIRES** — a hand-written "email is off" would rot the day someone switches it on, which is the defect this rule is a reaction to. **SCOPE: every channel the product has — email, SMS, in-app, and the customer portal once `BR-NOT-010` gains its fourth channel — and every surface where a person causes a send**, which is at least the bill run, account close-out, move-in/move-out, rate-plan change, payment receipts and the staff run summaries. **AND THE MOMENT MATTERS: the person who pressed the button sees it then**, not only in a delivery log they would have to go looking for. | PO ruling, relayed verbatim; the print-floor caveat, the derivation requirement and the correction of my own false claim are ours | `BR-NOT-005` · `BR-NOT-010` · `BR-BIL-036` (`OQ-091`) · `CR-048` *"wired end to end, not screens over a dead engine"* · `apps/notifications/services.queue_document` · `apps/notifications/rule_service.channel_switches` · `apps/billing/delivery_seam.event_for_bill` · B14 rules 32 and 33 · CLAUDE.md hard-won laws 2 and 7 |
| 2026-09-07 | 📣 **A TEMPLATE'S "IS THIS IN USE" SENTENCE BECOMES DERIVED FROM ACTUAL NOTIFICATION USAGE — PO ruling, and it forecloses the cheaper fix that was on the table.** PO verbatim: *"it should be dynamic and based on actual usage by notifications - can you fix it"*, said after finding on the live product that *Bill ready · e-bill email* announces **"Not in use yet — no wording has been written for it."** ⚠ **THE SENTENCE IS WRONG TWICE OVER AND BOTH HALVES ARE PROVABLE FROM ONE FILE.** In `06-backend/apps/notifications/catalogs.py`, `"email_bill_ready"` carries `used_by="Not in use yet — no wording has been written for it."` at ~line 990, and **`"email_bill_ready": _authored(...)` — the wording itself — sits ~280 lines BELOW IT IN THE SAME FILE**; `"sms_bill_ready"` carries the identical pair. And the PO's own screenshot shows a **live notification rule with that template selected and its Email channel switched ON**, so *"not in use"* is false as well. **`used_by` is a hand-typed string on a listing that nobody updates**, which is hard-won law 1 in its purest form — a sentence claiming a fact, believed because it is written down, contradicted by the file it lives in. **THE CHOICE THE PO CLOSED:** the lane was given two options — derive the sentence, or leave the literal and add a test that fails when a template has authored wording and still claims it has none. **The PO chose DERIVE, and a drift test is no longer acceptable as the substitute.** The reasoning is theirs and it is the stronger one: a check tells the next engineer the string is wrong, while derivation means the string cannot be wrong. ⚠ **"ACTUAL USAGE" IS FOUR FACTS AND NOT ONE, and flattening them loses the information the good literals carry.** (1) does any notification rule REFERENCE this template · (2) is that rule's CHANNEL switched on · (3) has wording been AUTHORED · (4) has anything ever been SENT through it. **Fact 4 is a trap on this product today**, and the PO's other screenshot names it: the notification screen says *"Nobody is reporting these back to us yet, because sending is not switched on. A zero here would look like every message had failed, which is not what is happening."* **So "never sent" must NOT render as "not in use" — a template wired to a live rule on a utility that has not enabled sending is IN USE AND WAITING**, and a derivation that reports silence as absence would ship the same class of lie in a new coat. ⚠ **THE HONEST-ABSENCE HALF SURVIVES AND MUST NOT BE FLATTENED INTO A BOOLEAN.** Where a template really is wired to nothing, the specific sentence stays — *"Not in use yet — closing an account does not send this."* names WHAT does not happen, which is worth more than "unused", and several of these literals carry that kind of real information (`customers/close_out.py`, `notifications/customer_events.py` and `rule_catalog.py` each quote theirs). **Derive the STATE; keep the SPECIFICITY.** ⚠ **AND THE DERIVATION CAN FAIL THE SAME WAY THE LITERAL DID — over a scope that silently excludes the answer.** CLAUDE.md records `G32` truthfully reporting **0 unresolved** across **21 live refusals it could not see**, because it resolved a key only where the helper was defined in the same file. **A derived sentence that cannot see some path by which a template gets used must PRINT WHAT IT SKIPPED BESIDE WHAT IT CHECKED** — a declared blind spot with no number attached is indistinguishable from an empty one. **SCOPE: the sweep covers EVERY `used_by` in the catalogue, not the two the PO happened to open**, and the report must state how many were wrong out of how many. `author not recorded` and `last edited` get the same test — if they are also unmaintained literals they are the same defect wearing a different label. | PO ruling, relayed verbatim; It keeps the number shape byte-identical, needs no DDL, behaves the same on PostgreSQL and sqlite so the suite exercises the real path, and happens to be gap-free because the bump rides the caller's transaction. **CONCURRENCY, STATED RATHER THAN ASSUMED:** the year is opened with `INSERT … ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING`, so two signups racing produce one row and **no exception** — which matters because a raised `IntegrityError` would abort the whole signup transaction (law 14); the bump is one `UPDATE … SET next_sequence = next_sequence + 1`, which re-reads under a row lock, so a second signup blocks and then increments what it finds. Two concurrent signups serialise on one row for the length of provisioning. At the rate a utility SaaS is signed up for, that is free. **THE UNIQUE INDEX IS STILL THE GUARANTEE** — if the counter is ever behind the rows, the insert fails and the retry bumps past it; the counter is the fast path, the index is the truth. **MIGRATION ORDER IS LOAD-BEARING:** `0041` seeds each year's counter from the highest number already issued and must run BEFORE `0042` turns the policy on, because FORCE applies to the table owner too and a context-free backfill would read zero rows *silently* and hand the next signup a number already taken. **S107 WAS CHECKED, NOT ASSUMED:** Settings → Billing plan reads through `TenantContextMiddleware`, which resolves the tenant from the path and SETs `app.tenant_id` before any view runs, so the screen still shows the plan; a policy over a context-free read would have been a live screen going blank rather than a test going red. | Eng-Lead (DEF-TEN-4446 lane) — no rule reversed, so no PO ruling sought (law 13) | 06-backend/apps/tenancy/migrations/0041_def_ten_4446_platform_order_counter.py · 06-backend/apps/tenancy/migrations/0042_rls_def_ten_4446_commercial_tables.py · 06-backend/apps/tenancy/platform_numbering.py · 06-backend/apps/tenancy/models.py · 06-backend/apps/tenancy/selectors.py · 06-backend/tests/test_def_ten_4446_commercial_rls.py · 04-docs/02-decisions/02-database-design-brief.md §3 · 12-governance/09-human-review-ledger.md · 12-governance/10-defect-log.csv |
