## 2026-08-20 · CR-018 PHASE 3 — THE SHARED CLASSES, AND THE QUESTION ROUTE B DID NOT ANSWER

**The ruling this builds under is `"Route B"`** (PO, 2026-08-19, recorded above).
Phase 1 migrated one screen and said plainly that it *"could not touch a single
shared class"* and that *"a Phase 2 for 179 shared classes remains entirely
unmeasured."* This is that measurement, on the widest family. **Version 2.29.9.**
Full working: `12-governance/reports/2026-08-20-cr018-phase3-button-spike.md`.

### 0 · THE ANSWER, SO NOBODY HAS TO READ THE REST TO GET IT

**Route B for a shared class means a COMPONENT, not a repeated string — and not
because a component is tidier. The repeated string does not work.**

`.btn` is written at **250 sites in 83 of 127 components**. The literal reading of
Route B — paste the 24-utility string at all 250 — was tried first and the parity
census printed **540 differing properties**: the primary button rendered
transparent with body-coloured text, and the small button rendered at the default
padding. **In CSS, `.btn-primary{background:accent}` beats
`.btn{background:transparent}` because it is later IN THE FILE.** Tailwind emits
one rule per utility and sorts them itself, so two utilities that set the same
property in one class attribute are a coin toss decided at build time. The class
attribute's ORDER is not the cascade.

So the kit is one module, filled in named SLOTS, and 250 call sites ask for it by
meaning (`variant="primary"`) rather than by name.

| | |
|---|---|
| call sites | **250** — `<button>` 192 · `<GuardedButton>` 36 · `<Link>` 20 · `<a>` 1 · `<summary>` 1 |
| migrated in this phase | **34 in 8 files**, plus **18 in 9 more** forced by the API change |
| CSS it replaces | 28 rules, 79 declarations, **9 stylesheets** |
| kit vs legacy, 8 variants × 4 states, every computed property | **16,768 comparisons, 0 differing** |
| 4 screens, 475 clickables | **11,875 comparisons, 0 differing** |
| full-page PNGs | **53 pixels differ on each — one 7×8 box at the sidebar version label this release bumped, and nothing else** |
| CR-016 conformance | **24 screens, every baseline number, PASS** |
| `npm test` | 99 files, 1,516 tests, PASS |

### 1 · SEVEN STYLESHEET RULES STYLE A BUTTON FROM ITS PARENT, AND ROUTE B HAS NO PARENT SELECTOR

This is the finding that decides whether Route B scales to shared classes, and it
is invisible to every census of class NAMES, because the button's own markup never
mentions the class:

```
.signin-actions       .btn { width:100%; justify-content:center }
.settings-row-actions .btn { font-size:12px; padding:2px 6px }
.ast-row-actions      .btn { padding:0 8px; font-size:12px }
.met-row-actions      .btn { padding:0 8px; font-size:12px }
.cus-note-meta        .btn { margin-left:auto }
.pay-result-head      .btn { margin-left:auto }
.download-menu-list   .btn { justify-content:flex-start }
```

The first screen census after migrating the call sites moved **1,416 properties on
273 buttons**. Every Assets row action grew from 12px/`0 8px` to 14px/`8px 14.4px`,
because `.ast-row-actions .btn` stopped reaching a button that had stopped carrying
`.btn`. **`tsc`, eslint, 1,516 unit tests, G31 and G34 were all green while it
happened**, and it is hard-won law 6 for the third time in three phases: the only
thing that saw it was a screenshot and a computed-style census.

Utilities have no parent selector, so each override travels down onto the button.
Re-measured after that: **0 differing**.

### 2 · AND THAT IS HOW WE FOUND B14 RULE 5 HAS BEEN BROKEN THE WHOLE TIME

Rule 5 is *"two button sizes only — default and small (12px)"*. The product renders
**four small-button paddings** at one conforming font size:

| | padding |
|---|---|
| `.btn-sm` — the declared small tier | 6px 8px |
| `.ast-row-actions .btn` / `.met-row-actions .btn` | 0 8px |
| `.settings-row-actions .btn` | 2px 6px |
| `.settings-icon-btn` | 0, forced to 32×32 |

**CR-016's rule E measures `distinctButtonFontSizes`** and has read
`["12px","14px"]` on 24 screens throughout. The rule says *sizes*; the guard reads
*type sizes*, and three of the four are descendant rules no reader of the markup
can see. Filed as **DEF-342**. They are now four NAMED sizes in one file rather
than three stylesheets, because collapsing them moves pixels on every list screen
and CR-018 §6 forbids that — **naming them is what makes the ruling askable.**

### 3 · ⚠ THE SAFETY NET DOES NOT REACH A COMPONENT API — OQ-280

Route B was bought to make an undeclared class impossible. Both readers —
`g31_declared_classes.py` and `src/styles/routeBUtilities.test.ts` — read
`className=` **ATTRIBUTES**. A component API keeps its strings in a module
constant. With `components/buttonKit.ts` listed on `route-b-migrated.txt`,
`items-center` → `itmes-center` gave:

```
npx vitest run src/styles/routeBUtilities.test.ts   → 5 passed
python3 10-scripts/gates/g31_declared_classes.py    → PASS, 0 undeclared
```

**A typo that would have flattened every button in the product was invisible to
the entire net** — DEF-327's failure mode walking in through the front door of the
migration bought to remove it. Closed for this family by
`src/components/buttonKit.test.ts` (139 lines, every kit token through the real
Tailwind compiler, in `npm test`, proved RED on that exact typo). **Closed for the
other 169 shared classes by nobody: OQ-280, raised rather than absorbed.**

⚠ **The first version of that check passed the sabotage too**, and the reason is
worth carrying: Tailwind's `compile()` returns an INCREMENTAL builder, so
`build([t])` returns the whole sheet including every candidate seen before. Every
token after the first looked alive. It is the vacuous green of G26, G27 and
DEF-323 reproduced by trusting an API's shape instead of measuring it, and it was
caught by sabotaging the check rather than by reading it.

### 4 · A COMPONENT API CHANGE IS 18 CALL SITES, AND THAT IS THE GOOD NEWS

`GuardedButton`'s variant prop was a CLASS STRING (`className="btn btn-primary"`).
Making it `variant="primary"` broke **18 call sites in 9 files** — instantly, at
`tsc`, by name and line. The same mistake in a class string is a screen that
renders unstyled and every check green. **That contrast is the strongest argument
for shape (b) that this spike produced**, and it is the answer to the brief's
question: nothing a call site needed could not be given, but it cost five wrappers
rather than one, because the kit is applied to five different elements
(`Button` · `ButtonLink` · `ButtonAnchor` · `ButtonSummary` · and `GuardedButton`
composing `Button`).

⚠ **`<summary>` is the case that proves the rule.** It is the open-control of a
`<details>` disclosure and cannot be a `<button>`. Writing
`className={buttonClasses(…)}` at that one site took **G31 from 0 to 1**: its
grammar pulled the quoted variant name out of the expression and reported it as an
undeclared class. Spelling that sentence out with the call written literally
tripped the same gate **a second time, from a comment.** So every element gets a
wrapper and the class string never appears at a call site.

### 5 · WHAT ELSE BREAKS THAT NOBODY WOULD PREDICT

* **`disabled:opacity-45` in the class attribute broke assertions across the test
  suite.** `expect(html).not.toContain("disabled")` is now true of no button in
  the product, and `/<button(?![^>]*disabled)/` matches none. Two assertions
  silently inverted. Route B writes STATE NAMES into the markup.
* **32 assertions in 19 test files read buttons by class name**; 18 broke here and
  the rest break as the family finishes. They are rewritten against
  **`data-variant`**, which the component writes and no caller can mistype — a
  stronger contract than the class name it replaces, and the thing that finally
  makes rule 5 countable (`[data-size]`).
* **Utilities beat the un-migrated shared classes on the same element.**
  `tailwind.css` is imported last (Phase 1 §3), so a migrated `<Button>` still
  carrying `.settings-icon-btn` takes the utility's font-size and padding, not the
  stylesheet's. Mixing migrated and un-migrated on one element is not neutral.
* **`--leading-btn: 1.2` had to be added to the theme.** `.btn`'s line-height has
  been 1.2 since the kit was ported and the ruled scale never named it, so
  `leading-[1.2]` is refused by `g34_type_scale_escape.py` and by the eslint rule
  beside it — both correctly. A transcription of a rendered figure, not a new
  decision, and it is the same move `--text-btn`/`--text-btn-sm` already made.

### 6 · SIZING THE REMAINING 169, WITH THE ERROR BARS POINTING BOTH WAYS

The family took **≈3 hours**, of which the two instruments, the slot-composition
discovery and the parent-selector discovery are **≈2 hours and are one-time**. The
mechanical part was ~40 minutes for 52 sites.

**≈35–60 hours for the other 169**, and the number is soft in both directions:

* **Buttons were EASIER than the median**: one family, one file, one concept, and
  245 of 250 sites were plain strings.
* **Buttons were HARDER in three ways that recur**: five host elements, seven
  parent rules, and a wrapper whose prop was a class string.
* **`.met-panel` (41 components), `.met-table` (30) and `.kicker` (26) are LAYOUT
  CONTAINERS**, whose utilities interact with their children's. Nothing here
  exercised that, and the slot-conflict trap of §0 is strictly worse between a
  parent and a child than within one element.
* **Every family will need its own `*Kit.test.ts`** until OQ-280 is ruled.

### 7 · THE RECOMMENDATION, STATED PLAINLY BECAUSE A SPIKE THAT ONLY CONFIRMS THE PLAN WAS NOT A SPIKE

**Continue, in shape (b), and stop calling it "styles in the markup" for shared
classes — for these it is "styles in a component".** The distinction is not
pedantic: it is what determines whether the gates can see the styles at all.

**The PO chose Route B on a reasoning about undeclared classes, and shared classes
are the case that reasoning does not cover.** For the 689 single-use classes,
Route B delivers exactly what it promised. For a shared class, the string moves
into a constant and the promise lapses unless each kit brings its own check
(§3) — which is affordable at ~140 lines per family and is a cost the CR never
counted. **That is not a reason to reverse the ruling; it is the condition under
which the ruling keeps its value, and it should be ruled on rather than absorbed.**

⚠ **`@apply` was NOT chosen and was not silently considered acceptable.** It keeps
the class name as the contract and preserves DEF-327's failure mode exactly; it is
Route A, the PO rejected it, and reversing that is a change request, not a lane's
judgment.

### 8 · WHAT THIS PHASE DID NOT COVER

* **The other 169 shared classes**, including all three of the big containers.
* **No `@media`, no responsive variant** (OQ-274 still open) — no button carries one.
* **No `::before`/`::after`**, no `@keyframes`, no `z-index` context.
* **The 28 button CSS rules are STILL DECLARED and must be**, because 74 files
  still name them. The bundle therefore GREW — CSS 138.31 → 141.79 kB raw — and
  the shrink only arrives when the last call site is migrated. **A phase that
  deletes no CSS is the normal shape of this work, not a failure of it.**
* **`.settings-icon-btn`, `.met-danger`, `.active`, `.table-page-btn`** are shared
  classes still on migrated buttons. `.table-page-btn` is a SECOND button
  implementation (8 declarations, composed with nothing) and was not touched.

## 2026-08-19 · OQ-280 COLLIDED — heading tracking renumbered to OQ-281, and G17 could not see it

**Two different questions were both called OQ-280.**

| | |
|---|---|
| **OQ-280 — KEEPS the number** | *"Route B's safety net does not reach a component API"* — CR-018 Phase 3, and it is **in `01-open-questions.md`**, which is the live registry |
| **OQ-281 — renumbered** | *heading tracking `-0.015em` vs r10 having none* — raised **and decided** by the engineering lane, and it **never entered the registry at all** |

**The registry wins**, per the ID-grammar rule that the registry is the allocator. The
decision-log entries that carried the old number are stamped rather than rewritten.

### ⚠ WHY G17 DID NOT CATCH IT, WHICH IS THE PART WORTH KEEPING

`g17_duplicate_ids.py` reads the **registry**. My OQ-280 was minted in
`02-decision-log.md` and **never written into `01-open-questions.md`** — so from G17's
position there was exactly one OQ-280 and nothing to report. **An ID minted in the decision
log and never registered is invisible to the duplicate-ID gate**, and the two lanes then
allocated the same number without either being wrong at the moment it allocated.

This is not a mis-scoped gate so much as a mis-scoped **habit**: the decision log is where a
judgement gets written down, and it is *not* where an identifier gets reserved. **Minting an
ID means writing the registry row, in the same commit.** Recorded as the rule; the gap that
made it possible is filed as **DEF-346** — ~~DEF-345~~, corrected: 345 had already been
issued to a different defect by the time this was filed, which is the *same* cite-before-file
mistake one paragraph later, and is why DEF-346 now covers both.

**It is also self-inflicted and worth saying so:** the lane's brief told it to mint OQs in
`12-governance/01-open-questions.md`, and mine did not follow the instruction I had written
for everyone else.

## 2026-08-19 · OQ-280 RULED BY THE LANE — the safety net follows the STRINGS, not the syntax

⚠ **This ruling is MINE, not the Product Owner's**, under *"Complete Cr 18 - dont wait for my
instructions"*. It does not reverse a PO decision; it decides how to keep one working.

### The problem, as Phase 3 measured it

Phase 3 planted `items-center` → **`itmes-center`** in `buttonKit.ts` and got
`routeBUtilities.test.ts` **5 passed** and G31 **PASS, 0 undeclared**. Both readers extract
from `className=` attributes. **A component kit keeps its utilities in module-level
constants** — `const STRUCTURE = "inline-flex items-center justify-center …"` — so the
strings move out of the readers' field of view the moment a shared class becomes a component.

**And Phase 3 established that shared classes MUST become components**: repeating utilities
at 250 sites produced 540 differing properties, because Tailwind sorts its own rules and two
utilities setting one property in a single class attribute are decided at build time, not by
author order. So this is not an edge case — **it is the shape all 173 shared classes are
going to take**, and 169 of them have not moved yet.

### The ruling: extend the shared grammar, do not write 169 tests

Phase 3's own mitigation was *"every family will need its own `*Kit.test.ts`"*. **Rejected as
the general answer.** That is 169 hand-written guards, each one a thing a future lane must
remember; the first family it is forgotten for is silent again, and nothing reports the
omission. **A discipline that must be repeated 169 times is not a safety net.**

Instead: **teach the ONE shared grammar to read kit constants**, so both readers see the
strings wherever Route B puts them. `07-frontend/classname-grammar/patterns.json` is now the
single place that knows what a class-name-bearing string looks like — OQ-277 built exactly
that, one commit before this problem needed it — so a `kit_constant` pattern there is picked
up by the Python gate and the vitest reader at once, for every family that exists and every
family that ever will.

**This closes the gap for all 169 at once rather than 169 times.** `buttonKit.test.ts` stays:
it asserts things about buttons specifically (B14 rule 5's two sizes) that no generic reader
could know.

### Why this is the right shape, stated so it can be argued with later

The alternative reading is that a component API is *supposed* to be opaque to a class-name
reader, and the real guard is the type system — Phase 3 showed a renamed prop breaking **18
sites in 9 files instantly, at tsc, by name and line**. **That is true and it is not enough:**
`tsc` proves the prop exists and says nothing about whether `itmes-center` is a utility
Tailwind will emit. The two guards answer different questions and we need both.

**Reverses if:** the kit pattern turns out not to be stable across families — if the second
and third kits hold their strings somewhere a regex cannot follow, the grammar is the wrong
layer and the answer is a compiler-backed check over built CSS instead.

### Ordering, and it is load-bearing again

**This lands BEFORE Phase 4 migrates any more families.** Do it after, and every family
migrated in between is a blind spot that has to be found rather than prevented — and Phase 3
has already shown what that looks like: 1,416 properties moved on 273 buttons with tsc,
eslint, 1,516 tests, G31 and G34 all green.

## 2026-08-20 · OQ-280 CLOSED — the grammar reads kit constants, and building it found two more shared bugs

**Built to the ruling of `2641a1a`.** `kit_constant` is now a pattern in
`07-frontend/classname-grammar/patterns.json`, consumed by `kit_tokens()` in
`g31_declared_classes.py` and `kitTokens()` in `routeBUtilities.test.ts`. One change, every
family present and future — instead of 169 hand-written `*Kit.test.ts`.

**RED-proved on the exact defect Phase 3 found**, not a planted analogue: `items-center` →
`itmes-center` in the real `buttonKit.ts` now fails by name —
`itmes-center (named by components/buttonKit.ts)`. Before this, that gave `5 passed` and
`PASS, 0 undeclared`.

### ⚠ WHAT BUILDING IT FOUND — two bugs, both shared by BOTH readers

Neither was in the brief. Both were caught by pointing the new reader at the **real** kit
rather than at a fixture, which is the whole argument for doing it that way.

**1 · A quoted OBJECT KEY read as a utility.** `{ "settings-row": "px-[6px]" }` — the key is
perfectly utility-*shaped*: lowercase, hyphenated, no scheme. Shape cannot tell it from a
class; only **position** can. The first version of the check reported `settings-row`, `link`
and `ghost` as utilities Tailwind would not emit.

**2 · Historical bug 1, recurring in a new reader.** `variant === "link"` inside a kit
constant contributed `link` and `ghost` as class names — the *same* comparison-operand
mistake that made G31 report 130 undeclared classes instead of 125. `class_tokens()` strips
comparisons; the new `kit_tokens()` did not, because I wrote it without mirroring that line.
**The file's own instruction — "keep the two bodies in the same shape" — is what I violated,
and the corpus is what caught it.**

**And fixing the two collided**, which is the part worth keeping: `{ "k": v }` and a ternary
`? "a" : "b"` both put a colon after a quoted string. Skipping on the colon alone threw away
the ternary's true branch. A key needs **both** sides — preceded by `{` or `,` **and**
followed by `:`. Corpus case **C16** is that collision, and both readers failed it
**identically**, which is the corpus doing precisely what OQ-277 built it for: textual
sharing catches drift in the *pattern*, and only the corpus catches drift in the *reader*.

### What this does NOT close

A kit constant whose value is **computed** — assembled at runtime, or read from an object the
regex cannot follow — is still invisible. Nothing today does that, and the day one does, the
grammar is the wrong layer and the answer is a compiler-backed check over built CSS.
Recorded as the reversal condition on the `2641a1a` ruling, unchanged.

## 2026-08-20 · DEF-342 — the guard is fixed; the DEFECT needs a PO ruling, and here is why

**The guard was measuring the wrong thing, and that half is now fixed.**
CR-016 measures `distinctButtonFontSizes`; **B14 rule 5 says two button SIZES.** A button's
size is its padding and its type **together**, so the check read one third of it and reported
conformance while the product rendered four sizes under one conforming font size.

`buttonKit.test.ts` now measures the shape `buttonClasses()` actually renders —
`py-… | px-… | text-…` per size — off the function that reaches the DOM rather than off the
constant maps, so a size that stopped being wired could not still be counted.

**Ratcheted at 4, not asserted at 2, deliberately.** Four is the truth today and a
permanently-red guard earns a `skip` rather than a fix. It may fall and can never rise; the
failure message prints every shape by name.

### ⚠ WHY IT CANNOT FALL TO TWO BY EDITING PADDING — the actual finding

r10's markup uses **`btn`, `btn-sm` and `btn-icon-sm` (229 uses)** and has **no `row` or
`settings-row` size at all**.

Our four exist because **our row actions are TEXT buttons squeezed into table rows**
(`py-0`, `py-[2px]`) where **r10 uses ICON buttons**. Collapsing `row` and `settings-row`
into `sm` would change row heights across the product in order to satisfy a rule whose real
violation is **B14 rule 15 — icons for row actions**.

**DEF-342 and DEF-337 are one root cause.** Closing DEF-342 means ruling on icon row actions,
which changes how every table row looks, and that is the PO's call rather than a padding
edit. Both rows stay open, now linked.

### Two false positives this cost, both mine, both worth recording

1. **`text-text` is a COLOUR, not a size.** The first draft filtered `/^text-/` and counted
   the text-colour utility as a font size. The ruled size names are listed explicitly now.
2. Building it is also what proved the point: the guard could only be written *correctly*
   once "what is a size" was answered, and answering it is what surfaced the r10 evidence.

**RED-proved** by adding a fifth size to the kit: the ratchet fails at 5 and names all five
shapes. Reverted; `buttonKit.ts` verified byte-identical to the branch afterwards.

## 2026-08-20 · ICON ROW ACTIONS RULED — OPTION A, and "only one reference point not two"

**The PO ruled, verbatim:**

> *"I will go with this A — Icons everywhere, per r10 and rule 15. Convert ~40 buttons in
> 10 files. Closes DEF-337 and DEF-342 together; four button sizes become three, and rule
> 5's 'two' becomes reachable for the first time. Ends the split — one product, one
> convention. Cost: real. It moves pixels on 16 tables, so by your own closure bar it needs
> a browser walkthrough, not a green suite. Estimate 10–14h including the walkthrough.
> Needs a shared icon module first (see below). - Tailwind, CSS, STylesheet, UI COmponents
> - we should ahve only one reference point not two;"*

**Two rulings, and the second is the wider one.**

### Ruling 1 — row actions are icons, everywhere

**The figure that was shown, in plain English:** the product renders row actions **two
different ways today**. Four files and seven tables already use 14px icons with an
accessible name (`SettingsReferenceData`, `SettingsRoutesCyclesTab`, `TemplateCatalog`,
`TemplateDetail` — 14 buttons, converted by CR-003/CR-004). **Ten files and sixteen tables
still render text**, roughly 40 buttons — Assets, Premises, Units, Users & roles, Chart of
accounts, Charge codes, Plans, Taxes & fees, Accounting, Allocation order, Custom fields,
Services. On Users & roles that is four red words in one cell, which is DEF-337 as reported
from the Silver Creek Water deployment on 2.28.0.

**The reference is r10 and it already draws every action we have.** Its `title` inventory
carries `Edit` (8 uses), `View` (14), `View asset` (5), `Reassign` (4), `Retire` (4),
`Deactivate` (5), `Remove` (5), `Edit mapping` (18), `Clear mapping` (18), `Remove rung`
(4), `Remove strategy` (3). It uses **one** icon size, `btn-icon-sm`, **229 times**, and has
**no `row` and no `settings-row` size at all**.

**Why this closes DEF-342 and not just DEF-337.** The four button paddings are not four
tastes, they are two contents: `0 8px` holds a WORD squeezed into a table row and `2px 6px`
holds a 14px SQUARE. Give every row action the same content and `row` and `settings-row`
collapse into one tier — four sizes become three, and B14 rule 5's "two" is reachable for
the first time since it was ratified.

**⚠ The closure bar applies and a green suite does not meet it.** This moves pixels on
sixteen tables. Closing evidence is a person clicking those sixteen tables in a browser
against a booted stack (PO 2026-08-18), and the two defects stay open until that happens.

**⚠ r10's own pattern is NOT copied in one respect.** r10 puts the action's meaning in
`title` alone, which is a mouse-only affordance — a keyboard or screen-reader user gets
nothing. The four already-converted files carry `aria-label` **and** `title`, both through
`t()`, and B14's own note on rule 15 says why: *"an icon with no name passes a text-absence
check and is unusable without a mouse."* **That pattern wins over r10's here**, and it is
the one thing in this conversion where the design authority is deliberately not followed.

### Ruling 2 — ONE reference point for Tailwind, CSS, stylesheets and UI components

*"we should ahve only one reference point not two"*. This is a general rule and it is
recorded as one, because it decides more than icons.

**What it rules on immediately:** DEF-348, filed hours earlier, found the pencil glyph that
rule 15 calls "edit" drawn **three times, byte for byte**, under two names — `EditIcon` in
`SettingsReferenceData.tsx:494`, `EditIcon` in `SettingsRoutesCyclesTab.tsx:144`, and
`PencilIcon` exported from `TemplateDetail.tsx:925`, all three
`d="M4 20h4L18.5 9.5a2.1 2.1 0 10-3-3L5 17v3z"` at `strokeWidth 1.6`. `TrashIcon` and
`PowerIcon` are each duplicated across the two tenancy files as well. **The shared icon
module is therefore a precondition of ruling 1, not a follow-up** — converting ten more
files without it would have produced a fourth pencil.

**What it rules on going forward:** it is hard-won law 5 ("one generated file, committed
once") widened from generated files to the whole UI surface, and it is the standing answer
to a question this repo keeps re-asking in different costumes — OQ-277 (the class-name
reader existing twice, closed by making the two share one grammar), DEF-344 (`.met-danger`
as a second danger tier beside `.btn-danger`), DEF-348 (three pencils). **Where a rule,
a token, a glyph or a component exists twice, the ruling is: merge to one and let the
duplicate be the thing that is deleted.**

### What is built, in order

1. `07-frontend/src/components/icons.tsx` — the rule-15 vocabulary, one export per verb,
   every existing duplicate re-pointed at it and deleted.
2. The ten text files converted, each button carrying `aria-label` + `title` through `t()`.
3. `row` and `settings-row` collapsed to one row-action tier; `buttonKit.test.ts`'s ratchet
   drops from 4 to 3 (it may fall and can never rise — that is what the ratchet is for).
4. A guard for rule 15, RED-proved **twice** as DEF-337's own prevention column demands:
   once on a bare text link, once on an icon with no accessible name — the second is the
   failure the obvious check misses.
5. The browser walkthrough of sixteen tables. Only then do DEF-337 and DEF-342 close.

## 2026-08-20 · ICON ROW ACTIONS — BUILT. What it cost, and the two things it found

The ruling above, executed. Six commits, `2.29.15` → `2.29.20`.

### The numbers, measured rather than estimated

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| Files rendering row actions as TEXT | 10 (16 tables) | **0** |
| Files rendering them as ICONS | 4 (7 tables) | **14** |
| Row-action cells in the product | — | **21**, holding **52** actions |
| Row-action container classes | 5 (`.ast-` `.met-` `.settings-` `.rating-` `.fin-`) | **1 component** |
| Button SIZE tiers (padding + box + type) | **4** | **3** |
| Implementations of the "edit" pencil | **4**, under 2 names | **1** |
| Icon vocabularies in the product | 2 (undiscovered) | 2 (**named**, DEF-349) |

The **10–14h estimate was accepted and the code took less**; the browser
walkthrough is the part that has not happened and it is the part the estimate
was mostly for.

### The two findings, and both are about checks rather than buttons

**1 · THE RULE-15 GUARD PASSED ON THE EXACT DEFECT IT WAS WRITTEN FOR.** G37's
accessible-name check searched `RowActions.tsx` for the string
`aria-label={props.label}`. That file renders THREE elements — `RowAction`'s
button and `RowActionLink`'s two branches — and all three carry it. So deleting
the attribute from the component that draws **every row action in the product**
left the string present twice and the gate printed **PASS** over a product full
of nameless icons.

It was found by one thing only: **DEF-337's prevention column demands the proof
be done on a nameless icon specifically**, rather than "prove it goes red". Had
that column said "RED-prove it", the text-link proof would have passed, the
guard would have shipped, and the failure it exists to catch would have been the
one failure it could not see. This is DEF-182's shape — *a check whose output
cannot distinguish pass from fail is worse than no check, because it is trusted*
— one gate later, and the third time this repo has hit it.

**2 · THE SHELL HAS A SECOND ICON VOCABULARY AND NOBODY HAD LOOKED (DEF-349).**
G37 refused `components/AppShell.tsx` on its **first run, before it had been
pointed at any defect**: seven inline glyphs at 24×24 stroke 2, against the row
actions' 16px stroke 1.6. DEF-348 counted the pencils and closed the **row-action**
family, because that is the family rule 15 names — and one level up was never
asked about. Allowlisted BY NAME rather than by pattern, so the exception is a
decision somebody wrote down; merging it would have put the product's entire
navigation into a commit about table cells.

### Where the pixels moved, and what has to be looked at

Sixteen tables. Five of the fourteen glyphs have **no r10 precedent** — commit,
archive, assignPlan, placement, temp_password — and are named in `icons.tsx` for
exactly this reason: whether a glyph MEANS the action to a person is the one
question no gate in this repo can answer.

Two smaller judgements worth a glance in the same pass:

* **Retire is `✕` and delete is the trash**, not one glyph for both — they sit
  in the SAME cell on the Assets registry, and a retired asset still exists.
* **The chart panel's "Import chart of accounts" stayed a WORD.** It was inside
  a `.settings-row-actions` box with no row under it — a panel action wearing a
  row-action container — so the BOX moved to `.settings-frame-toolbar` and the
  control did not change. Converting it because of the box it happened to be in
  would have been the migration deciding a design question.

### One rule was being quietly broken and the conversion is what surfaced it

Allocation order's up/down arrows were `disabled` at the first and last row
**with no reason given** — the one place BR-SHL-025 was not applied, invisible
while the control was a word that simply greyed out. `RowAction` has no way to
disable without saying why (`reason` and `disabled` are ONE prop, deliberately),
so the gap had to be filled: `settings.rules.sequence.atTop` / `atBottom`, added
to all eleven catalogues. **A component API that makes the rule structural found
a violation that a code review had not, twice over: the same prop shape is why
Chart of accounts lost its `<span title>` wrapper.**

### What is NOT closed

**DEF-337 and DEF-342 stay OPEN, and the reason is narrower than it was.**

The spec ran against a booted stack — `boot_stack.sh`, the built bundle on one
origin, signed in as Dana — and **both tests pass**:

```
rule 15 · 1,032 row action(s) across 12 screens
  assets 199 · premises 200 · units 200 · finance-gl 105 · settings-accounting 105
  settings-reference-data 78 · settings-templates 74 · settings-routes-cycles 24
  settings-services 20 · plans-rates 10 · settings-users 9 · billing-defaults 8
DEF-342 — one row-action size, not two: 1 distinct shape
```

Every one carries an accessible name, none renders a word, none renders an empty
box, and computed style says **one** row-action shape where there were two.
RED-proved in the browser too: `aria-label` removed from `RowAction`, rebuilt,
re-run — 14 findings, failing by name.

**So what is left for the PO is not "does it work", it is "does it MEAN".** Five
glyphs have no r10 precedent (commit · archive · assignPlan · placement ·
temp_password) and two judgements were made rather than transcribed (retire ✕ vs
delete 🗑 in the same cell; the chart-panel import staying a word). That is the
walkthrough, and it is minutes rather than the hours the estimate carried.

### ⚠ AND THE FIRST RUN OF THAT SPEC REPORTED A CLEAN PRODUCT OVER FIVE SCREENS IT NEVER REACHED

`641 row actions, all named` — over a walk where `/units`,
`/finance/chart-of-accounts`, `/settings/reference-data` (no `?list=`),
`/settings/custom-fields` and `/settings/rules` all rendered **zero**, four of
them not being routes at all. The floor was global — *"more than 20 actions
total"* — and two busy screens satisfy it.

**The spec's own comment warned about this one paragraph earlier**, citing
DEF-057 by name, which is the useful part: a warning in prose checks nothing.
Every screen now declares what it must find. The one screen that legitimately
has none — custom fields, because `CustomField` has **no seeder anywhere in
`06-backend/apps/**`** — is exempt BY NAME with that reason, and the exemption
is itself asserted, so a fixture that grows makes the exemption fail rather than
letting it become where checks go to die.

**That is the third time today a check reported success over the thing it was
pointed at** — G37's accessible-name search, this spec's coverage floor, and
DEF-182's `--stat` before them. The pattern is worth naming: each one produced
CONFIDENT OUTPUT, and in every case the output could not distinguish pass from
fail. Proving a guard RED is not a formality about the guard; it is the only way
to find out whether the guard can see.

## 2026-08-20 · GLYPHS ARE FOR TABLE ACTIONS, NOT FOR BUTTONS (PO ruling)

Shown the two judgements the icon conversion made rather than transcribed from
r10, the PO ruled on both. Verbatim:

> *"Retire is ✕ and delete is 🗑, not one glyph — they sit in the same cell on
> Assets and a retired asset still exists. - this only for table actions ; not
> for buttons"*
>
> *""Import chart of accounts" stayed a word. It was inside a row-actions box
> with no row under it; I moved the box, not the control. - okay"*

**Ruling 1 scopes the whole vocabulary, not just retire.** The ✕/🗑 distinction
stands **for table actions**, and B14 rule 15's glyphs do not reach an ordinary
button: a button says a word. So "Retire" as a page-header or confirm-dialog
control stays the word "Retire", and only the row-action ✕ is a glyph.

**Ruling 2 confirms the chart-panel import stays a word** — it was a panel action
wearing a row-actions container, and moving the container rather than the control
is what the PO wanted.

### What was already true, and what now keeps it true

**The product already obeyed ruling 1 when it arrived.** All **50** glyph uses
were row actions and **none** was a button's label — measured, not assumed. That
is the cheapest moment to write a rule down and the likeliest moment for it to be
broken later by someone who never heard it, so it is a check rather than a note:
`g37_row_actions.py` now refuses a rule-15 glyph inside a plain `<button>` or
`<Button>`, reading the glyph list out of `icons.tsx` so it cannot fall behind.

⚠ **AND ITS FIRST RED PROOF PASSED — THE FOURTH TIME TODAY.** This one was
different from the other three, and the difference matters: **the guard was
fine and the PROOF was broken.** The sabotage inserted `<TrashIcon />` into an
arrow function's body (`onClick={() =><TrashIcon /> seed.mutate()}`) instead of
between a button's tags, so the gate was never shown the defect and reported
PASS on a healthy tree — correctly. Re-done properly it fails by file, line,
glyph and rule.

**The lesson is one step further along than the other three:** a RED proof is
itself a thing that can be wrong, and a proof that does not fail tells you
nothing about which of the two — check or sabotage — is broken. **Read what the
sabotage actually produced before believing the result.** Printing the mutated
lines is what found it here, and it cost one command.

### The three glyphs still not ruled on

`archive` · `assignPlan` · `placement` · `temp_password` and `commit` have no
r10 precedent and were chosen by this lane. They are named in
`components/icons.tsx` for exactly that reason. **DEF-337 and DEF-342 remain
open on them**, and on nothing else: the shape of rule 15 is proved in a browser
(1,032 row actions, one size tier), so what is left is a judgement about meaning.

## 2026-08-20 · TAILWIND ONLY FOR NEW UI, FROM NOW ON (PO ruling)

**Verbatim:**

> *"Can you set the rule any new UI/screen we will use Tailwind only going
> forward"*

**Yes, and it is now a ratchet rather than a note.**

### What the rule says

**A new screen, a new component, or a new piece of UI is written in Tailwind
utilities. It does not add a class to a stylesheet.** Existing CSS is not
touched by this rule — the 172 remaining shared classes stay exactly where they
are until a migration phase takes them, and nothing has to be rewritten to
satisfy it.

### Why it was asked for, and why it is the right call

It answers the exact cost this lane put to the PO an hour earlier when they
asked *"what if we dont fixed it? what wil happen?"*. The honest answer was that
nothing breaks and nothing decays — but that the product would carry **two
styling systems side by side**, and *"every new screen, whoever builds it has to
pick one — and both are correct"*. That is a tax paid forever by developers, not
a bug, and it is the one part of stopping mid-migration that does not heal by
itself.

The ruling removes the choice. **The old system becomes a legacy surface that
only ever shrinks**, which is what makes a partial migration a stable position
rather than an abandoned one.

### How it is enforced — G31's declared-class count becomes a CEILING

`g31_declared_classes.py` already counts the classes every stylesheet declares:
**904** on the day this was ruled. That number is now a ratchet — **it may fall
and it may never rise.**

This is exactly the rule and not a proxy for it: a new screen written in CSS
adds declarations, and a new screen written in Tailwind adds none. A migration
that removes three classes and adds one still falls, and is still allowed.

⚠ **THE ESCAPE HATCH IS NAMED, NOT OPEN.** Some things Tailwind genuinely cannot
express — `@keyframes`, a `@font-face`, a deep `:has()` chain. Those go in
`g31_declared_classes.py`'s `NEW_CLASS_EXCEPTIONS` **by name with a reason**, the
same shape as G36's `ALLOWED_ORPHANS` and G37's `SVG_OWNERS`. An exception is a
decision somebody wrote down; a raised baseline is a rule that quietly stopped
being one.

### What this does NOT rule

* It does not say the remaining 172 classes must be migrated. That is still a
  cost/benefit call and the PO has not made it.
* It does not rule on Preflight (Phase 5), which is a separate whole-product
  change with its own 684-value measurement.
* It does not forbid EDITING an existing class — only adding a new one.

## 2026-08-20 · PIXEL-PERFECT IS RELAXED FOR PREFLIGHT (PO ruling)

**Verbatim, shown the measured before/after of Preflight enabled:**

> *"Im okay with this one also ; so we dont hav eto worry pixel perfect"*

### What it relaxes, and what it does not

**CR-018 §6 said "every screen renders identically to its pre-migration self".**
That held for every phase up to here and was the right bar for a CLASS
migration, where any movement is an accident. **Preflight is different in kind:**
it is a browser RESET whose entire purpose is to change what the browser was
doing, so "renders identically" and "Preflight enabled" are close to
contradictory. The PO has resolved that by relaxing the bar for this phase.

**It does NOT license breakage.** The distinction that matters:

| | |
|---|---|
| **A difference** | An unstyled `<input>` stops rendering in the browser's Arial 13.33px and inherits the app's Archivo 13px. A checkbox loses the UA's 3px margin. An inline `<svg>` aligns to the middle instead of the text baseline. **Accepted.** |
| **A defect** | An `<h1>` collapsing from 30px to 15px is not a heading any more. Eighty-four paragraphs losing every margin run their text together. **Still fixed.** |

So Preflight lands with its reset intact, and only the two changes that would
read as BROKEN are compensated.

### The heading decision this unlocks

Twelve `h1`s in this product have no size of their own; every other screen sets
one. Preserving 30px would have kept the browser's arbitrary `2em`. With
pixel-preservation relaxed, they take **the ruled scale instead** — OQ-275,
ratified 2026-08-19: `h1 40 · h2 32 · h3 25 · h4 20 · h5 16`. Those seven type
tokens were ruled and had **never been rendered by anything**; this is the
commit where they finally are.

⚠ **THAT IS A VISIBLE CHANGE ON TWELVE SCREENS and it is the PO's own ruled
scale**, not a migration's invention. It is called out here rather than buried
because it is the one thing in Phase 5 a person will notice.

### The measurement the ruling was made on

7,413 elements, 20 screens, before and after:

* **7,325 inert** — `border-style: none → solid` at width `0px`. Every number
  moves and nothing paints. This is the bulk of Phase 1's alarming "684".
* **4,228 visible**, and they concentrate on exactly the elements NOBODY HAD
  STYLED: 1,118 inline `<svg>` alignments, 194 unstyled `<input>`s inheriting
  the app font instead of Arial, 238 `<button>`s losing UA chrome. **Preflight
  is finding the gaps, which is what it is for** — DEF-211 was one of these
  found by hand.
* Screenshots of Assets, Units and Dashboard before/after are visually
  indistinguishable apart from the version stamp.

(1) THE LOAD STAYS ALL-OR-NOTHING; IT DOES NOT COMMIT PER CHUNK.** CR-026 step 4 named this as the one judgment to record, and `BR-MET-090` decides it rather than performance: **the run-level idempotency key is `uq_import_runs_idempotency (tenant, target, file_hash) WHERE status='loaded'`, and a half-committed run is not `loaded`** — so a worker killed after chunk 37 of 50 leaves 37,000 premises written, a run that still reads `validated`, and NOTHING anywhere that says which 37,000. All-or-nothing costs one long transaction (**101.5s measured at 50,000 rows**, Postgres holds it without complaint — the row lock is on the run, and the only reader of that row is a poller doing a plain SELECT, which MVCC never blocks) and buys the property the whole design rests on: **the run either loaded or it did not.** Resumability is TD-17's word for job bodies and it is honoured the only way this body can honour it — the job is idempotent because a re-delivered load of a `loaded` run returns the receipt (hard rule 6), not because it resumes mid-file. **(2) THE ASYNC BAR IS 5,000 ROWS, AND IT IS A ROW COUNT, NOT A CLOCK.** Measured on this tree at 50,000 real rows: transform **77.9s** (1.56 ms/row), validate **50.8s** (1.02 ms/row), load **101.5s** (2.03 ms/row). At the bar the slowest stage is **5,000 x 2.03 ms = 10.2s**, inside a 30s gateway timeout with 3x margin; at 5,001 rows the run goes to a worker. Below the bar NOTHING changes — same call, same 200, same synchronous answer — because a product that makes a 3-row import slower has been made worse, and the 79 tests that walk 3-row files are the contract that says so. **(3) LIVE PROGRESS CANNOT LIVE ON THE RUN ROW, SO IT LIVES IN A 1:1 SIDE TABLE (`import_run_progress`).** Every stage holds `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` on its `import_runs` row for the whole stage (DEF-529 put the lock inside the transaction, correctly), so a progress UPDATE to that same row **from any other connection blocks until the stage commits** — a column could only ever report 0% and then 100%, which is exactly the number a poller does not need. ## 2026-08-24 · OQ-354 option (A) APPLIED — a first deploy no longer needs an RLS bypass

**The ruling being executed** (PO, 2026-08-24, recorded at OQ-354), verbatim:

> *"You will ahve to do the migration step by step - you will ahve to consier a
> depands on b , b depends on c - so build the sequence of migration"*

That chose **option (A)** and ruled OUT option (B), the typed `BYPASSRLS` window —
which was then deleted from `10-scripts/13-provision-database.sh`. So there was no
remaining path to a first deploy at all until this landed: **the product could not
be installed on an empty database.**

**What was still owed, and is now done.** Three data migrations ended by clearing
tenant context to the **empty string**:

| File | Line |
|---|---|
| `apps/assets/migrations/0003_meter_types_and_read_methods.py` | `_leave_tenant` |
| `apps/metering/migrations/0016_br_met_101_common_area.py` | `_leave_tenant` |
| `apps/tenancy/migrations/0004_settings_families_logo_and_hosted_lists.py` | `_leave_tenant` |

Each now leaves the nil sentinel `00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000`.

**Why the empty string broke it, stated once so nobody re-derives it.**
`set_config(..., false)` is **SESSION** level, so `''` outlived the migration that
set it and every later migration in the run inherited it. PostgreSQL validates a
newly-created **FOREIGN KEY** with an ordinary scan, and under `FORCE ROW LEVEL
SECURITY` that scan is evaluated against the B2 §3 policy — where
`current_setting('app.tenant_id')::uuid` **raises** on `''` rather than simply not
matching. Each of the three migrations poisons *itself*: CreateModel (Django
DEFERS the FK constraints) → RunSQL (ENABLE + FORCE RLS) → RunPython (the clear)
→ exit, at which point the deferred FKs are created and validated against `''`.

**Why the nil sentinel is the answer and not a workaround: it is safe under BOTH
policy forms.** Under the original policy it CASTS where `''` raises, and matches
no row. Under DEF-639's repaired policy —
`NULLIF(current_setting('app.tenant_id', true), '')::uuid` — it is likewise a real
uuid matching nothing. The empty string only ever worked under the second, and
**historical policies are live at that point in a fresh run**. It is also already
the database- and role-level default installed by
`06-backend/db/001_tenant_context_default.sql`, so this restores the declared "no
tenant" default rather than inventing a value.

**Runtime is unchanged.** `core/tenancy.py` still clears a REQUEST's context to
`''` on purpose, because there a failed cast is the desired denial. The two
disagree deliberately and each file says so.

**MEASURED, not asserted** — PostgreSQL 16, role `smartbillhub` at
`rolsuper=f rolbypassrls=f`, one process, no bypass anywhere:

| Step | Result |
|---|---|
| empty database → `manage.py migrate` | **exit 0**, 171 migrations |
| tables created | **204** |
| tenant-scoped columns | **188** |
| `ENABLE` + `FORCE` row-level security | **187 / 187** |
| policies | **187** |
| `manage.py seed_demo` | **exit 0** |

The one tenant-scoped table without FORCE is `sessions`, which is deliberately
exempt — and independently confirmed as such the same day by the lane that used it
as the *failing control* in an RLS probe, proving that probe measured policy and
not connection.

**The append-only exception, and it obeys the rule it looks like it breaks.**
`.github/workflows/migration-guard.yml` blocks edits to committed migrations, and
its own text says *"DO NOT ADD AN ENTRY TO EXTEND THIS. A new exception is a new
PO ruling with its own decision-log row"*. **This is that ruling and this is that
row.** The exception is pinned by **(path, content) together**, not by path — so
it closes the instant it is used, cannot be borrowed by copying an exempt file's
bytes elsewhere, and any later edit to one of the three fails the guard exactly as
before.

⚠ **The tenancy file's hash MOVED rather than being kept beside the new one.** It
carried the earlier DEF-639 exception; editing it again changed its content, so
`786bb4e8…` no longer matches and has been REPLACED. A stale hash left in the list
would exempt nothing while reading as though it still did.

The matcher was proved on four cases before being trusted:

| Case | Result |
|---|---|
| the three exempt files, unmodified | ALLOWED |
| an unexempted migration edited | **REFUSED** |
| an exempt file edited one more time | **REFUSED** |
| exempt CONTENT copied to another path | **REFUSED** |

⚠ **HARD-WON LAW 4 — this does not reach a host that already migrated.** Those
`RunPython`s never run again there, so behaviour is identical, but such a host
still needs the two `ALTER … SET app.tenant_id` statements by hand, once, per
`06-backend/db/001_tenant_context_default.sql`.

⚠ **AND A FIRST DEPLOY NOW HAS A SECOND REQUIREMENT, FOUND BY RUNNING IT.**
`seed_demo` on the fresh database refused with
`FieldEncryptionUnavailable: SBH_FIELD_ENCRYPTION_KEYS is not set` — BR-CUS-092's
encryptor failing closed, which is hard-won law 3 working as intended (the unsafe
option is the one you have to type, and nothing is stored in plaintext instead).
`.env.example` documents the variable and its generator command thoroughly. It is
recorded here because a first-deploy runbook that lists only the database step is
now incomplete, and because editing `.env.example` reaches no host that already
has a `.env` — which the refusal message itself says.

## 2026-08-24 · NINE PO RULINGS, closing the move-out and service-request blockers

Put to the PO as a numbered list with a worked figure each; answered in one
message. **Verbatim, unedited:**

> DEF-652 🔴 - this is correct - A $62.14 bill with a 25% senior discount of
> $15.54 — is the 6.85% tax charged on $62.14 ($4.26); DEF-650 🔴- Make the
> owner a real party; DEF-653 - Refund the $13.12 now, or hold it until the
> dispute closes? hold until dispute close; DEF-654 - apply it to the final
> bill; DEF-648 - 6 steps; DEF-649 - Park it; DEF-651 - master account gets debt
> - if sub accoun tis unable to pay it ; even aftr deposite settlement;
> DEF-635 - confirm; DEF-634 - When we raise the request assing it a number;
> DEF-637 - Yes it should show $130

### 1 · DEF-650 → **THE OWNER BECOMES A REAL PARTY.** `BR-MET-105` is buildable.

*"Make the owner a real party"* — option (a) of the two the defect offered, and
the one with a precedent already on the same screen. `premises.owner_customer_id`
(the nullable FK W0 added) becomes the posting target: the empty-unit base
charge of **$30.50/month** accrues to a customer record, not to the free-text
`owner_manager` string. `MA-1408 · master` on the move-out premise panel is the
shape that already works, and `BR-CUS-083` uses the same shape for a developer.

**What this unblocks:** W7 task 7.15, and the move-out shortfall's posting
target. **What it still does not settle** — and W7 must not assume either:
whether the owner is billed **per empty unit or once per premises** (a 25-unit
building with 6 empty units is **$183.00 vs $30.50** on one bill), and what
happens **before** an owner customer is linked, since the column is nullable.
Both were flagged when BR-MET-105 was written and neither is answered here.

### 2 · DEF-653 → **HOLD THE EXCESS UNTIL THE DISPUTE CLOSES.** BR-CUS-081 gains a condition.

*"hold until dispute close"*. On the worked case: deposit + interest **$153.50**
against everything outstanding **$140.38** leaves **$13.12**, and that $13.12 is
**held, not refunded**, while **$48.00** of the $140.38 is disputed.

⚠ **THIS AMENDS `BR-CUS-081`, WHICH WAS CONFIRMED THE SAME MORNING.** That rule
said settle-and-refund with **no condition**; it now carries one. The rule is not
reversed — where nothing is disputed it still settles and refunds ($153.50
against $142.30 → refund **$11.20**, unchanged). What is added is: **an open
dispute on any part of the outstanding amount holds the excess**, because the
amount owed can still move. The move-out prototype's `Refusal · excess` panel was
right and the defect is closed in its favour.

### 3 · DEF-654 → **THE UNBANKED EXPORT CREDIT IS APPLIED TO THE FINAL BILL.**

*"apply it to the final bill"* — option (c) of four. The **$4.10** of solar export
credit a customer generated is **not forfeited**. It reduces what they owe at
closure, and only what remains after that follows the ordinary settlement path.
The prototype's *"unbanked credit of $4.10 is forfeited on close"* is **withdrawn**.

**Not settled and not assumed:** what happens when the credit EXCEEDS the final
bill — this ruling says where it goes first, not whether the remainder is
refundable. Raised again when W5 builds the settlement.

### 4 · DEF-648 → **SIX STEPS.** The list's four-segment bar is the defect.

*"6 steps"*. The move-out wizard's header — *"Six steps · final bill, deposit,
and what happens to the unit"* — is right, and `MVO-01`'s `4 of 4` STEP column
and four-segment progress bar are wrong. ⚠ **The two must be driven by ONE
declared step list, not two literals**, or this recurs the day a seventh step
appears. Step 4 stays conditional (`Shortfall · skipped`, greyed) — a skipped
step is still one of the six.

### 5 · DEF-649 → **PARK THE MOVE-OUT.** Task 5.1's *"every wizard"* means every wizard.

*"Park it"*. The move-out wizard gets `Save & exit` and `Park — waiting on`, like
move-in and like the service request.

⚠ **THE ARGUMENT AGAINST IT WAS REAL AND DOES NOT DISAPPEAR:** a half-closed
account **still holds its unit**, so a parked move-out blocks the next occupant's
move-in for as long as it sits. The ruling settles that parking is offered; it
does not settle what stops a parked move-out sitting forever. **W5 must build the
visible age with it** — `MVO-01` already shows rows waiting at `2 of 4` — and a
limit is likely needed. Raised, not assumed.

### 6 · DEF-651 → **THE MASTER ACCOUNT CARRIES A SUB-ACCOUNT'S UNPAYABLE DEBT.**

*"master account gets debt - if sub accoun tis unable to pay it ; even aftr
deposite settlement"*.

This is a **bigger rule than the question asked**, and it is recorded as what it
is. The defect asked which of two account numbers on one panel was the typo
(`A-11968` in the ledger row vs `11902` in the prose). **The ruling does not
answer that** — it answers where a shortfall GOES, which is more useful and is
new law: when a sub-account closes still owing after its deposit and interest are
applied, **the residue transfers to its master account**.

⚠ **SO TWO THINGS ARE NOW OPEN, NOT ONE.** (a) The A-11968/11902 discrepancy is
STILL unresolved and a transfer cannot be built against an ambiguous identifier —
it goes back to the PO. (b) This ruling interacts with **BR-CUS-082**, ruled the
same day, which says a debt surviving closure is chased with the dunning ladder
restarting at tier 1. If the debt moves to the master account, **who is chased —
the departed sub-account holder, or the master?** The two rulings do not agree by
themselves and W7 cannot build both readings.

### 7 · DEF-635 → **CONFIRMED.** Seven categories; `government` legacy.

*"confirm"*. `BR-CUS-094` stands as written: the vocabulary expands from four to
seven, `government` becomes a legacy code no new record may pick, every existing
row keeps it and bills exactly as it does today, and re-labelling is a human act
per record.

### 8 · DEF-634 → **A REQUEST IS NUMBERED WHEN IT IS RAISED.**

*"When we raise the request assing it a number"*. Consistent with the earlier
ruling (*"At creation — every draft is numbered"*) and with `BR-CUS-093`. The two
screen statements that disagree are the defect and are corrected.

⚠ **AND THE BUILD CANNOT HONOUR IT YET, WHICH IS ALREADY FILED:** the create path
requires `address_as_given` (step 3) plus `applicant_name`, so **no number exists
at form-open** and `Save as draft` is disabled with that reason. Honouring this
ruling literally needs a backend change — a request numbered before it has an
address — and that is the outstanding half.

### 9 · DEF-637 → **THE CONFIRMATION SHOWS $130.00.**

*"Yes it should show $130"*. The capture form totals **$130.00**; the detail and
the receipt both showed **$25.00**, which is what was actually collected. The
confirmation must show the amount **QUOTED** — $130.00 — with $25.00 shown as
collected and **$105.00 outstanding**, which is `BR-CUS-090`'s counter shortfall
already built and seeded.

## 2026-08-24 · DEF-652 — ⚠ MY DEFECT REPORT HAD A WRONG PREMISE, AND THE CORRECTION CHANGES THE QUESTION

The PO ruled *"this is correct - … the 6.85% tax charged on $62.14 ($4.26)"*.

**I filed DEF-652 saying no signed rule covers whether a discount reduces the tax
base. THAT WAS WRONG. Two signed rules cover it exactly, and I did not find them
before filing.**

* **`BR-RAT-071` (CONFIRMED 2026-08-19)** — *"DISCOUNTS APPLY AT R6, BEFORE TAXES
  — BUT EACH TAX PICKS ITS OWN BASE … CR-013 part 4 makes discount treatment
  **statutory and PER TAX**: some authorities levy on the pre-discount amount …
  R6 returns BOTH subtotals and lets R7 choose."*
* **`BR-RAT-106`** — `taxes.discount_treatment`, **`before` | `after`, default
  `before`**, and it is **BUILT** (DEF-502, `apply_discounts.py`), with tests
  pinning all three states.

**So the product already does both, per tax authority, and the prototype's
$46.60 is not a bug — it is the `before` treatment, which is today's default and
is lawful.** The `$1.07` I reported as a rule gap is the documented difference
between two treatments the product deliberately supports.

**WHICH MEANS THE RULING ANSWERS A DIFFERENT QUESTION THAN THE ONE I ASKED, AND
THE REAL ONE IS NOT SAFE TO ASSUME.** Taxing $62.14 is the **`after`** treatment.
Two readings, and they move different amounts of money:

**(A) Change the DEFAULT from `before` to `after`.** Every tax row no tenant has
explicitly configured re-prices. BR-RAT-106's own test says a NULL treatment is
*"the single behaviour the engine has always had, so a row nobody restated moves
nothing"* — changing it moves every one of them, on every discounted bill, and
issued invoices are immutable so the correction is a run, not a code change.

**(B) Configure THIS tax as `after`.** The Texas franchise fee in the worked case
gets `discount_treatment='after'`; every other authority keeps its own answer;
nothing already issued moves.

**NOTHING IS CHANGED UNTIL THIS IS ANSWERED.** Guessing (A) re-prices live bills
on an inference; guessing (B) leaves the PO believing a global rule was set. The
question goes back with both figures: on the worked bill, **`before` gives $3.19
and `after` gives $4.26**.

## 2026-08-24 · DEF-636 — "We call trash": the first ruling where the prototype LOSES

**PO verbatim, the whole ruling:** ***"We call trash"***.

Three words, and they settle a question that had two halves and one subject.

### What was asked

`04-docs/02-decisions/19-cr031-service-request-capture.md` §8.6 asked which
vocabulary is the product's, because B19 (extracted from r10) and the shipped
code disagreed in two places about the same ten services:

| | r10 / B19 §3 draws | the product ships |
|---|---|---|
| the name of one service | `Rubbish collection` | `Trash` |
| four badge letters | `D` storm water · `O` solar · `H` heating · `Y` battery | `St` · `So` · `Th` · `Ba` |

### Why they differ at all — this is not sloppiness on either side

Four of the ten services — storm water, solar, thermal/heat, battery — were
added by **OQ-273 AFTER r10 was drawn**. Their obvious initials were already
taken: `S` by Sewer, `T` by Trash, `B` by Broadband. r10 could not have known
about a collision that did not exist when it was drawn. Faced with it later,
**r10 invented new single letters and the product went to two characters.** Both
are correct answers; only one of them is already on screen.

### The worked case that made it a defect rather than a preference

The CR-030 W2 Accounts list **already renders `St`** in its service-chip column.
Building REQ-03.2 as B19 §3 drew it would have put **`D` on the request form and
`St` on the accounts list, for the same service, in the same product, two clicks
apart.**

### The ruling, and its reach

Signed as **`BR-RAT-118`** in the rating rule file. The PO answered the NAME
half; the badge half follows from the same sentence without a second question,
because both halves have the same subject and the same answer — **where the
drawing and the shipped product name the same service differently, the product's
name is the product's name.**

⚠ **THIS DOES NOT WEAKEN THE 2026-08-16 REFERENCE DEFAULT** (*"for this session
we will be refering to r10 - as default"*). That default settles **layout, copy,
flows and states**, and a service's own name is none of those. So the general
form, written down so the next divergence does not need the PO again:

> **Where r10 and the shipped product NAME the same thing differently, the
> product wins and the divergence is stamped in B19. Where they LAY OUT or
> SEQUENCE the same thing differently, r10 still wins. A name is not a layout.**

### What changed — and it is nothing in the running product

✅ **Nothing divergent ever shipped, so the ruling changed no behaviour.**
`serviceRequestShared.tsx` already imports `serviceBadge()` rather than
re-declaring letters, and every card renders `rating.service.<code>` from the
one catalogue where `rating.service.trash` = `Trash` (and its ten translations).
The two places still carrying r10's word were both **documents**:

* **B19 §3's service table** — `Rubbish collection` is now struck through with
  `Trash` beside it, kept rather than deleted so the divergence stays readable.
* **B19 §8.6** — closed, naming BR-RAT-118.
* The code comment that said *"DEF-636 is the row that decides which set wins"*
  now says which way it was decided, because a comment describing an open
  question after it closes is the staleness this repo keeps paying for.

Co-signed into the rule file the same commit, per hard-won law 9: the ruling is
written down when it is made, not at the end of the session.

## 2026-08-25 · W6 task 6.9a — the flat-service characteristic is a ROW, not a COLUMN

**Taken by the build, not by the PO, and B18 says so:** BR-MET-104 (PO 2026-08-24,
closing OQ-348) fixed **where** a flat service's pricing characteristic lives — on
the unit — and explicitly left **how many** open, assigning it to W6 *"before it
writes a migration"*. Task **6.9a** was inserted ahead of 6.1 for that reason.
Signed as **`BR-MET-108`**.

**The two shapes.** Trash, storm water and broadband bill on a characteristic
rather than consumption — container count and size, impervious area, speed tier.
One unit can take all three at once, so unit-level means either **a column per
service on `units`** or **a value table keyed by unit-and-service**.

### The precedent was examined and it does not carry

`metering.Unit.square_feet` is what the PO pointed at, and it is genuinely one
column because there is one of it. But it is a fact about the **unit** — true
whether that unit takes trash, storm water, both or neither. *"Three 96-gallon
containers"* is a fact about the unit's **relationship to the trash service**.
Different kinds of fact; the precedent stops there.

### The deciding argument is about money

A 25-unit building, 20 units on trash + storm water + broadband, 5 on trash only.

**Column-per-service.** `units` gains at least four columns — trash needs two —
and the five trash-only units carry NULL in three of them. **That NULL means
either "does not take this service" or "takes it and nobody recorded the
number", and those two price differently.** The first should bill nothing; the
second is an unpriceable bill that must refuse. One nullable column cannot tell
them apart, so the engine either prices an unrecorded impervious area at **zero**
— silently under-billing those units every month — or refuses service a customer
is entitled to.

**Row-per-characteristic.** A missing row is unambiguously *"no characteristic
recorded"*, and whether the service is taken is answered where it already lives:
the tenant's service list. The engine can refuse the second case **by name** and
bill nothing for the first. That building holds `20 × 3 + 5 × 1 = 65` rows.

### Two further reasons, either of which would decide it alone

**The unit of measure stays in a column, not in a column name.** Container count,
impervious square feet and a speed tier are three UoMs. Column-per-service
encodes each in its identifier (`storm_impervious_sqft`), which nothing can
validate, compare or migrate. `unit_of_measure` as DATA is the discipline hard
rule 3 already imposes on consumption — never assume the unit.

**B2 §2, the cross-module interface.** Rating reads these to price. Under
column-per-service a rating rule hardcodes metering's column name per service, so
**adding the eleventh service edits rating**. Under a keyed table rating reads
`(unit, service)` and the interface is stable across the catalogue. BR-MET-104
named B2 §2 for exactly this.

### What is decided, and what is NOT

Decided: the shape — `unit_id · service · key · value · unit_of_measure`,
tenant-scoped, one row per characteristic. **Not decided and not to be invented
by a lane:** the characteristic KEYS, their UoMs, and which services require one
before a bill can be produced. A service whose characteristic is required and
absent must **refuse with the absence named**, never price it at zero.

⚠ **This is AI-authored schema on a 🔒 path (migration ordering), under the PO's
2026-08-09 ruling.** It carries a row in `09-human-review-ledger.md` and is the
build's working shape — CONFIRMED, not ratified. **W6's migration may now be
written against it.**

## 2026-08-25 · FOUR RULINGS ON ELIGIBILITY AND THE DEPOSIT CARRY-FORWARD — and two of them land on a rule already signed

**PO verbatim, all four in one message:**

> *"1. What makes an identity match 'strong' enough to move money? **A — Name +
> date of birth + one government ID**; 2. A customer claims a low-income discount
> but hasn't shown proof yet. Discount on or off while we wait? **B — Hold it —
> bill $142.30**; 3. A discount needs re-certifying every year. The date passes
> and nobody re-certifies. Then what? **A — Discount stops on the date, bill goes
> to full price**; 4. Where does the list of discount programmes come from?
> **Each utility types its own list in Settings — matches how we did documents**"*

⚠ **I PUT FOUR QUESTIONS AND THREE OF THEM WERE ALREADY ANSWERED IN THE REPO.**
That is my error, and it is DEF-652's error repeated: I searched the customers
rules, found silence, and asked — without searching the RATING rules, where
`BR-RAT-076` and `BR-RAT-043` have covered questions 2 and 3 since 2026-08-19,
and where question 4's answer is not merely ruled but BUILT. Asking the PO to
rule on something already ruled spends the one resource this project cannot
manufacture. The rulings are recorded below anyway, because two of them **do**
add something the signed rules leave open — the shipped DEFAULT — and one is
genuinely new.

### 1 · The strong-match criteria — GENUINELY NEW, closes `OQ-364`

Nothing defined it. `BR-CUS-089` fixed only the consequence (money moves on
`strong` alone) and `service_request_service.link_customer` states in its own
words that *"`tier` is the clerk's, not ours … there is no automatic matcher
here."*

**Ruled: name + date of birth + one government ID.** The strictest of the three
offered — it refuses some genuine returners, and the PO chose that over the risk
of handing a stranger someone else's deposit. On the worked case, Rosa Alvarez's
**$150.00** (**$153.50** with the interest BR-CUS-057 would accrue) moves only
when all three agree.

⚠ **AND IT CANNOT BE BUILT TODAY, WHICH THE PO MUST BE TOLD RATHER THAN
DISCOVERING LATER.** It requires a **date of birth**, and `REQ-03.1` never
collects one — `DEF-638(2)` is open on exactly that. So the ruling is recorded
and the criteria stay unenforceable until the request form captures a DOB.
Until then `carry_forward_offer` refuses everything that is not already stored
as `strong`, which is stricter than the ruling, not looser — the safe direction.

### 2 · Unverified proof — the DEFAULT, not a reversal

⚠ **`BR-RAT-076` IS CONFIRMED (2026-08-19) AND SAYS THIS IS PER PROGRAMME:**
*"`proof_before_first_reduction` is a MONEY rule and is stored: true means an
unverified enrolment reduces nothing and the bill is charged in full."*

The PO's *"hold it"* is read as **setting the shipped default of that stored
flag to true**, NOT as removing the per-programme choice. Both readings honour
the words; only this one leaves the signed rule standing, and answer 4 of the
same message — *"each utility types its own list … matches how we did
documents"* — shows the PO thinking in exactly those per-tenant terms.

**Worked:** a $142.30 bill with a 20% assistance discount. Default: the customer
is billed **$142.30** while the claim is unproven, and the **$28.46** is applied
once proof lands. A utility that configures a programme otherwise still gets the
other behaviour.

⚠ **IF THE PO MEANT THE STRONGER THING** — that no programme may ever reduce a
bill before proof — that REVERSES a signed rule and needs its own re-sign. Put
back to them as a narrow question, not assumed.

### 3 · A lapsed recertification — the DEFAULT, and a mechanism that does not exist

⚠ **`BR-RAT-076` ALSO STORES THIS PER PROGRAMME**, with **three** behaviours
from r10's own select: *"notify 60 days ahead then drop · drop silently · never
expires."*

*"Discount stops on the date, bill goes to full price"* is recorded as **the
shipped default** — the first of those three, minus its notice — on the same
reasoning as ruling 2, and the same narrow question goes back if the PO meant to
delete the other two.

⚠ **AND NOTHING IN THIS PRODUCT READS THAT DATE.** Measured 2026-08-25 across
`06-backend`: `recertification_due_on` is written by `verify_enrolment`,
serialised by `enrolment_row`, indexed once — and consumed by **no runner, job,
queue, timer or command**. So *"stops on the date"* is a ruling with no
mechanism behind it: the date passes and the discount keeps applying. This is
the `held_excess_has_no_release_path` shape, and the panel says so rather than
implying a chaser exists. **Building the chaser is a task, and it is not W5's.**

### 4 · Where programmes come from — CONFIRMS what is already built

*"Each utility types its own list in Settings — matches how we did documents"* is
exactly the built behaviour: `create_discount` / `create_discount_version` /
`activate_discount_version` are tenant-authored, and `GET /discounts` already
serves them. **No change.** The precedent the PO names is `BR-CUS-095` (the
document checklist, ruled 2026-08-24), which is the right precedent — and its
sharpest clause is worth carrying across: *ship with nothing ticked*, so a
utility that configures nothing blocks nothing.

⚠ **B18 §5.5.5's `GET /discount-programmes` IS A SECOND NAME FOR AN EXISTING
ROUTE.** It is mounted, and it reads through the seam to the same table rather
than growing a parallel catalogue — `DEF-675`.

`service_characteristics` already keys on `(unit, service, key)` with
`unit_of_measure` as its own column, so trash storing `count = 3` and
`size = 96 gal` is two rows and needs no change. **BR-MET-108's shape decision
stands**, and this closes the "how many" half it left open.

### 2 · ⚠ AN ABSENT CHARACTERISTIC IS BILLED AS ZERO — AND THIS REVERSES `BR-MET-108`

**I recommended against this option explicitly, in the table the PO answered,
naming it the one to rule out. The PO chose it. That is their decision and it is
recorded as made, not re-argued.**

**What is being reversed, quoted:** BR-MET-108's own closing clause — *"A service
whose characteristic is required and absent must REFUSE with the absence named,
**never price it at zero**."* And the sentence one line above it, which was the
whole argument for rows over columns: a blank *"means either 'does not take this
service' or 'takes it and nobody recorded the number', **and those two price
differently**"*.

⚠ **BUT THIS IS NOT A FROZEN-RULE REVERSAL AND NEEDS NO RE-SIGN.** BR-MET-108 is
**AI-authored, CONFIRMED, and HUMAN-REVIEW-PENDING** — written by the build
yesterday under the PO's 2026-08-09 ruling *"AI will do it; we will review it
later as human."* **This IS that review, arriving and ruling differently.** That
is the protocol working exactly as designed, not a process breach.

**What survives and what goes:**
* ✅ **The SHAPE survives** — a row per characteristic, keyed by unit and service,
  with its unit of measure in a column. Nothing about ruling 1 or the storage
  changes.
* ❌ **The REFUSAL goes.** A missing characteristic no longer stops a bill.

**Worked, so the cost is on the record:** 25 units, 24 with a container count,
unit 12 blank. Under the reversed rule the run completes and **unit 12's trash
line is $0.00**. Nothing errors. The bill is delivered, the customer pays it, and
the shortfall recurs every cycle until somebody notices by other means.

⚠ **SO THE ABSENCE MUST BE RECORDED EVEN THOUGH IT NO LONGER BLOCKS.** Billing
zero is the ruling; billing zero *silently* is not something the ruling asks for,
and hard rule 7 plus the audit trail already oblige us to record what a money
path did. The build stamps the absence on the line and surfaces it, so a utility
can find every unit billed at zero for want of a number. **That is implementing
the ruling, not softening it.**

### 3 · A connection number is a Settings → Number format, with SEVERAL offered

*"we are maintaining the formats there - you ahve to give multiple formats"*. So
`connection` joins the existing number-series catalogue alongside `work_order`
(`WO-{0000}`), and the utility picks. The screens draw `CON-26-0110`, so
`CON-{YY}-{0000}` is among the options offered and is the sensible default —
**but it is a choice presented, not a format imposed.** This retires
`create_connection`'s `numbering_series_missing` refusal, which existed precisely
so no lane would invent a format (DEF-615's lesson).

### 4 · ⚠ BATCHING IS NOT A SYSTEM RULE — IT IS THE UTILITY'S TEMPLATES

*"We are making it flexible ; utility users can issue as many work order they
want … we will give them ready to use tempaltes - they will develope these
templats in work order section; then they can add as many they want - they can do
single or group"*.

**This changes what task 6.4 IS.** B18 frames it as batching logic — *"25 units →
7 orders; the split control"* — as though the system decides the grouping. It
does not. **The utility authors templates in the Work order section and issues
however many orders it wants, single or grouped.** `CON-26-0117`'s *5 of 7 orders
across 25 units* is therefore an OUTCOME of that tenant's templates, **not a rule
the engine applies** — and `work_order_templates` is a tenant-authored catalogue,
the same shape as discount programmes and the document checklist.

The drawn `Split into individual orders` control and *"5 orders for a single unit
— nothing to batch"* remain true as **affordances**, not as a computed policy.

### 5 · THE FIELD CONFIRMS, A HUMAN ACCEPTS, AND ONLY THEN DOES SERVICE GO LIVE

*"Work order will send the data and confirm from field; utility staff will review
these work order , accept them and use data from them to activate these services
or confirm the installation is completed"*.

**Three steps, and the middle one is new to the schema:** the field returns DATA
on the order → **a member of staff REVIEWS AND ACCEPTS it** → the accepted data
is what activates the service or confirms installation.

⚠ **THIS REFINES, RATHER THAN CONTRADICTS, THE HISTORY TAB'S *"Electric energised
— gate WO-4904 passed"* ATTRIBUTED TO `System`.** The system does energise, and
the gate does cause it — but the gate passes because **a person accepted the
field's data**, not because the field reported directly. So `is_gate` and
`gate_order_id` stay exactly as built; what is missing is the **acceptance step
and the field data it accepts**.

**What the schema does not yet have:** `work_orders` carries `outcome`,
`external_ref`, `completed_at` and `attachment_ref` — enough to say an order
finished, **not enough to hold what the field sent, who reviewed it, or when it
was accepted.** Recorded as owed; the acceptance is the thing that must be
auditable, because it is the human act standing between a field report and a
customer's supply going live.
