## 2026-08-25 · THREE PO RULINGS ON NEW CONNECT, AND ONE QUESTION WE ASKED BADLY

Three answers arrived in one message, in the PO's own words. Two close open
questions; the third is a change request, and the fourth thing in the message was
not an answer at all — it was the PO telling us a question was unreadable.

### 1 · OQ-367 — where the $14,435 lives → **the owner gets an account number**

> *"You will have to assign account number to owner and tag everything to account
> number"*

**Option (B) of the three put.** New Connect's step 7 offers three debtors for the
quote and only one of them named a party that exists at confirm time. The ruling
removes the difficulty instead of choosing between shapes: **the owner captured at
step 1 gets an ACCOUNT, not merely a customer record**, and the charge is an
ordinary account-shaped charge from that moment.

**The worked figure, unchanged from the screen:** `$185 × 25 = $4,625` ·
`$310 × 24 = $7,440` · `$45 × 50 = $2,250` · `$120 × 1 = $120` = **$14,435.00**,
tagged to the owner's account number at confirm. The commit manifest gains **one
account** — it created 1 customer, 26 units and **0 accounts** before.

**Why this is bigger than it looks.** B4's money math is ❄️ FROZEN on
**account-shaped** invoices, the ledger posts against accounts, and hard rule 7
wants an entity to name. A charge floating on a `connections` row would have needed
a **second, parallel money path** — a payable that is not an invoice, settled by a
payment that references no account — and every rule saying *"the account"* would
have gained a silent exception. **There is now one money path.**

It also makes **DEF-678** implementable: `NCT-03.9` says the quote is *"settled
before energisation"* and the state derivation had nothing to read a settlement
FROM. It can now read the owner account's balance.

→ **BR-MET-113**, which also records what the ruling does NOT settle: the account's
class (BR-CUS-083 already bills a developer via a **master** account — is this that
master?), whether the other two "billed to" options survive as ways of re-tagging,
and what becomes of the account once the units are sold.

### 2 · OQ-369 — outstanding work → **a human marks it**

> *"human will mark everything to start with"*

**Stored and human-authored.** The deciding case is item 3 of the drawn list:
*"Sewer on common area — **Left off, because common area has no water service**"*.
Items 1 and 2 are absences a query could recompute; item 3 is **a decision somebody
made and a reason they gave**, and no derivation can reconstruct a reason. A
derivation would also **re-raise item 3 forever**, because the sewer service
genuinely is absent and always will be.

**"To start with" is part of the ruling and is recorded as such.** Deriving
CANDIDATES later — the system suggesting *"50 meters have no number"* for a person
to accept, amend or dismiss — is not excluded. **What is excluded is the system
silently CLOSING an item a human opened**, which is the reason half of item 3
disappearing again.

→ **BR-MET-114**. Where the list is read after confirm is still not drawn
(`NCT-02.overview` has no such panel) — recorded as a design gap.

### 3 · "instead of energise can we use activated" → **CR-032, and the PO is right**

*Energise* is **electric jargon**. The platform seeds **ten services** and only
Electric, Solar and Battery are energised in any literal sense — water is turned
on, gas is lit, broadband is provisioned, trash is scheduled, sewer is connected.
One state token has to cover all ten and **`activated` is the only one of the two
that is true of every service**. `BR-MET-110` already avoids the word, using
*"service goes live"*.

**Measured, not estimated:** 3 backend files · 2 DB columns (`energised_at` ×2) ·
**0 CHECK constraints** (verified in migration `0026`) · 1 locale key × 11
languages · 5 documents · **0 rows already written**.

**Fast path** — no signed rule, no money, no data. ⚠ **But not a find-and-replace:**
the token is stored on `connections.state`, so it needs a `RenameField` migration or
a fresh database and an existing one disagree about a value silently. Captured as
**CR-032**; not yet executed.

### 4 · OQ-368 — **the PO could not read the question, and that is our defect**

> *"I didnot udnerstand what did you ask me"*

The standing instruction is that a decision goes to the PO *"in plain English with a
concrete figure — never as an ID to go and look up"*. The question as written opened
with `derive_connection_state()` and a state token. **That is us breaking our own
rule, not the PO failing to answer.**

It has been **re-put in the registry with no jargon in it**: *three letters are
picked at step 8; two go at confirm; the third is set for "when service goes live",
which may be three weeks later with nobody at the screen — what makes it actually
go out?* Three options, with the worked difference stated as a Friday-evening
build: **(A)** the letter sends itself at 9pm · **(B)** it waits in an outbox and
goes at 9.05pm, visible and cancellable · **(C)** somebody presses send on Monday.

**A second half of it has never been asked at all:** step 8 draws exactly two
send-times. Is that the list forever, or will a utility want *"three days before
the crew arrives"* or *"when the charges are paid"*? Only the two drawn are built.

**The lesson is the general one, and it is worth more than the answer:** when a
question comes back unanswered, re-read the question before re-asking it.

## 2026-08-25 · Two money rulings on the cut, and they interlock

**Both were put to the PO in plain English with a concrete figure, per the
standing instruction — never as an ID to go and look up — and both answers are
recorded here verbatim.**

### OQ-380 → BR-CUS-103 · base stops at the cut

Asked: *"when a service is cut, does the base charge keep running?"*, with the
figure — `A-11488`, cut 2026-08-18 owing **$612.75**.

**PO: "no".**

So a customer with no service pays nothing for it, and the cost of coming back
is recovered by the reconnection fee rather than by billing a standing charge
against a dead connection. `A-11488` still owes **$612.75** a month later.

⚠ **The product does the opposite today, and it does it by accident.**
`commit_cut` never touches billing — correctly, because DSC-02.4 forbids it
writing to `accounts` — so base runs on because *nothing was written to stop
it*. There was no wrong line of code to find. **The behaviour was an omission,
never a decision**, which is why it could not be read off the code and had to
be asked. Filed as **DEF-707**.

### OQ-381 → BR-CUS-104 · the fee lands at the cut

Asked with both amounts, because the whole difference is which one a customer
must pay: `A-11340` owes **$8,240.00**; the reconnection fee is **$75.00**; so
is the amount to clear **$8,315.00** or **$8,240.00**?

**PO: "does reconnection need $8,315.00 - this is correct".**

The fee becomes owed the moment the service is cut. ⚠ **It posts nowhere
today** — `commit_cut` writes it onto the disconnect case and
`mark_reconnecting` checks AR, two different places, so the gate lets a
customer through **$75.00 short**. Filed as **DEF-708**. The amount is never a
literal: it is the tenant's own `CC-RECON` code, and $75.00 is Brazos Bend's
configured figure.

### What the two together make — BR-CUS-105

Base stops at the cut; the fee lands at the cut. So **from the cut date onward,
nothing the passage of time does can change what a cut customer owes.**
`A-11488` owes **$687.75** on the day of the cut and **$687.75** on any later
day until it is paid.

**This is written down as a rule in its own right because it is the cheapest
guard either ruling has.** One test — run a bill cycle over a cut account,
assert the balance is unchanged — catches a violation of *either* rule without
knowing which: a base line that should not exist, or a fee that landed late.
A property that falls out of two rules is still a property somebody must not
break, and a derived property with no name is one nobody defends.

### What these rulings did NOT settle

**DEF-701's status question is now narrower and still open.** It asked whether
a cut account's sixth status belongs in class `billable_base_only` or
`billable`. BR-CUS-103 rules out `billable_base_only` — there is no base to
bill — but **it does not name the class**, and choosing one here would be
resolving a question by inference from a neighbouring answer. The narrowed
question goes back to the PO.

### D4 → BR-CUS-106 · the age accent is seven days

Put to the PO with the bound and the consequence, never as an id to look up:
*"a request's AGE turns amber past some number of days; the prototype shows 15d
and 11d amber and 5d plain, so the line sits between 6 and 11 and nothing says
where."*

**PO: 7 days — one week.**

Worked, on the eight seeded requests (ages 15 · 11 · 5 · 4 · 3 · 2 · 1 · 0):
exactly **two** accent, and the nearest row to the line is `5d`, two days clear.
Both drawn rows keep their meaning, which is why 7 was the reading offered
first.

⚠ **The obsolete guard must be REPLACED, not deleted.** `TC-REQ-14` was
deliberately asserted INVERTED — it proved a 15-day and a 2-day row were styled
*identically* — precisely so no lane could quietly pick a number while D4 was
open. Now that the number exists, deleting the case would leave the behaviour
unguarded; it must assert the real rule instead, **including the boundary at
exactly 7 days**, which is the half a "greater than" reading gets wrong.

### The work-order templates screen — the PO gave a third option, and it is better

Three were offered: defer it to R5, build it in the wrong module now, or open
R5. The PO answered:

> *"Just keep it black - and show note that Work orders not yet build"*

Read as **blank** — ship the screen as an intentional placeholder that states
its own absence, rather than deferring it silently or misplacing the code.

**This is a better answer than any of the three and it is worth saying why.**
Deferring leaves a menu entry that goes nowhere and a user who cannot tell
whether it is broken or unbuilt. Building it in `customers` puts a Work-module
screen in the wrong module and guarantees a later move. The placeholder does
neither: the code stays out of the wrong module, and the product tells the
truth about itself on screen.

⚠ **It is only honest if it SAYS SO.** Hard-won law 2 — built is not wired —
makes a blank screen a defect when it renders nothing and a feature when it
renders its own reason. The distinction is one sentence on the page, and that
sentence is the whole deliverable.

**No PO ruling is claimed here.** The PO's ruling — *"Just keep it black - and

`/work/templates`, rendered by `07-frontend/src/features/work/WorkOrderTemplatesPage.tsx`.

Three homes were possible and the reasoning is the whole value of the choice.

carries the mechanism — four `work` reference-data cards with `arrivesWithKey`
and no endpoint. **It was not chosen**, because the PO's own reframing of the

### 2 · It is LINKED, because an unlinked stated absence is the defect it warns about

Hard-won law 2 makes a blank screen a feature only when it renders its own
reason — and a screen nothing links to renders its reason to nobody. The two
sentences above now carry `Where work order templates will live`, so the copy
that says *"not built yet"* is one click from the page that says what that
means. Neither existing sentence was changed.

### 3 · ⚠ THE REASSURANCE THE LANE WAS ASKED TO PRINT WAS MEASURED AND IS FALSE

The obvious kind thing to write on that page is *"the seeded starter templates
already work, so connections still get their work orders — only editing them is
missing."* **Measured on this tree, 2026-08-25, it is not true**, and it is not
written:

* `sample_data._seed_work_order_template_starters` writes the per-service

* **Nothing reads them.** The only reader of `work_order_templates` is

  work plan. DECLARED, never batched"** — those orders were written directly.
* There is no writer either: `connections.py` publishes no

So the screen says what is true instead: **nothing on a new connection is
proposed from a template today, and work already recorded against a connection
is unaffected.** G38 exists because a screen claiming an ABSENCE is not the
absence; this is the same law pointed at a claimed PRESENCE, and it is the
cheaper half to get wrong — a false reassurance reads as competence.

## 2026-08-25 · DEF-709 — the demo estate gets a master account, and it is the DEVELOPER's

**The defect is DATA, not code.** `accounts.kind` (BR-CUS-068), `create_master_
account` as its only door, `kind` served on every account row, the `Master` pill
on S17 and S21 and the `f.kind` filter are all built and all wired — and **no
seeder anywhere had ever written a `kind='master'` row**, so every tenant this
product has ever planted rendered all of it against an empty set. The PO asked
for the feature to be built, which is the symptom. Every existing master-account
test builds its own master inline and passes, which is how it hid.

### The judgment: WHICH worked case gets seeded

Two signed rules work a master account with figures. **BR-CUS-083's is seeded;
BR-CUS-068/BR-MET-101's is not**, and the reason is invention cost, not
preference.

| | BR-CUS-068 · BR-MET-101 | BR-CUS-083 · BR-MET-116 |
|---|---|---|
| Worked case | 1408 Elm · 3 units + 2 common areas · **$41.20 + $28.40 = $69.60** | `SR-26-0043` → `CON-26-0117` · 500 Main St · 25 units · **$14,390.00** |
| What the estate already holds | a **single-family house with ONE unit** (`SCW-U-201`), the seat of `A-10432` — the account every B18 `[shot]` draws | the premises, its `owner_manager` **`Ridge Property LLC`**, the service request, the connection, its 25 units |
| What seeding it costs | re-shaping the demo's most-photographed premises into a three-flat block and inventing two more occupants | **ONE unit** |
| What it proves that is not already proved | nothing — the $69.60 comes out of the product end to end in `tests/test_br_cus_068_master_bill.py` | the pill, the filter and the detail pill have data on the estate |

The one unit is not invented either: **BR-MET-116 (PO 2026-08-25) states it as a
manifest** — *"the drawn manifest's `Units 26` = 25 apartments + 1 common area"*
— and states why it must exist, *"if there is common area you can add that in
premises"*. The payer is not invented: with no `contact` in the payload
`create_master_account` takes the premises' `owner_manager`, which BR-CUS-068
defines as the payer (*"payer = the premises' owner/manager"*) and BR-CUS-083
names as *"the developer"*. **No figure and no name is typed twice.**

**It also avoids OQ-366 by construction.** BR-CUS-097 moves a sub-account's
unpayable residue to its master and nobody has ruled whether the ladder then
chases the departed tenant or the master. A seeded master carrying a residue
would answer an open question by existing. This one carries none: it is a
build's owner account over an empty building, BR-MET-116's own *"unit will be
all vacant right now"*.

### Three smaller judgments, each with the thing it protects

1. **The common area is `SCW-U-324`, not the `SCW-U-350` a reader expects.** The
   build's twenty-five run `SCW-U-325…349`, so the 26th "should" be 350 — and
   **350 is already `18 Marten Row`**, the first `W7_SEATS` disconnect seat, with
   `A-10650 · Iversen, Britt` standing on it. 324 is the free slot below the
   block; renumbering a seat another lane drew an account on was the alternative.
2. **It is NOT in `W6_SEATS['units']`.** `_w6_units_for` reads that tuple and
   B18 §5.4.8's tile draws `UNITS 25`; a 26th entry there is exactly how a drawn
   figure silently becomes 26. It is seeded by its own function instead, and a
   test asserts the seat tuple still holds 25 and does not hold it.
3. **The account is created LAST in the customers block**, after the 48, ❄️
   GT-16, the estate and W5/W7. It takes the next number from the tenant series
   (BR-TEN-035), so seeding it anywhere earlier — in metering's block, where the
   connection lives — would have renumbered all 48 sample accounts.

### What was deliberately NOT done, and is owed

**`connections.owner_account_id` on `CON-26-0117` is not stamped.** That column
has exactly one lawful writer, `apps.metering.connections.create_owner_account`
(BR-MET-116's own door), and it is metering's while this seeder runs in the
customers block; calling it from customers needs a new declared seam contract,
and calling it from metering's block renumbers the 48 (judgment 3 above). So the
demo holds the developer's master account and the connection does not yet point
at it as its payer. **Stated, not skipped** — it is the natural next slice, and
it is the whole of BR-CUS-083's link.

### The RED proof, and the shape of it

The test asserts against the **SEEDED** estate through the real seeders' own
entry points, because a test that builds its own master account here would
reproduce the defect rather than catch it. Against the pre-lane seeders it goes
red on `assert 0 >= 1` — no `kind='master'` row on a fully seeded tenant.

## The local checkout keeps rewinding — DIAGNOSED, and the tool already existed

**Five times on 2026-08-25**, local HEAD went back to `42256218` — a commit from
**2026-08-24** — losing up to 152 commits from the working tree. Nothing was
ever lost, because everything had been pushed.

**The reflog is the diagnosis and it is unambiguous.** After a rewind, `git
reflog` holds NO entry for any of the day's commits; `HEAD@{1}` is yesterday's
commit. A `git reset` would have left a reflog entry. So the commits were never
made in the `.git` that is present afterwards: **the container's filesystem,
`.git` included, is restored from a session-start snapshot between turns, and
only what was PUSHED survives.** It is not a bug in the repo and no repo change
can prevent it.

**The check was written on 2026-08-20 for DEF-351 — the same phenomenon at 240
commits — and this session simply did not run it:**
`10-scripts/check_head_current.sh`. It fetches, compares HEAD to the upstream
tip, and prints the fast-forward recovery. **Run it as the FIRST command of
every turn**, not when something looks missing — every law-11 check in CLAUDE.md
is about what a commit CONTAINS and every one of them assumes HEAD is where you
left it. A rewind moves the pointer and touches no file, so all of them pass
over a stale tree.

The second half of the mitigation is what actually saved this session: **commit
and push after every step.** A push is the only durable act here.

## 2026-08-25 · DEF-712 — B14 rule 6 was UNFOLLOWABLE, and the audit of what still is (lane DANGERTIER)

**The finding, stated plainly:** the `danger` variant has been in `buttonKit`
since CR-018 Phase 3 and **no commit button in the product could reach it.**
`WizardFrame` commits through `StateFrame.WorkingButton`, which took
`working`/`children`/`onClick`/`type` and hard-coded `variant="primary"`. So a
disconnection — cutting off a household's water — committed through a button
styled exactly like Save, and **because no gate in this repo reads rendered
output, an UNOBEYABLE rule and an unfollowed one produce the same green.**

**Decision 1 — one optional prop per shared component, no parallel button.** The
W7 lane that hit this refused to draw its own danger commit beside the frame's,
and its reasoning is adopted here: a second button loses single-flight
(BR-SHL-019), the A18 §3 working state and the A18 §4
failure-with-entered-state-preserved. Three guarantees for one colour is the
wrong trade. Shipped: `WorkingButton` gains `variant?: CommitTier`,
`WizardFrame` gains `commitVariant?`, both optional, both defaulting to
`primary`, so the other thirteen `WorkingButton` sites and eighteen wizard
commits render byte-for-byte what they rendered before.

**Decision 2 — the tier is a NARROWED union, `"primary" | "danger"`, not
`ButtonVariant`.** Rule 6 has exactly two answers, so a `ghost` or `link` commit
fails to compile rather than being caught by a reviewer. `Extract<>` keeps the
names tied to `buttonKit`.

**Decision 3 — the FLOW declares destructiveness; the frame never infers it.**
There is nothing in `steps`/`commitLabel` a heuristic could read without
guessing: a label match on "disconnect" would style whatever a translator wrote
and would miss retire, reverse and write-off entirely.

**Decision 4 — the guard reads RENDERED OUTPUT, because the prop is not what was
broken.** Three suites read the commit button's own `class` attribute against
`buttonClasses("danger")`, in both directions (a declared commit is danger; an
undeclared one is primary). All five mutations — hard-coded primary, dropped
pass-through, dropped declaration, unconditional danger, removed working state —
were proved RED in a scratchpad copy per r11 step 2d, never in the shared tree.

### The audit rule 6 obliges — RECOMMENDATION ONLY, no screen was restyled

Changing how a commit button looks on a screen the PO has already seen is a
visible change to a ratified rule set, so only `DisconnectWizard` — the screen
the defect is about — was changed. The rest is put up for a ruling:

| Commit | Copy | Destructive under rule 6? |
|---|---|---|
| `AssetRetireWizard` | `Retire {asset} ✓` | **YES — `retire` is rule 6's own second example.** The strongest recommendation here |
| `DisconnectWizard` | `Schedule the disconnection ✓` | **YES — done.** ⚠ Note it SCHEDULES; the cut happens later, from `commit_cut`. The tier is still right: it is the commit that authorises a cut |
| `MoveOutWizard` | `Complete move-out ✓` | **BORDERLINE — a judgement, not a reading.** Service ends and the account closes, but at the customer's own request. Rule 6's four examples are all things done TO a customer or TO a record. Recommend: leave primary unless the PO reads move-out as destructive |
| `TransferWizard` | `Complete transfer ✓` | **NO** — service continues; it changes who is billed. (Owned by another lane during this work; untouched, as instructed) |
| `BillRunWizard` | `Send all now ✓` | **NO under rule 6, but it is irreversible and it is money.** Rule 11's consequence preview is the rule that governs it |
| `UploadReadsWizard` | `Post batch ✓` | NO — corrections are new rows (hard rule 4) |
| The other twelve | create/publish/activate/submit copy | NO — creations |

⚠ **AND THE LARGER HALF IS NOT A WIZARD AT ALL.**
`components/ConfirmDialog.tsx` — docstring: *"THE one destructive-action confirm
with consequence messaging"*, example consequence *"Write off 3 balances?"* —
commits through the same `WorkingButton` and **passes no tier**, across **30
non-test call sites** that delete, retire, archive, deactivate and roll back.
The prop now exists for it; nothing was changed. **This is the same defect as
DEF-712 with ten times the surface, and it is filed as `DEF-718` rather than
fixed here** — restyling thirty confirms on screens the PO has already seen is a
visible change to a ratified rule set and belongs to a ruling.

## 2026-08-25 · DEF-714 / DEF-201 — a fee line can be issued (lane FEELINE)

**The ruling implemented:** PO 2026-08-25, option **A · "Make issue read the
charge code"**. Three judgments were needed inside it and none of them was
ruled, so each is recorded with the number it turns on.

### 1 · The same defect was already on the register as DEF-201, and it is now the fix that row prescribed

DEF-201 (2026-08-17, **critical, open**) says it in its own title — *"A bill
carrying ANY fee cannot be issued at all"* — and its `prevention` column
prescribes exactly what was built: *"stage 6 stamps `charge_id` on fee lines,
then issue.py resolves rating.charges.gl_account_id per BR-BIL-010 (already
ruled — no OQ needed). Durable guard: a golden or issue test whose bill carries
a fee line, which no test does today."* **It sat open for eight days**, and what
made it urgent was not a new bug: BR-RAT-117 landed on 2026-08-22 and put a fee
line on the ordinary bill of every tenant with a recurring code, turning an
exotic refusal into a total one. DEF-714 is the re-report of DEF-201 from the
other end. Both are closed by this lane; the register said so first.

### 2 · What the charge id travels through — five hops, and every one of them dropped it

`billable_charge_codes` (add `id`) → `gather._charge_fees_for` →
`rating_seam.RatedLine.charge_id` → `pricing.LineCandidate` →
`finalize.PricedLine` → `rating_seam._as_rated_bill` →
`assemble_document` → `invoice_lines.charge_id` → `issue._gl_account_for`.
The seam adapter (`_as_rated_bill`) is the one that is easy to miss and it was
found by the test going red, not by reading: it rebuilds every line field by
field, so a field nobody adds there is silently None on the far side.

### 3 · A RETIRED charge code still answers with its account — judgment, and it costs a bill either way

`gl_account_id_for_charge` deliberately does **not** filter `deleted_at`, unlike
`charge_by_code` beside it. The two answer different questions: `charge_by_code`
is choosing a code to CHARGE (a retired code is not chargeable, IS-1), while
this read is asking where money a line ALREADY carries belongs. Worked: a clerk
retires `SVC-M` on the 3rd, the June run drafted on the 1st carries a **$12.00**
line, and the bill is released on the 5th. Filtering would refuse that bill with
no other account to fall back on. The ledger account's own liveness IS still
checked (`account_is_live`), because a stamp onto a retired ACCOUNT is
unrepairable — that is the ledger's question about the ledger's table.

### 4 · An unpublished rating read refuses the WHOLE bill, not just its fee lines

`gl_stamps_for_lines` refuses when `apps.rating.selectors.gl_account_id_for_charge`
is absent, exactly as it already does for `liability_gl_account_id_for_tax`.
Both halves land in one commit, so this is a posture for a mixed deployment and
never a state this repo ships: half an interface is not an interface, and a bill
issued with un-stamped lines is money in no bucket, permanently.

### 5 · WHAT IS STILL REFUSED — and the late fee is the one that matters

**A LATE FEE STILL CANNOT BE ISSUED.** `decisions._apply_to_account` puts an
applied late fee on the bill as a fee line whose amount comes from B4's own rule
(**$8.13** on the GT-10 reference bill) and which names **no charge code**, so
there is nothing for BR-BIL-010 to resolve and the bill refuses — by name, with
its own break code, and no clerk can close it on a screen. The chart seeds
**4200 Late-fee revenue** with no designation attached, so a fix has two lawful
shapes and the choice is the PO's, not a lane's: give `late_fee_revenue` a
twelfth designation, or make the late fee resolve a tenant charge code the way
BR-BIL-007 already says NSF and reconnect fees do. **Filed as DEF-719** (DEF-718 was taken by a sibling lane between reading
the register and writing to it — the shared-register race law 11 warns about,
caught by re-reading before the append); nothing was guessed here.

Also still refused, and correctly: a `discount` line (kind has no GL rule —
filed 2026-08-22), a charge code the tenant has not pointed at an account, and
one pointed at an account they have since deactivated.

### The worked bill, and it is what a human should be shown

Brazos Bend configures one recurring, auto-applied code — `SVC-M`, *Monthly
service fee*, **$12.00** — and points it at **4210 NSF & other fee revenue**.
Sarah Chen's June bill: electric usage **82.08** + base **18.50** = taxable
**100.58**, fee **12.00**, tax 8.25% of 100.58 = **8.30**, total **120.88**. It
issues; the entry debits AR **120.88** and credits 4100 **82.08**, 4105
**18.50**, 4210 **12.00**, tax **8.30**. **The tax is 8.30 and not 9.29**: the
fee is outside the tax base (B4.2), which is the half that would be silently
wrong on an immutable row. GT-1's ❄️ frozen 100.58 / 8.30 are reproduced
unchanged — `10-scripts/03-golden-verify.py` reads 33 PASS / 0 FAIL before and
after, byte-identical output.

## 2026-08-26 · CR-034 (b) — three judgments the rules did not make for us

The PO's re-scope asked the unit's Plan tab to show *"what exactly will be use
from plan for this unit when billing happens"* **for a stated period**. Three
places the signed rules ran out, each decided here rather than in a constant,
each with the case that decided it.

### 1 · A CALLER THAT STATES NO PERIOD GETS NO PERIOD — never a default month

`GET /units/{id}/pricing` takes optional `period_start` / `period_end`, and
`as_of` is the period **END** — BR-RAT-007's own pivot, quoted verbatim by
`rating.resolution.resolve_plan`: *"the plan version in force on the
SERVICE-PERIOD END DATE"*. With neither supplied the answer is
`period: null`, `as_of` = the tenant's today, `source:
"not_supplied_defaults_to_today"`, and the screen prints *"Showing what applies
as of 2026-08-25"*.

**The obvious alternative — default to the current calendar month — was worked
against a calendar and DECLINED.** On the 25th, a month default makes `as_of`
the 31st. A rate version **effective the 28th is not in force today** and would
resolve anyway, under a heading claiming to describe today. The same panel is
mounted on the move-in wizard's step 4, so the number a **customer signing up**
is shown would move by a filing that has not taken effect. A customer shown a
figure at sign-up holds the utility to it.

**Also decided by that:** the no-period answer is **byte-identical** to what the
endpoint served before this change, so the wizard is unchanged by construction
rather than by inspection. The month default remains a one-line change if the PO
wants it; it is a product decision with that consequence, so it goes to them.

### 2 · A MID-PERIOD PLAN CHANGE IS REPORTED, NEVER COLLAPSED

BR-RAT-114 / DEF-504: a customer who moved plans on the 15th is billed **once
per stretch, each on its own plan**. So a screen naming ONE plan as *the* plan
for a period would state something no bill will ever do.

**Worked, and asserted:** a unit on *Small Commercial* from 1 July and
*Residential* from 15 July, asked about 1–31 July, answers **both** stretches
with their dates, `splits_at: ["2026-07-15"]`, and the sentence *"a bill for it
would be split on 2026-07-15, with each part priced on its own plan"*. The
sections below resolve on `as_of` — **one DATE, which R1 answers with exactly
one plan** — and the payload says which date that was (`plan.resolved_on`).

Nothing picks a stretch. An empty assignment history is still **not** "no plan":
it falls back to the unit's current plan exactly as `billing/gather.py` always
has.

### 3 · WHICH MINIMUM FLOOR WINS IS NOT DECIDED BY A READ

Three places store a floor and they were scattered across three parts of one
screen: the plan's `minimum_bill_amount`, the plan-service line's
`minimum_amount`, and the rate-schedule version's `minimum_bill`. They are now
gathered under one heading.

**Worked: `15.00` (plan), `6.00` (electric service line), `5.00` (schedule
version) — printed side by side, and no fourth number.** Which one a bill
applies is **BR-RAT-016/028**, which is PROPOSED on GT-13 and **not ❄️ frozen**.
Deriving an "effective minimum" here would be billing math in a second place
where no golden test could ever see it, so the payload holds no total, no
`min()` and no comparison, and the screen says *"which one a bill applies is
decided by the billing rules, not by this screen"*. A test asserts the section's
keys are exactly `{plan, services, schedules}` and goes RED on `effective`.

### ⚠ AND ONE OPEN QUESTION THAT TURNED OUT NOT TO BE OWED

The lane was about to report that an OQ was owed for the CONTRACT section — *"no
contract object exists in this product"*. **It is not owed.** `CR-020` already
carries it: the PO's own contracts-on-plans request, captured 2026-08-20
(*"we will need another tab where we attach contracts required for various
plans … this requirement is not yet handled"*) and **HELD** by them 2026-08-21,
verbatim *"hold on dont proceed"*. `apps/rating/selectors.py` states the same
fact one module over (*"CR-020, deferred by the PO"*) and that is where the lane
found it.

**Two things follow, and both are the point of writing this down.** Minting an
OQ beside a live CR is one question under two ids — OQ-197's failure from the
other direction. And the screen does **not** use `ArrivesWith`: that component
promises a thing is on its way with a later story, and nothing is on its way
here. It says the work is *written down and paused*, with `CR-020` on
`data-cr`.

**A gate gap found by that, reported not fixed:** `G38`'s `TRACKS_ID` accepts
`DEF-###` and `OQ-###` only, so a stated absence tracked by a **change request**
cannot cite its row and reads as citing nothing. Nothing is wrong with the
ratchet — it is at 72 and this change leaves it at 72 — but the vocabulary is
one id-form short of the repo's own practice.

**And a smaller one, same shape:** `G32` is a ratchet at zero with no register,
so a lane that may not write catalogue copy must not mint a `message_key`
either. The three period refusals therefore reuse existing keys —
`metering.lookups.required`, `metering.cycle.bad_date` and
`billing.run.error.periodOrder`. **The third is billing's namespace raised from
metering**, which is a real coupling smell: if billing renames that key the
refusal goes silent, which is exactly what G32 exists to prevent. A
metering-namespaced twin is owed (`ledger.report.range_inverted` and
`reports.viewer.range_inverted` are the established precedent for such twins).

## 2026-08-26 · When a fix needs its own version — PO ruling

Asked whether DEF-714's fee-line fix should carry a `2.48.1` stamp. PO verbatim:

> *"if it is fixed, then no version bump required; if not fixed them you can
> icrease the version"*

**So a fix that lands inside a version's own span does not earn a patch number.
The version already names the build the fix is in.** DEF-714 was fixed at
`aca58970` and shipped inside what became **2.49.0**; no `2.48.1` exists and
none is owed.

**The converse is the useful half, and it is what the rule is really for: a
defect that is NOT fixed does not get quietly carried forward under the old
number.** When the fix lands later, that landing is a new version. A version is
a statement about what a build contains, not a receipt for effort — which is
why the change process makes step 7 a gate rather than a habit.

**⚠ AND THE STEP FAILED AGAIN THE SAME NIGHT IT WAS REPAIRED.** Hours after
2.48.0's entry was written to close a seven-release silence, **2.49.0 was
bumped across all four literals with NO CHANGELOG ENTRY AT ALL.** `G35` checks
that the four numbers AGREE; nothing checks that a version SAYS what it
contains, so the lockstep passed while the record went silent. The entry has
been written retrospectively.

**The gap is now named rather than left to recur:** a version bump and its
changelog entry are one act. `G35` cannot see the difference and no gate can —
this is the third documentation failure this session whose escape reason is
*"nothing automated reads prose for truth"*.

## 2026-08-26 · DEF-719 — the late fee books to a tenant charge code

Two lawful shapes were put to the PO with the trade-off in each. PO verbatim:

> *"A · The late fee uses a tenant charge code — like NSF and reconnect already do"*

**Rejected: a twelfth GL designation** hard-wiring the fee to the seeded
`4200 Late-fee revenue`. It would have made the late fee the one fee in this
product a utility cannot point at its own account, while BR-BIL-007 already has
NSF and reconnect reading theirs from the tenant's own codes. `4200` stays the
sensible default for the seeded code; it is no longer the only destination.

→ **BR-BIL-075.**

### ⚠ The half the ruling does not settle, recorded so nobody infers it

**NSF and reconnect are FLAT fees and their charge code carries the figure. A
late fee is not flat — its amount is computed by ❄️ FROZEN B4 math, and
`GT-10`'s `8.13` is a signed golden figure** (`usage 82.08 + base 18.50 + fee
8.13 + tax 8.30 = 117.01`, re-signed 2026-08-10 under HUMAN-GUIDE §6).

So "uses a tenant charge code **like NSF and reconnect**" is exact about the
GL account and **silent about the amount**, because the analogy breaks at
precisely that point. The ruling is recorded as settling **the account only**.

**A charge code whose `amount` overrode `8.13` would change a frozen figure.
That is a finance re-sign via HUMAN-GUIDE §6, not an implementation choice** —
and the CLAUDE.md rule is explicit that a ❄️ frozen figure means STOP. If a
tenant's late-fee code carries an amount, it is used for the account and
ignored for the figure, and that is stated on screen rather than silently
dropped.

**Why this is written down rather than asked again:** the PO answered the
question they were asked, correctly and completely. Re-asking would be the
DEF-682 failure — putting a question back to them that a signed rule (B4)
already answers. What is owed is not another question; it is that no lane
quietly reads the amount off the code because the sentence said "like NSF".

## 2026-08-26 · DEF-718 — the confirm dialog's danger tier, and the SIX confirms deliberately left alone (lane CONFIRMTIER)

**The ruling implemented**, PO 2026-08-26, verbatim:

> *"A. B14 rule 6 is ratified; the tier exists; the only reason they're wrong is
> that nothing could reach it until tonight."*

DEF-712 landed the tier on `WorkingButton` and reached the **wizard** commits.
`ConfirmDialog` composes that same button and passed **no tier**, so rule 6's
largest surface — **30 non-test call sites** — still committed through a button
styled exactly like Save. The fix is one OPTIONAL `confirmVariant?: CommitTier`,
absent meaning `primary`.

### The judgement the ruling did NOT make, and the number it turns on

The ruling says the destructive confirms are wrong. It does not say every
confirm is destructive, and **21 of 30 are** — so nine are a judgement, and the
judgement is recorded here rather than left in the diff.

**The standard used is the DEF-712 lane's, which the PO saw:** rule 6's four
named examples — disconnect, retire, reverse, write-off — are all things done
**to** a customer or **to** a record. `MoveOutWizard` was left primary on that
reading. The same standard, applied here:

| Confirm | Ruling | Why |
|---|---|---|
| 21 sites: delete · retire · archive · deactivate · roll back · remove | **`danger`, pinned** | Rule 6's subject, literally. Two of them (`PlanDetail`, `RateScheduleDetail`) are the word *retire* itself |
| Users & roles · Plans · Services | **COMPUTED from the action** | One dialog serves both halves — deactivate/remove **and** reactivate/temp-password; archive/delete **and** publish; disable **and** enable. Pinning either tier would be wrong half the time |
| Bill-run **bulk apply** | **primary** | Applies a chosen HANDLING to selected exception cases inside a run. Not a deletion; rule 11's consequence preview is the rule that governs it — the same reading DEF-712 gave `BillRunWizard`'s own commit |
| Close-export **send** | **primary** | A send to an external system (rule 4's `↗`), not a destruction. It IS money and it IS irreversible, and the consequence names the figures — that is rule 11's job, not rule 6's |
| Apply previewed rate changes · run the preview | **primary** | The first WRITES new rate versions (a creation, and corrections are new rows); the second merely fetches a preview |
| Numbering **reset** | **primary** | The word reads destructive and the act is not: the form refuses a number lower than the current one, so it can only move a counter FORWARD |
| Tenant **currency change** | **primary** | A settings change. Consequential, and rule 11 already makes it name both currencies; nothing is deleted, retired or reversed |

⚠ **WHY THE SIX MATTER MORE THAN THE TWENTY-ONE.** A tier that appears on every
dialog carries no information — the clerk stops reading it, and the twenty-one
places where it is true stop being warnings. That is why the negative half is
**asserted**, not merely left undone: `ConfirmDialogTier.dom.test.tsx` fails if
*Reactivate*, *Reset temp password* or *Enable* ever goes red.

**If the PO disagrees with any of these six, it is a one-line change and this
table is where to change it** — they are recorded as a lane's judgement under a
ruling that did not reach them, not as repo law.

### `AssetRetireWizard` — taken as included, then ruled in its own right

The lane was told to read the PO's message as approving `Retire {asset} ✓`
alongside the sweep, and to say it had been taken as approved rather than
separately ruled. **It was subsequently ruled on its own** — *"A. One line, and
it's the rule quoting itself."* (this log, same date). Both readings agree, and
that file's own `E4` exception had reported the primary tier and pointed at this
sweep; `E4` is now marked closed.

### What is checked, and the one hole left open

Every assertion reads the button's **rendered `class` attribute**, compared
**whole** — `toBe(buttonClasses("danger"))`, or `class="…"` with both quotes —
never by substring. **A substring match cannot see what follows it** (DEF-182),
so a mutation appending a class to every kit button was proved RED against the
whole-value form before it was trusted. The polymorphic screens are **clicked
open in jsdom**: a confirm dialog is state, and `renderToStaticMarkup` never
reaches one. A **census** case pins all thirty sites, so the thirty-first fails
until somebody classifies it.

**Ten mutations were proved RED first, in a `cp -a` copy, never the shared
tree** — including the shared frame's single-flight and its A18 §4
failure-with-entered-state-preserved, so the claim that they still hold is a
measurement rather than an assertion.

⚠ **THE HOLE, NAMED:** a commit button composing NEITHER shared component — one
hand-rolled in a screen — is still invisible to every gate here, because nothing
in this repo reads rendered output on its own initiative. Rule 6 is now ENFORCED
on these paths and nowhere wider.


## 2026-08-26 · CR-034 §7 — the discount CONDITIONS, and one PO reversal

### The PO's words that opened it

> *"We should show all discount plan offer and what condition are required to
> avail that discount ; when account is attached it will avail those discounts"*

### 0 · THE FINDING THAT DECIDED WHETHER THE SECTION COULD BE HONEST

The amendment named one hazard: if the only source of a "condition" is
`rate_plans.eligibility`, which `US-RAT-002 §5` marks **ADVISORY ONLY**, then
rendering it as a condition tells a clerk the product enforces something it does
not.

**It is not the only source, and the real one is a level down.** The conditions
live on `discount_versions` (`apps/rating/discounts.py`): `eligibility_summary`
at **line 401** (the sentence a human wrote — Silver Creek's five read *Age
65+ · Program enrolment · E-bill on · Autopay enrolled · Veteran ID*),
`eligibility_rule` at **398**, and the enrolment-and-proof block at **399-425**:
`enrolment_mode`, `verification_method`, `proof_required`,
`accepted_proof_kinds`, `proof_before_first_reduction`, `recertification_months
/ _notice_days / _grace_days`, `lapse_behaviour`, plus the caps, the floor and
the stacking columns above them. `_offered_discounts` was **already forwarding
`eligibility`** and the panel drew three columns and never printed it — a
rendering gap, which is the pattern this whole CR has followed.

**The hazard is real for the EVALUATION half and that half is stated, not
rendered.** Nothing in this product evaluates `eligibility_rule` — the model's
own note (*"ADVISORY IN THIS SLICE: no code evaluates it"*) and
`discount_services.py:42` (*"It does not evaluate eligibility"*).

### 1 · A CONDITION IS SHOWN AS RECORDED, NEVER AS CHECKED

`terms.eligibility_checked = {served:false, reason:"no_code_evaluates_a_
discount_eligibility_rule"}` travels on every row, and the screen prints
*"Nothing in this product checks this condition. Staff confirm it when the
account is enrolled."* — or, when a rule document exists, *"A rule for this
condition is recorded on the programme, and nothing in this product evaluates
it."* **Two sentences because they are two facts**: a rule recorded and unread
is not the same as no rule.

⚠ **AND THE RULE DOCUMENT ITSELF IS NOT SHIPPED TO THE CLIENT.** Only
`eligibility_rule_recorded: true`. Printing an unevaluated rule's clauses as
bullet points is the same false reassurance in a different font, and a test
asserts the word `age` from the fixture's own rule appears nowhere in the
payload.

**Why this direction:** a clerk who believes the software refuses unqualified
customers stops checking, and it refuses nobody. That is the expensive
direction of wrong, and the work-orders lane refused the same shape a day
earlier.

### 2 · THE PROGRAMME'S BUDGET IS DROPPED AT SOURCE, LIKE `enrolled` BEFORE IT

Silver Creek's SENIOR carries `budget_cap` **$12,312/yr**. It is not served to
this screen at all — not captioned, not hidden by the client. It is TENANT-WIDE,
and a dollar figure on a UNIT screen is read as that unit's however it is
worded, which is the reasoning `_offered_discounts` already applied to rating's
`enrolled` count.

**The line between the two kinds of money, stated because a later lane will meet
it:** `cap_per_bill` / `cap_per_year` / `cap_lifetime` ARE served, because they
are limits on **this customer's own reduction** — *at most $20.00 off one bill*
is a condition a person reading a discount needs. A budget is the programme's,
and it is not.

### 3 · ONE DATE GOVERNS THE WHOLE ANSWER

`plan_detail` and `plan_discount_rules` gained an optional `as_of` (default
`None` = the tenant's today, byte-identical to every previous answer), and
`unit_pricing` passes the service date it already resolved everything else on.
**Worked:** SENIOR filed v1 *Age 65+* to 31 July and v2 *Age 62+* from 1 August —
asked about July the screen says 65, asked about August it says 62. Before this,
the plan and the rate schedules followed the period and the discount followed
the day the screen happened to be open, and the panel's own heading names the
date, so the two would have contradicted each other in writing.

### 4 · THE FRAMING SAYS *ENROLLED*, NOT *ATTACHED*

The PO's third requirement is that the section read as *what WILL apply once
there is an account*. The line above the table is: *"An account attached to this
unit takes this plan, so these are the discounts it can be given. Each one is
granted by enrolling the account in it, and these are the conditions that
enrolment has to satisfy."*

⚠ **The softer sentence — *"an account here gets these"* — was written and
rejected.** BR-RAT-069: a plan binding grants a discount to nobody, and even an
`automatic` enrolment mode still needs an enrolment row. On a screen a clerk
quotes a **15.00%** figure from, promising a reduction the bill run will not
make is the failure the whole *available-vs-granted* split exists to prevent.

### 5 · A SIDE EFFECT OF SERVING THE CONDITIONS, FOUND AND CLOSED

`plan_detail` is not only a screen read: `rating.services._plan_snapshot` is
that payload minus three keys, and it is **stored inside every plan version
row**. Serving `terms` there put ~22 more leaves per offered discount into the
blob, and `_plan_snapshot_diff` shows **eight** changed leaves before it starts
counting.

**So the first plan edit after this shipped would have diffed an old snapshot
against a new one, reported the discount's conditions as what changed about the
plan, and pushed the operator's real edit off the row.** Nothing would have
failed and no gate would have objected.

**Ruled by the test the other three popped keys already pass — is it plan
CONTENT?** It is not: the conditions belong to the DISCOUNT VERSION and change
when a programme is re-filed while the plan is untouched. `terms` is popped in
`_plan_snapshot`; the discount BINDING stays, because that one really is the
plan's. `TC-15` pins both halves.

⚠ **AND A PRE-EXISTING ONE FOUND WHILE LOOKING, REPORTED NOT FIXED:** the same
snapshot already carries `discounts[].enrolled`, a LIVE TENANT-WIDE COUNT. It
moves when somebody enrols an account and this plan is not touched, so the next
plan edit diffs it as a plan change. It predates this lane, changing it changes
existing diff behaviour, and it is named here rather than smoothed over.

## 2026-08-26 · The unit Plan tab's default period — PO ruled B, against the recommendation

**PO, verbatim:** *"B Default to this month"*.

The question was raised by the CR-034 (b) lane in its own review-ledger row
(*"Is answering 'as of today' until someone picks a period the right default, or
should it default to the current month?"*), with a recommendation of **A**, keep
*as of today*. **The PO ruled B. That is the decision.**

**THE OBJECTION WAS SOUND AND ITS SCOPE IS WHAT ANSWERS IT — WRITTEN DOWN HERE
SO NOBODY "COMPLETES" THE RULING LATER.** On the 25th, a month-END `as_of`
resolves a rate version effective the 28th under a heading about now — and the
same panel is mounted on the customer-facing move-in wizard. So:

| Mount | Prop | Period it asks for |
|---|---|---|
| `UnitDetailPage` — the staff Plan tab | `showPeriod` | **the current calendar month** |
| `MoveInWizard` step 4 — a customer moving in | *(none)* | **unchanged: none. `as_of` = the tenant's today** |

**The default lives in the PANEL, keyed on `showPeriod` — never in
`getUnitPricing` and never in the endpoint.** Pushing it down would change the
wizard, which was never in question, and would reinstate exactly the hazard.
`GET /units/{id}/pricing` with no period still answers `period: null` /
`as_of` = the tenant's today (`test_cr034b_tc1`, unchanged).

**Two guards, in opposite directions, and the second is the one that matters:**
the Plan tab's tests seed the pricing response on the MONTH key and nowhere
else, so removing the default leaves every Plan-tab assertion measuring a
loading skeleton; and `MoveInWizard.test.tsx` renders step 4 twice — from the
no-period key (which draws the plan) and from the month key (which draws
nothing) — so a lane that ever pushes the default down goes red on the
customer-facing screen.

**Ruled at the same time and needing no change, listed because a signature
covers only what was shown:** the three minimum floors stay shown side by side
with no winner named (*"A for now. Which floor wins is BR-RAT-016/028, PROPOSED
not frozen."*), and the discounts keep showing the OFFER with the grant stated
as needing an account (*"A. Already built that way."*) — put to the PO precisely
so it could be vetoed, the risk being a clerk quoting **10.00%** to a customer.
Not vetoed.

## 2026-08-26 · BR-BIL-075 implemented — WHICH code, and what the lane did NOT read off it

Lane LATEFEE, closing **DEF-719**. The PO's ruling settled the SHAPE; three
things it did not name had to be settled to write the code, and all three are
recorded here rather than left in a diff.

### 1 · The code is `LATE`, and that was READ, not chosen

Nothing was picked. Billing's own field map states it against the exact column
this lane writes — `04-docs/05-modules/07-billing/03-field-map.md`, the
*Late-fee apply/waive* row:

> applied → draft fee line `invoice_lines.charge_id` → **LATE** (B2 `charges`)

and `EP-BIL-01-bill-run.md` §5 says the same (*"applied → draft fee line (LATE
charge code)"*). `BR-RAT-056` treats `LATE` as the late fee by name (*"`LATE` is
already pinned to the overdue portion by B4.1 ❄"*), and `EP-RAT-03` §4 seeds it
at 1.5% / $5.00 minimum — **BR-BIL-001's own figures**. So the identification
was already written down in three signed places and no open question was minted
for it.

It ships as `decisions.DEFAULT_LATE_FEE_CHARGE_CODE` with
`apply_decisions(..., late_fee_charge_code=)` overriding it — the same shape
`first_bill` uses for `CONN` and `disconnects` for `CC-RECON`. **A tenant who
renames their late-fee code is one argument away and NOT yet served by a
screen**, because no signed document says a tenant may rename it; that is not
raised as an OQ, it is simply not implemented and is named here so the next lane
sees the boundary rather than discovering it.

### 2 · The amount was NOT read off the code, and the code cannot see it

`_late_fee_charge_id` returns `str(charge["id"])` and nothing else. That is the
guarantee, not the comment above it: a function that never holds the row cannot
spend its `amount`. **`GT-10`'s 8.13 is unmoved** — `usage 82.08 + base 18.50 +
fee 8.13 + tax 8.30 = 117.01` — and a tenant whose `LATE` code is re-keyed to a
flat **$99.00** is still charged **8.13**, asserted on a real issued bill
(`tc6`). Reading the 99.00 would be changing a ❄️ FROZEN figure without a
finance re-sign under HUMAN-GUIDE §6.

⚠ **What is still OWED and is not done: the ruling says that ignored amount is
"stated on screen rather than silently dropped", and S31.3 renders no such
sentence.** It is not faked with a backend field nothing reads (hard-won law 2);
it is a frontend deliverable and is reported as outstanding.

### 3 · The refusal is run-wide, deliberately, and it is NOT a BR-BIL-055 breach

A missing late-fee code is a fact about the TENANT, not about one account, so
every late fee in the run is unbookable. `_late_fee_charge_id` therefore raises
out of `apply_decisions` — `api.run_calculate` renders it as a named 422
carrying `br_ref="BR-BIL-075"` — instead of holding accounts one at a time.
**It is resolved lazily**: a run in which nobody applied a late fee never asks,
so a utility that has never charged one cannot be stopped from billing by a code
it does not need (`tc7`). That is DEF-714's own failure mode, avoided on
purpose.

### 4 · The thing that is ruled, built, and still unreachable — DEF-733

`charge_codes.LATE` is seeded on every tenant (`lookup_defaults.json` +
`seed_demo.CHARGE_CODES`), so this is **not** DEF-700's trap. But **no seed
gives it a GL account**, and none gives one to any charge code — so a freshly
provisioned utility still cannot send a bill with a late fee until somebody maps
the code on S13, and the seeded chart's **4200 Late-fee revenue** sits unused
next to it. Filed as **DEF-733** and asserted as today's behaviour by `tc11`, so
the day a seed points `LATE` at 4200 that test states the change instead of
silently passing.

## 2026-08-26 · DEF-684 — a signed vocabulary is FETCHED, never typed (lane ACCTSTALE)

**The fix is one line of principle and four screens of consequence.**
`customersShared.ACCOUNT_CATEGORIES` was a four-code tuple — `residential ·
commercial · industrial · government` — and its comment gave a good reason for
existing: *"`account_types` is a PLATFORM table … Hardcoding them here is
therefore not a guess about a tenant's data; it is the platform catalog."*
**The reasoning held and the fact under it moved.** BR-CUS-094 (PO 2026-08-24)
expanded the signed vocabulary to SEVEN and marked `government` LEGACY, and the
tuple became one code short in one direction and one refused code long in the
other while **four screens read it**: S18 New account, S19 Move-in, the S14
common-areas master modal, and S17's own category filter.

**The judgment, and it is the reason this row exists:** a picker takes
`selectable`, a FILTER takes `selectable + legacy`. BR-CUS-094 keeps a legacy
code *"still a valid FK, still filterable, still priceable"*, so an account
already carrying `government` has to stay findable — hiding it behind a chip
would have made the additive migration lose live customers on a screen. One
literal category code survives on purpose: S18's `emptyCustomerForm()` default,
because a default is not a vocabulary — and it is pinned against
`AccountType.SEVEN_CATEGORIES` so a ruling that ever retires `residential` goes
RED instead of shipping a default the server refuses.

**FOUR SECOND SITES OF THE SAME SUPERSEDED FOUR WERE FOUND AND NONE IS FIXED
HERE**, each filed and each pinned by an `xfail(strict=True)` that goes RED the
day it is closed:

| Where | What it costs today | Filed |
|---|---|---|
| `services._resolve_account_type` — `POST /accounts` filters on `active` and never reads `legacy` | a legacy category is **written onto a brand-new account** and nothing objects; BR-CUS-094's *"unselectable on any form"* is enforced on the service-request door only | **DEF-736** |
| `services.SEED_ACCOUNT_TYPES` — still the four | the platform backfill would restore `government` **selectable** and never restore the four new codes | **DEF-737** |
| `rating.TAX_CUSTOMER_CLASSES` (+ its `endpoints.ts` mirror) | **no tax can be restricted to Agricultural, Institutional, Municipal or Builder-developer** — a money surface that fails closed, so it looks like a tax nobody configured | **DEF-738** |
| `notifications.template_models.CATEGORIES` / `TemplateCatalog.AUDIENCES` | those four categories get the **default letter** and a tenant cannot write them their own; BR-NOT-001 quotes the four verbatim, so widening it is a **re-sign**, not an edit | **DEF-739** |

⚠ **DEF-736 IS THE ONE THAT CHANGES WHAT DEF-684 MEANT.** Its register row says
the server *"refuses `government` on create"* — true of `POST
/service-requests/{id}/category` and **false of `POST /accounts`**, which is the
endpoint the three broken screens actually call. So the defect was not *"a clerk
picks a value that cannot be saved"*; on those screens it saved. **A visible
refusal would have been the better failure.**

## 2026-08-26 · DEF-722 — six statuses, four pill tones, and why this lane changed nothing (lane ACCTSTALE)

**REPORTED FOR A RULING, NOT DECIDED.** `accountStatusTone` keys off the
BEHAVIOUR CLASS, which was one-to-one with meaning until BR-CUS-107 (PO
2026-08-25) put a sixth status, `Disconnected`, into `non_billable` beside
`Pending activation`. **Both render the same neutral grey and they are opposite
facts** — one customer has not started, the other had their service cut for
debt. Nothing is FALSE, so no assertion fires and no gate can see it.

**The arithmetic is the argument, and it is why this is a PO judgment rather
than a lane's edit.** `StatusPill` has FOUR tones (A12 semantic tokens: status
meaning only, never decoration) and BR-CUS-055 now seeds SIX statuses,
tenant-extensibly. Six into four collapses something whatever we do, and every
available move trades this collapse for a worse one: `disconnected → danger`
makes *"cut, owes money, can come back"* look identical to *"moved out,
finished"*, and only one of them needs a clerk; `disconnected → warning` puts it
with `Vacation hold`, which is benign, temporary and customer-requested. A fifth
tone is a new visual vocabulary across every list in the product (B14 fixes the
pill set), not a change to one function.

⚠ **AND KEYING ON THE CODE IS NOT FREE EITHER.** BR-CUS-055 makes the status
list TENANT-EXTENSIBLE, and the class-keyed mapping exists precisely so a
tenant-added status gets a sensible colour instead of falling through to the
grey this defect complains about. Any fix must be code-first-with-class-fallback.

⚠ **THE SYMPTOM IS LATENT, WHICH IS THE ONLY REASON IT CAN WAIT.**
`Disconnected` is seeded (migration `customers/0025`) and **nothing assigns it**
— `commit_cut` writes no `accounts` column (DEF-701, open). No row in any tenant
carries it, so no clerk is confused by it yet. **The day DEF-701 closes it
appears on the first cut account**, and it should be ruled before then rather
than found by the PO on a live build. The whole argument is written onto
`accountStatusTone`'s docstring so the next reader meets it there.

## 2026-08-26 · CR-035 — a parked wizard changes nothing until it is executed (PO)

**Put to the PO in plain English with a worked case**, per the standing
instruction — never as an ID to go and look up:

> *"A clerk starts a move-in for **Unit 12, 500 Main St** on **26 August**, gets
> to step 3, and stops because they are waiting on a **$150 deposit**. They park
> it and come back on **2 September**. Between those dates — what does the rest
> of the product think is true about Unit 12?"*

Three shapes were shown, each with what Unit 12 would read between those dates:
**A** a parked drawer, unit reads **Vacant**, nothing else changes · **B** the
draft becomes a numbered service request `SR-26-0043` · **C** a real draft
move-in row, unit reads *"Move-in pending 1 Sept"*.

**PO RULING, verbatim:** *"Option A - Unitl move in executed, no records
updates."*

**→ BR-SHL-048, CONFIRMED.** A parked wizard is a saved draft of a form and
nothing more. Between 26 August and 2 September Unit 12 reads **Vacant**, no
account exists, no occupancy begins, no bill is affected, and the only place the
parked work appears is the clerk's own "Waiting on" list.

**THREE CONSEQUENCES THE RULING FORCES, each written down because a later reader
would otherwise re-decide them:**

1. **A parked draft carries NO FOREIGN KEY to the record it is about.** An FK is
   a relationship, and the ruling says there is none until execution. The unit
   id and account id a clerk has chosen are stored as plain values, copied, not
   referenced — so deleting a unit cannot be blocked by a forgotten draft, and
   no report, ageing bucket or occupancy query can reach a parked draft by
   joining to it. Only `tenant_id` and the parking user are real FKs.
2. **A parked draft is re-validated at execution, never trusted from the park.**
   Everything in it was true on 26 August. On 2 September the unit may be taken,
   the plan may have a new version, the deposit rule may have changed. The
   wizard resumes with what was typed and re-runs every check before it commits.
3. **IT SETTLES THE OPEN HALF OF BR-SHL-047 — in the opposite direction to the
   one that rule feared, and the new risk is stated rather than hidden.**
   BR-SHL-047 warned that *"a half-closed account STILL HOLDS ITS UNIT, so a
   parked move-out blocks the next occupant's move-in for as long as it sits"*.
   Under this ruling it holds nothing, because nothing is written — so **no
   parked wizard can ever block anything.** The cost lands elsewhere and is
   real: a parked move-out is invisible to the rest of the product, so the
   account **keeps billing** and nobody downstream knows a closure is coming.
   That is the trade the ruling accepts. The reminder date and the age on the
   "Waiting on" list are what stop a draft sitting forever; BR-SHL-047's
   unit-blocking limit is now **moot**, not merely unanswered.

**Filed and then corrected in the same session, because the escape reason is the

Its own docstring predicted this failure and prescribed the fix: *"a tax

## 2026-08-26 · DEF-722 — every status gets its own colour (PO)

**Put to the PO with the collapse spelled out, not as an ID:** the account list's
coloured pill has **four** colours and BR-CUS-055 seeds **six** statuses, so two
have to share. Three options were shown with what each one costs a clerk:
**A** add a fifth colour · **B** let `Disconnected` (cut, owes money, can come
back) share red with `Closed` (moved out, finished) · **C** let `Disconnected`
share amber with `Vacation hold`.

**PO RULING, verbatim:** *"have differnt color for diff pill - you can define
colors - recommendation: A"*

**→ Option A, and the second clause is a grant: WE choose the palette.**

**WHAT IS ACTUALLY WRONG, because the fix is not "add one colour".**
`accountStatusTone` keys off the **behaviour class**, not the status —
`billable` → success, `billable_base_only` → warning, `terminal` → danger, and
everything else → neutral. There are four classes and six statuses, so the
collapse is structural: `non_billable` holds **two members that mean opposite
things** — `pending_activation` (never started) and `disconnected` (cut off,
owes money, can come back).

**So the shape of the fix, which this ruling licenses:** the pill's colour is
chosen by the **status**, with the behaviour class as the FALLBACK — because
account statuses are tenant reference data (BR-CUS-055) and a tenant can add a
seventh tomorrow. Keying only on the status code would hand every tenant-added
status the same grey, which is the failure the earlier analysis identified;
keying only on the class is what we have. Both, in that order, is the answer.

⚠ **THE SYMPTOM IS LATENT AND THAT IS NOT A REASON TO WAIT.** Nothing assigns
`Disconnected` yet — `commit_cut` writes no `accounts` column (DEF-701, open) —
so today the collapse is invisible on screen. It becomes visible the day the cut
flow starts writing that status, and a colour scheme is far cheaper to settle
before there is a screen full of them.

## 2026-08-26 · CR-036 — the write mode is chosen at stage 1 or 2, not stage 4 (PO)

**The exchange, in full, because the question shaped the answer.** The PO asked
where the re-import option lives. Told *"Stage 4 of 5 — Load. It's the step after
Validate, the one where you confirm the commit"*, they ruled:

**PO, verbatim:** *"you need at step 1 or 2 itself - this is important decision
how you will process the data and upload it"*

**AND THE REASON IS IN THE SENTENCE, so record it rather than just the
instruction: the write mode is not a confirmation, it is a PREMISE.** It decides
what the file MEANS — a load, a correction, or a replacement — and every stage
before stage 4 is already reporting against an assumption about it that the
operator was never asked to make. Two things on the PO's own screenshots prove
the point:

  · `PRM.ADDRESS_ON_FILE` — *"No premises is already on file at this address"* —
    hit **9,881 of 9,881 rows** with action **Skip on load**. Whether that is a
    problem or the expected state of an update depends entirely on the write
    mode, and stage 3 renders it without knowing.
  · The rule beside it says, in as many words, *"This premise ID is already on
    file — **the write mode decides what happens to it**"*. The screen tells the
    operator the write mode is the deciding factor at the exact moment it is
    still refusing to show it to them.

**Recorded as CR-036 (g).** It is a CHANGE, not a defect — stage 4 does what it
was specified to do — but it is a change with a defect underneath it, which is
that stage 3's verdict is computed against an unstated assumption.

## 2026-08-26 · CR-036 (a) — a date is matched against the format the utility SELECTED, and a mismatch says so (PO)

**The exchange, kept whole, because the PO ruled on a hazard they were shown
rather than on a proposal we made.** They were told:

> *"`1/1/2026` reads the same either way, but `3/4/2026` is 4 March in the US
> and 3 April almost everywhere else, and neither reading throws an error."*

**PO RULING, verbatim:** *"youa re correct - when we match the date  wehave to
compare it date format that utility has selected. the format should match
otherwise it show the error saying - you setting says this data format and you
have given differnt and it does not match"*

**→ BR-MET-117, CONFIRMED. Two clauses, and the second is half the ruling.**

**(1) THE TENANT'S DECLARED FORMAT IS THE ONLY AUTHORITY.** The importer reads
the utility's own S8 Regional setting (`tenant_settings.date_format`, BR-TEN-020,
set at provisioning) and matches the cell against THAT. It never sniffs the
string, never falls back to a locale, never tries a list of formats until one
parses. **A format that "works" is not the same as the format that was meant** —
this is the whole hazard the PO was ruling on.

**(2) A MISMATCH IS AN ERROR THAT NAMES BOTH SIDES.** The PO wrote the sentence
themselves: *"you setting says this data format and you have given differnt and
it does not match"*. So the message states the DECLARED format and the value AS
GIVEN, together, in one sentence. ⚠ **This supersedes the message the PO
actually hit**, which read *"1/1/2026 is not a date this import can read"* with
the fix *"Use YYYY-MM-DD — 2026-04-01."* That message was wrong in two ways at
once: it implied no date format works, and it named a format the tenant had not
chosen.

**Worked, on the PO's own file — Ottumwa Water Works, rejected 9,881 of 9,881
rows.** Their unit CSV runs `1/1/2026`, `1/2/2026`, `1/3/2026` … `1/10/2026`.

| Cell | Under `MM/DD/YYYY` | Under `DD/MM/YYYY` |
|---|---|---|
| `1/1/2026` | 1 Jan | 1 Jan — the ONLY row where the readings agree |
| `1/2/2026` | 2 Jan | 1 Feb |
| `1/10/2026` | 10 Jan | **1 Oct** — nine months apart |

Both readings are valid dates and **neither errors**. Both even look sensible in
context: one unit per day through January, or one unit per month across ten
months. If that column feeds a service start, the wrong reading prorates a first
bill from the wrong month on 9,881 units, and it surfaces as a customer dispute.

**What the ruling does NOT settle, recorded so nobody assumes it did:** what
happens when the tenant has selected no format at all. Provisioning defaults it,
so this should be unreachable — but "should be" is exactly the assumption this
repo keeps getting caught by. Under (1) an unset format has no authority to match
against, so the safe behaviour is to REFUSE and say so, never to pick one. That
reading is not the PO's words; it is the consequence, and it is flagged rather
than smuggled.

**AMENDED the same session — clause (3), PO verbatim:** *"or when date matching
happen at transform level - show the format - and in case any issue highlight it
there itself"*.

The declared format is **printed on the Transform stage** beside the date column,
and a value that does not match is highlighted **there**, not one stage later.

**THE PRINCIPLE IS THE SAME ONE AS THE WRITE-MODE RULING AN HOUR EARLIER, AND IT
IS WORTH NAMING ONCE RATHER THAN RE-DERIVING IT PER SCREEN: a decision, or a
contradiction, belongs at the stage where the operator can still act on it
cheaply.** The PO has now hit the alternative twice in one session — a write mode
that decides what stage 3's verdict MEANS but is not offered until stage 4, and a
date column marked **`Matched`** on stage 2 whose unreadability surfaces on stage
3 as 9,881 identical rejects.

⚠ **AND SAYING `Matched` ABOUT A COLUMN WE CANNOT ACTUALLY READ IS THE DEFECT.**
The reject list is where it surfaced, not where it happened. `Matched` today
means *"this header was recognised as this target"* and an operator reads it as
*"this column is good"*. Those are different claims, and stage 2 is currently
making the weaker one in the louder voice.

## 2026-08-26 · BR-CUS-094 left THREE guards red and nobody read any of them (lane ACCTSTALE)

**This corrects the escape story for the whole DEF-684 family, and it is the
more useful finding.** The register's version is *"no gate compares a frontend
constant against a backend vocabulary"* — true of the screens, and it is not
what happened underneath. Mapping the backend suite's failure ordinals to names
while closing DEF-684 turned up **two existing guards that fired on the day the
ruling landed and were still red two days later**:

| Guard | What it has been saying since 2026-08-24 |
|---|---|
| `tests/test_def_273_tax_conditions.py::test_def273_the_class_vocabulary_mirrors_the_platform_account_types` | *"platform account_types are ['agricultural', 'builder_developer', …] and rating mirrors ['commercial', 'government', 'industrial', 'residential']"* — **DEF-738** |
| `tests/test_cr010_reference_list_inventory.py::test_a_fresh_tenant_receives_the_measured_number_of_rows_in_every_list` | *"a seeded list changed size … Differences: {'import_mappings': (3, 4), 'account_types': (4, 8)}"* — **DEF-748** |

Both were written for exactly this event. The second even prescribes the fix in
its failure message: *"it needs the PO's word (sign-off rule 2026-08-11) and
this table updated in the same commit — not a green suite."*

**So the class-level lesson is not "we needed another gate".** It is that
**a red test on a long suite is invisible**: the backend run is measured in tens
of minutes, it already carries unrelated failures, `-q` prints failures as `F` in
a progress bar, and nobody maps an ordinal back to a name. Two guards did their
job perfectly and the information died in a scrollback.

⚠ **THE PRACTICAL RULE THIS ARGUES FOR: a ruling that changes a SIGNED
VOCABULARY must sweep the guards that MEASURE that vocabulary, not only the code
that reads it.** BR-CUS-094 swept the model, the migration and the
service-request path, and left behind a rating mirror, a seeded-row-count
inventory, a notifications audience list, a backfill tuple, an account-create
resolver and four screens. Every one of those is a copy of the vocabulary, and
two of them were already shouting.

**Neither red is this lane's to close.** DEF-748 in particular must NOT be closed
by editing the expected number — the test says a seeded list changing size needs
the PO's word, and `account_types` is signed (B2 r5 #12, superseded by
BR-CUS-094). Put the figure to the PO in plain English: **a fresh tenant's
consumer-category list goes from four rows to eight — seven selectable plus
`government` kept as legacy.**
