## 2026-08-27 · A METER NUMBER IS ALLOCATED FROM THE TENANT'S SERIES, NEVER TAKEN FROM AN UPLOADED FILE

**PO verbatim:** *"here we should not allow usse to fill in Asset ID - we have number
system set in the settings, we shoudl call that function and get unique number and assign
it"*, said of step 3.10 of the four-uploads walkthrough — the point at which a meter is
assigned to a unit.

### WHAT IS RULED

The meters import **no longer takes `asset_no` from the file**. Every imported asset gets
its number from the tenant's `asset` number series, with the per-type prefix `BR-AST-026`
already enumerates (`M-` · `SM-` · `BF-` · `PV-` · `COM-` · `EV-` · `BAT-`).

### ⚠ THIS IS NOT A COLLISION WITH A SIGNED RULE, AND I CHECKED BEFORE ASSUMING EITHER WAY

It looks like one, because `_catch_up_target_series` carries the opposite reasoning in its
own docstring — *"An import takes its number FROM the customer's file — that is the point
of an import, and `BR-TEN-035` forbids renumbering what a customer already has."*

**It is not, and the reason is that `asset_no` and `serial_no` are two different columns.**

* **`asset_no` is OUR identifier** for the device — the "meter number", already allocated
  by the tenant's series under `BR-AST-026` whenever the column was left blank.
* **`serial_no` is the MANUFACTURER'S serial**, and it is untouched by this ruling. That
  is what ties a row to the physical device on the wall.

So `BR-TEN-035`'s protection — *don't renumber what a customer already has* — is satisfied
by the serial, which the file still supplies. This ruling makes the series the **only**
path rather than the fallback, and removes the two ways a file could previously go wrong:
a number colliding with one already issued, and a number in a shape the tenant's own
settings would never produce.

**`_catch_up_target_series` becomes unnecessary on this path** — it exists solely to move
the counter past numbers a file brought with it. Its docstring must be amended rather than
left standing (hard-won law 1), and it stays for any target still taking a number from a
file.

### THE ONE CONSEQUENCE, DECIDED HERE RATHER THAN ASKED

A utility migrating from an old system usually has **its own** meter reference — not the
manufacturer's serial, the number its previous software used. Under this ruling that
cross-reference has nowhere to go and would be **lost at import**.

**Decided: assets gain an `external_ref` column**, following the precedent `customers`
already set for exactly this problem. It is not overloaded onto `serial_no`, because a
utility's own number and a manufacturer's serial are different facts and a column that
holds either is a column that means neither. Recorded as work; no question is minted,
because choosing an existing in-repo pattern over inventing one is a build judgment.

### ⚠ THE SAME QUESTION EXISTS FOR THE OTHER THREE UPLOADS AND IS NOT ANSWERED HERE

Premises, units and accounts all have numbering series too, and all three still take their
identifier from the file. **The reasoning reads across, and applying it would be widening
a scope the PO did not widen** — the exact failure this log warned lanes about earlier
today over CR-040. It is raised on the walkthrough page as one line for the PO to settle
all three, and nothing is changed for them meanwhile.

### What must change in code

`_asset_column("asset_no", …)` leaves the meters template; the auto-mapper stops offering
it; `AST.NUMBER_ON_FILE`'s *"this meter number is already on file — the write mode decides"*
warning becomes unreachable on this target and is removed rather than left as dead
vocabulary; and the dry run states the numbers it will issue rather than echoing the file's.

### ADDENDUM, SAME DAY — THE TWO THINGS `asset_no` ALSO DOES, WHICH THE RULING MUST NOT TAKE WITH IT

Reading the code before dispatching found that `asset_no` is not only the number a
new meter is given. It has **two further jobs**, and a lane deleting the column
outright would silently break both.

**1 · It is the match key for "Insert & update".** `_eval_unit_service_free`
(`import_rules.py`) compares the seat's current holder to the row's own
`asset_no`, precisely so that **re-importing a file whose meters are already
seated reads as an UPDATE of the holder rather than a second meter on the seat**.
Take the column away entirely and every correction re-run becomes a pile of
"this unit already has an active meter" rejects.

`serial_no` cannot take over the job, and this is settled by a rule rather than
by preference: **BR-AST-026 makes a duplicate serial warn-but-allow**, so it is
not unique and cannot identify a row. `asset_no` is `UNIQUE (tenant, asset_no)`.

**Decided:** the column stays in the template but **changes meaning and header**.
It is no longer *"the meter number to give this meter"* — it is *"an existing
meter number, if this row is updating a meter already in SMARTBillHub; leave it
blank for a new one."* Blank is the normal case and the only case in Insert mode;
a value in Insert mode is an error, not a number to honour. **That is the PO's
ruling exactly**: they objected to being asked to invent an ID for a meter that
does not exist yet. Quoting a number this system already issued and shows on
screen is identifying a record, not inventing one.

**2 · It is how a sub-meter names its master** (`parent_asset_no`). This one is
**unchanged and needs no work** — recorded here so that a lane does not "fix" it.
`_eval_parent_meter_on_file` already requires the master to be **on file
already** (*"Load the master first, then re-run just the rejects"*), so the number
being cited is one we issued, readable from the Assets screen. Inventing does not
arise.

**Consequence for the first migration**, stated rather than discovered later: a
utility whose old system holds both masters and subs still loads the file twice —
masters, then subs — exactly as today. The ruling does not make that worse, and
the new `external_ref` column is what lets them match their own two lists up
afterwards.

## 2026-08-27 · DEF-1549 FIXED — a one-column lookup was costing a whole screen, once per import row (`v2.76.3`)

The Product Owner's twenty-row asset import timed out on the deployed build a
**second** time, hours after `DEF-1075` shipped. That fix was real — it removed
the `ensure_reference_catalogs` N+1, 1,920 queries down to 32 — and it uncovered
a larger one standing behind it. Gunicorn logged `[CRITICAL] WORKER TIMEOUT
(pid:44)` and killed the worker mid-row; the transaction rolled back and nothing
was saved.

### The numbers, measured rather than reasoned about

Driving the PO's own file (20 rows, `unit_ref` blank on all twenty) end to end on
the test harness:

| what | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| the 20-row commit, tenant with **no** customers | **1,092** queries | **292** |
| the 20-row commit, same tenant, **12 service points** | **5,892** queries | **292** |
| extra queries **per row** bought by the customer base | **+240** | **0** |
| `service_default_uom("water")` (12-point tenant) | **281** | **1** |
| `active_account_count("water")` for 12 points | **25** | **3** |
| `services_overview()` — the S8 screen — 12 points | **281** | **61**, flat |

**The +240 per row is the whole defect.** It is multiplicative in
`rows × services × points`, so it does not appear at all on an empty tenant and
grows without bound on a real one. At the 15–20 ms round trip of a remote
database, 5,892 queries is roughly **90 seconds** — past the 60-second gunicorn
timeout, which is exactly what the PO saw. On this harness at 0.2 ms it is one
second, and every test passes.

### The mechanism

`assets._create_asset_inner` asks `seams.service_default_uom(service)` **once per
row**. That walked `service_catalog()` → `tenancy.services_overview()` — the **S8
SCREEN read** — which builds `service_row(code)` for every active catalog
service, and each of those calls `customers.active_account_count`, which issued
**two queries per service point** (`service_point_ref`: the point row, then a
separate platform-catalog probe for its code) with no cache across calls.

### ⚠ The knowledge was already in the repo, and the call site never moved

`DEF-324` (2026-08-19) diagnosed this exact mechanism one function along —
`enabled_service_codes`, which spent **47 of one provisioning request's 118
seconds** answering a one-column question with a screen payload — and built the
cure: `service_default_uoms()`, whose own docstring names the cost, *"~150
queries a call"*. What was never published was the **singular** equivalent, so
every per-row caller kept reaching through the screen. That is the durable
lesson here and it is not about either function: **a batched cure does not
retire the un-batched call site, and nothing in this repo notices the ones left
behind.**

### The three fixes, and the one that was deliberately NOT built

**1 · `tenancy.selectors.service_default_uom` — the missing singular.** One
indexed query.

**⚠ Deliberately NOT `service_default_uoms().get(code)`, and this is the
judgment worth recording.** The plural filters `enabled=True`; the walk it
replaces did **not**, because `service_row` reports the stored `primary_uom` of a
present-but-**off** `tenant_services` row (New mandate 4 gives every catalog
service a row at provisioning). A tenant who switches a service off still has
meters on it. Narrowing the lookup would have turned every one of their reads
into a silent `unit_missing` refusal — **a regression wearing a speed-up's
clothes**, and no performance check anywhere would have caught it. The one-line
fix was the wrong one. A test now pins the switched-off case.

**2 · `customers.active_account_count` batches its point lookups** through a new
`metering.selectors.service_codes_for_points` (two queries, not two per point).
**Fixed at the source rather than routed around**, because fix 1 alone would have
taken it off the *import's* path while leaving it on everyone else's: its other
callers are the **S8 services screen** (`tenancy.selectors.service_row`, once per
active service, so ~10 × 2P on every render), the **BR-TEN-026 disable guard**
(`tenancy.services`), and `reports.queries`. Any utility with a customer base was
paying that on every visit to its own settings page and nobody had measured it,
because every tenant in the test suite is empty.

**3 · A per-request memo — NOT BUILT, and the reason is a trade, not an
oversight.** `DEF-1549`'s own prevention column asks for one as a backstop, the
way `DEF-1075` memoised `ensure_reference_catalogs` in a `ContextVar`. After fix
1 it would save **19 queries out of 292** on the PO's file — about 6%. Against that: `ensure_reference_catalogs` is safe to memoise
because `BR-TEN-036` makes seeded rows undeletable, so *"the catalogs exist"*
cannot become false inside a request. **`tenant_services.primary_uom` can.** It
is written by `update_tenant_service`, by `_apply_service_toggle` in both
directions and by provisioning — and provisioning **creates those rows and then
seeds meters in the same execution context**, which is precisely the shape where
a stale empty memo would hand every seeded meter `unit = None`. Four invalidation
sites for 6% is the trade that produces the next defect. **Reported, not
silently skipped.**

### The check that comes with it — and why the one already there could not see this

`test_def1080_assets_commit_path.py` already carried a `CaptureQueriesContext`
guard whose ceiling is computed live from the seed lists, and **it passed
throughout both outages.** Two reasons, and neither is carelessness:

1. **Its ceiling is the OLD defect's arithmetic.** 96 queries per row is what a
   per-row catalogue re-seed costs. `DEF-1549` cost **55 per row** on that
   fixture — a catastrophe in production, comfortably under a ceiling drawn
   around a different mechanism. *A bound is only as good as the widest thing it
   lets through.*
2. **The fixture multiplied the explosion by zero.** Ottumwa Water Works has no
   units, no accounts and **no service points**, so `P = 0`, the quadratic term
   vanished, and the harness measured the one tenant shape in which this defect
   is invisible.

So the new guard is **differential, and has no ceiling at all**: it loads the
PO's file on a bare tenant, plants an estate, loads a second file, and asserts
the two cost the same. That states the defect exactly — *does the customer base
multiply into the per-row cost?* — and cannot be defeated by a ceiling drawn
around the wrong mechanism. Proved RED against the tip first, verbatim:

> `AssertionError: the same twenty rows cost 1092 queries on a tenant with no`
> `customers and 5892 on the same tenant with 12 service points on file —`
> `240.0 extra queries PER ROW, bought by the customer base alone.`

⚠ **One of the new guards was written wrong and caught itself**, which is worth
recording because it is the same class of error as the guard it replaces. Its
first draft compared an **empty** tenant with an **estate** tenant and demanded
almost no growth. But going from no agreements to some agreements genuinely does
cost a little more — 41 → 61 queries — because each of the ten
`active_account_count` calls now issues its batched lookup, which it skips
entirely on an empty list. That step is **O(services), paid once**; the defect is
**O(points)**. A threshold cannot tell those two shapes apart. The check now
holds the estate non-empty on both sides and only changes its **size**: triple
the service points, and the query count must not move at all.

### What this leaves behind

* `metering.seams.service_catalog()` — the S8 screen read — now has **no caller
  left in `apps/`**; `service_default_uom` was the last one. It is kept, because
  it is a published seam and B16 §4.7 makes tenancy's screen payload metering's
  to read, and its docstring now states the measured cost and lists the five
  cheap reads that answer the questions people actually bring to it.
* **`GUNICORN_TIMEOUT` was not raised.** `docker-entrypoint.sh` says in its own
  comment that raising it hides the symptom, and a 20-row import must not need
  60 seconds.
* **Still not built, and it is the prevention both `DEF-324` and this row asked
  for:** nothing in this repo measures the query count of a *read*. Both defects
  were found by a human profiling a live request after a customer complained.
  Every check written here is a per-defect assertion in a per-defect test; there
  is no gate that would notice the third one.

## 2026-08-27 · OQ-840 CLOSED BY THE PO — THE INVENTORY PATH STANDS, AND THE STATUS IT WRITES IS NAMED · plus what "Insert & update" actually does

**PO verbatim, closing it:** *"2.3 Loads to INVENTORY Ready to assign · not billable yet - sorry my bad on asset -
this is valid scenario and we should accept the meters - what status you will ahve on this meters - please confirm
that and update in the diagram"*

### 1 · `BR-AST-045` STANDS UNCHANGED. NOTHING WAS BUILT AND NOTHING IS UNDONE.

The 2026-08-22 ruling — *"If they dont provide unit, its okay, we will still accept them and later we can update
it."* — is confirmed, not superseded. **This is the whole value of having asked instead of acting**: between the
PO's *"we should not do this path"* and this correction, the only thing that happened was a question and a row in
the register. Had a lane reversed the rule on the first sentence, the 1,262-row worked case, its tests, the commit
path and the screen would all have had to come back.

`OQ-840` is closed. The meter-numbering lane was dispatched with this path explicitly out of scope, so its work is
unaffected in both directions.

### 2 · THE STATUS, CONFIRMED FROM THE CODE RATHER THAN CHOSEN

`assets/services.py:961` — `stage_code = "active" if unit_id else "inventory"`. Against `BR-AST-031`'s five seeded
lifecycle stages, that resolves to exactly two outcomes, and the Unit column alone decides which:

| the row | stage written | behavior class | can it be read / billed |
|---|---|---|---|
| **no unit** | **Inventory / Spare** | `available` | no — until somebody assigns it |
| **names a unit** | **Installed / Active** | `in_service` | yes, from the moment it loads |

**Inventory is a full record, not a half-loaded one** — searchable, editable, assignable, and the destination a
rolled-back or unassigned meter *returns* to (`rollback_from_import` → *"the physical device the utility bought
goes back on the shelf"*). That is the answer to the PO's *"what status you will ahve on this meters"*, and both
walkthrough documents now state it on the diagram itself rather than in prose beside it.

### 3 · "DOES THE LOGIC CHANGE UNDER INSERT & UPDATE?" — YES, AND MORE THAN THE QUESTION IMPLIED

**PO verbatim:** *"In Asset upload - when user select insert and update - in that case your logic remain same or
does it change?"*

It is **not the same path with an extra branch**. `update_from_import` strips `asset_no`, `type`, `unit_id` and
every member of `BILLING_AFFECTING_FIELDS`, so a matched row skips the entire create decision tree:

* **no number is issued** — it already has one, which is why the numbering ruling does not reach this path;
* **the Unit column is ignored** — *"never moves the asset (its unit is the reassign flow's, not a file's)"*. A
  matched row therefore cannot be rejected for an occupied seat either: it is not asking for one;
* **billing facts are untouched** — a spreadsheet may not silently change what a meter charges for;
* **the status is untouched** — an update never moves a meter between Inventory and Installed;
* **spec fields only** change: make, model, install date, certification due, meter type, read method.

An unmatched row in that mode is simply a new meter and takes the full path. In **Insert new only**, a row naming
an existing meter is reported and not loaded — an error there, not an update.

**Why this belongs in the log rather than only in a diagram:** the write-mode fork was the FIRST decision in the
flow and neither walkthrough drew it, so every reader of those documents — the PO included — was shown a single
path and reasonably assumed the mode only widened it. The fork is now step 2.2 / 3.2, ahead of the numbering step.

### 4 · Documents updated the same turn

`asset-import-flow.html` renumbered 2.1 – 2.12; `four-imports.html`'s meter section renumbered 3.1 – 3.12. Both
carry the fork, the allocation step, and the two statuses on the diagram nodes.

### 5 · AND THE PO CORRECTED THE ORDER, WHICH WAS A REAL DEFECT IN THE DRAWING

**PO verbatim:** *"these decisiona should be taken just before updating teh record in the database - 2.4 The meter
number is ALLOCATED from your numbering settings not taken from the file - you ahve taken 2.3 and 2.4 way early in
the process - please udpate html document"*

**They are right, and the code already agrees with them** — the drawing was wrong, not the build. Allocation happens
inside `create_from_import` → `_create_asset_inner`, which runs in the **load** stage, inside the commit
transaction; `update_from_import` likewise. Both walkthroughs had drawn them as the *first* thing that happens to a
row, which reads as *"the number is issued when the file is read"*.

**Why the order matters and is not presentation:** a number issued before a row is known to be good is a number
**burned by a row that never loads**. The series would show gaps nobody can account for, and the gaps would grow
every time an operator re-ran a file to clear rejects. Because allocation sits inside the commit transaction, a
rollback takes the counter back with it and no number is spent — which is the same fact `DEF-577`'s
`_catch_up_target_series` comment already states from the other side (*"a run that rolls back must not leave the
counter moved for numbers it did not write"*).

Both diagrams are restructured around an explicit **COMMIT band**: every decision above it writes nothing; the
number is issued below it, as the row is saved. Steps are now 2.1 – 2.17 and 3.1 – 3.17.

**The lesson, recorded because it is general:** a walkthrough that draws a *decision* and a *write* as adjacent
steps in one line teaches the reader that they happen together. Where a five-stage pipeline's whole promise is
*"nothing is written until you commit at stage four"*, the drawing must show that line, or it quietly contradicts
the promise the same document makes two sections earlier.

## 2026-08-27 · BR-AST-049 IS BUILT — THE METER NUMBER IS ISSUED, THE UTILITY'S OWN NUMBER GETS A COLUMN, AND FIVE THINGS THE RULING DID NOT SETTLE ARE DECIDED HERE

This is the build of the ruling recorded above (*A METER NUMBER IS ALLOCATED FROM THE
TENANT'S SERIES, NEVER TAKEN FROM AN UPLOADED FILE* + its ADDENDUM) and of OQ-840's
same-day confirmations. Nothing in those entries was re-decided. What follows is the
five judgments they left to the lane, each with the figure it was decided on, plus
**one finding that CONTRADICTS the ruling's own premise** and had to be fixed for the
ruling to be true.

### ⚠ 0 · THE CONTRADICTION, FIRST, BECAUSE IT IS THE ONE THAT MATTERED

The ruling's safety argument is: *"`serial_no` is the MANUFACTURER'S serial, and it is
untouched by this ruling. That is what ties a row to the physical device on the wall …
So BR-TEN-035's protection — don't renumber what a customer already has — is satisfied
by the serial, which the file still supplies."*

**The file did not supply it. `serial_no` was not a column on any of the three assets
import targets.** It exists on the model and on the AST-05 form, and the import simply
never offered it — so a migration of 1,847 meters landed 1,847 rows whose only tie to a
physical device was a number we had just decided to stop reading. Taking `asset_no` off
the file without adding `serial_no` would have removed the LAST identifier the operator
controls.

`SERIAL_NO` is now a column on all three assets targets, with the header aliases
(`serial`, `serial no`, `serial #`, `device id`) a real export uses. **This is
implementing the ruling, not widening it** — the ruling asserts the column is there.

### 1 · `external_ref` IS UNIQUE PER TENANT — DECIDED YES, AND IT IS THEREFORE A MATCH KEY

`uq_assets_tenant_external_ref_ci`: `UNIQUE (tenant, lower(external_ref))`, PARTIAL on
`external_ref IS NOT NULL`, exactly `customers.external_ref`'s posture (BR-CUS-054).

**The worked figure that decided it.** A utility loads 1,847 meters. Blank `asset_no`
throughout, so we issue `M-00001 … M-01847`. They then find twelve rows with the wrong
multiplier and re-cut the same file. Their file holds no SMARTBillHub number — it never
did — so under number-only matching every one of the 1,847 rows reads as NEW:

* **without a unique legacy key:** 1,847 second assets, numbered `M-01848 … M-03694`,
  and no way to tell the two sets apart. Every seated row would in fact be stopped by
  `AST.UNIT_SERVICE_FREE` (*"this unit already has an active water meter"*) — 1,847
  rejects on a corrected file, which is the exact pile the ruling's ADDENDUM warns a
  lane about, arriving through a different rule.
* **with it:** 1,847 matches, 12 spec updates, 1,835 no-ops. Nothing duplicated.

So the column is unique, and `_key_of` falls back to it: `asset_no` first (an operator
quoting OUR number is naming a specific record), `external_ref` second. The two key
spaces are **namespaced** in one dict — `ext:<lowered ref>` — so a legacy string reading
`M-9001` can never silently address our own `M-9001`.

**`serial_no` could not take this job and that is settled by a rule, not a preference:**
BR-AST-033 makes a duplicate serial *warn-but-allow*, so it is not unique, and a
non-unique column cannot identify a row.

### 2 · `AST.NUMBER_ON_FILE` IS AMENDED **AND** A SECOND RULE IS ADDED — the question the dispatch asked

**The existing rule cannot carry the new error, and the reason is structural rather
than stylistic: the new error is the OPPOSITE PREDICATE, and the half the ruling
describes is one stage 3 cannot see.**

* Stage 3 **does not know the write mode** (DEF-543, and the mode is still changeable at
  stage 4). So *"a value in Insert mode is an error"* cannot be a stage-3 rule at all.
* `AST.NUMBER_ON_FILE` fires when a number **IS** on file. The ruling's new error is
  about a number that is **NOT** — an invented one. One rule cannot say both.

So, three pieces:

| where | what | severity |
|---|---|---|
| `AST.NUMBER_ON_FILE` (amended sentence) | *"This meter number names one already on file. Insert & update will update that meter; Insert new only cannot use it, because a new meter's number comes from your numbering settings."* | WARNING — unchanged, DEF-543 |
| `AST.NUMBER_NOT_ON_FILE` (**new**) | *"A meter number is issued by your numbering settings — leave this column blank for a new one."* | **ERROR / reject row** — mode-independent, so it can block |
| `_insert_mode_on_file_sentences` (dry run + load) | the mode-dependent half, where the mode is actually known | row outcome, never a run refusal |

The last row is deliberate: **1,846 good rows beside one bad one must still load.** A
run-level refusal would make the operator's fix *"cut the file again"* rather than
*"clear one cell"*.

⚠ **AND THE INSERT-MODE SENTENCE FORKS ON WHICH KEY MATCHED**, which the ruling did not
foresee because the second key did not exist when it was written. A match on a QUOTED
NUMBER is the operator's error and gets the numbering sentence. A match on
`external_ref` is the ordinary re-run — they supplied their own id exactly as the
template asks — and gets the ordinary *"already on file, use Insert & update"*.

### 3 · THE HEADER ALIASES MOVE FROM `asset_no` TO `external_ref`

`METER_NO` · `METER NO` · `METER #` · `METER NUMBER` · `SUB_METER_NO` · `DEVICE_NO`
were `asset_no`'s aliases. On a first-migration file every cell under those headers is
the OLD system's number — which is now precisely what `asset_no` refuses. Left where
they were, the product's own auto-mapper would have produced **1,847 identical
`AST.NUMBER_NOT_ON_FILE` errors on a file it mapped itself**.

`asset_no` keeps its own field name and its LABEL (`_auto_map`'s second pass), so the
shipped sample still maps itself — `test_def616__every_shipped_sample_maps_itself`
holds. That is what *"the auto-mapper stops offering it"* means in practice: no header a
utility would plausibly ship claims it any more, and an operator updating existing
meters maps it by hand, deliberately, which is the only case it is now for.

### 4 · THE DEDUPE KEY MOVES TOO, BECAUSE THE ALTERNATIVE WAS A DEAD CONTROL

`DEDUPE_KEY_BY_TARGET` keyed the three assets targets on `asset_no`. Under the ruling
`asset_no` is blank on every row of a normal file, so *"keep the latest row when a key
appears twice"* would have kept its checkbox, its sentence and its counter and matched
**nothing, ever** — hard-won law 2's exact shape. It keys on `external_ref` now, which
is the identifier a duplicated row in a migration file actually repeats, and which is
unique per tenant. `AST.EXTERNAL_REF_UNIQUE` (ERROR, in-file only) catches the pair when
the operator has NOT ticked the box, so the database's own refusal can never abort a
1,847-row commit over one duplicated cell.

### 5 · THE DRY RUN PROJECTS THE NUMBERS — IT DOES NOT ALLOCATE THEM

The ruling's last clause: *"the dry run states the numbers it will issue rather than
echoing the file's."* `will_issue` carries `{series_format, next_number, count, numbers
(first 5), last}`.

**It is a PEEK.** `assets.selectors.asset_no_preview_run` walks BE-06's `preview`
contract (*"validates + renders only, allocates nothing"*) by an OFFSET rather than
calling `next_number` N times. That is not a convenience — the PO ruled the same day
that allocation belongs inside the commit (*"these decisiona should be taken just before
updating teh record in the database"*), and a rehearsal is allowed to be run twice: N
allocations per rehearsal would burn numbers on rows that never load.

**PER ROW, IN ROW ORDER, because the prefix is per TYPE while the sequence is shared**
(BR-AST-026). A devices file of a backflow then a PV inverter takes `BF-00042` then
`PV-00043` off one counter; a single prefix for the run would print numbers nobody gets.
Only CREATING rows are counted — a matched row consumes none, and counting one for it
would shift every number after it by one.

**Absent, not zeroed, when the tenant has no `asset` series row**, so the screen says
*"your numbering is not set up"* rather than printing an invented range.

⚠ **ONE STATED LIMIT.** A CR-005 restart period rolls the counter back to 1 when the
period turns, so a rehearsal on the last day of a period can name numbers a commit on
the next day would not use. `asset_no_preview` has had the same limit since AST-W4 and
this inherits it deliberately rather than modelling a second, divergent answer.

### 6 · WHAT NAMES THE STATUS (OQ-840's ask), AND WHY NO NEW FIGURE WAS ADDED

OQ-840 asks that a preview reporting what it will write should name the stage. The
rehearsal already carries `will_create_in_service` and `will_create_to_inventory`
(DEF-1079) and **those two figures ARE the stage split** — `stage_code = "active" if
unit_id else "inventory"`. A third figure restating it would be a second source of truth
for one fact, which BR-REP-002's instinct forbids and which is how two counters come
apart. The screen labels them with the stage names; the engine keeps one derivation.

### 7 · WHAT WAS DELIBERATELY NOT TOUCHED

* **Premises, units and accounts** still take their identifier from the file. The
  reasoning reads across and applying it would widen a scope the PO did not widen.
* **`BR-AST-045`, the blank-unit → inventory path** — confirmed by OQ-840 the same day.
* **`parent_asset_no`** — unchanged, per the ADDENDUM, and stated here so no later lane
  "fixes" it.
* **`_catch_up_target_series` STAYS.** Its docstring carried the ruling's exact opposite
  (*"An import takes its number FROM the customer's file — that is the point of an
  import"*) and is amended (hard-won law 1); the function itself is still needed by the
  three targets that DO take numbers from files, and on the assets targets it is a no-op
  by arithmetic rather than by deletion, so removing it would silently re-open DEF-577
  the day anything there writes a number of its own again.

## 2026-08-27 · THE METER IMPORT'S SPINE, RE-ORDERED BY THE PO — the unit questions first, the meter's identity last, and "reject" where the rule said "warn"

**PO verbatim:** *"2.1 A meter row arrives -> 2.6 Is the Unit column filled in? -> 2.8 Does it match a unit already
on file? -> 2.10 Does that unit already have an active meter for this service? 2.12 Marked for the UNIT - 2.2 Does
this row name a meter already on file? if yes - ( in case of insert - reject it | in case of Insert & Update =
update the details), if no ( generate new meter number using settings -> numbers for meter), assing this unquie
number and upload the record - this is happy path and you can build rest of the flow around this"*

### 1 · THE ORDER IS THEIRS AND IT IS BETTER THAN OURS — and it matches the code more closely than our drawing did

We had drawn the meter's identity question FIRST and the unit questions after it. The PO inverted it: **seat the row
first, then ask what meter it is, then write.** Both walkthroughs are rebuilt on that spine (2.1 – 2.16 and
3.1 – 3.16), with the happy path drawn as a single green line and every rejection hung off it as a branch.

**Why theirs is right, and it is not taste.** `_eval_unit_service_free` already contains the special case that only
makes sense in this order: *"the seat's holder is this row's own meter — a re-import of a file whose meters are
already seated is an UPDATE of the holder, not a second meter on the seat."* The seat check runs for **every** row,
matched or not, and exempts the row's own meter. Under our ordering that exemption looked like a special case
bolted on; under the PO's it is simply what step 2.6 does. The diagram now labels both edges out of it —
*"yes — a DIFFERENT meter"* rejects, *"no — or it is THIS meter"* proceeds.

### 2 · THE ONE SUBSTANTIVE CHANGE: **"in case of insert - reject it"**

Today `asset_no_on_file` is a **WARNING** whose text is *"this meter number is already on file — the write mode
decides."* The PO has now decided it, and the decision is not a warning:

| write mode | a row naming a meter already on file |
|---|---|
| **Insert new only** | **ROW REJECTED** — "this meter already exists" |
| **Insert & update** | its **details are updated** |

That is a rule change, not a re-wording, and it is the numbering lane's to build: the same column that used to
carry a number for a new meter now does exactly one job — routing a row between *reject* and *update*. A blank
column is the normal case and always means "a new meter."

### 3 · WHAT THE PO'S WORDING SETTLES THAT OURS LEFT VAGUE

*"generate new meter number using settings -> numbers for meter"* — the diagram now names the setting by the path a
person clicks (**Settings › Numbers › Meter**) rather than by a rule id. Standing PO instruction: rules are put to
them in plain English, never as an ID to go and look up. The same instruction applies to what we draw.

*"assing this unquie number and upload the record"* — generation and assignment are drawn as two steps inside one
write box, because that is the guarantee worth showing: nothing above the box has changed anything, and if the
commit rolls back the counter rolls back with it.

### 4 · The lesson, which is the second time today the same one landed

**The PO corrected the same document twice — first on WHERE the write sits, now on WHAT ORDER the questions come
in — and both times the code was right and the drawing was wrong.** A walkthrough is not a decoration of the build;
a reader who cannot see the build reasons from the picture, and a picture that orders the questions differently
teaches a different product. The way to catch this without the PO's time is to read the drawing back against the
function that implements it, in order, before publishing.

## 2026-08-27 · OQ-790 CLOSED BY THE PO — the premises import CREATES the owner's master account, with a number from Settings › Numbering

**PO verbatim:** *"here 2.6 Marked, and waits for matching Flagged, not rejected - first time when we are
uploading premises and activating Tenant/utility at that time master account is not created; so in such case
you ahev to call master account creation logic by passing the details and generate account number using
Setting -> numbering and use this number to write premsies - you will have to udpaste your logic in html
diagram"*

### WHAT IS RULED — option (c), and the PO named the mechanism, not just the outcome

`OQ-790` offered four shapes. The PO chose **(c) MASTER IMMEDIATELY**, and specified how:

1. The premises import **calls the master-account creation logic**, passing the details the row carries.
2. The account number comes from the **`account` series in Settings › Numbering**.
3. That account is linked to the premises **in the same write**.

`ensure_owner_master_account`'s `NotImplementedError("OQ-790")` is the stub this closes. **The reasoning the
PO gave is the part worth keeping:** at first activation *nothing is on file*, so the "waits for matching"
state we shipped is not a rare edge — **on a first upload it is EVERY row**. A migration would land a
complete address book where not one address could be charged.

### ⚠ THE COLLISION WITH `OQ-500`, STATED RATHER THAN ASSUMED — because a supersession must be written down

`OQ-790` recorded that (c) *"contradicts the single-family ruling for every owner-occupier"*. Closing
`OQ-500` the same day, the PO ruled *"(b) — an owner-occupier"*, from which this log records that
master-ness is **"derived from whether anyone else occupies the premises, not chosen at creation"**.

**The reading taken, and it is a judgment rather than a re-ask (law 13):** the two rulings answer *different
questions*, and only one of them is about the owner.

* `OQ-500` decides **what shape an owner-occupier's own service account takes** — one regular account, not a
  master with a child pointing at itself.
* This ruling decides **when the party who OWNS an address acquires an account at all**, on a path where no
  occupancy exists yet to derive anything from.

The premises owner being a master account is separately CONFIRMED — the PO ruled it and then re-confirmed it
when a lane re-asked (*"this is repeat - I already confirmed"*). So creating a master here follows the
owner-side ruling and leaves the occupant-side derivation untouched.

**The consequence is stated plainly rather than buried, and it is the PO's to reverse:** a single-family
owner-occupier imported through this path acquires a **master** account at premises load, where
`OQ-500`'s derivation would have given them one regular account once occupancy became knowable. Nothing about
that is silent — it shows on the account, and it is one line to reverse if it matters.

### THE THIRD OBSTACLE IS ENGINEERING, NOT A QUESTION

`OQ-790` measured it: `create_master_account` attaches through the premises' **common-area units**, and a
brand-new premises has **no units at all**. That is a real blocker for a literal implementation and it is not
a reason to go back to the PO — it is the work. The creation path must anchor a master on the **premises**
rather than on a unit that does not exist yet. Recorded as work, with the measurement, so the lane building it
does not rediscover it as a surprise.

### WHAT THE LANE MUST CONFIRM RATHER THAN INVENT

**The owner's CATEGORY.** A seed lane learned this the hard way earlier today — its own test said *"A category
is a claim about a real party"* and failed a placeholder that invented one. If the premises template carries no
owner-category column, the created account must take a category the row actually states or a lawful "not
stated" — **never a guessed `landlord`**.

### The document is updated

`The Premises Upload` walkthrough now shows it: step **2.7** marks a new owner, step **2.12** creates the
master account with its number from Settings › Numbers › Account, and the happy path drawn in green is the
first-upload case — because on a first upload that IS the common path. The old *"loads and waits for
matching"* outcome is gone from the diagram and from the rule table.

## 2026-08-27 · AN EMPTY OWNER COLUMN LOADS THE PREMISES — `BR-MET-401` NARROWED TO THE SCREEN, NOT REVERSED

**PO verbatim:** *"in premises - 2.4 Does the owner name match a party already on file? what if owner column
is empty - in such case we create the premises and keep owner name empty - we cna edit and updaste it later
- updsate your diagram and add 4th flow after 2.4"*

### ⚠ THIS CONTRADICTS THE PO'S OWN DECISION 1 FROM EARLIER THE SAME DAY, AND THE SUPERSESSION IS STATED RATHER THAN ASSUMED

`BR-MET-401` exists because of this, verbatim: *"when presmies are created you have owner for it, without
owner how you can create premsies = owner = master account"*. It was built today, it is tested, and roughly
614 tests went red on the branch while it landed. **A second lane must not discover this contradiction by
tripping over it**, so it is written down here in full.

### THE READING TAKEN — a NARROWING, and it is minimal rather than convenient

**`BR-MET-401` stands for the premises CREATE SCREEN. The import accepts a blank owner and flags it.**

Three reasons this is the smaller change rather than a reversal:

1. **The two statements are about different acts.** Decision 1 answers *"how can you create a premises with
   no owner"* — asked of a clerk filling in a form, who knows the answer or can find it. Today's is asked of a
   **column in a spreadsheet**, of which the PO's own words are *"we cna edit and updaste it later"*.
2. **`BR-MET-401` ALREADY distinguishes contexts**, and for the same reason: *"THE REFUSAL IS ON CREATE ONLY,
   AND THAT IS NOT A LOOPHOLE"* — because a required field on update would make a ten-year-old address
   unsaveable. Import-create is a third context with the identical problem at a different scale.
3. **The measured consequence of the wider reading.** A migration is thousands of rows and half the owner
   answers are in a filing cabinet. Refusing those rows means a utility **cannot load its own address book
   until it finishes a research project** — and the addresses it cannot load are the ones its meters and
   accounts then cannot name either, because everything downstream resolves a premises.

**Stated for the PO to widen in one line if they meant the screen too**, which is the whole point of writing
it down rather than quietly picking.

### WHAT A BLANK OWNER COSTS, AND IT IS NOT NOTHING

No owner → **no master account** → that address has nobody to charge. It is a real premises: it holds units,
it holds meters, it can be read. It cannot be billed until somebody fills the owner in. The existing
`unmatched_premises_qs()` worklist is where those rows already surface, so the flagging half of this needs no
new machinery — which is the tell that the narrowing fits the build rather than fighting it.

### THE FOUR ANSWERS, now, and there is no fifth

⛔ **AMENDED 2026-08-31 BY CR-055 — ROW TWO NO LONGER SAYS *ROW REJECTED*, AND ITS LABEL WAS WRONG AS WELL AS
ITS OUTCOME.** The original table is kept below with the superseded cell struck through rather than deleted,
because the PO read this table's words on the published premises-upload picture and a reader arriving at
either has to be able to see that it moved.

| The Owner column | What happens |
|---|---|
| **empty** | The premises loads with **no owner**, flagged to be filled in later |
| **the name matches two or more existing owner records** *(the branch drawn as "several look alike" — see the correction below)* | ~~**ROW REJECTED** — the clerk says which; merging two landlords bills the wrong one~~ → **SUPERSEDED 2026-08-31 (CR-055): the premises LOADS WITH NO OWNER, flagged, exactly as the empty case does. The clerk still says which — merging two landlords still bills the wrong one, and the import still picks nothing — but refusing to choose no longer costs the operator the address.** |
| **one exact match** | That party is reused whole, with the account it already has. No second account |
| **no match** | A new party, and its **master account is created** with a number from Settings › Numbers › Account (`OQ-790`) |

### ⚠ THE BRANCH LABEL WAS THE DEFECT — *"several look alike"* NAMES THE WRONG THING (CR-055 task 4)

**Corrected wording, for the picture and for this table:** the branch reads **"the name matches two or more
existing owner records"**, and box 2.6 reads **LOADS WITH NO OWNER — FLAGGED**, never *ROW REJECTED*.

*"Several look alike"* reads naturally as *"several PREMISES name this owner"*, and that is exactly how the
PO read it on 2026-08-31: *"we need to allow 2.6 - owner can have multiple premises ownership"*. One owner
holding many premises is not merely allowed — it is the designed path, it is `Premises.owner`'s ordinary FK
with no cap, and box **2.7** (one exact match) is where those rows go. Box 2.6 was never about multiple
ownership at all; it is about **two or more OWNER RECORDS whose names collapse onto one search key**
(`_normalise_owner_name`: *Ridge Property LLC* and *Ridge Property, L.L.C.*).

⚠ **THE PUBLISHED PICTURE STILL CARRIES THE OLD WORDS.** The premises-upload page — CR-039 wave G, G1 — is

`resolve_owner_name`'s three answers become four. The document's step 2.4 now asks *"does the Owner column

## 2026-08-27 · THE UNIT UPLOAD — the premises is the only gate, the identity is the PAIR, and services are inherited by reference

**PO verbatim, two messages:**

> *"in -> What happens when you upload a unit file -> 2.1 A unit row arrives -> 2.4 Is the parent premises
> already on file? - this is the happy path - why you need unit label - unit lable you can use in - 2.13 On
> file — meters and accounts can now name it; also 2.7 Does this row name a unit that is already on file?
> premsies and unit name - not just unit name that combination is unique - updaet the diagram"*

> *"also in unit upload - 2.13 On file — meters and accounts can now name it - will you inherit Utility
> services from premises and assign them to Unit - or it is implied and no new changes required"*

### 1 · THE LABEL COMES OFF THE SPINE — a field check is not a decision

The label was drawn as the FIRST question the flow turns on. It is not one. **The only question a unit row
genuinely turns on is whether its parent premises exists**, because that is the one thing the import will not
create and the one thing there is no way to fix from inside the file.

The label **remains required**, and the reason is now stated rather than assumed: it is **half of what
identifies the unit**. It is caught as a field problem, alongside "every value has to be the kind of value its
column holds" — which is likewise not drawn, for the same reason. The spine is 2.1 – 2.11 now, not 2.1 – 2.13.

**Why the PO was right and the drawing was wrong**, generalised: a walkthrough that draws every validation as
a step teaches the reader that all refusals are equal. They are not — one of them means *go and load another
file first*, and the rest mean *fix this cell*.

### 2 · THE IDENTITY IS `premises + label`, NEVER THE LABEL ALONE — and this one is a correctness bug, not a drawing

**PO:** *"premsies and unit name - not just unit name that combination is unique"*.

Two buildings can each hold an `Apt 3B`. Matching on the label alone would find the wrong building's flat —
and in **Insert & update** it would **quietly overwrite it**. The premises is resolved first (2.2), so the pair
is only ever asked about once the address is known, which is what makes the pair cheap to match on.

**This raises a rule from WARNING to ERROR.** *"Unit label is unique within its premises"* was flag-only. It
is the identity key now: a second `Apt 3B` at one address is not a warning, it is two rows claiming to be the
same unit.

### 3 · SERVICES ARE INHERITED BY REFERENCE — implied, and NO CHANGE IS REQUIRED

The PO asked the right question and the answer is the good one, verified in code rather than assumed:

* **`Unit` has no services column.** `unit_detail_dict` and `unit_list_dict` serve
  `unit.premises.services_available`, **copied on read** so a caller cannot mutate the premises through a unit
  payload (`DEF-755`).
* **It is enforced in the other direction too:** adding a service to a unit validates against the premises'
  list and refuses when it is not offered, naming the **premises** in the refusal because that is where the
  answer must be fixed.

**Nothing is copied at import and nothing should be.** One source of truth means adding a service to an
address next year gives every unit in it that service immediately — no re-import, and no way for a unit and
its own address to disagree about what can be sold there. Copying would create exactly that drift.

**The migration hazard, stated because it is invisible otherwise:** a premises loaded with its services column
empty offers **nothing**, so every unit under it refuses every service. The symptom appears two uploads later,
when meters are rejected for a service the utility plainly does sell — and the fix is on the premises, not on
the unit or the meter. Both walkthrough pages now say so.

## 2026-08-27 · THE UNIT SPINE, FINAL — the plan is a step, and `premises + issued number` is checked immediately before the write

**PO verbatim:** *"in unit upload - 2.1 A unit row arrives -> 2.2 Is the parent premises already on file? ->
2.4 Marked for that premises -> then you need to check whether plan ID or Plan lable -> if plan yes -> 2.9 A
NEW UNIT NUMBER is generated Settings › Numbers › Unit -> then premises + New Unit ID = Unique -> if yes then
write it - this is the happy flow"*

### 1 · THE PLAN BECOMES A STEP, AND IT IS RESOLVED BY **ID OR LABEL**

*"whether plan ID or Plan lable"* — the file may name a plan **either way**, and both resolve to the same
plan. That matters more than it looks: **it means nobody has to look up an ID to write an import file.**
Staff know their plans by name.

**It does not become a gate.** A missing or unrecognised plan still loads the unit **unplanned** and flags it.
The asymmetry is the whole character of this upload and is now drawn rather than described: *the address is
structure, the plan is pricing.* A unit with no plan is a real flat you can price tomorrow; a unit with no
premises is a flat in a building that does not exist.

### 2 · TWO DIFFERENT UNIQUENESS CHECKS, AND CONFLATING THEM WOULD BE A BUG

The PO has now specified both, in two messages, and they are **not the same check**:

| | Asked at | On | Answers |
|---|---|---|---|
| **`premises + label`** | before the write mode fork | the file's own words | *is this row an existing unit?* — the match key |
| **`premises + issued number`** | immediately before the write | the number just issued | *can this row be written safely?* — the last guard |

**The second is not redundant with the series**, and the reason is worth stating so nobody deletes it as
belt-and-braces. The series guarantees a number unique across the tenant *at issue*. It cannot speak for a
series that was renumbered or reset, for numbers assigned by hand on the screen, or for two runs racing on one
address. **A number already in use at that premises is a unit two things could point at** — and a meter or an
account pointing at the wrong flat surfaces as a wrong bill, months later, with nothing in the record to say
why.

### 3 · WHAT THE FINAL SPINE IS

`2.1` row arrives → `2.2` **is the parent premises on file?** (the only true gate) → `2.4` marked for it →
`2.5` **plan by ID or label?** → `2.7` resolved, or `2.6` unplanned and flagged → `2.8` **does this
premises + label pair exist?** → `2.9` write mode decides (reject on insert · update on insert & update) →
**the write:** `2.12` number issued from Settings › Numbers › Unit → `2.13` **premises + number confirmed
unique** → `2.14` written → `2.15` on file.

**Three PO messages shaped this one diagram**, each removing something we had drawn as important and adding
something that actually was. The pattern across all three: **we drew field validations as decisions and drew
real decisions not at all.** That is the review to run on the other three pages before the PO has to.

## 2026-08-27 · SUB-METERS ARE ALREADY THEIR OWN UPLOAD — confirmed · and the numbering ruling BROKE how a sub names its master, which is fixed here

**PO verbatim:** *"asset logic is applciable to meters and devices - what are we going to do with sub meters ;
can you draw seperate diagram for sub mters and does that mean when we upload the assets we have to select
meters, sub mters, behind the meter and investor on step 1 - please confirm that"*

### 1 · CONFIRMED, AND IT ALREADY WORKS THAT WAY — the kind is chosen at step 1

`import_runs.TARGETS` already holds six: `premises` · `units` · **`assets_meters`** · **`assets_submeters`** ·
**`assets_devices`** · `accounts`. Each has its own column set, its own rule set, its own default mapping and
its own downloadable sample. **Nothing has to be built for this**; the answer is *yes, and it is already true.*

**⚠ ONE CORRECTION, and it matters because it would have become a fourth template nobody needs.** The PO's
list ends *"and investor"* — the fourth thing is **inventory**, and **inventory is a STATUS, not a KIND.** It
is where any of the three asset kinds lands when its Unit column is left blank. There is no inventory target
to choose and there must not be one. Stated on the sub-meter page as its own callout, because the same
misreading is available to anyone looking at the S49 tabs.

### 2 · THE REAL FINDING: THE NUMBERING RULING BROKE THE SUB-METER MIGRATION, SILENTLY

`_eval_parent_meter_on_file` resolves `parent_asset_no` against `world.asset_index`, which is keyed by
**lowered asset number** and nothing else. That was correct while a file supplied its own meter numbers.

**It is no longer correct.** Under the 2026-08-27 ruling, a master's number is **issued by us at import**. So
on a first migration:

1. the utility loads its masters, and we give each one a number **it has never seen**;
2. its sub-meter file names those masters by **its old system's** identifiers;
3. **every sub-meter row rejects** — *"Parent meter X was not loaded"* — for masters that were, in fact,
   loaded a minute earlier.

The only way through would be to load the masters, export the receipt, transcribe our numbers back into the
sub file, and re-upload. **That is not a migration path; it is a punishment.** Nothing in the meter ruling
anticipated it, and no gate would have caught it — the rule works exactly as written.

### 3 · DECIDED HERE, NOT ASKED — the master may be named THREE ways

Following the precedent `unit_ref` already sets on this very import (*"the unit's NUMBER, or the premises and
the unit together, or just the unit label"*), the parent reference resolves in order:

1. the master's **meter number** — for masters already on file before this run;
2. the master's **serial number** — what is stamped on the device;
3. the utility's **external reference** — the number its old system used.

**The last two are the ones a first migration actually holds**, which is the whole point. This is a build
judgment on an existing in-repo pattern rather than a new rule, so no question is minted — but it IS work,
and it is work the meter ruling created rather than work the sub-meter target was missing.

⚠ **A caveat the lane must handle rather than discover:** `serial_no` is **warn-but-allow duplicate**
(`BR-AST-033`), so it is not unique. A serial that matches two masters must **reject with "which one"**, never
resolve to the first. `external_ref` is unique and has no such problem.

### 4 · WHAT IS GENUINELY DIFFERENT ABOUT A SUB-METER, for the record

It is the meter flow with a **master block in front**: `ASSETS_SUBMETERS_RULES` is
`_assets_common` + `_assets_meter_rules` + three of its own (`AST.PARENT_ON_FILE` error,
`AST.ALLOC_WITHIN_MASTER` warning, `AST.UNIT_PREMISES_MATCHES_MASTER` warning).

**The one asymmetry worth stating in prose:** the Unit column may be blank — a sub-meter bought and not yet
installed is real — but the **master may never be**. *A sub-meter with no master is not in inventory; it is
nothing*: a device that measures a share of something, with no something.

**And an update must not re-hang a sub on a different master**, for the same reason it must not move a meter
between units: it changes what a bill is calculated from, and a spreadsheet is not where that is decided.

### 5 · The page

`The Sub-Meter Upload` — https://claude.ai/code/artifact/f292c167-7aeb-4fc7-b7cf-2b7cd1706c25 — steps
2.1 – 2.21, five rejections, the most of any of the six.

## 2026-08-27 · CR-046 WAVES B · C1 · D · F ARE BUILT — and wave B was NOT the field-read it looked like

Waves A and the ruling behind it are recorded above ("BR-AST-049 IS BUILT"). This is the
rest of the lane's scope, plus **three findings a reader needs and one correction to a
judgment this lane had already made**.

### ⚠ 1 · WAVE B'S PREMISE WAS HALF TRUE, AND THE OTHER HALF IS WHY `DEF-543` SURVIVED

CR-046 wave B says: *"`DEF-543` reasoned that an on-file number must WARN because 'the
write mode decides, and stage 3 does not know it'. That is no longer true. `CR-042` moved
the write-mode choice from step 4 to step 1, and stage 3 runs after step 1."*

**The CONTROL moved. The VALUE did not.** Measured before building anything:

* `ImportRun.write_mode` is declared, verbatim, `# IMPORT_WRITE_MODES — stage 4 only`,
  and is written in exactly two places, both inside the loaders.
* `extract()` never set it. `validate()` never read it.
* The client sent `write_mode` with `/dry-run` and `/load` **and with nothing else** —
  `validateImport` posted `{}`.

So at the moment stage 3 judged every row, the server did not know the mode, and
`DEF-543`'s sentence was still **literally true** — for a different reason than the one it
gave. That is worth recording rather than quietly fixing: a constraint outlived its cause
by five days, and the reason nobody noticed is that the two changes were read separately
and each was correct on its own.

**What was built:** `extract` records it, `validate` re-records it (stage 4's *Change it*
walks back to step 1 — DEF-770 — so a run can be judged more than once), `World.write_mode`
carries it, and `import_rules.resolve()` re-declares `AST.NUMBER_ON_FILE` per mode. The
client sends it at both stages; a server field no caller populates is dead UI (law 2).

**⚠ ABSENT IS NOT `insert`, AND THAT IS A DECISION.** A run extracted before this landed,
or by any other client, has `write_mode = NULL`, and the rule then keeps its pre-CR-046
warning. Defaulting an unstated mode to `insert` would make the mode that **rejects rows**
the one that arrives by silence — hard-won law 3, and DEF-127's rule that an absence must
not be spelled the same way as a value.

### 2 · ONE RULE CODE, TWO SEVERITIES — and the generic sentence retires

PO verbatim: *"Does this row name a meter already on file? if yes - ( in case of insert -
reject it | in case of Insert & Update = update the details)"*.

`AST.NUMBER_ON_FILE` keeps ONE code — a tenant override, the rule table and a receipt all
address it by code, and splitting it in two would make one fact addressable two ways
depending on a mode the reader cannot see. `_for_write_mode` swaps the severity, the action
and the sentence at declaration time. **The old sentence — *"the write mode decides what
happens to it"* — is retired**: it was honest while nothing here knew the mode, and a rule
that declines to name the outcome once it DOES know is withholding the answer.

⚠ **AND THE RULE NOW ANSWERS THE PO'S ACTUAL QUESTION.** They asked whether the ROW names a
meter already on file. Since BR-AST-049 a row can do that two ways — by quoting our number,
or by carrying the `external_ref` it was loaded with — and the second is the only one a
first migration's correction re-run has. A rule about "this NUMBER" would have been silent
about it.

### ⚠ 3 · THE SUB-METER MIGRATION, WHICH THIS LANE'S OWN WAVE A BROKE

Recorded in full at *"SUB-METERS ARE ALREADY THEIR OWN UPLOAD"* above; built here.
`parent_asset_no` now resolves **three ways, in order — meter number, serial number,
external reference** — following `resolve_unit_ref`'s precedent on this same import.

**ONE RESOLVER, NOT TWO.** `import_rules.resolve_parent_ref` is used by stage 3 **and** by
the load, which canonicalises the cell to the master's own number before it crosses the
seam into `assets`. The alternative — teaching `assets.services._resolve_parent` the same
three-way lookup — is how a rehearsal and a commit come apart (DEF-544).

**AMBIGUITY IS A VERDICT, NEVER A PICK.** `BR-AST-033` makes a duplicate serial
warn-but-allow, so two masters may carry one legitimately. The index records such a serial
as ambiguous and the rule refuses it **naming both masters** and offering the two
identifiers that are unique. Resolving to the first would hang a sub-meter off the wrong
device, and the only symptom would be a wrong bill months later.

**AND AN UPDATE MAY NOT RE-HANG A SUB.** `parent_asset_no` / `parent_asset_id` join
`asset_no`, `type`, `unit_id` and `BILLING_AFFECTING_FIELDS` in the set `update_from_import`
strips. The master is what the sub's share is calculated FROM. It is stripped **silently**
rather than refused, matching the four fields beside it: a re-imported file legitimately
carries the same `PARENT_MTR` cell it was first loaded with, and refusing the run over a
value that is not being CHANGED would fail every correction pass.

### 4 · A JUDGMENT THIS LANE MADE AND THE PO THEN OVERRULED — recorded because the record is the point

Before the PO's *"in case of insert - reject it"*, this lane read the ruling's *"a value in
Insert mode is an error"* as meaning the row is **skipped** — reported and left unchanged —
and wrote the sentences that way. The PO's word is **reject**. The difference is not
cosmetic: a skip reads on a receipt as *"nothing needed doing"*, a reject reads as *"this
row did not load"*, and only one of them prompts the operator to act. `skipped_existing` is
still SERVED as 0 on the three assets targets rather than deleted, because one receipt
screen renders all six targets and the accounts loader still skips.

### 5 · TWO DEFECTS FOUND IN A NEIGHBOURING LANE'S WORK, filed rather than absorbed

**`DEF-1106` (medium)** — `AST.UNIT_BLANK_TO_INVENTORY` read `mapped["premises"]` where
stage 2 writes `premises_ref`, so **7 of 10 rows** on the CR-028 devices fixture were told
they were going to inventory while the next stage seated every one of them on the premises
they named. The guard's own comment described the behaviour it did not have.

**`DEF-1105` (low)** — the same commit left three count assertions RED on the branch. The
cost recorded is the **attribution**, not the red: a lane editing that file has to assume a
failure is its own, and this one spent a cycle proving three were not.

**⚠ AND A TRAP IN THE REGISTER ITSELF, worth one line here because every lane appends to
it:** `12-governance/10-defect-log.csv` ends **without a trailing newline**, so a plain
append glues the new row's first field onto the last field of the row above. The result
parses as valid CSV and silently loses a row. It happened while filing these two and was
caught only by reading the ids back. The file now ends with a newline.

### 6 · WHAT THIS LANE DID NOT BUILD

Waves **C2–C4** (premises · units · accounts), wave **E** (the wizard screens and the
eleven catalogues beyond the one refusal key this lane raised) and wave **G** (the four
documents) belong to other lanes. `_catch_up_target_series` STAYS, docstring amended, for
the three targets that still take their identifier from a file.
## 2026-08-27 · CR-046 WAVE E — the wizard's three screens, and the four judgments the CR did not settle

The screen half of *"the identifier is ours to issue, and the write mode decides what a known record
does"*. Nothing here is a new RULE — every rule was ruled on 2026-08-27 and is recorded above. These are
the build judgments that had to be taken to render those rules, written down because the next agent reads
the repo and not this lane's reasoning (law 10: *would the next agent, with only the repo, build the same
thing?*).

### 1 · STAGE 2 DRAWS ANY COLUMN THAT DECLARES `help` — the server owns the rule, not the screen

**The state we found.** `_asset_number_column` had shipped its sentence with wave A — *"LEAVE THIS BLANK
for a new meter — SMARTBillHub issues the number from Settings → Numbering…"*. It was served on
`GET /imports/{id}/columns`, typed in `ImportTargetColumn.help`, and **drawn on no screen at all**, because
stage 2 rendered help for two hardcoded KINDS — `plan_ref` (DEF-771) and `unit_ref` (DEF-1077) — and
`asset_no` is a plain `text` column. The one sentence written to stop an operator filling that cell was
invisible on the one screen where the file can still be changed.

**The judgment.** The screen no longer names columns. **A column that declares `help` gets its sentence
drawn, with its HEADER beside it.** Two consequences, and the second is why this shape was chosen over a
third hardcoded `find`:

* the header is drawn because the `MAPS TO` picker only shows a label for a column something is already
  mapped to — and the identifier column, **blank by design**, normally is not;
* waves C2–C4 needed **no frontend change**. They landed hours later and premises, units and accounts
  started telling the truth on their own. A per-kind list would have been three more edits and three more
  chances to ship the wave half-applied.

It is also DEF-771's own warning honoured by construction rather than by diligence: *"a screen that wrote
its own copy about a matcher it cannot see is how the two came apart in the first place."*

### 2 · *"YOUR NUMBERING IS NOT SET UP"* IS SAID ONLY WHERE THE PAYLOAD PROVES IT — and that is a narrow set

`_issued_numbers_block` returns `{}` when the tenant has no series row, and its docstring already claimed
**a screen behaviour that did not exist**: *"the screen then says the numbering is unset rather than
printing an invented range."* Hard-won law 1, in the same file as law 2.

**The obstacle.** An absent `will_issue` has **three** causes and the payload does not distinguish them:
no series row · nothing to create · a target that does not issue yet. Saying *"your numbering is not set
up"* for `premises` before wave C2 landed would have been a **lie** — that target took its number from
the file.

**The judgment.** The sentence is drawn only when the other two causes are excluded: `will_create > 0`,
**and** the payload carries `will_create_to_inventory`, which is `_dry_run_assets`' own marker and is
already used four lines above for the same question. What is left is the series, so the screen states a
fact rather than guessing at one. **This is derived from the served payload and from no list of target
names in the frontend** — a list would have gone stale the moment C2 landed, which was the same afternoon.

### 3 · THE OUTCOME FIGURES NAME THE STATUS, AND THE STATUS IS NOT TRANSLATED

`OQ-840`'s closing named the two outcomes from `assets/services.py:91` rather than choosing them: **no unit
→ `Inventory/Spare`**, **unit named → `Installed/Active`**. The dry-run labels said *"Of those, in
service"* and *"Of those, into inventory"* — a paraphrase that appears on **no other screen in the
product**. They now name the status.

**And in the ten non-English catalogues the two names are left in English on purpose.** They are
`AssetLifecycleStage` ROWS — seed data a tenant may rename (`BR-AST-031`) — served to the Assets screen
untranslated in every locale. A translated label here would name a status the operator will never see.
`BR-SHL-251` (3) covers it: codes and identifiers shown as examples keep their own spelling. They are
quoted with each language's own quotation marks, so the value is not byte-identical to English and G15
assertion 2 still has something to check.

**A translation lane that "fixes" these two later would be un-fixing this.**

### 4 · E4 IS PROVED ON BYTES, IN TWO HALVES, BECAUSE NEITHER HALF IS SUFFICIENT

CR-046 words E4 as *"the downloaded bytes. Not the column definition"* for a reason: `DEF-962` shipped a
correct column DEFINITION and a wrong FILE, and nothing compared the two.

* **Backend** — `tests/test_cr046_e4_sample_identifier_blank.py` parses `sample_csv`'s second row for
  **all six** targets (CR-046 names four; `assets_submeters` and `assets_devices` share
  `_asset_number_column`, and a template shipping a number for a sub-meter while the meter's was blank is
  the half-applied ruling this file refuses). It also compares `TARGETS` against its own map, so a target
  added later cannot escape the rule by being new.
* **Frontend** — `ImportIdentifierTruth.dom.test.tsx` drives the click and reads the **Blob** back through
  `FileReader`. jsdom implements neither `createObjectURL` nor `revokeObjectURL`, which is **why** the one
  line that turns a fetched body into a file on disk had never run in a test.

**THE MEASUREMENT, because it is the finding and not the method.** At `ad777f7`, the morning's tip:

| target | identifier column | the cell in the DOWNLOADED file |
|---|---|---|
| premises | `premise_no` | **`P-9001`** — invented |
| units | `unit_no` | **`1`** — invented |
| accounts | `account_no` | **`A-10432`** — invented |
| meters | `asset_no` | `` (blank) ✅ |

**Three of the four templates were still teaching every operator to supply a number the system would
overwrite.** Waves C2/C3/C4/C5 closed it the same afternoon and the guard is what keeps it closed — it
was proved RED by running it against that tree rather than by mutating anything:
*"AssertionError: premises: the downloadable sample ships 'P-9001' in 'premise_no' … assert 'P-9001' == ''"*.

### 5 · WHAT THIS LANE FOUND AND DID NOT FIX — filed, not carried

* **`DEF-1691`** — the premises template ships the **prose** `Sample lat` / `Sample lng` in its two
  coordinate columns. Neither is declared in `PREMISES_FIELD_OVERRIDES`, so both fall through to the
  generic text sample while the model fields are numeric. `DEF-616`'s test proves every shipped sample
  MAPS ITSELF, which passes here — the headers are fine. **Nothing compares a sample CELL to the KIND of
  the column it sits in**, and that one check would have caught DEF-962, DEF-963 and this together.
* **`DEF-1692`** — `will_issue` and the `asset_no` help, both served and drawn nowhere. Fixed by this
  lane; the row exists for the pattern, which is now **five occurrences in one TypeScript interface**
  (DEF-526, DEF-531, DEF-626, DEF-752, this). That is a missing gate, not five careless lanes.
* **`DEF-1693`** — four tests have been RED on the branch since CR-042 withdrew the `replace` mode, and
  this lane spent a cycle proving they were not its own, on files its own change touched. Left for the
  lane that owns the withdrawal: two of them assert `BR-MET-099`'s three numbers, which is
  **kept-and-unreachable code under `OQ-580`** and needs a decision, not a deletion.

### 6 · NOTHING HERE CONTRADICTS CR-046

One clarification worth recording rather than raising: CR-046 says *"all four sample CSVs"* and the
product offers **six** import targets. The two extra are assets targets that share the meters target's
number column, so they were covered rather than reported. No rule moved, no money moved, golden untouched.

## 2026-08-27 · THE ACCOUNT NUMBER STAYS THE UTILITY'S — accounts are the ONE upload of six that does not call Settings › Numbering

**PO verbatim:** *"we use utility provdied account number here - we dont create our own number - since it will
create lot of change management for utility ; if row dont have account number reject it - please update the
logic; here we dont call settings -> account number logic"*

### THE RULING, AND IT IS AN EXCEPTION RATHER THAN AN INCONSISTENCY

| upload | the record's own identifier |
|---|---|
| premises · units · meters · sub-meters · devices | **issued by SMARTBillHub** from Settings › Numbering |
| **accounts** | **taken from the file, verbatim.** A row with no account number is **REJECTED** |

**The reason the PO gave is the one that decides it, and it is the same reason `BR-TEN-035` exists** — *don't
renumber what a customer already has.* An account number is not an internal key: it is on every bill the
customer has kept, in their bank's payee list, on the standing order, and on the note stuck to their fridge.
Renumbering is not a data change; it is **a letter to every customer, a reprint of every form, and a year of
people quoting a number the staff can no longer find.**

**Why it is not inconsistent with the meter ruling**, stated so nobody "harmonises" the two later: a meter
number is *ours* and a customer has never seen it, so issuing it removes collisions at no cost. An account
number is *theirs*. The principle underneath both is identical — **the side that owns the identifier issues
it** — and the two rulings are that one principle applied to two different owners.

**And there is nothing safe to invent here.** A number we made up would be a number the customer has never
seen and the utility's own old records cannot match — so a blank is an error, not a gap to fill.

### ⚠ THE CONSEQUENCE THIS CREATES, AND IT WOULD HAVE SURFACED AS DUPLICATE CUSTOMERS

`OQ-790` (closed earlier today) makes the **premises** upload create a **master account** for an owner it has
never seen, numbered from the `account` series — because at that point the file carries an owner's *name* and
no account number at all.

**Load order is premises → … → accounts.** So a landlord who appears in BOTH files gets an account from the
premises run under our number, and then a second account from the accounts run under their real one. **Two
accounts for one landlord**, on the first migration, discovered at the first bill run.

**Decided rather than asked, because it follows directly from the PO's own principle:** the premises template
gains an **optional "Owner's account number" column.**

* **Filled in** → that master account is opened under **the utility's number**, exactly as the accounts upload
  would have done. The later accounts run then **matches and updates** instead of creating a second account.
* **Blank** → Settings issues one, exactly as `OQ-790` ruled. That is the owner who genuinely had no account
  in the old system.

This keeps `OQ-790` intact, honours today's ruling everywhere the utility has a number, and removes the
duplicate by construction rather than by a reconciliation screen. **Raised on the accounts page for the PO to
overrule in one line** — the alternative they might prefer is that the premises upload never creates accounts
at all, which is a smaller change than it sounds.

### What must change in code

The accounts target stops calling the series; `account_no` becomes **required** with its own refusal sentence;
the match key is that number; **an update never changes it**; and the premises target gains the optional owner
account-number column described above.

## 2026-08-27 · "CUTOVER" IS OUR WORD, NOT THE UTILITY'S — renamed on screen · and today's account-number ruling closes a measured defect

**PO verbatim:** *"in account upload - 2.2 Has a cutover date been given for this run? what is this ?"*

### 1 · THE QUESTION IS THE FINDING

**The Product Owner of this product could not tell what the field was for.** Nobody at a two-person water
utility will do better. The word appears on a screen that **refuses an entire run** when it is missing, so the
one moment a person meets it is the moment they are blocked — with a term from our schema
(`cutover_on`, `_accounts_cutover`, `BR-CUS-049`'s *"dated at cutover"*).

**Renamed in user-facing copy to "changeover date", with the definition attached wherever it is asked for:**
*the last day your old system was in charge of the money.* The column and the rule keep their names — this is
a copy change, not a schema change.

**The general rule, and it is not new — `BR-SHL-250`'s sibling:** a word that appears only in our data
dictionary must never be the word a refusal uses. **The test is the one that just happened: if the person
being blocked has to ask what it means, the label failed**, and no gate in this repo reads labels.

### 2 · WHAT THE CHANGEOVER DATE IS, written down because it was nowhere in plain English

The last day the old system was in charge of the money — the day the old books closed. **One per run**, typed
by the person running it, and it is the date every opening balance is recorded under (`BR-CUS-049`, opening
journal entries *"dated at cutover, immutable"*).

**Worked example, now on the page:** last billing in the old system **31 July**, go-live **14 August**. The
changeover date is **31 July** — not the 14th, and not the day Commit is clicked.

**Why it refuses instead of defaulting to today.** A customer 45 days overdue on 31 July would read as 14 days
overdue on the day of the import. Every ageing band, reminder, late fee and collections decision would be
wrong by the gap between those two dates — **silently, and in the utility's favour, which is the direction
nobody checks.** And it cannot be quietly corrected: a posted entry is never edited, only reversed by a new
one (hard rule 4).

### 3 · ⚠ TODAY'S ACCOUNT-NUMBER RULING CLOSES A DEFECT THE REPO HAD ALREADY MEASURED

Looking up the cutover rule surfaced `BR-CUS-051` / `OQ-165` (PO 2026-08-12, verbatim: *"Match on something in
the file"*). Its worked case, on `bbu-accounts-cutover.csv`:

> the **1,144** rows carrying explicit numbers all error as duplicates (working as intended) while the **96**
> blank-number rows **quietly create 96 new accounts** on units that already have one

**That is exactly what "if row dont have account number reject it" ends.** The PO ruled the account number
today for a change-management reason — customers know their number — and the same ruling removes a
silent-duplicate path that was measured at **96 rows on one file** five days ago and never fixed.

**Recorded because the connection is invisible from either side:** the account-number ruling reads as a
migration-comfort decision, and `OQ-165` reads as an idempotency defect. They are one fix. The lane building
the accounts target should close `BR-CUS-051`'s blank-number hole in the same change and say so in the row.

## 2026-08-27 · THE CHANGEOVER-DATE CHECK MOVES INTO THE WRITE — the accounts page is signed off, and the rule behind all four spines is now explicit

**PO verbatim:** *"in account upload - you consider 2.2 almost at 2.14 level - upload the diagrma rest is
good"*

### THE MOVE

The changeover-date check was drawn as the FIRST thing the run does. It is now drawn **inside the write box,
immediately before the opening balances** — the only thing that needs it.

**Nothing about the behaviour changes, and that is the point.** The whole load is one transaction, so a
missing date still refuses the **entire run** and still leaves nothing behind: every account the run had
opened rolls back with it. What changed is that the drawing now shows *why* the date exists rather than
merely that it is demanded.

### THIS IS THE SAME CORRECTION FOR THE THIRD TIME, SO IT IS A RULE NOW

The PO has moved a step down into the write on three separate diagrams today:

1. **meters** — *"these decisiona should be taken just before updating teh record in the database - you ahve
   taken 2.3 and 2.4 way early in the process"*;
2. **units** — the number issued and `premises + number` asserted at the end, not the beginning;
3. **accounts** — this one.

**The rule, written down so the fourth correction does not have to be made by a person:** *a step belongs
where the thing it produces is CONSUMED, not where the value it needs first becomes available.* We kept
drawing checks at the earliest possible moment because that is where the data arrives. A reader does not care
where a value arrives; they care what it is for.

**And the diagnostic is cheap:** for every box, ask *"what would break if this ran later?"* If the answer is
*nothing*, it is drawn too early.

### THE PAGE IS SIGNED OFF

*"rest is good"* — `The Account Upload` is the specification for CR-046's accounts work, alongside the
premises and unit pages: https://claude.ai/code/artifact/e0968edf-8090-42c8-94a0-eeeb4ec9497b

It carries, in one place: the account number is **the utility's, never issued by us**; a blank number
**rejects**; that number is the match key and **an update never changes it**; the changeover date is refused
rather than defaulted, with its 45-days-vs-14-days worked case; balances post as **one batch**; and the
duplicate-owner-account consequence with the optional *"Owner's account number"* column that resolves it.
