correctly — `tenancy.services` is master data, a service renamed after issue must not re-title a bill already
sent (BR-BIL-030), and `test_us_bil_022_documents.py::…tc2` pins the render to two queries so a catalogue
lookup fails on the count as well as on the rule — and then drew the opposite conclusion from the right
premise: *so print the id*. The premise says STAMP IT, and stamping is what BR-BIL-030 is.

### WHAT WAS BUILT

Stage 6 freezes `id` and `name` per service into `bill_payload["services"]`, beside the `code` that was
already there. `documents._groups` reads that frozen map; the renderer joins nothing and its query count is
unchanged at two. `apps/tenancy/selectors.service_names_by_code()` is the new published read and
`apps/billing/tenancy_seam.service_names_by_code()` resolves it by name, memoised for one pass like its twin.

### FOUR JUDGMENT CALLS, TAKEN HERE RATHER THAN PUT TO THE PO (law 13)

**1 · The NAME is stamped, not just the id.** The cheaper fix stamps only the id and title-cases the code at
print time. It is wrong for two of the ten seeded services: the catalogue calls `storm_water` **Storm water**
and `thermal_heat` **Thermal/Heat**, and `.title()` invents *Storm Water* — a second name for one service,
which is the drift a catalogue exists to prevent. The name costs one read per bill at DRAFT time, where
reads are already happening, and none at render time, where they are forbidden.

**2 · Where a name is missing, the CODE is capitalised — `.capitalize()`, never `.title()`.** `water` →
`Water`, `storm_water` → `Storm water`, which is the catalogue's own spelling.

**3 · A bill issued BEFORE the stamp prints one NEUTRAL heading, not one per unnamed service.** Every bill
this product has issued is in that state, the PO's included. Two blocks both headed *Charges this period*
would be a grouping by an id the customer cannot see, so all unnameable service lines merge into the single
group the document already uses for a line naming no service at all, and the absence is recorded on the
result. **The id is never the fallback: no name is a better bill than a UUID.**

**4 · The new seam DEGRADES to `{}` rather than refusing, which is the opposite of its twin.**
`service_ids_by_code` refuses when tenancy publishes nothing, because a line with no `service_id` cannot
resolve a revenue account and the bill cannot issue at all. This one supplies a WORD. A deployment whose
tenancy lane has not landed must go on billing; what it gets is the neutral heading above.

**⚠ THIS DOES NOT REPAIR BL-2608-000048 OR ANY BILL ALREADY ISSUED.** Hard rule 4 — an issued bill is
immutable, and its payload was frozen without the name. Those bills stop showing a UUID (that is what
judgment 3 buys) and they do not gain the word. Only bills drafted from this commit forward carry it.

### THE SAME STAMP FIXED THE BAND ABOVE THE CHARGES

`documents._services` labelled its rows with the raw code — `electric`, `sewer` — and now uses the same
stamped name, which is B14 rule 32 clause 4 on the same surface. `tc8` and
`test_po_20260812_backbill_segment_estimate.py` asserted the lowercase code and were amended, each with a
note saying which defect moved it.

## 2026-08-31 · 🐞 THE BILL SAYS WHY A SERVICE WAS NOT MEASURED, IN WORDS — `DEF-2863`

**The PO's BL-2608-000048 printed `sewer   not read this period (tariff_prices_no_consumption)`.** B14 rule
32 clause 4 names that exact string, on that exact surface, in the ruling that created the rule the day
before.

**TWO FAULTS IN ONE STRING, and the second one is why this is not a translation job.** The visible fault is
an internal constant on a customer's bill. The quieter fault is the sentence around it: *not read this
period* tells a customer something went wrong and invites them to ask when somebody is coming to read the
meter. **For sewer, nothing went wrong and nobody is coming.** BR-RAT-015 bills sewer as a share of the
water usage charge; it has no register of its own, and there was never going to be a reading.

### THE JUDGMENT: A SENTENCE PER REASON, CHOSEN FOR WHAT HAPPENED

`documents.SERVICE_ABSENCE_SENTENCES` covers all ten values — billing's own seven and the ones metering
mints and stage 2 forwards — and they do not all say the same thing in different words:

| what the run recorded | what the bill now says |
|---|---|
| `base_only_account`, `tariff_bills_base_only` | no usage billed this period |
| `tariff_prices_no_consumption` (sewer) | not metered separately, billed from another service |
| `service_not_metered` | not metered, billed at a standing rate |
| `no_reading_supplied`, `no_read` | not read this period |
| `no_meter` | no meter on this service |
| `read_flagged` | the reading for this period is being checked |
| `asset_count_unavailable`, `asset_count_unit_unstated` | not counted this period |

**These are the CUSTOMER's words and they are deliberately NOT the clerk's.** The eleven locale catalogues
carry `billing.run.reason.*` for the S31.3 exception screen — *"Standing charge only, for an empty unit"* —
which is work to be judged. *"No usage billed this period"* is a fact about a bill. Reusing one set for both
surfaces is how a clerk's worklist ends up on a customer's paper.

**AN UNRECOGNISED VALUE PRINTS THE NEUTRAL SENTENCE AND NOT THE TOKEN**, and the token is recorded as a named
absence so it reaches the run report instead of the customer. A reader who sees one word less has lost
nothing; a reader shown `asset_count_unit_unstated` has been shown our internals.

**THE GUARD IS A WALK, NOT A LIST.** `tests/test_def_2863_absent_reason_sentences.py` collects every
`ABSENT_*` in `stages/measure_consumption.py` and every `READ_ABSENT_*` in `apps/metering/selectors.py` by
reflection and renders a bill for each, so a reason added on either side goes RED there instead of arriving
on a bill as a token. It asserts the collected set is non-empty first — a walk over nothing passes and proves
nothing.

**NOT FIXED HERE, and stated rather than implied:** the same eleven catalogues have no clerk label for
`tariff_prices_no_consumption`, `service_not_metered`, `no_meter`, `no_read`, `read_flagged` or either
`asset_count_*` value either, so the S31.3 exception screen shows the raw token for all seven. That is the
frontend half of the same rule-32 clause and it is not in this lane.

## 2026-08-31 · 📐 R2 IS THE ONE STEP THAT CANNOT RIDE THE EXISTING FORK POINT, AND WHY — CR-052 task 22, stated rather than attempted

**R1 and R7 were forked today and R2 was not. This records the difference, because "not done" and "cannot be
done the same way" are different facts and only one of them is a gap.**

**WHAT R2 DECIDES:** *plan version → exactly one RATE SCHEDULE VERSION per service*. **What the chain hands
back for it is `ServiceResolution.schedule_version_id` — an ID, and no rates and no tiers.** The ladder is
not on the chain's answer at all.

**WHY THAT MAKES THE EXISTING FORK POINT UNUSABLE, in one sentence:**
`resolution_switch.apply` runs at the END of gather's one impure pass — by which time `_tariff_config_for`
has already built every `TariffConfig` **from the live path's version** — so substituting the chain's version
id there would stamp the chain's version number onto prices read from the live one. The module's own
docstring says exactly this, and it is right: it would be **a lie on the bill**, and the worst kind, because
every figure would still be internally consistent.

**SO SERVING R2 MEANS REBUILDING THE TARIFF FROM THE CHAIN'S VERSION, which is a DATABASE READ**, and there
are only two places to put it — both real changes rather than an increment:

* **(i) inside `gather`, before the tariffs are built** — the chain answers R2 first and
  `_tariff_config_for` is handed the version to read. Clean on the bill, but it makes the chain run
  BEFORE the pass rather than at the end of it, which is `BR-BIL-871`'s *"ONE fork, at the end of the one
  impure pass; the chain runs at most once per account"* re-opened.
* **(ii) inside `resolution_switch`, as a read of its own** — a rating selector that builds a
  `TariffConfig` from a named version id. This keeps one fork and one chain call, and it puts a database
  read in a module written to substitute onto already-gathered facts. That is a design change to a 🔒 money
  path, not a bug fix, and it needs its own packet and a review-ledger row.

**NEITHER IS ATTEMPTED HERE.** Doing this quickly, at the end of a long session, on the module that decides
which rate table prices a customer, is the shape of this repo's worst register entries. **R2 is one packet
of work with a named choice at the top of it**, and that is what CR-052 task 22 can honestly claim today.

**WHAT TASK 22 HAS DELIVERED:** R7's fork (`discount_treatment` carried across, a chain tax with no live
counterpart refused by name) and R1's before it. **WHAT IT HAS NOT:** R2, above; and R4, which `BR-BIL-873`
binds to R3 — one base charge comes out of `resolve()` for the pair — and R3 is held on evidence until the
comparison runs over the widened population.

## 2026-08-31 · 🔎 WHERE `sewer base charge — — 0.00 USD` COMES FROM — `DEF-2864`, TRACED AND **NOT** FIXED, WITH THE REASON

**The PO's BL-2608-000048 prints a charge line for a charge nobody made.** The task was *either sewer has a
base charge and `0.00` is wrong, or it has none and the line must not print — find out which.* **It has
none**, and the mechanism is worth writing down because the next reader will otherwise re-derive it.

### THE CHAIN, END TO END

1. `apps/rating/sample_data.py::_plan_payloads` writes `plan_services.base_charge = "0"` for sewer, and its
   own comment says why: *"the workbook's §1 base column names one for electric and water and none for
   sewer, and a base nobody signed is a base this fixture does not invent."* `BASE_CHARGE_CODES` then
   declares charge code `BASE-S` at `"0"` to match, because `DEF-455` requires the two sources to *"agree to
   the cent by construction"*. Trash is configured identically (`OQ-317` retired its `$18.00` on
   2026-08-27).
2. `gather._base_charge_for` reads the charge code first (`BR-RAT-088`), finds `0`, finds the plan agreeing,
   and returns `Decimal("0")`.
3. `apps/rating/pricing/stages/price_usage.py::_base_lines` emits a line for any base that is **not None** —
   and its module docstring already states the right rule in its own words: *"`base_charge=None` means the
   tariff states NO base charge and NO base line is emitted — absence, not a base of zero … a 0.00 line the
   customer never agreed to is an invented input."*
4. `documents._groups` prints the stored line, correctly, because every figure on a bill is a stored row
   (BR-CUS-040).

**SO THE ENGINE ALREADY KNOWS HOW TO SAY *no base charge* — `None` — AND NOTHING CAN EVER PRODUCE IT.**
`_base_charge_for` returns a `Decimal` or raises; it has no third outcome. The fixture wrote `0` because a
blank is the ONE thing it must not write: `CR-013` part 1 makes a blank mean *this size is not served* and
`DEF-277` makes the bill refuse on it.

### WHY THIS LANE DID NOT FIX IT

Three repairs exist and each one is somebody else's call:

* **Suppress a zero base line in `_base_lines`.** One line, no money moves, and it collides head-on with the
  PO's ruling of **2026-08-19**: the two options put were *raise a billing exception* or *print a `$0.00`
  base line*, and the answer was **"print $0.00"**. Choosing the third option on our own is reversing a
  signed decision, which CLAUDE.md law 13 sends to the PO with the supersession stated.
* **Stop stating a zero in the fixture.** It makes every sewer and trash bill REFUSE, by that same
  `CR-013`/`DEF-277` rule. Strictly worse than the defect.
* **Give the configuration a third value** — *no standing charge*, distinct from *free* and from *not
  served*. This is the honest fix and it is a column, two screens and a migration decision about every zero
  already stored, not a defect repair.

**Recorded as `OQ-1221` with the three options in plain English and the figure ($0.00 either way — what it
costs is trust in the paper, on two of the ten shipped services).** `DEF-2864` stays OPEN and cites it.

⚠ **NOTHING ON THE MONEY PATH WAS TOUCHED.** `10-scripts/03-golden-verify.py` reads 33 PASS / 0 FAIL and
`tests/golden` 23 passed / 1 xfailed, unchanged, which is the statement that this lane moved no figure.

## 2026-08-31 · 🐞 A BILL NOBODY CAN ATTRIBUTE TO A UTILITY IS NOT A BILL — `DEF-2865`

**Six fields on the PO's issued bill printed an em-dash:** Utility, Address, Contact, Service address, Cycle
and Bill date. The bill showed a DUE date derived from a bill date it did not print.

**⚠ THE ABSENCES WERE ALL CORRECTLY RECORDED, AND THAT IS THE ONLY REASON THIS LASTED.** `documents._masthead`
and `_meta` name every one with its rule and its reason, and `test_us_bil_022_documents.py::…tc8` asserts they
ARE named absences. That test is the only one on them and it passes whether the gap is a week old or
permanent — so a gap read as a decision taken and honoured. **Hard-won law 1 says a comment claiming a
guarantee is not the guarantee; this is its mirror — a correctly recorded absence is not a plan to fill it.**

### WHAT IS STAMPED, AND AT WHICH MOMENT

| field | source | when |
|---|---|---|
| `utility_name` · `utility_address` · `utility_contact` | `tenancy.selectors.bill_masthead()` (new) | **issue** |
| `bill_date` | the run's own date, the SAME figure `_due_terms_for` gives the due date | **issue** |
| `cycle` | the run's cycle, its name else its code (`08-A`) | **issue** |
| `service_address` | the premises facts `gather._premises_geography` already returns | **gather** |

**The two moments are not interchangeable and the split is the judgment.** The utility's identity, the bill
date and the cycle are facts about the bill that was SENT, so they go beside BR-BIL-035's arrears and
BR-BIL-021's message at issue — a draft may sit for days. The service address is master data about the
ACCOUNT, so it goes beside the customer's name at gather: a premises re-addressed between the run and the
release must not print over a period billed at the old address (BR-BIL-030).

**THE NAME IS THE DBA FIRST**, then the legal name, then the tenant's provisioning name — never the
subdomain, which is a routing fact and not a name anybody chose. US-TEN-005 §5 already makes the DBA the
display name for remittance, and a customer knows the utility by the name on the truck.

**A PURPOSE-BUILT SEAM, NOT `company_profile()`.** That selector serves the S8 company tab and returns
fifteen keys including the EIN, the logo reference and the brand colours. Billing asking for the tab's
payload would make every future column on that tab a column billing receives, and would put the EIN one
dictionary lookup away from a document. `bill_masthead()` states what a bill may know: three strings.

**STAMPED, NOT JOINED, AND THE GUARD IS THE QUERY COUNT.** The render still issues exactly two queries and
touches neither `tenants` nor `cycles`; a utility that changes its trading name next year has not changed the
bill it sent this year. Same rule, same shape, as `DEF-2852` two commits earlier.

**WHAT IS STILL AN ABSENCE, AND IT IS THE RIGHT ANSWER RATHER THAN AN UNFINISHED ONE.** `Message` and `Ways
to pay` — the last two the PO listed — are stamped already, by `issue._stamp_bill_copy` since 2026-08-30,
from the pinned template version's own options. They print as absences on the PO's bill because **that tenant
has written neither**, which is a fact about their configuration and not a gap in the product. Nothing here
composes bill copy for a utility; the late-fee terms are their words to write. One edit on the Templates
screen fills both.

**And a tenant that has filled in no company profile still gets the dash and a named absence** — the document
reports `utility_identity_not_recorded` with its next step, which is what makes the S62 checklist item
actionable. Nothing is invented.

⚠ **NOT FIXED, AND FOUND WHILE HERE:** `document_correction.CORRECTABLE_PAYLOAD_KEYS` allows a key called
`bill_message`, and `documents._footer` reads `message`. A class-D document correction that "fixes the bill
message" therefore writes a key no renderer reads. It is a real defect in the correction path, it is not this
lane's, and it is stated here rather than left to be re-discovered.

## 2026-08-31 · 📐 THE ESTIMATE WINDOW OFFERS THE ACCOUNT'S OWN AVERAGE MONTH, AND QUESTIONS A FIGURE TEN TIMES ITS HIGHEST — DEF-2859 + DEF-2860

**Two judgment calls, both taken here rather than put to the Product Owner (law 13: a judgment recorded with
its reasoning is the deliverable). Neither moves a signed rule; the second fills a place where no signed rule
reaches.**

### The report these answer

The PO, working the deployed bill run on 2026-08-31: *"when I click on estimate it pop up window ; I dont
know what ; i add the estamate and submit - nothing happened"*. They typed **345** into an empty box, on a
water account whose neighbours read about **5.76 kgal** a month, and the product took it without a word — and
an estimate is a lawful bill input (BR-BIL-015), so 345 kgal prices as usage on a customer's bill.

### 1 · A STARTING FIGURE IS OFFERED, AND WHY THAT IS NOT A PRE-SELECTED DEFAULT

The estimate box opened **blank** while the same screen was printing, for a neighbouring account, *"water
bills an ESTIMATE (5.760000 kgal, trailing_3_avg, consecutive estimate #1)"*. The product knew a great deal
about this account's water and offered the clerk none of it.

**WHAT IS OFFERED:** the account's **own average month** for that service, over the twelve stored months
BR-MET-106 keeps, taken **verbatim** from the figure metering already computes for the account screen's
Usage tab. The window is prefilled with it and labelled with what it is and how many months are behind it.

**WHAT IS NOT DONE, and this is the load-bearing half:** billing does **not** average anything. Averaging
stored months in billing would be a SECOND estimation arithmetic living beside BR-MET-026's signed one, and
the two would disagree the first time a late read restated a month. The figure is asked for by name through
the seam billing already uses for the bill's twelve-month block, and is served or absent — never derived.

**WHY IT IS LAWFUL AGAINST BR-BIL-015 AND BR-BIL-061**, which forbid a pre-committed default: **those rules
are about the CHOICE, not about a field's contents.** The prohibition's own worked form is *"a select showing
its first option IS a default"* — because a select that is never touched still submits. **A prefilled text
box submits nothing.** The clerk has already made the choice (they picked *Estimate the reading* from the row
control, which is the recorded human act with a name on it), the window is titled with the account and the
service, the figure is labelled as this account's average and not as an answer, and **the estimate is
recorded only when they press *Record this estimate*.** Nothing is decided by omission, which is the thing
those two rules exist to prevent.

**AND WHERE THERE IS NO HISTORY THE BOX STAYS EMPTY** — no figure, no label, no comparison. An account we
know nothing about is one where a suggestion would be an invention.

### 2 · THE OUT-OF-RANGE QUESTION: TEN TIMES THE ACCOUNT'S OWN HIGHEST MONTH

**This is a GAP and not a rule violation, stated plainly.** BR-BIL-029's guardrail compares a **produced
draft** against a trailing average, and its case is `overcharge` — which `decisions.UNSUPPORTED_CASES`
disables outright, in its own words, because *"the guardrail compares a draft against the account's trailing
average, which is computed from billing history this module cannot yet query"*. A **typed estimate** is a
different moment: it is before any draft exists. No signed rule reaches it, so nothing was violated, which is
exactly why nothing went red.

**THE SHAPE CHOSEN — it asks, it never refuses.** When the typed figure is more than **ten times** the
account's own highest stored month, or less than **one tenth** of its lowest, the window says so and the
clerk must confirm before it records. Confirming records it, unchanged.

**THE WORKED FIGURE.** AC-2026-00001's water: highest stored month **8.10 kgal**, lowest **3.20 kgal**,
average **5.76 kgal**.
  * 345 kgal ÷ 8.10 = **42.6×** → **questioned.** This is the PO's own case.
  * 60 kgal ÷ 8.10 = 7.4× → **recorded silently.** A leak, a pool fill, an irrigation season.
  * 0.25 kgal × 10 = 2.5, below 3.20 → **questioned** at the bottom end too, because a decimal point moves
    both ways and an under-estimate is a bill the utility never collects.

**WHY TEN AND NOT THREE.** Three times a normal month is ordinary in this business — a leak, a filled pool,
the first month of irrigation — so a 3× threshold would fire on routine work and be clicked through, and **a
check that always fires is a check nobody reads.** Ten is the order-of-magnitude band: a decimal point in the
wrong place, or a register value typed where a consumption belongs. It is where the PO's own mistake sits, at
42.6×, and comfortably clear of a real big month.

**WHY IT ASKS RATHER THAN BLOCKS.** A genuinely enormous month exists, and a clerk who confirms it is making
precisely the recorded decision this screen is for — with their name on the row. A refusal would make a real
reading unbillable and send the work off-screen, which is the opposite of *"all the decisions are made on
screen and recorded"*.

**WHY THE COMPARISON MAY LIVE IN THE BROWSER.** It reads two figures the SERVER computed and decides whether
to ask a question. It derives no quantity, prices nothing, writes nothing, and is not a condition of
recording — the server's own rules (a quantity, its unit, BR-BIL-015) are unchanged and still the authority.
An account with no served history is never questioned, because there is nothing to compare against and a
guess would be worse than silence.

**THE DURABLE HALF IS NOT BUILT AND IS OWED:** this is a browser courtesy, not a rule. The rule-shaped
version of it is BR-BIL-029's guardrail on the produced draft, and that stays blocked on the billing-history
read `UNSUPPORTED_CASES` names. **This does not close that**, and a later lane must not read this row as
having done so.

## 2026-08-31 · ⚖️ THE `$0.00` BASE LINE STAYS ON THE BILL — `OQ-1221` CLOSED AS (a), AND THE 2026-08-19 RULING IS NOW RULED TWICE

**PO ruling: *leave it as it is*.**

**WHAT WAS SHOWN, and this is the record of it** (the standing instruction is plain English with a concrete
figure, never an ID to go and look up): *your bill shows a line reading `sewer base charge — 0.00 USD`;
nobody ever set a standing charge for sewer, so the customer is shown a charge line for something they were
never charged for; two of the ten services ship configured this way, so a customer on both reads two of them;
**no money moves either way** — every total is identical; and on 2026-08-19 you were shown these same two
options and chose "print $0.00", so it cannot change without you.* Three answers were offered — leave it ·
print no line for a zero · give the price book a way to say *no standing charge* — and the PO took the first.

**WHAT THIS SETTLES:**

* **`DEF-2864` CLOSES AS RULED BEHAVIOUR, not as a defect.** The line is correct output.
* **The 2026-08-19 ruling stands and has now been made twice**, the second time with the consequence on the
  page in front of them rather than as a hypothetical. *A zero means it is free and the bill prints `$0.00`.*
* **Option (c) is DECLINED BY IMPLICATION and that is written down rather than left to be re-asked** (law 13):
  no new column, no third state between *free* and *not available*, and no migration over the zeros already
  stored. A lane proposing any of those is reversing a decision, not finishing a stub.

**AND THE LANE THAT RAISED IT WAS RIGHT TO RAISE IT.** The one-line fix — skip a zero base line — is the
sort of change that looks like tidying and is in fact a reversal of a signed finance ruling. Law 13 names
exactly three things that legitimately reach the PO, and *a ruling that collides with a signed rule* is the
first of them. The cost of asking was one question; the cost of not asking would have been a silently
reversed ruling on a customer-facing document.

## 2026-08-31 · 📐 R2's FORK IS BUILT INSIDE `resolution_switch`, NOT INSIDE `gather` — CR-052 task 22, the choice named in the entry above, taken

**The entry earlier today — *R2 IS THE ONE STEP THAT CANNOT RIDE THE EXISTING FORK POINT, AND WHY* — put two
options on the table and attempted neither. This is the choice, its reasoning, and what was rejected. It is a
judgment call recorded with its worked evidence and NOT a question put to the PO (law 13: *a judgment call
recorded in the decision log with its reasoning is the deliverable; a question is the failure to make one*).**

### THE CHOICE: (ii) — `resolution_switch` rebuilds the tariff from the chain's version

**AND THE READ IT NEEDS ALREADY EXISTS AND IS ALREADY BATCHED, WHICH IS THE FACT THAT DECIDED IT.** The
option was written up as *"a rating selector that builds a `TariffConfig` from a named version id … a
database read in a module written to substitute onto already-gathered facts"*, and that framing overstates
what has to be built:

* **Rating already publishes the projection.** `selectors.pricing_inputs_for_version(version, service_date,
  size_class)` was split out of `pricing_inputs` on 2026-08-21 by `DEF-434` for the rate-change impact
  screen, precisely so that **there is exactly ONE projection of a stored version onto the engine's inputs**
  in the product. Its own docstring says why a second one is forbidden: *"a copy of it would drift on the
  first shape that gained a column — silently, because both copies would still produce a well-formed bill."*
  So billing does not write a projection here; it asks rating the question rating already answers (B1:
  billing asks, the owner answers). What is added on rating's side is a **six-line by-id wrapper** —
  `pricing_inputs_for_version_id` — that resolves the row inside the tenant and refuses a draft.
* **The read is already on the batching list, by name.** `seam_batch.BATCHABLE` carries
  `("rating", "pricing_inputs")` with the note *"the single heaviest read in the pass, and the one most
  obviously shared: every account on a plan resolves the identical version. Measured at 2,937 calls over 979
  accounts, of which 6 reach rating."* The by-id sibling collapses on the identical argument and is added to
  the same list, so it is **one read per distinct (version, date, size) for the whole pass**, not one per
  service per account. `2,937 → 6` is the measured shape of that collapse on the live path's own copy of
  this read.

**AND ON THE COMMON PATH IT IS ZERO READS, NOT ONE.** `TariffConfig.version_id` already records which version
priced this line (`DEF-276`, *"provable prices"*). When the chain's `schedule_version_id` equals it, the
rebuild is **provably** the same projection of the same version at the same date and the same size, so the
fork substitutes nothing and stamps the step. That is the case on **47 of 47** accounts of the seeded utility
(*R2 47 agree / 0 disagree*, measured 2026-08-31). The database read happens only where the two paths name
different versions — where a read is the only honest answer.

### WHAT WAS REJECTED, AND WHY

**(i) — move the chain INSIDE `gather`, before the tariffs are built.** Rejected on three grounds, and the
third is the one that would not have been visible from the write-up:

1. It re-opens `BR-BIL-871` — *"ONE fork, at the end of the one impure pass; the chain runs at most once per
   account"* — and `resolution_switch`'s own design note 2 gives the reason that rule exists: *"Two forks for
   one decision is how two implementations come to disagree, which is the defect this whole cutover exists to
   close."*
2. It breaks the shadow's guarantee that both sides look at the same account at the same instant. The
   adapter's input is `AccountBillingData` — the live path's **finished** output — and running the chain
   mid-gather means adapting a half-built one.
3. **It is not a call-site move; it is a second adapter.** `resolution_shadow.adapt` reads `data.readings`,
   `data.period_end`, `data.rate_plan_id` and the premises facts. Those are gathered before the tariff loop
   *today*, and nothing holds them there — a later lane reordering `gather_account` would silently un-build
   R2's fork with every test green. (ii) depends on no ordering inside `gather` at all.

**A THIRD OPTION WAS CONSIDERED AND REJECTED: re-derive `gather._base_charge_for` inside the switch.** It is
the obvious way to make the rebuild total, and `gather` forbids it in its own words at the place the base is
read — *"a second place that re-derives any of them is a second narrowing that can disagree with this one"*.
The refusal below is what replaces it.

### THE FACT THE CHAIN'S VERSION CANNOT SUPPLY, AND IT REFUSES BY NAME: **THE BASE CHARGE**

R7's fork carries `discount_treatment` across from the matching live rule and **refuses when there is no
match** rather than defaulting. R2 has the same shape of hole and it is the base charge.

`TariffConfig.base_charge` is not a field of the rate schedule version. It is `gather._base_charge_for`'s
answer over **three** stored figures — the charge code's amount (`BR-RAT-088`, which owns it), the plan's
figure, and the rate schedule version's own retired `base_charge` column — and **two of those three do not
travel on `TariffConfig`**. So a module holding only the gathered tariff cannot re-take that decision.

The version's column is the one input of the three that MOVES when R2 moves the version, and it is live in
two branches of that function: it is the value itself where no charge code is declared and the plan states
none, and it is a **tripwire** where one is — an unequal figure on the schedule raises *"the base charge is
stated in more than one place and they disagree"* by `BR-RAT-088`'s migration-artefact clause.

**So the rule R2's fork implements:**

* the chain's version and the live version are **the same** → the base cannot have moved; substitute nothing.
* they differ and **R3 + R4 are also served** → the chain supplies `base_charge` outright (that fork already
  exists), nothing is mixed, and the rebuild proceeds.
* they differ and **R3 + R4 are not served** → compare the two versions' own `base_charge` columns. Equal
  → the base is unaffected either way and the rebuild proceeds. **Different → REFUSE THE ACCOUNT BY NAME**,
  saying that the base on this bill was decided from a figure belonging to a version this bill would no
  longer be priced from. It is never defaulted and it is never carried silently: a ladder from one version
  beside a base from another is the *internally consistent lie* the earlier entry named.

**The size gate is carried across for the same reason** (`DEF-484`). If the chain's version prices some
connection sizes differently and this connection's size could not be resolved, the rebuild REFUSES with
`gather`'s own sentence rather than pricing the every-size ladder — *"that answer is right for a size the
schedule does not name and wrong for one it does, and the two are indistinguishable on the document."*

### THE SAFETY PROPERTY THIS FORK HAS THAT R1's DID NOT, MEASURED

`DEF-2839` is the trap next door: R1's plan id is **handed** to the chain and stamped back, so comparing it
compares one value with itself and switching it could never move a bill. **R2 is not that.** The chain
resolves the version independently — `resolve_schedule` walks `catalogue.schedule_versions` and applies its
own `in_force_on` — so an agreement is evidence and not an echo.

**AND THE TWO NARROWINGS ARE NOT IDENTICAL: THEY DISAGREE BY EXACTLY ONE DAY, AND THE CHAIN IS THE ONE THAT
IS WRONG.** `rating.selectors.in_force_version` matches `effective_to >= service_date`; `resolution
.ScheduleVersion.in_force_on` matches `effective_to > service_date`. `rating.services` closes a superseded
version with `previous.effective_to = new_from - timedelta(days=1)`, so **`effective_to` is the last day the
version prices** and the live path is right. On a service date equal to a version's `effective_to` the chain
finds the old version out of force and the new one not yet started, and **refuses the account** where the
live path bills it. Filed as its own defect rather than fixed here — it is a rating-chain defect, not part of
this fork — and it is the reason R2 must not be switched on before it is closed.

### WHAT THIS COMMIT CHANGES ON A BILL: NOTHING

`SERVED_BY_CHAIN_DEFAULT` is still `""` and `apply()` still returns its argument object unchanged on every
deployment. Golden-verify **33 PASS / 0 FAIL** and **`G61` PASS (130 frozen figures)** before and after.
`FORKED` goes from `{R1, R3, R4, R5, R7}` to `{R1, R2, R3, R4, R5, R7}` — six of eight. **What is still
unforked is `R3b` and `R6`**, and both keep the reasons already recorded.

## 2026-08-31 · ⚖️ CR-056 · THE OWNER-OCCUPIER HOLDS TWO ACCOUNTS AND RECEIVES ONE BILL — and an owner nobody has on file is flagged, never invented

**Two PO rulings, both taken from the options put to them, closing the two questions that blocked CR-056's
waves 4 and 6.**

### RULING 1 — an owner who lives in his own house gets TWO accounts and ONE bill

**PO chose (a):** *"Two accounts, one bill — the Master has no charges so it produces no document."*

**⚠ THIS SUPERSEDES THE 2026-08-27 RULING CLOSING `OQ-500`, AND THE SUPERSESSION IS THE POINT OF WRITING IT
DOWN.** That ruling said master-ness is derived from occupancy and is **never chosen at creation** — an
owner-occupier got one Regular Account and no master shape at all. **It is now the other way round: every
address gets its owner a Master Account, whether or not anything is shared, and whether or not the owner
lives there.** `BR-CUS-068` carries the old form and must be stamped SUPERSEDED at the sentence.

**WHAT THE CUSTOMER RECEIVES DOES NOT CHANGE, AND THAT IS WHY THIS IS THE CHEAP ANSWER.** He occupies the
only unit, so nothing falls to his Master Account; **an account with no charges produces no document**, so he
gets one bill from his Regular Account exactly as he does today.

**THE GENERAL RULE THIS RATIFIES, which is bigger than the case it was asked about:**

> **No lines, no document.** Decided at the END of the run, after pricing, never at the start — because only
> then do you know whether there was anything to charge. **A `$0.00` bill is not the harmless option:** a
> customer who receives one telephones to ask what it means, and several hundred a month is real postage and
> a real support load for a document that says nothing.

**FOUR CONSEQUENCES, each of which must be built or this reads as a fault instead of a design:**

1. **A silent Master Account must NEVER reach the exceptions screen.** That screen exists to catch a metered
   service point with nobody to bill. This is the opposite: the correct state, for most master accounts most
   months. Leave it firing and **every owner-occupier in the book is a false alarm every month.**
2. **On screen it must say what it is** — *nothing to bill this period* — rather than showing an empty table
   that reads as broken.
3. **An unoccupied unit that finds NO owner account IS a fault** and does belong on that screen. *"No lines
   because nothing falls to it"* and *"no lines although the premises HAS an unoccupied unit"* are different
   facts and only one of them is good news.
4. **The deposit is NOT taken twice.** A deposit secures OCCUPANCY, so it belongs on the Regular Account. The
   Master Account holds none unless something is actually owed on it.

**AND IT DEGRADES CORRECTLY, which is the argument that carried it.** The day he lets the house out his
Regular Account closes, the unit becomes unoccupied, and it falls to the Master Account **that already
exists** — no migration, no re-keying, no new account, no clerk step. Today that same day is a filed critical
defect: the charge has no posting target and the settlement refuses rather than post to a name. **Creating the
Master Account while he lives there costs nothing — it bills nothing and he never sees it — and it is the
only thing that makes the day he moves out ordinary instead of a hole.**

**WHAT WAS DECLINED, recorded so nobody re-proposes it:** combining both accounts onto one document (a fine
idea, addable later, but it buys nothing here and costs bill-assembly work in the one place where an error is
a customer's money); and making the owner-occupier's single account a Master Account on his unit (which would
put the master on a unit sometimes and on a premises other times — the exact conditional this model removes).

### RULING 2 — an owner name nobody has on file: load the address, create nobody, flag it

**PO chose (b).** A premises row naming an owner who is not on file **creates the premises and creates no
party.** The address loads, the owner is flagged for a human to search, and nothing is invented.

**IT REVERSES NO SIGNED RULE — it extends one the PO already made**, for the near-match case, and for the same
reason: opening an account here would mean inventing a customer out of a spreadsheet cell, with no phone, no
SSN, no licence and no way to tell two parties of the same name apart. **The import never invents a person.**

**⚠ AND IT SETTLES QUESTION 7 BY IMPLICATION, written down rather than left to be re-asked (law 13):**
addresses already on file carrying only a typed-in owner name get their owner's account **when the owner is
identified**, not at a migration that would invent one.

### WHAT THIS UNBLOCKS

`CR-056` waves 4 and 6 were explicitly barred until these two were ruled. **Both are now open**, and the seven
remaining questions — the empty-unit charge per unit or per premises (`$183.00` against `$30.50` on six
flats), automatic or approved reassignment on move-out, sale, two shared spaces on one service, the owner
record pointing at a tenant's account, and unallocated usage — **stay open and are not to be inferred from
these two.**

## 2026-08-31 · ⚖️ CR-056 · THE EMPTY-UNIT CHARGE IS LEVIED PER UNIT — `$183.00` on six flats, not `$30.50`

**PO chose (a): per UNIT.**

**THE WORKED FIGURE IS THE RULING, and it is six times the money.** Six empty flats at a `$30.50` standing
charge bill **`$183.00`** to the owner, not `$30.50`. The question was raised in the billing document as one
of two deliberately unanswered money questions, and it stopped being theoretical the moment the PO ruled that
every address gets its owner an account — under that model empty units reach the owner far more often than
they used to.

**WHY IT IS THE CONSISTENT ANSWER AND NOT MERELY THE LARGER ONE.** A standing charge pays for a CONNECTION —
a meter is installed at that flat, the service is available to it, and the utility carries that cost whether
or not anybody is living there. Six flats are six connections. Charging once per address would mean five of
the six meters are carried free while somebody lives in the sixth, and the same building would cost the
utility six times as much to serve when it emptied as when it was full. **The unit decides what it costs;
occupancy decides who pays** — which is the separation the rate-plan ruling already made, applied to the
question of how many times.

**NOTHING ABOUT THE PRICE CHANGES WHEN A FLAT EMPTIES.** Same meter, same tariff, same base charge, same
plan — the unit is priced exactly as it would be if a tenant lived there. **Only the name on the bill
changes.** That is why this needs no premises-level plan and no new table: plans attach to units today and to
nothing else, and a plan in two places would be two prices for one meter with the wrong one winning silently.

**WHAT THE OWNER SEES.** One document, one line per empty unit, each naming the unit it is for. Six lines
totalling `$183.00` on a six-flat block, not one line of `$183.00` with no way to tell which flats it covers
— an owner who cannot see which units he is being charged for cannot check the bill, and a bill that cannot
be checked is one that gets telephoned about.

**WHAT IS STILL OPEN AND IS NOT DECIDED BY THIS:** whether two shared spaces taking the same service (a
hallway and a car park both on water) carry the standing charge once or twice. That is the same shape of
question about COMMON PARTS rather than units, and it is not inferred from this ruling (law 13).

## 2026-08-31 · ⚖️ CR-056 · REASSIGNMENT IS PART OF MOVE-OUT AND IS STATED EXPLICITLY THERE; AND THE OWNER'S ACCOUNT TRANSFERS TO THE BUYER — our recommendation declined

**Two more PO rulings, closing questions 4 and 5 of the nine.**

### RULING 3 — a tenant moving out reassigns the unit as part of MOVE-OUT, and the move-out impact section must say so

**PO verbatim:** *"it is taken care during move out step - we have in impact section, we need to cover it there - expliciately"*.

**So the answer to *automatic or confirmed?* is neither of the two shapes we offered, and that is the useful
part.** It is not a new approval step and it is not a silent background move: **it is an existing, deliberate
act that already has a date, an actor and a screen**, and the reassignment is one more consequence of it —
belonging in the move-out's own IMPACT section beside the others, stated where the clerk can see it before
they commit.

**⚠ EXPLICITLY IS THE OPERATIVE WORD AND IT IS A REQUIREMENT, NOT AN EMPHASIS.** The move-out screen already
shows what the act will do. **The unit falling to the owner's account is a new consequence of that act and
must be drawn there in words** — which account it moves to, and that the standing charge continues on it —
rather than happening correctly and invisibly. A clerk who has to discover a money movement afterwards has
been given a surprise, and a surprise on a money path is a defect whatever the arithmetic did.

**AND IT MUST STATE THE REVERSE EDGE TOO:** when the next tenant arrives the unit leaves the owner's account
again. Same act, same section, same rule.

**WHAT THIS DOES NOT DECIDE (law 13, so nobody infers it):** what happens when the move-out screen finds NO
owner account to move the unit to. Under the ruled model there always is one — but "always" is a claim about
data that does not exist yet on premises already on file, and the previous ruling settled those as *the
account appears when the owner is identified*. So the impact section must have an honest branch for it, and
`CR-056` task 22 already names that case a fault rather than a silence.

### RULING 4 — he sells the property and the account TRANSFERS to the buyer

**PO chose (b): the account transfers.** ⚠ **OUR RECOMMENDATION WAS (a) — close his account, open the
buyer's — AND IT WAS DECLINED. That is recorded rather than folded into agreement**, because a declined
recommendation that quietly disappears is how a repo loses the reasoning behind its own rules.

**THE REASON WE GAVE FOR (a), AND WHAT NOW HAS TO BE HANDLED INSTEAD.** Hard rule 4: an issued bill can never
be edited, and journal lines are never rewritten. So on a transfer **the account keeps the seller's issued
bills, payments and ledger history**, and the buyer inherits an account whose past belongs to somebody else.
That is not a reason to reverse the ruling — the PO has weighed it — but it is a consequence the build must
answer rather than discover:

1. **The transfer is an EVENT ON the account with a date, never an edit of its past.** The seller's history
   stays exactly as issued (hard rule 4); the account gains a *held by* change from that date.
2. **Where the seller's liability ends and the buyer's begins must be a stated date**, not an inference from
   who happened to be linked when a bill ran. A part-period at the changeover is ordinary proration.
3. **The buyer must not be able to read the seller's bills.** One account, two parties in sequence: the
   document history has to be scoped by who held the account when it was issued, and that is a real access
   rule, not a cosmetic filter.
4. **The Customer # does not transfer.** It is the SELLER's, keyed on his identity and reused across his
   properties; the account changes hands and the number does not travel with it. The buyer's own Customer #
   attaches from the transfer date.

**⚠ POINT 3 IS THE ONE THAT COULD GO WRONG QUIETLY** and it is raised here rather than left to a lane: today
a document history is reached from the account and nothing filters it by holder, because until now an account
had one holder for life. Under this ruling that assumption is false, and nothing in the product objects.

### WHERE THE NINE STAND

**Ruled: 1 (two accounts, one bill) · 2 (flag the owner, invent nobody) · 3 (per unit — `$183.00` on six
flats) · 4 (part of move-out, stated explicitly) · 5 (transfers to the buyer) · 7 (settled by implication —
the account appears when the owner is identified).**

**Still open, and none of them inferred from the above: 6** (two shared spaces on one service — standing
charge once or twice) · **8** (may the owner record point at a tenant's account — today it is silent and
accepts it) · **9** (unallocated usage — the master meter against the sum of its units, three readings and no
rule; deliberately out of `CR-056`'s scope).

## 2026-08-31 · ⚖️ CR-056 · TWO SHARED SPACES ON ONE SERVICE CARRY ONE STANDING CHARGE FOR THE ADDRESS

**PO chose (a): one standing charge for the address.**

**A hallway and a car park both taking water are ONE water connection for the purposes of the standing
charge.** The owner pays the water base once, not twice, however many shared spaces the address has on that
service.

### ⚠ THIS LOOKS LIKE THE OPPOSITE OF THE PER-UNIT RULING AND IT IS NOT — the two together state one principle

The empty-unit ruling of the same day says six empty flats carry **six** standing charges (`$183.00` at
`$30.50`). This one says two shared spaces carry **one**. Read side by side that reads like a contradiction,
and a lane will eventually try to "reconcile" them unless the principle underneath is written down:

> **A standing charge follows the CONNECTION, not the space.**
> Six flats are six connections — six meters, six services the utility carries whether or not anyone lives
> there. A hallway and a car park on one address's water are **one** connection serving the common parts.
> Count connections and both rulings say the same thing.

**So the rule to implement is: one standing charge per SERVICE per address's common parts** — and, separately,
one per occupied-or-empty unit, which the previous ruling settled.

### THE SIGNED FIGURE IS UNAFFECTED, CHECKED RATHER THAN ASSUMED

**`1408 Elm Street` still bills `$69.60`.** Its two shared spaces are on **different services** — hallway and
exterior lighting on ELECTRIC (`base 12.00 + 146 kWh × 0.20 = $41.20`) and shared irrigation on WATER
(`base 8.00 + 5.1 kgal × 4.00 = $28.40`). One standing charge per service per address gives one electric base
and one water base, which is exactly what it bills today. **This ruling changes nothing at 1408 Elm and would
have changed it had both spaces been on water** — `$8.00` of base, on the one test this CR must not move.

### WHAT IT DOES NOT DECIDE

The USAGE is unaffected and is not inferred from this. Two shared spaces on one service still each consume,
and each one's consumption is priced — the ruling is about the **standing charge only**, which is the fixed
part that pays for having the connection at all. A lane reading this as *"charge the common parts once"* would
drop a car park's water usage, which is money.

### WHERE THE NINE STAND

**Ruled: 1 · 2 · 3 · 4 · 5 · 6 · 7** (7 settled by implication — the account appears when the owner is
identified). **Still open: 8** (may the owner record point at a tenant's account — today it is silent and
accepts it) · **9** (unallocated usage — the master meter against the sum of its units; deliberately outside
`CR-056`).

## 2026-09-01 · ⚖️ CR-056 · AN ADDRESS ALREADY ON FILE GETS ITS OWNER'S ACCOUNT WHEN THE OWNER IS IDENTIFIED — ruled explicitly, not inferred

**PO chose (b): the account appears when there is a person to attach it to.**

**⚠ THIS WAS RECORDED YESTERDAY AS *"settled by implication"* AND IT IS NOW RULED IN ITS OWN RIGHT, WHICH IS
NOT THE SAME THING.** An inferred ruling is a lane's reading of what the PO would have said; a stated one is
what they did say. The earlier entry drew it from the ruling on a blank owner column, correctly — and it stays
in the record as the inference it was, with this entry as the ruling that replaces it. **A repo that cannot
tell its inferences from its rulings will eventually defend one as the other.**

**WHAT IT SETTLES.** Hundreds of premises already on file carry a **typed-in owner NAME and no party record**.
Under the model every address must produce an owner's account — so the question was when theirs appears. The
answer: **not at a migration.** Nothing sweeps the existing book creating accounts for name-strings; each
address gets its owner's account at the moment a person is identified and attached, one at a time, by a human
who knows who that party is.

**IT IS THE SAME PRINCIPLE AS THE BLANK-OWNER RULING AND THE NEAR-MATCH RULING BEFORE IT**, now applied a
third time, which is worth naming because three consistent applications make it a rule rather than three
decisions:

> **The product never invents a party.** A name in a cell is not a person. The address loads, the owner is
> flagged for a human to identify, and the account follows the identification.

**THE COST, STATED PLAINLY:** for as long as an address carries only a name, it has no owner account — so an
empty unit there still has nowhere to post its standing charge. **That is the old defect, surviving on the
old data**, and it is the honest consequence of not inventing people. It ends address by address as owners
are identified, and `CR-056` task 22 makes the case visible rather than silent: an unoccupied unit that finds
no owner account **is** a fault and belongs on the exceptions screen.

**WHAT IT DOES NOT AUTHORISE (law 13):** a bulk "identify owners" tool that matches name-strings to parties
automatically. That is a matcher on a field that is not identity, on data nobody has verified, deciding who
owes money — the exact shape the deposit-carrying matcher rule already refuses. If such a tool is wanted it
is its own change with its own ruling.

### WHERE THE NINE STAND — seven ruled, two open

**Ruled:** 1 two accounts and one bill · 2 flag the owner, invent nobody · 3 per unit (`$183.00` on six
flats) · 4 part of move-out, stated explicitly in its impact section · 5 the account transfers to the buyer
(our recommendation declined) · 6 one standing charge per service for an address's common parts · 7 this one.

**Open, and neither inferred from the seven:** **8** — may the owner record point at a tenant's account?
Today it is silent and accepts it. **9** — unallocated usage, the master meter against the sum of its units;
three readings, no rule, and deliberately outside `CR-056`.

## 2026-09-01 · ⚖️ CR-056 · THE OWNER MAY BE LINKED TO A TENANT'S ACCOUNT — BUT ONLY AS A CHOICE THE CLERK MAKES ON PURPOSE. Our recommendation to refuse it was declined

**PO verbatim:** *"We ahve to give option to clark to select it ; if clark seelct it then we can link"*.

**⚠ WE RECOMMENDED (a), REFUSE IT OUTRIGHT, AND IT WAS DECLINED. Recorded rather than folded into
agreement.** The PO's answer is neither of the two ends we offered: not a refusal, and **not the silence we
have today either.**

### THE RULING IS ABOUT THE ACT, NOT THE OUTCOME — and that is the whole of it

**What the product does today:** `link_owner_master_account` checks that the account exists and belongs to
this utility, **and checks nothing else** — not its kind, not whose it is. A clerk can aim an owner's pointer
at a tenant's Regular Account and the product accepts it **without a word**. Nothing on the screen says what
kind of account was just chosen or whose it is.

**What is ruled:** the clerk is **OFFERED** the choice, sees what they are choosing, and the link is written
because they chose it. The same outcome the code already permits, arrived at deliberately instead of by
accident. **A clerk who has been shown the consequence and chooses anyway has made a decision; a clerk who
was shown nothing has made a mistake that looked like a decision.**

**SO THE BUILD IS A SCREEN CHANGE, NOT A GUARD.** The picker must state, for the account being chosen:
whether it is a **Master** or a **Regular** account, and **whose** it is. Choosing a tenant's account is
allowed and is not warned against as though it were an error — it is a legitimate arrangement a small utility
may genuinely want.

### ⚠ ONE CONSEQUENCE THE SCREEN MUST STATE, BECAUSE IT IS THE FAILURE THIS WHOLE CR EXISTS TO CLOSE

**A tenant's Regular Account CLOSES when that tenant moves out**, and a closed account is excluded from every
bill run. So an owner pointed at a tenant's account **works right up to the day it is needed and then stops** —
the empty unit's standing charge arrives at a closed account and has nowhere to post. That is the *"workaround
that dies on the day it is needed"* already filed as critical, and this ruling makes it a thing a clerk can
choose rather than a trap they can fall into.

**Therefore the choice must carry that sentence at the point of choosing** — *this account belongs to a
tenant and will close when they move out* — in plain words, no rule id (B14 rule 32 clause 4). Offering the
choice without it would satisfy the letter of this ruling and reproduce the defect underneath it.

**AND IT DOES NOT REPLACE THE OWNER'S OWN ACCOUNT.** Under ruling 1 every address gets its owner a Master
Account; this pointer is a separate, older mechanism. Where both exist the owner's own account is what the
model bills to, and a lane must not read this ruling as permission to skip creating one.

### WHERE THE NINE STAND — eight ruled, one open

**Ruled:** 1 two accounts and one bill · 2 flag the owner, invent nobody · 3 per unit (`$183.00` on six
flats) · 4 part of move-out, stated explicitly · 5 the account transfers to the buyer *(recommendation
declined)* · 6 one standing charge per service for an address's common parts · 7 the account appears when the
owner is identified · 8 this one *(recommendation declined)*.

**Open: 9** — unallocated usage, the master meter against the sum of its units. Three readings of the
question give three answers, none is ruled, and it is deliberately outside `CR-056`: pulling it in would
double the size of the schema wave.

## 2026-09-01 · ⚖️ CR-056 · UNALLOCATED USAGE IS DEFERRED, DELIBERATELY — and a deferral is a decision, so it is written down like one

**PO verbatim:** *"leave it for time being"*.

**ALL NINE QUESTIONS FROM *WHO GETS BILLED, AND UNDER WHAT NUMBER* ARE NOW ANSWERED. Eight are rulings and
this one is a deferral**, which is a different kind of answer and is recorded as such rather than left to
look like an oversight.

**THE QUESTION, for whoever picks it up:** a building's master meter reads more than the sum of its units.
100 kgal at the master, 92 across the flats — where do the 8 go? **Nothing anywhere in the product compares
the two.** Three readings of the question give three different answers — bill it to the owner, report it and
bill nobody, or treat it as a metering fault — and none of them is ruled.

**WHY DEFERRING IT IS SOUND HERE AND NOT A GAP LEFT OPEN.** It is not a consequence of anything `CR-056`
changes. The model moves the owner's account onto the address and gives him an identity; **the master-versus-
sum comparison does not exist today and will not exist any differently afterwards.** Nothing in this CR makes
it worse, and pulling it in would double the size of the schema wave for a question the PO has not needed to
answer.

**WHAT DEFERRED MUST NOT BE MISTAKEN FOR (law 13, so nobody infers it):**

* **It is not ruled as *bill it to the owner*.** Under `CR-056` an owner now has an account at every address,
  which makes that answer newly *possible* — and possible is not chosen. A lane that quietly posts a
  discrepancy to the owner's Master Account because there is finally somewhere to put it has decided this
  question without asking.
* **It is not ruled as *ignore it*.** The comparison still does not run; nothing reports the 8 kgal; nobody is
  told. That is today's behaviour continuing, not a judgment that it is correct.

**SO THE HONEST STATE IS: unmeasured, unreported, and unruled** — and when it is picked up it needs its own
change request, because whichever way it goes it is money moving on a rule nobody has signed.

### CR-056 IS NOW FULLY RULED — the tally

| # | Question | Answer |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Owner living in his own house | **Two accounts, one bill** — the Master has no charges, so no document |
| 2 | An owner name nobody has on file | **Load the address, create nobody, flag it** |
| 3 | Empty-unit charge per unit or per premises | **Per unit** — `$183.00` on six flats at `$30.50`, not `$30.50` |
| 4 | Tenant moves out — automatic or confirmed | **Part of move-out, stated EXPLICITLY in its impact section** |
| 5 | He sells the property | **The account transfers to the buyer** *(our recommendation declined)* |
| 6 | Two shared spaces on one service | **One standing charge for the address** |
| 7 | Addresses on file with only a typed-in name | **The account appears when the owner is identified** |
| 8 | May the owner point at a tenant's account | **Yes — offered as a choice the clerk makes on purpose** *(our recommendation declined)* |
| 9 | Unallocated usage | **Deferred** — its own CR when it is picked up |

**Two of the eight rulings declined our recommendation.** Both are recorded with the reasoning we gave and
the consequence the build now has to answer, because a declined recommendation that quietly disappears is how
a repo loses the argument behind its own rules.
