## 2026-09-01 · 🔧 BUILDING `BR-MET-1032` — THE FOUR JUDGMENTS THE RULING DID NOT REACH, DECIDED HERE (law 13)

The ruling above settled the three things it named: the FILE carries the whole number, the SCREEN
serves the last four, the STAGING TABLE holds a ciphertext with its blind index. Building it turned
up **four more decisions the rules genuinely did not answer.** None was put back to the PO — law 13:
*"a judgment call recorded in the decision log with its reasoning is the deliverable; a question is
the failure to make one."* Each is written with the argument against it, because three of the four
have a real one.

### 1 · THE FILE WE HAND **BACK** CARRIES THE WHOLE NUMBER TOO

When rows fail, the operator downloads a **failures file**: their own rows, unchanged and
un-reordered, plus a reason and a fix. `BR-CUS-673` says what it is for in as many words — *fix two
cells in the spreadsheet you already know and upload that file again.*

**It reads from the staging table, so encrypting the table forced a decision here that nobody had
made.** It is decided as: **the failures file DECRYPTS and carries the operator's own value.**

**Why, and the reasoning is not "it is more convenient".** A mask here would be redaction that BREAKS
the feature while looking like it hardened it — the same trap the ruling above already names once.
`crypto.normalise_identifier` strips the bullets, so a re-uploaded `••••6789` arrives as the
identifier **`6789`**: it matches nobody, and the row mints a SECOND customer number for a person
already on file. Nothing raises, and the receipt's counts all read correctly.

⚠ **THE ARGUMENT AGAINST IS REAL AND IS NOT DISMISSED.** `BR-CUS-092(c)` says the full value is never
in *"a list response, an export, a log line or an audit `details` blob"*, and a download is an export
by any ordinary reading. The reason it is accepted: **this file IS the spreadsheet the PO's ruling is
about.** *"in spreadsheet we will porvide entire SSN number if required"* — it goes to the
authenticated operator of the tenant that uploaded those exact rows minutes earlier, it is the same
bytes they already hold, and its only purpose is to be sent back. `BR-CUS-092(c)` is about surfaces
that SHOW a stored identifier to a reader; this is a round trip of the operator's own file.
**If that reading is wrong it is a defect to file, and the fix is to strip the identity columns out
of the failures file entirely rather than to mask them in place** — a masked cell that re-uploads as
a wrong number is the one outcome that must not happen.

### 2 · A MASKED CELL IN THE INLINE EDITOR OPENS **EMPTY**, AND AN IDENTIFIER CAN NO LONGER BE CLEARED THERE

Stage 3 offers *"Fix the rejects here — no need to re-upload"*: an editor over the row's own cells,
pre-filled with what is staged. Once a cell shows `••••6789`, pre-filling becomes dangerous — an
operator who clicks in and appends a digit sends `••••67891`, the server strips the bullets, and
**`67891` is filed as somebody's Social Security number** with nothing objecting anywhere.

So a masked cell opens **empty, with the mask as its placeholder**, and an empty masked cell is read
as *unchanged* rather than as *cleared*.

⚠ **THE COST IS STATED RATHER THAN BURIED: an operator can no longer CLEAR an identity cell from that
editor.** Clearing was how you said *"don't create a customer from this row"* without touching the
file. It is accepted because the two remaining acts are the two that are safe — leave it, or type the
whole number — and because the decision above already puts the operator's own file at the centre of
every correction. **If clearing turns out to matter, the fix is an explicit control that says so, not
a re-fill of the box.**

### 3 · A PHONE NUMBER IS NEITHER ENCRYPTED IN STAGING NOR MASKED ON THE SCREEN

The ruling says a staged identifier is stored the way a committed one is, and `customers.Customer`
encrypts **four** columns — SSN, driving licence, Tax ID **and phone**. Read literally that is four.
It is built as **three**.

**The rule that decides it is *"like every other surface in the product"*, which is the ruling's own
wording for the screen half.** `customers.selectors.customer_detail` serves `ssn_last4`,
`driving_licence_last4` and `tax_id_last4` — and serves **`phone` in full**. A phone is the utility's
contact handle and, in this repo's own words, *"a government identifier for NEITHER kind"*
(`BR-CUS-1022`).

**And for a cell shown in full, vaulting it would achieve nothing.** The visible cell is what the
screen draws, so a field served whole has to keep its plaintext there — an envelope beside a
plaintext cell is a SECOND copy of the value, not a protection of it. Encrypting the phone would need
the screen to be changed too, and that is a rule nobody has made.

⚠ **THE ARGUMENT AGAINST:** staging is now weaker than the customer record for exactly one column.
That is true, and it is the shape *"it is only staging"* was rejected for. The difference is that the
weakness is **inherited from a decision already taken and visible everywhere else** — the account
screen shows the whole phone today — rather than invented here for a parked row.

### 4 · THE BLIND INDEX USES `customers`' CONTEXT AND THE CIPHERTEXT DOES NOT

Two keyed values are written beside each staged identifier and they are bound to **different**
contexts, deliberately:

* **The blind index is computed under `customers.ssn`** (and its siblings). It **must** be: the index
  is an HMAC over `INDEX_SCHEME|context|normalised value`, so a token computed under any other
  context would be well-formed, deterministic and **useless** — every lookup would miss, every
  returning customer would be minted a second number, and nothing would raise. The contexts are read
  out of `customers.identity_match.CRYPTO_CONTEXT` through the metering seam and are **never copied**,
  because a mirrored cryptographic constant that drifts fails silently in exactly that way.
* **The ciphertext is bound to `import_run_rows.ssn`.** `crypto._aad`'s stated job is that *"a value
  lifted out of one column and dropped into another does not decrypt"*. A staged envelope is not a
  customer's, and writing one straight into `customers.ssn` must **raise** rather than quietly work,
  so the value goes through the door `customers` owns or it does not go at all.

**No argument against this one is recorded because none was found** — the two values do different
jobs and the split costs nothing. It is written down because it is the single non-obvious line in the
implementation, and a later lane "simplifying" it to one context would break matching in a way no
test outside `test_br_met_1032_staged_identity.py` can see.

### WHAT WAS MEASURED, BEFORE AND AFTER

Read straight out of PostgreSQL on a premises file carrying one owner, `Rosa Alvarez`, SSN
`123-45-6789`:

**BEFORE** — `raw` and `mapped`, and the payload the checking screen is polled with, all three:

    raw    = {"SSN": "123-45-6789", ..., "OWNER": "Rosa Alvarez", ...}
    mapped = {..., "owner_ssn": "123-45-6789", ...}
    rejects = [{... 'raw': {'SSN': '123-45-6789', ...}}]

**AFTER** — the cell is the mask, the value is an envelope, the index is beside it, and the screen is
served no more than it needs:

    raw     = {"SSN": "••••6789", ..., "__identity__": {"SSN": {"b": "bix1:…", "c": "sbh1:…"}}}
    mapped  = {..., "owner_ssn": "••••6789", "__identity__": {"owner_ssn": {…}}}
    rejects = [{... 'raw': {'SSN': '••••6789', ...}, 'masked': ['SSN']}]

**And the blind index equals the one the customer record carries for the same number**, which is the
assertion the whole feature hangs on: two premises rows presenting the same landlord still load as
**ONE** customer, not two.

---

## 2026-09-01 · 📐 THE ACCOUNT SCREEN SHOWS THE PLAN IT IS BILLED ON, READ THROUGH THE UNIT FK (PO ruling · `DEF-2419`)

**THE PO RULING, VERBATIM, 2026-09-01:**

> *"It should be foreign key - it should take it from Unit and display it there - that is important"*

**WHAT WAS SHOWN BEFORE IT WAS MADE**, so the signature is traceable to the statements it covers
(CLAUDE.md's rule on what counts as a sign-off — write down what was shown, not merely that review
happened):

* The PO asked why no plan is attached to any account, then opened the **unit** screen, which shows
  that same unit's plan correctly — *"Sample — Residential v1"* and *"ON PLAN SINCE 06/01/2026"*,
  against account **AC-2026-00001**.
* They were told, in plain English, that the account screen withholds the plan on the stated ground
  that *"the two match only until the first override"* — **and that there is no override and there
  cannot be one.** `accounts` carries no plan column of any kind, and `account_plan_assignments`
  (`BR-CUS-029`) was never built: **the divergence being guarded against has nowhere to be stored.**
* They were told the existing decision conflates two different things — **STORING** a plan snapshot
  on the account (correctly not done, because there is no DDL for it) and **SHOWING** the plan the
  account is billed on (a read that stores nothing).

The PO ruled on the DIRECTION: read it from the unit through the foreign key, and put it on the
screen. **They did not rule on the field name or the payload shape** — those are ours, and they are
recorded underneath as the build judgments they are.

### THE FINDING THAT MATTERS MOST: THIS WAS ALREADY RULED THREE WEEKS AGO

The PO ruled on **2026-08-11**, in the words *"from unit you will derive the plan"*, and this repo
records that ruling as SUPERSEDING `BR-CUS-029` for the derivation. `customers.services.
_account_and_unit_plan` has done exactly this since — account → `unit_id` → `units.rate_plan_id` →
`rating.selectors.plan_ref` — and the whole change-plan wizard is built on it.

**So the account HEADER was the single surface that never followed the ruling the rest of the module
already follows.** Today's ruling confirms it rather than changing it. That is worth naming, because
it is law 13's shape from the other side: an answer the repo already held, on a screen that had not
been brought into line with it.

### WHAT IS BUILT, AND WHAT IS DELIBERATELY NOT

**No new column and no migration.** *"It should be foreign key"* names a mechanism that already
exists: `accounts.unit_id` is in the reviewed cross-module set (B2 §2) and `metering.Unit.rate_plan`
is the plan. Nothing is stored; a field is read along a chain of keys the schema already has.

**A NEW field — `unit_plan` — and NOT a repurposing of `plan`.** `plan` stays `null` beside
`plan_snapshot_unavailable: "BR-CUS-029"`, exactly as before. Two reasons, and both are load-bearing:
`BR-CUS-029`'s contract says the account's OWN snapshot is not held, which is still true and must not
be contradicted; and a consumer that read the unit's current plan out of a key named `plan` would be
reading *today's* plan as *the plan that priced an old bill*, which is the one substitution the
original refusal was right to refuse. **The old refusal's premise was wrong; its caution was not.**

**A unit with no plan is a REAL absence and still says so.** `units.rate_plan_id` is nullable, and a
unit standing on no plan is an ordinary state — the new field is `None` there, and the screen states
it rather than printing an empty box.

**The 68-word paragraph is DELETED from the screen, not shortened.** B14 rule 33 puts RATIONALE at
**zero words on screen**; the sentence explained why a control was absent, which is precisely the
class the rule names. The reasoning moves into the code comment beside the render, which is what a
comment is for. Two keys (`customers.account.planNotShown`, `customers.account.planUnavailableWhy`)
leave all eleven catalogues with it.

⚠ **`customers.account.planUnavailable` IS NOT TOUCHED.** It is shared with the New-account and
Move-in wizards, where *"No plan recorded"* is the right sentence — those steps offer no plan field
and the account genuinely has none yet. Rewording it once before broke both wizards and three tests
caught it. One sentence per meaning.

**The label names the UNIT as the source.** What priced an old bill is that bill's Charges tab, not
this box; a box captioned only *"Plan"* would be read as the plan every past bill used. Three words,
per rule 33's label cap.

### THE ROLLBACK, STATED BEFORE SHIPPING

One field, one seam function, one render block. Reverting the render block restores the previous
stated absence exactly, because `plan` and `plan_snapshot_unavailable` were never changed; the seam
and the served field are then dead payload, not a wrong answer, and can be removed separately. **No
data is written by any part of this, so there is nothing to migrate back.**


## 2026-09-01 · 📐 THE COST CATEGORIES WIDEN TO SIXTEEN, CAPITAL IS REFUSED BY NAME, AND WHAT ENTERS BOUGHT-VERSUS-BILLED BECOMES A FLAG (`CR-060` T5 · T7c · `C15` · `C9` · `BR-LED-029` · `BR-LED-031`)

**Nothing here was put to the Product Owner.** `CR-060`'s C15 is already written and the two tasks
say what to build; every choice below is where the specification ran out and a lane had to decide.
Law 13: a judgment recorded with its worked figure is the deliverable, a question is the failure to
make one.

### WHAT THE PRODUCT COULD NOT RECORD BEFORE TODAY

A tenant could record a cost against **a service they sell, plus exactly two others** — O&M and
Infrastructure — and that second half was hardcoded. **No payroll, no insurance, no legal bill, no
postage, no fuel, no rent.** So the product's claim of *"everything in one place"* was not true, and
closing it is mostly seeding chart accounts.

**It is sixteen categories in five groups now**, and the fourteen new ones each get a chart account:
O&M splits into **labour 5210 · materials & supplies 5220 · contract services 5230** beside the flat
**5200** that stays; **Customer accounts** gains billing & collection **5400**, postage & printing
**5410**, meter reading **5420**; **Administrative & general** gains payroll & benefits **5500**,
insurance **5510**, professional fees **5520**, office & rent **5530**, vehicles & fuel **5540**;
**Taxes other than income** gains property **5600**, franchise **5610** and payroll taxes **5620**.
Infrastructure **5300** is unchanged. **The full seeded chart moves from 34 accounts to 48.**

### JUDGMENT 1 — THE FOURTEEN NEW ACCOUNTS SEED UNSIGNED, AND THAT IS THE ROUTE, NOT A GAP

**B5 line 74 is ❄️ FROZEN and carries no cost-of-service accounts at all.** Every cost row in this
chart arrived the same way: seeded `signed=False`, listed in `PENDING_FINANCE_RE_SIGN_COST`, and
**refused presentation as finance-signed by every surface that offers it** (US-LED-017 TC-5) until a
finance re-sign through HUMAN-GUIDE §6 flips it. That is what happened to the eight cost accounts on
2026-08-18 and to 4300 on 2026-08-28. **So this needs no PO turn to land** — the mechanism for "an
account exists and finance has not signed it" is already built, tested and served.

⚠ **AND THE TEST THAT ASSERTED `PENDING_FINANCE_RE_SIGN_COST == ()` IS REWRITTEN, NOT DELETED.** It
is the standing record of the 2026-08-18 re-sign and it must keep saying so: it now asserts that the
**eight** cost-of-service rows are still signed and that a code edit cannot un-sign them, and adds
that the **fourteen** widened rows are unsigned and every surface marks them. Deleting it would have
lost why the eight are signed at all.

### JUDGMENT 2 — CAPITAL IS REFUSED BY NAME, AND THE FIVE NAMES ARE OURS

`capital_assets` · `vehicle_purchase` · `equipment_purchase` · `plant_and_buildings` ·
`depreciation`. **A $40,000 truck recorded as a cost overstates this year by $40,000, understates
the next five years by the depreciation that never happens, and leaves the asset off the balance
sheet entirely** — the most common bookkeeping error at this size of utility. It does not need
solving, because it is solved elsewhere: `assets` already carries `purchase_cost`,
`depreciation_method`, `expected_life_years` and a computed `book_value_amount`.

**Two things this deliberately does NOT do.** It does not refuse `infrastructure`, even though the
fixture's CI-9 is **$12,500.00 of meters from Katy Meter Works** and meters are arguably capital:
that category is live, rows point at it, and re-categorising captured money is not this task's to
do. And it does not refuse `admin_vehicles_fuel` — **buying a truck is capital and running one is
not**, which is why the two are separate names.

**Depreciation is refused for a different reason and the message says which:** it is COMPUTED from
the asset's own life and book value and is never invoiced by anybody. `CR-060` T7f is the task that
posts it from the asset, and it is not this one.

### JUDGMENT 3 — THE RECOVERY EXCLUSION IS A FLAG, AND THE FLAG HAS NO DEFAULT

Until today the reconciliation asked **"is this code not a service?"** to answer **"does it enter the
bought-versus-billed denominator?"**, and with exactly two categories in existence the two questions
had the same answer. **With sixteen they do not.** A category added to the vocabulary and forgotten
in the excluded set would be treated as a commodity and sent to the billed-volume read — which is
how payroll ends up in a water ratio.

So every category declares `enters_recovery_denominator` in one place, **the field has no default so
a new category cannot be added without answering it**, and it is **False on all sixteen**. The
worked reason is the one already in `BR-LED-031`: a partial water denominator reads **−13.75%**, a
utility that appears to have delivered more water than it bought, and **a payroll figure in that
denominator is not a smaller error than −13.75% — it is the same error.**

**A constant-False flag is a check that cannot fail, so it is driven from a SYNTHETIC category whose
flag is True**, the same way `test_us_led_017_cost_chart` drives the unsigned-account mechanism from
a synthetic unsigned code. Without that, the flag would be decoration.

### JUDGMENT 4 — A VOLUME ON AN EXCLUDED CATEGORY IS INERT, NOT REFUSED

Refusing one was considered. **`BR-LED-030` is the PO's own ruling that the volume is optional and
that nothing refuses a cost-only invoice**, and an hours figure on contract services is meaningful to
the clerk who typed it. So it is stored, it enters no ratio, and **the row says so in its own
reason** rather than the figure sitting there looking as though it counted. There is a test that
captures payroll **with** a volume and proves water still reads **9.00%** and electric **5.50%**.

### JUDGMENT 5 — AN EMPTY CATEGORY GETS NO ROW ON THE RECONCILIATION

The reconciliation unions the tenant's live services with `COST_CATEGORIES`, so both categories
always appeared. **Union sixteen and Brazos Bend's July goes from 7 rows to 21, fourteen of them
"no volume denominator" for categories nobody bought anything in** — on the one screen whose value
is that the worst building is the first row.

**So: a SERVICE the tenant sells always gets a row** (workbook V-8's *"no purchases captured"*,
because the absence of a water purchase is information), **and a non-commodity category appears only
when it has purchases in the window.** July still reads exactly seven rows — water 9.00%, electric
5.50%, gas absent on the MMBtu/ccf mismatch, sewer and trash absent with no purchases, O&M and
Infrastructure absent with no denominator, **total $51,902.50** — because CI-8 and CI-9 are real
purchases in that window.

⚠ **CORRECTED THE SAME DAY, AND THE OLD FIGURE IS NAMED RATHER THAN QUIETLY REPLACED.** This
paragraph said **5 rows and 19** when it was written, from LE-12's illustration; the served table
was then MEASURED and is **7 and 21**. LE-12 lists five because it prints only the rows carrying
content, while the reconciliation also serves sewer and trash as *"no purchases captured"*. Both
numbers are true of different questions, which is exactly how a figure gets quoted wrong — so the
measurement is recorded here, and the test now asserts **7** rather than the membership check that
would have passed on either.

### JUDGMENT 6 — AN EXISTING TENANT GETS THE ACCOUNT ON FIRST USE (hard-won law 4)

**`seed_chart_of_accounts` runs at provisioning and nowhere else.** A tenant provisioned yesterday
would have got fourteen new categories in the picker and **no account in their chart to point any of
them at** — the capture would refuse, correctly, and tell them to pick an account that does not
exist. That is hard-won law 4 exactly: *a template change never reaches a host that already has a
`.env`.*

**So the account is minted on first use**, through the same lookup-and-top-up path
`ensure_service_revenue_accounts` already uses to mint 5140 the day a tenant enables Gas
(`BR-LED-038`). It writes the ledger's own table, audits the creation with
`source="cost_category_first_use"`, and carries the row's `finance_signed: false` into the audit
payload — which is the row a finance reviewer reads. **A tenant who has deactivated the account
keeps it deactivated**: rule 1 of the seed says the code stays theirs and nothing here resurrects
one.

### WHAT THIS DOES NOT TOUCH

**No migration** — `supplier_invoices.service` carries no CHECK constraint and no FK, deliberately
(the vocabulary is per-tenant data), so widening it is code and seed data. **No posting** — capture
still posts nothing, `OQ-200`'s ruling is untouched, and `CR-060` T6 is not started. **No money
math** — no B4/B5 figure moves, and the golden harness and the engine-verified goldens were run
before and after to show it.

### THE ROLLBACK, STATED BEFORE SHIPPING

Reverting the commit removes fourteen categories from the picker and the five refusals. **Rows
already captured against a new category keep pointing at their account**, which still exists in the
tenant's chart, and would then show a category the vocabulary no longer offers — the same state a
tenant reaches today by switching a service off, which the register already handles. **`T5` is
rollback-cheap precisely because it lands before `T6`:** while capture posts nothing, a
miscategorised row is a tidy-up.

## 2026-09-01 · 🔧 FIXING `DEF-2416` — "LEVEL IS DUE" CROSSES INTO PAYMENTS, AND THE ONE JUDGMENT THE RULING DID NOT REACH (law 13)

**No new rule and no new figure.** `BR-BIL-072` is the PO's ruling of 2026-08-11, verbatim *"Level
is due"*, closing `OQ-140` and `DEF-062`. On ❄️ WE-8's July bill the charges are **292.87** and the
level is **242.00**, so the bill ASKS for 242.00 and paying 242.00 settles the month. Billing has
answered that question since August through `selectors.amount_due_for`. **Payments never asked it**,
and measured every bill at `invoices.total`.

**WHAT THAT COST, IN THE ONE FIGURE THAT MATTERS: 50.87 A MONTH, FOR EVER.** A budget customer who
paid exactly the 242.00 they were asked for was recorded as still owing the 292.87 − 242.00
variance. The S22 bill picker offered a clerk a bill nobody owed; `outstanding_positions` added
50.87 to the account's balance, so the S34 debtors list showed a debtor who was not one; and
`ladder.run_ladder` reads that same balance, so the reminder and the disconnect notices went to a
customer who had paid on time. That is `DEF-062`'s own harm one module along, and both modules were
internally consistent and green throughout.

**THE FIX IS TO ASK, NOT TO COPY.** Both reads on `apps/payments/billing_seam.py` now resolve
`apps.billing.selectors.amount_due_for` BY NAME — the idiom that seam already uses for
`invoice_queryset` — and call it per bill. If billing ever stops publishing it, the seam falls back
to the issued total and REPORTS `bill_amount_due_unavailable` rather than re-deriving the level out
of `bill_payload` itself. `apps/customers/payment_plan.py` states the reason once and it is the
reason here: *"a second copy of a ruled figure is how two figures start disagreeing."*

### THE JUDGMENT — WHAT "PREVIOUS BALANCE" MEANS ON THE NEXT BILL

**This is the decision the ruling did not reach, and it is ours (law 13).** `apps/billing/
payments_seam.prior_position_for_account` builds `BR-BIL-035`'s balance-forward block — *previous
balance − payments & credits = open balance* — and it derived the middle line **by subtraction**:
`allocated += total - balance`. That was exact for as long as every bill's ask WAS its total.

The moment payments began measuring a budget bill at its level, the same subtraction would have
printed, on the bill of a customer who had paid **nothing**:

    Previous balance   292.87
    Payments & credits  50.87
    Open balance       242.00

Three lines that foot, and the middle one a claim about a payment that does not exist.

**DECIDED: previous balance is what the earlier bills ASKED for, and payments & credits is what was
actually allocated.** Both operands are taken from the seam's own carried facts (`amount_due` and
`allocated`), so the block foots BY CONSTRUCTION rather than by arithmetic, and every line is a
figure somebody can point at. The block for that customer now reads **242.00 · 0.00 · 242.00**.

The alternative — keep summing totals and take `allocated` from the seam — was rejected because the
three lines then stop footing (292.87 − 0.00 ≠ 242.00), and `PriorPosition`'s whole contract is that
they foot however the split is drawn.

**❄️ NOTHING FROZEN MOVES.** `amount_due` equals `total` for every bill that is not budget-billing,
so ❄️ WE-1's `45.00 − 0.00 + 247.87 = 292.87` and ❄️ PE-4's carried **57.13** are byte-identical, and
a test asserts the ordinary case beside the budget one for exactly that reason.

### WHAT MOVED ON THE MONEY PATH, SAID PLAINLY

**A payment now settles a budget bill at its level**, so 242.00 closes the month and anything beyond
it carries as account credit under `BR-PAY-010` — what any other overpayment already does. Paying
short still leaves a real, chaseable balance: **200.00 against the 242.00 ask leaves 42.00**, not
92.87, and the ladder still runs on it. No rounding site was added, no B4/B5 figure moved, and the
allocator is untouched — it still reads `balance` alone and this seam still owns the subtraction.

`CR-059` CS-4 said in terms *"no money logic moves and the allocator is untouched"* and that is why
the read lane filed this rather than fixing it. **This is the defect fix, not that change**, and
moving what a payment settles is the whole of what the defect asks for.

### WHAT IS NOT TOUCHED, DELIBERATELY

The **settle-up** month and the variance chain are billing's and `OQ-142` is still open on which
account the settle-up line touches. Nothing here ages, rounds or posts.

### THE ROLLBACK, STATED BEFORE SHIPPING

Reverting the commit puts both seam reads back on `invoice.total`, drops `amount_due` from the
open-bills row, and restores the subtraction in the balance-forward block. Every ordinary bill is
unaffected either way. What comes back is the defect: budget customers reading as owing their
variance, on the debtors list and in the ladder.

### AND A SECOND ENTRY THE SAME DAY — `DEF-438` IS NOT WHAT ITS ROW SAYS

`DEF-438` has read *"the R1–R7 resolution chain has no production caller at all"* since 2026-08-21
and it was true for ten days. It is not true at **2.123.0**: `CR-057` shipped
`SBH_BILLING_RESOLUTION_STEPS` defaulting to **R3,R4**, so the chain prices the base charge of every
account on every deployment that has not deliberately rolled it back. **R1, R2, R5, R6 and R7 are
still served by the bill run's own narrowing**, so the row is `partially-fixed` rather than closed.

**Three comments were still describing the old world and are corrected** (hard-won law 1). The one
that mattered was `gather.GATHER_RULED_PATH_REFUSED`, which said the refusal *"cannot be raised"* —
it can, and `DEF-2923` is what it looked like the first time a tenant with no `is_base` charge code
declared for a service met it.

## 2026-09-01 · 📐 `DEF-2487` AND `DEF-2805` DO NOT SHARE A FIX — THE FIRST MAKES THE SECOND MORE REACHABLE

Recorded because the two rows sit next to each other in the register, both are about a
big import surviving, and the obvious reading — *"one fix closes both"* — is wrong in a
way that would cost the next lane a day.

**`DEF-2487` is about the sixty-second wall in FRONT of the worker.** A 1,048-account
commit ran inline inside a web request; `docker-entrypoint.sh` runs gunicorn with
`--timeout 60`; the worker was killed at 60.8 seconds with the transaction open and
zero accounts written. **It is fixed** — `ASYNC_ROW_BAR_BY_TARGET[(accounts, load)] = 100`
against a measured 90–94 ms per account, so anything above 100 rows goes to a BE-07
worker, a deferral REFUSES when no worker would run it, and a queue nothing has claimed
reports itself `stalled` on the screen after 30 seconds.

**`DEF-2805` is about the hard kill INSIDE that worker.** `CELERY_TASK_TIME_LIMIT` kills
a task outright; `core.jobs.start()` admits `queued → running` and `failed → running`
and nothing else, so the re-delivered message for a hard-killed job raises `JobsError`
and **the record keeps saying `running` for ever.** Nothing reaps it and nothing can
resume it.

**So the relationship is the opposite of shared:** `DEF-2487`'s fix moves the accounts
commit ONTO the path `DEF-2805` describes, and it lowers the bar to 100 rows, which puts
**almost every real migration** on it. The soft limit is what keeps the hard kill rare —
it raises inside the task with 300 seconds of headroom, so the ordinary failure path
writes the row and the checkpoint survives — but the backstop behind it is still open.

**Nothing is changed here.** `DEF-2805`'s own prevention column names the two ways to
close it (admit `running → running` when the record's worker is demonstrably gone, or a
management command that fails a job running longer than the hard limit) and says both
need a decision about **what proves a worker is gone**. That decision is not taken in
passing while closing a different row, and its severity (`medium`) is judged against a
condition only a live database can show.

## 2026-09-01 · 💰 `CR-059` CS-36 — WHEN A BILL IS CORRECTED, THE PAYMENT COMES OFF IT FIRST (tasks 14 · 19)

The one gap in `CR-059` that is fully wired, reachable today and puts a **wrong number in
front of a paying customer**. Ajinkya pays **100.00** for a **100.00** bill, on time. Staff
correct the bill to **80.00**. The correction writes four correct things — a credit note for
−100.00, a replacement bill at 80.00 carrying the ORIGINAL due date, the original moved to
`corrected`, an audit row — **and never touches the payment.** So his 100.00 goes on pointing
at a bill that payments can no longer see, and the product says two different things at once:

| | what it said | what it says now |
|---|---|---|
| His account screen | outstanding **80.00** · credit **0.00** · **six days late** | outstanding **0.00** · credit **20.00** · **not late** |
| The books | receivable **−20.00** (the utility owes him 20.00) | unchanged — **−20.00** |
| The difference | **100.00, reported by nothing** | **none** |

He also entered the collection ladder, and the first notice was for a bill he had overpaid.

**The whole fix is ONE inserted step:** between the credit note and the replacement, release the
allocations — one negative mirror row per payment, hung off that payment, editing nothing. Then
the credit position rises by itself (it is computed from rows) and the replacement bill's
existing draw-down consumes it. **Nothing else was built:** both halves already worked and were
starved of this one input.

**SEVEN JUDGMENTS WERE OURS TO MAKE. Each is here with its worked figure** (law 13 — a judgment
recorded is the deliverable; a question is the failure to make one).

**1 · The release is PER PAYMENT and NET, not one mirror per original row.** CS-36 describes
*"one negative allocation row mirroring each original row"*, which is what a bounced cheque
writes. Copied literally it is wrong on the second run: a replay would mirror its own negative
rows back into POSITIVES and re-apply the whole **100.00** to a bill nobody owes. Summing per
payment instead makes a replay find **0.00** still applied and write nothing, which is the
idempotency CS-36 asks for **without minting a new key** — and it is also right on a bill whose
payment already bounced, where the net is 0.00 and there is nothing to release.

**2 · An unreachable payments module REFUSES the correction.** This is the OPPOSITE of the rule
one function away: `apply_credit_at_issue` reports and lets the bill issue, because a deployment
that cannot reach payments must still be able to bill. Here, proceeding writes the credit note,
issues the replacement and leaves the money on a bill nothing reads — **the exact 100.00 silence
above, with nothing reporting it.** A loud refusal that leaves the bill correctable beats a
silent wrong number reaching a customer (hard-won law 3).

**3 · The release refuses to run outside an open transaction.** CS-36 makes the ORDER a rule and
says why it has to be one: *"it is invisible in the code and will otherwise be tidied into the
wrong order."* Two failure modes, both customer-facing — after the replacement issues, the
replacement draws on a credit that does not exist yet and goes out unsettled at the ORIGINAL due
date (overdue on arrival); in a transaction of its own, a failure between the two leaves a
customer holding **100.00** of credit against no bill. The ordering half is asserted by test
against the real correction; the transaction half is enforced by the service itself, so a future
caller cannot lose it by omission.

**4 · "Already paid in full" is measured at what the bill ASKS, not at its total.** ❄️ WE-8's
budget bill totals **292.87** and asks for **242.00**. Measured at the total, a customer who paid
exactly what they were asked reads as **50.87** short and no warning appears — `DEF-2416` in a
new place, and a SECOND definition of "settled", which is the shape of this whole defect. It
reads billing's own `amount_due_for` (`BR-BIL-072`, the PO's *"Level is due"*).

**5 · The warning is raised on a RESTATEMENT only.** A goodwill concession leaves the bill
untouched (PO 2026-08-11, *"you dont touch the bill"*) and a document correction moves 0.00, so
on neither can an existing payment go anywhere wrong. Raising it on all three would be noise on
the two where there is nothing to notice.

**6 · The release posts NO journal line, and the consequence is named rather than left.** No
money moves: the cash is in the books, the credit note has reversed the original's revenue and
receivable, and the replacement posts its own. ⚠ The released money therefore sits in the books
inside **`1200 Accounts receivable`** rather than in **`2400 Customer credit`**, because
`credit.apply_credit_at_issue` posts nothing either. **The AR control still ties out to the
penny** — 0.00 owed − 20.00 held = **−20.00**, against **−20.00** in the books — which is the
assertion CS-36 asks for and the one that would have caught the original defect. Reclassifying
between two ledger accounts is a finance question about the credit-application path and was not
taken here.

**7 · No route and no role gate.** Every other change in this wave adds a door; this one does
not. The only caller is the correction, which already carries the workflow's approval
(`BR-BIL-014`), and a second way to release an allocation would be a way to move a customer's
money that no approval covers.

**A SENTENCE ON SCREEN STOPS BEING A PROMISE AND STARTS BEING TRUE.** The S30 preview has told
approvers, on every downward correction, that *"if the original was already paid, the difference
stays on the account as a credit and comes off the next bill; they can ask for it back
instead"*. Until today the difference did not stay on the account and did not come off the next
bill. Nothing on any screen has to change for it to become true — which is why nobody noticed.

**Rules written:** `BR-PAY-1072` (the release, append-only) · `BR-PAY-1073` (no journal line;
the tie-out is the proof) · `BR-PAY-1074` (before the replacement, in one transaction).
**Nothing frozen moved:** `10-scripts/03-golden-verify.py` **33 PASS, 0 FAIL** before and after
(document self-consistency — it imports no application code), engine-verified coverage unchanged
at **14 of 61 GTs**. Nothing here rounds anything: every figure is a Σ of stored allocation
amounts with its sign flipped.

## 2026-09-02 · 📐 THE COLLECTION LADDER NOW RUNS ON A SCHEDULE — AND THE THING THAT MADE THAT SAFE WAS A DEFECT NOBODY HAD FILED (`CR-059` CS-10, task 54)

`CR-059` CS-10 asked for one thing: register a job so the collection sequence advances
without a person pressing a button, **on the utility's own business day rather than on
UTC**. Its Backend paragraph also says *"the idempotence it needs already holds — one
step per account per pass is enforced in the engine, so a double run cannot double-notice
anybody."*

**That sentence is false, and it is the whole of `DEF-3150`.**

### THE FIGURE, IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Every step of the sequence has its date worked out from **the oldest unpaid bill**, and
from nothing else. So take a customer whose bill fell due on **1 July** and look at them
on **1 September**. The friendly reminder was due 4 July, the ten-day disconnect notice on
14 July, the five-day on 19 July and the certified final on 22 July — **all four are
overdue at the same moment.** The engine takes one step per *pass*, so:

    pass 1  →  the friendly reminder goes out
    pass 2  →  the TEN-DAY DISCONNECT NOTICE goes out
    pass 3  →  the five-day notice
    pass 4  →  the certified 48-hour final, which costs about $8.00 to post

Four letters, one afternoon, one customer — and each pass was individually correct. A
clerk could already do this by pressing *Run* four times on the Outstandings screen; a
scheduled job would do it whenever the message queue re-delivered a task, which it is
configured to do on purpose.

### THE JUDGMENT — ONE LETTER PER CUSTOMER PER BUSINESS DAY

The engine now records the day it last wrote to a customer and takes no further step for
them that day. This is not a new rule: the engine's own note has said *"an account 58 days
overdue must not receive four notices in one afternoon"* since it shipped, and the
collections summary in `CR-059` §7 says the same. What was missing was anything enforcing
it. The guard reads the **same** record the manual screen writes, so it counts a clerk's
letter and the job's letter as one and the same — press the button in the morning and the
6 a.m. sweep the next day still moves on normally.

Two details that were decided rather than assumed, both recorded here because a later
reader would otherwise have to guess:

* **It is tested LAST, after all five of the reasons the sequence stops.** Those five are
  facts about the customer — what they owe, what they agreed, what their doctor said — and
  their order was ruled. This one is a fact about the *run*. So a customer who is both
  under the $25.00 floor and already written to today is reported as under the floor,
  which is the answer that is still true tomorrow.
* **A re-run for an earlier date is also stopped.** The engine deliberately allows a job
  to be re-run "for last Tuesday". Doing that against a customer written to since would
  post a letter to somebody who has already moved on, and would stamp last Tuesday's date
  over a newer one. So any letter dated on or after the day being re-run stops the pass.

### THE SCHEDULE ITSELF, AND THE THREE THINGS IT REFUSES TO RUN WITHOUT

**It runs on the utility's clock, and that is the requested change.** A single scheduled
job has one clock for the whole system, and eleven utilities in eleven time zones do not
share a 6 a.m. So the job wakes every fifteen minutes and asks each utility one question:
*is it your hour yet, on your clock?* At **11:05 UTC on 22 August** a utility in Texas is
at **06:05 on the 22nd** and its sequence runs for the 22nd; at **04:30 UTC** the same
utility is still on the **21st**, and a job running on the server's clock would have
chased that customer on the wrong date entirely.

Three things stop it, and all three are the safe direction:

1. **It is switched OFF for every utility until somebody turns it on.** Installing this
   code chases nobody. The alternative — a deployment that starts writing to customers on
   its own — would be a change to a utility's collections practice made by a software
   release. The hour is stored beside the switch and starts at **6 a.m.**, which is early
   enough that a notice printed overnight is on a desk when the office opens; it is a
   starting value on a screen, not a rule.
2. **No medical-hold list, no run.** A customer with a medical certificate is excluded
   from every step of the sequence. The engine is handed that list and never works it out
   for itself — a clinical fact is not payments' to infer. `apps/customers/disconnects.
   medical_hold_for` has existed since 2026-08-25 saying of itself *"AND NOTHING CALLS IT
   YET"*, and **this is its first caller.** If it cannot be reached, the scheduled run
   stops for that utility rather than running with nobody excluded. A clerk pressing the
   button is looking at the account; a job at six in the morning is looking at nobody.
3. **No settings, no run.** The existing rule already refuses rather than falling back to
   defaults, in its own words: *"an unreachable setting is not a setting."* One
   misconfigured utility stops itself and not the others.

### WHAT IT STILL CANNOT DO, SAID OUT LOUD RATHER THAN LEFT TO BE FOUND

* **The partial-payment pause has never worked and this does not fix it** (`DEF-3151`).
  A customer who pays part of what they owe is supposed to be left alone if the payment
  clears the utility's percentage. The engine can do it; **nothing in the product has ever
  told it what the customer paid** — not the scheduled job and not the Outstandings
  button. Worked on the fixture the rule was ruled against: **$150 against $948 is 15.8%**,
  and the engine cannot even reach that arithmetic because the $150 never arrives. Closing
  it needs an answer to a question nobody has asked: *paid recently — over what period?*
  (`OQ-1320`). Both are carried on every scheduled result rather than left silent.
* **Nothing records that the sequence ran** (`OQ-1321`). The screen work asks Outstandings
  to say *when it last ran, what it did and when it runs next*. Three of those four are
  answerable from settings and are published; *when it last ran* and *what it did* are
  not, because no table holds a record of a pass. That table belongs with the screen that
  reads it, which is task 55.
* **On the host this product is deployed to, it does not fire at all** — and not because
  of anything in this change. The deployment notes already record that that host needs
  three things done on it before any scheduled work runs there. Registering the job does
  not change that, and this is stated rather than implied.

### THE SENTENCE ON THE SCREEN

Outstandings prints **"Nothing runs the collection sequence overnight. It only moves when
someone asks it to from this screen."** in eleven languages. It is now capable of being
false — but only where the scheduler is actually running **and** that utility has switched
it on, and neither implies the other. So it is withdrawn exactly there and kept
everywhere else. Withdrawing it wholesale would print a promise the product does not keep,
which is hard-won law 1 with the sign flipped. The replacement panel is task 55's, and
`DEF-3154` holds the gap.

### AND THE ONE THAT WENT THE OTHER WAY — `CR-059` CS-19 WAS ALREADY BUILT (task 13)

CS-19 says *"Payments publishes the figure; billing never asks for it"*, so a customer who
paid their deposit at the counter is charged for it again on their first bill. **Billing
has asked for it since 2026-08-15.** The two modules are joined by name at the moment of
the call rather than by an import, which is exactly why searching the code for a caller
finds nothing — and `apps/payments/credit.py` still carried the sentence **"⚠ NOTHING
CALLS IT"** on the function itself, which is where the CR's line came from (`DEF-3152`).

What genuinely had never been done is CS-19's own proof. The existing tests stop at the
priced draft; that file says of itself *"This file never issued one."* **That is not a
detail** — it is how `DEF-181` survived for weeks, with the deposit priced perfectly on a
bill that could not be issued at all. So the missing half is now proved on the **issued**
bill, on the signed figures: **$150.00 asked, $150.00 paid at the counter, and no deposit
line on the bill** — not a $0.00 one, which would say a deposit was charged and waived.
Part-paid: **$150.00 asked, $50.00 paid, $100.00 billed**, untaxed.

Task 13 is therefore **landed as already-built plus its missing proof**, and the two stale
sentences that sent this lane looking for work already finished are corrected in place
(`DEF-3152`, `DEF-3153`).

## 2026-09-02 · 📐 A CREDIT NOTE GETS A NUMBER, AND THE SIGN-OFF PANEL STOPS PRINTING A DATABASE ID (`CR-059` CS-37 · tasks 27/28/29)

**The breach, as `CR-059` filed it.** The bill-run sign-off panel names the credit notes in
a run, and where a note had no number it fell back to the row's **database id** — so a
finance user signing off a run read a sentence with a raw UUID in it. **B14 rule 31 forbids
it outright**, ratified 2026-08-31 in the PO's own words: *"no Databse ID on screen - that
is a rule"*.

**And the fallback was not an edge case — it was the ONLY branch that ever ran.** Every
credit note in the product carried `credit_note_no: null`, because the tenant's **Credit
memo #** series was seeded, formatted `CM-0001` and **never asked for a number by any code
in the product**.

### What landed

**Both writers now mint a number.** `corrections.execute_credit_only` (the goodwill
concession) and `corrections.execute_restatement` (the full reversal) each call
`_allocate_credit_note_no` inside their own existing `@transaction.atomic`. Two credit
notes raised in one bill run take **`CM-0001` then `CM-0002`** — consecutive, proved by
running both corrections through the real writer and the real series
(`tests/test_cr059_cs37_credit_note_identity.py`).

**The id fallback is deleted, not softened.** `release._credit_note_label` now names a
credit note by its number, or — on a historic row that has none — by **the bill it was
raised against and the date**, and where neither exists it says so in words. CS-37's
rollback note is explicit that restoring the fallback is not an option: *"it is a rule
breach, not a safety net."*

**The account can be asked the question it could not be asked before.**
`GET /accounts/{id}/credit-notes` and S21's new **Credits** tab. Before this, to find every
credit note a customer had ever been given somebody had to open each of their bills one at
a time — and `ix_credit_notes_account`, the index built on (tenant, account) for exactly
that lookup, had **never had a query run against it**.

### Four judgments where the rules ran out, each with its worked figure

**1 · A MISSING SERIES ROW IS REPORTED, NEVER FAKED, AND NEVER STOPS THE CORRECTION.**
CS-37 says a credit note takes its number from the series; it does not say what happens on
a tenant provisioned before that series existed. Two readings: refuse the correction, or
write the row unnumbered and say so. **The row is written unnumbered**, on
`runs._allocate_run_no`'s established posture (*"a missing series row is REPORTED, never
faked… refusing to create the run instead would stop a utility billing over a settings
gap"*) — and CS-37's own rule is what makes it safe, because *"historic rows keep a null
number; they are NOT back-filled"*, so a numberless credit note is already a state every
reader must handle. The gap travels as `numbering_series_missing` on the correction's audit
context, the same code `create_run` uses.

**2 · THE FROZEN FIGURE DOES NOT MOVE, AND IT IS ASSERTED RATHER THAN ASSUMED.** ❄️ GT-6 is
*a $25.00 goodwill credit against a $247.30 invoice leaves the customer owing $222.30*,
finance-signed 2026-08-08. Giving a credit note a NAME cannot change what it is WORTH, and
the panel still reads **gross 247.30 · credits 25.00 · amount 222.30**. A test asserts all
three, so drift goes red.

**3 · THE PANEL'S CREDIT-NOTE NAMES ARE PUBLISHED AS DATA, NOT AS PROSE.** The server
already composed a sentence naming the notes, and that sentence carries a PO ruling, a date
and the GT-6 worked figure — none of which belongs on a clerk's screen (B14 rule 32: no rule
id or internal code in clerk-facing copy; gate G28: no internal reference reaches a screen).
So `RunSummary` now publishes `credit_count` and `credits_named` **structurally**, S31
renders a one-sentence line from its own catalogue, and the prose stays where it was, for
the support line. A run with **no** credit notes draws no line at all — a stated absence is
closed by default (rule 32).

**4 · THE CREDITS TAB BORROWS BILLING'S COLUMN WORDS RATHER THAN MINTING ITS OWN.** S28's
bill-detail panel already lists these rows under **Credit note · Amount · Reason · Issued**.
The tab reuses those four keys and `Bill #` from the account's own recent-bills panel. One
concept, one vocabulary, on two screens — which is what B14 is for — and **five fewer new
keys** across eleven catalogues.

### Where the tab sits, and why

Tenth tab, **immediately after Payments**. A customer ringing about a credit they were given
is looking at what they paid and what they were let off in one conversation; putting it at
the end of nine tabs would answer the question in the wrong place.

### What is NOT done, stated rather than left to be found

* **No historic row is back-filled.** The row freezes at issue, and a migration that
  rewrote history would be exactly what the freeze exists to prevent. The
  bill-and-date branch is therefore **permanent**, not transitional.
* **Nothing nets a credit note into a balance.** Neither the outstanding figure nor the
  account credit reads this table, and making a READ start doing so would give the account
  balance two sources of truth in two modules — the smaller alternative CS-38 rejects by
  name. CS-38 owns that half.
* **No rendered check of S31 exists**, and this work does not claim to be one. The backend
  test scans every string the panel serves for a uuid, and a `BillRunWizard` case scans the
  rendered page — but B14's own status table says no gate in this repository reads rendered
  output, and that is still true.

## 2026-09-02 · 📐 CS-34's "THE REFERENCE MAY BE AMENDED" COLLIDES WITH HARD RULE 4, AND THE COLLISION GOES TO THE PO (`CR-059` CS-34 · task 41)

**What CS-34 asks for.** A mistyped cheque number changes nothing financial and cannot be
fixed. Its cost is real: the reference is what a bank line is matched on, so a wrong one is
an unmatched line and a reconciliation nobody can finish.

**Why it stopped short of writing.** CS-34's first new rule is *"the reference and memo may
be amended"*. CLAUDE.md hard rule 4 says a payment accepts **no UPDATE and no DELETE, ever**
— and that is a database trigger, not a convention (`payments/0002`,
`payments_payment_immutable`). **`CR-059` §2 lists thirteen signed statements this change
request reverses and hard rule 4 is not among them**, so the supersession would have been
ours to assume. Law 13 puts that on the Product Owner.

⚠ **AND THE VERSION THAT "WORKS" WOULD HAVE SHIPPED GREEN.** Those triggers are PostgreSQL
only and the test suite hardcodes in-memory SQLite, so the one-line `update(confirmation=…)`
passes every test in this repository and raises on the first real cheque — law 14, one
module along from where it was learned. A test case records that limit rather than leaving
it to be discovered, and a second case proves the refusal on a real cluster.

**So the question is raised with its three readings** (widen the trigger's allow list · a new
append-only amendments table · correct by reversal, which already works), and **most of
CS-34 is built anyway**: the named endpoint — deliberately not a PATCH, and no PATCH, PUT or
DELETE is added to any payment path — every money field refused BY NAME, the tender refused
once the payment is in a deposit batch, the required note, and the audit row's shape composed
and asserted. Only the write raises, naming the question.

**One judgment taken rather than asked.** CS-34 names five fields that may never be amended;
the refusal list carries **sixteen**. A list that enumerated only the five it happened to
mention would let the sixth through the day somebody sent it, which is the *"a route that
accepts a partial body invites the next field to be added to it"* failure the spec is written
to prevent, one layer in. An unknown field is refused too, for the same reason: silently
dropping one is how a clerk comes to believe a correction landed.

## 2026-09-02 · 🔧 AN ID ALLOCATOR THAT SCANS PROSE READS CLAUDE.md's OWN EXAMPLE AS A REAL ID — AND PROPOSED `OQ-12346`

**Found while allocating ids at push time** (`CR-059` CS-34 lane), and worth a row
because the mistake is invisible in the output: the allocator printed a number, the
number looked like a number, and only a human comparing it to the register would
have noticed it was **eleven thousand above every real question in the product.**

**WHAT HAPPENED.** Law 11's last clause says to re-derive allocated ids from the
PUSHED world at push time. The helper written for it scanned `OQ-\d{3,5}(?!\d)`
across the open-questions register, the decision log, the change register and the
reservations file. **The decision log and the change register both quote
CLAUDE.md's Screen-IDs paragraph**, and that paragraph contains the literal
examples `OQ-12345` and `OQ-123456` — written there to explain why the lookahead
is load-bearing. So `max + 1` came back **`OQ-12346`**.

**THE LOOKAHEAD WAS RIGHT AND THE CORPUS WAS WRONG.** `DEF-2804` is about the
PATTERN — three digits silently reading `OQ-1190` as `OQ-119` — and the fix for it
was correct and is unchanged. This is the other half: **a vocabulary's maximum is
read from ITS OWN REGISTER, never from prose that quotes examples of it.** The
open-questions register's real maximum at the pinned tip is `OQ-1321`; this lane
took **`OQ-1322`**.

**AND A SECOND ID WAS SKIPPED ON PURPOSE, WHICH IS `DEF-1787` WORKING.** The
defect register at the tip ends at `DEF-3155`, so `max + 1` is `DEF-3156` — and a
sibling lane's own commit message on this branch already says *"it is filed as
DEF-3156"*, meaning that row exists in a worktree that has not pushed. Every
`max + 1` reads the pushed world plus its own checkout, so both lanes would have
computed the same number correctly. **A gap is harmless — ids are never reused —
and a duplicate in a 3,000-row register reads as a register rather than as an
error.** So this lane took **`DEF-3158`** and left 3156 to its author.

**The cheap generalisation, for whoever writes the next allocator:** scan the
REGISTER for the vocabulary you are allocating from, and nothing else. Add the
decision log or a change request to the corpus and you are asking prose for a
maximum, which is what prose is worst at.

## 2026-09-02 · 💵 THE LAST THREE SERVICES THAT COULD NOT BILL NOW BILL — AND THE ONE JUDGMENT IT TOOK WAS WHICH UNIT A CAPACITY LINE IS PRICED PER

**Plainly, and this is the whole result.** A utility that ticks only Solar, only
Broadband or only Battery at signup used to get 70 addresses, 118 units and **no
bills at all** — every one of its 48 customer seats was refused. It now gets
**96 bills**, the same number a Trash utility gets. **Nine of the ten services a
person can buy now produce bills**; the tenth is Sewer, which correctly cannot be
sold on its own because it is priced as a share of the water bill and there is no
water. Measured on a real PostgreSQL 16.13, one utility per service, through the
same sign-up the product uses. This closes `DEF-3156`.

**What was actually missing.** Two fixes landed the day before and each looked
complete from its own side. One gave these three services a demo estate; the
other made the price list follow whatever service the utility sells. Neither
wrote a price-list entry for a service billed on **what is installed** rather
than on what a meter reads. A service the price list has no entry for is simply
absent from it — which looks exactly like a service the utility does not sell —
so nothing anywhere counted the difference, and the customers could not be opened
for want of a plan. The three now get the same three things Trash has had since
its own fix: a price-list entry, a line on the plan, and a base charge.

**Every figure on those bills is $0.00, and that is the answer rather than a
gap.** No signed figure prices solar, broadband or battery, and the rule for a
service whose sizing nobody has recorded is already decided — *"Bill it as
zero"* (`BR-MET-108`) — so the bill carries a line saying so instead of a
silence. Worked: a solar customer's June bill reads `solar usage 0 × $0.0000 =
$0.00`, a `$0.00` base and `$0.00` tax. The day somebody records how solar is
sized and what it costs, both figures move together and the same bills carry real
money.

**THE ONE JUDGMENT, MADE HERE RATHER THAN ASKED (law 13), WITH ITS COST STATED.**
A price has to be quoted *per something* — the product refuses a quantity with no
unit on it, on purpose (hard rule 3). The unit chosen is **`month`**, and three
candidates were rejected for reasons worth keeping:

* **`kW DC`, `Mbps`, `kW`** — the units `BR-TEN-170` names for how each of these
  services is *sized*. Using one would answer an open question — `OQ-370`, which
  sizing fact each service has and in what unit — inside a fixture, which is the
  one thing a seeder may never do.
* **`panel`, `kW block`** — `BR-RAT-022`'s own examples. They belong to the
  `capacity` pricing model, whose input is `account_capacities`, a table with no
  DDL in any signed document, so that model cannot produce a bill from seeded
  data at all.
* **A word for the equipment counted** (`panel`, `modem`, `battery`) — the most
  honest of the three, and rejected because none is in the platform's unit
  catalogue: a clerk reopening the schedule would find a unit the picker cannot
  offer, and minting catalogue entries would itself answer `OQ-370`.

`month` is in `lookup_defaults.json.uoms`, is offered to every service, and is
already what `SERVICE_DEFAULT_UOMS` declares broadband's unit to be — so
broadband takes it from its own row rather than from a constant, and the seeded
schedule satisfies the 2026-09-02 schedule-unit-versus-billed-unit ruling
(`uom_gate_for`) **by construction** rather than by luck.

⚠ **AND THE COST IS REAL AND IS WRITTEN AT THE LINE THE FIGURE SITS ON.** The
quantity that reaches the bill is `BR-RAT-090`'s **count of installed
equipment**, and a count is not a measure of months — the same mistake `DEF-497`
records, where the trash schedule read *$15.00 per MONTH* against a quantity of 3
CARTS. **It is harmless here only because both factors are zero**: no capacity
equipment is seeded, so the count is 0 on every unit, and the price is a stored
0. So the price and the unit are ONE decision — whoever signs a real capacity
price must move the unit in the same commit — and `core.sample_fixture
.CAPACITY_UOM` says exactly that where the number lives.

**What did not move.** `10-scripts/03-golden-verify.py` reports **33 PASS / 0
FAIL** before and after — document self-consistency, which is what that number
is — and the engine-verified count is **14 of the 61** signed golden tests on
both sides. `GT-15`'s two capacity figures still price from real rows unchanged:
**solar 4 × $10.00 = $40.00** and **battery 2 × $12.00 = $24.00**. A water
utility's seeded bills are byte-identical.

**One copy fix came with it, because this lane made it reach more people.** A
plan for a utility with no metered service described itself as *"Sample plan.  at
a $0.00 monthly base; usage is not priced on this plan yet."* — two spaces where
the service name goes, and a clause about usage on a plan that prices none. It
has been true of every Trash-only utility since `DEF-2414`. It now reads *"Sample
plan. Trash — billed on the equipment recorded at each unit, with no monthly
base."*

**Reported rather than fixed, because it is not this lane's and it is red on the
branch already:** `tests/test_us_rat_schedules.py` has **14 failing cases** and
`tests/test_def2799_seeded_size_axis.py` **1**, identically at the pinned tip
`c7df5026` and with this change — verified in a detached worktree. Thirteen of
the fifteen fail inside `_guard_base_charge_code` on
`rating.schedules.no_base_charge_code`, which is `DEF-2923`'s gate becoming
unconditional once the ruled chain states the base; the last asserts that battery
size bands still raise, which `DEF-2408` deliberately stopped doing when the PO
dissolved that question.

## 2026-09-02 · 💰 A GOODWILL CREDIT NOW REDUCES WHAT THE CUSTOMER OWES — AND THE ONE THING WE HAD TO DECIDE WAS WHICH SIDE POSTS IT (`CR-059` CS-35 · CS-38 · tasks 8/22/24)

**The problem, in one sentence.** A utility gives a customer **$25.00** off a **$247.30**
bill, the books record it correctly, an email goes out telling the customer about it — and
then every figure the customer and the clerk can read still says **$247.30**, the next bill
is worked out without the $25.00, and the collection ladder chases them for the lot. Of
everything `CR-059` found, this is the only one where the customer has been told something
in writing that the product then contradicts.

**Why it happened, and it is not a bug in the accounting.** The concession is written into
its own table, `credit_notes`, and posted correctly. But what a person reads comes from two
other sums: **what is owed** is bills less payments applied, and **credit on account** is
payments less what they met less refunds. **Neither of them has ever looked at credit
notes**, and nothing was ever going to make them — so the money was real in the books and
invisible everywhere else.

### The three decisions this took, each with its worked figure

**1 · WHICH SIDE POSTS THE CONCESSION — and the answer is BILLING, exactly as it does
today.** `CR-059` left this to the build and warned what it costs to get wrong: *"a double
post here is a real 25.00 of invented money."* Payments now records a credit row for the
same $25.00 so the balance moves, and **that row posts nothing at all**. The books keep the
one entry billing already writes — **$25.00 out of write-off, $25.00 into customer credit**
— which is the entry the Product Owner ruled on 12 August. The alternative was to move the
posting to the payments side; we did not, for three reasons: it would reverse a ruling
nobody asked to reverse, it would file new concessions under a different source from every
one already recorded (one event in two shapes, on rows nobody may go back and fix), and
this module already works this way — when a customer's credit is used up by their next
bill, that too writes the record and posts nothing, because the money reached the books
when it arrived. **Asserted, not promised:** the test counts the journal entries either
side and requires exactly one.

**2 · THE CREDIT SITS ON THE ACCOUNT; IT DOES NOT PAY OFF THE BILL IT CAME FROM.** There is
an open question on file (`OQ-215`) asking precisely whether a goodwill credit reduces
**that** bill to $222.30 or sits as credit and comes off the **next** one. Its own words are
that this *"needs one sentence from the PO and is not a thing an implementer may pick"*, and
that the signed $222.30 is reached either way. The engine already implements the second
reading, so the credit row is written to carry rather than to meet a bill — **recording it
the ordinary way would have paid $25.00 off that very bill and quietly settled the open
question on a money path.** So: the bill still says **$247.30**, credit on account reads
**$25.00**, and what the customer owes is **$222.30**.

**3 · THE UTILITY STOPS CHASING MONEY IT IS ALREADY HOLDING.** This is the judgment nobody
had written down. The collections list and the notice ladder both worked off the bills
alone, so an account holding real credit was chased for the gross. `CR-059` says plainly
that after this change *"the balance, the next bill and the collection ladder all agree with
the letter"*, so the amount we chase is now the bills **less the credit we hold**: on this
case **$247.30 − $25.00 = $222.30**, and the notice quotes $222.30.

**And the deliberate limit on that.** A credit can go **below zero** — a bounced cheque
whose change was already refunded leaves **−$57.13**, and the Product Owner ruled on 11
August that this is *"a real debt"* and is never to be shown as zero. It still is not: the
figure is unchanged everywhere it appears. What we decided is narrower — **a negative credit
does not make the chase bigger.** There is no bill behind it, and a ten-day disconnect
notice would be telling the customer that bills are unpaid which are not. The list says so
out loud rather than dropping it silently.

⚠ **THIS DOES NOT FIX `DEF-3121` AND MUST NOT BE READ AS IF IT HAD.** That defect is an
approved write-off that reduces the books and leaves the debt on the collections list —
**$948.20 at 91 days late, before and after.** A write-off writes no payment and no credit,
so the account's credit is unchanged and it is still chased in full. It stays open.

### What CS-35 added underneath, because CS-38 could not be built without it

The payments table has always had three kinds of row — **payment, credit, adjustment** — and
the screens have always known how to draw all three. **Nothing had ever written anything but
`payment`**, and the recording service did not even accept the choice, so the only way to put
a goodwill credit on an account was to record a **fake payment**: money the utility never
received, sitting in the day's takings. Three things now depend on which kind it is:

* **It never goes to the bank.** A credit is left out of the day's deposit and **named in the
  result** rather than dropped, so a clerk whose drawer does not tie can be told why. Worked:
  a day with **$100.00 cash and a $25.00 credit** banks **$100.00**, and the credit is listed
  as *not cash*.
* **It posts to its own account.** A credit uses the account its reason is mapped to
  (Settings → Accounting → GL mapping — a column added on 17 August that until today
  **nothing had ever read**), and where a reason is not mapped it uses the same **write-off**
  account a goodwill concession already uses, so the two can never drift apart. It never
  touches undeposited funds: no cash arrived, and no bank line is ever coming to explain it.
* **It needs an admin.** A new figure on Settings → Accounting → Finance controls sets the
  amount above which giving money away needs a System Admin, and **it ships at $0.00 — so
  today every credit does.** That is the strict end on purpose: a utility that wants a clerk
  to be able to hand out $10 types the number and is seen typing it. A clerk may still
  **take** $25.00 — taking money is not giving it away.

### The refusal that had expired three weeks earlier (task 8)

The *Issue credit* button on an account was switched off with the explanation that **which
account a goodwill credit should be charged to had not been decided**. It was decided on
**12 August** — *"a separate write-off account"* — and the code implementing it was written
the same week and has been running since. The same expired sentence was in three places: the
server's reason table, the corrections module's own docstring (a paragraph saying that
executing a concession *"raises rather than choosing"*, describing a path that in fact
executes), and the words on the screen. **All three are corrected.**

**The button stays off, with an honest reason instead of a dead one:** every credit note this
product can write is raised **against one bill**, inside the bill-correction workflow. There
is no account-level writer for one to call. The route to a goodwill credit today is to open
the bill and correct it as a concession.

**On-screen wording, reported rather than changed** — the catalogue files are another lane's
this week: `customers.account.action.issueCreditBlocked` should read *"Credits are raised on
a bill. Open the bill to credit it."*

**And a wiring claim that was never true.** The screen's own comment said these refusal
sentences came from the server, *"not sentences typed here — so the day a billing lane
publishes it, the reason stops being true in exactly one place."* The server's table has
never reached that screen; the words are a translation string. So the reason lives in **two**
places, and on 2026-09-02 they disagreed, which is exactly what that comment promised could
not happen. Corrected in the file.
## 2026-09-02 · 💵 FOUR PAYMENTS BACKENDS THAT NOBODY COULD REACH ON A SCREEN, AND THE SENTENCE THAT SAID SO (`CR-059` tasks 6 · 10 · 12 · 20, `DEF-3158`)

**The shape of all four is the same and it is worth saying once.** A backend
landed on 1 September. The screen half did not. So the product held the
behaviour and a person could not get at it — and in three of the four cases the
screen was actively saying something that had stopped being true.

### The figure that matters most, because a clerk acts on it

`BL-2608-018410` was issued at **247.87**. A **200.00** payment left **47.87**
outstanding. Until today a clerk taking money against that bill could not aim it
at 47.87 at all: *"A specific bill"* and *"Split across bills"* have been
confirmed law since 11 August and the allocator has executed both since that
day, but they rendered **disabled**, because nothing served what each open bill
still owed and a picker built on the bill list would have offered **247.87** as
the figure to aim at. **Money aimed at 247.87 on a bill that owes 47.87 is a
wrong allocation nobody looking at the screen can see is wrong**, which is why
the two shipped switched off rather than shipping over the wrong number.

`GET /accounts/{id}/open-bills` landed 1 September and `OQ-154` closed. The
picker is built, the two choices are live, and **the sentence that said they
could not be is deleted from all eleven catalogues.**

### Three judgments this lane made, with what decided each

**(1) The eleventh tab on the account screen is `Plan`, and it sits after
`Credits`.** CS-23 asks for *"the plan tab"* and there was none. It goes beside
Credits rather than at the end because the three money tabs answer one
conversation — what the customer paid, what they were let off, and what they
agreed to pay in instalments — and that is the order somebody on the phone asks
them in. The credit-note lane's tenth tab set the precedent six hours earlier.

**(2) The settlement panel rides INSIDE the preview's sixth section, not in a
tenth one.** `BR-BIL-044` says *"nine sections, all required, none collapsible
away"*, which is a ratified contract and not a layout preference — a lane may
not widen it. `the_customers_balance` is already the section about the
customer's money, and it already carries the `reallocation_plan` sentence that
promised this behaviour and that nobody executed until 1 September. The figures
now sit beside the sentence that promised them. A test asserts the nine stay
nine.

**(3) `min(available, corrected_total)` is the whole of the settlement
arithmetic, and the existing account credit is part of `available`.** CS-36's
three worked shapes all fall out of one line — down 100.00 → 80.00 takes 80.00
and returns 20.00; up → 120.00 takes 100.00 and leaves 20.00 owing; part-paid
60.00 → 80.00 takes 60.00 and leaves 20.00 owing — and adding the account's
existing position is what stops the panel over-stating *still owed* for a
customer who was already in credit. **A NEGATIVE position buys nothing**:
`credit_position_for_account` returns a signed figure and deliberately does not
floor it (`BR-PAY-041`, PO 11 August, *"Yes, it's a real debt"*), and its own
docstring says the caller is what decides that a debt settles nothing. This is
that decision. The debt is still SHOWN — hiding it would be a screen deciding
what a clerk may know about a customer's position.

### Two rule-31 breaches were found in the panels this work touched, and both are closed

Neither was reported by anyone. Both were read while editing the file beside
them, which is the way every one of these has been found.

* **The month-close checklist printed a function name.** An item nobody could
  compute rendered the read it wanted, so a finance user closing the month read
  `apps.payments.selectors.unreconciled_batch_count(start, end) -> int | None`
  on screen. B14 rule 31 names *"a module path, a file name, a function name"*
  outright. The provenance is not deleted — the rule's own sentence moves it to
  `title`, where a support engineer still finds it.
* **The correction preview printed the server's own English.** The warnings list
  rendered `warning.detail`, so a clerk correcting a bill in a closed period
  read *"(BR-TEN-038: a closed period posts to the earliest open one)"*. Two
  rules forbid it — BR-SHL-020 r2 (PO 19 August, *"server detail text should not
  reach customer screens"*) and rule 31 — and the fix is the contract payments'
  own `ProblemList` already follows: the server sends a code, the screen renders
  the language, and the detail keeps travelling for the audit trail.

### `DEF-3158` and the check that would have caught it

Seven screens printed a shortened database id where a number belongs, and
**Budget Bills had no alternative at all** — `01a00000` was the visible value on
every row, every time, not a last resort. Six of the seven had a number field
already and only needed the fallback replaced. The seventh did not: nothing
served the account's number to that tab, so `budget_status_row` serves it now,
read through the reviewed cross-module FK the table already carries, exactly as
the pending queue reads it.

**Why nothing caught it, and this is the useful half.** Rule 31 has three
enforcers and this walked past all of them: `G28` inspects STRINGS and this is a
runtime expression; the two checks that read rendered output cover `S30` and
`S15` alone. And a truncation defeats even those — **`01a00000` is not
uuid-shaped.** It has no dashes, it is eight characters, and it reads like a
reference number, which is why seven lanes wrote it in good faith.

**`G69` is the mechanical source pattern the defect's own prevention column
prescribed** — `<expr>.<id-ish>.slice(` — at a **ceiling of zero**, because all
seven were fixed in the commit that added it and a baseline file for an empty
set is where a rule quietly stops being one. It was proved RED against the real
defect: restoring two of the seven from the tip produced
`FAIL: 2 site(s) put a TRUNCATED DATABASE ID on screen`. **It reads SOURCE, and
its own PASS line says so** — a whole uuid built through a variable still passes
here, and rule 31's rendered half stays unenforced outside those two screens.

### What did not move

No frozen figure. `settlement_preview` READS and writes nothing; the picker
computes no bill balance (the seam did the subtraction and this adds nothing to
it); the plan strip decides no instalment (it mirrors
`plans.earliest_unmet_installment`'s predicate so the screen cannot promise a
different row from the one the service links). `G31` is at **470/470** before
and after — `features/payments/` is not Tailwind-migrated, so every class the
picker and the strip use is one a stylesheet already declares.

**And a number that fell.** `G27`'s translation-coverage debt was **572 against
a baseline of 558** and had been over at every one of the last sixty commits
(`DEF-2394`). Fifteen of the keys in that number belonged to three other lanes
that had reported them and could not write them, because the locale files were
somebody else's this week. They are written. The debt is **555** — under its
baseline for the first time since it was set — and `G32`'s unresolved refusal
keys fell from 7 to 6 with them.
