## 2026-09-04 · `BR-CWP-102` — a credential is not a fifth write point, and the gate that asked the question was right

`G81` went red on `apps/portal/credentials.py` with twelve complaints of two
shapes, and the two shapes have **different answers**. Separating them is the
whole of this entry.

### The `apps.notifications` import — the gate was right and the code changed

`credentials.py` imported `apps.notifications.services` to queue the one-time
code. `G81`'s clause 4 refuses that anywhere under `apps/portal` — *"a write
reached through a service is still a write"* — and it named the file.

**The tempting move was to add `credentials.py` to the gate's allow-list, and
that is the move that turns a guard into decoration.** What was done instead is
the shape **every other module already uses**: `seams/notifications_seam.py`
RESOLVES `notifications.queue_document` by name at call time, exactly as
`apps/metering/seams.py` and `apps/customers/seams.py` do. No file under
`apps/portal` imports another module's services, and `G81` now has nothing to
allow.

**And it turns out not to be an exception at all.** `metering/seams.py` states
the rule in its own words: `outbound_messages` is *"the one table B1 opens to
cross-module writes (B2 r16 #7)"*. The portal was never asking for a fifth write
point; it was using an exception the platform made years of commits ago, and it
was reaching for it the wrong way.

### The `.save()` calls — a third class of write, now `BR-CWP-102`

`credentials.py` and `session.py` write `portal_credential`, `portal_session`
and `portal_one_time_code`. Those are the portal's OWN tables, which is a case
`BR-CWP-001` does not describe: its four kinds — a payment, a service request, a
meter reading, a preference on an account — are all rows in the **utility's
book**, and **none of them is about who is allowed to look**.

**Decided, and written into `02-business-rules.md` as `BR-CWP-102` rather than
left in a gate's data file:** authentication material is a third class. It
changes no balance, no bill, no reading and no preference, and deleting every
row in those three tables would cost a round of password resets and nothing
else. **The test a future lane applies: a file allowed to write here writes a
row the PORTAL ITSELF OWNS and never a row in the utility's book.** The day a
file in that list writes an `Account`, an `Invoice`, a `Payment` or a
`MeterRead`, it IS a fifth write point wearing a different coat — a ruling for
the Product Owner, not an edit.

⚠ **This is a build decision under law 13 and one word reverses it.** It was
not put to the PO because nothing about it collides with a signed rule, touches
a ❄️ FROZEN figure, or needs a fact only they hold.

### Why the question had to be asked twice, and that is the expensive part

**The declaration was already written, in the same commit as the code, with this
reasoning in it** (`5cb4d970`). A whole-file pathspec commit at `5bfc2492`,
from a base that predated it, removed the five lines by subtraction —
hard-won law 11's mechanism two, in the file where it costs most, because those
lines are **a gate's data**. `G81` went red for the whole branch, named a file
whose author had already declared it, and two lanes spent effort re-deriving an
answer that was in the reverted text. `DEF-CWP-3754`.

**The durable half of the fix is not the restore.** It is that the rule now
lives in `02-business-rules.md`, where a whole-file commit to a code file cannot
silently drop it, and that the notifications reach was **removed** rather than
re-declared — so the allow-list entry that got reverted is no longer what stands
between this code and the gate.

## 2026-09-04 · WAVE E — GETTING IN: six judgments, and the one thing a defect row would have made worse

`CR-068` wave E builds the customer's own front door: `portal_credential`, `portal_session`,
`portal_one_time_code`, the seven authentication endpoints, and the balance read behind
`CWP-018`'s consequence panel and Home's tile. Everything below is a decision the rules ran out
on. Nothing here went to the Product Owner, and law 13 is why: every one of them is ours to make
and write down.

### 1 · The password hash is the deployment's configured one, and the field map said `Argon2id`

`03-field-map.md` §1 types `password_hash` **Argon2id**. **`argon2-cffi` is not installed on this
deployment** — `import argon2` fails — so Django's `PASSWORD_HASHERS` resolves to PBKDF2, which is
what `apps/identity/services.py` has hashed every staff password with since 2026-08-09.

Three options were weighed. Adding the dependency puts a package install between this wave and a
working portal, on a network where `npm ci` already hangs; hand-rolling Argon2id is inventing
cryptography; using `make_password` accepts the field map's figure being aspirational today.

**Chosen: `make_password`/`check_password`, the ACTIVE configuration.** The reason is not
convenience — it is that **two hashing policies in one product is worse than one slower hash**. A
deployment that adds Argon2id to `PASSWORD_HASHERS` upgrades staff and customers together and
re-hashes each row on its next sign-in, because that is what Django already does. Two policies
means somebody upgrades one and not the other and nothing says so. The field map is stamped and
this is the record.

### 2 · `outstandings()` is named by the execution plan and is deliberately not composed

Wave E's `E3` says the balance read composes `outstandings()`. **It does not, and this is the one
place this lane departed from its own task text.**

`outstandings()` is the COLLECTIONS view. Read it: it joins `AccountCollectionState`, the live
`PaymentPlan`, `_notice_summaries` and `DeliveryReturnEvent`'s unresolved bad-address flag onto
every row it returns. **Four facts, and every one of them is either on `BR-CWP-052`'s held-back
list or above the issued bill (`BR-CWP-041`).** Composing it would mean assembling the customer's
own collection ladder into a portal response object and then remembering, in every serialiser
forever, to drop it. That is one missing line away from a customer reading the notice count
against their own account.

**`billing_seam.outstanding_positions` is the same arithmetic without them** — and it is what
`outstandings()` itself composes, so nothing is reimplemented and `CR-068` §2d's *no arithmetic of
its own* still holds. `open_bills.open_bill_position` supplies the per-bill detail.

⚠ **`customer_open_bill_position()` was also named and is also not used, for a different reason:**
it keys on the CUSTOMER, and `BR-CWP-008` says a session carries *a set of (account, what they may
do) — **never a customer id on its own***. It happens to give the right answer today because
`portal_delegate` is empty; the day a bookkeeper is invited it silently would not.

### 3 · The owing figure is the NET one, and the other two are served beside it

`outstanding_positions` returns `balance` net of the credit the utility already holds (`CR-059`
CS-38), while `open_bill_position` returns the gross. They disagree on any account holding credit.

**Chosen: `owing` is the NET figure**, because CS-38's own words are *"the balance, the next bill
and the collection ladder all agree with the letter"* and a portal showing a fourth number is the
exact defect CS-38 closed. `bills_open` and `credit_held` are served beside it and named, so a
screen never has to subtract to explain the difference. On `US-CWP-024` TC-2 the two are equal:
four accounts at `$142.18`, `$0.00`, `$318.04` and `$412.60`, none holding credit, totalling
**`$872.82`**.

### 4 · A credential and a session are a THIRD class of write, and `BR-CWP-001` does not name them

`BR-CWP-001` allows exactly four kinds of row: a payment, a service request, a meter reading, a
preference on an account. `G81` enforces it and refused this lane's first draft by name.

**A credential is none of the four, and adding a fifth `kind` would be the erosion `CR-068` §13
warns about in as many words** (*"Nobody ever decides to allow a fifth; a lane just needs one more
field"*). It is also not a companion of any of the four.

**Chosen: `credentials.py` and `session.py` join `STAFF_WRITE_MODULES` with the reasoning written
into `write_points.py`, and `MODULE_WRITE_TABLES` names exactly the three models they may write.**
The test, stated so a future lane can apply it: **a file there writes a row the PORTAL ITSELF owns
and never a row in the utility's book.** The four kinds are about the utility's records; none of
them describes *who is allowed to look*. Deleting every row in these three tables would cost a
round of password resets and change no balance, no bill and no reading.

⚠ **The dict's NAME is now wrong and is not renamed.** Two of its five entries are not staff
writes (`applications.py` has not been one since wave C). The string is read by `G81` and by `G84`;
renaming it is a mass shared-file edit for no behaviour (law 11), so the meaning is written down
instead.

### 5 · `SOURCE_TYPES` gains `portal`, and it is not a tidiness edit

The outbound queue's `CHANNEL_FLOOR_BY_SOURCE` is keyed on `source_type`, and **`account` — the
nearest existing kind — carries a PRINT floor** since the `BR-NOT-024` amendment of 2026-08-30.
Queueing an enrolment code under it would have created a `pdf_print` row as well as the SMS one:
**a six-digit login code posted by letter, arriving four days after it expired.**

`portal` is added to `SOURCE_TYPES` and deliberately **not** added to the floor dict. A code is not
a document, there is no envelope for it, and it is worthless within ten minutes. This is a
one-constant widening of another module's published vocabulary rather than a write into it, and the
comment beside the value carries the whole reason.

### 6 · The gate-number collision that took the whole suite down — recorded HERE and not as a defect row

At about 08:44 this morning two gates were both registered as `G89` (`g89_dead_custom_properties`
and `g89_provider_error_seam`), and `_assert_registry_sane` — written that same morning to catch
exactly this — **refused to start the suite at all**. Not one gate ran on the branch for roughly
twenty minutes. This lane found it by running `run_gates.py` and had a defect row half written.

**It is recorded here instead, and the reasoning is worth as much as the fact.** The style lane
fixed it in `2c926ba7` by the terminating rule the refusal message itself names — *the gate that
landed later renumbers* — within minutes, and `DEF-CWP-3734` and `DEF-GOV-3654` already carry this
escape twice. **A register row describing a state that no longer exists is worse than none**, and
the coordinator said so before this lane pushed it.

**What is genuinely new, and is why this paragraph exists at all:** the CONSEQUENCE changed. Until
this morning two lanes sharing a gate number produced a citation that resolved to the wrong gate —
bad, and silent. Since the registry check landed it produces **zero gate coverage, branch-wide,
until somebody notices**. That raises the value of the fix the existing rows already name and
nobody has built: **an allocator that reserves a gate number against the REMOTE, the way
`file_defect.py` already reserves a defect id.** Every one of the four occurrences in two days is a
lane correctly computing *the next free number* from a directory listing that cannot see a
sibling's unpushed worktree. It is a lane of its own and it is written down here so the next lane
taking a gate number starts from the measurement rather than from the surprise.

⚠ This lane also read `14-id-reservations.md` line 656 (*"`G90` and up are UNUSED and free"*) and
found it already stale by one number when it came to push. **Gate numbers were re-derived from the
pinned tip at push time and not at file-creation time**, which is the standing instruction, and it
is the only reason `G91`/`G92` are not a fifth occurrence.

## 2026-09-04 · The three shipped waves were run against ONE product, and the first proof of any of them turned out not to be reproducible

**Who decided:** the coordinating session, on its own judgment. Nothing here was put to
the Product Owner — none of it collides with a signed rule, none of it moves a ❄️ frozen
figure, and none of it is a fact only they hold (hard-won law 13).

### Why this was done at all

Three waves shipped inside about four hours — the integrations grid (`2.129.0`), the Work
shell and its anchor (`2.130.0`) and the value-mapping screen (`2.131.0`) — and **each was
proved against its own private database by the lane that built it.** Every one of those
proofs was honest and none of them answered the question a reader of this branch would
actually ask: *do the three work together?* Three green walkthroughs on three databases
are not one green product.

### What was run, and what it printed

One PostgreSQL 16 database at the branch tip, migrated, `seed_demo`, then
`load_sample_data --tenant brazosbend` — 1,232 rows across nineteen sample blocks, every
block loaded. One Django server, one built front end, one browser. Then all three
walkthroughs in sequence:

| The walkthrough | Checks | Result |
|---|---|---|
| The integrations grid | 15 | green — 17 cards, the screen drawing exactly what the server served, 36 state words all *Not set up* |
| Their words, mapped | 35 | green — fourteen kiosk words, two mapped to one of ours, *12 of 14 not mapped*, and an unmapped row's border read back as the theme's red |
| The Work shell and the anchor | 38 | green — 18 open orders across 5 connections, the leak investigation on `77 Cedar Ct` with a dash under CONNECTION |

**88 checks, no failures**, plus the terminal half of the Work demonstration: a leak
investigation accepted with no connection, the same raise refused by the service in a
five-word sentence, and refused again by the database — `new row for relation
"work_orders" violates check constraint "ck_work_orders_has_anchor"`. Row-level security
on `work_orders` was read out of `pg_class` as **enabled and forced**, with its
tenant-isolation policy, rather than taken from a comment.

### The finding, which is worth more than the green

**The Work walkthrough failed five checks the first time, and every one of them read like
a broken product.** 0 rows drawn, no order on `CON-26-0122`, 0 connections spanned, the
leak investigation absent, an empty column list. Nothing was broken. Its `HOW TO RUN IT`
block named `<scratch>/cr070a_terminal.py` — **a file in nobody's repository** — and did
not make clear that `load_sample_data` is required rather than optional.

That is filed as `DEF-WRK-3633` and fixed in the same commit: the terminal half now lives
beside the walkthrough as `10-scripts/render-checks/cr070-a-terminal.py`, and the header
names that path.

**Two rules follow, and they are ours, recorded here rather than asked about:**

   only its author can reproduce is not a proof — hard-won law 1 applied to a procedure
   rather than to a guarantee.
   worktree before signing off.** The wave A lane's run was green and its script was on
   its disk; both facts were true and together they hid this.

### One more thing this turned up, in the fix rather than in the product

The first version of the committed script deleted only rows typed `unspecified` and its
own docstring claimed it was idempotent. Running it twice left **two** leak
investigations and the walkthrough read **19** rows where it had read 18. The claim was
wrong before the code was, which is law 1 again, this time inside the repair. It now
clears every anchorless order on that address and the count returns to 18 on a second
run — verified, not asserted.

## 2026-09-04 · CR-070 wave C — Settings tells the truth: four judgment calls, and one fixture that is owed rather than done

**The wave, in one sentence a person can read:** the four Work cards that had said
*arrives with Work* for three weeks now hold real rows a utility edits, and Work → Parts
is a price list that deliberately counts nothing.

### 1 · The five lookup cards use the GENERIC list routes, and only Parts got a screen

Task C1 asked us to *"check whether `BR-SHL-035`'s generic `kind: "list"` reference-data
routes can serve the four cards"* before writing fifteen handlers. **They can, and they
do.** Five of the six cards — job types, priorities, skills, safety kits, parts
categories — are `kind: "list"` and ride the existing `GET/POST/PATCH /lookups/{code}`
with one handler class each in `apps/work/lookups.py`. The endpoint count falls from the
plan's 21 to **four Work-specific routes** (the parts register's own CRUD) plus the
generic ones. The sixth card, Parts, is `kind: "link"` and navigates to `/work/parts`,
following `BR-TEN-033`'s own precedent (the Document & message templates card navigates
and does not list) — because a register with six columns and a segmented control is a
SCREEN, and putting a weaker second one inside a Settings modal would give a utility two
parts registers that disagree.

### 2 · Two cards carry a detail column, and which one is a choice

`BR-SHL-035` allows ONE detail column per card. Job types carry **default priority** —
of the four columns the card could show (duration, customer-present, default template,
priority), it is the one that decides *when the job is due*. Priorities carry
**`sla_hours_text`**, the server-rendered *"4 h"* rather than the bare integer, so hard
rule 3's unit travels with the number in one serializer instead of eleven catalogues.

### 3 · The register is named *Register*, not the drawing's *Stock register*

`Work-025.png` labels the first segment *Stock register* and draws On hand · Reorder at ·
Location · a reorder banner. The commitment card for the same screen says *"No stock
levels, no reorder points"*. **The card wins** (`DEF-WRK-3550`), `OQ-WRK-1490` is OPEN,
and a register with no stock must not be named after what it does not hold. The
walkthrough asserts all five forbidden words absent from the page AND the three keys
absent from `GET /work/parts` — ten checks, because a screen that merely declines to draw
a column over a payload that carries one is one line from the thing the rule forbids.

### 4 · ⚠ THE PARTS FIXTURE IS OWED, AND IT IS WRITTEN DOWN HERE SO IT IS NOT DISCOVERED TWICE

Task C3 names a fixture — `MTR-E1P 96.0000` · `SEAL-01 0.2200` · `MTR-W58 92.4000` ·
`GSKT-STD` — and **no seeder in this repository plants it.** The five LOOKUP lists do
seed, at tenant provisioning, through `apps/work/services.seed_reference_list`; measured
on a freshly provisioned Brazos Bend that is **8 job types, 4 priorities, 8 skills, 4
safety kits, 4 parts categories**. But `parts` is a REGISTER and not a lookup list, and
`apps/tenancy/sample_data.py`'s `SAMPLE_MODULES` has no `work` entry at all, so
`load_sample_data` leaves the register **empty**.
**What we did instead, and why:** `10-scripts/render-checks/cr070-c-terminal.py`, in the
repository, planting the four parts idempotently — the same answer wave A gave to the
same problem (`DEF-WRK-3633`: a proof only its author can reproduce is not a proof).
**What is still owed:** a `work` sample module, which would seed those four for every
lane, every demo and every future wave. It was NOT added in passing because
`SAMPLE_MODULES` is a shared registry whose prose count three gates read, G72 is RED on
that very count today (19 entries, four sentences saying *eighteen*), and a lane quietly
making it twenty is exactly how that number went wrong the first time.

### 5 · A note on what the browser found, because none of it was in the code

Three assumptions in the walkthrough were wrong and the product was right each time: the
card badge state is `seeded` and not `present`; the add form sits behind *+ Add entry*
rather than opening with the card; and the Work strip has FOUR tabs because wave B's
*Awaiting approval* landed while this was being written. The third is worth keeping —
`WorkShell.tsx` warns in its own header that two lanes edit `WORK_TABS` in the same hour,
and the check going RED is that warning being right rather than a failure.
**And a fourth, found only by running it twice:** the walkthrough ADDS a skill, so its
second run failed two checks over a perfectly healthy product. A walkthrough that passes
only on a virgin database reads as a broken screen ever after; the fixture now resets in
both directions and the run scored **62 of 62 twice**.

## 2026-09-04 · The captured packs give layout; r10 gives the style — and six shipped screens did not

**PO ruling, verbatim, in two messages half an hour apart**, on seeing the Integrations grid, the connect modal, the portal's Overview and the portal's Branding screen:

> *"you ahve to folow the stylegudie that we have approved from R10; style guide na dtailwind component remain same - thi sis not in line with style guide - also toolkit is not align"*

> *"this Screen does not follow the Styleguide that we agrred for application. UI screens layout and details you can folow from Screens that we capture from document, but style guide should be from r10 agreement"*

### What this changes, and what it does not

⚠ **IT AMENDS THE RULING OF 2026-09-03 THAT *the pack is the layout authority*.** That ruling was made when a Work wireframe and prototype r10 disagreed about what a screen contains, and it is still right about **what a screen contains and how it is arranged**. It was never a licence to invent a visual language, and it was read as one.

The split the PO drew is exact, and it is now B14 rule 36:

| | Comes from |
|---|---|
| What is on the screen, and where | the captured pack for that module |
| What it **looks like** — buttons, chips, fields, panels, type, colour | `05-prototype/r10-2026-08-16/UI-RULES.md` |
| How you comply without deciding it again per screen | the shared component kit in `07-frontend/src/components/` |

### The six breaches, all in code that passed every gate

1. **A wireframe style shipped as product.** The connect modal drew four production panels in `border-dashed border-info-700` with `font-mono uppercase tracking-wider` legends — a customer-facing form that looks like a sketch of itself.
2. **The danger colour spent on a sign-in.** *Sign in with Microsoft* rendered filled red. `r10` rule 6 reserves that tier for destructive commits — disconnect, retire, reverse, write-off.
3. **The danger colour again, on Save.** The Branding screen's primary commit is not destructive and must not wear it.
4. **A wall of checkboxes.** *Services shown on the front page* is a multiple-choice field, and `r10` rule 9 says those are removable chips plus an add control, **never** a wall of checkboxes. Named, and broken anyway.
5. **The kit ignored.** Category chips and segmented controls were hand-rolled as raw `<button>` elements while `Button`, `buttonKit`, `FilterBar` and `SegmentedControl` all exist. Four screens acquire four different chips this way.
6. **A column so narrow the text wrapped one word per line**, eleven lines of it, on the Branding preview. That one is not a style question — it is a broken layout, and **no test in this repo could see it**, because every suite asserts on text content and text content is identical however it wraps.

### Why every gate was green

Nothing here is catchable by the checks this repo has. B14's own status table says most of its rules are RATIFIED and UNENFORCED because **no gate reads rendered output** (hard-won law 6), and the browser walkthroughs that do read it were written to assert the things their own authors were thinking about — a state word, a count, a computed `display` — never *does this look like the rest of the product*.

**Two of the six are mechanically catchable and a gate is owed for them:** the annotation style in a file under `features/`, and a raw `<button>` in a screen where the kit's `Button` would serve. The other four need a person or a rendered-output check with a wider eye.

### What follows

The screens above are corrected onto the kit rather than patched in place, because patching one screen's chip is what produced four different chips. Where the kit lacks a piece, **the piece is added to the kit** — one component, one visual decision, every screen.

## 2026-09-04 · ADDRESSES HAVE ONE HOME, AND EVERY OTHER ENTITY BORROWS IT — `BR-MET-1161`, and it is the same ruling as CR-072

**The Product Owner, verbatim, immediately after the CR-072 scoping:**

> *"also note we are having addresses at one place now - Premises and Units -> then they flow to {Meters, Sub meter, assets} + { accounts} -> from there it flows to Routes and Cycles -? and bill derives it again dueing billing. Simialrly work orders are either related to Accounts/Customers  or they are related to Assets or premises and Units - so they will also draw addresses from same place that we we can maintain the integrtiy, we can keep all service points = units, premises valid and intact, along with GIS data, and use it for all entities as well as maps - this is important to udnerstand - it will flow in Customer web portal /Self servcie portal also"*

### What it says

One place holds where something IS: **`premises` and `units`**. Everything else that needs an
address — a meter, a sub-meter, an asset, an account, a route, a cycle, a bill, a work order, a
page of the customer portal — **reaches it by walking the chain, and stores none of its own.**

The chain the PO drew, and it is the chain the product already has:

```
premises  ──►  units  ──┬──►  service points ──►  meters / sub-meters / assets
   │                    │
   │  (lat, lng, GIS)   └──►  accounts  ──►  invoices ──► the printed bill
   │
   └──►  routes and cycles (through the service point)
   │
   └──►  work orders — anchored on account, premises, asset or connection,
                       and reading the address through whichever anchor it has
```

**And that is why it is the same ruling as CR-072.** CR-072 said *one destination for a build*;
this says *one home for an address*. Both are the PO refusing a second place to look at the same
fact. The reason is the one they gave: **integrity** — two copies of an address are two answers to
*where is this*, and the map, the route sheet, the envelope and the crew's phone will eventually
disagree.

### What is already right, measured rather than assumed

| | |
|---|---|
| `premises.address_line / city / state / postal_code` | the one address of record — **required**, not nullable |
| `premises.lat` / `premises.lng` | `NUMERIC(9,6)`, the GIS the PO names. 46 of 79 sample premises carry them |
| `units` | carry **no address at all** — a unit is `(premises, label)`, and it borrows |
| `service_points` | carry no address — 174 of them, all reached through the unit |
| `assets` | carry no address — reached through the service point |
| `work_orders` | carry **no address column**, and `ck_work_orders_has_anchor` refuses a row with none of its four anchors. The address is whatever the anchor's premises says |
| `interruptions.location_text` | free text **on purpose** (`BR-CWP-027`) — a passer-by reporting *"the corner of Elm and Third"* is not naming a premises, and `premises_id` stays NULL until a clerk resolves it |

**So the shape the PO describes is the shape that is built.** That is worth stating plainly rather
than quietly: the ruling is a *confirmation and a fence*, not a rework.

### The one place it is NOT right, and it is a door rather than a leak

`customers.addresses.kind` accepts **two** values — `mailing` and `service` (`services.py:989`,
`ADDRESS_KINDS`, straight from B2 §2). A `kind='service'` row is a second, independent, editable
copy of a service address hanging off the account.

**It is not in use, and that is measured, not hoped:**

* rows of `kind='service'` in the tip database: **0** (against 51 `mailing`);
* code paths that READ one: **none.** The only four hits for the string are the tuple that permits
  it, the validator that checks against that tuple, and a docstring in `selectors.py:1641`
  explaining why the mailing selector refuses to fall back to it.

So today it is a door standing open onto a room nobody has entered. Under this ruling **the door
closes**: `ADDRESS_KINDS` becomes `("mailing",)`, the account's service address is derived from
`account → unit → premises` and is never stored, and a write asking for `kind='service'` is refused
by name with the reason.

⚠ **B2 §2 declares both values, so this SUPERSEDES a signed schema statement** and is recorded as
such rather than edited into B2 in passing. It is not a ❄️ FROZEN B4/B5 figure — no money math
moves — so it does not need a finance re-sign; it needs this row, the rule below, and the gate.

### What this makes a rule — `BR-MET-1161`

> **An address is stored on `premises` and nowhere else.** A `unit` refines a premises by label, not
> by address. Any other entity that needs to know where something is — asset, service point,
> account, route, cycle, invoice, work order, portal page, map pin — **derives it by walking to the
> premises**, and declares no address column of its own. The coordinates (`premises.lat/lng`) travel
> the same way, so a map and an envelope cannot disagree.
>
> **Two exceptions, both narrow and both already built:**
> 1. **`customers.addresses` `kind='mailing'`** — where the BILL goes, which for a landlord, a
>    managing agent or anyone who has moved is deliberately not where the meter is. This is not a
>    duplicate of the premises address; it is a different fact.
> 2. **`interruptions.location_text`** — what a stranger typed. It is a report, not a record, and it
>    resolves to a `premises_id` when a clerk says so.
>
> A third copy is a defect, not a feature.

### Where it flows to the customer portal, since the PO named that too

The portal shows a customer *their* address. Under this rule it shows the **premises** address,
reached `account → unit → premises`, and `apps/portal` gains **no address column and no address
copy** — its seams read, exactly as they do now. The portal today has none, which is why this is a
fence rather than a fix.

### Cost of the fence, stated

Closing `kind='service'` costs one line in `ADDRESS_KINDS`, a refusal message, and a gate. Leaving
it open costs nothing **today** and costs an unresolvable disagreement the first time an importer,
a lane or a customer writes one — because at that moment there are two service addresses for one
premises and no rule says which is true.

### The third home, decided here rather than put back (law 13)

`tenancy.ServiceCentre.address` is a bare text address on the utility's own walk-in counter, and it
does **not** borrow. That is deliberate: a service centre is not a property that takes service, has
no `premises` row and never will, so there is nothing for it to walk to. It is a **different fact**,
like the mailing address — the utility's own place on a map, not a customer's.

It appears on a map beside premises pins, which is exactly why it needed deciding rather than
assuming. Recorded as `BR-MET-1161`'s exception 3, and named in `G85`'s allow list with that reason
in one line, so a later lane cannot read the entry as "an address slipped through".

### What broke by closing the door, and it is the whole reason this needed a defect row

`DEF-CUS-3653`. The account header's identity chain drew `1408 Elm St · A · Austin, TX 78704`, and
the third part came from `serviceLocality(detail.addresses)` — a lookup for the `kind='service'` row
this ruling retires. **Closing the door would have made that function return `null` on every account
forever**, with `tsc` green, every test green, and the line simply gone from the screen. That is
hard-won law 2 in its exact shape: not a crash, not a placeholder, an absence nobody can see.

Fixed in the same commit, and fixed by walking rather than by restoring the copy:
`metering.selectors.premises_locality` publishes three columns of one indexed row; `customers.seams`
names it; `account_detail_dict` serves `premise_locality`; the header composes the same sentence from
it. **`account → unit → premises`, which is the chain the PO drew** — so the fix and the rule are the
same act.

⚠ One test writes a `kind='service'` row directly through the model
(`test_cr053_print_set.py::test_a_service_address_is_not_used_as_a_mailing_address`). It is **left
standing and its docstring amended**: nothing was migrated, so rows written before today can still
exist, and *"an old service row is never used as a mailing address"* is now a guard on LEGACY data
rather than on a state the product can reach. Deleting it would remove the only test covering the
rows this ruling leaves behind.

### The gate

**`G85 one-address-home`** — parses every model in `06-backend/apps/` with `ast` and fails a fourth
model that declares an address-shaped column. Proved RED twice on the real tree (`lat`/`lng` on
`WorkOrder`, `postal_code` on `Contact`), both reverted, and green on the tree as it stands with
exactly the three homes.

⚠ **`state` and `country` are deliberately not triggers, and that is measured.** A first draft
included `state` and **eight of its eleven hits were workflow columns** — `DisconnectCase.state`,
`ServiceRequest.state`, `Connection.state`, `WorkOrder.state`, `Transfer.state`,
`ImportRunProgress.state`, `Tenant.state`, `ConnectionService.state`. A gate that is 73% false
positives earns an allow-list entry per commit until it means nothing.

## 2026-09-04 · THE REUSE AUDIT THE PO ASKED FOR — what CR-068 and CR-069 actually reuse, measured

**PO verbatim:**

> *"also please check in Cr 68 - you are using existing end point as much as possible for self service - dont rewrite and repeat same code again - be critical about it , apply product engineering mid ; apply similar approach for integration also"*

Audited by reading every route, every import and every seam of `apps/portal` (2,442 lines, 13 files)
and `apps/integrations` (5,580 lines, 18 files), plus `src/portal` (1,733 lines) against
`src/components`. **Findings, not reassurance** — three of the four are good and the fourth is a
defect.

### 1 · The portal's WRITES reuse the existing services. Good.

`apps/portal/services.py` has one write path and it calls
`customers.service_request_service.create_from_portal` and
`metering.interruption_service.create_interruption`. It does not create a `ServiceRequest` itself.
`write_points.py` declares the four permitted writes AS DATA and `G81` fails a fifth. **Nothing is
rewritten here.**

### 2 · The portal's READS go through seams, and one of them is legitimately NOT a reuse.

`portal/seams/customers_seam.py` defines `request_progress_view(row)` returning six keys — the
reference, the state and three dates. `customers` already has `service_request_reads.detail()`, which
serves eight tabs. **Serving that to a guest would leak the applicant's name, address, documents and
fees**, so this is a different view of the same row, not a second copy of an existing one; the
docstring says so and `BR-CWP-024` is the rule. **Reuse would have been the bug here.**

⚠ One misplacement, minor and worth naming: `customers_seam.premises_postcode` reaches into
`apps.metering.models` from inside the *customers* seam, while `metering_seam.py` exists one file
along. It works and reads one column; it belongs in the metering seam.

### 3 · The integration substrate reuses the platform's kernels rather than growing its own.

Measured by its imports: `core.jobs` (not a second queue — `jobs.py` registers two kinds on
`core.jobs.set_job_handler` and routes them to the `integrations` queue), `core.crypto`,
`core.money`, `core.pagination`, `core.permissions`, `core.tenancy`. **It imports no other `apps.*`
module at all**, which is what a substrate should look like.

And `codecs.py` is the case worth citing, because it went the right way on purpose: it did not copy
`billing/print_formats.py`'s registry, it **generalised it into `NamedRegistry` and made
`print_formats.NAMED_FORMATS` an instance of that**. One mechanism, two lists.

`scrubbing.py` is genuinely new and needed: `integration_run.provider_error` is the one column where
another tenant's data can arrive (a mail server quoting the message it refused), and RLS cannot help
because the leak is inside a row the tenant is entitled to.

### 4 · The one real duplication is on the SCREEN, not the server — `DEF-CWP-3655`.

`src/portal` is 1,733 lines and imports the shared component kit **four times** (3 × `StateFrame`,
1 × `Button`). Meanwhile `portal/components/content.tsx` exports its own **`Panel`** and **`Chip`**,
and `primitives.tsx` its own **`PageHead`** — and the kit already has `Panel.tsx`, `StatusPill.tsx`
and `PageHeader.tsx`. The portal `Chip`'s own comment states the duplication in as many words:
*"the staff kit's tones, its own markup"*.

**The sharpest detail is the timing.** `components/Panel.tsx` gained a `title` prop TODAY under B14
rule 36, and its comment says why: *"Three screens of `CR-068` wave D had each written their own
`<section>` with their own border and their own small-caps `<h3>`."* That fix landed one component
away from the portal's own `Panel`, which survived the pass untouched.

### The rule this leaves behind, so the running lanes inherit it rather than re-deriving it

**Before writing a portal route or a portal component, the question is not *"what does this screen
need"* — it is *"what already serves this, and why is it not enough?"* An answer of *"it serves too
much"* (a guest may not see a clerk's tabs) is a reason to write a narrower view and to say so in the
docstring. An answer of *"it looks slightly different"* is not a reason at all — that is the case B14
rule 36 already settles, and it is the one that produced four different chips.**

Wave E — the signed-in customer's bills, payments and usage — is where this will cost the most,
because `billing`, `payments` and `metering` already serve every one of those reads for staff. The
rule above applies hardest there and it is written down now rather than after the code.

## 2026-09-04 · The eight screens corrected onto r10 — six judgments the rules did not settle, and the two that collide with r10 itself

B14 rule 36 was ratified this morning and this is the pass that applies it: the captured packs
still decide what is on each screen, `05-prototype/r10-2026-08-16/UI-RULES.md` decides what it
looks like, and the shared kit is how a screen complies without deciding it again. Six of the
decisions below were ours to make (law 13 — a judgment recorded with its reasoning is the
deliverable, a question is the failure to make one), and the last two are recorded because they
**collide with r10's own markup**, which is the one case law 13 says must be stated rather than
assumed.

### 1 · `BR-INT-001` NEVER SAID *dashed*, AND TWO FILES SAID IT DID

`IntegrationsTab.tsx`'s header cited the rule as *"a coming-soon Connect is dashed AND refused at
the API"*. The rule's own words, in `04-docs/05-modules/13-integrations/02-business-rules.md`, are
**"card renders 'Coming soon' + wave label, Connect disabled at UI AND API"**. It says disabled. It
has never said dashed. A hatched rectangle reached a customer's screen with a rule id beside it,
and both the screen test and the browser walkthrough asserted the hatching as a success. This is
hard-won law 1 exactly: a comment claiming a rule is not the rule. The button is the kit's,
disabled, and the rule is honoured more precisely than it was.

### 2 · THE CARD'S ACTION IS `btn-sm`, CONTENT WIDTH — MEASURED FROM r10, NOT PREFERRED

`SMARTBillHub.dc.html` line 7727 draws an integration card's action as
`class="btn btn-primary btn-sm"` and a connected card's as `btn btn-secondary btn-sm`; neither
carries a width. Ours was `w-full` at the default size — a slab across the card rather than a
button on it, on eleven cards at once. The line is quoted in the file so the next lane does not
have to re-find it.

### 3 · THE DESTRUCTIVE COMMIT ON THE BRANDING SCREEN IS *Reset to defaults*, NOT *Save*

r10 rule 6 gives the danger tier to a destructive commit. On CWP-070 the two header actions were
*Reset to defaults* as the calm outlined secondary and *Save* as the loudest thing on the page —
and Reset is the one that writes `EMPTY_FIELDS`: it wipes the strapline, the office hours, the
emergency number and the whole front-page service list in one press, with no undo. The emphasis
was inverted. Reset takes the danger tier; Save keeps the primary, because **r10 draws every Save
as `btn btn-primary`** (`Save charge`, `Save tax`, `Save rules`, `Save mapping`).

### 4 · THE LIVE PREVIEW IS A MINIATURE OF THE PAGE, NOT A NARROW COPY OF IT

The preview rendered the real `FrontPageView` into a four-of-twelve column — **329 pixels, measured
on the running product at a 1440-wide window** — while `CardGrid3` is `md:grid-cols-3` and `md:` is
a **viewport** query. The browser saw a 1440px window, drew three columns, and gave each card about
90px: eleven lines of one word each, and the *Sign in* button on top of the info icon.

Two ways to fix it and the choice matters. Restyling the front page to fit a narrow box would make
the preview legible and **wrong** — it would stop being a preview. So the page is laid out at the
width a visitor's browser really gives it (`GuestFrame` caps its main column at 1100px) and the
whole thing is scaled down to the panel, so every line break is the one a customer will see. The
scale is measured with a `ResizeObserver` rather than hard-coded, because this panel is a different
number of pixels on a laptop, a wide monitor and a phone.

### 5 · THE EMPTY STATE'S CTA STEPS DOWN A TIER RATHER THAN DISAPPEARING

An empty Parts register drew `+ Add part` twice in the same red — once in the page header, once in
the middle of the screen. B14 rule 4 / BR-SHL-044 allow one primary; r10 rule 17 wants the empty
state to name *"the action that fills it"*. Both are satisfiable: `EmptyList` grew an optional
`ctaVariant`, **absent means `primary` so all 27 other call sites are byte-for-byte unchanged** —
the same shape `WorkingButton` used when it grew its tier prop on 2026-08-25 — and Parts passes
`secondary`. Nothing else in the product moves.

### 6 · THE RATIONALE LEAVES THE SCREEN AND THE CATALOGUE KEYS STAY

B14 rule 33 says rationale is **zero words on screen**. Work > Templates printed 96 words of it.
The three paragraphs are preserved verbatim in the file's own header — deleting rationale is not
deleting information, it is moving it to the place that keeps it. The three catalogue keys
(`work.templates.whatItIs`, `.instead`, `.noDate`) are **left in all eleven catalogues rather than
swept out**: they are unreferenced now, and removing eleven values from files three other lanes are
editing tonight is the mass shared-file rewrite law 11 exists to prevent. A sweep belongs with the
wave that fills that screen.

### ⚠ 7 · *Sign in with Microsoft* IS SECONDARY, AND r10 DRAWS THE ANALOGOUS BUTTON PRIMARY

B14 rule 36 breach (b) is explicit: *"`Sign in with Microsoft` was rendered in the danger colour,
which r10 rule 6 reserves for destructive commits — the loudest colour in the product spent on a
sign-in."* **r10's own connect wizard draws `Sign in to {name} →` as `btn btn-primary`**
(`SMARTBillHub.dc.html` line 7816). The two disagree, and the disagreement has a cause worth
recording: **this theme's accent and its danger ramp are the same red.** `--color-accent` is
`#ec3013` and `--color-danger-500` is `#e0341a`; r10 makes primary and danger the SAME HUE
deliberately and separates them by FILL (`.btn-danger` is `background: transparent; border: 2px
solid var(--color-accent)`), while `buttonKit.ts` separated them by using a different ramp. So a
filled primary and a filled danger are, on screen, nearly the same button.

Ruled by this lane, and the reason is rule 4 rather than colour: **`↗` is r10's grammar for sending
to an external system**, and this button hands the clerk to Microsoft. It is not this form's
commit — it is the door out of it. Secondary. **This is the change in the whole pass I am least
certain of, and it is the one to look at first.**

### ⚠ 8 · THE PORTAL'S SECOND COMPONENT KIT IS MEASURED AND BASELINED, NOT FOLDED

`src/portal` is **1,733 lines and imports the shared kit four times** (three `StateFrame`, one
`Button`) while defining its own `Panel` **twice** — in `content.tsx` and again in
`primitives.tsx`, which is drift inside the drift — plus a `Chip` whose own comment says what it
is: *"the guest surface's status chip — the staff kit's tones, its own markup."* Five component
names collide with the kit.

**It is not folded tonight and that is a judgment, not an omission.** It is a wave rather than a
hunk: 35 exports, and swapping the portal's `Chip` for the kit's `StatusPill` changes how every
guest screen looks — a visual decision a person should see, not one a lane makes at speed in files
another lane pushed twenty minutes earlier. What ships instead is the instrument: **G86 clause (c)
refuses any NEW component whose name the kit already exports**, over a baseline of the five, and
that baseline may only shrink. One hand-rolled button in `content.tsx` is folded onto the kit's
`Button` because clause (b) caught it and it is one line. `DEF-CWP-3655` carries the rest.

### WHAT THE GATE CAN AND CANNOT SEE, SAID OUT LOUD

`G86` refuses three things: a dashed panel with a monospace uppercase legend (baseline **0**), a
`<button>` in a screen file that draws its own box (baseline **6**, ratcheted), and a component
under a name the kit already exports (baseline **5**, ratcheted). All three were shown RED on the
real breaches first.

It **cannot** see the other four things B14 rule 36 records — a wall of checkboxes where rule 9
wants chips, the danger colour on a sign-in, on/off drawn as a word in a box, and a column so
narrow the text wraps one word per line. The last is the sharpest illustration of hard-won law 6
in the repository: **every suite here asserts on text content, and text content is byte-for-byte
identical however it wraps.** A geometry assertion is added to the CR-069 wave B walkthrough for
the one thing a browser can answer — the field slot's border must be SOLID and its legend must not
be typewriter type — and that assertion **used to say `dashed` and was pointed at the defect**.

## 2026-09-04 · CR-068 wave D — four judgments, and one signed rule that collides with another signed rule

**Who:** the CR-068 wave D build lane. **Nothing here was put to the Product
Owner** — law 13: the repo is where an answer lives, and three of these four are
ours to decide and write down. The fourth is a collision between two CONFIRMED
documents, which law 13 says legitimately reaches the PO *when the supersession
must be stated* — it is recorded here rather than asked, because the reading
below leaves **both statements literally true** and supersedes neither.

### 1 · `help_answer_feedback` is written by `tenancy`, and `BR-CWP-001` is not bent

**The collision, quoted from both sides.** `BR-CWP-001` (CONFIRMED — blueprint
§2 Figure 1, `CR-068` `PR-17`, `R12`): *"The portal may create rows of exactly
**four** kinds: a payment, a service request, a meter reading, and a preference
on the account. Every other portal operation is a read."* And
`03-field-map.md` §2 (CONFIRMED — `CP-34`): `help_answer_feedback` is *"the
portal's smallest write and the one that makes the help screens improvable"*,
with `US-CWP-072` §1 calling it *"the smallest write in the portal"* in as many
words. Both are ratified. Built literally, they cannot both be obeyed.

**The reading taken, and why it needed no ruling.** `help_answer_feedback` is a
**tenancy** table (`03-field-map.md` §2 puts published content in `tenancy`),
and **B2 §2 forbids a cross-module write** — so `apps/portal` could not write
that row wherever the endpoint were mounted. The route therefore lives in
`apps/tenancy/published_content_api.py` and wears the portal's own guest guards.
That is not a way around the rule; it is the only place the row can legally be
written from.

**And the four kinds are untouched.** Every one of them is a row about a
CUSTOMER'S ACCOUNT — a payment, a request, a reading, a preference. This row is
about a published paragraph: it carries the answer, the language it was read in,
the event and the day, and **no customer, no account, no session and no
address** (`BR-CWP-021`). It can change nothing a customer owns, which is
`BR-CWP-026` satisfied. `write_points.py` still declares exactly four and `G81`
still refuses a fifth.

**The figure a reviewer can check:** the portal package contains **zero** ORM
writes outside `services.py` and the two staff modules, and `G81` says so on
every run. Filed as `DEF-CWP-3727` so the two documents are not read as
agreeing.

### 2 · A demo clock, and why it fails closed

*"Closed today · Opens Thursday at 9:00am"* and *"Closed November 26 —
Thanksgiving Day"* are computed from the clock and the tenant's holiday
calendar and typed by nobody (`BR-CWP-096`) — which is the rule's whole point
and also means **the two sentences can only be SEEN on a Wednesday in
November**. The walkthrough has to be able to stand on that day.

So `PORTAL_CLOCK_OVERRIDE` exists in `config/settings/base.py`, and
`apps/tenancy/published_content._clock_override()` honours it **only when
`DEBUG` is true**. `DEBUG` is False in `base.py` and in `production.py`; only
`local.py` turns it on. On any deployed build the variable can be set,
exported, or left in a `.env` by accident — hard-won law 4's exact failure — and
a customer's opening hours still come from the real clock. The unsafe option is
the one you have to type, twice.

### 3 · The fixture writes no holiday row, and finding that out is the best proof in the wave

The fixture was written to seed *26 November, Thanksgiving* into
`holiday_calendars`, and its first test run said the label was **Thanksgiving
Day**. Provisioning already seeds the eleven US federal holidays
(`apps/tenancy/us_holidays.py`, PO ruling 2026-08-11) and the fourth Thursday of
November 2026 is 26 November — so **a brand-new Pine Hill closes both counters
on Thanksgiving having done nothing at all**, which is a better demonstration of
`BR-CWP-096` than any fixture would have been. `seed_holiday` is kept as a
belt-and-braces `get_or_create` for a tenant provisioned without the seed.

⚠ **And the label that ships is the calendar's, not the story's.** `US-CWP-074`
§4 writes *"Holiday: 26 November, Thanksgiving"*; the product spells it
`Thanksgiving Day`. The screen shows the **utility's own word** — the label is
data, not copy — so the figure that ships is the calendar's. Recorded rather
than quietly reconciled.

### 4 · A language's own name is not a catalogue line

`Deutsch` is `Deutsch` on a Korean screen, because that is what its speakers
call it. Eleven catalogues each holding eleven copies of the same eleven strings
would be 121 lines that can only ever be identical, and 110 of them would read
to `G15` as **English pasted in untranslated** — which is exactly what they
would be. `Intl.DisplayNames` answers instead
(`07-frontend/src/portal/components/languageName.ts`), and the same reasoning
gives the weekday names and the clock: **the server sends a weekday number and
an `HH:MM`, and the screen writes the sentence from a catalogue frame in the
reader's own language.** No English sentence is assembled and then translated,
which is B14 rule 35 met by construction rather than by care.

⚠ **The ten non-English catalogues are `NATIVE-REVIEW-OWED`** — 191 lines
written by somebody who is not a native speaker of ten of the eleven. Rule 35's
own instruction is to say so rather than imply eleven fluent authors.

### 5 · What this wave did NOT decide

`OQ-1398` — who keeps the answers current, and in how many languages — is
**OPEN and was not answered**. The store, the three statuses, the eleven
variants and the **visible** `needs_translating` state are built; nothing
assigns a translation, chases one, notifies anybody, or promises on any screen
that it will happen. A test asserts the absence
(`HelpAndCentres.test.tsx`: *"no screen promises a translation workflow"*), so a
later lane cannot add the promise by accident.


## 2026-09-04 · CR-068 wave B — seven judgments the rules did not settle, and one branch that was broken while nobody could see it

**The wave:** a passer-by reports a burst main from `/{tenant}/portal`, keeps
`RP-26-0412`, and looks it up later; a clerk sees it on the worklist with channel
*Customer portal*. Stories `US-CWP-002`, `007`, `008`, `009`, `010`. Everything
below is a call this lane made because the signed rules did not reach it —
written here because the next agent reads the repo and not this session
(hard-won law 9).

### 1 · A report is given its OWN reference, and it is not the clerk's SR number

Every portal document writes `RP-26-0412`, and the product's service-request
series renders `SR-26-0057`. Two readings were possible and the third is what
shipped: **a report raises BOTH records, and the number a stranger is handed
names the INTERRUPTION**, from a new thirtieth series `interruption_report`
(`RP-{YY}-{0000}`, group *work*). The clerk's `SR-` number is a clerk's
vocabulary and is deliberately **not served to a guest at all**.

The alternative — one number for both — fails `Track`: `US-CWP-010` looks up a
report AND a move-out request with one box, and a single series cannot tell the
two records apart. **Worked figure:** Pine Hill's counter starts at 412, so the
first report is `RP-26-0412`, the second `RP-26-0413`, and a smell of gas
consumes nothing at all — the walkthrough asserts the gap is exactly one.

⚠ **AND EVERY TENANT PROVISIONED BEFORE TODAY HAS NO ROW FOR THAT SERIES.** The
counter is not zero, it is ABSENT, so the guest form refuses with *"No report
numbers are set up"* on a utility seeded yesterday. `tenancy.
seed_reference_data_for_tenant` is the repair door that module publishes for
exactly this and the fixture now calls it; a REAL utility already live needs the
same refresh, and the CHANGELOG says so out loud (hard-won law 4: a template
change never reaches a host that already exists).

### 2 · The interruption is a COMPANION row, not a fifth write point

`BR-CWP-001` names four kinds of row the portal may create and `G81` refuses a
fifth. A report creates **two** rows: the service request a clerk works, and the
interruption it is about — a record `BR-CWP-001` predates, because the blueprint
drew it and nothing had built it.

**The judgment: it is declared as a `companions` entry on the service-request
write point rather than as a fifth `kind`**, and `write_points.py` carries the
three conditions that made it lawful — the companion has no independent door,
it is written by the owning module's own service in the same transaction, and it
CREATES and changes nothing that existed. **The day one of those three is not
true, it is a ruling and not an edit.** Adding a fifth `kind` would also have
failed `G81`, which is the gate doing its job rather than an obstacle to route
around.

### 3 · The guest write is a SECOND door beside the role gate, never a widening of it

`create_request` is `@require_role(SYSTEM_ADMIN, BILLING_CLERK)` and there is
nobody signed in on a public form. Three shapes were possible: fabricate a clerk
actor in the portal, widen the existing gate, or add a narrow door.

**What shipped is the third, and it lives in `customers` rather than in
`portal`** — the module that owns the rule owns the exception to it. A
portal-side function that faked a clerk to get past `@require_role` would put
the decision to bypass a guard in the module the guard was written to constrain,
where no reviewer of `customers` would ever see it.
`create_from_portal` takes **no `actor` parameter at all**, accepts seven fields
and refuses every other by name, forces `channel = customer_portal`, and links no
account. Its actor object carries **no role**, so passing it to any
`@require_role` function raises — which is the property that makes it safe to
hand around. `allocate_number`'s body moved into `_allocate_number` so the guest
path can number a row without a role; **every path a staff member can reach still
runs the gate.**

### 4 · Track reaches two series and not three, and says so

`US-CWP-010` TC-7 looks up a PAYMENT reference. A payment's second fact is the
postcode of the service address, three joins away through a `payments` seam
**wave P builds** with quick pay itself. Writing that join on an unauthenticated
endpoint a wave before the module that owns the read is how an
account-disclosure route gets built by accident.

**So a payment reference is refused IDENTICALLY to an unknown one** — which
`TC-3` requires of every wrong pair anyway, so the boundary is narrower here than
the story asks and never wider. `selectors.TRACKABLE_SERIES` names the two, and
the test asserts the boundary rather than passing quietly over an absence.

### 5 · The lockout is keyed on the tenant ID, not the slug

`BR-CWP-023` says per tenant, per form, per address. A slug is a word a utility
can change on Settings: changing it would silently unlock every door in the
middle of an attack, and re-using a freed slug would inherit somebody else's
lock. The id is what the request already resolved and it never moves.

### 6 · *Crew on site* is the warning tone, not the brand one

`09-component-inventory.md` puts CREW ON SITE in the brand colour beside OVERDUE
and BOUNCED. **`r10` rule 6 keeps the loudest colour in the product for a
DESTRUCTIVE COMMIT** — disconnect, retire, reverse, write-off — and a crew
arriving to fix your water is the best news on the screen. It renders in the
kit's warning tone, and a test asserts the tone rather than the words. Recorded
because it is a divergence from a document, not an oversight.

### 7 · Track needed a door, and `CWP-001` has no card for it

`CWP-012` is drawn with no entry point: the front page's six errand cards do not
include it and no other screen links it. A screen nobody can reach is hard-won
law 2 with the arrow reversed. **It goes in the guest frame's nav**, beside the
other things a guest does without signing in.

### 8 · What this wave broke, and what broke under it

`DEF-CWP-3735` — `POST /public/reports` answered **500 on the branch**. Wave C
correctly folded three request shapes behind one write-point function (G81 allows
exactly one public function per declared write kind) and updated its own callers,
not wave B's. Nothing could see it: G81 read `write_points.py` against
`services.py` and both halves of that pair were consistent; ruff and black do not
resolve a module attribute; every backend test of the path was green in the
worktree it was written in and was never re-run against the merged tree. **Two
lanes found it within the hour, independently, and both by running the product.**

`DEF-CWP-3650` — a push of mine deleted 39 catalogue keys in all eleven
languages, by re-deriving the BLOB from a pinned tip while the CONTENT had been
read from an earlier one. The only thing that saw it was law 11's own arithmetic:
`11 insertions, 39 deletions` where `11 / 0` was intended.

### 9 · What this wave did NOT decide

`OQ-249` (planned work) is untouched — `US-CWP-011` is another wave's and is
blocked older than this module. `OQ-CWP-1510`'s response-time targets are
MEASURED and printed, never asserted. And **the consumer-upload re-sign is asked,

## 2026-09-04 · TWO THINGS THE PRODUCT OWNER SAW ON A LIVE PORTAL: NO BRAND COLOUR, AND ONE REQUEST IN TWO PLACES

Said while looking at `smartbillhub.bynry.com/silver-creek-water1/portal` — the real deployment, not a
fixture — with the front page (`CWP-001`) on screen. **Verbatim, both sentences:**

> *"the Style Guide , coloars are not matching."*

> *"all the request coming from portal should go in Service request. if we have to icnrease the
> defination of Service request we should do it"*

### One · THE COLOUR, AND IT IS NOT A TASTE DISAGREEMENT — IT IS `DEF-CWP-3736`

**The page is greyscale, and it is greyscale by construction rather than by choice.** Measured on the
tree, four facts:

1. `07-frontend/src/portal/` writes **zero** brand-colour classes. Not the wrong ones — **none**. A grep
   for `(bg|text|border)-(accent|brand|primary)*` across the whole directory returns nothing.
2. The API **does** serve the utility's own colours: `GET /portal/public/front` carries
   `brand_primary_hex` and `brand_accent_hex`, and the sample utility's are `#EC3013` / `#E15B47`.
3. The frontend **does** receive them and set them: `GuestFrame.brandStyle()` puts them on the frame as
   the CSS custom properties `--brand` and `--accent`.
4. ⚠ **AND NOTHING READS EITHER ONE.** A grep for `var(--brand)` and `var(--accent)` across every
   stylesheet in the product returns **nothing**. The theme's variable is spelled **`--color-accent`**,
   and r10's own CSS reads `var(--color-accent)` in twenty places — `.btn-primary`, `.btn-ghost` and the
   rest. The two properties the portal sets are consumed by nobody.

**So the tenant's brand colour is fetched over the wire, threaded through three components, written onto
a DOM element, and lands nowhere.** That is hard-won law 2 in its exact form — built, styled, tested,
wired to nothing — and it is worth noting that `GuestFrame`'s own docstring describes behaviour that does
not happen: *"every `var(--brand)` falls back to the ink it sits in"*, of a `var(--brand)` that appears
nowhere in the repository. Law 1: a comment claiming a guarantee is not the guarantee.

**Why every check was green.** The test fixtures set `brand_primary_hex: "#EC3013"` and the tests assert
the style attribute is present — which it is. No test asks whether any rule consumes it, and **no gate in
this repo reads rendered output** (law 6). `G86 house-style-controls` refuses a hand-rolled button and a
wireframe style; it does not ask *"is this screen the right colour"*. The PO found it by opening the
page, which is the only thing that could have.

**Classified a DEFECT and not a change**, per `13-change-process.md` step 1: the style guide was agreed on
2026-08-16 and ratified again as B14 rule 36 two days ago. Nothing new is being asked for; we did not
implement what was already signed. Filing our own misunderstanding as a "change" would convert our error
into the customer's new requirement.

### Two · THE SERVICE REQUEST — `CR-072`, and the second sentence is the ruling

Full analysis in `12-governance/change-requests/CR-072-portal-requests-are-service-requests.md`. The short
version, and the honest part first:

**The ruling is ALREADY MET for three of the portal's four shapes.** Start service, quick ask and — half
of — report all write through the one declared write point, and `G81` has failed a fifth write from any
portal file since wave A. The architecture the PO is asking for is the architecture that exists.

**The one place it does not hold:** a problem report creates **two** records — a `service_requests` row
*and* an `interruptions` row — and hands the stranger the **interruption's** `RP-26-0412`, while the
`SR-` number the same call created is deliberately withheld. A clerk has two rows; the customer holds the
number of the one that is not the request.

**The build judgment, decided here rather than put back to the PO (law 13):** `interruptions` is two
different things wearing one table. **The report** — *a stranger said there is water in the road* — is a
request, and becomes the service request. **The confirmed interruption** — *supply is off on Elm St
between 1400 and 1500, back by 18:00* — is not a request at all; it is the utility's operational record,
opened by a clerk who has judged the reports real, and it may gather many of them. Today the foreign key
runs one-to-one in the wrong direction, which is what forces a second row per report.

**What that makes concrete:** the guest is handed the `SR-` number; a report no longer opens an
interruption; `service_requests` widens to carry what a report needs — which is the PO's own second
sentence, *"if we have to icnrease the defination of Service request we should do it"*, and the reason
this did not need a question put back.

**What is NOT in scope, so a later lane does not read absence as oversight:** a payment and a
self-submitted meter reading stay where they are — neither is a request, and routing a bill payment onto
a clerk's worklist is not what was asked.

### The pattern worth naming, because this is the third time

`CR-070 §W` — *"you cannot have two differnt screen"*. `BR-MET-1161` — one home for an address.
`CR-072` — one destination for a request. **Three rulings in two days, all the same instinct: the PO
keeps refusing a second place to look at one fact.** A lane proposing any new table, screen or reference
series should expect to answer *"what already holds this, and why can it not hold this too?"* before it
is built, not after it ships.

## 2026-09-04 · THE PORTAL'S COLOUR, MEASURED IN A BROWSER — THE DIAGNOSIS WAS HALF RIGHT, AND THE HALF IT MISSED IS THE HALF THAT WAS BROKEN

`DEF-CWP-3736` was filed this morning from the PO's own words on the live deployment —
*"the Style Guide , coloars are not matching."* — with a four-fact diagnosis ending
**"nothing reads either one"**. This lane was asked to test that reading rather than agree with
it. **It does not hold, and the correction matters more than the agreement would have.**

### What was actually measured

A real Chromium, the real dev bundle, `GET /portal/public/front` stubbed with a tenant hex
that is deliberately **not** the theme's stock accent — `brand_primary_hex: #0F7B6C`,
`brand_accent_hex: #B45309`, against a theme whose `--color-accent` is `#ec3013`. Read back
with `getComputedStyle`, on `CWP-005`:

| what | before |
|---|---|
| `--brand` on the guest frame | `#0F7B6C` — the tenant's, set |
| `--accent` on the guest frame | `#B45309` — the tenant's, set |
| `--color-accent` on the guest frame | `#ec3013` — **the product's, unmoved** |
| **primary button background** | **`rgb(236, 48, 19)`** — `#EC3013`, the product's stock accent |
| the `InfoBar` "i" | `rgb(15, 123, 108)` — `#0F7B6C`, **the tenant's** |
| non-grey colours on `CWP-001` | **2**, one of them a service chip the API coloured |

**So `--brand` is NOT unread.** Fifteen source sites write `text-[var(--brand)]`,
`border-[var(--brand)]` and `border-l-[var(--brand)]`, Tailwind compiles an arbitrary value
into a real declaration, and thirteen elements on `CWP-005` render the tenant's teal. The
original grep was for `var(--brand)` **in stylesheets**, and this product's styles are in the
markup since Route B — so the grep was looking in the one place Route B moved them out of.

**Two things were genuinely wrong, and neither is the one that was written down:**

1. ⚠ **THE KIT READS A DIFFERENT VARIABLE, AND THE KIT IS WHERE THE COLOUR IS.**
   `buttonKit.ts` writes `bg-accent`, `text-accent` and `hover:bg-accent-600`; Tailwind emits
   those as `var(--color-accent)`. `--color-accent` is a **theme constant**, and no tenant has
   ever been able to move it. So every primary button, every ghost button, every link and every
   accent rule on the guest surface has rendered the PRODUCT's red on every utility in the
   world. The tenant's hex reached the decorations — an `i`, an asterisk, a left rule — and
   never the controls.
2. ⚠ **`--accent` (the tenant's `brand_accent_hex`) IS read by nothing at all.** Zero
   `var(--accent)` anywhere, in markup or stylesheet. That half of the original diagnosis is
   exactly right, and it is the half `G90` below goes red on.

### ⚠ AND THE REASON EVERY TEST AND EVERY WALKTHROUGH WAS GREEN IS A COINCIDENCE IN THE FIXTURE

The sample utility's `brand_primary_hex` is **`#EC3013`**. The theme's `--color-accent` is
**`#ec3013`**. They are the same colour. So on every fixture, every screenshot and every
walkthrough this repo has ever run, a button painted with the product's constant is
byte-for-byte the button painted with the tenant's hex, and **no assertion could have told
them apart.** The defect is only visible on a utility whose colour is not ours — which is
what a live deployment is. `CR-068` wave A's own decision row claims *"the front page appears
in the utility's own colours"*; it was written in good faith and it was never true.

### The fix, and the judgment inside it

**One variable, the one the stylesheets already read.** `brandStyle()` now sets
**`--color-accent`** from `brand_primary_hex`, and `--brand` is deleted rather than kept as an
alias: two names for one colour is the fifth chip problem in a custom property.

⚠ **THE HOVER AND ACTIVE SHADES HAD TO MOVE WITH IT, AND MISSING THAT WOULD HAVE BEEN A NEW
DEFECT.** The primary tier is `bg-accent hover:bg-accent-600 active:bg-accent-700`. Overriding
only `--color-accent` leaves a teal button that turns **red** under the pointer. The two darker
steps are therefore **derived, not invented** (hard-won law 5 — one source, derive the rest):
`color-mix(in srgb, var(--color-accent) 88%, black)` and `… 72%, black`. Checked against the
stock ramp on the stock hex: `#ec3013` derives `#d02a11` / `#aa230e` where the hand-picked
ramp holds `#dd2b0f` / `#ae1800` — within a couple of steps, and a derivation that follows any
tenant's colour beats a literal that follows one.

**`brand_accent_hex` is honoured NOWHERE, deliberately, and that is filed rather than hidden**
— `DEF-CWP-3737`. `--color-accent-2` is declared in two files and read in none, so there is no
token a second colour could fill and no signed rule in r10's `UI-RULES.md` or B14 saying what a
second accent is FOR. Setting it anyway would move the dead wiring one variable along, and
`G90` would refuse it by name. Deciding this here rather than asking is law 13; recording it is
law 9.

### `DEF-CWP-3655` — the second kit, and why it is the SAME defect

The reading this lane was asked to test was that the portal is colourless *because* it
hand-rolled its own components. **That holds, and it is now measurable rather than plausible.**
The pieces that carry the tenant's colour correctly are the ones that reach the kit —
`primitives.StatusChip` wraps `StatusPill`, `CommitButton` wraps `WorkingButton` — and the
pieces that lost it are the ones drawn by hand from raw utilities. `content.tsx`'s `Chip`
re-implements four tones the kit had already measured for contrast (`DEF-722`); its `Panel`
and `primitives.tsx`'s `Panel` are two bordered surfaces under one name, one directory from
`components/Panel.tsx`, which grew a `title` prop THIS MORNING under B14 rule 36 for exactly
this reason.

**What moved, and the visual delta it costs, stated rather than discovered later:** the kit's
`Panel` gains `trailing` (a header-row slot) and `tone`, and `as` accepts `aside`. Every one of
the 149 existing call sites renders byte-identically, because both new props are optional and
absent takes the old path — asserted, not assumed. The portal's nine `content.Panel` sites and
nine `primitives.Panel` sites become the kit's, which means the guest surface's panel picks up
the kit's `bg-surface` / `border-divider` / `text-h5` heading in place of three private
opinions about the same three things. **That is the change the PO asked for in rule 36's own
words, and it is a change a person can see** — recorded here so the next reviewer meets it as a
decision rather than as a surprise.

### `G90` — a custom property set by a component and read by nothing

The durable half. Both sides are greppable: the properties a `.tsx` writes into a style object,
and every `var(--name)` in the whole frontend — stylesheets **and** markup, which is where this
product's styles live and where the original grep did not look. A name in the first set and not
the second is wiring that goes nowhere.

**It would have gone red the day `GuestFrame` landed**, on `--accent`, and it goes red today on
the same one — proved by running it against the tip before the fix. It generalises past colour:
any `--foo` a component writes and nothing consumes is the same failure. Baseline **zero**, and
the one pre-existing hit (`--text-display`, in `styles/tailwindTheme.test.ts`) is excluded
because a test that names a token is not a component wiring one.

## 2026-09-04 · THE COLOUR PRECEDENCE, RULED — `BR-CWP-099`

**Product Owner, verbatim**, on being shown that the portal sets `--brand`/`--accent` and that nothing
reads either:

> *"default will be our style guide and then we will allow utility users to change it"*

### What it settles

**Ours first, theirs on top.** A utility that has chosen no colour gets **`#ec3013`** — the product's own
accent, r10's — and a utility that has chosen one gets theirs. In that order, and the order is the whole
ruling.

⚠ **IT SUPERSEDES A SENTENCE THE CODE STATES TODAY**, and the sentence is half of `DEF-CWP-3736`.
`GuestFrame`'s docstring says, in as many words: *"No hex is invented for a tenant that has none: the
variable is simply absent and every `var(--brand)` falls back to the ink it sits in."* **Falling back to
the ink it sits in is grey.** So an unbranded utility was designed to render colourless, deliberately,
and that design is now reversed: absence of a tenant colour means *use ours*, never *use none*.

### Why this makes the fix smaller rather than larger, which is worth stating

The theme already defines `--color-accent: #ec3013` at `:root`, and r10's own CSS reads
`var(--color-accent)` in twenty rules. **So the default the PO has just ruled for is already in the
product and needs no code at all.** What the portal needs is not a fallback chain, a second variable or
an invented hex — it is to stop writing `--brand` (which nothing reads) and instead override
`--color-accent` (which everything reads), and to do so **only when the tenant has a colour**. A tenant
with none then renders in the product's accent because nothing overrode it.

Two build cautions, recorded because both are silent failures:

* **An empty string is not the same as absent.** `style={{"--color-accent": null}}` writes nothing, which
  is right; `""` would override the default with garbage and return exactly the tenants with no colour to
  greyscale. It needs a test, not a comment.
* **The accent has a nine-step ramp beside it** (`--color-accent-100` … `-900`), and `.btn-primary:hover`
  reads `--color-accent-600`. Overriding only the base leaves a tenant's blue button with the product's
  red hover. Deriving the ramp with `color-mix` or overriding only the base and accepting the mismatch
  are both defensible; **leaving it undecided is not**, and the lane owes the decision with its worked
  figure.

### What this does NOT say

It does not say where a utility changes their colour — that is `Company → Profile`, already built
(`US-CWP-070` TC-6) — and it does not make the colour a portal setting. It is read from the tenant, not
copied, so a change follows on the next load.

## 2026-09-04 · THE PO SETTLES THE PRECEDENCE: OUR STYLE GUIDE IS THE DEFAULT, A UTILITY'S HEX OVERRIDES IT

Said while `DEF-CWP-3736` was being fixed, and it answers the one design question the defect left
open. **Verbatim:**

> *"default will be our style guide and then we will allow utility users to change it"*

**Two consequences, and the second is the one the code got wrong.**

1. A utility **with** a brand hex gets their hex.
2. A utility **without** one gets **`#ec3013`, r10's own accent — not grey, and not nothing.**

⚠ **`GuestFrame`'s docstring stated the opposite in as many words** and is now stamped
SUPERSEDED in place rather than deleted, because that docstring is where a regression would show
first (law 1). What it said: *"No hex is invented for a tenant that has none: the variable is
simply absent and every `var(--brand)` falls back to the ink it sits in."* **The ink it sits in is
GREY**, and grey-when-unbranded is half of what the PO was looking at.

**The ruling makes the implementation SMALLER, not larger, and that is worth saying because the
tempting reading is the other one.** `tokens.css` already declares `--color-accent: #ec3013` at
`:root`. That declaration IS the style guide's default and it needs no code at all. The tenant's
hex is then a single override of that same variable on the guest frame, written only when they
have one. There is no second variable, no fallback chain, and no `??` anywhere: **a utility with
no colour renders in the product's accent because nothing overrode it.**

### The two failure modes this creates, each with a test

**An empty string is not a colour.** `brand_primary_hex: ""` must write NOTHING. Writing
`--color-accent: ""` would override the style guide with garbage and land the unbranded tenants —
the exact population this ruling is about — straight back in greyscale. The guard is that the
write is conditional on a truthy hex; `FrontPage.test.tsx` TC-1c asserts it for both `null` and
`""`, and asserts the absence of the property rather than the absence of a hex, because only the
absent property lets `:root` win.

**The ramp is nine steps and the base is one of them.** `.btn-primary` is
`bg-accent hover:bg-accent-600 active:bg-accent-700`. Override only the base and a tenant's teal
button turns the **product's red** under the pointer — a new defect wearing the old one's fix.

**Decided: derive the two steps the guest surface can actually render, with `color-mix`.** Measured
first — the only accent tokens reachable from any guest screen are `--color-accent`,
`--color-accent-600` and `--color-accent-700`, so three properties are written and nine are not.
The worked figure, on the stock hex so it can be compared to the hand-picked ramp:
`color-mix(in srgb, #ec3013 88%, black)` = **`#d02a11`** against the ramp's `#dd2b0f`, and
`… 72%, black` = **`#aa230e`** against `#ae1800`. Within a step or two, and — the reason to prefer
it — a percentage follows *any* tenant's colour where a literal follows only ours. One source, the
rest derived (law 5).

**The alternative was considered and rejected in writing, as the coordinator asked:** override only
the base and accept that hover is the product's red. It is cheaper and it is defensible on a page
with one button; it is not defensible on `CWP-006`, `CWP-008` and `CWP-010`, where the commit
button is the thing a stranger is looking at when they press it, and a colour that changes identity
on hover reads as a broken page rather than as a hover.
