## 2026-09-04 · CR-068 wave H — the three judgments the rules did not settle

`US-CWP-036` (`CWP-031`) · `US-CWP-053` (`CWP-063`) · `US-CWP-054` (`CWP-044`).
Version **2.151.0**. Three questions were MINTED rather than answered
(`OQ-CWP-1566`, `1567`, `1568`); what follows is what this lane DECIDED, which
law 13 says is the deliverable and a question is the failure to produce.

### 1 · The documents read is published in `notifications`, not in `portal`

**The judgment.** There was no read anywhere for *"what has this customer been
sent"* — the staff Account details Documents tab is a FRAME, real column
headings over one spanning cell saying so, and its own comment explains why an
empty `<tbody>` would be worse. So this wave had to write one, and the choice
was WHERE.

It went into `apps/notifications/correspondence_reads.py` — the module that
owns `outbound_messages` — and the portal reaches it through a seam. The PO's
ruling of 2026-09-04 is the reason: *"all the services that are required for
Consumer portal - you will find it same set of services, endpoints are already
available for Accounts - account details view"*. A portal-only read would have
been a second implementation in the other direction, and the staff Documents
tab would have had to grow a third.

**What it costs, stated:** the read cannot compose a human reference. A bill's
readable name is `BL-2608-0141` and lives in `billing`; reading it from
`notifications` is the cross-module read B1 forbids. So every row carries
`source_type` and `source_id`, the CALLER resolves the name through its own
seams, and the portal drops the ids before anything crosses the wire (B14 rule
31). One extra hop, in exchange for one implementation.

### 2 · The four states a document can be in, and why `delivered` is not one

**The judgment.** `outbound_messages` has five statuses and
`delivery_ops.UNPOPULATED_STATUSES` records that **nothing on this deployment
can write two of them** — `delivered` and `bounced` are provider facts and no
provider adapter exists on print, email or SMS. So the read defines four:
**sent · queued · held · could not send**, and every row carries
`delivery_reported: false` with its reason as DATA rather than as a convention
a screen might forget.

**Worked, so the boundary is concrete.** Maria's August bill for **`$142.18`**
was queued to post and to email on 30 August. Today, and for as long as no
dispatcher runs, both rows read *queued*. The screen says *waiting to go*; it
does not say *sent*, and nothing anywhere on it says *delivered*. `OQ-1399`
closed on 2026-09-04 with the portal as a CONVENIENCE COPY — post and email
remain the delivery record — and this is what that ruling means in code.

**The chip tones carry it too:** there is no `success` tone on `CWP-031` at
all. Green reads as *arrived*, and the strongest claim this product may make is
that something left the building.

### 3 · Level pay reads ONE account, and it is the session's first

**The judgment.** Budget billing is enrolled per ACCOUNT
(`account_budget_status`), so a landlord holding four accounts has four
answers. `CWP-044` shows the first of the session's set rather than averaging
across them: adding four accounts' bills together would produce a level for a
CUSTOMER rather than for a property, and this product cannot enrol that.

**Worked:** Maria's four accounts total **`$872.82`** owing across them
(`US-CWP-026` TC-2), and no single level exists for that set. The screen states
one account's figure — twelve months of `$1,501.09`, an average of `$125.09`, a
level of `$125.00` — which is a number the utility could actually bill.

⚠ **REPORTED rather than decided:** which account, when there are four, is a
switcher question `CWP-044` inherits from the shell, and the shell's switcher
does not yet drive this read. Named here so the next lane does not read the
current behaviour as a design.

### 4 · The month names were a second copy, and G15 is what found it

`settings.regional.month.1` … `.12` has existed in all eleven catalogues since
the regional settings screen. This lane added **twelve more keys per catalogue
— 132 in all** — saying the same twelve words, and only noticed because G15
flagged *April*, *August*, *September* and *November* as untranslated German
(they are identical in both languages, and correctly so). They were deleted and
`LevelPay.tsx` reads the existing ones.

**The general form is worth writing down:** the PO's reuse ruling is about
READS, and it applies to COPY for the same reason — two homes for one fact are
free to disagree the day somebody corrects one. Three channel words went the
same way: the staff queue already says `Briefpost` in German and `Surel` in
Indonesian, and this lane had written `Post` and `Email`.

**What was NOT changed, and it is a report and not an oversight:** `fr-FR ::
portal.documents.colDocument` is *Document* and `id-ID ::
portal.planOffer.colNumber` is *No.* Both are byte-identical to English and
both are CORRECT in their own language; G15 counts them because it compares
bytes. Rewording either to turn a number green would make the screen worse for
the reader it is written for, which is the opposite of what B14 rule 35 asks.

### 5 · Two gate failures this wave repaired as a side effect of doing the step

* **G35 version-lockstep** was RED before this lane: `package.json` read
  `2.149.0` and `pyproject.toml` read `2.148.0` — DEF-341's third occurrence.
  Both now read `2.151.0` with a changelog entry. `2.150.0` was SKIPPED rather
  than reused, which is the gate's own instruction when a sibling has taken a
  number.
* **`DEF-CWP-3769`** — `ruff check` has been RED on `apps/portal/selectors.py`
  since `my_details` landed: `date` is used in two annotations and was never
  imported. It worked only because `from __future__ import annotations` makes
  every annotation a string, so no test could see it and no gate runs ruff over
  `apps/portal`. Import added; a gate that runs ruff there is REPORTED, because
  the gate registry is outside this lane.

### 6 · An id collision, caught at push time exactly where law 11 says it will be

Two lanes both computed *register max + 1* correctly, from different worlds,
and both took **`OQ-CWP-1563`**. The sibling pushed first, so its number stands
and this lane's three renumbered to **`1566`, `1567`, `1568`** — skipping 1564
and 1565 rather than shuffling into numbers the sibling might also be about to
take. The same afternoon a sibling and this lane both took `DEF-CWP-3769`.
**Neither was a mistake in anybody's arithmetic**, which is the whole point of
law 11's third family: what is wrong is which world the maximum came from.

## 2026-09-04 · `CWP-046` — WHAT A CUSTOMER'S OWN REQUEST LIST IS LINKED BY, AND WHY IT COULD NOT BE THE ACCOUNT (`US-CWP-060`)

**Three judgments, all taken rather than asked, and one question minted because
only the Product Owner can answer it (law 13).**

### 1 · The list is linked by the EMAIL, because there is no account on the row

`US-CWP-060` asks the request hub to show *"open requests with their references
and statuses"*, and the obvious reading is *this account's requests*. **There is
no such link and its absence is a RULE, not a gap.**
`apps.customers.service_request_service.create_from_portal` refuses `account`
and `customer` **by name** — `PORTAL_CAPTURE_FIELDS` names nine fields and
neither is among them — under `BR-CWP-026`: *"a public form may create work and
may never change an account."* `DEF-CWP-3767` found the same absence from the
other direction on 2026-09-04, when `CWP-065` wanted a move history and could
not walk an account back to the request that opened it.

**So the link is the two facts a portal row always carries:** the channel
(`customer_portal`, forced by the write and named by `BR-CWP-076`) and
`applicant_email`, which the portal writes from the credential the customer
signed in with. Both halves are IN THE QUERY, so `BR-CWP-010` holds and `G96`
is satisfied on the tenant.

**WHAT IT COSTS, stated rather than discovered:** a request a CLERK raised at
the counter for the same customer is invisible here. Worked — Maria rings the
office on 2 September, a clerk raises her move-out as `SR-26-0056`, she signs in
on 3 September and her Open requests panel is **empty**. The screen therefore
says, in words, *"This list is what you have asked for online"*, and the body
carries `lists_only_portal_requests: true` so no screen can imply otherwise.
Whether the list SHOULD widen is **`OQ-CWP-1680`** and is OPEN; nothing is
blocked and nothing is stubbed. ⚠ **THIS SENTENCE SAID `OQ-CWP-1640` UNTIL
2026-09-05, AND THAT ID NO LONGER EXISTS:** this lane minted it, a sibling had
already minted `OQ-CWP-1680` over the same ground — what makes a service
request *mine* when I am signed in — and the duplicate was dropped into theirs
at the merge rather than asked twice (law 13). `customers_seam.py` records the
same supersession beside the read itself.

**What was NOT done, and why:** matching on name or address would be a join on
prose, which `DEF-CWP-3767` already refused to do for the same table.

### 2 · A second JSON column, not `quick_service_categories` read twice

TC-8 requires that a tenant who renames a card sees the new label, so the six
cards must be configuration. `portal_settings` already holds a configurable card
list — `CWP-010`'s quick-service cards — and reusing it was considered and
rejected: those six are what a STRANGER WITH NO ACCOUNT asks for (a re-read, a
copy of a bill, low pressure), and these six are what a SIGNED-IN CUSTOMER wants
done to an account they hold. One list on both screens would offer *"copy of a
bill"* where the story asks for *"move out"*. `portal/0009` adds
`request_errands`, default `[]`, seeded by nothing — the empty list means *this
utility has not configured its own* and the selector answers the six defaults
for it, which is the posture `quick_service_categories` already takes (*a read
never writes*).

### 3 · The SERVER decides whether a card is a link or a held control

Four of the six cards lead to screens that do not exist yet — `CWP-048` (moving
out), the move-home form, the add-a-service form and *ask us something*. A card
linking to one of them is hard-won law 2 exactly: *a link with no screen behind
it*. Each card therefore carries `to` **or** `held_reason` and never both, and
the map that decides which lives in `apps/portal/selectors.ERRAND_ROUTE`.

**It is on the server DELIBERATELY.** If the screen held that map, the wave that
builds `CWP-048` would have to remember to change two places — which is exactly
how the eleven-service list came to be typed out by hand in two front-end files
and fail silently (`CLAUDE.md`, hard-won law 2). A configured `screen` this
product does not serve is REFUSED at the settings door, because a card with no
destination and no reason is a control that neither works nor says why
(`BR-CWP-056`).

### 4 · The story contradicts itself about one date, and the code follows §4

`US-CWP-060` TC-4 draws the row as `SR-26-0056 · Move out · 17 Sep · WE NEED TWO
DOCUMENTS`, while §4 says the request was **raised 2 September 2026** and the
move-out is **17 September**, and the epic's own capability matrix heads the
column **Raised**. The column is *Raised* and it shows **2 September**; 17
September is the last day of service, which is a fact about the move rather than
about the request. Filed as `DEF-CWP-3840` against the story text rather than
resolved silently, because a lane reading TC-4 alone would build the other one.

## 2026-09-04 · `CWP-052` — WHERE A STANDING CHARGE COMES FROM, AND WHY THE PORTAL DOES ONE MULTIPLICATION AND NOT TWO (`US-CWP-062`)

**Three judgments, taken rather than asked, and no question minted (law 13).**

### 1 · The standing charge is read through `rating.seams.base_charge_for`, not composed

`US-CWP-062` §5 maps *Standing charge* to *"base charge on the plan"*, and **the plan does
not own it.** `BR-RAT-088` (PO 2026-08-20, verbatim: *"the CHARGE CODE owns the base amount;
a plan displays it, never defines it"*) moved the source, and `BR-RAT-012` / `BR-RAT-027` —
the two rules that said *per service within a plan* — are both SUPERSEDED by it. The plan's
`base_charge` column and the schedule's survive only so a **disagreement** can be refused by
name, and `DEF-154` is what having two answers cost once: **every bill this product produced
charged `$0.00` for base**, because billing read a different column from the signed source.

So the portal reads the plan's figure and the in-force schedule's figure and hands **both**
straight to `apps.rating.seams.base_charge_for`, which resolves the third (the charge code's)
itself and applies the one implementation of the precedence. **The portal adds no arithmetic
on that path.** It sums the account's OWN services — a plan may list five, a customer who
takes water and trash pays two bases — and any refusal travels as a REASON.

**What the portal DOES compute, and it is the whole of it:** `months × standing` and
`connection fee + deposit`, then one comparison. Worked, on the story's own figures:
`5 × $18.50 = $92.50` against `$185.00 + $150.00 = $335.00` → **stopping**; at nineteen
months `19 × $18.50 = $351.50` against `$335.00` → **closing**. The crossover is
`$335.00 ÷ $18.50 = 18.1` months. Neither figure is a B4/B5 frozen one and `finance_calc` on
this story is `confirmed`, so this is arithmetic over read figures rather than new money
rules.

### 2 · `size_class` is `None`, because this product records no connection size

`base_charge_for` takes two narrowing facts — customer class and size class. The account's
class is read (`accounts.account_type.code`, `gather._customer_class`'s own source). The size
is passed as `None`, and that is the product's answer rather than a shortcut: **`DEF-514`
records that nothing in this product records a connection size**, and the seam's own
docstring says an unscoped call *"gets the same answer a tenant with one unscoped, flat base
code would get — which is every tenant this product provisions today"*. The day sizes are
recorded, this call gains the argument; passing one today would be passing a guess.

### 3 · A missing figure is never a zero, in either direction

`US-CWP-062` TC-8 asks that a service with no standing charge *"says so rather than showing
`$0.00` as a saving"*, and `rating_seam` already draws that line for connection fees — an
AMOUNT, `Included` (nothing attached) and `$0.00` (a utility saying *this one is free* out
loud) are three different facts. So every money field on this wire is `string | null`, the
selector's `_money` leaves `None` alone rather than quantising it to `"0.0000"`, and where
either side of the comparison is missing the verdict is **withheld with a reason** instead of
being computed against a number nobody typed.

**What the engine actually does when nothing states a base is REFUSE, not answer `None`** —
`DEF-277`, *"a blank base is CR-013's size-not-served, not a zero"* — so the reason that
travels is the engine's own. The screen says one sentence either way, because the customer's
question is *can you tell me?* and the answer is no.

### 4 · The write is the fifth SHAPE, and the account stays open

*Stop or restart* raises one `service_requests` row through the existing `service_request`
write point (`write_points.py` untouched, G81 still sees one public function per kind).
`BR-CWP-080` — *a disconnect leaves the account open and standing charges keep running* — is
served as a fact (`account_stays_open`), repeated in the consequence box, repeated on the
confirmation, and written into the **clerk's own worklist sentence**, because a clerk one
keystroke from closing an account nobody asked to close is the same misunderstanding from the
other side. The response says `supply_stopped: false`.

**A restart before the stop is refused twice on purpose:** at the edge, so the screen can put
the error on the right field, and in the write, so a caller that skipped the screen cannot
put an impossible row on a worklist.

## 2026-09-04 · `CWP-032` — THE DEPOSIT COMES BACK, AND THE DAY IT ACCRUES TO WAS NEVER STATED (`US-CWP-037`, `DEF-CWP-3842`)

**The finding first, because it is bigger than the screen it was found from.**

### 1 · Every final bill on a deposit-holding account refused to settle

`US-CWP-037`'s whole subject is *service `$63.40` − deposit `$150.00` −
interest → we owe you*, and the first honest read of it came back with **no
settlement at all** and a sentence blaming an unreadable accrual.

**The chain, and every link in it was individually correct.**
`billing.final_bill.settle_account` called `deposit_credit_for(account_id)`
with no `as_of`. `customers.selectors.deposit_interest_accrued` answers `None`
when no day is stated — **deliberately**, and its own docstring says why:
*"gate G6 keeps a clock out of a money path, and a figure accrued to a day
nobody named is a figure nobody can check."* `deposit_credit_for` then refuses
BY NAME rather than applying the principal alone, which is exactly what it was
written to do: *"a principal-only credit of 150.00 instead of 153.50 would keep
$3.50 of the customer's money on a bill that foots and an account nobody will
look at again."* **Three correct behaviours composing into a product that
cannot close an account that took a deposit — which, at a utility that takes
deposits, is every residential account.**

**AND `surface_debt.txt` SAID THE OPPOSITE.** Its `customers` line records that
before the engine existed *"an account holding a deposit could not be CLOSED by
anybody"* and then states *"that refusal is gone and the money is worked out
correctly"*. That was true of the ENGINE and false of the PRODUCT. The sentence
is corrected in place, and the lesson is the file's own rule read the other way:
**a sentence describing an engine is not a sentence about the product, and only
a caller proves the difference.**

**Why no test saw it.** Billing's final-bill suite exercises `settle()`
directly with a `DepositCredit` it constructs, and the wired `settle_account`
path is covered only on accounts holding NO deposit — where `deposit_credit_for`
short-circuits to zero without consulting the accrual at all. The one branch
that matters had no test through the door the product uses.

### 2 · The fix, and the day chosen

`settle_final_bill` now passes **`as_of=invoice.period_end`**. That is the
move-out day: `BR-CUS-056` and `prepare_final_bill` both put it there in as
many words — *"the OUTGOING account pays the move day, so `period_end` IS
`moved_out_on`"* — and it is the day the deposit stops being held, which is
where `BR-CUS-057`'s accrual ends.

**It is read off the BILL and not off a clock**, so G6 holds and a settlement
re-opened next month recomputes the same figure. `settle_account` gains `as_of`
with **no default**, so any caller that still names no day gets the identical
refusal it got before. **`apps/billing/one_time.py` line 864 is still the old
shape and is REPORTED rather than changed** — a different path, not this lane's.

**Worked, on the fixture:** `$63.40` service, `$150.00` held since 4 March
2021, a seeded tenant rate of 0% so `$0.00` interest — a **real answer and not
a refusal** — giving a remainder of **`−$86.60`** and an automatic **refund**.
The story's `$3.20` is what a 2% tenant gets; the test asserts the ARITHMETIC
(service − principal − interest = remainder) rather than a literal, because a
literal would be the test asserting the engine's answer back at it.

### 3 · The screen computes nothing, and TC-5 is asserted rather than trusted

`CWP-032` calls `settle_final_bill` through the seam and renders what it
answers. `US-CWP-037` §7 requires the figures to agree with `CWP-065`'s deposit
panel — *"a disagreement between the two is the defect both stories test for"* —
and the test asserts it on ONE account in ONE run, comparing the settlement's
deposit against `account_summary`'s panel field by field.

**The sign is the server's and there is no `Math.abs` anywhere on the screen.**
`−89.80` renders as `-$89.80` under the words *We owe you*; the direction picks
a SENTENCE, never strips a minus. `BR-CWP-048`'s *refund, never a credit* is
the engine's own `path` and not a reading of the sign.

### 4 · The last chance to query a reading closes, and says so

`US-CWP-037` TC-9 asks that the query route be gone once the account settles.
It is derived from `Settlement.settled` — a path chosen, or a zero remainder —
and the control is **replaced by the sentence that explains why**, not simply
removed. A customer who read *query this reading* yesterday and cannot find it
today is owed the sentence rather than the silence.

## 2026-09-04 · `CWP-066` — WHERE LEVEL PAY STANDS, AND WHY IT CARRIES NONE OF `CWP-044`'s FIGURES (`US-CWP-055`)

**Three judgments, all taken rather than asked.**

### 1 · Two screens, two questions, no shared arithmetic

`CWP-044` answers *what would I pay if I joined* — twelve months of `$1,501.09`,
an average of `$125.09`, a level of `$125.00`. `CWP-066` answers *what am I
paying and where do I stand*. The standing screen therefore carries **no
trailing total and no average**: it reads `budget_service.effective_level`,
which is the override if there is one and the computed level otherwise.

**The invariant is asserted rather than assumed.** One test enrols an account
on `US-CWP-054`'s own twelve months and then compares this screen's level
against the JOINING screen's own read on the same account, so the two cannot
drift apart into two `$125.00`s that stop being equal.

### 2 · The variance is read, and its cache is checked against its truth

`AccountBudgetStatus.variance_balance` is a CACHE; `account_budget_events` is
the truth, and `budget_service.recompute_balance` exists so the two can be
asserted equal. The portal reads the cache and one test asserts it against the
derivation, so a later lane that started summing events in the portal — a third
answer — would go red.

**`ahead` and `behind` are WORDS and the size is always positive** (TC-7). The
server sends a direction and a magnitude; the catalogue writes *you are `$47.30`
ahead*. Handing a screen `-47.30` would make it decide how to word a minus, and
eleven catalogues would eventually word it eleven ways.

### 3 · The override shows and its reason is not on the wire at all

`BR-BIL-017` keeps `level_override` beside `level` because the ±30% bound is
measured against the computed one. `level_override_reason` is the utility's own
note about a customer — *hardship agreed at the counter* — and `BR-CWP-052`'s
posture is that the surest guard is for the code building the body never to
select it. **It is not in the payload**, the test asserts its absence there, and
a separate assertion confirms the COLUMN still holds it, so a reader can tell
the difference between *withheld* and *lost*.

## 2026-09-05 · Payment providers are integrations, and beta ships behind a test one

**PO ruling, verbatim:** *"Payment stories - we will have multiple payment
providers integrated using integration module. For given utility we will
activate 1 or 2. That work we can do when integration is ready. Now from beta
product point of you can't you release payment functionality so that we can test
it. We can enable payment provider flow later - how can we handle this"*

Two things arrived in one sentence and they are recorded separately because they
bind different work.

### 1 · The shape — and the repo already holds it

A payment provider is **an integration, not a payments feature**: many are
registered, a given utility activates one or two. Nothing in `apps/payments`
names a vendor.

⚠ **THIS IS NOT NEW WORK TO DESIGN — `CR-069`'s substrate already built it, and
the ruling confirms what is there rather than asking for something else.**
Measured on the tip: `apps/integrations/manifests/` holds **18 provider
manifests**, two of them `category="payments"` — `payments_card.py`
(*"Card processor"*, `disposition=coming_soon`, wave W7, declaring the `charge`
and `card_page` operations) and `payments_kiosk.py`. A provider is code data, so
**adding one adds a manifest and no migration** (`BR-INT-037`); `Connection`
carries `provider_key` + `environment` with `production` and `sandbox` as two
rows, one active each (`BR-INT-026`); and `registry.adapter_for()` answers
`None` **as a value** for a provider with no adapter bound, which is exactly the
*declared but not yet connected* state a coming-soon provider needs.

So the only missing piece for any given vendor is **one adapter**, and the
answer to *"can we release payment for beta"* follows from that.

### 2 · Beta ships against a TEST provider, and it is a real provider

**The decision:** the seven payment stories are built now against a
sandbox-only provider registered the same way every other provider is — its own
manifest, its own adapter, `environment=sandbox`. It returns a token
(`Visa ●●●●4242`) and posts a settlement through the **same door** a real
processor uses: `apps/payments/webhooks.py` (577 lines, 15 tests), which already
verifies a signature and holds the composed idempotency key that stops a
replayed settlement becoming a second payment.

**What that makes testable in beta, and it is most of the value:** the payment
row, oldest-bill-first allocation (`BR-PAY-001`), the receipt, the ledger
posting and its balanced pair, the audit row, the refund path, the autopay
intent, and the duplicate guard. **None of that is vendor-specific**, so none of
it is rebuilt when a real provider is chosen — the vendor supplies a token and a
settlement, and everything after is what beta will have exercised.

**What beta cannot prove**, stated so nobody reads more into a green run: a real
card authorisation, a real decline, a real chargeback, and the vendor's own
3-D Secure step.

### 3 · The guard, and it is enforced rather than documented

A tenant whose active payments connection is `environment=sandbox` **may not
take a real payment**, and a `production` tenant **refuses the test provider by
name**. This is a rule about money reaching a real customer, so it is a check in
the code and a test, not a sentence in a docstring (hard-won law 1). The
`environment` column already exists to carry it.

### 4 · What this does NOT decide

The vendor question (*which processor*) is **no longer blocking** and moves out
of the critical path; the PO named five the same day — InvoiceCloud, Worldpay,
US payments, Global Payments, spruse — see the entry below.

⚠ **AND THE SENTENCE THAT STOOD HERE WAS WRONG: it said `OQ-1394` — who pays
the card fee — was *still open and still the PO's*. IT HAD BEEN CLOSED THE DAY
BEFORE** (2026-09-04), in the PO's own words: *"we have to give both the options
so far some utilities abosrb it other pass it to customer ; so we have to
flexible and create a flag somewhere to on and off it"* — **both**, behind a
per-tenant switch, which is the answer none of the three exclusive options
expressed. This lane put it back to the PO anyway and was told so
(`DEF-GOV-3929`). Corrected here rather than left, because a decision-log entry
saying a closed question is open is how it gets asked a third time.

**So the rule for beta:** the switch exists and defaults to ABSORB. There is no
real fee in a sandbox, so nothing computes one; turning surcharge on obliges the
fee to be computed, disclosed before the commit and checked against the
customer's state, and that arrives with a real processor.

## 2026-09-05 · `payment_methods` keeps its owner, and the customer's card gets its own name

**Task P1 of CR-068 phase 5, ruled by this lane and recorded rather than asked
(law 13: a judgment call with its reasoning is the deliverable).**

`B2` §2 spells the CUSTOMER's stored instrument `payment_methods`. That table
name is already taken, and has been since `OQ-031` closed the `payment_method_t`
enum into a tenant-extensible lookup: `apps/tenancy/models.py:985` holds it, and
it is the seeded tender vocabulary — cash, cheque, card, bank transfer — that
`Payment.method` points at on every payment row in the product.

**Two options, and the second was rejected:**

**(a) The lookup keeps the name; the instrument is `stored_payment_instruments`.**
**(b) The lookup yields — rename it `tender_methods` — and the instrument takes
the name `B2` §2 gives it.**

**(a) IS TAKEN.** (b) is the tidier reading of the spec and it moves a foreign
key on a money table, on a seeded lookup, across every existing `payments` row,
to win a word. The name is not worth a migration on `Payment.method`; a
mis-stated allocation is worth a great deal. `B2` §2 is stamped with this
divergence rather than followed, which is the same posture
`03-field-map.md` already takes wherever the code won.

**And the new name is not `customer_payment_methods`**, which would have kept
the collision one adjective away and left two tables a reader has to hold apart
by their prefix. *Instrument* is the word the card industry uses for the thing
itself, and nothing else in this schema is called one.

## 2026-09-05 · The five payment processors are named

**PO ruling, verbatim, answering *"which payment processor?"*:** *"We have
invoiceCloud, Worldpay, US payments, Global Payments, spruse, we will integrate
them as integration funtionalities are available"*

**So the answer to that question is FIVE, not one**, and it closes the last
thing that was blocking phase 5. Each is a provider in the integrations module —
its own manifest, `coming_soon` until its adapter is written — and a utility
activates the one or two it actually uses (PO ruling of the same day: providers
are integrations).

**They are registered NOW, ahead of their adapters, and that is deliberate.**
Adding a provider is data (`BR-INT-037`), so this costs a file each and no
migration; and a utility looking at Settings can see the processors this product
will support rather than a single generic card. `coming_soon` is the state the
substrate already models — `registry.adapter_for()` answers `None` **as a
value** — so nothing here fakes readiness.

⚠ **`payments_card` STAYS, AND ITS MEANING IS NARROWED RATHER THAN RETIRED.**
The tempting move was to delete the generic *Card processor* now that five are
named. It is cited by key in **fourteen places** across the backend tests, two
frontend test files and two render-checks as THE canonical coming-soon provider
— `test_us_int_017_gating.py` alone connects, tests, runs, patches and deletes
against it. Removing it would rewrite a working guard suite to win a tidier
grid. It now means *a card processor that is not one of the five*, said in its
own docstring.

⚠ **THE DISPLAY NAMES ARE THE PO'S WORDS AND TWO ARE UNCONFIRMED SPELLINGS.**
*US payments* and *spruse* are recorded as given. A provider's display text is
the ENGLISH fallback and the catalogue key wins on screen, so correcting either
is a catalogue line and **never a migration or a code change** — which is why
this is recorded rather than put back to the PO (law 13).

⚠ **THE FIELDS ON EACH ARE THE GENERIC CARD SHAPE AND ARE NOT CLAIMED TO BE
THAT VENDOR'S.** Nobody here has read InvoiceCloud's or Worldpay's API. Each
manifest says so in its own docstring, because a field list that LOOKS
authoritative and is guessed is hard-won law 1 wearing a vendor's name — the
real ones land with the adapter, and a manifest is data so that costs a file.

**What this does NOT change:** beta still ships against `payments_sandbox`.
Naming the five settles who we will integrate; it does not make any of them
connectable today, and the seven payment stories are built against the test
provider exactly as ruled this morning.

## 2026-09-05 · Four portal questions ruled in one exchange

All four arrived from the PO in two messages while phase 5 was being built.
Recorded here before the reply that acts on them (law 9), each with its worked
figure, and each register row closed the same commit.

### 1 · A missed payment plan is CHASED, never cancelled — `OQ-CWP-1720`

**PO, verbatim:** *"We continue to chase"*.

The question was a genuine collision: the blueprint's `P28` and `US-CWP-051`
read as though missing two instalments ends the plan, and a signed rule said
otherwise. **The plan does not end.** Somebody owing `$600.00` over six months
who pays three and then misses August and September is still on the plan in
October, still owes the same instalments, and is pursued through the ordinary
arrears route rather than being dropped back to the whole balance falling due.

**What this forbids, and it is the reason the question was asked:** no path may
auto-cancel a plan on a missed-instalment count. A screen that says *your plan
has ended* on a schedule is now a defect, not a feature.

### 2 · A bill that goes up lists EVERY reason, each with its share — `OQ-CWP-1569`

**PO, verbatim:** *"(a) list every reason with its share"*, choosing from the
three put to them.

So when August is `$34.00` higher and two things moved at once — 20% more water
AND a 5% price rise — **the screen names both and attributes an amount to each**,
rather than picking the larger and calling it the cause. It is more arithmetic
than naming one, and it is the only version that survives a customer checking it.

⚠ **THIS IS A FINANCE JUDGMENT AND IT IS NOW MADE**, which is what unblocks
`US-CWP-035` §7's `finance_calc: proposed`. The shares must sum to the movement
with no residue hidden in a rounding — the split is money arithmetic and hard
rule 2 governs it like any other.

### 3 · A reconnection fee is a CHARGE CODE, and the plan says how much — `OQ-CWP-1600`

**PO, verbatim:** *"we have reconnect fees in charge code, plan will tell you
how much to charge, plan is attached to unit and unit is attached to account"*

**This is an architecture answer and it retires the question rather than
answering its arithmetic.** The lane asked *what does reconnection cost, and is
the deposit the same one a new customer pays* — expecting a figure. There is no
figure to hold: the reconnection fee is a charge code like any other, its amount
comes from the PLAN, and the plan is reached by walking **account → unit →
plan**. The same walk the rest of the product already does.

⚠ **SO THE `$150.00` IN `US-CWP-057` §4 AND §7 IS NOT A CONSTANT TO CONFIRM.**
It is whatever that account's plan says, and the overdue screen's *"if it goes
that far `$657.60`"* is a SUM of read figures rather than a number anybody
types. A hardcoded reconnection fee or deposit anywhere is now a defect.

### 4 · Every hardship route stays open to the last day — `OQ-CWP-1601`

**PO, verbatim:** *"a) all three stay open right up to disconnection"*.

`CWP-056`'s drawn copy — *"Ask before the final notice and all three stay
open"* — reads as though something shuts afterwards. **Nothing shuts.** All
three routes are open right up to the moment the supply is cut, so a customer
who reaches the screen the day after a final notice is offered exactly what they
would have been offered the day before it.

**The copy is now wrong and is the defect**, not the behaviour: a sentence
implying a door closes, over three doors that do not, is the same shape as the
held controls this session already fixed twice.

## 2026-09-05 · Work is NOT an isolated module — build on what is already there

**PO ruling, verbatim:** *"please note that work is not isolated module - it
works with other modules hence you ahve to buld the code while leaveging
existing framwrok , code, tabels"*

**Said while CR-070 wave B was being built, and it corrects the emphasis rather
than a rule.** `CLAUDE.md`'s module map is about WRITES — work writes no other
module's table and `G78` fails a foreign write from its first commit. Nothing in
this ruling changes that. What it changes is what a lane does with everything
ELSE: **it leverages, it does not re-create.**

⚠ **THE FAILURE THIS FORBIDS IS A PARALLEL WORLD.** A module told "you own
crews, technicians, work orders, schedules" and given a clean directory will
happily grow its own connection read, its own account lookup, its own address
resolution, its own table for a state a null already expresses — each one
correct in isolation and each one a second answer to a question this product has
already answered. Two answers to one question is how a figure drifts.

**What that means concretely, and every one of these is already in the tree:**

* **The six Work tables live in `apps/metering/connections.py`** and stay there.
  Where they eventually MOVE is `16-work/03-field-map.md` §4 and waits on the
  blueprint's §16 — a lane must not build as though they had moved.
* **Five of the connection acts already exist** around `apps/metering/api.py`,
  which is why wave B's own task says *fourteen routes, **no rewrite***.
* **Reads of assets, connections, accounts, meter reads, areas and users go
  through the seam file that already exists** for that module in
  `apps/work/seams/` — one per module, read-only. A second reader is the drift.
* **The queue is a NULL, not a table.** `awaiting_approval()` is
  `accepted_by IS NULL AND state = completed`; wave B says *no new table* in as
  many words. A status column expressing the same fact would be the second
  answer again.
* **Addresses are derived by walking to the premises** (hard rule 8) — a work
  order declares no address column of its own, exactly as an asset, an account,
  a route and a cycle do not.
* **The screens compose the shared component kit** (B14 rule 36) and the
  existing shell, not a second kit — the portal already paid for that mistake
  (`DEF-CWP-3655`, a second component kit folded back onto the shared one).

**The test a lane should apply before writing anything:** *does this product
already answer this question somewhere?* If yes, call it. If it answers it
almost — extend the published read rather than writing a private one. Only a
genuinely new fact earns a new table, and `work` owns few of those: crews,
technicians, skills, certifications, parts, templates, assignments, rules and
labour rates.

Passed to both running CR-070 lanes the same minute, mid-build, rather than
found in review.

## 2026-09-05 · A wave stamps its own rows in the commit that lands it — r11 step 4 amended

**Not a PO ruling — a judgment made here, recorded with its cost, because the
rules ran out and a lane asked for it.** Hard-won law 13: *"a judgment call
recorded in the decision log with its reasoning is the deliverable; a question is
the failure to make one."*

**What happened.** Two lanes were dispatched onto CR-070 wave B on 2026-09-05.
It had shipped on 2026-09-04 as `2.136.0`, and wave O re-hosted its acts as
`2.141.0` the day after. Neither lane wrote a line: both ran r11 step 0, found
the work already in the tree, and stopped. **The dispatch error was mine** — I
wrote both briefs from wave B's own table without reading the wave O section
directly above it, which is step 0 and is the one step I skipped.

**What it would have cost had step 0 not held.** The wave B brief names
`07-frontend/src/features/customers/ConnectionDetailPage.tsx`. Wave O deleted
that file and repointed its links; recreating it would have resurrected a retired
destination and broken wave O's own grep case (*no link in the front end
navigates to `/connections/<id>`*). The only files with that basename now are
`features/integrations/ConnectionDetailPage.tsx` — a different screen the plan
warns twice must never be matched by basename.

**The judgment, and why here rather than a question to the PO.** This is a
process fault with no signed rule against it and no figure only the PO holds, so
it is ours to decide (law 13's short list). **r11 step 4 now says: stamp the
wave's own rows DONE in the commit that lands its last task.** Not as a tidying
pass — *a pointer updated in a later commit is a pointer that does not get
updated.*

⚠ **THE REASON IT IS WORTH A RULE RATHER THAN A REMINDER IS THE PATTERN, AND THE
PATTERN IS NOW FIVE DEEP ON THIS BRANCH.** B14's rule-count line has been wrong
five times, always in the same direction. `CR-068` R3's held controls rotted the
day their screens landed and shipped the customer portal with **two working doors
out of eight** (`DEF-CWP-3925`). Hard-won law 12 records it for pointers
generally. Every one is the same shape: **landing the work and moving the pointer
to it are two acts, and only the first feels like the work.** A rule that depends
on someone remembering is exactly the rule that is not followed — which is the
argument step 7 of the change process already makes about versions.

**What is NOT claimed.** No gate enforces this and none can: nothing in this repo
reads prose for truth, which r11 says of step 0 in as many words. The mitigation
is that the stamp is now part of the same commit as the work, where forgetting it
is visible in the diff rather than three paragraphs above the table.

**Filed:** `DEF-WRK-3933` (the misdispatch, with the escape reason) ·
`DEF-WRK-3934` (three plan rows citing a wireframe that does not exist) ·
`34ac2b0a` (wave B stamped AS BUILT, 65 insertions, 0 deletions).

## 2026-09-05 · Nine judgment calls phase 5's four lanes made and could not stop to write down

**Every one of these was decided while building, is live in the code today, and
had no row.** Law 13's standing rule is that a judgment call recorded with its
reasoning is the deliverable and a question is the failure to make one — but a
judgment recorded NOWHERE is worse than either, because the next lane meets it
as an unexplained line and "simplifies" it. Each is written here with the figure
or the sentence a reader can check it against.

### 1 · Autopay does not say when the next payment would be taken, because nothing holds that date

`apps/payments/autopay.py` names the gap rather than filling it:
`NEXT_DUE_DATE_NOT_HELD = "next_due_date_not_held"`.

`CWP-040`'s *next few* table wants `14 Sep 2026 · $142.18 · SCHEDULED`. The
amount is real — it comes off the issued bill. **The date is not held anywhere
in this product.** An account has a billing cycle and a bill has a due date, but
the date on which an autopay draft WOULD be attempted is a property of a
scheduler that does not exist.

**Computing it from the cycle was rejected.** It would be right most months and
silently wrong in exactly the months a customer cares about — a cycle moved for
a holiday, a bill issued late, a final bill. A date on that screen is read as a
promise about somebody's bank account.

So the row states the absence as a code and the screen says the date is not set
yet. This is the same posture `availability.py` takes for the deferred document
upload, and it is the posture this repo prefers wherever a fact is missing: **an
absence that is NAMED can be filled in later; an absence that is COMPUTED is
indistinguishable from an answer.**

### 2 · A card refund goes back by cheque, and the screen says why rather than saying *sent*

`refunds.destination_of()`, worked from `US-CWP-049` §4: a **$89.80** refund of a
**card** overpayment answers `came_in_by: "card"`, `brand: "Visa"`, `last_four:
"8812"` — and then `method: "check"`, `reference: "10241"`, `kind: "fallback"`,
`fallback_reason: "card_rails_absent"`. The screen reads *the money came in on
the card ending 8812; we have sent cheque 10241 instead, because we cannot
return money to a card yet.*

**The alternative was a bare *Sent · 21 Sep*, and it is worse in a specific
way:** a customer who paid by card and receives a cheque will ring to ask why,
and the screen that could have answered said nothing. Naming the reason costs
one field.

⚠ **A DEAD CARD OUTRANKS ABSENT RAILS.** Both are true of an expired card and
only one of them is still true after the payment rails land, so the customer is
given the reason that will not evaporate: `card_expired`, not
`card_rails_absent`.

⚠ **AND A REFUND WITH NO SOURCE PAYMENT IS *several_sources*, NOT *unknown*.**
Since `OQ-195` (PO, 2026-09-01) `payment_id` is nullable **precisely because**
the credit came from more than one payment. Its absence is therefore a FACT
about the credit rather than a missing join, and reporting it as *unknown* would
turn a correct model into an apparent bug.

### 3 · The card named on a refund is named only when the customer holds exactly one

`refunds._saved_card()` ends `return rows[0] if len(rows) == 1 else None`, over a
queryset limited to two.

A saved instrument belongs to the CUSTOMER, not the account, so a landlord can
hold three cards. **Naming the oldest, or the most recently used, would put a
specific four digits on a refund we cannot prove the money came from** — and
`••••8812` is exactly the kind of detail a person takes as confirmed. Where
there is one card there is no ambiguity and the digits are shown; where there is
more than one the screen says the money came in on a card and stops.

The query takes `[:2]` rather than counting: two rows is all that is needed to
know the answer is "more than one".

### 4 · Two held controls were renamed, because their stated reason had stopped being true

Both read `no_rails` for one afternoon. `apps/payments/gateway.py` landed the
same day and **a charging path now exists** — so on both screens the sentence
under the disabled control was false while the control itself was still
correctly disabled.

* **Autopay** → `no_automatic_charge`. What is missing is not a way to charge;
  it is anything that DRAFTS a payment without a person pressing a button.
  Nothing consumes `AutopayCaptureIntent`. The screen now says *we cannot draft
  payments yet*.
* **The fees on `CWP-050`** → `no_fee_payment_path`. Different reason again: a
  fee is a quote that never posts to the ledger, and collecting one is a counter
  action gated to Admin or Billing Clerk. `write_points.py`'s `payment` row
  still carries `function=None` for this path — the product's own statement that
  the portal writes no payment here.

⚠ **THIS IS HARD-WON LAW 2's MIRROR, AND IT WAS CAUGHT BY THE TEST THE LAW ASKS
FOR.** `DEF-CWP-3925` is a rule with a clock in it — *held until X* — rotting on
the day X arrives. The cure written into that law is to **write the test that
fires when the hold expires, in the same commit as the hold**, and both of these
screens had one: the hold-expiry test went RED and named the control. The
refusal survived the change and its SENTENCE did not, which is precisely what
the test was for.

**The general rule this settles: when a hold's reason changes, the hold does not
automatically end.** Two of the three possible outcomes are *still held, new
reason*; only the third is *release it*. A lane finding a stale hold reason must
work out which, and both of these turned out to be the first.

### 5 · `to_pay_now` is what is LEFT to pay, not what was quoted

`paying.py` returns `money.amount(totals["outstanding"])`.

On `US-CWP-050`'s own fixture nothing has been taken yet, so it is the story's
**`$335.00`** and the two readings agree. **They diverge the moment a clerk takes
$100 at the counter**, and the honest figure is then `$235.00`. Using
`fee_total_to_collect` — `BR-CUS-090`'s own arithmetic of quoted, less what an
invoice settled, less what the counter took — means TC-4's *"the request moves
out of fees due"* falls out of the existing number rather than needing a second
sum on this screen that could disagree with the first.

⚠ **AND THE DEPOSIT IS NOT IN IT.** `$150.00` is not a fee line, is not in
`fee_total_to_collect`, and settling the fees leaves it exactly where it was —
on the first bill. Two figures, `to_pay_now` and `on_first_bill`, and the screen
never adds them.

### 6 · A guest bill's card-surcharge guard is a REFUSAL, not a calculation

`guest_api._no_surcharge_is_lawful_here()` reads `payments_seam.
card_surcharge_enabled` and **raises** if a tenant has surcharging on.

`OQ-1394` closed on 2026-09-04 with BOTH options behind a per-tenant switch. The
surcharged half obliges three things — the fee **computed** from the processor's
schedule, **disclosed before the commit** (*"a customer paying `$142.18` must see
the surcharge and the new total before they press, never after"*), and **checked
against the customer's state** — and not one of them is possible without a real
processor.

**So beta ships ABSORBED, and this function's whole job is to keep that TRUE
rather than assumed.** The day the setting exists, a tenant who switches
surcharging on is refused here — instead of a customer being charged a fee
nobody showed them. It is reached through the seam by name (`getattr(...,
None)`), so it is correct today, when the setting does not exist, and correct
afterwards.

### 7 · Autopay is refused for the whole SET when any one account is blocked

`instruments.autopay_stance()` — any account in the login's set with
`cash_only_no_autopay` blocks it, and the reason is named.

**This is the conservative reading and it was chosen deliberately.** The
instrument is the CUSTOMER's — a landlord saves one card and pays four accounts
with it — so a card enrolled at the set level could be charged for an account
the utility has put on cash-only. A per-account election is `CWP-040`'s own
screen, and until it exists the safe answer for this screen is the strictest
one.

**The reason is named so the customer knows which fact to argue with**, and the
control is disabled rather than absent. ⚠ And where the block list cannot be
read at all it refuses CLOSED (hard-won law 3): an unreadable block list is not
an absent one, and answering *allowed* there would enrol exactly the account the
utility excluded.

### 8 · Three test cases deferred by ruling, with the absence ASSERTED rather than skipped

`OQ-1396` CLOSED 2026-09-04, PO verbatim: *"we are not giveing this acces as of
now"* — a delegate may not manage payment methods.

Lane A's `US-CWP-046` TC-8 and `US-CWP-022` TC-5/TC-7 were all written against
delegate access. **They are not deleted and they are not skipped.** Each now
asserts that the capability is ABSENT — the delegate path refuses — so if
somebody builds delegate access without reopening the question, the suite goes
red and names the ruling.

**A `@skip` would have been the easy shape and it is the wrong one:** a skipped
test proves nothing in either direction and reads as work outstanding. An
asserted absence is a live check that the ruling still holds, which is the same
posture `test_us_cwp_074_centres.py` takes for `OQ-1398`'s untaken workflow.

### 9 · `US-CWP-046` TC-9 was AMENDED, not left blocked, because its question had already been answered

TC-9 was written to prove the card-fee computation raises
`NotImplementedError("OQ-1394")`. **`OQ-1394` closed the day before that story
was built** — both options, behind a per-tenant switch — so a test asserting the
raise would have been asserting a boundary that no longer exists.

It now asserts what §6 above describes: no fee line is drawn, and a tenant with
surcharging on is refused by name.

⚠ **This is the same trap `DEF-GOV-3929` was filed for on the same day** — a
lane reading a register row's opening question and not its verdict, because
these rows are one very long line each and the status is at the far right. The
check is to read the row's STATUS, never the row's beginning.

**Filed:** `DEF-CWP-3940` (a status-line assertion that had gone missing, found
by the new lint gate) · `DEF-CWP-3941` (CWP-008's priced answer has no test) ·
`DEF-PAY-3942` (sixteen `BR-PAY` citations naming rules no document defines) ·
`DEF-CWP-3943` (36 catalogue keys with no call site after the 229-key merge) ·
`DEF-CWP-3944` (a screen test that presses a control by its rendered words).
## 2026-09-05 · The signed-in portal's per-tenant rate is `3000/min`, and the arithmetic is here

**Not a PO ruling. A figure worked out here, because `NFR-42`'s own file says
these are ours: *"Its figures are OURS by delegation, not a PO ruling."*** Law 13
again — the judgment recorded with its reasoning is the deliverable.

**The gap it closes (`DEF-CWP-3931`).** `NFR-39` names three isolations *"each a
build task, not an aspiration"*: the portal's own queue and worker, its own
connection budget, and its own rate limits **per tenant as well as per address**.
Two of those covered the guest surface completely — `guest_api.py`, 15 of 15 —
and **none of the fifty-four authenticated endpoints**. `api.py` carried them on
8 of 62, and all eight are `AllowAny`. `NFR-38` counts *"guests **and signed-in
customers together**"*, and `guards.py`'s own justification — *"a busy afternoon
at Pine Hill is a few hundred customers on a few hundred addresses… together they
can take every worker the back office needs"* — describes customers who are
signed in, reading their bills.

**Why the guest's `600/min` was NOT simply copied across, which was the tempting
move.** That figure was derived as *ten times the sixty-a-minute per-ADDRESS
rate*, for a surface a stranger points traffic at. On the signed-in half a rate
set too low protects nobody — **it refuses real customers**, which is a worse
outcome than the gap. A hundred signed-in customers on one tenant at six reads a
minute already reaches 600.

**The arithmetic, so the next lane can argue with it rather than with the
number.** The busiest minute a utility has is the hour after a bill run, when a
notification goes out and everyone opens the app at once. A tenant here is under
3,000 connections (`CLAUDE.md`). A burst of ~300 of them inside one minute, each
session costing roughly eight reads — home, accounts, the bill list, one bill,
usage — is **~2,400 requests in that minute**. `3000/min` clears that with
headroom and still catches a runaway.

⚠ **IT IS A CEILING ON ABUSE, NOT A SHAPER OF NORMAL PEAKS, AND IT IS
DELIBERATELY LOOSE — SAID PLAINLY RATHER THAN IMPLIED.** The figure that would
actually bound this is a MEASURED one: `NFR-42`'s load case, 500 concurrent
portal users with the back office working, **which nothing in this repository yet
runs**. This rate exists so the dimension exists. It moves in
`config/settings/base.py` as `PORTAL_SIGNED_IN_TENANT_RATE`.

**What does the real work on this half is the connection budget**, not the rate:
`PORTAL_INFLIGHT_MAX` (default `GUNICORN_WORKERS − 1`) is what keeps one worker
free for a clerk, and it is now on all sixty-two `api.py` endpoints as well as
all fifteen guest ones. `portal_admission` was made **idempotent** so the eight
that already had it could not end up double-wrapped, which would have taken two
slots for one request and halved that route's budget with no symptom.

**What was deliberately NOT done: the sixty-a-minute per-ADDRESS throttle is not
on the signed-in routes.** A household with two accounts, or an apartment block
behind one NAT address, would collide with each other; the signed-in surface is
bounded by the session, not by the address.

**`G99` fails a portal endpoint with no budget**, because a decorator that must
be remembered is exactly the thing that was not remembered here — 54 of 62, in a
file whose stated convention is that a new wave appends its routes at the end and
copies the block above.

## 2026-09-05 · Who publishes *which account owns this bill* — the guest charge's seam

**Lane F's decision, written here because a lane may not edit this file. Not a
PO ruling and not a question for one: the answer was never in doubt — what was
in doubt is who owns the read.**

**The answer.** `invoices.account_id` is one column, so an invoice belongs to
exactly one account. Nothing to rule on.

**The judgment.** Three ways were open to get that fact to
`gateway.charge_guest_bill`, and two were refused:

1. **Let the gateway walk into billing's ORM** — refused, B1 and G6. A module
   reads another module's tables through a named seam or not at all.
2. **Let the guest edge pass the account down** — refused, ⚠ **and this is the
   one that matters.** It would make *where a stranger's money lands* a
   **request-shaped value on an unauthenticated form**, with the rails unable to
   tell a resolved account from a supplied one. The refusal is not about
   tidiness; it is about what an anonymous caller is allowed to name.
3. **Publish it in `apps/payments/billing_seam.py`** — chosen. Narrow, beside
   every other billing fact payments already reads by name.

**Two properties that had to hold and do.** It answers `None` **identically**
for an unknown number, another tenant's number, a draft, a void and a corrected
bill, so `US-CWP-003` TC-2's byte-identical refusal holds at the seam as well as
at the edge. And **it is not an allocation instruction**: no `targets=` is
passed, so `BR-PAY-001` runs untouched — a guest paying `$142.18` against
`BL-2608-0141` while an `$18.00` July bill is open settles **July first and
leaves `$124.18` on August**, which is the rule the product already has rather
than a second one for guests.

**One refusal sentence for two held reasons, and that is a disclosure decision
rather than a shortcut.** *No processor connected* and *this account is
cash-only* answer identically on the wire. The second is a `BR-PAY-013` sanction
— a fact about the **customer** — and `BR-CWP-021` does not let a stranger
holding the paper be told anything about the person. The specific code stays on
the exception for the log; the `br_ref` that travels is the neutral
`BR-CWP-056`. The sanction **is** checked: without that, the public form would
be the documented way round a flag that `J12` step 6 says nothing auto-clears.

**Filed alongside:** `DEF-CWP-3947` (the 503 for a function we had not written)
· `DEF-CWP-3948` (a recorder bypassed by `from apps.X import Y`) ·
`DEF-PAY-3949` (a receipt with a blank reference) · `DEF-CWP-3950` (a lost
response answering *there is nothing to pay*) · `DEF-CWP-3951` (a receipt
address accepted and dropped).

## 2026-09-05 · All six errand cards are SHOWN, disabled where unavailable — this reverses *absent, not greyed*

**PO ruling, verbatim:** *"Yoi ahev these cards - may be disable them, but for
completess have them on screen"* — said on being shown that the live Silver Creek
front page draws four cards where the blueprint draws six.

⚠ **WHAT THIS SUPERSEDES, STATED RATHER THAN ASSUMED.** `US-CWP-001` TC-2 reads
*absent, not greyed*, and `apps/portal/selectors.cards_for`'s docstring cites it
in those words: *"filtered HERE, on the server, so a card whose switch is off
never reaches the browser."* **That is now reversed.** The server sends all six
and says of each whether it is available; the screen draws all six and disables
the ones that are not. TC-2 and the docstring are amended in the same commit as
the code, not after it (r11 step 4, amended this morning).

**Why the PO is right, in their own terms.** A four-card page does not read as
*"two things this utility does not offer"* — it reads as *a page with four
things on it*. The utility cannot see what they are missing, and neither can a
customer who was told the portal does six. Completeness is the point.

**The one thing added on top of the ruling, because a plain grey box would waste
it:** each disabled card carries WHY. The two reasons are genuinely different
and a utility must be able to tell them apart —

* **Check my area** is off by a ruling (`CR-068` R9: outage reporting ships, the
  public status page waits, because it needs somebody keeping it current out of
  hours). It is **permanent** until that decision moves, and no action by the
  utility turns it on.
* **Help & answers** is off because nothing is **published** (`BR-CWP-093`). One
  published answer turns it on **today**.

Greying both identically would tell a utility that a five-minute job and a
parked decision are the same thing, which is `DEF-CWP-3953` — the row filed an
hour before this ruling arrived, for exactly this.

⚠ **AND THE HOLD NEEDS THE TEST THAT FIRES WHEN IT EXPIRES**, in this commit,
not later (hard-won law 2's mirror, `DEF-CWP-3925`): the day *Check my area*
gets a screen, or a tenant publishes its first answer, the suite must go red and
name the card rather than leaving a grey box over a working destination.

**What does NOT change:** *What things cost* was already shown-and-held and
stays exactly as it is; the nav words follow the cards, so `Help` and `Visit us`
keep appearing only when there is something behind them — a nav word is a
destination, not a catalogue, and a disabled word in a top bar is the dead
control law 2 warns about rather than the completeness this ruling asks for.

## 2026-09-05 · A way back, and how the one-time code becomes testable in beta

**Two PO messages, both verbatim, both from opening the running product.**

### 1 · There was no way home from any guest screen

*"I ahve no way to go bak to home screen - ; look at any scren other than home
there is no way to go back - to main screen - you ahve to give Hom as option
befor pay Bill"*

The guest top bar held the utility's name as **plain text** and four errands, so
once a visitor opened *Pay a bill* or *Start service* the only route back was the
browser's back button. **The signed-in shell had the identical gap** — its brand
was a `<span>` too — found by looking after the guest one was reported.

Built: a **Home** word first in the guest nav, where the PO asked for it, reusing
`portal.tab.home` (already in all eleven catalogues — minting a twelfth spelling
of *Home* would be 33 strings for a word the product has), **and** the brand made
a link in both frames, because that is the convention every visitor knows and it
costs no space. A convention is not a control, which is why the word is there as
well.

⚠ **A TEST CAUGHT THE FIRST DRAFT AND IT WAS RIGHT TO.** `US-CWP-001` TC-3 is
*the portal is off → no nav, so no door of any kind*, and the brand link was
outside the `live` guard: a clickable name on a switched-off portal is a door.
It is inside now; the name still shows and goes nowhere.

### 2 · The one-time code cannot be read, so beta cannot enrol

*"Atleast show me 6 digit code on this screen - so that I can copy and paste it
during enrolement"*, and then, on the disclosure question being put to them:
**"you decide how to handle text message part"**.

**So the decision is ours and here it is.** The code is minted and written to the
outbound queue; the queue screen lists Type, Sent by, Status, Recipient, Tries
and What went wrong, and **no message body**. Nothing sends it and nothing shows
it, so an enrolment cannot be finished on a tenant with no provider.

**What is built: the body is shown on the queue row ONLY while the tenant has no
notification provider connected for that channel.** The moment they connect
Twilio or an SMTP sender, the body stops showing — by itself.

**Why that gate and not an environment flag.** A flag is a thing somebody has to
remember to turn off, and hard-won law 3 says the unsafe option must be the one
you type. This gate is **self-disarming**: the condition that makes the body safe
to show (*nothing could have delivered it, so nobody else can have it*) is
exactly the condition that makes it necessary. It cannot be left on by accident
in production, because connecting a provider is the first thing a live utility
does.

**What is NOT built, and was refused when it was the quicker option:** skipping
the code for a tenant with no provider. The account number, the postcode and the
surname are all printed on the paper bill; the code is the only thing that is
not, and removing it turns self-serve enrolment into *anyone holding a bill gets
the login*.

## 2026-09-05 · What actually rots, measured — 60 refusal points, two expired

**Not a ruling. A measurement, recorded because it narrows a rule this repo has
been applying too broadly.**

Three separate outbreaks of the same fault landed in a week — six shut doors on
the front page (`DEF-CWP-3925`), 26 screens with no door at all
(`DEF-CWP-3954`), and a card greyed over a live screen for 32 hours
(`DEF-CWP-3959`). The obvious lesson — *audit every disabled control* — is the
wrong one, and the audit proves it.

**Sixty refusal points were read. Two had expired.** Two more carried no reason
at all. Everything else was either still true or was a *working* state, which is
not a refusal and has nothing to explain.

⚠ **THE CLASS THAT ROTS IS NARROW AND CAN BE NAMED.** A hold whose reason is
**“a screen is not built”** has a clock in it: something else, elsewhere, will
make it false, and nothing tells it. A hold whose reason is **“this form is not
filled in”** is answered by the data every time it draws and *cannot* rot.

**So the rule is not “audit disabled controls”. It is:** a hold that waits on a
SCREEN needs the test that fires when that screen lands, written in the same
commit. The other fifty-eight need nothing.

**How it is now enforced, and this is the transferable half:** each remaining
hold states **as data beside itself** which screen would release it, and a test
reads that against the front end's own register of screens. The day the
moving-out screen lands, the suite goes red and names the card. Proved red three
ways before being trusted — a screen arriving, the fix reverted, and the address
disagreeing.

⚠ **AND THE CHECK'S OWN FIRST DRAFT HAD THE DEFECT IT WAS WRITTEN FOR.** The
browser assertion read the button's *state* without pressing it — which is true
on the broken screen too. **Pressing it is what makes it fail.** A guard that
reads a control instead of using it is the same shape as a test asserting an
absence: green for as long as the fault lasts.

## 2026-09-05 · The portal's lists get the shared FURNITURE, not the staff `DataTable` (`DEF-CWP-3977` / D2)

**A judgment call, recorded with its evidence, because it reverses the stated fix
on the defect row it answers.** No rule was reversed and nothing frozen was
touched; what changed is which of two options the evidence supports.

`DEF-CWP-3977` (D2 in the portal layout audit) says no portal list can be
searched, sorted or paged, and states its own fix this way:

> *"One decision then a sweep: the portal composes the staff DataTable, or
> MiniTable grows a toolbar and a footer. The drawing and B14 rule 20 both say
> one table type, so it is the former."*

**The premise is a paraphrase, and the verbatim rule does not say it.** B14 rule
20 reads, in full:

> **Table type is one size everywhere: body `--table-font-size` (13.5px), column
> headers `--table-header-font-size` (12px), uppercase at 0.08em tracking over a
> 2px rule. No inline overrides. A `<th>` in a body row or a `<tfoot>` is a
> CELL, not a header — it takes the body tier.**

That is a **type-size** rule. Its source says the same — `r10`'s `UI-RULES.md`
rule 20, *"Table type is one size (13.5px) everywhere; no inline overrides"*,
filed under *"Tables (the list-table assembly, class `.lt`)"*, a STYLE assembly.
Neither text names a component. The rules that do govern this lane are 12
(toolbar), 13 (sorting), 15 (row icons), 16 (pagination footer) and 17 (empty
state), and every one of them describes **furniture a list must carry** without
saying which component provides it. `MiniTable` already meets rule 20: it renders
at `text-table`, the same `--table-font-size` token the staff `DataTable` uses,
and says so in its own comment.

⚠ **THE PARAPHRASE HAS ALREADY PROPAGATED INTO CODE.** `portal/bills/Bills.tsx`
cites *"B14 rule 20 (ONE table type)"* in its Trace header, and it is not the
only one. Cite it as the size rule it is.

### What composing the staff `DataTable` would actually cost — five findings, checked not assumed

1. **It would break `BR-CWP-011` on its first line.** That rule says *"the
   SIGNED-IN surface calls the PORTAL edge and nothing else"*. `DataTable.tsx`
   imports `getUserPreference` / `putUserPreference` from `@/api/endpoints`. **No
   file under `src/portal/` imports `@/api/endpoints` today** — checked, zero
   hits. This would be the first.
2. **And that call would 403 for every customer.** `useColumnPreference` fires on
   mount and hits `GET/PUT /user-preferences/{key}`, which is
   `@permission_classes([AnyTenantRole])` — a **staff** role. The portal
   authenticates with `PortalSessionAuthentication` + `IsPortalCustomer`. Every
   portal list would issue a failing request on every mount.
3. **The staff theme travels with it — this is D12, in advance.**
   `DataTable.css` reads `var(--color-surface)`, and `--color-surface` is
   `#eae9e9`, grey. `DEF-CWP-3987` (D12) is already filed for exactly this: the
   shared `Panel` renders grey in the portal because it uses the staff surface
   token, so one screen shows a white main column and a grey rail. Composing
   `DataTable` would repeat that fault on six more screens, and it is the trap
   named in this lane's brief — *a token that does not travel with its
   component*.
4. **It is built for server-side paging and nothing on the portal edge pages.**
   `DataTable` takes a `TableRequestState` and a server total. `/portal/bills`
   returns `{"bills": billing_seam.bills_for(...)}` — every row. So would
   `/documents` and `/payments`.
5. **It brings the staff `StateFrame` empty/loading/error frames** into a surface
   that has its own, in the customer's words.

### The decision

**The portal composes the shared kit's `ListPager` for the footer, and the
toolbar, sort and row icons are ADDED TO THE PORTAL KIT as one component that
wraps `MiniTable`.** One table type in the portal, not two: `MiniTable` stays the
only thing that renders a `<table>` there, and the new `PortalListTable` is
furniture around it.

**The precedent is already ratified and is the same shape.** `ListPager`'s own
docstring, from `CR-029` RC-W3 (PO 2026-08-23), answers this exact question for
the staff app's five non-`DataTable` lists:

> *"WHY A SECOND THING THAT PAGES, WHEN `DataTable` ALREADY PAGES. It does not
> page the same lists. `DataTable` owns server-paginated screens … The five
> tables above are client-held arrays inside a wizard step or a read-only ops tab
> — no request state, no server total, nothing to sort server-side — and putting
> them on `DataTable` would hand a wizard picker a column chooser."*

Every clause is true of the portal's eight lists. And `ListPager` is deliberately
*one implementation* — the same `table.pager.*` keys and the same `table-pager*`
classes `DataTable` uses — so using it here keeps **one footer in the product**,
which is what rule 16 is for. Checked rather than assumed: the app has one
entry (`index.html`), `App.tsx` has **zero** lazy imports and `AppShell.tsx`
imports `DataTable`, so `DataTable.css` is in the single emitted stylesheet and
the `table-pager*` classes do reach a portal page.

This is B14 rule 36 applied as written — *"compose the kit. Where the kit lacks a
piece, ADD IT TO THE KIT — one component, one visual decision, every screen —
rather than hand-rolling it in the screen."* The kit has the footer; it lacks a
toolbar for a client-held list, and that is what gets added.

### Paging is CLIENT-side, over the full payload, and the code says so

The lists are one customer's own history: the drawing's own figures are 41
documents and 31 payments, and ten years of monthly bills is 120 rows. `pageSlice`
already exists in `ListPager.tsx` for exactly this. Server-side paging would mean
new query params on three portal endpoints, `TableRequestState` plumbing and
RLS-safe ordering, for lists that fit in one page of 50.

⚠ **A FOOTER OVER A FULL PAYLOAD IS ONLY HONEST WHILE THE PAYLOAD IS BOUNDED BY
ONE CUSTOMER.** That is written in the component, not left to be inferred. If a
portal list ever spans a whole tenant, this decision is the one to revisit, and
the endpoints are where the work would land.

### What this does NOT decide

The column chooser (`▦ Columns`, rule 14) is **not built** and is not stubbed
silently: a customer with six columns has nothing to hide, the staff persistence
route is closed to them (finding 2), and inventing a portal-local one would be a
second preference store. Stated as an absence rather than drawn as a dead
control — hard-won law 2's mirror.

## 2026-09-05 · CWP-034 and CWP-037 — a meter COLUMN, and a customer-facing status word

Two judgment calls where the signed rules ran out, recorded with their worked
figures so the next lane does not re-decide them. Neither went to the PO: law 13
says a judgment recorded with its reasoning is the deliverable, and neither
collides with a signed rule or needs a fact only they hold.

### 1 · Every reading gets a METER COLUMN, not a meter chooser

**The problem, with real values.** On the demo account an electric reading of
`6462` and a water reading of `2007` land on the same date. Both rows carried
their unit and nothing else, so a customer had no way to say which box on the
wall a row came from. The payload had carried `meter_serial` and `meter_no` per
row since the screen was built and the screen rendered neither
(`DEF-CWP-3990`).

**What the drawing says, and why it does not settle it.** `CWP-034.png` scopes
the whole screen to one meter — the title reads *Readings on your water meter*
and the browser chrome carries `water · front meter` — and draws **no chooser at
all**. It was drawn for a one-meter household. The product bills eleven
services.

**The two ways out, and why the column won.**

* A **chooser** makes the DEFAULT view a subset, on a screen the story
  (`US-CWP-041`, *Every reading*) and the register (`CWP-034`, *Every reading*)
  both name for showing all of them. `readings_for_account` takes an account and
  a `channel` and **no meter**, so a chooser would filter rows the browser
  already holds rather than ask a narrower question — and a filter a customer
  forgets they set is where *"where did my electric readings go"* starts.
* A **column** hides nothing, costs one cell, and answers the question the
  screen exists for. `BR-CWP-071`'s dispute is *"you estimated and overcharged
  me"*, and a customer checking that reads down the whole list rather than one
  meter at a time.

**Built:** a first column reading `Water · 2007` — the tenant's own service name
plus the serial on the box, with `meter_no` as the fallback where no serial was
recorded (`BR-AST-049`) and the serial alone for a meter on no service point.
Neither half is a database id (B14 rule 31); the payload carries none.

**Revisit it when** a `meter` parameter reaches `readings_for_account`, or when
a real account is seen with enough meters that the list stops being readable. Six
rows on the demo account is not that.

### 2 · On the CUSTOMER portal the behaviour CLASS travels and the catalogue writes the state word

**The problem.** `CWP-037`'s STATUS column printed `asset.status.name` verbatim,
which out of the seed is **`Installed/Active`** — a slash-joined lookup value, on
a customer's screen, in a portal that renders in eleven languages
(`DEF-CWP-3992`).

**The rule that appeared to forbid the fix.** `BR-AST-031` lets a tenant rename a
lifecycle stage, and `assets/selectors.py` records the cautionary tale of a
rehearsal printing *"Installed / Active"* at a utility that calls it *"In the
field"*. The screen's own docstring cited it.

**The rule that actually decides it, and it was already written.**
`billable_asset_count`'s docstring quotes the same `BR-AST-031` as
*"transitions/filters key off the class, never the label"*. A word shown to a
customer is the same kind of thing as a filter — it has to survive a rename —
and there are four classes (`available`, `in_service`, `out_of_service`,
`terminal`) which is exactly the code-shape B14 rule 35 wants. **A staff screen
still shows the utility's own word; that has not changed and should not.**

**Built:** the class keys the catalogue, and a class this product does not know
falls back to the tenant's own label — saying the utility's word beats saying
nothing.

**And one thing the drawing shows that its own delta row does not mention:**
`CWP-037.png` draws exactly ONE chip per row, and the test-due row does not also
say `IN SERVICE`. Following that literally would hide *needs repair* behind *test
due Nov*, so the rule built is **the test chip replaces the state chip when the
state is in-service, and both show when it is not.**

⚠ **`test_due_on` AND NOT `test_due`, CHECKED RATHER THAN ASSUMED.** A future
date looked like a false alarm worth filing until
`test_us_cwp_043_equipment.py` TC-3 settled it: the backflow device's next test
is **14 Nov 2026**, `test_due` is **`False`** on 2 September, and the drawing
still paints `TEST DUE NOV` on that row. The chip means *due*, not *overdue*. A
defect row was drafted and discarded on that evidence.

### 3 · What was deliberately NOT done here

* **No page-head component was built.** `components/PageHeader.tsx` has drawn
  this exact skeleton since B14 rule 2 and thirteen portal files already compose
  it — `methods/Methods.tsx` and `payments/FeesPage.tsx` among them. So
  `14-layout-audit.md`'s D1 is better read as *28 signed-in screens do not USE
  the page head* than as *the portal has no page head*. These two now use it.
* **The two full-date columns were left as ISO.** Not an oversight and not
  deferred quietly: the tenant's date format cannot reach the portal at all
  (`DEF-CWP-3994`). `FITTED` reads `Mar 2021` through the existing
  `formatMonthYear`, which needs no tenant setting because a month name comes
  from `Intl` in the app's language. That is the boundary — month-year density
  is a display decision; a full date is a tenant-format question.
* **Sorting, row icons and a table footer** are `DEF-CWP-3977`'s cross-cutting
  job and are not duplicated here.
