## 2026-09-05 · A tip's `×` closes it for the visit and nothing remembers it

**Ours to decide, and decided rather than asked** (hard-won law 13: what
legitimately reaches the Product Owner is a collision with a signed rule, a
frozen figure, or a fact only they hold — this is none of the three).

`08-screen-layouts.md` `CWP-062` draws a `×` on the tip bar. `BR-CWP-095` says
what makes a tip appear — **on, in season, one per screen, top of the list
wins** — and says nothing at all about a customer putting one away.

**So there were two honest readings and one dishonest one.** Remembering a
dismissal needs a per-customer row keyed to a tip: a table, a migration, a
write endpoint and a retention answer, for a bar that is seasonal and at most
one line long. Drawing no `×` contradicts the drawing. **Drawing a `×` that
silently does nothing is the dishonest one** — it is `DEF-CWP-3925`'s shape, a
control that looks live and is not.

**The `×` closes the bar for as long as the page is open.** That is a working
control with no promise attached to it, and it is what the two screens now
ship. A tip the customer has read is a tip they scroll past next time, which
is the cost; a schema nobody asked for is the alternative.

**If the Product Owner ever says a dismissed tip should stay dismissed**, this
becomes a portal-owned per-recipient row — the same shape `US-CWP-067` builds
for the message count, and it should be built once for both rather than twice.

## 2026-09-05 · The portal's surface is a token the portal moves, not a second component

`DEF-CWP-3987` — every signed-in screen with a rail drew a **white main column
beside a grey one**. The portal's `Card` writes `bg-[white]`; the shared
`Panel` writes `bg-surface`, which is `#eae9e9`, the staff app's surface and
correct there.

**Three ways to fix it and only one is not a fork.** Recolouring `Panel` moves
149 staff call sites. Giving `Panel` a `surface` prop puts a second visual
opinion inside a component whose whole point is that it holds one. **Moving
the variable on the portal frame** — which is exactly how the tenant's own hex
already reaches every `bg-accent` in the portal — leaves the shared component
untouched and means the lists lane's `DataTable` and `FilterBar` arrive
correct without knowing the portal exists.

⚠ **AND IT IS WRITTEN UNCONDITIONALLY, WHICH IS THE PART WORTH RECORDING.**
`brandStyle` writes nothing for a utility that has chosen no colour. Folding
the surface into it would have left the rail grey on precisely the unbranded
tenants — the same defect with a smaller blast radius and a harder story.

## 2026-09-05 · `CWP-038` Pay now — the three faults that stopped a payment, and the two judgment calls behind the fix

**Lane:** portal money screens (`CWP-038` · `CWP-039` · `CWP-041`).
**Version:** `2.169.3`. **Defects closed:** `DEF-CWP-3970`, `DEF-CWP-3971`,
`DEF-CWP-3972`, `DEF-CWP-3946`.

### 1 · The rules ran out twice, and here is what was chosen

**(a) A standing panel needs a trigger, and the wireframe does not draw one.**
`38.1` says delete *Show me where it goes* and make `WHERE IT WILL GO` standing.
It does not say *when the server is asked*. Two readings were available: price
only the pre-selected whole balance and leave a typed amount unpriced until
blur, or price whatever amount is current. **Chosen: price whatever amount is
current, debounced 250 ms.** The reason is `38.1`'s own: the panel exists for the
person paying PART of a balance, and that is precisely the person who types.
Pricing only the pre-selected figure would have kept the letter of the row and
lost the case it was written for.

⚠ **It is safe to fire without a press for a reason that is checked rather than
assumed:** `pay_now_seam.preview` writes nothing, says so in its own docstring,
and answers `writes: []` so a caller can prove it. The only call in this product
that takes money is still a button a person presses.

⚠ **And the key is re-sent, never re-minted.** The seam answers `key or mint()`,
so every re-price after the first carries the string the first one returned —
`US-CWP-045` TC-7 survives the change and its assertion is unaltered.

**(b) An unpriced amount still needs a held reason, and `heldNoPreview` is gone.**
Deleting *"See where it goes first."* leaves the gap between a keystroke and the
server answering. **Chosen: a new five-word key, `portal.payNow.pricing` —
*Working out where it goes.*** It is a true sentence about a state rather than an
instruction to press something that no longer exists. B14 rule 33, five words,
eleven catalogues each in its own language (rule 35).

### 2 · The one figure worth writing down

`$40.00` against a `$142.18` bill reads **`$102.18` left owing, before anything
commits, with nothing clicked.** That is the assertion the screen exists for and
it is now reached on mount rather than after a press. Every figure is the
server's — `allocate_payment`, the same code that will apply the money — and no
subtraction is written in the browser.

### 3 · What was deliberately NOT done

* **`primitives.tsx` was not touched.** Row `38.6` (bold money inside each amount
  option) needs `RadioList`'s `label: string` widened to `ReactNode`. That file
  is the kit lane's and had uncommitted edits in it; a second author on one file
  is hard-won law 11's `DEF-165`, which reverted a customer-facing money fix with
  a correct file count and a green suite. **The two-line hunk is written into the
  delta row** so it costs the owner seconds rather than a rediscovery.
* **Row `38.7` (*Just the August bill*) is not a copy edit** and was not done as
  one. The screen holds a bill NUMBER and no month; the wording needs `issued_on`
  through the shared date formatter the kit lane is building, and writing a second
  formatter here is the thing that lane exists to prevent.
* **No page head was built.** `components/PageHeader.tsx` is the shared one and
  thirteen portal files already compose it.

### 4 · Two process findings, both from this lane's own mistakes

**(a) A whole-file CSV round-trip is a mass shared-file rewrite.** The first
helper written to mark four defect rows fixed used `csv.DictWriter` over all 1803
rows; Python normalises quoting, so `git diff --numstat` came back **56 lines
changed for 4 rows edited** — 52 other lanes' rows republished in this lane's
spelling. Nothing lost, no gate objecting, damage only to the record.

**(b) And being line-surgical was still not enough, because the register has
MIXED LINE ENDINGS.** 16 of its 1822 lines end `\r\n`. `Path.read_text()` opens
in TEXT mode, so universal-newline translation flattens those 16 before the first
edit and writing back publishes the normalisation: **20 lines changed for 4 rows
edited**, and the 16 were byte-different for real, not a diff artifact.
**What found both was reading `git diff --numstat` as ARITHMETIC rather than as a
glance** — hard-won law 11's own instruction, and 20-for-4 is exactly the size of
discrepancy a glance calls close enough. The helper now reads and writes BYTES
and puts each row's own line ending back.

## 2026-09-05 · Wave P — five flows, four judgments the rules did not cover

**Not rulings. Four judgments made by the build lane and recorded with their
worked figures, because law 13 says a judgment recorded with its reasoning is
the deliverable and a question is the failure to make one.**

**1 · `move_in` IS ONE TOKEN, NOT TWO — the plan's "four values" is three.**
Task `P1` asks for four new values on `work_orders.source`: `service_request`,
`move_in`, `transfer`, `reconnect`. But r10's eighth drawn source is
*Move-in wizard*, and this wave's move-in door is the same fact — one flow, one
moment, one reason a job exists. So the code declares **fourteen** tokens and
`move_in` appears once, with *Move-in wizard* as its catalogue label. **Worked
against the alternative:** two tokens meaning one thing gives a report that
groups by reason two rows a person has to add up by hand, and nothing tells them
the rows are the same thing.

**2 · THE MIGRATION IS `metering/0049`, NOT `work/000N`.** `P1` says the columns
go in a Work migration. That is not buildable: Django resolves `model_name`
inside the migration's own app and `workorder` is declared in
`apps/metering/connections.py`, so an `AddField` on it from `apps/work/migrations`
raises before it runs. The same reading `metering/0044` and `0045` already took.
Both corrections are stamped into the plan's own task row.

**3 · WHICH HALF OF THE TEMPLATE LIST EACH FLOW SEES.** `P2` says the offer is
*"the published templates that fit"* and does not say what fits. The split
chosen, and it is not arbitrary: `sequence >= 1` is the set of jobs that BUILD a
service, so New Connect and an approved SERVICE REQUEST are offered those — a
request is an application to build something. `sequence` 0 or absent is work on
a service that already EXISTS: a final read, a turn-on, a changeover read, a
reconnect visit. **A move-out, move-in, transfer and reconnect all act on a live
connection, so offering them *Meter set* would be offering to build the thing
the customer already has.** `E2`'s reader carries both predicates as one
parameter — one reader, never a second copy — and both clauses stay in the query.

⚠ **THE CONSEQUENCE, STATED BECAUSE IT WILL LOOK LIKE A BUG:** the 24 seeded
starters are ALL connection-sequence jobs, so **a brand-new utility is offered
NOTHING on a move-out until it publishes a template of its own.** The panel says
so in its own words. The alternative — seeding four more starters — was refused:
it would move a figure (24) that wave E's tests, `G101` and the plan all assert,
and it would put this platform's guess at a utility's own job list into their
account. The templates are theirs to author; wave `D`/`E` is what made that
possible.

**4 · THE FIFTH SCREEN IS NOT BUILT, AND IT IS STATED RATHER THAN IMPLIED.**
`P4` names *the reconnect on the account's disconnect surface* as the fifth
host. There is no host: `commitCut`, `markReconnecting` and `restoreService`
have no client function and no caller anywhere in `07-frontend`, so the ladder
on screen stops at *schedule the cut*. The backend door is open and tested and
the shared panel is ready for it. **Building the reconnect ACTION — its date,
its arrears gate, its five refusals — is the disconnect surface's own work**,
and a tick-list shipped over a button that does not exist is hard-won law 2 in
its plainest form. Filed as `DEF-WRK-4003`.

## 2026-09-05 · `CWP-039` and `CWP-041` — the two judgment calls, and a drawn HOLD that had expired

**Lane:** portal money screens. **Versions:** `2.170.1` (`CWP-039`), `2.172.1`
(`CWP-041`). **Defects closed:** `DEF-CWP-3973`, `DEF-CWP-3974`, `DEF-CWP-3975`.
**Defect filed against another lane:** `DEF-WRK-4005`.

### 1 · A wireframe's HELD state is a fact about the day it was drawn

`13-wireframe-delta.md` row 39.2 calls `+ Add a method` *"a brand primary
button"*. **The image does not.** Cropped at 4x, `CWP-039.png` draws it
brand-bordered with **grey** text — this kit's HELD presentation, and the very
same reading `DEF-CWP-3993` established for `CWP-034`'s *Send a reading* the
same day. So the delta row is wrong about the tier for the second time in one
file.

**And the image is out of date about the STATE, which is the more useful
finding.** Its own note says why it was drawn held: *"Rests on: nothing — the
stored-instrument table is described in the schema notes and was never
created."* That table exists now, and `POST /portal/payment-methods` writes a
row through `instruments.save_instrument`. **A held control over a working path
is `DEF-CWP-3925`, which this product has paid for eight times.**

**Chosen: the drawn POSITION, the live TIER.** Written down because the general
form is worth more than the instance — **read a drawn hold as evidence of a
DEPENDENCY, then go and check whether the dependency landed.** That is hard-won
law 2's mirror arriving through a picture instead of through code.

### 2 · A full-width button was never a width, and the cause is one the kit hides

Row 39.5 reads *"renders as a full-width bordered button"*. Nothing sets a
width. `Card` is `flex flex-col`, so **a control placed directly inside it
stretches to the card**, and every correctly-sized control in this portal
happens to sit inside a `flex` row. Measured in a browser: **1060px before,
121px after**, with an identical class list on the control both times.

**The test asserts the PARENT, not the width** — a width assertion in `jsdom` is
a fiction, and the parent is the actual rule.

### 3 · `REFERENCE` was two faults, and the second one was a database id

`DEF-CWP-3974` was filed as *the portal serves the wrong field*. It is that, and
it is also a **fixture** fault, and the fixture half is the worse one:

* `confirmation=f"SAMPLE-{invoice.invoice_no}"` — a **bill number** in the
  cheque-number column;
* `confirmation=f"SAMPLE-PLAN-{plan.pk}"` on the plan down payment and
  `f"SAMPLE-PLAN-{plan.pk}-{seq}"` on each instalment — **a UUID on a
  customer's screen, B14 rule 31, arriving from the FIXTURE rather than from
  the screen.** Every review of the screen passed over it because the screen is
  serving a real column with a real value in it.

**Built:** each tender seeds the reference that tender really produces (a cheque
number · `Chase ••••4021` · `Visa ••••8812` · nothing at all on cash), and the
SEAM decides the shape once — `#10188` — so the browser holds no second
definition of *what is my reference*. Exercised directly: seven cases, including
the two that must NOT be touched (a clerk who already typed `#10188`, and a
bank's alphanumeric reference).

⚠ **SAID PLAINLY BECAUSE IT WOULD OTHERWISE BE ASSUMED: a tenant seeded before
today keeps `SAMPLE-…` until it is seeded again.** Changing seed CODE changes no
row already written — hard-won law 4's shape for data.

### 4 · Red per CELL and not per ROW, on purpose

`PortalListTable` takes `rowMuted` and no tone, and it is another lane's file
this week. Wrapping the four cells this screen owns gets the drawing without a
second author in a shared file (`DEF-165`). **If a `rowTone` lands later this
collapses to one prop and the test still asserts the right thing** — that the
reversal's cells are marked and the row beneath is not, never how.

Verified in a browser: `rgb(168, 22, 0)` on four cells of the bounced row, grey
on the row it undoes, ordinary ink on the rest.

### 5 · What this lane found in someone else's file

`routeBUtilities.test.ts` is RED on the branch tip and not because of this lane:
`components/RaiseFieldWork.tsx:122` asks for **`text-danger`**, a shade-less
token this theme does not emit, so **a refusal on the field-work panel draws in
the ordinary body colour**. `tsc`, eslint and any `toContain` all pass on it —
`DEF-974` exactly, arriving through a shade rather than a file. Filed as
`DEF-WRK-4005` with the one-token fix written out; **not fixed here, because
that file is another lane's and had uncommitted work in it.**

**The transferable part is about the gate rather than the token:**
`routeBUtilities.test.ts` answers the only question that can be asked about a
utility and it is not in the run a lane does for its own screen. **Run it
whenever a commit adds a class, not only when it changes a stylesheet.**

### 6 · What was NOT proved, and why

The box's PostgreSQL credentials for `smartbillhub` changed mid-session and
every lane's `runserver` began answering 500. **`CWP-041` was therefore rendered
against a stub API rather than the fixture**, which is weaker in one way and
stronger in another: it is not the real payload, and it is the only way to put
the wireframe's **bounced pair** on screen at all, because the fixture has no
reversal in it. `CWP-038` and `CWP-039` were both walked against the real
database before it broke. **Shared credentials were left alone rather than
re-keyed on this lane's judgment.**

## 2026-09-05 · Every hold in the portal now says what would release it — the four judgments behind `G103`

**The problem in one sentence:** a greyed control that says *"arrives later this
year"* over something that shipped last week has now happened four times in a
week, and no check in this repo could see any of them.

The four are `DEF-CWP-3925` (the front page had two working doors out of eight),
`DEF-CWP-3959` (*Something else* grey for 32 hours over a screen live since
01:27 that morning), `DEF-CWP-3962` (the bills list holding *Pay* after *Pay
now* shipped) and `DEF-CWP-3824` (*New answer* disabled over a `create_answer`
that has worked since `2.138.0`). **The mechanism is the same every time and it
is not carelessness:** a hold is a rule with a clock in it, correct on the day
it is written, and landing the thing it waits for is a different act from
releasing the control that points at it.

**Why nothing caught it.** `G13` asks whether a prop is PASSED. `G100` asks
whether a screen is POINTED AT — and it credits a held control as a pointer,
which it states about itself. The one check that existed,
`tests/test_cwp_holds_expire.py`, covers the three errand cards on `CWP-046`.
**The question *is this refusal still true* belonged to nobody**, which is the
same shape as the question `DEF-CWP-3954` records — *has anything started
pointing at this screen* — one turn further on.

### 1 · The register is keyed by the REASON, not by the call site

The obvious design gives `HeldButton` a required `releases` prop. It was
rejected: there are held controls in **five lanes' files** today, so that design
is one commit touching five lanes' work at once, which is hard-won law 11's
mechanism two with extra steps.

**The reason string is the thing that makes a claim about the world** — *"is not
ready yet"*, *"arrives later this year"* — and therefore the thing that becomes
false. So `07-frontend/src/portal/routing/holds.ts` is keyed by the reason's
i18n key. It is one new file, owned by nobody else, and a lane adding a hold
adds one row to it or `G103` fails the merge.

The convention the scan relies on is one the catalogues already follow without
exception: a hold's reason key contains `Held`, `held` or `Blocked`. **All 35
live holds match it.** A key that does not is invisible to the gate; that is
written into the gate's own docstring rather than left to be discovered.

### 2 · Seven kinds, and only two of them are actually guarded

| kind | what releases it | guarded? |
|---|---|---|
| `screen` | a `CWP-###` gaining a row in `PORTAL_SCREENS` | **yes** |
| `endpoint` | a named Python symbol being defined under `06-backend/apps/` | **yes** |
| `server` | nothing — the server re-answers it on every draw | cannot rot |
| `form` | nothing — the person has not filled the form in | cannot rot |
| `policy` | a ruling, which means a CR | cannot rot silently |
| `fact` | nothing — it was never a refusal | cannot rot |
| `unwatched` | something no automatic check can see | **no, and it says so** |

**Today that is 1 guarded, 12 unwatched, 22 that cannot rot.** The gate prints
those three numbers on every PASS.

### 3 · `unwatched` is the judgment call, and it is an admission on purpose

Twelve holds wait on a capability with **no screen id and no symbol** — a PDF
download, SMS activating in W8 by wave order, *"Ring us to answer this offer"*
over an offer the portal serves read-only. Nothing mechanical can watch those.

Two options: guess the symbol the implementer will use, or say so. **Guessing was
rejected** — a check that silently fails to fire is `DEF-182`'s flaw, a check
that is trusted because its output looks like a pass. So an `endpoint` row only
ever names a symbol that is **already defined** (the hold has already rotted and
the gate is red today) or one the seam convention forces.

The precedent for the admission is already in the repo: `ERRAND_HELD_UNTIL`
carries `None` for two cards for exactly this reason, and says *"a hold with no
expiry is the weaker kind."* **Counting them out loud is the difference between
an admission and an implication.**

### 4 · Scope is "any file that DECLARES a portal screen"

Not `src/portal/**`, which would have missed `DEF-CWP-3824` entirely — that hold
is on a **staff** Settings screen. Not the whole staff app, which would drag in
several hundred unrelated files. **A file carrying `data-screen="CWP-###"` is in
scope wherever it lives**, which is the same mark `G100` and the walkthrough
already read. One fact, three readers, no second map to keep in step.

### 5 · Two flaws the self-test found before the gate was trusted

Both are the same species — **a gate reading the wrong span of text**:

* **A key that appears only in a comment.** `PayNow.tsx` explains at length that
  `heldNoPreview` was REMOVED and why (`DEF-CWP-3970`). A scan that counted that
  mention demanded a register row for a hold that does not exist — and would
  have taught the next lane to delete the explanation to make the gate pass.
  `G100` records the identical lesson. Comments are stripped before scanning.
* **A template whose interpolation is named `held`.** `Overdue.tsx` writes
  `` t(`portal.protections.kind.${held.kind}`) ``. A pattern looking for the word
  inside the backticks reported a live protections label as an unregistered
  hold. **Normalise `${…}` away FIRST, then ask whether what remains is a hold
  key** — the order is the whole fix.

### 6 · And the gate's own contract caught this lane in the act

The first draft of `g103_holds_cannot_rot.py` had `run() -> int`. It was green
by hand and **would have been reported as *gate returned invalid status*** by
`run_gates`, which does `status, detail = module.run()`. That is `DEF-GOV-3733`
exactly, one day after it was written into `CLAUDE.md`, and it was found by
reading the runner rather than by trusting `python3 <gate>.py`. **The red proof
that matters was taken through the registry**, on `settings.portalHelp.addHeld`
over `create_answer`.

### 7 · What this lane did NOT take, and why

`DEF-CWP-3945` — a clerk pins a help answer to a screen and the customer never
sees it — is **left open with its row corrected**. The row read *"the back end
serves it"*; measured, `apps/portal/` cannot reach `attached_answer()` at all.
Three links are missing: a reader on `portal/seams/tenancy_seam.py`, a field on
a screen's payload, and a caller for the card. **The worked example is
`tip_for_screen`, one content type over.** Not built here because `CWP-060`'s
placements are the bill, usage and overdue screens, which belong to two other
live lanes today.

⚠ **A FIFTH ENTRY, ADDED THE SAME DAY BECAUSE THE LANE'S OWN FIRST DRAFT WAS
THE THING WORTH RECORDING.**

**5 · THE LAW-14 CASE PROVED NOTHING UNTIL IT WAS PROVED RED.** The first draft
of `test_us_wrk_039_from_flows_pg.py` asserted that the nested
`transaction.atomic()` inside `from_flows.raise_for` is what stops a database
error in the raise from losing a move-out. It was sabotaged by deleting that
savepoint, run against a real PostgreSQL — **and it still passed.**

**The savepoint is not what saves it.** Every one of the five doors raises AFTER
its own transaction has committed, so there is no open transaction for a failed
statement to poison. The savepoint is a genuine second line of defence and not
the mechanism.

**The case now asserts the real guarantee and it was proved three ways on a live
PostgreSQL**, each run about five minutes:

| what was broken | result |
|---|---|
| nothing | PASS |
| the savepoint deleted (ordering alone) | PASS |
| the raise moved inside the flow's transaction (savepoint alone) | PASS |
| **both** | **FAIL — *"the account was lost at COMMIT"*** |

**The lesson is `DEF-182`'s, one level along:** a check whose sabotage does not
bite is worse than no check, because it is trusted — and the only way to find
one is to break the thing it names and watch. Writing the sabotage down in the
docstring is what makes it re-runnable by the next lane.

## 2026-09-05 · Integrations connects; Runbooks transforms — the boundary, ruled before either is built

The PO is adopting the Runbooks capability and asked where it overlaps CR-069. Reading
the specification against the change request found five meeting points; the ruling drew
one line through all of them.

**PO verbatim:** *"I want integration to just make the conenction nad manage the
conenction, Runbooks will handle the logic , ETL and record udaptes, and we will abel to
keep record, audit of it as part of runbooks."* And, on timing: *"right now notng to be
done; you just write this rule in the CR69 - and leave it there we will handle CR 69 and
Runbook together once CR70 is completed."*

Recorded as `BR-INT-054`, and written into `CR-069-integration-substrate.md` with the
five overlaps set out.

**The worked case that makes the line concrete.** A bank file lands. Integrations
connects to the bank, authenticates, pulls the file, and records that a batch arrived on
that connection — and stops. Runbooks reads the batch, decides which payment matches
which account, writes the payments, and keeps the run record and the audit of what it
decided. Today no such division exists and the temptation runs the other way: the
integrations module already holds `IntegrationRun` and a codec layer, and it would have
been natural for the next wave to grow matching logic into it.

**What the ruling prevents rather than commissions.** Nothing is to be built against it
yet. Its whole value is that a wave built between now and CR-070's completion cannot put
transformation on the integrations side and need unpicking later. **The one live lane it
could have touched — wave `F`, isolating one tenant's hanging connection — is unaffected,
and the ruling is what settles it:** an hour earlier I had raised whether `F` should
isolate *the runner* (because Runbooks says both share one) or only *connections*. Under
this ruling the runner is not integrations' concern, so `F` stays as briefed. That
question is now answered rather than open, and no lane was redirected.

⚠ **Two events Runbooks needs and integrations does not emit** —
`batch.landed(connection, batch_id, subject_type)` and `feedback.landed(provider,
batch_id)`, which six runbooks trigger off. The `emit()` already in
`apps/integrations/codecs.py` is a different thing entirely (it writes records OUT
through a codec) and must not be mistaken for this. Unscoped, deliberately, until the
two are taken together.

**Found at r11 step 0 by the CR-070 wave I build lane, before a line was written.**
This is exactly what step 0 is for, and it is the only thing that could have found
it: nothing in this repo reads prose for truth.

**What the brief and the plan said.** Wave I's own header reads *"Blocked by:
`OQ-WRK-1495` bounds the reschedule message only"*, task `I1` says
`notify_reschedule()` raises `NotImplementedError("OQ-WRK-1495")` and the response
carries `reschedule_notice_kind_unruled`, and task `I6` is listed as **blocked**,
to be done *"after `OQ-WRK-1495`"*.

**What the register said.** `OQ-WRK-1495` was **CLOSED on 2026-09-04**, option
**(a)**. PO verbatim: *"(a) — filing an appointment change beside disconnection
notices distorts every monthly report"*. A rescheduled visit sends on a **new
message source kind, `appointment`**, with its own wording.

**So the wave had no blocker at all, and `I6` was not a later task.** Every one of
the nine `OQ-WRK-*` questions — `1490`, `1491`, `1492`, `1493`, `1494`, `1495`,
`1496`, `1497`, `1561` — is closed. Two module summaries still counted six stories
carrying a blocking question; the true number is one, and it is `OQ-376`, which is
metering's and which the `1495` ruling says in as many words it does **not** close.

**The six documents corrected, dated, before any code was built on them:**
`10-execution-plan.md` (the wave header, `I1`, `I3`, `I6` and the story index row),
`EP-WRK-05-dispatch.md` (§1's stub paragraph, the BR table, TC-5, §5's mapping row,

`05-user-stories.md`, `01-overview.md`, and journey `J62` steps 3 and 4.

⚠ **THE CLOSURE'S OWN ARITHMETIC WAS ALSO STALE, AND IT IS THE MORE DANGEROUS HALF.**
The ruling says the platform constant grows *"from ten kinds to eleven"*. It was
written on 2026-09-04 — the same day `CR-068` wave E added **`portal`** to
`notifications.SOURCE_TYPES` for reasons of its own. So the constant already stood
at **eleven**, and `appointment` makes **TWELVE**. A lane implementing the ruling
literally would have asserted a count of eleven and gone red against its own correct
code — or worse, "fixed" the count by removing a kind the portal needs.

**Why this is a decision-log row rather than a question to the PO** (law 13's short
list): the ruling is made, the option is chosen, and the only thing wrong is a number
in the prose around it. Re-asking would manufacture the inconsistency law 13 exists
to prevent.

**The pattern, and it is now the sixth on this branch.** Closing a question and
un-marking the stories it blocked are two acts, and only the first feels like the
work — identical in shape to B14's rule-count line (wrong five times, always in the
same direction) and to `CR-068` R3's held controls, which rotted the day their
screens landed and shipped the portal with two working doors out of eight
(`DEF-CWP-3925`). **Filed as `DEF-WRK-4028`** with that escape reason.

**The consequence for what wave I ships:** the Change effects box's first line is
*Customer notification — the customer is told the visit moved*, not *not yet sent;
being decided*; `US-WRK-031` TC-5 flips from *asserting a stub* to *asserting the
kind by name*; and the marker `reschedule_notice_kind_unruled` never enters the
codebase. A wave that shipped the stub would have been hard-won law 2's mirror — a
refusal that outlived its reason, over a send the PO had already specified.

## 2026-09-05 · The PostgreSQL blocker's blast radius, measured rather than assumed

`DEF-WRK-4027` stopped every PostgreSQL migration on this branch: a trigger the
database refused to compile, so `manage.py migrate` died at
`work/0009_rls_force_dispatch.py` and **no PostgreSQL database could be built at all**.
The obvious follow-on question is the one worth writing down: **for how long, and whose
"proved on PostgreSQL" claims from today are therefore worthless?**

**Sixty-five minutes.** The file landed at 16:05 in `c760b753` (CR-070 wave G · G1) and
was fixed at 17:10 in `5ab3d2df`. Every commit in that window was read and **not one of
them claims a PostgreSQL run.** The only two that mention PostgreSQL at all are the fix
itself and `3ef9b3fc`, which is about a gate *not* using PostgreSQL. Wave G's own
`80117906` names PostgreSQL once, and it is a citation of hard-won law 14 about
savepoints, not a claim of a run.

**So the claim that prompted the question stands.** CR-070 wave P reported *"all 12 also
pass on real PostgreSQL"* at 13:39 (`9476fda6`), two and a half hours before the blocker
existed. Nothing needs re-proving.

Recorded because the honest answer to *"did this invalidate other people's evidence"* is
a list of commits and their times, and the next person to ask it should not have to
rebuild that list.

## 2026-09-05 · G5 was pointed at a database where tenant isolation cannot exist — and then at a role that ignores it

`DEF-GOV-4024`. G5 is the tenant-isolation gate. Its first half said *run the suite*, and
it did not say **where**, so it ran `pytest -m isolation -q` with no settings override —
which picks up the `config.settings.test` pinned in `pyproject.toml`, which hardcodes
in-memory SQLite. SQLite has no row-level security, so four fifths of the suite skipped
itself and the gate reported **PASS**.

Measured on this branch: **46 passed, 192 skipped, exit 0.** Of the 192, **168 carried the
vendor reason** — *"needs live PostgreSQL"* — which is a case that did not run.

This is `DEF-101` one level up. That defect taught that a skipped TEST is green; this is a
skipped SUITE being green. And the cure was already written in this very file's docstring
— *"a rise in the skip count is a regression"* — as a sentence with nothing reading it.
Hard-won law 1, in the file whose entire subject is tenant isolation, thirteen days later.

**The second finding is larger than the first, and it is why this took a day rather than
an hour.** Pointing the suite at PostgreSQL is not the same as pointing it at a role that
row-level security applies to, and from inside the gate the two look identical. The local
development role `smartbillhub` is `rolsuper = t`, and **a superuser bypasses every
policy**: the deny is never evaluated, every "another tenant cannot see this" case reads
its neighbour's rows, and the suite goes red for a reason that has nothing to do with the
code. Measured: **36 failed, 201 passed, 1 skipped** in twenty minutes — and among the 36
is the suite's own canary, `test_the_role_this_suite_runs_as_is_genuinely_subject_to_rls`,
which exists to say exactly this. A gate that simply "used PostgreSQL" would have handed
36 red tests about nothing to whichever lane ran it next.

**So the gate now has three honest states and no fourth:**

* a reachable PostgreSQL whose role is genuinely subject to RLS → run it, and judge the
  result, including a **FAIL on any skip at all** (the standing figure on PostgreSQL is 0);
* PostgreSQL reachable but the role holds `SUPERUSER` or `BYPASSRLS` → **SKIP**, naming the
  role, because the environment cannot prove the guarantee and a lane cannot fix a cluster
  role from inside a merge;
* nothing reachable → **SKIP**, and never a fall back to SQLite called a pass.

**Judgment calls made here, so the next agent does not have to re-make them.**
*The role check is a SKIP and not a FAIL*, because the code under test is not what is
wrong. *A hardcoded fallback DSN is acceptable in this one file* — DEF-524's warning is
about a hardcoded path that keeps reporting PASS after what it names moves, and this one
can only ever cause a SKIP, which is visible. *The gate's test database carries a digest
of every migration file*, the pattern `config/settings/test.py` already proves
(`DEF-GOV-3778`), because on PostgreSQL a reused test database persists and would happily
serve a schema three migrations out of date; and without reuse the gate costs every lane
twenty minutes, and a gate too slow to run is a gate that does not run.

**Proved RED before being trusted, through `run_gates`' own import path and not
`__main__` (hard-won law 7, and `DEF-GOV-3733` on the second half of it):** forcing the
old SQLite settings back produced `FAIL — 168 isolation case(s) skipped with the VENDOR
reason`, where the same code on the same branch had said PASS; and the role check produced
`SKIP — the role 'smartbillhub' on localhost:5432 holds SUPERUSER` in 2.4 seconds.

## 2026-09-05 · Wave I's four judgment calls, and why the audit is per FIELD while the history is per ACT

**Recorded because the rules ran out and a lane had to decide** (law 13: *a
judgment call recorded in the decision log with its reasoning is the
deliverable; a question is the failure to make one*).

**1 · ONE AUDIT ROW PER FIELD, AND AS MANY HISTORY ROWS AS THE ACTS REQUIRE.**
Two signed documents disagreed, and only one reading satisfies both.
`US-WRK-031` TC-1 changes the technician AND the window and expects
`unassign` + `assign` rows and **two** audit rows. `J62` step 3 assigns and
schedules and expects one `assign` row, one `schedule` row and **two** audit
rows. Per-act auditing gives TC-1 three; per-submitted-field gives J62 four.
**The rule that satisfies both is: one `audit_log` row per FIELD a dispatcher
changed, while `work_order_assignments` takes as many rows as the acts need.**
Reassigning a job is TWO history rows — somebody LOST it, and recording only the
gain leaves *"who had WO-4821 on Tuesday morning"* unanswerable — and ONE field.

**The cost of that choice is a refactor, and it is the honest one.**
`dispatch.record_act` bundled the append, the cache refresh and its own audit
row. The wrong fix is a second function in `edit.py` that creates a
`WorkOrderAssignment` — the parallel world the PO ruled against the same day
(*"work is not isolated module … buld the code while leveraging existing
framwrok, code, tabels"*). So the shared half is extracted as
`dispatch.append_act` and both callers use it: `record_act` = `append_act` + one
row per act, `save_order_edit` = `append_act` + one row per field.

**2 · `blocked_by` AND `follows_order_id` ARE TWO COLUMNS BECAUSE THEY ARE TWO
FACTS.** `blocked_by` says *do not start me yet* — sequencing, written by any
wave that orders work, uninteresting once the blocker finishes. `follows_order_id`
says *I exist BECAUSE that one failed* — provenance, permanent. **Derive
`EP-WRK-10`'s FIRST-TIME FIX from `blocked_by` and it is wrong every month,
quietly**: every ordinary two-step job counts as a return visit and nothing on
the report shows it.

**3 · THE CONSEQUENCE CHAIN TAKES NO SAVEPOINT, WHICH IS THE OPPOSITE OF LAW
14's ADVICE AND DELIBERATE.** Law 14 is about a LOOP that must survive one bad
row (`bulk_act` over eight orders). The failed-outcome chain is one human act
over one order, and `US-WRK-034` TC-3 says *a refusal anywhere rolls the whole
acceptance back*. An accepted failure with no follow-up is precisely the state
`BR-WRK-054` exists to prevent, and it would be INVISIBLE — the order reads
*accepted*, correctly, and nothing ever raises the return visit. So the chain
runs inside the caller's transaction and catches nothing, and its docstring says
a lane "hardening" it with `try/except: pass` would convert a loud failure into
a silent one.

**4 · `failed_outcome` IS A FIFTEENTH SOURCE TOKEN, AND ADDING IT IS THE
OPPOSITE DIRECTION FROM `DEF-WRK-3726`.** `BR-WRK-054` and `J66` both name
`source = failed_outcome`; wave P closed the vocabulary at fourteen and
`ck_work_orders_source` refuses anything else — so the chain would have been
refused **by PostgreSQL, inside a supervisor's Accept**, naming a constraint
rather than a cause. `DEF-WRK-3726` forbids a wave NARROWING a vocabulary it
does not own, because that starts refusing writes other waves make. Adding a
token refuses nothing that worked yesterday. ⚠ **And it had to be a migration
rather than a Python edit:** `metering/0049` builds its CHECK from a LIVE import
of the tuple, so appending a token silently changes what that migration *would*
create while every database that already ran it keeps fourteen — Python accepts
the raise and PostgreSQL refuses the INSERT, which is the one failure nobody can
debug from the symptom.

⚠ **A FIFTH, AND IT IS AN OBSERVATION RATHER THAN A DECISION: THREE GUARDS WERE
FOUND RED IN ONE AFTERNOON AND NONE OF THEM WAS BROKEN.** `G78` named
`dispatch.py:69` by line. The print-floor test named `portal` in its own
assertion message. A PostgreSQL-only proof failed on a NOT NULL column added
three commits earlier. Every one of them did exactly what it was written to do,
and every one had been failing for a day or more. **The missing thing is not a
better guard — it is anything that routes a change to the guard about that kind
of change.** `DEF-NOT-4032`, `DEF-WRK-4033`, `DEF-WRK-4034`, and
`DEF-WRK-4035` left OPEN because renaming four seam functions would satisfy the
assertion and leave the breach.

## 2026-09-05 · The tenant-isolation suite, run for the first time on a role it can be proved against

`DEF-GOV-4036` unblocked the run; this is what it says. **50 failed, 184 passed, 1 skipped,
7 errors in 855 seconds**, as `sbh_gate_iso` — `NOSUPERUSER NOBYPASSRLS CREATEDB`, a member of
the `sbh_rls_probe` role so the probe's `SET ROLE` is permitted.

**Read the three numbers together, because each is a different measurement of the same suite
on the same commit:**

| run as | result | what it can prove |
|---|---|---|
| in-memory SQLite (what `G5` did until today) | 46 passed, 192 skipped, exit 0 | **nothing** — no row-level security exists there; 168 cases skip with a vendor reason |
| the superuser app role, on PostgreSQL | 36 failed, 201 passed, 1 skipped | **nothing** — a superuser bypasses every policy, so no deny is ever evaluated |
| a role RLS genuinely applies to | **50 failed, 184 passed, 1 skipped, 7 errors** | this is the real one |

The single skip in the third run is the honest one and worth quoting, because it is the
mirror image of the whole problem: *"the app role is itself NOSUPERUSER/NOBYPASSRLS here, so
there is no bypassing connection to contrast the probe against."*

⚠ **50 RED IS NOT 50 LEAKS, AND SAYING SO WOULD BE WORSE THAN SAYING NOTHING.** The names in
this suite are written to describe a breach — `a_second_tenant_sees_none_of_the_first_tenants_customers`
— so a failing one reads as a catastrophe whatever the assertion underneath it says.
`test_lone_star_ridge_sees_only_its_own_discounts` fails `assert 6 == 5`: the tenant sees six of
**its own** discounts where the fixture expected five. That is seed drift. Every finding sorts
into one of three buckets and the counts must be given separately: **a real leak** (a policy
missing, wrong, or not `FORCE`d), **a missing deny** (the row is not readable but a query with
no `app.tenant_id` is not refused outright, which `BR-AUD-002`/`DEF-639` require), and **a stale
fixture**. The triage is running and no number in it is claimed here.

**What is already established, and is the point of recording this at all:** the figure that
mattered for three weeks — *the isolation gate is green* — was measuring a suite that could not
run. The first honest reading is 50 red. Whatever the triage returns, the interesting fact is
that nobody could have known either way, and the gate said the guarantee held.

## 2026-09-05 · The isolation proof is a WAVE-CLOSE act, not a continuous one

The first real isolation receipt was taken tonight and `G5` reported it **STALE within
minutes** — a sibling landed `tenancy/0040` during the twenty minutes the suite took, and the
migration digest moved. The triage lane raised the consequence rather than working around it:
*"on a branch with eight lanes and this much migration churn, a digest-keyed receipt will be
stale more often than not, so G5 will usually say 'no current proof' rather than pass. Worth
deciding whether that is the intended steady state."*

**It is, and this records why the obvious alternative was refused.**

The tempting fix is to invalidate more narrowly: digest only the migrations that can move the
policy surface, and let a column rename or a data backfill through. **That is a judgment made
in a regex, and a wrong one keeps a dead proof alive silently.** It is the
check-that-cannot-fail shape this gate was rewritten because of (`DEF-GOV-4024`), rebuilt
inside the cure. A conservative digest is occasionally annoying; a clever one is occasionally
a lie, and the lie is invisible.

The genuinely correct invalidation would key on the **policy catalogue itself** — the 269
tables, their `FORCE` flags and their policy predicates — because that is precisely what the
proof proved, and a migration touching nothing else would leave it identical. It was not
built, and the reason is worth stating: computing it needs the built test schema, which is the
twenty minutes the receipt exists to avoid. It stays available if the cadence below turns out
to be wrong.

**So the posture: a proof is taken when a wave closes**, in the way `G12`'s browser run
already is — not maintained continuously against a branch taking migrations all day. In
between, `G5` says what is true, in five seconds: that no current proof exists. **A gate that
says "unproven" is doing its job; the failure this whole episode was about is a gate that says
"proved" when nothing ran.**

⚠ **The number in the first receipt is 49 failed, 198 passed, and that is not a verdict on
the product.** The triage established that none of those is a leak: 2 were mis-shaped denies,
now fixed, and 46 are fixtures written against a connection that bypassed row-level security
(`test_def_123_tc8`'s own comment: *"the Django connection in tests is the table owner"*). The
receipt records the state honestly and a later lane is repairing the fixtures.

## 2026-09-05 · `pkill -f` in a shared container is law 11's hazard one layer down

Recorded from the wave J lane, which hit it three times in one session and named the
generalisation itself.

**A `pgrep -f` or `pkill -f` pattern matches far more than you mean it to.** A pattern like
`vite build` or `test_us_wrk_030_push_pg` matches **the monitor shell that contains the
pattern in its own command line**, and it matches **another lane's identical process** just as
readily as your own. Twice it killed that lane's own watchers. The third time it would have
reported a sibling's build as its own run still hanging — a false diagnosis that leads
straight to killing someone else's work.

**The parallel with law 11 is exact and worth stating, because it is the same mistake about
the same thing.** Law 11 exists because in a shared tree a commit is a statement about FILES
while you only ever author HUNKS. Here, in a shared container, a signal is a statement about
every process matching a STRING while you only ever started ONE. Both go wrong by being
broader than the author's intent, both look successful, and in both cases the damage lands on
a sibling.

**So: resolve the pid, verify it is yours, then signal that pid.** `/proc/<pid>/cwd` says
which worktree a process belongs to, which is the only check that can tell a sibling's work
from your own. A lane that started a server should record the pid it got rather than searching
for it later by name.

Small, and it belongs here rather than in `CLAUDE.md`: nothing was actually lost, the fix is
one habit, and the laws file has taken three amendments today already. Promote it if it costs
somebody real work.

## 2026-09-05 · CR-070 wave L — the offline day, one sync, and the read that posts (2.195.0)

**Six judgments this lane made where the rules ran out, written down before they were
reported to anybody.** None of them is a PO ruling; all six are ours, and each is
recoverable from the code it lives beside.

**1 · The close carries the HANDSET's time, and `submit_field_result` gained a parameter
for it.** Three jobs closed at 10:20, 12:05 and 16:07 reach the server at 17:40.
`accept_field_result` dates every set read from `completed_at` (`BR-TEN-043` — an event
date, never a wall clock), so a wall-clock stamp would move a whole offline day's readings
into the wrong billing period, on a money path, with nothing on any screen to show it. A
time in the FUTURE is refused rather than trusted: a handset's clock is the handset's, and
a close dated tomorrow would date a read into a period nobody has billed.

**2 · Which meter a reading posts to is a QUESTION, not a derivation — `OQ-WRK-1723`.**
`BR-WRK-015` gives a reading specification six columns and **none of them names a meter**.
For a job with one meter the order's own asset anchor is the answer and nothing is decided.
A meter EXCHANGE has two — `48,221 kWh` on the old meter and `1,204 kWh` on the new — and
the only thing separating the two readings is the wording of a prompt a tenant edits freely
on Settings. Posting both to the anchor would write a second read on the OLD meter: a wrong
number on a billing path, from a guess. **So `post_set_reads` refuses a job with more than
one posting reading, by name, and the acceptance rolls back.** Everything else ships.

**3 · The field read lands on the `total` channel, not on a channel called `field`.**
`US-WRK-046` TC-1 and `J61` both say *channel `field`*, and that reads as a SOURCE rather
than a register. A channel in this product names WHICH REGISTER was read (`BR-MET-059`);
a read on an invented `field` channel would sit where no tariff prices it and no
consumption delta walks it — invisible to billing while looking correct on the reads list.
WHO read it is already recorded twice. Filed as `DEF-WRK-4073`; the documents are the
documentation lane's to amend, because a build lane correcting a spec to match its own code
is how a spec quietly becomes whatever was built.

**4 · Metering's door drops the caller's unit, and we report it rather than route around
it.** `commit_event_reads` builds each staged row from five keys and `unit` is not one of
them, so a `unit` a caller passes is neither honoured nor refused — it is IGNORED. The unit
on the committed read is the REGISTER's own (`BR-MET-143`), which is the right source; what
is missing is the CHECK that the two agree. `03-field-map.md` D-13 anticipated this and
ruled it *"metering's story, filed not worked around"* — `DEF-WRK-4072`. The seam carries
the unit anyway (so nothing moves the day metering reads it) and compares the register's
stamped unit against the measured one on the way back out, raising and rolling the
acceptance back on a disagreement. **That is one caller's check and NOT a substitute for
the door refusing.**

**5 · An `attachment` item in a sync batch CONFIRMS a photograph, it does not carry one.**
A JSON batch cannot hold an image and the pre-signed PUT was dropped at 100 KB
(`BR-WRK-047a`), so the bytes travel `#77` and the batch item names the key. Refused when
no such row exists, because answering *accepted* over a photograph the server does not have
is a claim of a guarantee that is not the guarantee.

**6 · A `material` item is written by `sync.py` because `#75` is not built yet.** Wave K's
`K2` onward is still running. It writes the one column `costing.py` already reads and
invents no rule — `used_qty` NULL means *nobody has said* and `0` means *asked for and not
used*, which is why `J65`'s unused gasket is a real outcome. **When `PUT …/materials/{mid}/
used` lands, this should call it rather than keep a second writer.**

### And one lesson from the lane's own mistake, which is the part worth reading

`DEF-WRK-4079`. The headline law-14 test — *a duplicate key inside a batch does not poison
the rest, on PostgreSQL* — **passed with the savepoint deleted.** It set its duplicate up in
a separate call, so by the time the batch arrived the key was already in the receipts table
and `sync_batch`'s cheap `exists()` read answered *duplicate* **without ever raising
`IntegrityError`**, which is the only event a savepoint protects against. Green with correct
code, green with broken code, on a real database, in the configuration it was written to be
conclusive in.

**Nothing but the sabotage could have found it**, and only a sabotage aimed at the exact
mechanism. The general form is worth more than the fix: **when a guard protects a SECOND
path behind a fast path, a test that only ever takes the fast path proves nothing** — and
the way to find out which path it took is to break the guard, not to read the code. That is
the fourth occurrence in this repository of an assertion passing for a reason other than the
one it names (`toContain("disabled")` matching a Tailwind variant; `not.toContain("<p")`
matching `<path>`; `--stat` answering *is every change mine*).

## 2026-09-05 · CR-070 wave L `L7` — the walkthrough, and the five things it found (2.195.0)

**The phase-2 launch is declared on a demo that was RUN.** `L8` deliberately withheld it for
several hours because `L7` had not been executed, and a launch declared over an unexercised
walkthrough is the claim hard-won law 1 exists to stop. This is the record of what running it
actually cost, because **every one of the five findings below was invisible to 245 frontend tests,
15 backend cases on SQLite, 6 on real PostgreSQL, `tsc`, eslint and every gate** — which is law 6
in one paragraph: *no gate looks at rendered output*.

**1 · A cold `goto()` while offline loads NOTHING, and the run reported it as a dead screen.**
The close pane came back completely blank and the check said *the witness is absent* — which reads
exactly like a broken route. It was not: `page.goto()` with the context offline cannot fetch the
document or the bundle, so the browser had no app at all. **A technician does not retype a URL in
a meter pit; they tap, and a tap is client-side routing inside a page already loaded.** The
walkthrough now pushes history and dispatches `popstate`, which is both faithful and the only way
the next finding means anything.

**2 · A zero-requests assertion that passed because nothing had loaded.** *No request reached the
server while offline* was green — over a blank page. This is `DEF-WRK-4079`'s shape a second time
in one wave: **an assertion passing for a reason other than the one it names.** It is now paired
with a POSITIVE — the three closes are read back out of the handset's own IndexedDB store — so the
pair says something: the work happened, and none of it went over the wire. It also counts WRITES
rather than attempts, because the close pane legitimately asks the server whether the job may close
and that request is attempted and fails; counting attempts would have failed the check over correct
behaviour.

**3 · A batch whose close arrived before its safety ticks was refused BY NAME, and the server was
right.** The first draft queued only the close. `BR-WRK-037` is re-derived on the server from
`ticked_at` and never from the client's word, so the close was refused and the run went red. The
fixture now works the job properly — mandatory safety ticks first, in capture order, then the close
— which is `J65`'s own shape and exercises the ordering guarantee instead of stepping around it.

**4 · The read pipeline refused the acceptance with `unit_missing`, and that is `US-WRK-046` TC-5
happening for real.** The fixture had taken the first asset it found — `BAT-0001`, a battery with
no unit recorded — and metering answered *unit_missing* and rolled the WHOLE acceptance back, order
still on `Work-009`. **The product was right and the fixture was wrong.** A walkthrough that had
"fixed" this by loosening the assertion would have thrown away exactly the guarantee hard rule 3
exists for. It picks a kWh meter now.

**5 · Assertions written against COLUMN names rather than the keys the endpoint serves.**
`read_at` and `current_value` are the columns; `assets.selectors._fold_row` publishes `date`,
`reading` and `unit`. Both came back `undefined` — an assertion against a key nothing serves fails
over correct data and reads precisely like a missing feature. The same class as (2): a check that
cannot distinguish its own bug from the product's.

### And one property that was added on purpose: the walkthrough is RE-RUNNABLE

A second run against the same database was refused by `BR-MET-059` — one read per meter per date —
because the first run had already posted for that meter on 15 March. Correct, and a proof that only
works against a database it has never touched is a proof somebody will one day be unable to
reproduce. It now CHOOSES its meter: the first kWh meter whose history is free on the day the
reading is dated to. **Proved by running it twice in a row, green both times.**

⚠ **The same fragility exists in wave J's walkthrough and is recorded here rather than fixed from
this lane.** Its technician lookup keys on `row.user_id` from `GET /work/crews` — and a person row
on `Work-023`'s one table deliberately carries `name` and `slug` and **no `user_id`**, because B14
rule 31 makes the name the visible value. So that lookup can never match; wave J passed only
because it ran against a database with no technicians, took the create branch, and never exercised
the find. Re-running it against its own output would fail.

## 2026-09-05 · Two faults moved from a gate to the moment of writing — and the one that could not move

**The finding this acts on, in the words of the lane that cleared `G46` for the third time
in one day:** *"`file_defect.py` doesn't validate severity, so a lane filing from memory has
an even chance of the wrong word and G46 can only speak once the row is on the branch. Same
shape for the keys: nothing stops a wave landing a raised `message_key` with no sentence.
**A validating allocator would end both; a gate never can, because it runs too late.**"*

That is right, and the general rule is worth stating once: **a gate is a net under the
trapeze. Where a cheap check can run at the moment of writing instead, the fault never
lands** — and nobody spends an evening cleaning it up. Both halves below were built that
way. What is more interesting is the half that could NOT move, and why.

### 1 · The defect register: refuse the word, never correct it

`file_defect.py` now refuses a severity outside `critical/high/medium/low` **before it
touches the network**, and the refusal names the survivor: *"`major` was mapped major->high
on 2026-09-05 across seven rows, keeping each filer's intent — so write `high` if that is
what you mean."* Fed `DEF-WRK-4079`'s and `DEF-MET-4081`'s own arguments, the tool that
wrote them prints a row containing `"major"`; this one exits 1 and writes nothing.

**It refuses and never corrects, and that is `G46`'s reasoning rather than a new one:**
*"`blocker` might mean `critical` and might mean something the filer could tell you and the
script cannot."* So `blocker`, `trivial` and `cosmetic` are refused with the allowed list
and **no suggestion at all** — nobody ever ruled what they become, and a script that guessed
would destroy the evidence the register exists for. Only the two words somebody actually
ruled on carry a mapping.

**The status vocabulary narrows on write and not on read.**
`12-governance/15-defect-register-truth.md` §7 measured nine values where six would do and
named the sequence: *"stop the tools emitting the losing spellings, let the 37 affected rows
be corrected as they are touched for other reasons."* `close_defect.py` now writes only the
six; `G30` and `G46` still accept all nine, so **not one existing row was touched** — a mass
rewrite of a file ten lanes append to is the operation this repo has lost work to twice.
The two halves live in `10-scripts/register_vocabulary.py` as
`*_ACCEPTED_ON_READ` ⊇ `*_WRITABLE`, in one place, because three modules holding three
copies of one vocabulary is how the severity column got two vocabularies to begin with.

### 2 · The refusal that reaches a clerk as silence

Since the PO suppressed `params.detail` on 2026-08-19, a `message_key` with no catalogue
entry does not render as an ugly dotted string — **it renders as nothing.** The clerk
clicks Save, the server refuses correctly, and the screen has no sentence to show. There
were 57 of those in the Work module alone, and five more landed *while the repair for the
first 59 was being pushed*.

**The check now lives in `ApiError.__init__`** — the one constructor every catalog refusal
in this codebase passes through — enabled under the test settings and off everywhere else.

**Why there and not in a `conftest` fixture.** A fixture fires in the same runs, but it
belongs to the shared suite, it is skipped by any run that does not import it, and its
failure names the TEST rather than the raise. The constructor fires wherever the code is
exercised and names the line. There is also no earlier point available: **there is no tool a
lane invokes to "raise a refusal"** the way `file_defect.py` is invoked to file a row — a
lane types the raise into a service and then runs its own test, so that run IS the first
moment the fault can be seen.

**Why it derives from `BaseException`, which looks like overreach and is not.** The code
around such a raise is full of handlers that would swallow an ordinary exception —
`except Exception` in the request path, and `pytest.raises(errors.ValidationError)` in the
very tests that exercise refusals. `test_tc7b_a_rule_with_an_unknown_trigger_is_refused_at_
the_door` is the concrete case: it covers two of the five keys that landed silent, and an
`Exception` subclass raised from inside `ValidationError.__init__` would be caught by its
own assertion. The guard would have reported green over the exact fault it was written for.

**Why it is OFF in production, which is law 3 the right way round rather than an exception
to it.** The unsafe direction here is RAISING: a missing sentence in production would turn a
clean 422 into a 500, so the customer loses the refusal they were entitled to and gains a
fault report they cannot read. `G32` covers production and needs nothing at runtime.
⚠ **When it IS on and the catalogue cannot be read, it raises rather than waving keys
through** — a check that silently degrades to always-true would have reported a clean run
over all 57.

### 3 · The part worth reading: what the runtime check saw that no gate can

It found two things on its first broad run, and neither was a lane's mistake.

**a. Thirteen clerk-facing refusals that render as silence, in the blind spot `G32`
declares about itself — `DEF-MET-4093`.** `G32` resolves a positional `message_key`
helper **only when the helper is defined in the same file**, and says so:
*"A helper imported from a sibling module is still invisible; that is a KNOWN and stated
limit, not a silent one."* `apps/metering/premises_owners.py` imports `_field_error` from
`apps/metering/lookups.py`, and `apps/rating/discount_services.py` does the same. **Four
premises-owner refusals and nine discount refusals** are matched by nothing, and `G32`
reports `0 unresolved` over them on every run — truthfully, of everything it can see.
A clerk saving a premises owner with no category, or a discount with a value over 100%,
clicks and **nothing happens.**

**The transferable lesson is not "G32 has a limit" — it is that A DECLARED BLIND SPOT WITH
NO NUMBER ATTACHED IS INDISTINGUISHABLE FROM AN EMPTY ONE.** The docstring is honest and
the trade behind it is sound (keying helpers by bare name across the tree merged two
unrelated `_cap` functions and returned English sentences as keys). What nobody did was
**measure** it. Two of the thirteen turned three tests red the first time the runtime check
ran; the other eleven came from asking the same question statically across every helper in
the tree instead of per file.

**b. Eight of the twenty MECHANICAL fallback keys have no sentence either — `DEF-SHL-4092`.**
`default_message_key(code)` derives `errors.<code>` when a caller supplies none;
`biz-immutable`, `biz-locked`, `biz-window`, `biz-approval`, `biz-completeness`, `biz-cap`,
`biz-sod` and `sys-drift` resolve to nothing. **No lane ever types these**, so they appear
in none of the literal forms `G32` matches; and they appear in no `t()` call, so `G18` and
`G15` cannot see them either. They sit in the gap between the two directions. One is
reachable today: a staff member converting a premises owner to a master account, where the
owner owns no premises or owns several (`apps/metering/premises_owners.py:883`).

**They are NOT folded into the per-raise check, and the scoping is a judgment worth
recording.** The derived keys are a CLOSED SET OF TWENTY owned by `core/errors.py`.
Checking them per raise would report ONE of them — whichever code a test happened to
exercise — and only where coverage reaches. They get a check of their own that names the
whole set and all eight at once, which does not depend on coverage and is the stronger
question to ask about a fixed list.

### 4 · Neither is fixed here, and that follows a ruling rather than a preference

The fix for all twenty-one is **copy in ELEVEN catalogues**. Adding it to `en.json` alone
turns `G15` red on ten counts of *missing*; adding the English string to the other ten turns
it red the other way, and B14 rule 35 says a catalogue is written in its own language rather
than mechanically translated (PO, 2026-09-03: *"it sound like local person language and not
mechanical translations of English"*). `g112_computed_key_gaps.txt`, written the same day
for the same class of fault, records the conclusion: **a lane cannot honestly invent copy in
ten languages it cannot check.** The copy belongs to the modules that own these screens.

So the thirteen are parked in `06-backend/core/refusal_keys_parked.txt` under **the same
three properties that file is held to**, and all three are asserted rather than described:

* **NARROW** — the exact key, never a prefix. `rating.discounts.value` does not cover
  `rating.discounts.value_sign`; both are listed, and a one-character sibling of a parked
  key is still refused.
* **LOUD** — the figure THIRTEEN is asserted by name, and the defect row states it in plain
  English.
* **EXPIRING** — a parked entry fails the suite in **both** ways it can go stale: the key
  gains a sentence, or its raise site goes away. Proved red both ways before being trusted.

**Why a park list at all, rather than letting the thirteen raise.** Letting them raise turns
thirteen tests red at once for a reason none of them names, and the next lane deletes the
guard rather than writing the copy. A ratchet that starts at today's number and may only
fall is the same discipline `G32`'s own baseline, `G15`'s and `G112`'s all use.

### 5 · What the guard cost the existing suite, measured

Across all **833** backend test files there are **13** literal `message_key=` constructions,
and **four** name a key with no sentence. Two are tests whose whole subject is *"a refusal
whose `message_key` nobody has written words for"*; the other two use an illustrative key
where any two strings would do. All four now carry
`override_settings(REFUSAL_KEYS_MUST_RESOLVE=False)` **with the reason written beside them**,
which makes those tests say out loud what they were already doing silently.

⚠ **AND ONE HONEST CORRECTION ABOUT HOW THIS WAS MEASURED**, because it is the same trap the
repository keeps recording. Mid-run, `grep -c UnresolvedMessageKey` over the pytest output
returned **0**, and that was read as *the guard fired zero times*. It was not: **pytest
prints failure tracebacks only at the END**, so the count was measuring how far the run had
got, not what it found. The true figure was three failures from two live keys. **A check
run against a stream that has not finished is a check that cannot fail** — the `--stat`
shape again, one layer down.

## 2026-09-05 · CR-070 wave L's leftovers — the desktop leg, and what activating a journey means

**Lane:** the wave-L leftovers lane (`L4`'s desktop half · `J61` and `J65` activated).
**Version:** no bump — this finishes wave L's own tasks rather than raising a change.

### 1 · A journey is activated by a test that RUNS, so these two are `.py` and not `.spec.ts`

`10-execution-plan.md` line 282 says a demonstrating wave *"writes the `.spec.ts` beside
the other journey specs, runs it green on the build, removes the banner"*.

**There are no other journey specs.** No `.spec.ts` exists anywhere in this repository;
`08-qa/01-e2e/` holds journeys, an expectation dataset and a stack booter, and no runner
for such a file. So writing `J61.spec.ts` would have produced **a check that cannot
fail** — the shape hard-won law 7 spends four paragraphs on — and it would have been the
**fourth** wave in a row to record an activation that did not happen: `E6` said `J60` was
activated, `H3` said `J67` and `J62`, `I3` said `J66`, and all five still carry their
banners today.

**The judgment, and it is ours to make (law 13):** a journey file is defined by this
repository as *"the handoff contract — what upstream leaves in the DB for you and what
you must leave for downstream"* (CLAUDE.md, the dependency rule). That is a claim about
the DATABASE, so the spec belongs where the database is: `06-backend/tests/`.

* `06-backend/tests/test_j65_offline_day_one_sync.py` — **6 cases, green**
* `06-backend/tests/test_j61_connect_field_accept_live.py` — **8 cases, green**

**What an activation asserts, decided here so the next five are consistent:** the
journey's own *"This journey leaves (for downstream)"* paragraph and its INVARIANCE row,
one case per clause. **Not** the step table — a case per drawn cell is a second copy of
the journey, free to disagree with the first. `J61`'s spec builds its fixture through
`J65`'s OWN helper, so the join between the two is what goes red if either half moves;
two journeys proved against two fixtures prove nothing about the handoff.

Each was proved RED first, through pytest — the harness that runs it (`DEF-GOV-3733`):
breaking the idempotency key fails the re-sync case; taking the read's date from the wall
clock fails the completion-date case; posting the read at Close fails both invariance
cases. Every file was restored and verified by subtraction.

### 2 · Wave L's letter check was passing for the wrong reason

`BR-WRK-057` — *the letter is refused, not misfiled* — is one of the four rules
`CR-070` §11's phase-2 exit test names, and **it was not being exercised.**

Wave L's walkthrough raised its three jobs on a premises and a meter and **no
connection**. `dispatch_communication` returns at its very first guard when
`order.connection_id is None` — *"an order with no build sends nothing, and says so"*
(`DEF-WRK-3635`) — answering `queued: False, no_connection: True` and **never reaching
the message queue at all**. The check read `queued:false OR OQ-376`, so the first half
was true for the wrong reason and the run was green.

**A check that cannot tell *the platform refused this letter* from *there was no letter*
is not checking the rule.** The fixture now stands its jobs on a build as well as a
meter, `tracks` is asserted to be `OQ-376` by name, and the same hole is closed in
`J61`'s spec, whose own first draft reproduced it exactly.

It also made the desktop walk unreachable: `Work-009`'s eye builds its link from
`row.connection.home`, so a row with no build renders a **disabled** eye and the drawer
this wave was meant to demonstrate could not be opened from the queue at all.

### 3 · The drawer now says what the acceptance did with the letter

`WorkOrderAcceptResult`'s own docstring has said, in capitals, since 2026-09-04:
*"`queued` CAN BE `false` WITH A REASON, AND THE SCREEN MUST SAY SO."* No screen did.
The drawer's consequence box promises *"tells the customer their service is live"*, the
letter is refused at the queue, and a supervisor pressed the button and was never told
the promise had not been kept — **hard-won law 1 with the comment living in a type.**

`Work-003` now renders *What this acceptance did*: the service state, and the letter as
**sent · already sent · no new connection · not yet sendable**. Four answers because
`dispatch_communication` gives four, and `DEF-WRK-3635` is the reason *no build* and
*the platform refused* must not share a sentence.

⛔ **The server's own refusal string is never printed.** It names the `SOURCE_TYPES`
constant and lists its whole vocabulary — written for a log, and B14 rule 32 forbids an
internal code in clerk copy. The SHAPE of the answer picks a clerk sentence; the question
travels in `data-tracks`, which is not a visible value and is therefore not a rule 31
breach. Eight keys in all eleven catalogues, each in its own language (rule 35).

### 4 · Three journey boundaries had closed while the journeys sat unactivated

`OQ-WRK-1492` (who may accept), `OQ-WRK-1494` (the web-blocked login) and `OQ-WRK-1496`
(retention) were **all ruled on 2026-09-04**, and on 2026-09-05 `J61` steps 8 and 9 and
`J65` step 12 still described their stubs — *"is caught into allow, logged ONCE"*,
*"the test is xfail"*, *"`retention_policy()` raises"*. Every clause false.

This is `DEF-WRK-4030`'s exact shape one document further on, and it is why CLAUDE.md's
prime directive now says **the status column decides**. Had the specs been written from
the bodies they would have asserted stubs for questions the PO had already answered.
**All three were amended, dated, BEFORE the specs were written** (step W: before the
thing that depends on it, never "at the end"). `OQ-376` is the one boundary that remains
OPEN, and it is asserted rather than resolved.

### 5 · `DEF-MET-4101` — every meter read displays one day early, and it is not this
wave's

Found by RENDERING the page (law 6). A read's date is a **calendar date**:
`read_import._parse_date` normalises every one to `00:00:00Z` **on purpose**, and its own
docstring gives the reason — that normalisation IS what makes `UNIQUE (asset, read_at,
channel)` behave as the per-date key `BR-MET-052` describes. But
`assets/selectors._fold_row` serves it as a **raw instant**, and `DateCell` — correctly,
by its own documented contract — converts an instant into the tenant's timezone. Brazos
Bend is America/Chicago, so the read wave L dates `2026-03-15` is **drawn as
03/14/2026**, and the whole Reads tab is shifted, not just field reads.

**Every check in the repo compares UTC dates and the screen renders local ones, so the
two never meet.** Wave L's own walkthrough asserted the read against the API payload from
inside the browser and went green, correctly — *a check that fetches JSON from inside a
browser is not a check on what the browser drew.*

**NOT FIXED HERE, and the reason is the blast radius rather than the difficulty.** The
one-line fix — serve `read_at.date()` so `DateCell` takes its calendar-date path —
changes the shape of a published API field on four consumers this lane cannot sweep.
⚠ **And the tempting fix is at the other end and would be silent:** storing the
completion MOMENT instead of its date makes the screen right and **disables the
one-read-per-meter-per-date guarantee**, because that guarantee IS the midnight
normalisation. Written down so the next lane does not discover it by breaking it. The
walkthrough asserts the drawn date and names the row, so **the day the fold is fixed that
line goes red and points at the fix** (law 2's rule for a hold).
