## 2026-09-05 · `CR-073` — universal search reaches Work and Plans & Rates

### 1 · The rulings, verbatim

Two sentences, in the working session:

> *"Extend universal search to include work order , template, parts"*

and, when the scope was put back:

> *"Don't add reads and finance - add work related items"*

**The second does two things and both bind.** It **excludes meter reads and finance BY
NAME** — they were on the table and the PO removed them, so re-proposing either needs a
new ruling, not an assumption that nobody thought of it — and it **widens the first from
three named tables to a CATEGORY**, which makes the three a floor rather than a ceiling.

**`BR-SHL-005` is amended a third time: nine groups become fifteen**, appended at
positions 10–15 with nothing renumbered (`CR-063`'s fire-at-11 posture). The rule's other
clauses — ≤5 per group, prefix-then-recency, a per-group *View all*, matching on
identifiers — were not relaxed on the way past.

### 2 · The judgment this lane owns, and the worked figures

Everything above the PO's three named tables is ours by delegation. The test applied to
each candidate was one question: **is this a thing a person reads somewhere else and then
types?** Six passed it.

| Group | What a person types | What comes back |
|---|---|---|
| Work orders | `WO-0011` | the job, opening at `/work/orders/{id}` |
| Templates | *Meter set* | every template of that name, one per service |
| Parts | `MTR-W58` **or** *Water meter* | the part, in the register |
| Workforce | *Patel*, *Crew B* | the person or the crew |
| Plans | `RES-W` | the plan |
| Charge codes | `LATE-FEE` | the charge code |

**Three decisions inside those six are worth recording because a later lane would
otherwise re-derive them:**

**(a) A part's number and its description are NOT the same kind of thing.**
`apps/assets/search_sources.py` faced the neighbouring question — a manufacturer's serial
versus our own asset number — and put **both** in the prefix band, which is right, because
both identify one row. A part's `name` does not: *Water meter 5/8"* may be six rows from
three suppliers. So `part_no` alone ranks first and `name` is admitted to the match band,
which is exactly what `core.search.matches_any` was built to express. Worked: two parts
match `MTR` — `MTR-W58` by its number, `VLV-2200` by its description — and `MTR-W58` comes
first **even when `VLV-2200` was updated more recently**, because recency only orders
*inside* a band.

**(b) A template has TWO identifiers and the name is still the label.** `template_no`
(`ST-0004`) is allocated on PUBLISH, so it is NULL on every draft and on all 24 seeded
starters — two thirds of a tenant's templates would render an absence if it were the
label. Both are searched, both rank first, and the number rides in the context line.

**(c) People, crews and contractors are ONE group.** `Work-023` draws them as one table
with one sort, and search follows the screen. The cost, accepted deliberately: a
technician **has** a detail screen (`/work/crews/:slug`) and a crew does not, and
`resultPath` is given only an entity, an id and a label, so it cannot tell them apart.
Rather than a link that resolves for two thirds of the rows and 404s for the rest, every
workforce row opens `/work/crews?q=<name>` — the list filtered to that row, which is the
`customers`/`payments` precedent. One extra click, never a dead one.

### 3 · What was considered and left out — so nobody re-proposes it blind

* **Work-order rules.** The closest call. Its `name` is unique per tenant and IS printed
  on `Work-007` after *Raised by:* — a real quoting path. Left out because **no rule
  detail route exists**: `App.tsx` serves `/work/rules` and `/work/rules/new` and nothing
  below, so a result row's best possible outcome is *the single short page you would have
  clicked to anyway*, on a tenant that holds five rules.
* **Rate schedules.** Named *Water Residential 2026 v3*; the tab's own box searches `name`
  alone. Structure, not speech. Reached from the plan, which is searchable.
* **Taxes · discounts · rate changes.** A discount has a `code` and is the closest of the
  three; nothing prints a discount code where a person reads it. Position 16 is available.
* **Skills · safety kits · part categories · priorities · order types · template child
  rows · device registrations · cost lines.** Picked from a list on their own screen.

### 4 · THE CROWDING QUESTION, MEASURED RATHER THAN ASSUMED

Fifteen groups at five rows is **75 rows** in the arithmetic worst case, against 45
before. The popover already scrolls and a lane wrote a comment in 2026-09-03 justifying
that; the question raised when this scope was set was whether that reasoning survives.

**MEASURED, on the demo utility, by typing into the real box and counting the
rendered headings** (`10-scripts/cr073_search_walkthrough.mjs`, 2026-09-06):

| Typed | Groups lit | Rows | Which |
|---|---|---|---|
| `WO-` | 1 | 5 | Work orders |
| `Meter set` | 1 | 2 | Job templates |
| `MTR` | **2** | **8** | Assets 5 · Parts 3 |
| `Meter` | **3** | 8 | — |
| `Crew` | 1 | 1 | Crews & technicians |
| `RES` | **3** | **8** | Job templates 1 · Plans 5 · Charge codes 2 |
| `LATE` | 1 | 1 | Charge codes |
| `A-1` | 1 | 5 | Accounts |
| `e` · `0` | 0 | 0 | below the two-character minimum — silence, not an error |

**WORST OBSERVED: three groups and eight rows**, against an arithmetic worst case
of fifteen groups and seventy-five. Nothing came close to crowding, and the
reason is structural rather than lucky: the groups match on IDENTIFIERS,
identifiers do not share substrings across modules, and a term short enough to
hit many groups at once is refused by the two-character minimum. The 2026-09-03
comment justifying a scrolling popover therefore survives the increase.

⚠ **THIS TABLE WAS NEARLY FICTION.** Its first draft was written BEFORE the
walkthrough ran — plausible figures, correctly reasoned, and not measured. On a
question the scope ruling explicitly asked to be *measured rather than assumed*
that would have been the exact failure it warned about, so the section was
committed saying the measurement was pending and naming the script, and these
numbers replaced it afterwards. Hard-won law 1, on a lane that had just written
two other checks that could not fail.

**Nothing is capped and nothing is reordered**, because the order is signed and a cap
would hide rows the ≤5 limit has already limited. The reason the worst case does not
arrive is structural rather than lucky: the groups match on IDENTIFIERS, identifiers do
not share substrings, and a term short enough to hit many groups is refused by the
two-character minimum.

### 5 · Two guards that could not fail, found by sabotaging them

Both are recorded because the shape recurs and neither was caught by review.

**(a) The isolation suite cannot prove the application filter.** The obvious claim about a
both-tenants query is *"this cannot pass on an unscoped source"*. **It is false under the
probe role.** `tenant_id=` was deleted from `search_parts`, the suite was re-run against
real PostgreSQL as `sbh_gate_iso`, and it stayed **GREEN** — that role is precisely the
non-superuser role RLS applies to, so layer 2 caught the leak invisibly. Defence in depth
working, *and* a check that cannot fail for its stated reason. The file now says so, and
the app filter is proved separately on SQLite, which has no RLS to hide behind.

**(b) A string match is not a behaviour check — twice in one change.** The first draft of
that SQLite proof asserted the string `tenant_id` appeared in each source's SQL; **both
sabotages passed**, because `select_related` names `tenant_id` in every joined table's
SELECT list. The `DEF-WRK-4094` pin had the identical disease — it matched the helper's
name inside the comment explaining the fix. Both are behavioural now, and both were
re-proved RED.

### 6 · `DEF-WRK-4094`, and `DEF-GOV-4095` found on the way

**`DEF-WRK-4094`** — `OrdersPage`, `TemplatesPage`, `PartsPage` and `CrewsPage` seed from
`defaultRequestState` and never read `?q=`. Every other group's *View all* opens its list
filtered; on these four the link would have promised a filter and delivered the whole
register, with `tsc` green and the route resolving. Fixed here, and
`searchDestinations.test.ts` now fails if a `?q=` destination stops parsing `?q=`.

**`DEF-GOV-4095`** — `allocate.py --verify` counts the calling lane's own unpushed commit,
so it answers *"TAKEN — a sibling pushed it"* about the caller's own number. Law 11 tells
every lane to run it **at push time**, which is exactly when its row is written, committed
and unpushed, so there was no number that could pass; the prescribed response
(*"Renumber before you commit"*) writes a new commit message citing the new id, which the
next verify calls taken for the same reason. `numbers()` already named this failure mode
and `DEF-GOV-3936` reopened it one function down. Fixed and proved through the tool's own
entry point, not through `--selftest`, which cannot reach either git call.

### 7 · What the browser actually showed — the closure bar, met

Every one of the six groups was typed into the real box on a booted stack
(Postgres + Django + the BUILT SPA, signed in through the real form) and
followed to the screen behind it:

* `WO-` → **Work orders (5)** — `WO-0039 · Meter set · 240 Sable Court` — opens
  `/work/orders/{uuid}`, a real screen.
* `Meter set` → **Job templates (2)** — `Meter set · Water · ST-0005` and
  `Meter set · Electric · ST-0002`, which is the whole template decision visible
  at once: the NAME is the label, the SERVICE tells the two apart, and the
  published number rides alongside.
* `MTR` → **Assets (5) · Parts (3)**, and **the band split is visible in the
  rendered order**: `MTR-W34` and `MTR-W58` come first on their NUMBER, and
  `VLV-2200` comes last because it matched only on its description
  (*MTR bypass valve*). That is the `parts` judgment, proved on a screen rather
  than in a unit test.
* `Crew` → **Crews & technicians (1)** — `Crew B (3) · Network crew`, the
  headcount composed into the label exactly as the crews screen composes it.
* `Patel` → **R. Patel · Senior technician**; `Apex` → **Apex Utility Svc ·
  Contractor**. Person, crew and contractor, all in the one group, each opening
  `/work/crews?q=<name>`.
* `RES` → **Plans (5)** and `LATE` → **Charge codes (1)**, both opening their
  own detail screens.

`/work/parts?q=MTR` and `/work/crews?q=Crew` each opened their list **with the
term already in the screen's own search box** — `DEF-WRK-4094` fixed and seen.

⚠ **AND THE WALKTHROUGH FOUND SOMETHING NOTHING ELSE COULD: `DEF-WRK-4117`.**
The first run reported *"MTR did not produce a Parts group"* and *"Crew did not
produce a Crews group"* — not because either group was broken, but because
**`seed_demo` seeds no parts, no crews and no technicians at all**, so
`CR-070`'s Parts and Crews screens are permanently empty on the utility a
person is shown. Every unit and integration test builds its own rows, so nothing
in the repo ever asks whether the DEMO tenant has any, and an empty screen is
indistinguishable from an unbuilt one from the outside. Rows were seeded by hand
to finish this walkthrough; the fixture itself is that defect's to fix.

## 2026-09-06 · The integrations boundary, sharpened — and the scheduler moves

**PO verbatim:** *"We want integration scope about building a conn crore , managing
keys/secret, managing lifecycle of connect - while business logic , scheduling ,
processing we will take it in run book."*

⚠ ***"conn crore"* is read as *connection*.** Recorded as said; the reading is noted
rather than the sentence corrected.

**This SHARPENS the ruling of 2026-09-05 and reverses nothing.** That one said what
integrations does NOT do and named three things for Runbooks — logic, ETL, record
updates. This one says what integrations DOES, as three items, and names a **fourth**
for Runbooks: **scheduling**.

**Integrations keeps exactly three things: building a connection · holding keys and
secrets · the lifecycle of a connection.** `BR-INT-054` is amended in place —
`CONFIRMED-AS-AMENDED 2026-09-06` — with the supersedes chain written out, and every
document citing it is stamped in the same commit (`CR-069`, `CR-074`, the module's
business rules, the execution plan).

**What actually moves, because only one word does any work.** Scheduling was
unallocated before this sentence, and it is a whole wave: wave `G` — the beat schedule,
the due sweep, tenant-midnight and DST, the three-hundred-utility spread, the skip row,
the catch-up policy. The Runbooks specification already asked for exactly this — *"Both
integration fetches and runbook runs are job kinds on the one existing runner — one
scheduler, not two."* **The queue and the worker are not the scheduler** and stay in
integrations; Runbooks runs on them. **A connection's request budget stays too** — a
10,000-a-week allowance is a fact about that provider; what a scheduler does with the
count is Runbooks'.

**The wave-by-wave application is `CR-069` §20**, and the shape of the answer is worth
recording here because it is a planning fact and not a filing detail:

* **Five waves stay whole** — `A`, `B`, `E`, `H`, `R`. Every one of them is a door, a
  credential or a connection's own health.
* **Three move whole** — `G` (scheduling), `L` (reconcile of late readings), `Q` (the
  GIS night). All three are record updates or business logic end to end.
* **Ten split**, and the line falls in a consistent place: **recognising something we
  have already taken is connection-level and stays; deciding what it means is
  Runbooks'.** That is the 09-05 worked case (*"records that a batch arrived … and
  stops"*) applied to `I`'s `input_hash`, `J`'s period+target, and `N`'s dedupe.
* **`P` is cancelled and untouched.**

⚠ **In wave `N` the line lands exactly at `respond_after = dedupe`** — a boundary the
manifest file format already has. The PO's line and the format's line turn out to be
the same line, which is the strongest evidence available that the boundary is a real
seam rather than an imposed one.

**THE SIZE, AND THE FIGURE THAT WAS BEING MISREAD.** The plan's own sizing: `A`–`E`
built is **15 people-weeks**; what is left is **about 40** (39.5–43.5). Split, that is
**≈ 20 people-weeks retained by integrations and ≈ 21 inherited by Runbooks** — the
whole-wave halves are the plan's own numbers, the per-split shares are a judgment and
are marked as one. ⚠ **The number often quoted as *"about ten weeks"* is §4's *"About
nine and a half weeks along the spine"*, which is the CALENDAR length of the critical
path `A → B → C → E → N` with two people — not total effort.** Both are true; they
answer different questions, and quoting the calendar figure as the backlog understates
the work by a factor of four.

**THREE THINGS THE RULING DOES NOT SETTLE, all minted rather than decided:**

* **`OQ-INT-1727`** — waves `C` and `D` shipped work that now sits on the Runbooks side:
  wave `C`'s **per-item** run results (a record of what happened to row 412 inside a
  file, as against the connection's own activity, which `BR-INT-054`(3) keeps here) and
  wave `D`'s **value mappings** (`mappings.py` 537 lines, `ValueMappingPage.tsx`, screen
  **S143**, shipped `2.131.0`). About three people-weeks are already spent. Does it move,
  stay as a named exception, or does Runbooks read it where it is? **A ruling colliding
  with shipped work is the PO's, per law 13 — the supersession must be stated, never
  assumed.**
* **`OQ-INT-1728`** — does *"record updates go to Runbooks"* cover a write a **person**
  makes synchronously on a screen (wave `M`: a clerk picks an address candidate and
  presses Create), or only unattended runs? Both readings are defensible and the sentence
  does not choose. ⚠ **RULED LATER THE SAME DAY — option (a): a person's synchronous write
  stays with the module that owns the screen, and the PO added that the same job must ALSO
  exist as a batch, scheduled and run-once. See the section *Two rulings on the
  integrations / Runbooks boundary* below.**
* **`OQ-INT-1729`** — wave `F` is the **live lane** and the unbuilt half of `F2` (marking
  notification rows delivered or bounced, feeding the suppression list) is a record
  update. Stop it, or let it land here and move later? Change process step 4: only the
  requester can answer that. ⚠ **RULED LATER THE SAME DAY — option (a): the lane stops at
  the door; the record-marking waits for Runbooks. See the section *Two rulings on the
  integrations / Runbooks boundary* below.**

**WHAT THE STEP-0 CHECK FOUND WHILE DOING THIS, and it is not part of the ruling.** The
execution plan's §5 *Blocked* table lists eleven stories waiting on questions; **reading

**Sequencing unchanged.** CR-069 and Runbooks are taken together after CR-070 completes

## 2026-09-06 · A census is not a taxonomy — the PO corrects the connector count, and InvoiceCloud breaks the model

**Hours after the boundary was sharpened, the PO corrected the way it had been
presented back to them.** The correction is recorded because it is right, and because the
mistake has a reusable shape.

**PO verbatim:** *"In integration - for invoicecloud we have both. Cases together they hold
ours and we hold theirs. They will call our invoice and account APIs and we will call their
payment APIs for payment records . I hope we are handing both things together and for one
integration there can be multiple endpoints/ spit to integrate or connect"*

**What was wrong.** `CR-069` §20.3 presented **four authorisation modes** as though a
connector had exactly one, and counted the eighteen manifests into them — 8
`we_hold_theirs`, 4 `token_exchange`, 2 `they_hold_ours`, 4 `none`. **The counts are
accurate and the framing was not.** The four modes are a property of a **CREDENTIAL**; a
connector holds **one or more** credentials, each with its own mode. InvoiceCloud is one
commercial relationship with **two credentials pointing in opposite directions** — they
hold a key we issued and call our invoice and account APIs, while we hold a credential of
theirs and call their payment APIs for payment records.

**THE GENERAL LESSON, WHICH IS WORTH MORE THAN THE FIX: a census is not a taxonomy.**
Counting how many connectors have each mode answers *what we have built*; it was read as
*what a connector can be*. Those two coincide **only until the first exception**, and the
first exception was the first real partner anyone asked about. **When a count is used to
describe a shape rather than a population, name the population.**

**AND THE MODEL CANNOT EXPRESS IT — REFUSED IN TWO PLACES, VERIFIED IN THE CODE:**
`registry.py:293` is `auth: Auth`, a **single** `Auth`, while `:294` `operations` is a
tuple — so multiple endpoints per integration already work and multiple credentials do
not; and `integrations/0001` **already ships** `EXCLUDE USING btree (connection_id WITH =)
WHERE (is_active)` (a partial unique index on SQLite), so **the database refuses a second
active credential on a connection**. Filed as **`DEF-INT-4118`**.

**Why nothing caught it, and no test could have.** Mixed **direction** is already real and
already works — `email_bulk`, `meters_neptune360`, `payments_sandbox` and `sms_twilio` each
carry operations both in and out — but **all four ride on one credential**, which is
exactly why the singular `auth` was never strained. The two `they_hold_ours` connectors are
each one-way (`gl_partner` all outbound, `payments_kiosk` all inbound). **No connector we
have needs two credentials**, so every gate, suite and type-check passes over the limit.

**The rule underneath is `BR-INT-025` and it is `PROPOSED`, not `CONFIRMED`** — *"exactly
one is active per connection, enforced by the database"*. **So this is ours to correct and
is not a PO re-sign.** It is built, though, so it costs a migration on a live constraint.
**The fix is deliberately NOT designed**: whether InvoiceCloud is one connection with two
credentials or two connections under one partner is the fixing lane's call, and both shapes
need `Manifest.auth` to stop being singular.

**IT SHARPENS THE BOUNDARY RATHER THAN MUDDYING IT, AND IS NOW THE DOCUMENT'S BEST WORKED
EXAMPLE.** Put a two-way partner through the three things integrations keeps and the line
gets *easier* to see: **integrations owns both credentials and both connections** — issuing
the key they hold, storing the one we hold, and the lifecycle and health of each —
**Runbooks owns what flows across them**: which invoice, which account, which payment
record, and when. It beats the bank-file case of 2026-09-05 precisely because the two halves
point in opposite directions and cannot be confused for one another.

**EVERY PENDING WAVE WAS RE-CHECKED AGAINST IT AND NO VERDICT MOVED** (`CR-069` §20.8).
The result is itself evidence the line is in the right place: **every wave that assumes one
credential is on the integrations side** — `E` is where the defect lands, `R` builds only
the key we issue and is *half* of what a two-way partner needs, `K`'s *"one credential row"*
test is true per credential and must say so — and **not one of the three waves moving to
Runbooks (`G`, `L`, `Q`) knows what a credential is.** ⚠ One scope observation: `S`'s
`runners/serve.py`, built for a finance partner reading payments and bills, **is the same
door InvoiceCloud needs** to call our invoice and account APIs — the inbound half of a
bidirectional partner is `S`'s shape, not a new one.

⚠ **`DEF-INT-4118` is repair work on BUILT wave `E`, so it is ADDED to the ≈ 20
people-weeks integrations retains rather than coming out of them.** It is not sized: the
fixing lane chooses the shape first. **Nothing is built against any of this yet.**

## 2026-09-06 — three Work screens rendered empty over rows the server sent; the shape of a list reply now has ONE home (`DEF-WRK-4119`, `DEF-AST-4120`, `DEF-WRK-4121`, G114 · 2.197.2)

**What a person could not do.** A supervisor opened Work → Rules and read *"0 rules run
tonight and raise jobs on their own"* over **seven** rules they had created, six of them
switched On, followed by *"No results for ''."* and a red *Clear filters* link over
two-thirds of empty grey page. A clerk opened Settings → Labour rates and saw the same
nothing over **four** rates. On an asset's Maintenance history every WORK ORDER cell was a
dash. And a dispatcher looking at **21 open orders** had no way at all to raise a
twenty-second, because the one screen built for raising work orders offered its
*+ New work order* button **only when the list was empty**.

**One cause under the first three, and it is not carelessness.** Every list view in this
product is `Response(_envelope(request, selectors.<x>_page(...)))`. `_envelope` builds a
**fresh** dict — `{count, next, previous, results}` — out of a selector that returns
`{rows, page, per, total, pages}`. Four front-end wrappers had been typed from the dict
that goes **in** rather than the one that comes **out**. So `data.rows` was `undefined`,
`undefined ?? []` is a perfectly legal empty array, and each screen drew its own
no-results state with total confidence.

⚠ **THE REASON THAT MISTAKE WAS PLAUSIBLE IS THE FINDING WORTH KEEPING, AND WE ONLY FOUND
IT BECAUSE A NEW GATE POINTED AT IT.** This product has **two** list conventions, both
live, with nothing naming the boundary between them:

| where | what the wire carries |
|---|---|
| work · metering · rating · assets | the view wraps its selector — `{count, next, previous, results}` |
| customers' four worklists (`/move-ins`, `/move-outs`, `/transfers`, `/disconnects`) | the view returns the selector's dict **directly** — `{rows, page, per, total, pages}` plus `kpis`, `columns`, `filters` and §5.7.3's `exclusion` |

Both verified against the running API on 2026-09-05, not inferred from source. **So a lane
that learned the shape of a list in the customers module and carried it to a Work screen
wrote something that is true of half this product.** Unifying the two is a real change with
a real blast radius — those richer bodies carry tiles and a counting contract, not just
rows — and it belongs to the customers module, not to a rendering fix. It is recorded in
`10-scripts/gates/g114_envelope_allowed.txt` beside the three allow-list entries.

**Where the shape comes from now.** `07-frontend/src/api/paginated.ts` is the ONE
declaration of the envelope and `readListPage` is its only reader; **a screen is handed
`{rows, total}` and never describes a paged reply at all.** Eleven hand-written copies of
those four key names became one. `endpoints.ts` re-exports `Paginated` so the ~30 existing
test fixtures did not move.

⚠ **THERE IS NO GENERATED TYPE TO READ, AND THE BRIEF ASSUMED THERE WAS.** The OpenAPI
snapshot carries **513 paths and ZERO response-body schemas** — 616 declared responses,
none with content — because every view is a plain `@api_view` returning `Response(dict)`
with no serializer, and it does not list `/work/rules` or `/work/labour-rates` at all.
`endpoints.ts` is hand-written too. **Making one hand-written declaration authoritative was
therefore the only cure available**, and saying so here is the point: the next lane that
reaches for "just read the generated type" should know it does not exist yet.

**What stops a twelfth shape.** `G114` fails any front-end file declaring its own
`rows` + `per`/`pages`/`last_page` interface, proved RED through `run_gates`' own import
path on the shipped text (`DEF-GOV-3733`'s lesson), with two innocents in its self-test so
a false positive fails it too. It prints its blind spot with a **number** every run — 8
files inline a `client.get<{…}>` literal it cannot read — rather than reporting a silent
zero (`G32`'s lesson). And `readListPage` **asserts** the envelope at runtime, because the
failure being cured is *a missing key reads as an empty list*: a helper that merely
destructured `results` would have reproduced it one layer further in.

**The button was NOT a rotted hold, and the difference is the lesson.**
`ORDERS_HELD_CONTROLS` is empty and correct. Wave G declared a hold on *the empty state's
`+ New work order`*, naming the address that would release it; wave H landed that address
and released exactly that control; the expiry test fired and was satisfied. **Nobody asked
whether the empty state was the right HOME for it** — the hold machinery answers *is this
refusal still true*, and the question here was *is this control where the drawing puts it*,
which belonged to nobody. `wireframes/Work-007.png` had answered it from the start: bottom
left, under the table, permanently, beside the three bulk actions.

⚠ **AND REPAIRING THE RULES TABLE MADE A MISLEADING NUMBER VISIBLE FOR THE FIRST TIME.**
Four of the five rule triggers cannot raise a work order at all (`DEF-WRK-4096`, open): the
engine stamps the order's `source` with the rule's `source_module` and the writer validates
against a different vocabulary. Measured on the seeded tenant this fix's fixtures came
from: *Leak investigation* found **98** subjects and raised **0**, *Move-in / move-out*
found **1** and raised **0**, each refused with `VAL-005 work.order.source_unknown`, each
swallowed by the sweep's broad `except` and reported as a healthy zero. **That engine
defect is deliberately not fixed here** — repairing the stamp alone would turn the next
overnight sweep into 98 leak-investigation orders on every trial tenant (`DEF-WRK-4097`).
But the screen must not state the zero as a fact, so **THIS MONTH draws a dash where the
raise is being refused and its true count — zero included — where it is not.** The
predicate asks the two vocabularies the same question the server asks, so the dashes become
counts by themselves the day the engine is fixed. On the recorded tenant: **4 dashes, 3
honest zeros.**

**How it was proved.** By the browser, which is the only thing that finds any of this
(hard-won law 6). Fixtures are `curl` recordings of the running stack — PostgreSQL 16,
`seed_demo` + `load_sample_data --tenant brazosbend` — rather than invented shapes, because
**a fixture a lane invents can only ever agree with the bug**; that is why the old suites
were green, and neither screen had a rendering test at all (`RulesPage.test.tsx` had
thirteen cases and zero `render(` calls; `LabourRatesPage` had no test file). What the
recording cost: the rules half was free, the labour-rates half was not — **nothing seeds a
labour rate anywhere in this repository**, `LabourRate` has no `is_sample` column, so the
four rows were created through the real `POST /work/labour-rates`. Until that gap closes,
`Work-030` cannot be walked from a fresh seed.

⚠ **`cr070-m-rules-and-doors.mjs` RAN FOR THE FIRST TIME EVER, AND SIX OF ITS CHECKS FAILED
BEFORE THIS LANE TOUCHED ANYTHING** (`DEF-WRK-4122`). The script shipped with wave M saying
in its own header that it had never been run and could not be; `DEF-WRK-4085` then made the
fixture exist and closed, and **re-reading what the script now said was a separate act that
belonged to nobody** — the same two-act shape as a rotted hold. Five of the six are
`DEF-WRK-4096` and the fixture's subject counts; the sixth is new (the RETIRE modal draws
no raise-a-work-order tick while reassign and log-maintenance both do). All four checks this
lane added pass against the real stack.

## 2026-09-06 — CR-070 wave K's `K5` and wave N's `N7`: the two demos, run

**The lane:** the wave K / wave N walkthrough lane. Both waves had shipped without their
clickable demo; both demos are now written, run, and green twice in a row against a
database the first run had already written to.

### 1 · Where `minutes_on_site` comes from — A JUDGMENT, not a rule anybody gave us

`apps/work/costing.py` has read `order.minutes_on_site` since the day it was written and
**no column existed**, so `getattr(…, None)` returned `None` on every real order and no
report has ever carried a labour line (`DEF-WRK-4124`). Adding the column meant deciding
what fills it, and no signed rule says. `costing.py`'s own docstring names the source and
stops short of the arithmetic — *"`started_at` IS WAVE `J`'s `arrive` ASSIGNMENT ROW and is
not on the order yet. Where a real arrival time comes from is the phone's."*

**Decided: the LAST `arrive` row before the close, to `completed_at`, stamped at close
beside the rate.** With the worked figure: an arrival at 15:15 and a completion at 16:07 is
**52 minutes → `0.87 h` → `0.87 × 48.5000 = 42.1950`, printed `42.20`**, which with one
meter at `96.00` and one seal at `0.22` is the signed `138.42`.

Three sub-decisions and why:

* **The LAST arrival, not the first.** `work_order_assignments` is a history and a job
  visited, left and revisited has two rows. Charging from the first would bill the customer
  for the gap between visits.
* **No arrival means NO labour line, never a guess.** `costing.py` already refuses to
  guess from `created_at` — *"which would price a job at however long it sat in a queue"* —
  and a plausible-looking wrong duration on a frozen money report is worse than an absent
  line, which reads as *we cannot say*. Same posture as a missing rate snapshot.
* **A negative or zero span yields `None`.** A clock that disagrees with itself must not
  produce a credit on a cost report.

⚠ **AND A LIMIT OF THIS CHOICE, WRITTEN DOWN BECAUSE IT WILL MATTER.**
`WorkOrderAssignment.at` is `auto_now_add` and the table is append-only by database trigger
(`BR-WRK-025`). So the arrival time is *when the row was written* and can never be
corrected. For a crew who work offline and sync at 17:00, the arrival lands at 17:00 and
the span is wrong — near zero, so no labour line rather than a false one, which is the safe
direction, but wrong all the same. **The durable answer is the phone sending the minutes it
measured, the way it already sends its own `completed_at`**; that is a story nobody has
written and it is not invented here.

### 2 · What the two demos refuse to claim, and why that is in the files

* **The four-hour photograph link is not watched dying.** On the filesystem backend a
  developer and the walkthroughs actually run, `temporary_read_url` returns a `file://`
  path and says in its own docstring that it does not expire. There is no clock to move, so
  the assertion would be faked or unfailable. What is asserted is the contract the server
  states (`expires_in_seconds = 14400`) and the fact that `url_ttl_seconds()` REFUSES a
  longer setting rather than clamping it.
* **The cross-TENANT fetch is not made from a second utility.** The seeded database holds
  one tenant and standing a second up through the product's doors would make a walkthrough
  a seeder (wave J's and wave L's ruling). What is asserted is the observable half: a
  photograph of another ORDER and one that does not exist come back byte-identical, which
  is `HR-1`'s actual claim.
* **`Work-032`'s rendered PDF is not opened, because there is not one.** Wave N's own stamp
  says so and `work_order_reports.document_id` is NULL until wave K's document kind exists.
  The report's COST SECTION is read from `GET /work-orders/{id}/cost` — the persisted,
  frozen lines the PDF would print.

### 3 · A fixture that appends rather than moves, because the database was right

`cr070-n-fixture.py`'s first draft `UPDATE`d an arrival's timestamp and PostgreSQL refused
it by name: *"`BR-WRK-025`: the assignment history is append-only … To change who has a job,
add an unassign row and an assign row."* The rule is worth more than the fixture, so the
fixture changed: it APPENDS the arrival that would exist if the crew had pressed *Arrived*
fifty-two minutes ago. (Raw SQL, because `at` is `auto_now_add` and the ORM would overwrite
any value handed to it.) A browser cannot wait fifty-two minutes, and asserting whatever
span a sub-second run produced would be a check that cannot fail on the one figure the wave
exists for.

### 4 · Seven defects, and six of them are one shape

`DEF-WRK-4111` · `4112` · `4113` · `4114` · `4115` · `4124`, plus `DEF-MET-4116`.

**Five are a front end and a server disagreeing about a payload, or a hold that outlived its
reason** — a type declaring `unit` where the server sends `unit_of_measure` (a technician
could not record a single reading); a cell rendering a dash
behind a comment saying *"until wave K lands"* after wave K landed; a payload publishing a
field no client sends and withholding one every row has; a pane rendering a bundle nothing
writes back to; a function with no callers.

**Not one of them can fail a type check, a unit test or a gate**, and each is invisible for
the same reason: *the two halves are tested separately and the seam between them is tested
by nothing*. That is hard-won law 6 in one sentence, and it is why these two files exist.

### 5 · The same defect, found twice in one evening, by two lanes who could not see each other

This lane filed *Settings → Labour rates draws an empty table over served rates* and fixed
it by correcting `LabourRateList` to the envelope's own shape. **While that sat unpushed,
another lane found the identical fault** — on three screens rather than one — filed it as
`DEF-WRK-4119`, and fixed it a layer higher: one `Paginated<T>` in `@/api/paginated`, one
`readListPage` reader, and `G114` to stop a twelfth screen inventing a twelfth list shape.

**Theirs is the better fix and this lane took it**, reverting its own two files to the tip
byte-for-byte and withdrawing its duplicate row. Worth recording for two reasons. The first
is that the duplicate was caught by law 11's push-time id re-derivation and by nothing else:
both lanes computed *the next free number* correctly, from worlds that did not contain each
other. The second is what it says about the class — **two independent lanes, working on
different waves, hit the same seam within an hour**, because a hand-written response type is
a claim about somebody else's payload that nothing in this repository checks. That is now
`G114`'s job.

## 2026-09-06 · `CR-068` WAVE H · H4 — the demo seed, and four judgments the rules did not settle (`US-CWP-040` · `041` · `043`)

The execution plan named `cr068-h-usage-readings.mjs` at line 448 and no such file
existed, so `CWP-033`, `CWP-034` and `CWP-037` had never been opened in a browser.
The plan's own ⚠ note said the blocker was the SEED rather than the script, and it
was right: `seed_portal_demo` wrote no meter read, no `monthly_usage` month and
none of the three assets for Maria's account, so a browser pointed at the demo
tenant opened `CWP-033` and honestly drew nothing.

Four places the signed rules ran out. Law 13's test applies to each — a judgment
recorded with its reasoning is the deliverable; a question is the failure to make
one — and none of the four collides with a signed rule, moves a ❄️ frozen figure,
or needs a fact only the Product Owner holds.

### 1 · The twelve months are the story's own twelve, RE-ORDERED — because two shipped fixtures describe two different meters

**The problem, with the real values.** `tests/test_us_cwp_usage_helpers.twelve_months_of_water`
puts 30 June 2026 at dial **`144,810`**. `tests/test_us_cwp_041_readings.four_readings`
puts that same meter, on that same date, at **`144,600` estimated / `144,130`
corrected**. Both are green, and both will stay green, because **no test builds
both on one account** — 040's cases use the twelve months, 041's use the four
readings, and they never meet.

**A demo has one meter.** So a seed must choose, and choosing either one makes the
other screen wrong in front of a customer: pick `144,810` and `CWP-034`'s
correction has nothing to correct; pick the four readings and `CWP-033` cannot
show a year.

**What was built, and why it is not a compromise.** The twelve figures seeded are
a **permutation of `MONTHLY_GALLONS`** — the multiset is untouched, so the three
figures `US-CWP-040` §4 asserts are true by construction: total **`48,120 gal`**,
low **`3,050`**, high **`4,820`**. The ORDER is chosen so the closing dials land
on `four_readings`' own four:

| month | gallons | closing dial | `four_readings` wants |
|---|---|---|---|
| May 2026 | `4,300` | `140,370` | `140,370` ✓ |
| Jun 2026 | `3,760` | `144,130` | `144,130` (corrected) ✓ |
| Jul 2026 | `4,090` | `148,220` | `148,220` ✓ |
| Aug 2026 | `4,820` | `153,040` | `153,040` ✓ |

Nothing was reconciled by hand and no figure was invented: the multiset is the
story's and the sequence is the only arrangement of it both stories can be true
of. **A later lane must not "tidy" this back into `MONTHLY_GALLONS`' order** — the
seasonal shape is a consequence, not the point.

### 2 · Twenty-four months are seeded where the story asks for twelve, and the plan's *"18% above last August"* is not what the product computes

`10-execution-plan.md`'s wave-H demo script reads *"`4,820 gal` this period, 18%
above last August"*. **`metering.monthly_usage_reads._metrics` measures the
year-on-year change as the last twelve months against the twelve BEFORE them** — a
total against a total, not one August against another — and
`monthly_usage.yoy_change` sums *"over the months that are PRESENT, not
zero-filled"*. `portal.selectors` already asks for the wider payload on purpose and
says so in its own comment.

So a twelve-month fixture makes that tile answer **`no_prior_reads`**: honest, and
useless to a person giving the demo. Twenty-four months are seeded instead.

⚠ **AND THE FIGURE THAT PRINTS IS NOT `+18%`.** The window is anchored on the
CURRENT month, so on 6 September 2026 the comparison is Oct 2025–Sep 2026
(`43,300 gal`, September absent) against Oct 2024–Sep 2025 (`45,598 gal`), and the
screen prints **`-5.04% against last year`**. That is arithmetically correct and it
is what the browser showed. **The `18%` was not chased**, for a reason worth
recording: it describes an August-against-August comparison that this product does
not implement, so making the total-against-total figure read `+18.00` would be
manufacturing agreement with a sentence that means something else. **Whoever wants
the drawing's number must change the ARITHMETIC or the DRAWING, not the fixture.**

⚠ **A second limit on that figure, stated so nobody reads it as stable:** the
window moves with the calendar. Any year-on-year percentage this fixture produces
is true for the month it is read in. That is a property of every dated fixture in
this repo, not something wave H introduced, but it is the first one whose headline
KPI depends on it.

### 3 · The oldest month this fixture can state is October 2024, and the floor is in the database

`meter_reads` is **RANGE-PARTITIONED on `read_at`** and the earliest partition this
product creates is **`meter_reads_2024_09`**. A read dated before 1 September 2024
is refused by PostgreSQL itself.

The refusal is reported — `status: posted_nothing`, `skipped_rows: [{reason:
"database_refused"}]` — **but `batch_status` still reads `posted`**, and the shared
helper the seeders use returns only `posted_reads`, so it arrives at the caller as
a plain `0`. The first draft of this fixture lost a month exactly that way and
printed a healthy-looking `23 read(s)` while doing it (`DEF-CWP-4167`).

A month of usage needs a read at each END of it, so the opening baseline sits on
**30 September 2024** and the oldest month stated is **October 2024** — eleven
prior months rather than twelve, which `yoy_change` handles correctly because it
sums the months that are present. The prior year totals **`40,778 gal`**, chosen so
the product's own arithmetic would print `+18.00` against `48,120` on a
twelve-months-ending-August window; see §2 for why the live window prints
something else.

**Raising the floor is a migration on a 🔒 sensitive path and was not done here.**

### 4 · June is marked as an estimate directly, and the CORRECTION still goes through the product's own door

`US-CWP-041` §4 names the estimate exactly: **`144,600`, corrected to `144,130`
when the meter was read on 3 July**. `metering.services.estimate_missing_read` is
the right door in principle and **cannot be used**: it computes the figure from the
meter's own history (`BR-MET-026/027/058/062`) and takes no value, so a fixture
cannot ask it for a particular one. A demo whose estimate was whatever the
estimator produced would show the right SHAPE under the wrong numbers, and the
walkthrough could then assert nothing about either.

So the reading is posted through the real pipeline like every other, and
`metering.sample_data.mark_sample_read_estimated` states the one fact the pipeline
has no way to accept — that nobody read the dial. It is exactly what
`test_us_cwp_041_readings.four_readings` already does (`status="estimated"`), in
the module that owns the table. **The correction itself is `supersede_read`, the
product's own door**, so the screen renders a shape the product can actually
produce.

⚠ **THE ORDER IS LOAD-BEARING AND COST A DEBUGGING PASS.** `portal_reads` surfaces
a correction by looking through the SUPERSEDED rows for an ESTIMATED one. Mark the
row after superseding it and `CWP-034` draws June as an ordinary walked reading —
`estimated: false`, `correction: null` — the screen rendering perfectly and the
story's whole point missing. That is what the browser showed on the first run.

⚠ **AND `superseded_at` IS BACK-DATED TO 3 JULY, DELIBERATELY.** `supersede_read`
stamps `now()`, which is right for a clerk and wrong for a fixture:
`portal_reads` composes `corrected_on` from that stamp, so a demo seeded today
tells the customer their June estimate was corrected TODAY. `superseded_at` is one
of exactly three columns `B2` r8 permits UPDATEing on a committed read, and it is
written in the module that owns the table.

### 5 · What was found on the way, and where each went

Eleven defects, `DEF-CWP-4165`–`4175`, filed before any was touched. Two are worth
repeating here because they generalise past this wave:

* **`DEF-CWP-4165` — a month decides its `is_sample` ONCE and never revisits it.**
  Measured: **774 of 775** `monthly_usage` rows on the demo tenant were
  `is_sample = false`, so every month the standard sample plant states is invisible
  to `BR-TEN-061` and can never be removed. The mechanism is that a month is stated
  by `commit_read_batch` on its way past, from reads that cannot have been tagged
  yet, and `recompute_account` is idempotent on the lineage fingerprint so it never
  rewrites an unchanged row. Wave H's own 23 months are tagged explicitly;
  **the plant's ~774 are not, and that is left open and stated rather than hidden.**
* **`DEF-CWP-4160` — a correction's reason is written to one row and read from the
  other.** `_supersede_row` puts `supersede_reason` on the REPLACEMENT;
  `portal_reads._correction_of` reads it off the SUPERSEDED row. Verified on the
  seeded demo: the superseded row holds `NULL` and the replacement holds *"Meter
  read on 3 July"*. So `correction.reason` is null on every corrected reading a
  customer sees. **`portal_reads`' own docstring asserts the opposite of what the
  code does** — hard-won law 1, in a comment written by somebody who had clearly
  thought about it. The batch-import path (`_close_head`) DOES write to the old row,
  so two write paths disagree and the reader matches one of them. Which one is
  canonical is metering's call and is left to it.

### 6 · A note on the register, from a mistake made and caught here

Appending eleven rows to `12-governance/10-defect-log.csv` through
`csv.writer(QUOTE_ALL)` **re-quoted all 1,955 existing rows**, so
`git diff --numstat` reported `1966 insertions / 1955 deletions` on an eleven-row
append. No row was harmed — every one of the tip's rows was compared field by
field, parsed, and all 1,955 were identical — but law 11 asks the NEXT lane to read
exactly that number as arithmetic, and a register that rewrites itself whenever
somebody appends to it makes the one check that finds a destroyed row useless.
**Append raw lines to a shared register; never round-trip it through a serialiser.**

## 2026-09-06 · CR-068 WAVE J — WHAT A BROWSER SAW ON THE FINAL BILL, AND THE THREE THINGS THIS LANE DELIBERATELY DID NOT FIX (`2.197.11`)

The wave J walkthrough (`cr068-j-self-read-and-final-bill.mjs`) is on disk and
green. Five defects came out of it. **Two were fixed here and three were left,
and the reasons for leaving them are the part worth recording** — each is a
place where the rules ran out and a judgment was made rather than a rule
applied.

### 1 · The fixture sets a deposit-interest rate, on purpose

The seeded tenant pays **0%**, so `deposit_interest_accrued` returns a real
`$0.00` and `settle_account` never exercises the accrual at all. The decision
row of 2026-09-04 (`DEF-CWP-3842`) already records that and quotes the fixture's
answer as `−$86.60` rather than the story's `−$89.80`. **That is precisely the
branch that row also records as having no test through the door the product
uses** — billing's own suite covered `settle_account` only on accounts holding
NO deposit.

So `cr068-j-fixture.py` sets `billing-defaults.deposit_interest_rate_annual` to
**2**, through `save_settings_family` with a real System Admin actor, and the
engine answered **`$16.50`** on `$150.00` held since 4 March 2021 to a move-out
of 17 September 2026. The screen then printed
**`$63.40` − `$150.00` − `$16.50` = `−$103.10`**.

⚠ **THE WALKTHROUGH ASSERTS THE ARITHMETIC AND NEVER THE LITERAL, AND THAT IS A
RULE RATHER THAN A STYLE.** `US-CWP-037` carries `golden_tests: []`, so `$89.80`
is a story's illustration and **not** a ❄️ frozen B4/B5 figure; the answer moves
with the tenant's rate, and a hard-coded `−$89.80` would be the walkthrough
asserting the engine's answer back at it. What must hold — and what is asserted,
on the rendered cells — is that the lines a customer can add up **do** add up to
the total printed under them.

### 2 · NOT FIXED: the arrears line (`DEF-CWP-4191`)

On the *you owe us* half the panel lists `$289.10` − `$150.00` − `$16.50` and
states **`$296.82`**. The `$174.22` difference is what the account already owed
before its final bill, because the deposit settles *"everything outstanding"* —
the PO's own words closing `OQ-158` on 2026-08-12 — and **no line on the screen
names it**.

`billing_seam.final_bill_for` serves both `service_charges` and `charges` and
warns in its own docstring that a screen given one of the two *"would either
hide the arrears or misname the service charge"*. The screen reads
`service_charges`. So the server needs no work at all.

**The judgment: this lane did not add the missing line.** The fix is a fourth
row whose LABEL is new customer-facing money copy, in eleven catalogues, under
B14 rule 35 (written in its own language, never translated from English).
Inventing that sentence is not a walkthrough lane's call — the same reasoning
`DEF-CWP-3986` used when it refused to build `WarningBar` with no stated copy,
and the same reason this lane did not invent a hold's wording either. What is
settled and written down is that the figure exists on the wire and the work is
one row plus one sentence.

### 3 · NOT FIXED: *Query this reading* on a refund bill (`DEF-CWP-4192`)

`Settlement.settled` is `path is not None or remainder == 0` and
`settle_account` picks the refund path automatically — *"nobody chooses whether
to give back money that is not theirs"*. So a *we owe you* bill is `settled`
from the instant it is first read, `query_reading_open` (`not settled`) is
false, and the control **can never draw on it**. Confirmed in a browser across
two accounts: CLOSED on the refund, OPEN on the owed.

Wireframe P18 draws *Query this reading* on the `$89.80` refund screen. **So the
drawing and the engine disagree about who gets a last chance to query a closing
reading, and the leaving customer who is OWED money is the one sent to the
telephone.**

**The judgment: this is a product decision and not a lane's.** Both readings are
defensible — the engine's *"the path is decided, so the account is closing"* and
the drawing's *"tell us now, while it is still cheap"* — and whoever owns
`BR-CWP-056` has to pick one. What a lane can settle is that they currently
disagree, which nothing had noticed, and **why nothing had**: the component test
proves the control renders by feeding it `path: "refund"` together with
`query_reading_open: true`, a pair the server cannot produce. Two green suites
describing opposite screens.

### 4 · NOT FILED: `We owe you -$103.10`

The screen prints the server's signed remainder under a sentence that already
carries the direction, so a customer reads *we owe you minus one hundred and
three dollars*. The drawing reads `We owe you $89.80`, positive.

`FinalBill.tsx` states the intent in its own docstring — *"a negative remainder
is drawn as we owe you `$89.80` by choosing a SENTENCE, never by stripping a
minus"* — and then prints the minus. **Recorded as a delta row and NOT filed as
a defect**, because the code's stated reason (the minus lets a customer check
the column) is a real argument and the drawing is evidence rather than law. It
is named here so the next person to read that docstring knows the code and the
comment disagree.

### 5 · The stale-question fan-out, done in full (`DEF-CWP-4194`)

`OQ-1393` was closed on 2026-09-04 and **six live sentences across two documents
still told a lane to stub against it** — the execution plan's story list, its
demo script step 5, its exit test, its *Blocked by* line, task J1, and task J4;
plus four in `US-CWP-042`'s body, whose frontmatter had been correctly updated.
All ten are amended, dated, with the ruling quoted.

**The half that is real work, and it is not a documentation edit:** the ruling
requires a provenance flag on **every** customer reading — *"you will also ahve
to flag that this reading is reacievd from Cosnumer"* — and
`READ_SOURCES = ("ami", "manual", "import")` has no value for it. B2
`meter_source` names the same three. A customer's own reading is **not
`manual`**, which means a person the utility SENT. The catalogues already carry
`portal.readings.how.self_read` — *You sent it in* — in all eleven languages,
and a browser confirmed on 2026-09-06 that **no reading in this product can wear
it**.

## 2026-09-06 · Two rulings on the integrations / Runbooks boundary — a person's write stays with its screen, and the SAME job is also a batch, twice (`OQ-INT-1728` and `OQ-INT-1729` CLOSED)

**Both questions were minted earlier the same day**, when `BR-INT-054` was sharpened and
`CR-069` §20 classified all nineteen waves against it. Both were put to the Product Owner in
plain English with their figures, and both were ruled the same day. They are recorded here
verbatim, with the date, per the ratification rule — **a signature covers only what was
shown**, so what was shown is written out below rather than referred to by id.

### 1 · `OQ-INT-1728` — option (a), AND A SECOND REQUIREMENT ARRIVED WITH IT

**PO verbatim, 2026-09-06:**

> *"(a). Every other Runbooks example is a batch nobody is watching. Routing a form submit
> through a runbook to write one row while somebody waits is a different animal, and slower
> for no benefit. Keeps ~3 of wave M's 4 weeks here. - we provide both option schedule it as
> a batch job or you run it one time as a batch job"*

⚠ **THE CLAUSE AFTER THE DASH IS AN ADDITION, NOT A RESTATEMENT, AND IT IS THE PART A LANE
WILL MISS.** Everything before the dash answers the question that was asked. Everything after
it asks for something nobody had asked about — and it reads like a paraphrase of (a) because
it says *batch* twice. It is not. **(a) is about where a synchronous write LIVES; the second
clause is about what else must EXIST BESIDE IT.**

**WHAT (a) SETTLES.** A record update a person makes **synchronously on a screen, while they
wait**, stays with the module that owns the screen. It does not become Runbooks' work merely
because it writes a business record. `BR-INT-054`'s *record updates go to Runbooks* is read as
being about **unattended** processing — which is what every other example in the Runbooks
specification is: a nightly file, a reconcile, a night report. So wave `M`'s Create — Priya
types an address, the City answers in under a second, she picks a candidate and presses
**Create**, and a premises is written — is **integrations' work, stays here, and is not
blocked**.

**WHAT THE SECOND CLAUSE ADDS.** The same work must **also** be available as a batch, **in two
forms**: **scheduled**, and **run once, on demand**. One job therefore has **three ways to do
it**, and a lane builds all three rather than choosing one:

| | The way | Whose |
|---|---|---|
| **1** | the person's synchronous write on the screen, while they wait | **the screen's module** — this is what (a) rules |
| **2** | the same work **scheduled** as a batch job | **Runbooks** — scheduling is Runbooks' under `BR-INT-054` as amended 2026-09-06 |
| **3** | the same work run **once**, as a batch, started by a person | **split — and it is the one that reads two ways**: the trigger is the screen's, the running is Runbooks' |

⚠ **DO NOT COLLAPSE 2 AND 3 INTO ONE. The PO named both**, in one sentence — *"schedule it as
a batch job **or** you run it one time as a batch job"* — and a lane that builds a scheduler
and treats the on-demand case as "just running it early" has delivered half of what was asked
for.

**WHY ROW 3 SPLITS WHERE IT DOES, written down so nobody has to infer it: a person pressing
*Run it now* is TRIGGERING, not SCHEDULING.** Scheduling is deciding *when* — the beat, the
tenant's own midnight, the spread across three hundred utilities, the skip, the catch-up — and
that whole body of work moved to Runbooks on 2026-09-06. A button that starts one run decides
nothing about when; it is a person saying *now*. So the button, the screen it sits on and the
sentence the person reads afterwards belong with the screen, and the job it starts runs on
Runbooks' runner like any other job. **This is not a new distinction:** `BR-INT-054`'s own
amendment already says wave `H`'s sweep body is *"triggered by Runbooks' scheduler once `G`
moves — that is integrations work running on a shared clock, not a split of ownership."* This
is the same sentence with a person in the place of the clock.

**THE FIGURE, AND EXACTLY WHAT IT COUNTS.** Wave `M` is **four people-weeks** and (a) keeps
**roughly three of them with integrations** — that is the figure that was put to the PO and
the figure they ruled on. ⚠ **It counts row 1 only.** The two batch forms the second clause
requires are **not inside that number, are not sized anywhere in the plan, and are not
commissioned by this ruling.** Sequencing is unchanged: `CR-069` and Runbooks are taken
together after `CR-070` completes (PO, 2026-09-05). What this ruling changes is **who owns
each piece, and what the finished shape has to include** — not what anybody builds tomorrow.

### 2 · `OQ-INT-1729` — option (a): the lane stops at the door

**The Product Owner chose option (a): the lane stops at the door, and the record-marking waits
for Runbooks.** ⚠ **The words of the option are OURS, from the register — what the PO
supplied is the CHOICE.** It is recorded as a choice rather than dressed up as a quotation,
because a signature covers only what was shown and inventing a sentence for the PO is the
worst possible way to break that.

**What stays with integrations and is finished here:**

* **`F1`** — the hard timeout, the per-connection concurrency cap, the breaker, backoff with
  jitter, *Not working*. Connection lifecycle, unambiguously integrations', and **BUILT**.
* **`F2`(a) the send half** — per-item `execute()` results becoming the dispatcher's verdict
  through notifications' own service function. **BUILT**, and now behind `F1`'s guard.
* **`F2`(b) the feedback door** — `POST /integrations/webhooks/{key}` and the pipeline
  *authenticate → dedupe → reply at the declared position → persist raw*. That is **landing
  what arrives**, which the sharpened `BR-INT-054` keeps here in as many words. It **stays,
  and it is finished here.** ⚠ It is **NOT started**: `apps/integrations/inbound.py` is
  still wave B's stub raising `NotImplementedError("US-INT-044")`.

**What is NOT built now, and waits for Runbooks:** marking notification queue rows
`delivered` / `bounced` with the provider's own sentence, and feeding the suppression list
`J17` expects. Those are record updates on another module's rows, and the sharpened
`BR-INT-054` puts them on the Runbooks side.

⚠ **NOTHING IS WASTED BY STOPPING, AND THAT IS THE REASON THIS ANSWER WAS CHEAP: THAT HALF WAS
NEVER STARTED.** The question read like a collision — change process step 4, in-flight work
against a changed rule — but the collision was with a **plan**, not with code. No line is
deleted, no test is discarded, and no shipped behaviour changes. It is recorded because the
next reader will assume that stopping a live lane cost something, and here it cost nothing.

**`F3`, `F5` and `F6` are unstarted, and each was checked against the line rather than
assumed:**

* **`F3` — mostly integrations', and part of it is already done.** The `S8` card, the `S142`
  breaker note (*Not working · the mail server is not answering*) and the skipped-window row
  are a connection's own health and stay; the `last_test_text` half landed on 2026-09-05. The
  delivery dashboard's ***not reported*** is read off the **manifest** — whether the provider
  declares a feedback operation at all — so it is connection-level and stays too. ⚠ **What
  cannot be built yet is the delivered/bounced COUNTS behind it**, because nothing will mark a
  row until Runbooks exists — and `BR-INT-027` already makes that screen correct without them:
  the absence is words, forever, and never `0`. **The rule written for honesty is what lets
  the wave stop cleanly.**
* **`F5` — buildable whole.** Every step of `cr069-f-dead-mail-server.mjs` is the breaker, the
  skip row, the send count and the *not reported* string. None of it needs a marked row.
* **`F6` — and this is the one worth a human's eye.** `F6` closes **phase 2** on six stories,
  and `US-INT-023` **can no longer be completed here**: its feedback half is now Runbooks'.
  **This lane's judgment, recorded rather than put back to the PO (law 13): phase 2 closes
  with `US-INT-023` delivered TO THE BOUNDARY and the remainder named in the story**, rather
  than phase 2 being held open indefinitely for work that has deliberately moved to a project
  with no home in this repository yet. It is a planning consequence of the ruling, not a fact
  only the PO holds — but it is flagged here and in the plan, because a phase closing on a
  story that is half-elsewhere is exactly what reads as drift six weeks later.

### 3 · What this lane did NOT do, and what it found on the way

**No code.** No batch runner was built, wave `F`'s code was not touched, and wave `M` was not
started. `OQ-INT-1727` — the shipped work now on the Runbooks side, waves `C` and `D`, about
three people-weeks with screen **S143** live at `2.131.0` — **stays OPEN**. It was not put to
the PO here, and no lane may answer it by choosing.

**The fan-out, because closing a question is not a status edit.** Both rulings were walked
across every surface in one commit: the register row's **status AND its body**, this log, the
integrations module's `02-business-rules.md` (`BR-INT-054`), `CR-069` §20.4 · §20.5 · §20.7,
the execution plan's §0a · wave `F` · wave `M` · §5 · §8.2 · §8.3, `05-user-stories.md`, and
the two epics whose stories the rulings bound — `EP-INT-06` (`US-INT-023`) and `EP-INT-12`
(`US-INT-042`).

⚠ **AND THE WALK FOUND A STALE CITATION WITH NOTHING TO DO WITH EITHER RULING: `OQ-INT-1471`
WAS CLOSED ON 2026-09-04** — *"(b) type it, marked unchecked"* — **and `EP-INT-12` §8 still
listed it as `OPEN`, while `05-user-stories.md` still carried `US-INT-042` as *blocked* on
it.** The register's status column and two module documents had disagreed for two days, which
is the exact shape the prime directive warns about: a lane briefed from that epic would have
stubbed a branch the PO has already ruled is a **build**. Both are corrected in this commit.
**The lesson is the one already written down — closing a question is a fan-out — and it is
recorded again because the miss was found by walking somebody else's question, not by any
gate.**


## 2026-09-06 · CR-069 wave I — where the boundary actually fell, and four judgments made on the way

**The wave is the worked case of the 2026-09-06 boundary sharpening** (`BR-INT-054` as
amended, `CR-069` §20.4), so the split was ruled before the lane started and none of these
four is a question. They are recorded because the rules ran out at each of them and the next
agent would otherwise re-decide them differently.

**1 · THE IDEMPOTENCY KEY IS (tenant, connection, content-hash) — THE CONNECTION IS IN IT.**
`BR-INT-020` C says *"content hash computed BEFORE parse (file in)"* and stops there; it does
not say what the hash is scoped to. Two bank connections at one utility — Chase lockbox and
BofA lockbox — can each receive a file with byte-identical content, and **neither should
refuse the other's**: they are different relationships with different banks, and a lockbox
file that happens to collide is not a duplicate of anything. Scoping to the connection also
means a utility that re-connects the same bank starts a fresh history, which is the same
answer `US-INT-010` gives for the connection's own lifecycle. **Worked figure: Chase sends a
40-row file; BofA sends the identical 40 rows; both are ACCEPTED, and a second Chase copy is
refused.** Asserted in `test_tc6_two_banks_at_one_utility_do_not_refuse_each_other`.

**2 · A REFUSED DUPLICATE CLOSES `skipped`, AND THE RUN ROW IS WRITTEN BEFORE THE VERDICT.**
`skipped` is *we did not ask* (`BR-INT-024`), and it is right here: nothing was parsed and
nothing was handed on. The ordering matters more than the word. `record_arrival` opens the
run row **before** it asks whether the file is a duplicate, so **a duplicate that arrives is
still recorded as an arrival** — a utility asking *did Wednesday's upload reach you at all*
is owed a row that says yes. Refusing before recording would make the second arrival
invisible, which is the failure `US-INT-033` names.

**3 · TESTABILITY IS A FACT ABOUT THE CONNECTION, AND THE MANIFEST CANNOT SAY SO.**
`BR-INT-019` says a provider with no safe instance declares it in its manifest
(`Operation.test_action = None`). The bank card breaks that in half: over **SFTP** it has a
perfectly good safe instance — list one folder — and over **upload** it has none at all,
because there is no folder to list. A manifest is data read once at `AppConfig.ready()` and
cannot branch on a connection's config field. **The manifest therefore keeps its
`test_action` (the SFTP case, the one that CAN be tested) and the adapter answers an upload
connection honestly with `ok=false` *Nothing to test until first use.*** This is not a gap in
`BR-INT-019` so much as a case the rule did not reach; it is written here rather than left
for the next reader to rediscover from the code.

**4 · `test()` REFUSES RATHER THAN PRETENDS WHEN NO SFTP CLIENT IS INSTALLED.** There is no
SFTP library on this deployment, so `FOLDER_CLIENT` is unbound. `test()` answers `ok=false`
*No folder client is installed.* — it does **not** return a green result it has not earned.
`BR-INT-019` was written against exactly this temptation (*"I have seen this method built as
'does the API key parse' more times than any other mistake in this space"*), and a `test()`
reporting success because it never dialled is that mistake wearing better manners. The gap is
recorded in `cr069-i-same-file-twice.mjs` through `lib/knownGaps.mjs`, so it goes red in BOTH
directions: install a client and leave the sentence, and the walkthrough fails for being
stale.

### What the build found, and one of them would have shipped broken

⚠ **`finish_run` WOULD HAVE ERASED THE HASH IT WAS REFUSING ON.** The argument was
`input_hash: str | None = None` and it was assigned unconditionally. All five runners in the
module omit it, so closing an arrival's run row set the column back to NULL — and **the next
arrival of the same file would have found nothing to match.** The duplicate refusal would
have been incapable of firing, with every test in the repository green. A `KEEP` sentinel now
distinguishes *not supplied* from *deliberately null*.

⚠ **AND SABOTAGING IT TAUGHT SOMETHING WORTH MORE THAN THE FIX.** Breaking only the
ASSIGNMENT left all thirteen cases GREEN — `finish_run` saves with `update_fields`, the
column was not in the list, and the blanked value never reached the database. **There are two
halves to that guard and `update_fields` is the deciding one.** Breaking both — the original
form — fails two cases, and the second is the one that matters: `FAILED
test_tc4_the_same_file_twice_is_refused_naming_the_first_by_date`. Written into the test's
docstring so the next lane sabotages the half that decides.

⚠ **A CHECK WRITTEN THIS SAME HOUR WAS LOOKING AT THE WRONG THING.** The boundary test
grepped `arrivals.py` for `stage_import` — which its **docstring names**, because explaining
where the boundary falls is what that docstring is for. It walks the AST now and asks whether
the module IMPORTS the processing half. Prose cannot trip it and an import cannot hide from
it.

⚠ **THE WALKTHROUGH COULD ONLY EVER HAVE PASSED ONCE.** It posted a FIXED file, and the
product's guarantee is that the same bytes are refused forever — so its second run read `409`
where it expected `201` and every later assertion drifted onto rows the first run had left
behind. That is not flakiness; it is a check that is true once and false after, which is
worse than one that fails. The file now carries the run's own stamp in its header, and the
refused row is found **by its trace id** rather than by being the first `skipped` row on the
screen.

### Two live screen defects, both older than this wave

**`skipped` was missing from the frontend's `RunOutcome` union while the server had been
sending it since wave `F1`'s breaker.** A word the server can send and the client's type does
not know is **not a type error anywhere** — the value simply arrives, every branch falls
through to its default, and the screen renders whatever the default happens to be. It
rendered **`0 of 0`**: a perfectly formatted lie for a run nothing was attempted on. The
catalogue key was missing too, so the raw enum word `skipped` reached a clerk in all eleven
languages (B14 rule 32). Both fixed here; the run's list cell reads *Not attempted*.

### Where the plan blurs the boundary, said out loud rather than quietly crossed

**The plan's `I1` cell contradicts its own wave heading.** `I1` reads *"→ the bytes handed to
`apps.payments.payment_import.stage_import / commit_batch` through `seams/payments.py` … the
run's counts (`899 / 1 / 0`) and a receipt artifact naming row 412"* — and the heading four
lines above it, together with `CR-069` §20.4, assigns **every one of those clauses to
Runbooks**. `I1` predates the 2026-09-06 sharpening and was never rewritten. **It was not
followed**, and a test now walks `arrivals.py`'s AST so the line cannot be re-crossed
quietly. The same is true of `I2`'s S38 and S35, which are screens over the processing half.

## 2026-09-06 · THE IDEAL CUSTOMER PROFILE MOVES FROM "UNDER 3,000 CONNECTIONS, 1–2 STAFF" TO ELEVEN SERVICES AND 80,000–100,000 ACCOUNTS (PO ruling · `2.199.0`)

⚠ **SUPERSEDED THE SAME HOUR, BEFORE ANYTHING WAS BUILT FROM IT — SEE THE ROW "THE ICP, CORRECTED THE SAME HOUR" BELOW.** The figure in this row — **80,000–100,000 accounts** — **IS WRONG.** It was read from a first, garbled statement of the profile; the PO restated it in full and the real ruling is **North American utilities up to 40,000 accounts (tiers T7/T6/T5) with 10–20 staff**. Two of the three consequences this row reasons about are withdrawn with it: the **capacity model needs no re-run** (40,000 is exactly the top of T5 and is already the largest tenant `B6` models), and the **staffing question is answered, not open** (10–20 staff, ruled). The **eleven-services assumption stamped below is withdrawn too** — the corrected ruling says nothing about service counts, so there was never anything to assume. **Nothing was edited from this row: no document, no epic, no defect and no code.** It is kept, with this banner, because deleting it would hide that the misreading happened at all.

**The ruling, verbatim, and it is the whole of what was said:**

> *"I want you to change the defination of ICP - we will use this applciation for Utilities
> having upto 1 utiltieis servie we supposert and accoutns uptpt 80k to 100K"*

**The new profile, as this repo will now state it:** a utility taking **up to eleven of the
utility services this platform supports**, with **up to 80,000–100,000 accounts**.

**What it supersedes:** *"small utilities/submetering, under 3,000 connections, 1–2 staff"* —
`CLAUDE.md` line 3, both READMEs, `B1` §1, `B2`'s sizing note, `B6`'s planning table and
`09-infra`'s orientation. That sentence had been the product's stated market since the first
commit and is cited by roughly forty backend and front-end docstrings as the reason a list is
unpaginated, a sort happens in Python, or a set is built in memory. **Those citations are now
standing on a number that no longer exists**, which is recorded as a defect below rather than
edited here.

### ⚠ ONE WORD IS AN ASSUMPTION AND IT IS STAMPED AS ONE, NOT BURIED

*"upto 1 utiltieis servie we supposert"* is read as **ELEVEN** — the number of services this
platform supports — and **that reading is this lane's, not the PO's.** The message carries
four other typos in two lines (*uptpt*, *supposert*, *accoutns*, *defination*), so a dropped
numeral is much the likeliest explanation, and the alternative reading — a utility taking
**one** service — would contradict three things ratified within the last five days: the
eleven-service seed order, `CR-063`, and the real utility being onboarded on **Fire** as the
eleventh service. A single-service ICP would also make the eleven-service sign-up tick-list
and `SignupWizard.test.tsx`'s assertion of eleven pointless.

**It is recorded as OPEN TO CORRECTION.** If the PO meant something else, the correction costs
one sentence here and a re-run of the same fan-out; nothing was built on it. **No code
behaviour anywhere depends on this reading** — it is a sentence about who we sell to.

### THE THREE CONSEQUENCES, NAMED RATHER THAN QUIETLY ABSORBED

**1 · The public Pricing page now contradicts the product's own stated market, and the numbers
that would fix it belong to the PO alone.** Three live tier lines in **eleven locale
catalogues** say *"Up to 300 active connections"* (`public.plan.starter.f1`), *"Up to 1,000"*
(`growth`) and *"Up to 3,000"* (`scale`), at $1,000 / $5,000 / $8,000 a month
(`04-docs/01-spec/13-copy-and-microcopy.md`, seeded by
`tenancy/migrations/0005_seed_subscription_plans.py`). **A prospect with 80,000 accounts reads
a Scale tier that stops at 3,000 and concludes the product is not for them.** These are
commercial figures — `NFR-5` already says connection counts are *"commercial only"* and never
technical ceilings — so **not one of them has been touched.** Filed as `DEF-TEN-4222`: three
numbers are needed from the PO, and until they arrive the page is wrong on the most public
screen the product has.

**2 · The capacity model does not cover a 100,000-account tenant, and this lane did not re-run
it.** `B6`'s capacity math (PO-directed 2026-08-08) models 1,000 utilities as
`800 × 100 + 180 × ~4,000 + 20 × 40,000` accounts — **1.6M platform-wide, ≈2.7B rows over
three years**, with `journal_lines` the largest table and `NFR-24` requiring partitioning above
50M rows/yr. Its own planning-table correction states *"max observed tenant size for design =
**40,000 accounts**"*. **The new profile is 80,000–100,000 — two to two-and-a-half times the
largest tenant ever modelled**, and `journal_lines` grows at ~18 rows per account per month, so
the largest table scales with exactly the number that moved. **The arithmetic was deliberately
NOT re-run here**, because `NFR-27` already sets the precedent that re-running this math
requires **Eng-Lead sign-off** (it does so for the AMI gate, for a 30–60× read volume). Filed
as `DEF-TEN-4217`.

**3 · "1–2 staff" is now false, and it is a different question from the other two.** A utility
with 100,000 accounts does not run on one or two people. This is NOT the same as the portal
concurrency amendment: `NFR-38` (PO, 2026-09-03) already moved the PLATFORM's concurrency
assumption to *"500 concurrent portal users spread across many tenants"* while explicitly
holding that *"the old 1–2 staff per tenant line stays true of STAFF"*. **That last clause is
what this ruling breaks** — the staff figure itself, not the portal figure. `B6`'s planning
table still reads *"Concurrency | low (1–2 staff/tenant)"*, and the sentence is cited in
`ledger/services.py` and `PlanWizard.tsx` as the reason a screen is honest at tens of rows and
not at hundreds. **`NFR-38` is EXTENDED rather than contradicted**, and no concurrency number
is invented: the staff figure is marked superseded-and-unquantified, because what replaces it
is a fact only the PO or ops holds. Filed as `DEF-TEN-4218`.

### THE GOOD NEWS, VERIFIED RATHER THAN ASSUMED — AND THE ONE PLACE IT IS NOT TRUE

**Nothing structural blocks this, and each claim was read before it was repeated:**

* **`NFR-5`** — *"No hard per-tenant account/connection caps anywhere (design rule above;
  connection counts commercial only)"*. Confirmed at `06-non-functional-requirements.md:34`.
* **The design rule under the planning table** — *"no table, index, or code path may enforce a
  maximum account count per tenant"*. Confirmed at line 24.
* **The planning table's own connections row** already read *"~5,000 and above — indicative,
  **not** a hard cap"*. Confirmed at line 9.

**So the architecture never assumed 3,000, and this ruling breaks no schema, index or cap.**
That is stated wherever this edit lands, because a reader meeting a large jump in the stated
market will otherwise assume the worst.

⚠ **BUT `NFR-3` IS A DIFFERENT MATTER, AND IT IS THE FINDING THIS LANE DID NOT EXPECT.**
`NFR-3` says *"Server pagination universal; NO unbounded list endpoints"* — and **at least
four shipped endpoints are deliberately unpaginated, each citing the 3,000 ceiling BY NAME as
its justification**: `GET /outstandings` (*"Unpaginated ON PURPOSE, and the reason is the
product's own ceiling"*), `GET /cheques`, the bank-reconciliation batch list, and their two
front-end mirrors. Worse, `payments/outstandings.py`'s own header records exception (6):

list is bounded by the debtor count"***. **These are not sentences — they are behaviour whose
correctness argument was the ICP.** One row per debtor at 3,000 connections is a screen; at
100,000 accounts it is an unbounded list sorted in application memory on every request. Filed
as `DEF-PAY-4219`, **high**. No backend code was touched by this lane.

### WHAT WAS EDITED, AND WHAT WAS DELIBERATELY LEFT ALONE
