carry a period as its unit"*. `ton-hr` is an ENERGY — a ton of cooling delivered for an
hour — so leaving it would quote a price per ton-hour against a quantity measured in
connected tons. That is `DEF-497` on a live money path.

`BR-TEN-171` goes **59 → 64**: the three `TH-CW-*` ranges are WITHDRAWN and eight
connected-tonnage capacities take their place — `TH-T5` `TH-T10` `TH-T25` `TH-T50`
`TH-T100` `TH-T200` `TH-T400` `TH-T800`, in `ton`. `capacity_uom_for_service
("thermal_heat")` answers `"ton"`, so **thermal SUMS like solar rather than counting
like trash**: a building with a 100-ton and a 25-ton connection is **125 tons**.

Fixture `V2.48.0.10 → V2.48.0.11`. `uoms` 27 → 28 with `ton`. Migration
`tenancy/0043_cr080_thermal_capacity_basis.py`, DATA ONLY.

### 2 · THE MEASUREMENT, RE-RUN BEFORE MIGRATING RATHER THAN QUOTED FROM THE CR

On a seeded development database at the tip: every `tenant_services` row for
`thermal_heat` is **`metered`** and **`enabled = false`**, with **0 thermal service
points, 0 thermal assets and 0 thermal invoice lines**. **Nothing bills thermal, so no
customer is re-billed and no issued invoice is contradicted** — CLAUDE.md hard rule 4
is not engaged because there is nothing issued to engage it. That is the cheapest this
change will ever be, and it is the argument for doing it now.

### 3 · NO ❄️ FROZEN FIGURE MOVES — CHECKED, NOT ASSUMED

`04-docs/02-decisions/04-money-math-rules.md` contains **no thermal figure at all**.
B5's only mention of `thermal_heat` is the revenue-account addendum — account **4170**,
a GL designation and not an amount. **`GT-1`–`GT-61` price no thermal line.** So this
needs no finance re-sign under HUMAN-GUIDE §6. The check was run rather than inherited
from the CR row, because *"checked, not assumed"* is what the CR asked for.

### 4 · JUDGMENT 1 — THE PER-TON RATE, `$12.5000` PER CONNECTED TON PER MONTH

⚠ **THIS RETIRES A FIGURE THE PRODUCT OWNER PERSONALLY APPROVED, WHICH IS THE PART
THAT NEEDED WRITING DOWN.** `METERED_USAGE_PRICES["thermal_heat"] = "0.0450"` —
`$0.045` per ton-hour — was put to the PO in plain English with a worked figure and
approved (`CR-062` E6, step 5 judgment 3). **A capacity service has no ton-hour**, so
it has nothing left to multiply.

⚠ **THE MAP IS NOT LEFT EMPTY, AND THE REASON IS A COLLISION WORTH RECORDING.** A
sibling lane seeded **`gas` at `$1.15` per `ccf`** into this same map **hours earlier
the same day** (`DEF-RAT-4516`, closing `OQ-1290`), on the PO's *"please fix this gap -
One real gap, and it is money. Gas bills $0.00 usage"*. The two changes are
independent and both stand, and the map's own rule is what decides it: it holds a flat
price for a **metered** service, so gas belongs there and thermal no longer does. **A
first draft of this CR asserted the map would be empty; that assertion would have gone
red on a sibling's correct change**, which is law 11's *"read the failures you did not
cause"* arriving from the other side. ⚠ And their decision row's worked figure —
*"Thermal on the same estate billed 30,000 × $0.045 = $1,350.00"* — is retired by this
one; it was true when it was written that morning.

**The delegation this replacement is authored under, PO verbatim:** *"you can research
in amrket at Municiapl utility in north amrica and put it there"*.

**What the research found, with the utility and the year on each figure:**

| Utility | Kind | Figure | Year |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Lansing Board of Water & Light**, Lansing MI, Rate CW1 Commercial Chilled Water | municipal | Contract Demand **`$50.00` per ton** (Excess Demand `$70.00` above 105% of contract); commodity `$0.15469` per ton-hour; **the Capacity Charge IS the minimum monthly charge** | FY2024-25, effective 2024-10-01 (`$49.49`/`$69.30` in FY2023-24) |
| **City of Mesa, Arizona**, District Cooling | municipal | a monthly capacity charge per **Rated-Ton** plus a per **Ton-Hour** energy rate; a Ton-Hour is defined as **12,000 BTU** and a Rated-Ton as the building's cooling need from square footage and anticipated usage | FY2024/25 and FY2025/26 rate books |
| **District Energy St. Paul**, Minnesota | district energy | demand is the building's peak capacity **in tons**; demand charges recover infrastructure and O&M, energy charges recover production | current |
| **JEA**, Jacksonville FL, District Energy System Tariff | municipal | the demand charge is set on **tons of billable demand** to recover debt service and capital renewal | current |

⚠ **WHY `$50.00` IS NOT COPIED ACROSS, AND THIS IS THE WHOLE JUDGMENT.** Lansing bills
its `$50.00` on **Billing Demand — *"the maximum instantaneous demand (tons) supplied
during the billing period"*** — a MEASURED monthly peak, which in a Michigan January is
near zero. **The PO's model is Mesa's**: a charge on CONNECTED tonnage, twelve months a
year, whatever the weather. A rate levied every month on installed capacity must be
well below one levied on a summer peak, or the same building pays several times more
for the same service. Taking a Great Lakes cooling season as roughly three
full-equivalent months of billed peak out of twelve: **`$50.00 × 3 ÷ 12` = `$12.50` per
connected ton per month**, i.e. `$150` per ton-year, which sits inside the ordinary
North American municipal district-cooling capacity band.

⚠ **WHAT COULD NOT BE VERIFIED, STATED RATHER THAN SMOOTHED OVER.** The Lansing and
Mesa rate PDFs are both refused by this environment's network egress policy — `WebFetch`
answers `EGRESS_BLOCKED` and a direct `curl` gets `CONNECT tunnel failed, response 403`
— so the `$50.00`, the `$49.49` and the Ton-Hour definition are quoted from search
results rather than read off the tariff. **The STRUCTURE — a monthly per-ton capacity
charge on connected tonnage — is corroborated by four independent North American
municipal utilities. The exact cent is one utility's, read at one remove.** A later
lane with network access should open the two PDFs and either confirm or correct this
row; that is cheaper than re-deriving it.

**Worked, on the PO's own two numbers:** a **100-ton** connection bills `100 ×
$12.5000` = **`$1,250.00`** a month; a **200-ton** connection bills **`$2,500.00`**; a
building with a 100-ton and a 25-ton connection is **125 tons** = **`$1,562.50`**.

### 5 · JUDGMENT 2 — THE EIGHT TONNAGES, AND THE REFRIGERATION-TON READING

The PO named two values and invited the rest: *"i will ahve 100 tonne or 200 tonne
etc"*. The ladder doubles from a small commercial bay (5 tons) to a hospital plant
(800 tons), which is how equipment catalogues are actually shaped, and **25 and 100 are
deliberately kept** because they were the boundaries of the three withdrawn ranges — a
tenant reading its own list sees the numbers it already had, now as capacities it can
multiply.

⚠ **WE READ *"tonne"* AS THE REFRIGERATION TON (12,000 BTU/hr), NOT THE METRIC
TONNE.** The reading is recorded in the CR row, in `BR-TEN-171`, in the code and here,
so the PO can correct it in one word. The evidence: the three withdrawn size classes
already said *"tons"* (*"Thermal chilled water ≤25 tons"*), and the City of Mesa's own
district-cooling rate book defines a Ton-Hour as 12,000 BTU and bills on a
*"Rated-Ton"*. **If they meant 1,000 kg of anything, the ladder and the price move and
nothing else does.**

**Neither the eight nor the `$12.50` is a ratified figure.** They are seeded DEFAULTS a
tenant edits on Settings → Service sizes — the same posture as fire's six, which are
still `OQ-1360` — and no screen, document or report may present them as anybody's
tariff.

### 6 · JUDGMENT 3 — `klb` STAYS, AND `OQ-560` IS UNTOUCHED

`OQ-560` — thermal STEAM's bands — **stays OPEN**, and `steam_size_classes()` still
raises. `klb` (thousand pounds of steam) keeps the ALT slot of
`SERVICE_DEFAULT_UOMS["thermal_heat"]` because it is the unit of the half of thermal
that question governs; dropping it would leave the map silent about steam, which reads
like steam was settled.

⚠ **AND THE HAZARD THE CR WARNED ABOUT DOES NOT HOLD, WHICH IS WORTH RECORDING BECAUSE
THE NEXT LANE TO MOVE A UNIT WILL HIT THE SAME QUESTION.** The CR warned that
`_derive_uom_service_scope()` derives a unit's service scope FROM
`SERVICE_DEFAULT_UOMS`, so dropping `klb` there would *"silently rescope a catalogue
entry"*. **It cannot — for `klb` or for `ton-hr`.** `_seed_uoms` resolves a row as
`stated or SEEDED_UOM_SERVICE_SCOPE.get(code)`, and **both units STATE `"service":
"thermal_heat"` in `lookup_defaults.json`**, where the fixture wins. So `ton-hr` leaves
the map, keeps its stated scope, and `BR-TEN-071` deletes it from nobody: a utility
that meters chilled-water energy still has the unit to pick. `klb` is kept anyway, so
the derived and the stated statements still agree in both directions.
`test_cr080_thermal_capacity.py` asserts the finding so it survives this session.

### 7 · JUDGMENT 4 — THE TONNAGE IS A UNIT FACT, NOT A DEVICE

`connections.UNIT_CAPACITY_CHARACTERISTIC` gains `"thermal_heat": "connected_capacity"`,
so thermal is the **second** service whose capacity is recorded on the unit rather than
carried by installed equipment. The reason is storm water's own: **nobody installs a
ton.** A connected tonnage is the size of the building's SERVICE CONNECTION; the
chiller is the utility's, in the plant, serving hundreds of buildings, and a basement
heat exchanger is not sized per customer in anything this product records.

**Route thermal down the equipment path instead and the failure is silent:**
`billable_asset_size_classes` returns an empty list on every unit,
`total_installed_capacity` sums to `0`, and every thermal line prints **`$0.00`** on a
document that foots perfectly. That is `DEF-2388` exactly, one service over, and no
gate in this repo can see it.

**It is the only capacity service that is unit-recorded AND sums.** Storm water is
unit-recorded and has one assessment per unit; solar, battery and broadband sum but ask
the equipment; trash and fire count. Unlike storm water, **nothing is divided**: an ERU
is assessed on a PREMISES and spread across its units because hard surface belongs to
the property, while a chilled-water connection is made to a UNIT and is that unit's
whole capacity.

### 8 · THE SEEDED ESTATE, AND WHAT A THERMAL CUSTOMER'S BILL LOOKS LIKE NOW

**Before:** 48 `TH-5000…TH-5047` meters, an opening read and three months of readings,
scaled by `CONSUMPTION_SCALE["thermal_heat"] = 500` into ~4,500 ton-hours a month at
`$0.045` — about `$202.50` on the reference customer.

**After:** a service point per unit with its connected tonnage recorded on it. 45
houses at 5 tons (`$62.50`), **two commercial units at 100 tons (`$1,250.00` — the PO's
own figure)**, the municipal depot at **200 tons (`$2,500.00` — their other one)**, the
mill at 400 tons (`$5,000.00`), and one unit deliberately unconnected so `BR-MET-108`'s
ruled **`$0.00`** stands beside real numbers on a real document. **1,025 connected tons
= `$12,812.50` a month**, before `BR-RAT-101`'s outside-city 1.5x reaches two of the
houses.

`SERVICE_METER_PREFIX`, `CONSUMPTION_SCALE`, `METERED_USAGE_PRICES`, `BACKBONE_BASE`,
`SEASONAL_SHAPE` and the per-class band map each lost their thermal entry in the same
commit. `BASE-TH` moved from `BACKBONE_BASE_CODE` to `CAPACITY_BASE_CODE` **with its
letters unchanged**, exactly as `BASE-SW` did on 2026-09-02 — `create_charge` is
idempotent on `code`, so minting a new one would leave every existing tenant holding
both, and its ABSENCE from the capacity map is what cost fire a whole tenant's billing
on 2026-09-02 (`DEF-3087`).

### 9 · ONE THING FOUND THAT THIS CR DID NOT GO LOOKING FOR

`07-frontend/e2e/CR-004-reference-crud.spec.ts` had been **missing fire's six `FL-*`
codes since 2026-09-02**: its per-list count assertion read **53** where the fixture
held **59**. This lane had to touch that array for its own three codes and could not
leave a count it knew to be wrong, so all six are added and the array is now 64 and
byte-for-byte the fixture's.

**That is `DEF-971` recurring exactly as that defect predicted** — *"a test nobody runs
is a comment, and hard-won law 1 says a comment is never a guarantee"* — for the second
time, found the same way both times: a human opening the file for another reason.
`DEF-971` stays OPEN, and its own cheap remedy (a unit-level check that every literal
in this spec matches `lookup_defaults.json`, needing no browser and no server) is still
unbuilt and is still the thing that would have caught both.

### WHAT WAS DELIBERATELY NOT DONE

**`OQ-560` is not closed.** **No steam band is invented.** **No stored UoM is
backfilled** — a seeded default is never a backfill (`BR-TEN-1180` clause 6), so the
migration moves the basis and nothing else. **No new asset type was minted for a
thermal connection**, because recording the tonnage on the unit needs none, and minting
one would have answered `BR-AST-042`'s question inside a fix for a different one.


### 10 · WHAT THE BILL ACTUALLY READS, AFTER BOTH LANES OF THE DAY

Re-verified in a browser on a second seeded utility built from the MERGED code, because the first walkthrough predated a sibling's change by a few hours. A 5-ton house's June bill now reads:

```
Thermal / Heat                          2 lines      $82.50
  thermal_heat usage        5 ton  $12.5000        $62.50   4170 — Thermal/Heat
  thermal_heat base charge    —        —           $20.00   4170 — Thermal/Heat
```

⚠ **THE `$20.00` IS NOT THIS CR'S AND IT SURVIVED THE MOVE BY CONSTRUCTION, WHICH IS THE PART TWO LANES CROSSING ON ONE DAY COULD EASILY HAVE LOST.** A sibling researched a municipal monthly base for thermal under the same PO delegation hours before this CR moved the service off the metered path — and `capacity_base_charge_codes` and `capacity_plan_services` BOTH call `service_base_amounts.base_for(code, fixture.CAPACITY_BASE)`, so the figure was picked up on the capacity path with no edit at all. **Had they read `fixture.CAPACITY_BASE` directly, a researched figure would have reverted to `$0.00` and no check in this repo would have said so.** `test_def2397` asserts it on the capacity path now.

The other observed figures: the outside-city houses bill **`$18.75` per ton** (`$12.50 × 1.5`, `BR-RAT-101`) for **`$93.75`** of usage, and on the first tenant `THERMAL_UNIT_WITH_NONE` billed `BR-MET-108`'s ruled **`$0.00`** beside them. Settings → Services & UoM reads **Thermal/Heat · On · Capacity · ton · klb**, and all eight tonnages are on the size list with all three `TH-CW-*` gone.
## 2026-09-07 — `CR-078` BUILT: THE LATE FEE COMES FROM THE PLAN'S CHARGE CODE, AND NO CODE MEANS ZERO

**PO ruling, verbatim (2026-09-07):** *"this is wrong - you ahve to take late fees form
charge code mentione din the plan - if plan doent provide you that charge code then you
have to put zero on late payment. - Logic aplplied ot Minimum late fee $5- - you can
link these defaults in Charge code - we have a charge code for late payment"*, and on
the ❄️ frozen figure: *"you capturd it correctly - please apply them - raise CR if
required"*. Finance re-signed the same day (`12-governance/09-human-review-ledger.md`).
Shipped as **2.228.0**. Rule: **`BR-RAT-1011`**.

### THE FIGURE DID NOT MOVE, AND THAT WAS CHECKED RATHER THAN ASSUMED

The seeded `LATE` charge code carries **1.5% with a $5.00 minimum** — the same two
figures the Billing-defaults screen holds — so the fee is the same whichever copy the
engine reads. Measured on the sample utility, a real account: **AC-2026-00050**,
invoice `BL-2608-000100`, **$5,247.31** overdue, six days past a five-day grace →
**$78.71** with the plan naming `LATE`, `max($5.00, 0.015 × 5,247.31)`. With the code
taken off that plan: **$0.00**, and no fallback.

`GT-8` and `GT-10`'s ❄️ **$8.13** is untouched, established by READING the tests
rather than by assuming: `tests/golden/test_gt08_late_fee.py` builds `PERCENT =
Decimal("0.015")` in Python and hands it straight to `assess_late_fee`, and
`tests/golden/conftest.py` hands GT-10 a `RatedLine(amount=Decimal("8.13"))`. **Neither
reads a database, a plan or a charge code**, and `assess_late_fee` itself is unchanged
byte for byte — the change is a layer above it. Re-run anyway: golden suite 23 passed
/ 1 xfailed, `03-golden-verify.py` 33 PASS 0 FAIL.

### THE ORDER WAS THE RISK, AND ONE STEP OF IT SILENTLY DID NOTHING

`rating/0026` adds the column; `rating/0027` fills it; only then does anything read it.

⚠ **THE FIRST BACKFILL WROTE NOTHING AND REPORTED `OK`.** It used a plain
`RatePlan.objects.filter(...).update(...)`, and `rate_plans` carries `FORCE ROW LEVEL
SECURITY` with the B2 §3 policy, so a migration — running with `app.tenant_id` at the
database default of all zeros — **cannot see one tenant row**. `manage.py migrate`
printed `Applying rating.0027… OK` over **eight seeded plans that stayed NULL**.
Nothing raised. That is `tenancy/0031`'s own warning in a second costume — *a green run
over an empty table is not evidence about a backfill* — except here the table only
LOOKED empty, and the consequence would have been every late fee on every live tenant
going to $0.00 while obeying the prescribed order perfectly.

**Found by doing what the CR said: proving it by query.** The fix is the shape
`assets/0011` and `assets/0003` already use — walk the tenants, `set_config
('app.tenant_id', …)` per tenant, one savepoint each (law 14), and **LOG THE COUNT**,
because a migration whose only output is `OK` cannot tell 8 rows from 0. Measured on
PostgreSQL 16, forward and reverse: **`pointed 27 rate plan(s)` across 9 tenants, 0
tenants left without a code**; `manage.py cr078_late_fee_codes` says the same from the
other side: `TOTAL: 27/27`.

### THREE ANSWERS, NOT TWO — THE JUDGMENT THIS LANE MADE AND WHY

The ruling reads *"if plan doent provide you that charge code"*, which presupposes a
plan. So a plan that **cannot be read at all** — an absent or malformed id, another
tenant's — is NOT the ruled zero; it is a data fault and it **REFUSES BY NAME**
(`late_fee.LateFeePlanUnreadable`, `decisions._late_fee_charge_id_for_plan`). Zero is
reserved for a plan that exists and names no live code, which is a thing a human at the
utility did.

**Collapsing those two was the whole danger.** An account whose plan cannot be read
could not have been priced either; answering "no late fee" for it would make it free
for the rest of its life with nothing going red — the same silent failure the CR's
ordering exists to prevent, reached from the other side.

### THE ZERO IS LAWFUL AND MUST NEVER BE INVISIBLE

Three things buy that back. (1) A NEW plan starts pointed at the tenant's seeded code
(`services.default_late_fee_charge`) — without it the backfill fixes today's plans and
every plan created tomorrow charges $0.00 with nothing raising, which is `CR-068` R3's
clock-in-a-rule shape. It is a default **on the plan**, visible and clearable, not the
engine fallback the PO rejected. (2) `selectors.plans_missing_late_fee_charge` and
`manage.py cr078_late_fee_codes` COUNT the plans in the zero state, per tenant.
(3) Gate **G121** fails on a non-empty count and refuses a re-introduced read of
`late_pct`/`late_min_amount` on the late-fee path. Both halves were proved RED through
`run_gates`' own entry point and then green again.

### WHAT WAS ALREADY BUILT AND IS NOW WRONG (change-process step 4)

`BR-BIL-075`'s TC-4 and TC-5 asserted that a tenant with no `LATE` code **REFUSES the
whole run by name**, with the reasoning *"dropping the fee is money the utility decided
to charge and never charged"*. That reasoning was right when the missing code meant the
fee could not be BOOKED; it is answered rather than ignored now, because the drop is
counted rather than silent. Both tests are amended IN PLACE with the old assertion
quoted in the docstring — `test_def_719_late_fee_charge_code.py` tc4/tc5 — rather than
deleted, so a later reader can see what was reversed and by which ruling.

### WHAT WENT BACK TO THE AGENDA RATHER THAN BEING DECIDED

**`OQ-RAT-1766`, OPEN.** `plan_penalty_rules.late_fee_pct` and `late_fee_min` are a
per-plan override of the tenant default and are **no longer read by the fee path**.
Whether they should still override the charge code was never put to the PO, and the
finance re-sign says in its own words that a fifth decision returns to the agenda. The
ruling was implemented literally — the charge code is the source — and the interaction
is raised, not guessed. The GRACE half (`grace_days`, `grace_mode`) is untouched and
still falls back to the tenant (`BR-BIL-008`/`BR-BIL-002`).

### PROVED BY CLICKING (the closure bar, PO 2026-08-18)

`10-scripts/cr078_late_fee_walkthrough.mjs`, against a built SPA on a real PostgreSQL:
sign in → plan editor step 6 → the **Late fee charge code** picker renders with the
label *"Late fee charge code"*, **29 options** of that utility's own codes, and the
empty one reading ***"No late fee on this plan"*** rather than a blank → clear it,
commit the wizard, the server serves `late_fee_charge: null` → put it back, it returns.

⚠ **AND THE WALKTHROUGH WAS WRONG TWICE BEFORE IT WAS RIGHT, BOTH TIMES IN THE
DIRECTION THAT MATTERS.** It first clicked a `role="tab"` that this screen does not
have, then bailed on hop 0 because `Continue` had not rendered yet — and both times it
reported ***"the control is not wired"*** over a control that was wired and three
clicks away. Then it clicked a save button beside the field, when `WizardFrame` commits
only from the final step, and truthfully reported that the server had not changed.
**A check whose failure mode is *I looked in the wrong place* is hard-won law 7's
`looking at the wrong thing`, produced by the check written to avoid it.** Each is
fixed with the reason written beside it in that file.

## 2026-09-07 · NOTHING IN THE DEMO HAS EVER REACHED `CLOSED`, AND THE DATE THE FIXTURE DECLARED IS ONE THE PRODUCT REFUSES

**How it was found.** The Product Owner asked whether `Active` was the right
status on an account. It was. Counting the rest of them on a freshly planted
`brazosbend` gave:

    69 Active · 1 Marked disconnect · 1 Pending activation · 1 Vacation hold
    0 Closed · 0 Disconnected
    select count(*) from accounts where closed_at is not null   →   0
    select count(*) from move_records where kind = 'move_out'   →   0

Two of the six seeded statuses are unreachable in the demo and they are
unreachable for different reasons. `Disconnected` is a known, documented gap:
`lookup_defaults.json`'s own comment says it is *"seeded as reference data ONLY"*
and names the two consequences that must be closed first. **`Closed` was nobody's
gap at all.** It is the TERMINAL state — the one the whole move-out flow exists to
arrive at, with a `Close out` button on the account screen pointing at it — and no
seeded tenant this product has ever planted has held a single account in it.

**IT IS NOT A PRODUCT DEFECT, AND THAT WAS WORTH ESTABLISHING BEFORE FIXING
ANYTHING.** `services.move_out` was driven against the real seeded estate, in a
transaction that was rolled back afterwards, on `AC-2026-00042` (unit
`SCW-U-042`, the fixture's own `CASE_MOVED_OUT`):

    move_out(actor, AC-2026-00042, {"moved_out_on": "2026-07-31"})
      → status  active/billable → closed/terminal
        closed_at        2026-07-31
        final_read_state due
        move record      MVO-26-0001   (the first this series has ever issued)
        letter           email_move_out_final, queued
        both July and June invoices untouched

Every column `BR-CUS-030` names is written. **Nothing had ever called it on the
demo estate.** `core/sample_fixture.account_plan()` has carried a `moved_out_on`
key on `CASE_MOVED_OUT` since the fixture was written and a grep over the whole
backend returns **the definition and no reader** — hard-won law 2 in data form.

**AND THE DATE THAT FIELD CARRIED IS ONE THE PRODUCT REFUSES.** The same probe
with the fixture's own literal:

    move_out(actor, AC-2026-00042, {"moved_out_on": "2026-07-15"})
      → BIZ-STATE customers.account.move_out_behind_issued_bill
        BR-BIL-004, issued_through 2026-07-31

This estate bills WHOLE MONTHS, and that account's July bill `BL-2608-000088`
covers 2026-07-01 → 2026-07-31. A move-out dated the 15th is a tenancy ending
behind a bill already issued for it, which is exactly what `US-CUS-005` TC-6
refuses — *"corrections route via J6, not move-out backdating"*.

**THE JUDGMENT, and it is ours rather than the PO's (law 13).** The move-out day
is now DERIVED — `fixture.move_out_on()` returns the last day of the last BILLED
period, which is **2026-07-31** today. Three things make that the only lawful
date rather than a compromise:

  * `BR-BIL-004` forbids anything earlier while July is issued;
  * `BR-CUS-056` — *"the outgoing account pays the move day"* — makes the July
    bill this tenancy's FINAL bill, with **nothing to prorate and nothing to
    reissue**, so CLAUDE.md hard rule 4 is not approached at all;
  * the month after it is the unbilled one the Product Owner runs, and the
    fixture's own August oddity already says the house is empty by then
    (*"the tenant's final bill was cut … and the meter has been standing still
    since"*).

It is derived and not typed because a literal is precisely what went wrong.

**WHAT WAS BUILT.** One new sample-data block,
`customers:seed_sample_move_out`, the twenty-seventh, placed **after**
`payments:seed_sample_cycle_collections` and before the payment-plan blocks. The
position is the feature: a closed account's behaviour class is not in
`OCCUPYING_BEHAVIOR_CLASSES`, so it leaves `accounts_in_cycle` and no bill run can
see it — put the block above either billing block and that account is billed
NEITHER month and the estate silently loses two bills. The block calls
`services.move_out` and nothing else; it never writes a status or a date directly,
because a seeder that did would put the demo in a state the product's own door had
never been asked to produce, which is the gap being closed.

**ONE ACCOUNT, NOT FIFTY**, and it keeps its unpaid bill. `_july_share_for` leaves
unit 41 unpaid (41 % 4 == 1), so the closed account carries **$139.72** still
owed. `BR-CUS-082` (CONFIRMED, PO 2026-08-24, *"(b) continue, ladder restarts"*)
rules that a debt surviving closure is still chased, and until now that ruling had
no worked case anywhere a person could open. Paying it off to make the demo tidy
would delete the only example of the rule.

**A SECOND THING WAS SILENTLY DOING NOTHING, AND THE SAME ABSENCE HID IT.**
`_seed_cr039_move_records` skips any account whose `closed_at` is NULL, and the
comment justifying its position said *"three of its five transfers COMMIT (which
closes their outgoing account)"*. **That stopped being true on 2026-09-01**, when
the PO ruled *"dont create new account - we reassing that account"* and
`commit_transfer` became `transfers.reassign_account`, which closes nothing and
asserts `"account_closed": False` on its own audit row. So the demo held ONE move
record, a move-IN, and the `MVO-` series had never issued a number. The comment is
corrected and the record now comes from `move_out` itself.

**WHAT NOBODY ASKED, WHICH IS THE PROCESS LESSON.** Every check on the status list
asks whether the six ROWS EXIST; none asks whether a row is ever ASSIGNED. The
seed count is compared against SEATS, not against STATES. `DEF-CUS-4628` records
it, and `tests/test_def_cus_4628_seeded_move_out.py` is the check that goes red if
the terminal state stops being reached.

## 2026-09-07 · `DEF-WRK-4518` — THE ORDER DETAIL RESOLVES ITS NUMBER ONCE, AND THE ROW AS FILED WAS HALF RIGHT

**Two defects were fixed and two more were filed. The correction to the row is the part
worth reading first, because a later lane will otherwise build from a claim that is not
true of the running product.**

### 1 · WHAT THE ROW SAID, AND WHAT WAS ACTUALLY ON SCREEN

`DEF-WRK-4518` as filed says the work-order detail *"loads NO data on any order"* and
that *"every field on the Overview tab renders an em-dash"*. Measured on 2026-09-07
against a real PostgreSQL and a real browser, on the branch tip `1c157a23`:

* **Opened by CLICKING a row — the screen worked.** Six requests, six `200`s, and the
  header drew `WO-0016 · Meter set · Queued · Planned · 14 Willow Bend`, with Type
  `Meter set` and Service `electric` on the Overview tab.
* **Opened at `/work/orders/WO-0016` — the screen was empty.** Fourteen routes,
  fourteen `404`s, a dash in every field, and **nothing on the page saying so.**

The cause of the difference is that **every producer of that address passes the UUID**
— `OrdersPage`'s eye (`workOrderDetailPath("", row.id)`), `NewOrderWizard`'s redirect,
and global search's `searchDestinations` — while the route parameter is spelled
`:orderNo`. So the parameter has always been NAMED after the number and always been
HANDED an id, and the filing lane reasonably built the address the parameter's name
promises.

**The remaining two dashes on that screen are honest and are not a defect.** `Raised by`
reads `row.source`, which is `null` on a seeded order, and `Template version` reads
`checklist.template_version`, which is `null` on an order with no template. The API was
asked directly and returns `null` for both.

### 2 · WHAT WAS BUILT — OPTION (b), AND THE REASONING HELD

The two options were (a) a by-number door on the whole route family, or (b) the page
resolves number → id once. **(b) was built**, and nothing in the code contradicted the
three reasons given for it: one new endpoint against fourteen changed ones; the URL
keeps a human reference; and a by-number vocabulary spread over fourteen routes would
make every future route on the family choose a door.

**No by-number lookup existed under any name.** The whole backend was searched for a
resolution of `order_no` to a row: `platform_numbering.py` allocates one and
`connections.py` writes one, and nothing reads one. `GET /work-orders/by-number/{order_no}`
is new, is `AnyTenantRole` like `GET /work-orders/{id}`, and **resolves through the same
assembler** (`dispatch.order_row`) so the two doors cannot drift apart.

**It is tenant-scoped, and that is load-bearing rather than routine.** `order_no` comes
from a per-tenant series, so `WO-0016` exists in more than one utility and names a
different job in each. This is the one read in the module that could answer across a
tenant boundary if its filter were dropped, and a single-tenant fixture would never
show it — so `test_def_wrk_4518_order_by_number.py` raises the same number in two
utilities and proves each sees only its own.

**The screen accepts BOTH spellings rather than one being made the winner.** A uuid goes
straight to the id route, so every existing link keeps working byte for byte; anything
else goes through the lookup, which answers with the whole row — so resolving costs no
extra round trip. **Measured after the fix: `/work/orders/WO-0016` makes ONE lookup call
and five id calls, all `200`.**

### 3 · THE PART THAT ACTUALLY MATTERED, AND IT IS NOT THE ADDRESS

The address was one bug. **What let it survive is that a failed read was invisible**, and
that is now fixed as its own thing: `OrderDetailPage` had **no loading branch and no
failed branch**, so `data === undefined` reached the fact list and every `<Fact>` turned
it into a dash. A page of dashes because it is still loading and a page of dashes
because everything 404'd are the same picture.

**The dash is not the bug.** A dash is the right answer for a value that is genuinely
absent — two on that very screen are exactly that. The bug is a dash standing in for
*we do not know*, which is a different fact and needs different words. The screen now
takes `BillDetailPage`'s three-branch shape (law 5, B14 rule 36): `LoadingSkeleton`
while pending, `FailedWithRetry` naming the failure, the page only when the row is
there. `/work/orders/WO-9999` now reads **"This work order could not be opened — No work
order here answers to WO-9999"** with the HTTP status and a support reference, instead
of fourteen dashes.

### 4 · THE CHECK, AND THE SECOND DEFECT IT FOUND ON ITS FIRST RUN

**`G122` asks the general question**: every `.tsx` under `features` that draws a
`<FactList` from a `useQuery` of its own must consult that read's PENDING state and its
ABSENT state. Mutations are excluded deliberately — `markComplete.isPending` is a button
spinner, and the three `isPending` references on the broken file were all mutations,
which is how a looser check would have passed over it.

Measured over the whole front end: **nine such screens, eight guard both states, one
does not.** That one is `TemplateDetailPage.tsx`, and it is **`DEF-WRK-4637`**, filed
rather than fixed here: an unknown or foreign template id leaves the header on the word
**"Loading" for ever** — checked in a browser, still Loading after twenty seconds — with
Edit, Duplicate, Deactivate and Delete drawn live over nothing. **A permanently-Loading
header is worse than a dash, because it makes a false claim rather than an empty one.**

`G122` was proved red **through `run_gates.py`'s own path** (`_assert_registry_sane()`
then `module.run()`), not through `__main__` — `DEF-GOV-3733` is exactly that mistake —
and it exits `1` on the defect and `0` on the fix. Its baseline may only shrink, and its
PASS line prints what it skipped beside what it checked, because a declared blind spot
with no number is indistinguishable from an empty one.

**`G122`'s first draft was itself wrong in the instructive direction.** It demanded
`if (query.isPending)` — an early return — and reported `NewAccountWizard`, which
answers the question perfectly well by passing `loading={unitsQuery.isPending}` to the
control that draws it. **A gate that dictates the SHAPE of a correct answer rather than
asking whether the question is asked manufactures work and then gets suppressed.** It
asks the question now. Loosening it also revealed that `BillRunWizard` already complied,
and the ratchet refused to pass until its now-undeserved baseline line was deleted.

### 5 · THE THIRD FINDING — ONE SCREEN CONTRADICTING ITSELF (`DEF-WRK-4635`)

Raising `WO-0040` from template `ST-0006 v1` to get a populated screen produced this:
**Overview said `Template version v1` and Checklist said "This job was raised without a
template".** The branch was right (no tasks and no safety rows means nothing to draw);
the SENTENCE asserted a cause the branch never tested, and a template published with no
steps is lawful. Fixed by choosing the sentence on `template_id` rather than on the row
counts, with a second string. **`US-WRK-032` TC-7 could not have caught it** — its
fixture sets `template_id: null`, which makes the old sentence true.

### 6 · WHAT WAS DELIBERATELY NOT DONE

**No in-app link was changed to carry the number.** B14 rule 31 governs the visible value
of a FIELD, and ids in URLs are this product's settled norm — bills, plans, charge codes
and templates are all addressed by uuid. Changing four call sites to make the URL match
the parameter's name would be a bigger, riskier change than the defect warrants and was
not asked for.

**The parameter is still named `:orderNo`.** Renaming it would touch the route constant,
the screen registry, `App.tsx` and every test that spells the pattern out — the mass
shared-file rewrite law 11 exists to prevent — and the screen now serves both spellings
correctly, so the name is no longer a trap. It is recorded here so the next lane knows
the name is a survival rather than a statement.

**`DEF-WRK-4637` was filed, not fixed.** It is a different screen with its own tabs and
its own four commit buttons, and folding it into this lane would have made one commit
answer for two screens.

### 7 · ONE THING THIS LANE HIT THAT IS WORTH THE FOUR LINES

**A defect id collided between filing it and pushing it, and `allocate.py --verify`
caught it.** This lane took `DEF-WRK-4630` from the register's maximum; by push time a
sibling had pushed `DEF-GOV-4630` to the branch tip. `allocate.py defect --verify 4630`
answered **"TAKEN — a sibling pushed it. Renumber before you commit"**, and the row is
`DEF-WRK-4637`. That is `DEF-1787`'s exact shape — both lanes computed the maximum
correctly, from different worlds — and the tool worked as its own docstring says it
would: it cannot reserve, it removes the stale read, and it catches the rare case at the
only moment the answer can be final. **Run the verify in the same breath as the blob
re-derivation, every push, unconditionally.**

**No template was renamed.** The 2026-09-06 ruling that the two *Meter set* templates are
lawful by construction stands. Every place that matches a template by NAME was searched
again while looking for a by-number lookup; `_exchange_template_id` is still the only
one, and it still refuses an ambiguous name.

## 2026-09-08 · THE PRODUCT OWNER RULED ON EIGHT QUESTIONS ABOUT PUTTING A RATE CHANGE THROUGH

A clerk walkthrough on 2026-09-08 put a 4% water rise through the rate-change wizard in a
real browser, as the rates clerk at Brazos Bend Utilities. It took **four attempts**, hit
**three refusals all discovered on the last screen**, and the task as set — an October
effective date — **could not be completed at all**. Seven defects were filed
(`DEF-RAT-4641` to `DEF-RAT-4647`). Nine questions went to the PO in plain English with a
figure each; **eight were answered on 2026-09-08 and are recorded here verbatim so nobody
asks again (hard-won law 13).**

### THE EIGHT RULINGS

**1 · The review screen shows the prices already in force, not the ones being saved.**
PO: **"(b) Old and new side by side, with the change."**
So step 5 reads back `$4.2400 → $4.4096 · +4.00%` per band, including rows that did not
move, marked as unchanged. The percentage is computed for the clerk. Chosen over showing
the new prices alone because a mistyped digit is visible as `+40.00%` in a way three
absolute figures are not.

**2 · Two boxes ask for a reason; the obvious one is optional and the required one is not.**
PO: **"(a) One box only"** — required, blank, written to both the audit record and the
version history. The optional "What changed" box is removed.

**3 · The new version was recorded under the previous version's note and docket number.**
Put to the PO twice: the first framing was not understood ("help me to understand this - I
did not understandn"), and was restated in plain terms — the history now describes a 4%
change as *"+6% across tiers · PUC #W-2025-1184"*, a figure and a state-commission docket
belonging to a different filing. **Settled by ruling 2 and not separately asked again:**
with one box, blank each time, nothing is carried forward and the record cannot be wrong
this way. The reading was stated to the PO and stands unless contradicted.

**4 · The end date arrives pre-filled from the version in force and is only checked at save.**
PO: **"(b) Pre-fill, but check it the moment the start date changes."**
So the end date clears when the start moves, and the screen says on the field that it did.

**5 · The overlap refusal names the wrong version and describes a rule the code does not enforce.**
PO: **"(b) Allow inserting a version between two existing ones."**
Both halves: the message names the version that actually blocks the date and offers one
that works, **and the rule changes** — today the server requires a new version to start
strictly after the newest one's start (`_guard_window`, whose own docstring says so while
its message says "may not overlap"). It becomes: a version may start anywhere not already
billed, and the version it lands inside closes the day before.

**6 · Nothing lets a clerk schedule a rise before an already-filed one.**
**Answered by ruling 5 and not asked again.** The PO's answer to 5 is verbatim the option
that was offered as 6(b), so insertion is allowed and an October rise becomes possible.
The reading was stated to the PO explicitly.

**7 · Activating silently truncated a pending 2027 filing from open-ended to 31 days.**
PO: **"(a) Warn on the review screen, by name and date, and require a tick."**
Contiguous windows stay — that behaviour is correct and deliberate. What changes is that
the review names the filing ("2027 filing · adds conservation pricing"), its new end date,
and Activate stays disabled until the tick.

**8 · The impact step reported 75 of 75 accounts unpriceable and every figure blank.**
PO: **"(a) Allow it, but record on the version that impact was unknown - show the warning
and allow it."**
So activation is still permitted. The warning is explicit, the per-account reason is
recorded and shown as a breakdown, and the version carries the fact that impact could not
be computed together with who activated it anyway.

**9 · The tax detail page holds Edit disabled over a wizard that exists and works.**
PO: **"(b). This is the fifth time a hold has outlived its screen. The test is what stops
a sixth."**
So both halves: turn Edit on for the tax kind, and add a test that asserts every held
control's destination is **still unbuilt**, by address and by screen id — not that the
control is disabled, which would freeze it.

### WHAT WAS DRAWN, AND WHAT WAS NOT BUILT

The PO asked for wireframes before any implementation, verbatim: *"can you draw the
wireframe first, let me review it and then we implement the change."* Seven panels were
drawn as an artifact — each showing today beside the proposal — and **no code was changed.**
Every figure in the drawings is real, read out of the running product during the walk: the
three water bands, the 75 accounts across two plans, the 2027 filing and its note, the
clerk's own name.

### THE ONE TO BUILD FIRST, IF IT IS ONLY ONE

**The side-by-side review (ruling 1).** It is screen-only, it touches nothing else — the
comparison table has exactly one other caller and is fed different data there — and it is
the only one of the eight where today's behaviour can put a wrong price into force without
the clerk ever seeing it. The test that keeps it fixed is one assertion: type a price on
step 3, assert the same string appears on step 5.

## 2026-09-08 · PLANS & RATES IS SIXTY SCREENS BEHIND SEVENTEEN ADDRESSES, AND 106 OF ITS SENTENCES SAY SOMETHING IS NOT THERE YET

The PO asked for a count of the Plans & Rates screens and a redraw based on the analysis.
Both numbers below are read out of the code, not estimated, and both are worth keeping
because **the number everyone quotes is wrong by a factor of three and a half.**

### THE COUNT · 17 ADDRESSES, 60 SCREENS

`screenIds.ts` holds **17 paths** under `/plans-rates`. What a clerk can actually reach is
**60**, because one address serves six tabs and every detail page and wizard has its own:

| Surface | Why it is more than one | Screens |
|---|---|---|
| The list | one address, six tabs (`RATING_TABS` 5 + `RateChangesTab`) | 6 |
| Plan detail | 8 tab ids in `PlanDetail.tsx` | 8 |
| Rate schedule detail | overview · matrix · billing-rules · plans · versions | 5 |
| Charge code detail | `DEFINITION_TABS.charge` | 5 |
| Discount detail | `DEFINITION_TABS.discount` | 5 |
| Tax detail | `DEFINITION_TABS.tax` | 6 |
| Plan wizard | 8 steps | 8 |
| Rate schedule wizard | `basics · sizes · structure · effective · review` | 5 |
| Charge code wizard | `basics · amount · review` | 3 |
| Discount wizard | `basics · value · eligibility · effective · review` | 5 |
| Tax wizard | `TAX_WIZARD_STEPS` | 4 |
| **Total** | | **60** |

### THE FINDING THAT CHANGED THE DELIVERABLE

**All sixty are one of three shells** — a list (6), a detail page with tabs (29), a wizard
step (25). So the redraw is **three designs, not sixty**, and drawing sixty would have
concealed the only structural fact worth having. What the three do not share today is a
consistent answer to four questions each has to handle: what to show when a figure cannot
be computed, when to refuse, where an action lives, and how a tab says it is empty.

### THE MEASUREMENT WORTH KEEPING · 106 ABSENCES

**106 sentences in the English catalogue under `rating.` tell a clerk that something is not
there yet** — a figure that cannot be shown, a field not stored, a list that cannot be
named, a calculation that does not exist. Counted by key prefix: `rating.plan` 23,
`rating.rate` 13, `rating.discountWizard` 10, `rating.planDetail` 10, `rating.rateDetail` 8,
`rating.taxWiz` 7, `rating.definition` 6, `rating.charges` 5, `rating.chargeWizard` 4,
`rating.plans` 4, and 16 more across nine smaller areas.

**They are honest, and that is the good part** — an unbuilt read that says so is far better
than one that renders a plausible zero. **The cost is that they are the dominant experience
of the module.** On the four detail pages opened in a browser that day, the summary tiles
were empty more often than they were filled, which trains a clerk to stop reading them.

**The rule proposed, and it replaces most of the 106 without removing any honesty: a tile
that cannot be computed is not drawn.** Three tiles that mean something beat four where two
are dashes. A genuine absence is stated ONCE, in the tab that owns it, rather than as a
permanent dash in a summary read forty times a week.

⚠ **AND THE HONEST LIMIT WAS STATED TO THE PO RATHER THAN GLOSSED:** some of the 106 are
not copy at all, they are reads nobody built, each deferred separately by somebody who was
right at the time. Which of them to build is a scoping conversation, not a design one. The
redraw makes the remaining absences **quieter, not fewer**, and says so in its own footer.

### FOUR DEFECTS FILED FROM THIS ANALYSIS

`DEF-RAT-4648` three live rate schedules and one plan carry an internal question id in the
clerk-facing name, unmarked, in the same list as the schedule that bills 75 accounts —
**data, not code, so no gate can see it** · `DEF-RAT-4649` the list says "9 sizes" and the
detail says the schedule does not price sizes separately; both statements are true of
different facts and nothing compares two screens' claims about one object · `DEF-RAT-4650`
a charge code reports **0 plans** while the rate wizard attributes every water size's base
to that same code — the tile is truthful about the one table it reads, and a zero renders
as a fact rather than as an absence · `DEF-RAT-4651` step 3 offers a per-connection-size
price on nine controls and says underneath that bills ignore it, **while the charge-code
path refuses the same thing server-side** — the product does both, in two places, and which
one is right is a PO decision rather than ours.

### WHAT WAS DELIVERED, AND WHAT WAS NOT

Three artifacts, and **no code was changed**: the customer portal redrawn to 54 screens in
journey order (adding the landing page, the two language screens and the guest payment
receipt, none of which existed), the rate-change wizard fixes drawn from the PO's eight
rulings, and this count with its three shells. The PO's standing instruction holds — draw
first, review, then implement.

## 2026-09-08 · FOUR PRODUCT OWNER RULINGS ON THE CUSTOMER PORTAL'S DESIGN, FROM REVIEWING THE WIREFRAMES

The PO reviewed the portal wireframes screen by screen and ruled on four things. All four
are design law for the portal from now on, and all four came from the PO looking at drawings
rather than from any gate — which is hard-won law 6's shape applied to a design review.
**Nothing is built; the drawings were updated and republished.**

### 1 · QUICK PAY KEYS ON THE BILL NUMBER, NOT THE ACCOUNT NUMBER

PO, verbatim: *"on this scren we need to start with bill number not with account # also when
bill is search you ahve to show Account #, name, service address, Bill # , Bill period etc so
that user can understand"*.

**The reasoning, recorded because it generalises:** the person paying without signing in is
**holding one bill** and wants that bill paid. The bill number is the most prominent thing on
the paper in front of them and names exactly what they intend to pay. An account number asks
them to think about a relationship. It also removes a real ambiguity — an account with two
unpaid bills has one account number and two possible answers to *"how much"*.

**What a found bill shows, ruled:** bill number · bill period · issued date · account number ·
name on the account · service address · amount due · due date. The PERIOD earns its place —
a landlord paying a tenant's bill, or somebody with two properties, recognises the month and
the address long before a number.

⚠ **THE SECURITY COST WAS STATED TO THE PO RATHER THAN GLOSSED.** Bill numbers are sequential
(`BL-2608-000042`), so bill-number-plus-ZIP is guessable. The mitigations are not optional:
rate-limit by address and by ZIP, refuse after a few misses, and **never say which half was
wrong**. The reward for a successful guess is one bill's amount and service address, and the
ability to pay somebody else's bill — a nuisance rather than a theft, and a real one.
The landing page and the sign-in page were changed to match, so all three say bill number.

### 2 · TWO HEADING BARS, AND EXACTLY TWO

PO, verbatim: *"on each desktop screen - you need to keep heading bar constatant and consistent
across all sceens - there are 2 scenraios - guest user and registerd user - so 2 heading bar"*.

Applied to all 54 screens — **17 guest, 37 signed in, one bar per desktop frame, verified by
count.**

* **Left, on both:** the utility's name, same place. Guest: the five things a stranger can do
  without an account. Signed in: **who and which account** — name, service address, account
  number.
* **Right, on both:** language FIRST, because somebody who cannot read the page must be able
  to fix that from anywhere. Then the phone number (guest) or **the amount due and its date**
  (signed in) — the two numbers most visits are about, in the same place on every screen.
  Then the one identity action: Sign in, or Sign out.
* **Second row:** only the signed-in bar has one — seven sections with the current one marked.
  A guest has no sections to move between; their tasks are in the bar itself.
* **A back-link or a wizard step rail sits UNDERNEATH the bar, never inside it.** Those change
  per screen; the bar is the thing that does not.
* **Why not one bar:** a single bar would have to show either an account or a sign-in prompt,
  and guessing wrong is worse than either — a customer who sees a sign-in link assumes they
  were logged out, and a guest who sees an account number assumes they are looking at somebody
  else's. Two bars make the state legible before anything is read.

### 3 · FOUR SCREENS THAT DID NOT EXIST, AND THE ORDER

PO, verbatim: *"you did not build landing screen, all screens for guest login , language
selection for guest and register user"* and *"arrange these screen in logical order and
renumber them"*.

**Four screens were missing entirely and are now drawn:** the **landing page** (the public
front page had no design at all — its primary action is *Pay a bill*, not *Sign in*, because
most visits are a payment and most of those people have no account); **choose your language,
signed out**; **the guest payment receipt** (the signed-in receipt can say *"a copy is in
Payments"* and this one cannot, so the reference is the loudest thing after the amount); and
**your language, signed in**.

⚠ **THE LANGUAGE RULING HAS TWO HALVES AND THE SECOND ONE IS THE PRODUCT BUG.** Every language
is written **in its own language first** — *Español*, not *Spanish* — because somebody who
reads no English cannot find "Spanish" in a list. And **there are TWO language settings that
can disagree**: the one on the account decides what a bill and a shut-off notice arrive in;
the one in the browser decides what the site looks like. A customer who sets the site to
Spanish reasonably assumes their bill follows. Screen 53 names both, flags the mismatch, and
offers one tap to align them — without forcing it, because different on purpose is legitimate.

**The order is the journey, renumbered 01–54:** before you sign in (14) · starting and stopping
service (4) · your account (5) · the bill (5) · paying (6) · when money is tight (9) · what you
used (3) · asking us something (4) · you and your settings (4). Two of the 54 are second
addresses for a screen already drawn (`/home`, `/ask`), listed so no route is unaccounted for.

### 4 · A SCREEN DRAWN AS IF THE SEARCH HAD ALREADY HAPPENED

PO: *"Track a report - Desktop · 1280 - search is not included"*. The desktop frame opened
straight into a found report with no way to look one up — the phone frame had the field and
the desktop did not.

**Worth keeping because it is a drawing failure with a product lesson in it:** fixing it
exposed that the screen had only ONE way in, a reference on a scrap of paper, and losing that
scrap is exactly what turns a self-service check back into a phone call. It now also accepts
**a phone number the reporter left**, returning everything reported from it in the last 90
days, rate-limited for the same reason quick-pay is.

## 2026-09-08 · TWO MORE PORTAL RULINGS, AND ONE OF THEM IS THE NO-HARD-CAPS LAW SHOWING UP IN A DRAWING

### 5 · TIPS ON THE HELP SCREEN — AND THE PRODUCT ALREADY SAYS HOW MANY

PO: *"here we need tips also - without crowding it - please add tips"*.

Drawn as **one line**, in a quiet band below the common questions — never above them, and
never beside the phone number, which is what that screen exists for.

⚠ **"WITHOUT CROWDING IT" IS NOT A DESIGN JUDGMENT HERE; IT IS ALREADY THE RULE.** A tip
record (`tips`, `published_content_models.py`) targets **one screen, never a list**, carries
an optional `month_from`/`month_to` and an `is_on` switch, and where two match one screen the
lower `position` wins — **exactly one renders** (`BR-CWP-095`). The drawing follows the data
model rather than inventing a carousel, which is why it cannot crowd anything.

**Two things the drawing states that the model implies and nobody had written down:**

* **When no tip matches there is NO BAND AT ALL** — not an empty box, not "no tip today". The
  seeded demo depends on it: its freeze-warning tip is off **and** out of season, on purpose
  (two independent reasons, `US-CWP-073` TC-3), and the portal home is expected to show no tip
  container.
* **The same one-line band, in the same place relative to the content, on every screen a tip
  targets** — usage, usage-looks-high, send a reading, past due, help. One design applied
  wherever a utility has written a tip; not a Help-page feature. The seeded set is six tips on
  six screens, and *Usage* and *Usage looks high* are two of them, which is why an all-year tip
  and a seasonal one can both be on without either hiding the other.

### 6 · "WHERE TO FIND US" NEEDS A SEARCH, AND THE REASON IS A REPO-WIDE LAW

PO: *"you will need search bar on this - utility may have many service centers"*.

The drawing showed **three** places and a scroll. That is right for one utility and wrong for
the next: a city system can have a dozen counters, drop boxes and partner payment agents, and
a customer wants the one near **them**, not the one near the head office.

⚠ **THIS IS `NFR-3` AND `NFR-5` ARRIVING IN A WIREFRAME, WHICH IS A PLACE NOBODY CHECKS FOR
THEM.** The repo's flexibility law is stated as *no hard caps anywhere* and *universal server
pagination*, and it is enforced — where anyone looks — against endpoints and tables. **A
drawing that assumes three rows is the same defect one layer up, and no gate reads a
drawing.** It is the identical shape as the four breaches CLAUDE.md already names, where an
unpaginated list was correct at the old ceiling and 13× short at the new one.

**Ruled and drawn:** search by **town, ZIP or name**; filters that name the errand rather than
the feature — *takes cash · open now · open Saturday · start or stop service · drop box*;
server-side paging with the count stated (*"showing 3 of 14"*); and **no cap on how many
service centres a utility may have.**

**"Takes cash" is the filter that decides the journey**, because paying cash is the only
errand no other channel can do — and the nearest office may be the one that cannot.

⚠ **AND THE MIRROR CASE IS DRAWN TOO, because it is the same law read the other way:** with
two or three places the search and the filters are **absent entirely**. A search box over
three rows is furniture, exactly as a chooser with one option is.

## 2026-09-08 · FOUR MORE PORTAL RULINGS — START AND STOP SPLIT, THE HEADING BAR RESHAPED, AND AN ACCOUNT CARD ON HOME

The PO kept reviewing the wireframes screen by screen. Four more rulings, all from looking at
drawings. **The portal set is now 60 screens; nothing is built.**

### 7 · START AND STOP ARE FOUR STEPS EACH, DRAWN SEPARATELY AND BUILT AS ONE

PO, verbatim: *"please show all 4 screens - address, when , about you, check; and show
seperate screens for stop - when you develope you can use same code internally"*.

**Start service** is now `1 Address · 2 When · 3 About you · 4 Check`, and **stop service**
`1 Which property · 2 When · 3 Where the final bill goes · 4 Check`. One screen each became
nine (the resume screen sits between them).

**The PO's own build instruction is the important half and is recorded as design law:** they
are **drawn as two flows and built as one component**. The stepper, the read-back, the change
links, the what-happens-next panel and the refusal behaviour are identical work; only the
fields and the copy differ. It is written into the group heading and into screen 23's spec so
a lane cannot read the two flows as two implementations.

**Three things the split made possible that a single form could not hold:**

* **Address is step 1 of start**, because every other question is wasted if the answer is no —
  and the check says WHICH services and, where known, **who supplies the rest** (*"electric
  here is Pedernales Electric"*), which saves a second search and a call.
* **Step 3 is where people abandon**, so it carries the document drop, a panel saying why each
  field is asked (a date of birth into a utility form needs a reason), and **"Send my ID
  later"** as a real option with its cost stated — the commonest reason this form is
  abandoned is a licence that is upstairs, and somebody who leaves to fetch it does not
  come back.
* **Stop step 2 carries the warning that generates the moving-day call:** *you are billed up
  to and including your last day.* People pick the day before they move and then have no
  water while loading a van. One sentence prevents an emergency call and a $45.00
  reconnection fee.
* **Stop step 3 is its own step on purpose.** Buried at the foot of one form the forwarding
  address is the field people skip, and **a final bill posted to the house they just left is
  the most expensive small failure in the product.** Given its own step, with the $150.00
  deposit figure beside it, it becomes the field they came to fill in.

⚠ **AND STOP STEP 1 IS SKIPPED FOR MOST PEOPLE** — one account with nothing optional means
nothing to choose, so the flow opens on *When* and says "step 1 of 3". Same rule as every
other chooser in this product: one option is furniture.

### 8 · THE RESUME SCREEN OPENS ON THE FIELDS, NOT ON A CHECKLIST

PO: *"on this sceeen you will ahve to show field to take input from user and aldo dropbox to
add documents"*.

The first drawing listed what was still needed and made the person press *Carry on* to reach
it. **That is one more tap between somebody holding their licence and the thing that takes a
photograph of it.** Redrawn so the unfinished step IS the page: the fields, the drop zone,
**take a photo** (the one that matters on a phone), still-needed fields marked with one line
saying why, and what is already done as a small panel beside it with change links.

### 9 · THE SIGNED-IN HEADING BAR IS TWO ROWS, MENU FIRST

PO: *"here header bar should ahve menu - and below that we should have a line for account -
this should be consitent across registered user login"*.

**Row one:** the utility's name, then the seven-section menu, then language and Sign out.
**Row two:** a quieter line carrying **who and which account** — name, service address,
account number — and, on the right, **the amount due and its date**.

The reason for the order, recorded because it is the general rule: **the menu goes where a
menu lives**, and the account line is not navigation — it is the answer to *whose account am
I looking at*, which a landlord needs on every screen and which anyone about to phone is
asked for first. Applied to all **39** signed-in desktop frames.

### 10 · A BIG ACCOUNT CARD ON HOME, MASKED, WITH A SWITCHER

PO: *"can you give big account identifier on home screen - name account #, service area,
Utility services, assets, phone # and email ID, govt ID - last 4 digits etc - you can mask
these detials - and also seletor for multiple account if he has"*.

Drawn as a wide card under the bars: **account number · name · service address · service
area, route and cycle · services · plan · equipment installed · phone · email · the ID on
file**, plus a footer line for open-since, autopay, paperless and deposit.

**Masking, ruled:** phone, email and the government ID are **masked by default and revealed
on request** — `(•••) •••-0148`, `m•••••@example.com`, `Driving licence ••••4417`. Enough to
confirm it is the right record; not enough to be read over a shoulder in an office, a library
or a shared kitchen. Only the last four of an ID is ever shown. **The account number is NOT
masked** — it is printed on every bill and quoting it is exactly what a customer is asked to
do.

⚠ **AND THE TENSION WITH THIS SCREEN'S OWN RULE WAS RESOLVED RATHER THAN IGNORED.** Home's
question is *what do I owe*, and its own line says nothing else belongs above the fold. So on
desktop the card is a single band **above** the amount due, and **on a phone it sits BELOW
it** — compact, four rows, with *all account details* expanding the rest. On the width where
space is scarce the money wins and the identity is one tap away. The switcher is the
exception: on a phone it goes **above** everything, because every figure on the screen
belongs to the account it names, and a landlord who pays the wrong property's bill has been
failed by that control.

## 2026-09-08 · ADDENDUM TO RULING 10 — THE HOME ACCOUNT CARD, TIGHTENED IN THREE PLACES

The PO reviewed the account card drawn under ruling 10 and cut it in three places. Small
changes, recorded because each carries a reason that generalises.

**Equipment shows REFERENCES, not descriptions.** PO: *"just show IDs not details … W-2209,
8841-C, F-0118 - this is enough"*. So `8841-C · W-2209 · F-0118` replaces *"Electric meter
8841-C / Water meter W-2209 · 5/8" / Fire line F-0118 · 2""*.

⚠ **THE REASON IS WORTH MORE THAN THE CHANGE: a customer already knows what is installed at
their own house.** What they cannot produce from memory is **the number a clerk asks for on
the phone, or a plumber needs off the meter**. The description is the half they can supply
themselves; the reference is the half they cannot. Three references fit on one line where
three descriptions took three. Sizes, ownership and full descriptions stay one tap away on
the equipment screen.

**Account status goes on the card.** PO: *"+ account status"*. Drawn as a chip and a date —
**Active since Jun 2, 2026** — in the room the equipment change freed. The footer line was
re-cut to carry the settings that change what happens NEXT month: autopay · paperless ·
budget billing · deposit held · anything past due. *"Open since"* moved up into the status,
so nothing is stated twice. **A customer reading this card is deciding whether anything needs
their attention, and status is the single word that answers it.**

**A six-month chooser on the bill panel.** PO: *"please give me drop down to select last 6
months - on this - August bill · BL-2608-000077"*. The panel now carries the month and its
total — *August 2026 · $191.00 ▾*.

**Why it belongs on Home rather than on the bills list:** the commonest reason to leave this
screen is to compare this month with last, and that round trip is **three screens to answer
one question**. Choosing a month redraws the panel in place, and **the bill number, period
and due date follow it** — so nothing on screen can belong to a different month than the
heading says, which is the failure this kind of in-place chooser usually introduces.

Two states came with it: fewer than six bills lists only what exists (**a first bill means no
chooser at all** — one option is furniture, as everywhere), and an older paid month shows
*"Paid Jul 19"* where the due date was, with **no Pay button**.

## 2026-09-08 · THE PO ASKED WHETHER THE DOORS WERE RIGHT, AND FIVE OF NINE DRAWINGS WERE WRONG

PO: *"are you sure you ahve correct doors for these screens - When money is tight? please
double check"*, and then, looking at the budget-billing drawing: *"youa re saying on this
screen user can come from home - but Im not sure your home scren gives door for this screen"*.

**They were right, and it was worse than the one screen.** Every inbound reference to the
nine routes was then read out of the portal source. **Five of the nine back-links in the
wireframes were assumed rather than read**, and two of the corrections turned out to be
product defects rather than drawing ones.

| Screen | Drawn | The code |
|---|---|---|
| Past due `/overdue` | ← Home | **← Bills**, and only Bills |
| The plan we can offer `/plan-offer` | ← Past due | **← Payments** |
| Your plan `/plan` | ← Home | **← Payments** |
| Budget billing `/level-pay` | ← Home | **← Help paying**, and only that |
| Money back `/money-back` | ← Home | **← Payments** |

### THE TWO PRODUCT FINDINGS

**`DEF-CWP-4652` · Past due has no door from Home.** Its only door is the *Where things
stand* list at the foot of Bills. It is not in the nav, and `Home.tsx` links to `/pay-now`
and `/ask-for-a-plan` and nothing else — *"overdue"* appears in that file only as a comment
and a status-to-tone map. **The customer who is behind lands on Home**, and the screen that
tells them what happens next is two clicks away behind a list. Protections, whose only door
is Past due, is deeper still.

**`DEF-CWP-4653` · Budget billing sits behind hardship.** The one inbound link to
`/level-pay` in the whole portal is from *Help paying*. It is a mainstream product for
anybody with a summer-and-winter bill, and routing it exclusively through a screen about not
being able to pay makes it hard to find and, for some people, off-putting. It is not among
the seven errand cards on Payments — where *Your plan*, *The plan we can offer* and *Money
back* all are.

### WHAT THE AUDIT CONFIRMED

All nine routes exist and are registered. `/level-pay/standing` has two doors from Budget
billing. The Payments errand grid is real and rendered, so three screens reached only through
it are genuinely reachable. **`/ask-for-a-plan` has three doors — Past due, Help paying and
Home — the most of any screen in the group, which is right for the thing a struggling
customer most needs.**

### ⚠ THE LESSON, AND IT IS ABOUT THE ORDER OF WORK

**A route existing is not a door.** Two different questions were being confused: *is this
screen built* (yes, all nine) and *can a customer get to it from where they are standing*
(no, for two of them). The first is in `screenIds.ts` and every test asserts it. **The second
is nowhere, and nothing checks it** — G13 asks whether a prop is passed, and the hold-expiry
work asks whether a refusal is still true; both are about controls that exist. **This is the
opposite shape: a live, routed, tested screen that nothing points at.** Every test passes,
because each screen is tested at its own address.

**And the drawings were the wrong way round.** The doors were drawn from what seemed sensible
and only checked when the PO asked. Reading them first would have found both defects before a
single frame was drawn, and would have cost one grep. **For the remaining eight groups the
doors get read before anything is drawn**, and each screen's spec carries a *How you get here*
row naming its real inbound links.

## 2026-09-08 · THE WHOLE PORTAL'S DOORS, AUDITED — TWO FLOWS HAVE NO DOOR AT ALL

After the *when money is tight* audit found five wrong back-links, the PO named the fault
exactly: *"all your screens are good - only problem is door to that screen. when you mention
that door is from x screen - when we check x screen we dont find the door there - rest is
good."*

So **every inbound link in the portal was extracted from source** — literal `to=`/`to:`,
template-literal paths, and programmatic `navigate`/`<Navigate>` — and matched against the
registered route list. **Nine back-links in the drawings were assumed rather than read, and
two whole flows have no door of any kind.**

### THE TWO UNREACHABLE FLOWS

**`DEF-CWP-4654` · Stop service.** `/stop-or-restart` has **zero inbound links anywhere**.
Not Home, not My details, not Your account, not Bills, not among the seven errand cards on
Payments, not in the nav. Its only mentions outside its own route registration are two
backend calls in `portalClient.ts` and its own docstring. **The route is registered, the
screen is built and tested, and nothing points at it** — while moving out is one of the
commonest reasons anybody opens a utility portal.

**`DEF-CWP-4655` · One service centre.** `/visit/:slug` likewise. `/visit` has two doors, so
**the list is reachable and the detail is not**: a customer sees three addresses and cannot
open one for its hours, its payment methods or directions — which is exactly what decides
whether they make the journey.

### "MY DETAILS" WAS A HABIT, NOT A ROUTE

Four screens were drawn as reached from My details — **payment methods, autopay, equipment,
documents**. **None of them is.** They come from Payments, Payments, Usage and Bills. The
error is worth naming because of *why* it survived: My details is where those things feel
like they belong, so the sentence read plausibly to everyone including the author.

### ⚠ THE RULE, AND WHY NOTHING CATCHES THIS

**A route existing is not a door.** Two questions were being confused all along:

* **Is this screen built?** — `screenIds.ts`, `portalRoutes.tsx`, and every test asserts it.
* **Can a customer reach it from where they are standing?** — **nowhere, and nothing checks
  it.**

`G13` asks whether a prop is passed; the hold-expiry work asks whether a refusal is still
true. **Both are about controls that exist.** This is the opposite shape — a live, routed,
rendered, tested screen that nothing points at — and **every test passes on it, because each
screen is tested at its own address, which is the one place a door is not needed.**

**The check that would close it:** every registered portal route must have at least one
inbound link from a screen reachable without typing the address. It would have caught all
four of today's door defects — the two unreachable flows, Past due's missing door from Home,
and budget billing sitting behind hardship. Parameterised routes need the template-literal
form counted, which is what made the first pass of this audit report seven false positives
before it was corrected.

**And the working habit, which costs one grep:** read the doors BEFORE drawing the screen.
Every screen's spec now carries a *How you get here* row naming its real inbound links — and
where the answer is *nothing*, it says so.

## 2026-09-08 · A THIRD DOOR GAP, FOUND THE SAME WAY AS THE FIRST TWO

PO: *"how to go to this screen 04 Create your sign-in? I did not udnerstand from where we are
going to this screen"*.

**`/enrol` has exactly two doors:** the **landing page** — one of the three beneath its
sign-in form — and the **guest payment receipt**, offered to somebody who has just paid
without an account, which is a good moment to ask because they have proved they hold a bill.

**`DEF-CWP-4656` · The dedicated sign-in screen has neither.** `/sign-in` offers *Forgot your
password?* and nothing else. Anybody who arrives there directly — from a bookmark, an emailed
link, or **the *Sign in* word in the guest top bar, which is on every signed-out screen and
goes to `/sign-in` rather than to the landing page** — cannot create an account from there.
It is the most obvious place in the product to look for it.

⚠ **THIS IS THE THIRD GAP FOUND BY THE SAME QUESTION IN ONE SESSION**, after `/stop-or-restart`
(no door at all) and `/visit/:slug` (list reachable, detail not). All three were found by a
human asking *where do I reach this from*, and none of them can be caught by anything that
exists: each screen is correct in isolation, each is routed, rendered and tested, and every
test passes because a screen is tested at its own address.

**The pattern in the three is worth more than any one of them.** Two different kinds of
absence keep appearing: **no door anywhere** (stop service, one service centre) and **a door
that is not where a person looks** (enrolment, budget billing, past due). The first is
mechanically checkable — every registered route should have one inbound link from somewhere
reachable. **The second is not, and it is the more common one.** It needs somebody to ask
*where would a person go looking for this*, which is exactly what the PO did four times
today and what nothing automated will ever do.

## 2026-09-08 · `DEF-CWP-4656` IS WITHDRAWN — THE THIRD GAP WAS NOT A GAP

The section immediately above is **wrong** and stays here unedited, because a decision log
that quietly deletes its own errors teaches nobody anything.

**`/sign-in` has always offered a way to create a sign-in.** `SignInPage` renders
`FrontDoorView` — the *same component* the landing page renders — and that component carries
the enrol link at `signin/FrontDoor.tsx:124`, under a heading whose key is
`portal.signIn.otherDoors`. The screen was correct the whole time. The register row is marked
`invalid`, not `fixed`, because there was nothing to fix.

⚠ **THE ROW CONTRADICTED ITSELF AND THAT WAS READABLE WITHOUT OPENING ANY FILE.** Its own
`surface` field says the two inbound links to `/enrol` are *"signin/FrontDoor.tsx line 124 and
guest/QuickPayDone.tsx line 270"* — while its title says the sign-in screen has none. Line 124
IS on the sign-in screen. The row named its own refutation in the sentence next to the claim.

**How it happened, because the mechanism is the useful part.** The audit grepped for the
screen's *file* — `signin/Enrol.tsx` — and for links *to* `/enrol`, and never asked the third
question: **what does `SignInPage` actually render?** Four of the portal's guest screens are
thin wrappers around a shared view, so the file that owns a route is not the file that draws
it. A door audit that reads route files and link sites, and never follows a route to the
component it mounts, is blind to exactly this shape — and it will report the absence
confidently, because from where it is looking the link genuinely is not there.

**Which is why the guard is written the way it is.** `everyRouteHasADoor.test.ts` reads every
`.tsx` under `src/portal` and does not care which file a link lives in. It found the two real
gaps and it never had an opinion about `/sign-in`, because the link is in a file it reads.
**The false finding came from a human method, and the mechanical one was right.** That is the
opposite of the usual lesson here and it is worth recording as such.

## 2026-09-08 · CR-085 WAVE 1 SHIPPED — FOUR DOORS AND THE GUARD · `2.232.0`

PO: *"now start development - doors first, then the bars"*. Doors are done; commit `2fde39e6`.

| Defect | What a customer could not do | The door added |
|---|---|---|
| `DEF-CWP-4654` | **Stop service, at all** | Your account, and My details |
| `DEF-CWP-4655` | Open one service centre from the list | *Where to find us*, built through `usePortalPath` |
| `DEF-CWP-4652` | Find out what happens next when behind | Home, beside *Ask for a plan* |
| `DEF-CWP-4653` | Find budget billing without going via hardship | Payments, as an eighth money errand |

⚠ **`DEF-CWP-4655` WAS WORSE THAN A MISSING DOOR AND THAT IS THE FINDING TO REMEMBER.** The
link was **built**: `CentreCard` has always taken an `href` and always drawn a *see this*
link. `CentresPage` handed it `` `visit/${slug}` `` — **relative, no leading slash, no
tenant** — which from `/{tenant}/portal/visit` resolves to `/{tenant}/portal/visit/visit/{slug}`
and is not a route. So the list showed three addresses and opened none of them. **A missing
door is visibly missing; a door that renders, reads correctly in the source and goes to a 404
looks finished in every review** — `tsc` passes, and the page's own test asserts the link is
PRESENT and never asks where it goes. This is hard-won law 2's fixture clause in its other
form: a test that cannot tell a working link from a broken one.

**The guard, and what it honestly cannot do.** `everyRouteHasADoor.test.ts` asserts, per
registered route, that something in the portal links to it — 49 routes, two red at the
pristine tip and both real. Proved red **in the harness that runs it**: reverting the
`CentresPage` href to the relative form fails `/visit/:slug` by name, and the file was
restored byte-identical before the green run.

It catches **no door anywhere**. It does **not** catch **a door that is not where a person
would look** — Past due and budget billing both HAD doors and were both still wrong. Nothing
can check that; it needs somebody to ask *where would a person go looking*, which is what the
PO did four times. **This is the cheap half, and saying so is the point.**

⚠ **THREE LINK FORMS EXIST IN THE PORTAL AND A CHECK KNOWING TWO OF THEM CONDEMNS WORKING
SCREENS.** Built matching quoted paths only, it failed five HEALTHY routes; adding backticks
still missed `` `/bills/${n}/document` ``; both together still condemned `/pay/check` and
`/pay/done`, which the quick-pay wizard reaches by `navigate()` with no anchor at all.
**The false positives mattered more than the true findings** — a guard that cries wolf on five
real screens is silenced by whoever meets it next, and then catches nothing. Law 7's
*incapable of passing* is as useless as *incapable of failing*.

**Proved:** portal suite 65 files / 754 cases green; `tsc` clean; guard red then green on the
real defect. The eleven catalogues carry one new sentence each, written in its own language
per B14 rule 35.

## 2026-09-08 · CR-085 WAVE 2 — THE ACCOUNT LINE GETS ITS OWN ROW

PO, reviewing the portal wireframes: *"here header bar should ahve menu - and below that we
should have a line for account - this should be consitent across registered user login"*.

⚠ **THE INFORMATION WAS NOT MISSING, WHICH IS WHY NOBODY HAD FILED IT.** The account WAS on
screen — squeezed into the top row between the utility's name and *Help*, as a `truncate`d
label or a bare `<select>`, competing for width with five other controls. So on a narrow
window **the one fact a customer needs in order to trust the page — *which of my properties
am I looking at* — was the first thing clipped**, and it was never labelled as an account at
all. Its own row costs 40 pixels and takes it out of that competition entirely.

**The switcher MOVES; it is not copied.** Two account controls in one frame would be two
answers to one question, and a customer who changed the top one and saw the bottom one
disagree would be right to distrust both.

**The guest bar needed no change and that was CHECKED rather than assumed.** `GuestFrame` is
already one shared component drawn on every signed-out screen, already grows instead of
clipping (`DEF-CWP-4440`), and already carries the language control the PO asked for on
2026-09-07. Two bars were asked for; one of them already existed.
