⚠ **`account_no` ON SCREEN IS NOT A BREACH OF B14 RULE 31, AND THE DISTINCTION IS WORTH
WRITING DOWN BECAUSE IT WILL BE ASKED AGAIN.** Rule 31 forbids a DATABASE id as the visible
value of a field. `account_no` is the utility's own printed reference — it is on the bill, a
person reads it down the phone, and a clerk asks for it; `account.id` is a uuid nobody has
ever read aloud. They are different fields and only one of them means anything to a person.

⚠ **A TEST WHOSE SUBJECT IS *THE ID MUST NOT APPEAR* HAS TO BE GIVEN DATA WHERE THE TWO ARE
DIFFERENT.** The shell fixture defaults `account_no` to `ACC-${id}`, so with a uuid id the
fixture's own account number CONTAINS the uuid and the assertion fails **on the fixture
rather than on the screen**. It went red exactly that way and the fix was in the test.

**What the browser walk covers and what it cannot.** Ten signed-in screens carry the bar at
`y=107`, height 40, reading the same account, and at 390px it wraps rather than clips. **The
multi-account case is NOT walked and cannot be** — the seed has one portal login on pine-hill
holding one account, so the switcher never renders on this data. `select=0` in the walk's
output is the SINGLE-account rule being kept, not evidence about the switcher. What proves
the switcher moved INTO the bar is `PortalShell.test.tsx` asserting the ORDER of the markup:
the header closes before the bar opens, and the bar opens before the `<select>`. **Naming
which check covers what is the point** — law 7's *reporting zero over a scope it silently
excludes* is a walkthrough that skipped a case reading exactly like one that covered it.

⚠ **AND A CLASS TYPO WAS CAUGHT IN REVIEW THAT NO CHECK WOULD HAVE CAUGHT.** The bar was
written with `mx-aut0`. Tailwind emits nothing for a class that does not exist, so the row
would simply not have been centred — silently, with `tsc`, 759 tests and every gate green,
because the class IS in the DOM. That is CLAUDE.md's B14 rule 21 note in its plainest form,
and the only thing between it and production was reading one's own diff.

## 2026-09-08 · THE RATE SCHEDULE'S READ SCREEN — SIGNED OFF, AND THE VOCABULARY IT SETTLED

PO, on the redrawn rate schedule Overview: *"this is good and signed off"*. Recorded here
because four of the decisions behind it are **vocabulary rulings that reach far past this one
screen**, and the next lane must not re-litigate any of them.

**1 · The GL account has ONE name and it is `GL account`.** PO: *"revenue acount is not
volcabolory we use"*. Checked rather than assumed: the product says **GL account** in nine
places — `finance.gl.col.account`, `finance.je.col.account`, `finance.export.col.account`,
`ledger.je.line_account_required`, `rating.charges.col.gl`, `rating.plan.glLabel`,
`rating.taxes.col.gl` (as *Liability GL account*), `settings.accounting.edit.title`,
`settings.accounting.failedTitle`. Exactly one screen said *Revenue account*:
`rating.rateDetail.glLabel`. **That one is the outlier and it moves**, not the nine.

**2 · A history tab is called `Audit`.** PO: *"we dont user Versions & filings - just call it
audit or what we use at other places"*. Eight detail screens already do —
`assets.detail.tab.audit`, `billing.bill.tab.audit`, `customers.account.tab.audit`,
`metering.premises.tab.audit`, `metering.units.tab.audit`, `settings.cycles.detail.tab.audit`,
`settings.routes.detail.tab.audit`, `work.order.tabs.audit`. Plans & Rates was the only module
using its own word (`rating.*.tab.versions`).

⚠ **3 · A COUNT ON A RATE SCHEDULE IS UNITS, NOT ACCOUNTS, AND THE REASON IS LOAD-BEARING.**
PO: *"sicne we attached plans to Units - hence this should be units"*. A plan is assigned to a
**unit** — `units.rate_plan_id`, with `unit_plan_assignments(unit_id, rate_plan_id,
assigned_from, assigned_to)` recording every assignment and its dates. An account is billed
*because* it occupies the unit. **So counting accounts undercounts by every vacant unit** — and
a vacant unit is precisely the case whose base charge lands on a landlord's bill under the PO's
own ruling of 2026-08-27 (`base_charge_only_units`, closing `OQ-531`: *"when bill is generated
for A - we should consider common areas and U6 to U10 base charges"*). The two rulings are the
same fact seen twice.

**4 · Five tabs are three.** Overview, Rate matrix and Billing rules answered one question and
are one tab in four blocks — what it prices · the rates · how it bills · what a schedule may and
may not do. Plans and Audit stay.

**5 · No chart.** PO: *"we dont need graph … table is enough"*. The tier chart plotted three
bars a clerk had already read as numbers on the row beneath, and it could only ever draw ONE of
the seven structures — a flat, seasonal, time-of-use, demand, capacity or percent schedule has
nothing to stack. The block ranges are the column headings (`0–2 kgal`, not `Tier 1`), which is
what the chart's captions carried, so nothing was lost with it.

⚠ **AND THE SCREEN SHOWED NO CUSTOMER CLASS AT ALL** — not the header, not a field, not the
list — over a column that exists (`Tariff.account_type_id`) and a wizard whose own note admits
the picker is missing. It decides which base charge applies and therefore what a customer pays.
See the entry below on `applies_to_customer_classes`.

## 2026-09-08 · ONE BASE CHARGE PER SERVICE WAS AN ASSUMPTION IN THE SCREENS, NOT IN THE PRODUCT

PO, reading the redrawn base-rates step: *"You did not allow user to select this from drop down
- user might create 2 base rates for 2 consumer class - residential and industrial - youa re
assupming that there will be only 1 base rate for water or elctric or gas or any service"*.

**They are right, and the capability has existed in the database for weeks.** A base is narrowed
by **THREE** things before `resolve_base_charge` picks one: the **service** (`charges.service_id`),
the **meter size** (`ChargeCodeAmount.size_class`) and the **account type**
(`charges.applies_to_customer_classes` — a JSON list of platform `account_types.code` values,
`NULL` or `[]` meaning every class). Its own docstring quotes the PO's earlier words —
*"and Account type you will have select 1 base charge out of so many charges … then you need to
derive which base rate to select"* — and states the exact case: **water base is $8.00 residential
and $15.00 commercial, one service and two amounts.** That data is in the shipped fixture.

⚠ **WHAT WAS MISSING WAS TWO PICKERS, AND ONE SCREEN ACTIVELY DENIED THE COLUMN EXISTED.** The
charge-code wizard rendered a stated absence reading *"A charge code carries no customer-class
column, so it cannot be limited to one."* — **false since the column landed**. The rate-schedule
wizard admitted its own half in a fold-away note: *"A rate schedule can be limited to one
customer class, and this screen does not offer the picker yet."* So no clerk could express what
the engine could already price, and every screen read as though one service had one base.

**The fix is two pickers and one label, not a schema change:** a customer-class picker on the
charge code, a customer-class picker on the rate schedule, and the base cell naming the code
**and** the class it resolved from (`BASE-W-RES · Residential`).

⚠ **AND `applies_to_customer_classes` DOES NOT MAKE TWO MATCHING BASE CODES LEGAL — IT MAKES
THEM SEPARABLE.** Where two survive the narrowing the engine still refuses and names both
(`DEF-468`). Two codes on one service is now how a utility prices two classes; it is not a
precedence question and nothing chooses between them silently.

## 2026-09-08 · BASE RATES STAY ON THE CHARGE CODE — asked, considered, declined with a worked case

PO: *"shall we capture base rates directly in rate schedule itself instead of charge code; that
will allow us to consolidate all rates at one place"*. A fair question, and the answer is no.

**The case that decides it is the PO's own ruling of 2026-08-27** (`base_charge_only_units`,
closing `OQ-531`): a master account's bill carries the **base charges of every vacant unit** on
its premises. A vacant unit has no occupying account, therefore no plan, therefore **no rate
schedule**. Put the base on the schedule and those units have nothing to charge, and the
landlord's bill silently loses a line per empty unit — the class of failure that does not show
up in testing.

Three supporting reasons, none sufficient alone:
* **A base charge is a bill LINE, and only a charge code knows how to be one** — GL account,
  taxability, waivability, *show as its own line on the bill*. A rate schedule carries a GL
  account and none of the rest.
* **One code serves many schedules.** Change `BASE-W-RES` once and every schedule and plan
  carrying it follows. On the schedule it is N numbers and N chances to mistype one.
* **This would be the base's THIRD home.** The engine once read it from
  `tariff_versions.base_charge`, which defaults to `0` and which no tenant had typed into, so
  **every bill this product produced charged $0.00 for base** (`DEF-154`). `BR-RAT-088` then
  moved it to the charge code and calls a schedule still carrying one *"a migration artefact
  that must be refused"*.

**What the PO actually wanted is a SCREEN outcome, not a storage one** — see all the rates in
one place. The base is already shown on the rate schedule, read-only, per size, now named with
its class and linked to the code that owns it. If that is not enough, the offered next step is
to let a clerk EDIT the base from that screen while it stays STORED on the charge code: one
number, one home, two doors, no migration, and neither the vacant-unit nor the $0.00 failure is
reachable. Offered to the PO; not built.

## 2026-09-08 · THE CHARGE CODE'S FIRST STEP — SIGNED OFF, AND WHY IT LOST THREE THINGS

PO: *"all are good now"*, after three rounds. What the sign-off ratifies, so nobody rebuilds it:

**The type is a SELECT, not five radio cards.** Five cards each carrying a five-word hint took a
third of the screen to ask one question with one answer. The hints are not lost — they are a
column in the table below, where five options can be read side by side, which is how a person
picks between five things.

⚠ **AND THE TYPE DECIDES WHAT THE NEXT STEP ASKS FOR, WHICH NOTHING SAID.**
`ChargeCodeWizard.stepTwoSections()` maps it: `recurring → recurrence + proration`,
`one_time → proration`, `refundable → deposit`, `penalty → event`, and **`adjustment → nothing`,
because it is absent from the map and falls through to `[]`**. A clerk met that for the first
time *after* pressing Continue. The table states it before the choice, which is also when the
choice is still cheap to change. Adjustment's empty row is drawn with its reason — an
adjustment has no recurrence, no deposit and no trigger — because a blank row reads as a screen
that failed to load.

**Help appears only where it prevents a refusal.** Seven fields carried eight lines of it. What
survives: the code is uppercased and must be unique, and blank customer classes means every
class. *Description (shown on the bill)* needs no sentence explaining that it is shown on the
bill. This is B14 rule 32 applied literally, after the PO said *"too much content"* for the
fifth time.

**Step 1 is identity only.** The customer class moved to step 2 — see below.

## 2026-09-08 · AN AMOUNT DIFFERS BY CLASS **AND** CAPACITY, AND ONLY TWO OF THREE COULD BE WRITTEN

PO: *"Conenction fees, disconnections fees, deposites, penalties - these and simialr to these
are based on consumer classes - currenlty I cannot set differnt deposites for differnt calsses.
based charges are based on customer category and capacility of the assets or units"*.

**The engine narrows an amount by THREE things — service, customer class, connection size — and
the screens could express two.** The class was an inclusion list on the CODE
(`charges.applies_to_customer_classes`); the size was a flat table on the AMOUNT
(`charge_code_amounts`, unique on `(tenant_id, charge_id, size_class)`). So *residential 2" is
$45 and industrial 6" is $220* had no single place to be written. Drawn now as **one grid,
classes down and sizes across**, which is the shape a utility actually prices in.

⚠ **WHAT THE GRID COSTS IS ONE COLUMN, AND IT IS NOT A LANE'S TO ADD.**
`charge_code_amounts` has no account-type column, so a class cannot be a row. Until it does, the
supported answer is **one code per class** — `CONN-RES`, `CONN-IND` — each with its own size
amounts, which prices correctly and reads as a workaround. The grid is drawn as the design and
the workaround stated beneath it; **adding the column is the PO's call and is recommended**,
because two codes puts the deposit story (already a grid) and the fee story (not a grid) in
permanently different shapes for no reason a utility would recognise.

⚠ **AND TWO OF THE FOUR THINGS THE PO NAMED ALREADY WORK — SOMEWHERE ELSE, WHICH IS THE REAL
FINDING.** **A deposit is not a charge code at all.** `plan_deposit_rules` is keyed
`(rate_plan, account_type_id)` — a class × amount grid — and has been since `BR-RAT-020/023`.
The late fee is the same shape: its percentage, minimum and grace are plan settings. So
*"currently I cannot set different deposits for different classes"* was **false and reasonable
to believe**, because the charge code is where a person looks and no screen pointed anywhere
else. Screen 02 now carries a table naming, for each kind of charge, how it varies by class and
**where you set it**. The lesson generalises past this case: when one question is answered in
two objects, the screens must say which — an absence on the screen a person opens is
indistinguishable from the feature not existing.

## 2026-09-08 — FOUR RULINGS ON WHAT A PLAN CARRIES, AND ONE OF THEM WAS ALREADY RULED

Put to the Product Owner as four gaps found by reading the plan wizard against
the model while redrawing it. All four answered in one reply.

### 1 · Customer sub-type on a plan — NOT REQUIRED

`rate_plans` carries `account_subtype_id`, the API accepts it, accounts carry a
sub-type and it imports from a spreadsheet — and no wizard step asks for one.
Raised as the only true product gap of the four.

**PO ruling, verbatim:** *"Customer sub-type is never asked, and the plan stores
one - not required; - i will add it as charge code"*.

So a utility that needs different pricing for, say, multi-family inside the
Residential class expresses it as a **charge code**, not as a plan sub-type. No
step is added. `account_subtype_id` stays on the model, written by nothing in
the wizard; it is not retired here because nothing was asked about retiring it.

### 2 · The grace-day basis — CONFIRMED, KEEP IT ON SCREEN

`plan_penalty_rules.grace_mode` decides whether grace days run from the bill
date or the due date — which decides **which day** a late fee lands — and the
wizard drawing had no control for it.

**PO ruling, verbatim:** *"The grace-day basis was in the same position - this
is okay"*.

⚠ **SUPERSEDED WITHIN THE HOUR BY RULING 5 BELOW**, which takes the whole
late-fee block off the plan. The basis is still a real fact that must be
recorded somewhere — the ruling above says so — and ruling 5 says where: the
charge code, not the plan. Left here because *"this is okay"* was a genuine
answer to a genuine gap, and the reason it moved is worth reading.

### 3 · The plan's own late-fee minimum and percentage — ALREADY RULED 2026-09-07

**PO ruling, verbatim:** *"The plan stores its own late-fee minimum and
percentage alongside the late-fee charge code. - we should not have this - we
will take it from charge code"*.

⚠ **THIS IS THE SAME RULING THE PO MADE THE DAY BEFORE, AND IT IS ALREADY
BUILT.** `CR-078` / `BR-RAT-1011`, 2026-09-07, verbatim: *"you ahve to take late
fees form charge code mentione din the plan - if plan doent provide you that
charge code then you have to put zero on late payment"* — finance re-signed the
same day, shipped as `2.228.0`. `late_fee_terms_for_plan` reads `percent` and
`minimum` off the charge code the plan names; a plan naming none charges
`$0.00`.

**So the PO was asked to decide something the repo had already decided**, which
is exactly the failure CLAUDE.md law 13 exists to prevent, and the grep that law
prescribes would have found it: `BR-RAT-1011` is in this file. Recorded here as
the miss it was, not as a new decision.

What is genuinely left is narrower and is **not** a question for the PO: the
ruling moved the READER and left the WRITER. `plan_penalty_rules.late_fee_min`
and `late_fee_pct` are still validated by the API and still served by the
selector though nothing reads them, and `RatePlan.late_fee_charge`'s own comment
still says *"`PlanPenaltyRule.late_fee_pct` NULL falls back to the tenant's"*,
which was true before `CR-078` and is false now. Filed as **`DEF-RAT-4660`**.

### 4 · Proration per plan — WANTED, AND IT COLLIDES WITH A FROZEN FINANCE RULE

Raised as: nothing on a plan says what happens when a customer joins or leaves
part-way through a cycle.

**PO ruling, verbatim:** *"yes we should give option to user to select this"*.

⚠ **THE STATEMENT THIS WAS ANSWERING WAS WRONG AND THE CORRECTION CHANGES THE
ANSWER'S COST.** The gap was put to the PO as *"proration lives on the charge
code, so it cannot differ per plan"*. It does not live on the charge code: the
charge-code wizard names *Part-period charging* as a **stated absence** —
*"cutting the amount to the days a customer actually had the service … is not
stored on a charge code yet"* — and nothing stores it anywhere.

**Proration is `B4.3`, and `B4.3` is ❄️ FROZEN and finance-signed**: by calendar
days, one `service_days / cycle_days` factor for the whole account, the base
charge **always** prorated, usage prorated only when there is no move-in read
(amended 2026-08-11, PO/finance, HUMAN-GUIDE §6). `GT-3` pins it: a move-in on
day 16 of 30 with a `$30.50` base gives **`$15.25`**.

So letting a plan choose *charge the whole period* would contradict *the base
charge is always prorated* on a signed figure. Under CLAUDE.md's change process
step 2 that is a **STOP**: it needs a finance re-sign through HUMAN-GUIDE §6,
not a chat instruction. It is drawn in the wireframe as a **proposal marked as
awaiting that re-sign**, and no code is written against it.

**The narrow version that needs no re-sign, offered as the alternative:** the
plan states which of B4.3's existing answers applies to it — nothing new, a
read-back of the frozen rule per plan — which is documentation rather than a
choice. Whether that is worth having is with the PO.


### 5 · The late-fee block and the deposits block leave the plan entirely

Raised implicitly by drawing them on step 6, minutes after ruling 2.

**PO ruling, verbatim:** *"please note in plan - we dont need these - we have
added them in charge code - When a bill is late / Late fee / LATE — Late payment
fee, 1.5% of the amount / Grace days / 10 / Counted from / The due date / A bill
due 09/20 that is unpaid on 09/30 is charged 1.5%. / Leave the late fee empty
and this plan charges nothing for a late bill. // Deposits / Customer class /
Deposit / Residential 150.0000 Remove / Commercial 400.0000 Remove"*.

**Both blocks go. The principle underneath is the one the PO has now applied
five times in one day, and it is worth stating once as a rule:** *a plan names
charge codes; the charge code carries the money and everything that varies it.*
Amounts vary by customer class and by connection size, and the charge code got
both of those today — so a deposit of `$150.00` for Residential and `$400.00`
for Commercial is one charge code with a class column, not two rows on every
plan that exists. A late fee is the same: `CR-078` already reads its percentage
and its minimum off the charge code, and the timing terms follow the money.

⚠ **AND THE PLAN DOES NOT LOSE THE ABILITY TO NAME ONE — IT ALREADY NAMES IT
TWICE.** `LATE · Late payment fee · 1.5% of the amount · On an event` is on
**step 4** with every other charge code the plan carries. The step 6 picker was
a *second* place to name the same code, which is the duplication these rulings
keep removing. Removing it removes the duplicate, not the capability.

**Where they show instead: the REVIEW.** Step 8 lists the late fee and the
deposits under Billing terms, read-only, sourced from the attached charge codes
and marked as coming from them — the same treatment the PO ruled for base
charges earlier the same day (*"we might have multiple base charges so in review
we will show the correct ones"*). A reviewer still sees what the plan does; they
just cannot set it in two places.

⚠ **WHAT THIS DOES NOT DECIDE, AND IT IS THE ONE THING A LANE MUST NOT ASSUME:**
`plan_penalty_rules` still exists and still carries `grace_days` and
`grace_mode`, and `plan_deposit_rules` still exists and is what the customers
lane reads for a deposit (`BR-CUS-023`, `BR-RAT-020/023`). This ruling is about
**where a clerk sets them**, not about which table stores them. Whether the two
tables are retired, and what reads a deposit once it is a charge code, is not
answered here and is open.

## 2026-09-08 — THE PLANS & RATES SCREEN RULINGS, AND WHY EACH ONE

Twenty-odd rulings across one working session, on the wireframe the PO reviewed
screen by screen. The drawings live outside the repo by standing PO instruction
(*"dont write research in repo - just pick up the values that we need to set"*);
the DECISIONS are here, because a drawing nobody can find is a decision nobody
inherits.

### The rule underneath most of them, stated once

**A plan names charge codes; the charge code carries the money and everything
that varies it.** The PO applied this five times in one day — to deposits, to
late fees, to base charges, to customer sub-type and to per-class pricing — and
every time the answer was the same shape: one code with a class column beats a
row repeated on every plan that exists.

### Tax wizard · four steps became three

The Remittance step left the wizard entirely. `taxes` carries 37 fields, the
server requires three to save one (`name`, `kind`, `jurisdiction`), and exactly
**19 can never be changed once a tax is live** — `TAX_RATE_HISTORY_FIELDS`. The
wizard now asks for those 19 and stops; the other 18 are edited on the tax's own
page for the life of the tax. Not one field on the old step 3 is frozen by a
bill, so collecting them before the first bill was asking early and asking twice.
**`effective_from` moved to step 2** — it was the one frozen field on that step,
buried among seven that are not.

Code, bill label and tax type also left step 1. That dissolved the paragraph
explaining *tax type is not the same as the basis on the next step*: **a sentence
written to undo a collision is cheaper to fix by removing the collision.**

### Tax view · four tabs became three, then Remittance folded in too

PO, verbatim: *"overview and Remittance & filings - you can merge it in Overview
only"*. This SUPERSEDES the argument made earlier the same day for keeping
Remittance separate (a different job for an outside bookkeeper). Overview ·
Plans · Audit.

### Discounts · a choice of more than two is a dropdown

PO, verbatim: *"these should be drop down"*, for Type (five radios) and for
Enrolment. Now the pattern, ruled twice — the charge code's Type on 2026-09-06
and this. **The sentence explaining each option moves INTO the option**, so a
reader no longer counts across a row of radios to match the third sentence to
the third button.

⚠ **The enrolment dropdown made a refusal unnecessary, which is the better
outcome.** *Automatic enrolment* plus *proof required* was an impossible
combination the product policed with its best inline refusal message. Three real
answers in one dropdown, and the impossible fourth cannot be expressed. **A
refusal that can no longer fire beats a refusal written well** — and the message
is not lost, it is the model every other inline check was written from.

### One action set on every detail screen

PO, verbatim: *"the button duplicate retire and edit as per other screen make it
uniform for all screen"*. Five detail screens carried five different sets: the
same button called **Edit**, **Edit rates**, **Edit as new version** and
**Correct with a new version**; Retire in the middle on two and last on two; a
quiet outline on three and the loud primary on two. **Duplicate · Edit · Retire**,
in that order, at that weight, on all five. What editing DOES still differs — and
that belongs in a sentence under the title, never in a fourth name for the same
button. A hold stays where a hold is true (Duplicate on a plan).

### Plan wizard · the eight steps stay, the content does not

* **Step 2 · services is a multi-select**, not five tick-boxes for a list of
  eleven; the switched-off services are named INSIDE the list, greyed, with
  where to switch them on.
* **The outside-city surcharge stopped asking for arithmetic.** *"Type 1.15 to
  charge 15% more"* is a multiplier a clerk computes, in a product where a
  neighbouring field takes a percentage and another takes a fraction — **15
  typed into it would have charged fifteen times the bill.** It is a plain
  question with two answers, then a percentage that reads back *a $100.00 bill
  outside the city becomes $115.00*.
* **Step 3 lost the base-charge column** — PO: *"dont show base charge here let
  user only select the rate schedule; we might have multipe base charges so in
  review we will show the cororect ones"*. It showed ONE base per service where
  a service can have several, because the code is picked by class AND connection
  size, and it was read-only anyway.
* **Add buttons on charges, taxes and discounts.** Rows could only be removed, so
  a plan built with the wrong thing had to be started again.
* **Step 7 contradicted itself in two lines.** *"Who may be put on this plan"* is
  a permission; *"they never block an assignment"* is the opposite; both were on
  screen four inches apart with the same fact said a third time below. It is not
  a gate — a row like *Meter size · is · 5/8 inch* is a written note, stored,
  shown, and **read by nothing at billing time**. The heading now agrees with the
  fact, and the dates moved out because dates are not eligibility.

### Step 8 and the plan's Overview are now the same card

PO supplied a reference layout and ruled: *"there is no point user clicking on 10
thing to review the entire plan"*. Seven read tabs — Overview, Rate schedules,
Base rates, Charges, Taxes, Discounts, Eligibility — became **one banded card**,
and the review step uses the same component with the same bands in the same
order: **rate schedule → charge codes → discounts → taxes → other terms**, which
is the order a bill is made in. A clerk who checks a plan before publishing
recognises the page afterwards.

Three things the merge exposed, each worth keeping:
* **Base rates was two columns printing the same number**, kept only so a rare
  disagreement between plan and charge code would show.
* **Rate schedules, Charges and Taxes each had a column that could print an
  apology** — *"this was not in the list this page read"* — because the row came
  from the plan and its cells from a separate scan of the first 200 records.
* **A count is nothing without its denominator**: *28 of 74*, not 28; and the
  combined **7.25%** a clerk was adding up in their head on every call.

Presentation rules ratified with it: **an absent value is italic and grey, never
bold** (*not set*, *no rate*, *nothing dated*) — a plan with no city tax looked
identical to one with a city tax of zero; **figures right-aligned in the
monospaced face** so a column can be scanned; and **every row states when it
applies** in plain words. The band labels were first drawn at 9.5px grey and the
PO rejected them — *"too small and grey colored to be recognized by user"* — so a
section heading gets its own ground, a marker in the accent, real size and real
weight.

### The plan's second tab is Units, and it did not exist

PO: *"second tab can be units and last tab can be audit"*. The plan showed a
count of 74 and never said 74 of what. **A plan attaches to a UNIT**, so it is
units — and the vacant unit is the row that matters: no account, no customer, and
a base charge that still reaches the owner's bill. Services on it use the
badge the product already ships (`ratingShared.tsx`), because **the letter cannot
be derived from the name** — six of eleven services collide on their initial.

### Every screen now names its own server work

PO: *"in case there are any back end related changes - please map it to respect
screen level details section"*. Eight screens carry one; one says explicitly that
it needs nothing. The three that matter:

1. **`charge_code_amounts` has no customer-class column at all** — it is unique
   on `(tenant_id, charge_id, size_class)` — so a $45.00 residential connection
   fee and an $85.00 commercial one are the same row and the class × size grid
   cannot be stored. Needs the column, the column in the unique key, and a
   migration. ⚠ **`charges.applies_to_customer_classes` is NOT this**: it says
   who a code reaches, not what each of them pays.
2. **`GET /taxes/matched-premises` takes the boundary and nothing else.** The
   count now narrows on class and service too; until they are passed, the number
   on screen is the boundary's count and not the tax's reach — the one way that
   safeguard misleads rather than fails.
3. **The outside-city conversion must happen on the server.** The plan stores a
   multiplier and the screen now asks for a percentage; a scale conversion
   written into a screen is the same trap one layer up.

Two are honest absences rather than tasks: no read works out how many accounts
are ELIGIBLE for a discount, and no endpoint lists the units on a plan (the count
exists; the list does not).

---

## 2026-09-08 — CR-087 A1: what one charge code is allowed to say about price

`CR-087` task A1 asked for one thing — a customer-class column on
`charge_code_amounts` — and building it needed five judgments the signed rules do
not make. Nothing here was put to the Product Owner and nothing here contradicts
a signed rule; it is recorded so the next agent does not have to re-derive it,
and it is what the human-review ledger row of the same date asks a reviewer to
look at.

**1 · The class is a CODE, not a UUID, and that is a deliberate break with the
nearest precedent.** `plan_deposit_rules` keys its customer class with
`account_type_id`, a UUID. This column does not follow it. The reason is the
resolver rather than taste: `resolution.AccountFacts.customer_class` is a code
string and `charges.applies_to_customer_classes` is a JSON list of code strings,
and the chain narrows by comparing those two. A UUID here would put two columns
on the same object that narrow by different keys, and would force an id→code
lookup on the hot path of every read.

**2 · NULL is not a class, it is EVERY class.** This is what makes the change
additive: every row written before today keeps pricing exactly what it priced,
and the reading matches the one `applies_to_customer_classes` already takes,
where NULL or `[]` means every class.

**3 · A class-specific row BEATS the every-class row.** A code carrying $45.00
for everybody and $85.00 for Commercial quotes a commercial connection **$85.00**
and a residential one **$45.00**. The database cannot express this — two partial
unique constraints keep the rows apart and say nothing about which wins — so the
precedence lives in the two reads and is asserted by test, not assumed.

**4 · TWO partial unique constraints, because one would not work.** PostgreSQL
treats NULLs as DISTINCT in a unique index, so a single constraint over
`(tenant, charge, size_class, customer_class)` would have allowed **two
every-class rows for one size** — exactly the duplicate the old three-column key
refused. The pair is `uq_charge_code_amounts_size_and_class` (where the class is
NOT NULL) and `uq_charge_code_amounts_tenant_charge_size` (where it IS).

**5 · THE FINDING THAT WAS NOT IN THE CR, AND IT IS THE ONE THAT WOULD HAVE COST
MONEY.** `charge_code_amounts` is read from more places than the CR names.
`selectors.base_charge_from_charge_code` — `BR-RAT-088`'s live base read — already
TAKES a customer class and uses it to decide which CODES apply, then built its
per-size dictionary with **no ordering and no narrowing at all**. The moment two
rows could exist for one size, that read kept whichever the database returned
last: a residential 5/8" water connection was quoted **$34.00**, the commercial
base, with no error and no refusal. It is fixed with the same rule as the
catalogue, and the test was watched failing on that exact figure first.

⚠ **The general shape is worth more than the fix: a column added to a table is
only added once, and every read of that table is a place it has to be added
again.** `size_amounts` is built in **two** separate places in `selectors.py`
(`_charge_size_amounts` for the plan detail's charge rules, and `charge_row` for
the charge code's own screen) and adding the field to one of them served a field
that existed on one screen and not the other. Both now carry a comment naming the
other.

**What is NOT decided here and is nobody's ruling yet:** what a bill should do
when a class-specific row exists for a size the every-class row does not state.
Today the class row wins and the size is priced. That was never put to anyone, it
is named in the ledger row as outside the signature, and a reader who needs it
decided should raise it rather than infer it from this paragraph.

---

## 2026-09-08 · CR-087 lane C — what the discount screens actually needed, and three places the drawn spec and the running code disagreed

Lane C of CR-087 owns the discount screens and the rate schedule detail's action
row. Four judgments below were ours to make; each is written with its worked
figure because the rules ran out and a question would have been the failure to
decide (CLAUDE.md law 13).

### 1 · The server already refused the impossible pair. What it did not do was say who to blame.

`PRB-14` says a POST setting *automatic* enrolment together with *proof required*
is **"accepted and stored"** today. **It is not, and has not been since CR-013
part 3.** Measured at the route on real PostgreSQL before a line was changed: the
POST comes back **422**, `code=VAL-002`, `key=rating.discounts.automatic_with_mandatory_proof`.
`_validate_version` GATE 1 has been there all along.

**What was actually wrong is one field name.** The refusal named
`proof_required` and nothing else — correct while the screen drew a tick-box for
it, because the message landed on the box the clerk had just ticked. With the
pair replaced by one dropdown (below) **there is no tick-box left to point at**,
and a field error naming a control the form does not draw is a refusal nobody
can act on. Both halves make the contradiction, so the refusal now names both
and a screen highlights whichever control it has.

The document's claim is filed as a defect against the blueprint rather than
quietly corrected, on CR-087 §1's own precedent — *"a DEFECT in the document, not
the product"*. The gate stays whatever any one form can draw, for the reason
`DEF-384` gives on a different endpoint: a client that cannot express a state is
not a server that refuses it.

### 2 · The proof list opens with the option that needs it

GATE 2 on the server requires *accepted proof kinds* **only when proof is
required**. The wizard drew all ten tick-boxes on every programme, so a discount
that asks for nothing offered ten decisions with no consequence. They are behind
the third dropdown option now — which is the moment a utility actually decides to
demand a document, and where BR-RAT-079's *Restricted* marking belongs.

### 3 · The worked example on step 4 went, rather than becoming live

The second-approval panel carried five sentences: the rule, the conflict between
two signed policies, a worked example (**$7,332 a year is $611 a month**) and the
approval authority. It is **two** now, and **both bars stay because the bars are
the question** — $500 against a projected monthly subsidy, $10,000 against the
budget cap typed above.

⚠ **The obvious improvement was refused deliberately.** Quoting the clerk's OWN
budget cap back at them as a monthly figure means dividing money on the screen,
which is `DEF-364`'s shape exactly: the server owns every money conversion and
this wizard prints no figure it did not receive. So the example is gone rather
than computed. Who may activate is not lost either — it is on the two lifecycle
buttons at the foot of the review step, where a person is about to press one.

### 4 · The enrolment dropdown's third option is not a value any vocabulary holds

`discount_versions` stores `enrolment_mode` and `proof_required` in two columns
and CR-087 moves no column, so the screen's three choices —
`automatic`, `apply_and_approve`, `apply_and_approve_with_proof` — are a
SCREEN vocabulary translated to and from that pair.

**A stored pair that is the impossible one resolves to *with proof*, and the
direction is a decision.** No row can hold it, but the function must answer for
one rather than render a dropdown with nothing selected. Keeping the PROOF and
dropping *automatic* grants no subsidy nobody checked; the other reading would
enrol every qualifying account on a programme written to demand a document.

---

## 2026-09-08 — CR-087 LANE D: FIVE JUDGMENTS THE RULINGS DID NOT COVER, MADE HERE RATHER THAN ASKED

The PO ruled the plan wizard's steps 1–7 on 2026-09-08 (the entries above). Five
things those rulings imply but do not state had to be decided before a line was
written. CLAUDE.md law 13: *a judgment call recorded in the decision log with its
reasoning is the deliverable; a question is the failure to make one.* Each is
recorded with the worked figure it turns on.

### 1 · The outside-city surcharge: the API takes a PERCENT and the COLUMN does not move

The ruling says the screen asks for a percentage and *"the conversion belongs on
the server … It must not be converted in the browser."* It offers two shapes and
picks neither: *"Either the API accepts a percent and converts once, or the column
changes."*

**Decided: the API accepts a percent; the column keeps the multiplier.**

`rate_plans.outside_city_factor` is read by `resolution.py`, `gather.py`,
`resolution_catalogue.py` and the audit snapshot, and it is the number every
priced line is MULTIPLIED by. Changing the column would move a value four
readers already agree on, on a 🔒 money path, to save one conversion on one
screen. Adding a second accepted key on the way IN moves nothing that has been
priced.

So `PLAN_FIELDS` gains **`outside_city_percent`**, `POST`/`PATCH` accept it, and
the server converts once:

    multiplier = 1 + (percent / 100), quantized to SIX places

**Worked, and it is the CR's own figure:** a clerk types `15`; the server stores
`1.150000`; a `$100.00` bill outside the city becomes `$115.00`. `0` stores
`1.000000` — *somebody typed nothing extra*, which is a different stored fact
from NULL (*this plan does not surcharge*), and the selector already refuses to
collapse those two.

**A payload naming BOTH keys is refused, and that is deliberate.** Two answers to
one question cannot be reconciled by precedence without one of them silently
losing; the refusal names both fields. `outside_city_factor` stays accepted
because the seeder, the sample fixture and every integration that already writes
a multiplier must keep working — this is additive, not a replacement.

**The read half:** `plan_detail` serves `outside_city_percent` (derived,
`(factor − 1) × 100`, six places) and `outside_city_percent_display` (two places,
the string a screen prints) BESIDE the unchanged `outside_city_factor`. Percent
to six places, display two, per CLAUDE.md hard rule 2. Nothing client-side scales
anything.

### 2 · Removing the step-6 late-fee picker must not make a new plan charge $0.00

Ruling 5 of the day takes the late-fee block off the plan, and the picker for
`late_fee_charge` with it — it was *"a second place to name the same code"*.

**The hazard nobody stated:** `create_plan` reads `"late_fee_charge" in cleaned`
to tell *the payload said nothing* from *the payload said null*. A wizard that
kept sending the key as `""` → `null` would create every new plan with **no late
fee at all** — `$0.00` on every late bill, which is `CR-078`'s ruled-but-empty
case arriving by accident on every plan built after this change.

**Decided: the payload stops sending the key entirely.** A create then takes
`default_late_fee_charge()` — the tenant's seeded `LATE` code, written onto the
plan where a human can see it — and an edit leaves the stored value untouched.
The capability is not lost: `LATE` is attached on **step 4** with every other
charge code, and step 8 reads the terms off it.

### 3 · The four penalty fields and every deposit row are PRESERVED, never cleared

The ruling moves where a clerk SETS them and explicitly keeps the tables:
*"`plan_penalty_rules` still exists and still carries `grace_days` and
`grace_mode`, and `plan_deposit_rules` still exists and is what the customers
lane reads for a deposit."*

**Decided: the draft keeps carrying `penalty` and `deposit_rules`, reads them
back from the plan, and re-posts them unchanged.** This is `DEF-422`'s discipline
applied again — a wizard that dropped a field from the payload because it stopped
drawing a control would silently clear a stored fact on the next rename. A plan
that today asks Commercial for `$400.00` still asks for it after a rename through
this wizard; the only thing that changed is that the wizard is no longer where
that figure is typed.

### 4 · What "a filtered catalogue" means, stated as a rule so the number is checkable

The PO asked for an Add button *"they can select ad nad from the chagre code"*
and the CR sizes it as *"6 codes, not the utility's 41"*. Nothing says what the
filter IS.

**Decided: a plan may add a charge code when BOTH are true —**
  * **class** — the code's `applies_to_customer_classes` is empty (*every class*)
    or contains this plan's customer-class code; and
  * **service** — the code's `service` is null (*any service*) or is one of the
    services this plan carries.

Both halves are already stored and already served on `charge_row`, so this
narrows a list rather than inventing a taxonomy. An EMPTY list and a NAMED list
are different facts and the filter reads them that way, which is the posture
`charge_row` itself takes.

**Worked on the demo utility:** a Residential plan carrying Electric alone offers
the codes scoped to Residential-or-all AND to Electric-or-all; every Commercial-
only code and every Water/Gas/Sewer-only code drops out. The count on screen is
stated as *N of M*, never as a bare N — a count without its denominator is the
thing the same day's rulings removed from the review.

**A code already on the plan whose row the filter would now exclude is NEVER
dropped.** It stays listed with its own note. Narrowing what may be ADDED is a
convenience; silently removing what a plan already carries would be a pricing
change nobody asked for.

### 5 · A service with no rate schedule is refused on step 3, and the refusal is a REFUSAL

The blueprint: *"a service left with no rate schedule was only refused five
screens later."* It does not say whether step 3 should refuse or merely warn.

**Decided: step 3 refuses Continue.** Every other presence gate in this wizard
sits on the step that collects the value, and the whole complaint is that this
one did not. It caps at six words (B14 rule 33) and names the service.

⚠ **It refuses CONTINUE and never SAVE DRAFT.** `BR-RAT-031` allows a
half-finished draft, and a clerk building a plan ahead of its rates is a real
case the step-2 copy already defends. What has gone is discovering it on the
final press.

### Footnote · two lanes filed the same defect with the same id, forty minutes apart

`file_defect.py` allocated **`DEF-RAT-4663`** to this lane for the stale
assertion at `PlanWizard.test.tsx:704`. By the time the work was ready to push,
the tip already carried `DEF-RAT-4663` — **lane A, the same number, the same
defect**, filed minutes earlier from its own worktree, where this lane's
allocator could not see it. Both allocations were correct arithmetic against the
world each could see, which is exactly the shape CLAUDE.md law 11 records for
2026-09-04.

**The row was DROPPED rather than renumbered, and that is the part worth
reading.** Law 11's clause says renumber when two lanes take one number; it
assumes two DIFFERENT defects. Here the content was the same finding, so a
renumbered row would have been a duplicate entry in a 2,339-row register — the
thing that reads as a register rather than as an error. Lane A's row stands, and
it names this lane in its own prevention field: *"that file is lane D's under
CR-087 D3, which is rewriting the same step."*

**What caught it was the unconditional re-derivation at push time**, not a gate:
rebuilding the register from the pinned tip put lane A's row and this lane's
side by side. The check that mattered was reading them, not counting them.

## 2026-09-08 · CR-087 lane C, part two — the discount detail's three tabs, the count that decides take-up, and one action set on two screens

### 5 · What "the count that decides take-up" turned out to be, and what it is NOT

The redraw asks for the missing take-up figure and says the count already on the
screen *"says accounts where what it counts is units a plan is assigned to"*.
**On the discount detail that second half is not true of any count there**, and
checking it is what produced the rest of this entry.

`enrolled` counts `discount_enrolments` rows, and that table carries an FK to
`customers.Account`. **It says accounts and it counts accounts.** Relabelling it
*units* would have made a true label false. The count that really does say
accounts over a query counting units is `schedule_applied_to_accounts` — whose
own docstring reads *"Units on a current assignment whose plan attaches this
schedule"* — served as `applied_to_accounts` and drawn on **four** labels across
the rate schedule and the plan. That is filed as `DEF-RAT-4664` for the lane that
owns those tiles, not fixed here.

**So the take-up denominator was BUILT rather than relabelled:**
`discount_offered_unit_count` — units on a CURRENT plan assignment whose plan
carries the discount — served as `offered_units` and drawn as a fourth tile,
*Offered to · 86 units on a plan carrying it*, beside *Enrolled accounts · 31
accounts with an open enrolment*.

⚠ **THE TWO ARE DELIBERATELY NOT DIVIDED INTO ONE ANOTHER.** They are different
populations: a vacant unit has no account and cannot enrol, so `31 of 86` drawn
as one fraction would assert that accounts and units are the same thing. Each
tile carries a caption saying what it counts, and a reader gets take-up by
reading two adjacent tiles that are both true.

⚠ **AND IT IS NOT CALLED *eligible*, WHICH IS WHAT `PRB-20` ASKS FOR.**
Eligibility on a discount is `eligibility_summary` — a sentence a person typed,
*"Age 65 or over"* — and nothing in this product evaluates one. **Offered is a
fact about plans and is computable; eligible is a fact about people and is not.**
Drawing the first under the second's name would be a wrong number rather than a
missing one, which is the exact distinction the tile it replaced was built on.
`PRB-20` stays open, and the Overview says in one sentence that neither a
month's subsidy nor a count of who qualifies is worked out anywhere.

### 6 · The tile that was replaced had never shown a figure

*Programme cost per month* held a quarter of the KPI strip and was an em-dash on
**every discount that has ever existed** — it needs a period-scoped aggregation
over issued bills and R6 is not wired into `apps/billing`. A permanently blank
tile is not a stated absence, it is furniture. The absence is now stated in
words on the Overview, in the same sentence as the eligibility gap, and the slot
carries a number.

### 7 · The discount's last tab is now called Audit, and it renders exactly what it did

Every other module in the product calls this tab `audit` — assets, premises,
units, accounts, bills, cycles, routes, work templates — and Plans & Rates alone
said *Versions*. The tab is renamed and **what it draws has not moved**: still
the object's own version table, never a filtered `audit_log` query. §10 is
emphatic that the wrong implementation is the plausible one, and the
source-as-text guard that keeps it honest is untouched. `isHistoryTab` is the one
place that knows both spellings, because the charge and the tax have not been
renamed yet and are other lanes' screens.

### 8 · A hold whose reason had quietly stopped being true

`Duplicate` and `Retire` on the definition detail were disabled carrying
*"Duplicate, Edit and Retire arrive with the full-page wizard for this object.
This screen reads a definition; it does not change one yet."* Two of the three
wizards have shipped since that was written, `Edit` is live on the charge and the
discount, and the screen changes a definition through three lifecycle acts —
**so the sentence was false in three of its clauses and read as a decision
somebody had taken.** That is hard-won law 2's mirror: a dead control over a live
screen.

What is still true is narrow, and is what it says now: **"Nothing copies or
retires this yet"** — six words, B14 rule 33's cap. And the hold carries the test
law 2 asks for: the day a `duplicateDiscount` or `retireCharge` lands in
`endpoints.ts`, `DefinitionDetail.test.tsx` goes red and names the buttons to
release.

### 9 · A test was stricter than the rule it cited, and E1 is what exposed it

`RateScheduleDetail.test.tsx` asserted **exactly one** `data-variant="primary"`,
citing BR-SHL-044. E1 makes the header *Duplicate · Edit · Retire* with the first
two at secondary weight and Retire in the danger tier, which leaves the page with
**none** — and BR-SHL-044 clause (c) says in as many words that *"a tab may
legitimately have NO header action"* and that the slot must accept empty. B14
rule 4 forbids a SECOND primary competing with the first; it does not require one
to exist. The assertion is now *at most one*, and the rule is unchanged.

`Edit rates` also lost its second word. *"No screen offers a fourth spelling of
Edit"* — the five detail screens carried `Edit`, `Edit rates`, `Edit as new
version` and `Correct with a new version`. What editing DOES still differs and
stays in a sentence on the screen.

### 10 · Two reds this lane did not cause, dated rather than dismissed

CLAUDE.md law 7's first habit, and both were measured rather than assumed.

* **Six discount-read tests** fail `assert 6 == 5` because CR-062 seeded a sixth
  sample discount and the fixtures still expect five. Re-measured with this
  lane's change reverted to the branch tip: the identical six fail. **The
  isolation triage of 2026-09-01 diagnosed this correctly in this very log and
  filed nothing**, so it has had no owner for a week — `DEF-RAT-4670`.
* **One plan-wizard test** asserts a sentence CR-078 deleted on 2026-09-07. The
  string is absent from the tip's own `en.json`, so the test cannot pass —
  `DEF-RAT-4671`.

Neither is CR-087's, and saying so with a date is the point: two lanes once
reported the same red in good faith as *"pre-existing, not mine"*, and one of
them had caused it.

## 2026-09-08 · CR-087 D4/D5/E1/E2 — the plan's review and its page become one card, and the seven judgments that took

**PO rulings this executes, verbatim, all of 2026-09-08:** *"can you merge all
these into 1 Overview / Rate schedules / Base rates / Charges / Taxes /
Discounts / Eligibility … there is no point user clicking on 10 thing to review
the entire plan. - second tab can be units and last tab can be audit"* · *"this
categories are too small and grey colored to be recohnized by user"* · *"for
services - use E and W we have build"* · *"the button duplicate retire and edit
as per other screen make it uniform for all screen"*.

Eight tabs became **Overview · Units · Audit**, and step 8 of the wizard and the
plan's page are now drawn by ONE component — `PlanSummaryCard.tsx` — in five
bands, in the order a bill is made in: **rate schedule → charge codes →
discounts → taxes → other terms**. Nothing was deleted; seven tabs' content is
in the card or in the two blocks around it.

**Seven judgments the rules did not settle, each with what it costs.**

**1 · The Rate schedule band's fourth column is the SCHEDULE'S NAME, not its
tier prices.** The blueprint draws `4.0000 · 6.5000 · 8.0000` under a *Rate*
heading. Those figures are on the tariff VERSION and are not served to this
screen; assembling them would be a second price renderer whose every figure this
screen invented. The column names the schedule a clerk clicks through to, and
the shape (*tiered by kgal*) sits beside it.

**2 · The "Change already dated" column is NOT repeated inside the card.** It
was a fifth column on the Rate schedules tab AND a banner above every tab. The
banner survives — it is the half that reaches a reader who never scrolls, and it
already names the schedule and formats the date through the one date formatter.
Saying it twice on one page is B14 rule 32 broken in the direction nobody
notices.

**3 · The Base column has ONE source, and the precedence decides it.**
`Base rates` drew the charge code's amount AND the plan's own, side by side,
kept so a rare disagreement would show. The card draws one column: the CODE's
amount where a code owns it (`BR-RAT-088`), the plan's stored figure where none
does, an absence where neither exists — **never `$0.00`, which reads as "this
service is free"**. `OQ-238`'s two-figure conflict is unchanged and is still
refused by the bill run; what moved is that the screen no longer draws two
columns printing the same number to surface it.

**4 · A binding the catalogue scan MISSED is not "no schedule".** The plan names
a tariff the scanned page did not carry. Drawing *no schedule* there would be a
lie told confidently, in italic, with every check green — and only one of those
two facts means the service is unpriced, which is a publishing refusal. The two
render differently.

**5 · The deposit rows show their amounts and NOT the customer class.**
`plan_deposit_rules` carries `account_type_id` and an amount; the plan's page
does not load the account-type vocabulary, and printing the id would break B14
rule 31. So one row states the amounts with *by customer class* beside them. The
wizard, which does hold the vocabulary, could name them and does not — one shape
for one band. **What this costs is stated rather than hidden:** a reader sees
`$150.00 · $400.00` and must open the plan to learn which class is which.

**6 · The take-up cell shows the ENROLLED count and names the missing half.**
The blueprint asks for *"28 of 74"*. The 74 would be the UNIT count, which
answers a different question, and nothing in the product works out how many
accounts are ELIGIBLE (`PRB-20`). A ratio one half of which is another
question's answer is worse than a bare count with its gap named.

**7 · `BR-SHL-044`'s single action slot now holds the DANGER tier, and no button
on the plan header is `primary`.** `E1` makes Duplicate and Edit secondary
weight and Retire the danger tier, so this page's one commit is destructive.
BR-SHL-044 asks for `status-pill → secondaries → ONE primary` and its own clause
(c) says the slot may be EMPTY, so it is about the slot holding one action
rather than about that action's colour. **The count in `PlanDetail.test.tsx`
moved from one `primary` to one `danger`** and is asserted in both directions,
so a lane that quietly restores a primary fails.

**`Edit as new version` is now `Edit`, and BR-RAT-037 has not moved an inch.**
E1 says no screen offers a fourth spelling of Edit. The builder still collects
the reason, the server still refuses without one, and the version still bumps —
what changed is that the button stopped carrying the policy in its label. **The
sub-line's sentence was a pointer that rotted the moment the label changed**: it
read *"Composition edits run through Edit as new version."*, naming a control by
a name that no longer exists. It now states the RULE instead of the control —
*"Editing a published plan writes a new version; this one keeps its own
history."* — in all eleven catalogues.

**Duplicate stays HELD with a five-word reason and an EXPIRY TEST.** B14 rule 33
caps a refusal at five or six words; the old sentence was 26. The hold rests on
one fact — no endpoint copies a plan — so the test asserts THAT FACT
(`endpoints.duplicatePlan` is undefined), not the disabled attribute, which
would pass forever. Hard-won law 2's other half: *when you write a hold, write
the test that fires when the hold expires, in the same commit*.

**PRB-19 · the combined tax rate is the SERVER's, and it closes a second defect
on the way.** `plan_detail` serves `tax_lines` — one row per tax that reaches
the plan, level first, with the authority, the name and the served percent — and
`combined_tax_rate_display`, summed on the stored six-place fractions and
rounded ONCE. 6.25% + 1.00% = **7.25%**, which a clerk was adding in their head
on every call. It also removes the browser-side join: this screen used to fetch
`GET /taxes` at 200 rows and match by jurisdiction, so a tax past that page
produced a cell reading *"this was not in the list this page read"*. That
request is gone. **A plan with no tax serves `null`, never `"0.00%"`** — *not
set* and *zero* are different facts, which is E2 one layer down.

**PRB-21 · the units, paged in SQL.** `GET /plans/{id}/units` hands the
paginator a QUERYSET, so `count` is a `COUNT` over the whole set and the page is
a `LIMIT`/`OFFSET`; only the page's rows are enriched through one new seam.
Every other list read in this module builds the full list and lets the API slice
it — correct at T7 and the exact breach CLAUDE.md names on `GET /outstandings`
at T5. The address is WALKED to the premises (hard rule 8) and services travel
as CODES so the screen draws the badge: the letter cannot be derived from the
name, six of the eleven collide.

**E2 · what "read as a band" was built to mean.** A band label is an `<h4>` at
`text-h5` with its own ground and an accent marker — the rejected version was
9.5px grey at 65% opacity. An absence is italic and grey; a figure is
right-aligned and tabular. The three are exported as constructors so an adapter
cannot invent a fourth kind, and the test asserts the DIFFERENCE between a *not
set* cell and a `0.00%` cell rather than the presence of one class.

**Two facts the merged tabs carried that the card cannot, kept as their own
lines on the Overview:** the units count has no inside/outside-city split
(`PRB-24` — `premises` has no `inside_city_limits` flag), and a schedule being
DRAFTED while its current prices are live never appears in the band, because
`schedule_card` fills `draft_version` only when nothing is in force. The second
is stated ALWAYS rather than only when something is pending — a plan with no
dated change is exactly where "nothing is coming" is most likely to be misread.

**A pre-existing red found, dated — and NOT filed, because a sibling had
already filed it.** `PlanWizard.test.tsx:704` asserts the sentence *"Anything
left blank falls back"*, which left all eleven catalogues on **2026-09-07 19:10
UTC** in commit `99e9e564` (CR-078 / `BR-RAT-1011`). This lane dated it with
`git log -S` rather than assuming — CLAUDE.md law 7's habit (1) says *was this
red before I started* is a claim about history and must be checked like one —
and then allocated `DEF-4670` for it.

⚠ **THAT ROW WAS DROPPED BEFORE IT REACHED THE BRANCH, AND HOW IT WAS CAUGHT IS
THE PART WORTH KEEPING.** `push_paths.sh`'s register guard refused the push,
naming two lines of the tip that the version about to be pushed did not contain:
`DEF-RAT-4670` and `DEF-RAT-4671`. Lane C had filed the *same* red minutes
earlier as **`DEF-RAT-4671`** — and had taken `DEF-RAT-4670` for a different
defect entirely. So this lane's allocation was both a DUPLICATE of one row and a
COLLISION with another, and `allocate.py --verify 4670` had answered *"still
free on every branch"* truthfully forty minutes before, because at that moment
it was.

**The lesson is the one law 11 already states and it is worth one more worked
case: an allocated id is a blob, and it goes stale exactly like a file.** The
verify is only true at the instant it runs; two lanes reading the register in
the same hour will both be right and will still collide. What made the
difference here was not the allocator — it was the guard reading the register as
ARITHMETIC at push time, which is the only check in the chain that runs after
the sibling has pushed.

## 2026-09-08 · CR-087 lane C — the revert this lane caused, how it was found, and the two lanes that built the same thing

### 11 · `REDERIVED_FROM_TIP=1` was true of thirteen paths and asserted over eighteen

`push_paths.sh` refused this lane's second push twice, both times correctly. The
first refusal named the eleven catalogues and the two registers — a sibling had
pushed to all thirteen. They were re-derived from the pinned tip, my keys and my
rows re-applied, and the push run again. It refused a second time on the
**base-is-the-tip** check that `DEF-GOV-4061` added, because by then the tip WAS
the base I was passing.

`REDERIVED_FROM_TIP=1` is the escape hatch for exactly that, and it was passed
honestly and wrongly: **thirteen of the eighteen named paths had been rebuilt
from the tip, and five had not.** Those five were source files, a sibling lane
had pushed to every one of them, and the push reverted all five.

⚠ **EVERY CHECK CLAUDE.MD LAW 11 PRESCRIBES PASSED ON IT.** The file count was
right. My own hunks were present. `git show` carried nothing foreign. The
frontend and backend suites were **green**, because the work I had deleted had
its own tests in files my push did not touch.

**What caught it was the numstat read as ARITHMETIC** — `55 insertions, 119
deletions` in a file I had only added a function to. That is the one check the
law names for this class, it is printed by the helper without being asked for,
and it works. The repair was a three-way merge rather than a force, so both
lanes' work is on the branch. Filed as `DEF-GOV-4674`.

**The lesson is about the flag, not the operator.** A flag that asserts a
property of *every* named path, passed by someone who has established it for
*most* of them, is a check that is one careless moment from being disabled. The
prevention filed with the defect is to make it take the paths it covers.

### 12 · Two lanes built the same mechanism in the same hour, under two names

CR-087 merges the tax's tabs (lane B) and the discount's (lane C) into one
Overview each. **Both lanes independently discovered that a merged tab is not a
longer list** — folding three or four tabs into one flat grid puts *Cap per
year* beside *Programme owner* — and both added the same thing to
`DefinitionPresentation`: several headed groups of fields, keyed by tab id,
winning over the flat `panels`.

One called it **`blocks`** with `DefinitionBlock {id, titleKey, noteKey?,
fields}`; the other called it **`sections`** with `DefinitionSection {headingKey,
fields}`. Lane B's landed first, so **`blocks` is the name and `sections` is
gone** — two mechanisms for one job is two places to fix a rendering bug and one
place to forget it.

The same thing happened one layer down, to the same two lanes, on the same
screen: both noticed that `Duplicate` and `Retire` were held behind a
thirty-two-word reason that had stopped being true, and both wrote a six-word
replacement — `notBuilt` and `heldNoRoute`. **`heldNoRoute` was retired from all
eleven catalogues** rather than left beside its twin.

⚠ **THE FINDING IS WORTH MORE THAN THE TIDY-UP.** Two lanes reading the same
screen against the same ruling reached for the same missing piece within an
hour, which says the piece was genuinely missing rather than either lane's
invention — and it says a CR that hands one shared component to four lanes
should name the shape they will all need before they start, or pay for it in
merges.

## 2026-09-08 — CR-085's remaining work, cut into waves

The Product Owner asked for *"wave 1 and 2"* of CR-085. Its **eleven** waves had all
landed, so what they were asking for is the first two waves of what is still open — the
portal blueprint's **24 specifications**, which `CR-085` §4 item 4 names as a scoping
decision nobody had taken.

**Nobody had cut them into waves, so this session did, and the cut is by WHAT A CUSTOMER
IS TRYING TO DO rather than by screen or by size.** A wave that is one job a person has
can be walked end to end and judged by whether that job got easier; a wave that is "six
screens" cannot.

| Wave | The job | Specifications |
|---|---|---|
| **1** | Money a customer is trying to control — the commitments they make, and the proof they get back | `CPB-02` autopay · `CPB-18` budget billing · `CPB-03` and `CPB-21` the plan we can offer · `CPB-22` and `CPB-01` the guest payment and its receipt |
| **2** | What a customer is trying to find out — what they used, what it cost, what is at their address | `CPB-06`, `CPB-07` usage · `CPB-08` why it costs this · `CPB-04`, `CPB-09` readings · `CPB-10` equipment |

**Left for later waves, deliberately:** documents (`CPB-14`, `15`, `19`, `20`), requests
(`CPB-05`, `11`, `12`), the dispute (`CPB-13`), the landing page (`CPB-24`), and the 37
screens naming no door (`CPB-23`).

⚠ **`CPB-16` AND `CPB-17` ARE IN NO WAVE ON PURPOSE.** They are *Ask a question*, and
`CR-085` §4 item 1 records that `/ask` versus `/ask-a-question` is an OPEN question the
Product Owner has not ruled on. Building either spec would settle it by accident, which is
the failure the prime directive exists to prevent. They wait for a ruling.

**What this decision costs if it is wrong:** nothing structural. A specification can move
between waves at any time; the grouping is a running order, not a commitment. It is
written down because the next agent reading *"start wave 1 and 2"* in the chat history
would otherwise have no idea which six screens that meant.

## 2026-09-08 · CR-085 blueprint, wave 2 — the two comparisons a customer arrives with, and the month an absence names

**`CPB-06`** (*"Usage compares against the same month last year"*) and **`CPB-07`**
(*"Usage compares against last month"*) were both open because, in the blueprint's
own words, *"Nothing on the server works out a month-on-month change. Working it
out in the browser would put a figure in front of a customer that no staff screen
and no bill can reproduce."*

Both are now arithmetic in `apps/metering/monthly_usage.py` —
`month_on_month()` and `same_month_last_year()` — surfaced through
`monthly_usage_reads._metrics`, which is the ONE object the staff Usage tab (S21)
and the portal's `CWP-033` both read. That placement is `CPB-07`'s own acceptance
sentence: *"and a clerk looking at the same account sees the same 5%."*

### The judgment nothing signed covers, and it is about ABSENT months

`BR-MET-106` makes an unread month **ABSENT, never `0`**. So *"against last
month"* has no single obvious meaning on an account with a gap in it, and two
readings were open:

* **(a) walk back to the nearest month that HAS a figure, and NAME it.** June
  `1,000 kWh` → August `800 kWh` reads *"20.00% less than June"*.
* **(b) refuse when the immediately preceding calendar month is absent.**

**(a) is what shipped.** The screen names the month it compared with, so
*"20.00% less than June"* is unambiguous where a bare *"20% less than last
month"* would not be, and nothing is subtracted from a zero that would tell a
customer they used nothing in a month nobody walked. **(b) would answer
*"nothing to compare with"* on an account holding two perfectly good figures.**

**And `same_month_last_year` takes the OPPOSITE choice deliberately**: it is the
same calendar month or it is nothing. That comparison exists because usage is
SEASONAL — an August against an August holds the weather roughly still, which is
the whole reason a person asks it — so July 2025 is not an answer to *how does
this August compare*, and an absent August 2025 is REPORTED
(`no_same_month_last_year`) rather than substituted with the nearest month to
hand. One function walks back and one does not, because they answer different
questions.

Recorded rather than put to the Product Owner (hard-won law 13): nothing signed
rules it, it collides with no signed rule, and it moves no ❄️ FROZEN figure.

### Worked, on the numbers the tests assert

| | this month | against | difference | percent |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `CPB-07`, the blueprint's own case | Aug 2026 `760 kWh` | Jul 2026 `800 kWh` | **`-40 kWh`** | **`-5.00%`** |
| `CPB-07`, a gap in between | Aug 2026 `800 kWh` | **Jun** 2026 `1,000 kWh` | `-200 kWh` | `-20.00%` |
| `CPB-06`, the blueprint's own case | Aug 2026 `800 kWh` | Aug 2025 `714 kWh` | **`+86 kWh`** | `+12.04%` |
| Ana's live account (`pine-hill`) | Aug 2026 `800 kWh` | Jul 2026 `800 kWh` | `0 kWh` | `0.00%`, direction **`same`** |

⚠ **`direction` IS A THIRD VALUE AND NOT A SIGN.** `more` · `less` · `same`,
because *"0% more"* is not a sentence anybody says. It travels as a CODE and the
catalogue writes the word (B14 rule 35).

⚠ **THE PERCENTAGE IS CARRIED AT SIX PLACES AND DISPLAYED AT TWO** (CLAUDE.md
hard rule 2), rounded ONCE on the server, so the two surfaces cannot round
differently. **THE DIFFERENCE CARRIES ITS UNIT OR IT IS NOT SERVED** (hard rule
3): `difference_display` and `unit` are `None` together, so there is no state in
which a screen holds the number and not the unit — which is the *"Monthly average
800"* defect of wave H, generalised into a shape that cannot recur.

⚠ **AN EARLIER MONTH OF EXACTLY ZERO KILLS THE PERCENTAGE AND NOT THE
DIFFERENCE.** *A percentage change from nothing is not infinity, it is
unanswerable* — `yoy_change`'s own words for `prior_year_zero` — but *"800 kWh
more than July"* is still a true sentence, so it is still served.

### This does not touch `yoy_change`, and the difference matters

The decision log of 2026-09-04 recorded that the product's year-on-year figure is
*"a total against a total, not one August against another"*, and that **whoever
wants the drawing's number must change the ARITHMETIC or the DRAWING, not the
fixture**. This is that arithmetic, added BESIDE the existing one. `yoy_change`
is unchanged, `+18%`-style fixture chasing is still not done, and the two answer
different questions: *is this year heavier than last year* against *is this
August heavier than last August*.

## 2026-09-08 — Premises & Units: four rulings, one of which narrows a signed rule

Raised while the Product Owner reviewed a walk of the property and unit screens.
Recorded here the same session they were made, because the conversation does not
survive and the next agent will read the repo.

### 1 · A unit may carry its own parcel and its own map point

PO, verbatim: *"youa re correct address is on premsies/property - but GIS data for
unit might change and hence we have to have parcel ID and GIs details on Unit
also"*, and confirming the reading put back to them: *"The address half stands. The
coordinate half narrows: a unit may carry its own point and parcel, and where it
does, that is the truth for that unit. Where it does not, it uses its building's."*

⚠ **THIS NARROWS `BR-MET-1161` — CLAUDE.md HARD RULE 8 — AND THE SUPERSESSION IS
STATED RATHER THAN ASSUMED.** That rule puts an address in one home and carries
`premises.lat/lng` the same way *"so a map and an envelope cannot disagree"*. The
**address half is untouched**: an address is still stored on `premises` and nowhere
else, and a unit still refines a premises by LABEL. What moves is the COORDINATE
half, and only for a unit: a unit may hold its own `lat`, `lng` and parcel, and
where it holds them they are the truth for that unit. Where it does not, it reads
its building's — the fallback is the rule, not an implementation detail, and the
screen states which of the two it is showing.

**Why the PO ruled this way, in their own terms:** a unit's GIS *"might change"* —
a cabin in a park, a pad, a wing of a campus is somewhere its site office is not.

**What it costs, measured rather than estimated:** `G85` treats `lat`, `lng`,
`latitude` and `longitude` as address-shaped names and fails on a fourth home. It
will go RED the moment a unit gains coordinates. **That is the guard working.** Its
allow list moves in the same commit as the column, with this ruling quoted beside
it. ⚠ **CLAUDE.md hard rule 8 must be stamped in that same commit** — it is the
citing document and it states the coordinate clause verbatim. It is NOT stamped
today, deliberately: the column does not exist yet, and a rule amended before the
code is a comment claiming a guarantee (hard-won law 1).

### 2 · The existing reference number BECOMES the Parcel ID

PO, verbatim: *"you can make reference # = Parcel ID"*, overruling this session's
recommendation that a parcel be a NEW field beside it.

**The recommendation was over-cautious and the measurement says so: `premises.external_ref`
is NULL on all 673 properties across every tenant.** Nothing is overwritten and no
utility loses data. The field is labelled *External / GIS ref* today, which tells a
clerk nothing; it becomes **Parcel number** — the assessor's number for the plot.

### 3 · A property cannot be shut down while anything on it is live

PO, verbatim: *"if you ahve units - active, assets or active accounts, you cannot
shut down building pr premises."*

This answers the question this session had left open (refuse · warn · cascade) and
the answer is **REFUSE**. Active units, assets still attached, or open accounts each
block a property's deactivation. The refusal names what is blocking and links to the
list that clears it, so *"why not"* is also the route to *"then do this first"*. A
unit's version is the same rule with one term: an open account on it blocks it.

⚠ **NEITHER A PROPERTY NOR A UNIT HAS A STATUS CONTROL TODAY** — both pages show a
status badge and offer no way to change it, and the unit page advises deactivating
as though a button existed. So this ruling creates the control as well as its refusal.

### 4 · A property carries one or more utility services

PO, verbatim: *"you also need to assign one or more utility services to Premises."*
The column exists (`premises.services_available`, a subset of the tenant's enabled
services per `BR-MET-003`); what the ruling settles is that assigning them is part
of recording a property rather than an afterthought. Drawn as removable chips with
an add control on both the create and the edit form, which is what B14 rule 9
already requires of any multiple choice.

### What was NOT decided, and is not being inferred

Whether a unit's own point should be REQUIRED for any class of property. It is
optional and falls back, on this session's judgment: making it required would mark
all 1,109 existing units incomplete overnight for no gain. If a utility with a cabin
park wants it enforced, that is a new ruling.
