## 2026-09-17 · EMAIL AS A PLATFORM SERVICE — FIVE PO RULINGS, AND TWO QUESTIONS THE PRODUCT OWNER COULD NOT ANSWER BECAUSE THEY WERE BADLY ASKED

Seven questions were put to the Product Owner about the SendGrid and Postmark
email connectors. **Five were answered. Two came back *"i did not understand"*,
and that is OUR defect and not theirs** — `DEF-1931`'s rule runs in every
direction, not only for a ruling put up for signature: *"if a paragraph cannot
be read aloud to someone who has never seen the register, it is not finished."*
Both are re-asked in plain words, and the badly-worded originals are kept here
so the failure is visible rather than tidied away.

| # | Question as put | PO, verbatim | Reading |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Do we have a Postmark account, and has it been submitted for approval? | *"yes we have"* | The 1–2 day Postmark review is not a risk on our path |
| 2 | Do we have a SendGrid account and a key? | *"yes we do"* | Restricted Access → Mail Send → Full Access, as asked |
| 3 | Our account, or the utility's own? | ***"our account - we will provdie servcie to utilities as platform provider"*** | ⚠ **THE PLATFORM HOLDS THE CREDENTIALS AND SELLS EMAIL AS A SERVICE.** See the consequences below — this is the largest of the five |
| 4 | What is our real, internet-reachable webhook host? | *"i did not understand"* | **BADLY ASKED — re-asked below** |
| 5 | Which utility goes first, and who controls their DNS? | *"i did not udneratnd"* | **BADLY ASKED — re-asked below** |
| 6 | Bill as a PDF attachment, or a secure link to the portal? | ***"secure links"*** | ⚠ Settles the 10 MB question entirely — see below |
| 7 | Is text/SMS in scope now or later? | ***"later"*** | `sms_twilio` stays `coming_soon` with no adapter. Not this scope |

### What ruling 3 costs, and none of it is optional

**`AUTH_MODES` cannot express it today.** The closed vocabulary is
`we_hold_theirs · they_hold_ours · token_exchange · none`. *We hold OUR OWN
credential and send on the utility's behalf* is none of those. A new mode is
needed and it is **not** a cosmetic addition.

**A platform credential has no tenant, and `integration_credential` has RLS
ENABLED AND FORCED** — verified in `pg_class`: `integration_credential` and
`integration_connection` both read `t|t`. Hard rule 1 forbids touching a tenant
table without `app.tenant_id`, so **a platform-level credential cannot live
there.** `platform_number_series` is the precedent for a non-tenant table.

**Isolation becomes ours to provide.** One account serving many utilities means
one shared suppression list and one shared sending reputation by default: utility
A's bounces sit beside utility B's, and one bad campaign degrades delivery for
everyone. **No gate in this repo would see that** — it is not rows crossing a
tenant boundary, it is reputation and suppression data doing so. The two
providers answer it differently and the difference is commercial: **SendGrid
subusers require Pro plan or above; a Postmark Server is the normal unit and
costs nothing extra.** Not ruled; recorded so it is decided rather than
defaulted.

**It reopens pricing.** `DEF-TEN-4222` deferred the pricing page — *"Keep it as
it is for timebeing … thats when we take care of pricing model"* — and states it
is reopened by the pricing-model work **and by nothing else**. Charging utilities
for email IS that work. Counting is feasible (`OutboundMessage` is tenant-scoped,
`delivery_counts.py` exists); charging for it is not built.

### What ruling 6 settles, and what it opens

**Postmark's 10 MB limit stops mattering.** It was the strongest argument against
Postmark for bill delivery, and a secure link removes it — a link is bytes.

⚠ **It moves work to the customer portal rather than removing it.** A consumer
clicking that link must reach their bill without a password they do not have, so
the link carries its own authority: it must expire, be single-purpose, and be
revocable. **That is a security design and it is not written anywhere yet.**
Nothing about it is decided by this row.

### The two questions, re-asked in plain words

**4 · Is there a copy of SmartBillHub running on the internet that SendGrid can
reach?** When SendGrid finishes delivering an email — or fails — it telephones us
back to say so. To telephone us it needs a web address that works from the
outside world. Our build environment is sealed; nothing outside can reach it. If
there is a live deployment we can point them at, everything works end to end. If
there is not yet, we build and test the callback against recorded messages and
**we will not know it truly works until there is one.**

**5 · Which utility goes first, and who there can change their website settings?**
Even using our own SendGrid account, the emails will say they come FROM THE
UTILITY — `billing@ottumwawater.gov`. For Gmail and Outlook to believe that and
not file it as spam, whoever runs that utility's website must add three short
records to their domain settings. It is a ten-minute job for them; getting it
asked for, approved and done usually takes **one to three weeks**. ⚠ **That wait
is theirs and we cannot shorten it, and everything we build is finished long
before those records are** — which is why it is worth starting on day one rather
than at the end. **The alternative, if that wait is unacceptable: the emails say
they come from US instead.** No waiting, and the consumer sees a sender that is
not their utility, replies come to us, and their own domain gets no benefit.
That is a product decision and it has not been made.

## 2026-09-17 · A FULL MAILBOX AND A DEAD MAILBOX STOP BEING THE SAME THING — THE SENDGRID/POSTMARK OUTCOME VOCABULARY, AND FIVE JUDGMENT CALLS MADE RATHER THAN ASKED

`DEF-NOT-5626` · `BR-NOT-1032` (PROPOSED) · migration
`06-backend/apps/notifications/migrations/0018_def_not_5626_normalised_outcomes.py`

Two email providers are being connected. **Each of them telephones us back to say
what happened to every message, and each uses its own words.** SendGrid sends
`delivered · bounce · deferred · dropped · spamreport · unsubscribe`; Postmark
sends `Delivery · Bounce` — with a hard/soft **Type** carried on the one event —
`· SpamComplaint · SubscriptionChange`. **Neither vocabulary may escape its
adapter.** The product holds six words and nothing else in it ever learns which
provider a utility is on:

    delivered · bounced_hard · bounced_soft · complained · unsubscribed · failed

`OutboundMessage.STATUSES` held five: `queued · sent · delivered · failed ·
bounced`. **Four of the six had nowhere to go.**

### The one that matters, with the figure

**`bounced` is ONE word for TWO opposite instructions.** A **hard** bounce means
the mailbox does not exist — sending again cannot succeed, and enough refused
messages degrade the sending reputation *every utility on this platform shares*
(the platform holds the credentials, per the PO ruling of this same day: *"our
account - we will provdie servcie to utilities as platform provider"*). A
**soft** bounce is a full mailbox on a Tuesday — temporary, and `BR-NOT-005`'s
retry ×3 with backoff is already the product's answer to it.

**Collapsing them loses a real consumer's bills for ever, or retries into a dead
mailbox for ever.** There is no third outcome and no safe default.

The split is enforced where it cannot be forgotten rather than where it reads
well: **`delivery_ops.REQUEUEABLE_STATUSES` carries `bounced_soft` and
deliberately does not carry `bounced_hard`, `complained` or `unsubscribed`.** A
clerk pressing *Re-queue* on a hard bounce is refused by the VOCABULARY, and the
refusal is a sentence written for them — *"this email HARD bounced … The customer
still gets this document: print is the floor on every customer document
(BR-NOT-024) and that row was never touched."*

### FIVE JUDGMENT CALLS, RECORDED AS OURS (hard-won law 13) SO THEY CAN BE DISPUTED HERE

**1 · `bounced` STAYS LAWFUL AND NO ROW WAS REWRITTEN.** `BR-NOT-013` (PO ruling
2026-08-15) says *"`delivered` and `bounced` can never be written by anything in
this repo"* — both are provider facts and no email adapter with a feedback door
has ever existed. So no code path has ever written one, and the count measured on
the seeded lane database on 2026-09-17 was **0 rows in `outbound_messages` in any
status at all.** Even so, the rule is not *"there is nothing to migrate"* but
*"an unclassifiable bounce has no truthful successor"*: guessing one into
`bounced_hard` would suppress a live consumer's address on no evidence and move
their bills to paper for ever; guessing it into `bounced_soft` would retry into a
dead mailbox for ever. `bounced` means **a bounce of unknown kind**, keeps its
place in `STATUSES`, on the failures index and in `REQUEUEABLE_STATUSES` (the one
action available on it), and is never written again. There is no data migration
in `0018` and that is the decision, not the shortcut.

**2 · `unsubscribed` IS NOT A FAILURE AND IS OFF THE CLERK'S FAILURES LIST.** It
is the one outcome of the six that is a person exercising a choice. Three places
used to carry a hand-written `(failed, bounced)` pair — the partial index
`ix_outbound_msgs_failed`, `selectors._apply_order` and `delivery_ops.failures` —
and all three now read ONE tuple, `models.ATTENTION_STATUSES`, which holds five
and not six. Three hand-maintained copies is how a new status becomes invisible on
the one screen built to show it (hard-won law 7, *reporting zero over a scope it
silently excludes*). An unsubscribed consumer appears on the blocked-addresses
screen instead, where a person can see the choice and undo it if it was a mistake.

**3 · A COMPLAINT MAY ARRIVE AFTER A DELIVERY, AND A BOUNCE MAY NOT.**
`ALLOWED_TRANSITIONS` gains `delivered → complained` and `delivered →
unsubscribed`, because a person must OPEN the mail to mark it spam or click
unsubscribe: the provider reports `delivered` first and the complaint minutes or
days later. Refusing that move would leave a real report with nowhere to go — the
gap this whole slice exists to close, arriving one layer down. **The delivery fact
is not destroyed:** `sent_at` is stamped and never cleared, `attempts` is never
reset, and the payload stays in `provider_response`. The status says *the last
thing we were told*; the columns say *what happened*. That is the same reading
`delivery_ops.mark_returned` already uses for a returned letter, which
deliberately does not move the status because *"a returned letter WAS sent."*
**`delivered → bounced_hard` stays REFUSED:** a mailbox cannot both accept and
refuse the same message, so a provider telling us both is a provider we have
misread, and the refusal is how we find out instead of overwriting a delivery.

**4 · `UNPOPULATED_STATUSES` STAYS AT TWO, AND THE COST IS FILED RATHER THAN
HIDDEN.** That tuple is SCREEN-FACING: each value on it is paired with a plain
sentence in `delivery_counts.NOT_REPORTED`, it rides `GET /outbound/summary` to a
clerk, and `correspondence_reads._LEFT_THE_BUILDING` reads it to decide what a
CUSTOMER is told about their own document. Putting `bounced_hard` on it would
print a machine word on a clerk's screen with no sentence behind it (B14 rule 33
— a fact is at most six words, and rationale is zero words on screen). The
machine-facing list is `models.PROVIDER_OUTCOME_STATUSES` instead. ⚠ **The
consequence is real and is `DEF-NOT-5627`:** a row carrying one of the four falls
through to `could_not_send` on the customer portal, which is honest for the three
failures and **false for `unsubscribed`** — that message arrived. Nothing writes
any of the four today, so nothing renders it today; it goes live on the day the
first adapter lands, which is why it is a defect row and not a comment.

**5 · `BR-NOT-1032` IS *PROPOSED*, NOT *CONFIRMED*, BECAUSE IT AMENDS A SIGNED
RULE.** `BR-NOT-005` is the PO's, from 2026-08-08, and it names the lifecycle
*"statuses queued→sent→delivered/failed/bounced"* — five words. Adding four is an
amendment to a confirmed rule, and a lane may not widen one by editing a
dictionary; `CHANNEL_FLOOR_BY_SOURCE` set that precedent on 2026-08-30, when the
merge lane put the widening back to the PO instead of taking it. So the rule is
written down PROPOSED, the supersession is stated rather than assumed, and the
row in `12-governance/09-human-review-ledger.md` carries the four plain-English
statements to put to the Product Owner, with the figure in statement 3. **Nothing
in this repo writes any of the four new words**, so no behaviour a customer can
see depends on the amendment before it is ruled.

### What was proved, and what it cannot prove

**RED FIRST, on real PostgreSQL 16** (hard-won law 7, and law 14's warning that
the default suite runs on in-memory SQLite): `bounced_hard` was put back on
`REQUEUEABLE_STATUSES` — exactly what a later lane "simplifying" the two words
into one would do — and the run read `1 failed, 5 passed` with
`AssertionError … Left contains one more item`, i.e. **both rows re-queued and no
refusal was raised**, while the five vocabulary cases in the same file stayed
green over it. That asymmetry is the point: asserting that `"bounced_hard" in
models.STATUSES` proves nothing at all about what the product DOES with one.

The migration was applied to a live PostgreSQL 16 and the predicate read back out
of `pg_indexes`:

    CREATE INDEX ix_outbound_msgs_failed ON public.outbound_messages
      USING btree (tenant_id, created_at DESC)
      WHERE (status = ANY (ARRAY['failed','bounced','bounced_hard','bounced_soft','complained']))

⚠ **WHAT NONE OF IT PROVES: that an outcome can ARRIVE.** `BR-NOT-013` still
holds — no email adapter with a feedback door exists — so every row in those
cases is CONSTRUCTED, and this slice ships WORDS rather than a writer. It is
hard-won law 2's *built is not wired*, stated out loud in the migration's
`exceptions:` line, in `models.PROVIDER_OUTCOME_STATUSES`' own comment and here,
rather than left to look finished.

## 2026-09-17 — CR-115-BRC05 lane 4: three ways into the inbound door, and a setting that varies by the kind of message

**The problem, in one figure.** The inbound door served **one** verification
style and there are **three** connectors' worth of styles in flight. It read a
credential out of the header the manifest names. SendGrid presents **no**
credential — it signs the body — and Postmark puts HTTP Basic credentials in the
URL. So of the connectors the email work is about to add, the number the door
could authenticate was **zero**, and the only way to accept either call was to
turn authentication off on a route that writes delivery state (`DEF-INT-5628`).

### Judgment 1 — the signature algorithm vocabulary is SYMMETRIC ONLY, and that is a design decision rather than a limitation

`inbound.py`'s standing rule is *ONE AUTHENTICATOR, NOT TWO*:
`runners/serve.resolve_caller` identifies a caller by the blind index of what it
presented and then applies six guards — unknown, revoked, expired, allowlist,
connector off, scope, utility live. A second resolver would be two answers to
*may this machine in* drifting apart in silence.

A signature style has nothing to present, so the question was how to keep one
authenticator. **The answer taken: a SHARED-SECRET signature is a statement
about possession.** Recomputing an HMAC proves the caller knew the same bytes we
hold, so the door hands those bytes to `resolve_caller` as *what the caller
proved knowledge of* — which is literally true — and every guard goes on being
applied in the one place it always was. `serve.py` was not edited; it is
`HUMAN-OWNED` and nothing in it needed to move.

**That equivalence is false for an asymmetric algorithm**, where the stored
value is a PUBLIC key: verifying proves the sender holds a private key we have
never seen, and the public half identifies a connection without proving anything
about possession. So `SIGNATURE_ALGORITHMS` is `("hmac_sha256",)`, an asymmetric
name is refused at LOAD by name, and
`test_signature_algorithms_are_symmetric_only` pins the tuple so the day
somebody adds one the suite goes red and the identification question is asked
instead of assumed (hard-won law 2 — a hold with a test on it).

⚠ **WHAT THIS COSTS, STATED RATHER THAN LEFT TO BE FOUND: SendGrid's real Event
Webhook may well be the asymmetric case.** The specification this lane was given
describes it as an HMAC over `timestamp + payload` against a stored Verification
Key, and that is what is built; SendGrid's own documentation is not readable
from this environment. **Which algorithm the going-live manifest declares is the
manifest lane's to establish**, and if it is ECDSA that lane does not get to add
a word to the vocabulary quietly — the test refuses, and the design question
above has to be answered first.

### Judgment 2 — a failed verification answers `None` rather than raising

The obvious shape is for the verifier to raise `DoorRefused`. It does not.
`resolve_caller` has no early return, computes every guard whatever the first
says, writes the refusal record and holds the answer to the **40-millisecond**
floor so the ways of being turned away cannot be told apart by timing them.
A raise from the verifier would be a refusal that skipped all of that and came
back faster — the timing oracle `BR-INT-044` exists to close, arriving through
the fix for something else. So there is ONE refusal path with ONE floor.

### Judgment 3 — where the webhook secret lives is a SEAM with one arm built and the other NAMED

**PO 2026-09-17, verbatim:** *"our account - we will provdie servcie to
utilities as platform provider"*. We hold the SendGrid and Postmark accounts and
sell email as a service. That does not by itself say where a webhook
verification key lives, because two shapes remain open: a **subuser or Server
per utility** (the key is then an ordinary tenant secret) or **one platform-level
webhook for everybody** (the key belongs to no tenant).

`apps/integrations/webhook_secrets.py` is the one function that answers it.
`scope_for()` returns `per_connection` today and says so; the platform branch is
named in the docstring with the reason it cannot be bolted on —
`integration_credential` has RLS **enabled and forced**, so a row belonging to no
tenant yields nothing for every key including the right one (hard rule 1, and
law 7's *incapable of passing*), and the non-tenant precedent is
`platform_number_series`.

⚠ **NO NEW `AUTH_MODES` VALUE WAS MINTED.** That vocabulary genuinely cannot
express *we hold our own account and send on their behalf* and will need one —
but the subuser-versus-shared question is unruled, and a word minted now would
put a guess inside a closed vocabulary the registry refuses by name. A later
lane mints it, after the ruling.

### Judgment 4 — the notification classes are notifications' own five, and the specification's four do NOT map

`registry.Field.per_class` is the general mechanism — *this setting varies by the
kind of message* — with `default` required as the fallback and the keys checked
against `apps/notifications/catalogs.py` `CR_CATEGORIES` through
`seams/notifications.notification_classes()`. One list, read rather than copied.

**Why that axis and not the other**, written down because it is not obvious:
notifications carries two. `rule_catalog.CATEGORIES` (six) answers *what part of
the business SCHEDULES a message*; `catalogs.CR_CATEGORIES` (five) answers *what
part of the business SENDS one*. A per-class connector setting is resolved at
SEND time, and what a sender holds is an `OutboundMessage` with a
`template_code` — `catalogs.listing_for(code).category` turns that into one of
the five. The rule axis is not reachable from a message at all.

**The four names in the Postmark specification are not those five and no
parallel taxonomy was invented.** *Operational* maps to Service & field;
*Financial* spans two (Billing and Payments); **Security and Internal have no
home at all** — there is no security category and no template class for a login
code or a password reset, and *Internal* exists only on the axis a sender cannot
reach. And the five leave **Collections** unspoken for by the specification,
which is a deliverability decision rather than a cosmetic one. Routed to the PO
as `OQ-INT-12404` with three options; the mechanism is built and no mapping is
guessed.

### THE ID WENT WRONG TWICE IN ONE AFTERNOON, IN OPPOSITE DIRECTIONS, AND THE SECOND ONE WAS REAL

**First, a FALSE alarm.** `10-scripts/allocate.py defect --verify 5624` answered
**"TAKEN — a sibling pushed it. Renumber before you commit"** — and at that
moment the sole holder of `DEF-INT-5624` anywhere on any remote ref was **this
lane's OWN pushed `inbound.py`**, cited in code one commit before the register
row was appended. No defect register on any branch contained the number. The
allocator scans code and commit messages as well as the registers, which is
right and is what makes it useful, but its verdict **cannot tell *a sibling took
this* from *you took this yourself a commit ago***. Acting on it then would have
renumbered a live citation for nothing. It was settled by looking, in one
command — `git grep -l "DEF-INT-5624" <every remote ref>` named the file and the
ref — which is the discipline `DEF-CWP-4187` prescribes for *"was this red before
I started"*: the claim is about history, so check it like one.

**Then, forty minutes later, a REAL one.** Re-verified against a newer tip, the
number was taken for real: a sibling had pushed **`DEF-MET-5624`** into the
register. `DEF-INT-5624` would have been the **twentieth** shared defect number
in this register — `DEF-GOV-5621` counted the first nineteen the same day — and
`G17` fails a duplicate NUMBER whatever the module segment says, because the
segment is not part of the number. **Renumbered to `DEF-INT-5628`**, in the
register row and in all six citations: `inbound.py` (2, already on the branch and
therefore corrected in the open), the test file (1) and this log (3).

**The lesson is the one CLAUDE.md law 11 already states and this pair sharpens:
`--verify` is not a reservation and is only true at the instant it runs.** Both
answers were correct about the world they were asked about; the first world
included my own unpushed intent and the second included a sibling's push. So it
is run **at push time, unconditionally, and its answer is checked by looking**
rather than acted on — the false alarm costs a `git grep`, and the real one costs
five minutes of renumbering instead of a duplicate nobody can count.

### THE RED PROOF, SABOTAGE BY SABOTAGE — including the one that did not bite, and why that is the best result in it

`10-scripts/` has no harness for this, so it was four edits to
`inbound.signature_verified_secret` made one at a time, each followed by the
matching cases **through the real view** (`DEF-GOV-3733`: a gate proved through
an entry point nobody uses is no proof of the thing that matters). Run on real
PostgreSQL, `--reuse-db`, with a shared counter configured.

| sabotage | the false pass it models | result |
|---|---|---|
| 1 · a MISSING signature header returns the secret | the classic: `None == None` is true, and a verifier that forgets to DEMAND a signature admits everyone who sends none | **RED** — `test_a_missing_signature_is_refused` failed |
| 3 · the timestamp is concatenated and never aged | an HMAC has no clock in it, so one captured call is a permanent key | **RED** — both `…stale_timestamp…` and `…from_the_future…` failed |
| 4 · a failed `compare_digest` returns the secret anyway | the check runs and its answer is thrown away | **RED** — `…wrong_signature…` and `…different_body…` failed |
| 2 · NO SECRET STORED reads as *nothing to check against* | a connector half set up admits anybody | **STAYED GREEN — twice, and the second time the reason is worth more than the proof** |

⚠ **SABOTAGE 2, FIRST ATTEMPT, WAS A SABOTAGE THAT DID NOT SABOTAGE.** It set the
key to `""` and let the HMAC run; a caller signing with the REAL key then failed
`compare_digest` and was refused for a different reason than the one being
tested. The transcript shows `2 passed` where `2 failed` was expected — **and a
lane reading only the tick would have recorded a red proof that never happened.**
That is hard-won law 7 pointed at the proof instead of at the check: *ask what
would make THIS pass wrongly*, including when *this* is your own sabotage.

⚠ **THE SECOND ATTEMPT WAS FAITHFUL — an early `return "nothing to check
against"` — AND THE CASES STILL PASSED, BECAUSE THE PROPERTY IS DEFENDED
TWICE.** `verify()` does not answer *yes*; it answers **WHAT THE CALLER PROVED
KNOWLEDGE OF**, and that value then has to identify a real credential row
through `resolve_caller`'s blind index. A verifier that invents an answer
therefore cannot admit anybody: the invented bytes hash to no credential and the
one authenticator refuses exactly as it would for a wrong key. **The design
choice that keeps ONE authenticator is what makes this false pass unreachable**,
which is a better outcome than a test that catches it — and the two cases stay,
because they pin the property rather than the mechanism.

**Restored and green: 46 of 46** in
`tests/test_cr115_inbound_verification.py`, with `inbound.py` byte-identical to
HEAD afterwards (checked, not assumed).

### AN ENVIRONMENT FINDING THE OTHER LANES NEED, AND IT COST AN HOUR HERE

**Six of the forty-six failed for two reasons that had nothing to do with this
work, and both present as a broken test.**

1. **With `JOBS_EAGER=false` and no Redis running**, every case that LANDS a
   delivery dies in `kombu` with `Error 111 connecting to localhost:6379`.
   `redis-server` is installed in this image and was simply not started.
2. **With Redis up but no `CACHE_URL`**, those same cases answer **429**, not
   200. That is `rate_limit_store` refusing because the cache backend is
   `locmem`, which is not in `SHARED_BACKEND_MODULES` — **the guard working
   exactly as its own guard-list entry says it must**: *"a rate limiter that
   opens when its counter breaks is a rate limiter an attacker turns off by
   breaking the counter"*, and *"a server with no `CACHE_URL` answers nothing
   but come back later on its partner routes"*.

**So any suite that drives a partner or inbound door needs BOTH**:
`redis-server --daemonize yes` and `CACHE_URL="redis://127.0.0.1:6379/1"`
beside the `DATABASE_URL`. With both, the file runs **46 passed in 35s**.
⚠ **Neither failure names the cause at the tail of the traceback** — one is a
`kombu` stack and the other is a bare `assert 429 == 200` — which is the
`LANE-ENVIRONMENT.md` lesson (*read the HEAD of a pytest error*) arriving in a
third costume.

### A NEAR-MISS WORTH THE LINE: A SABOTAGED FILE IS A LOADED GUN

Two sabotage runs overlapped for about a minute, because the first had been
left waiting on a file that a `pkill` then created. For that minute
`apps/integrations/inbound.py` held `return secret  # SABOTAGE` on the
credential path **in the shared-looking working tree**, and an ordinary pathspec
commit naming that file would have published it with a correct file count, its
author's own hunks present and nothing in `git status` to notice — CLAUDE.md
law 11's *stale index is a loaded gun*, with the gun loaded by a test harness
rather than by git. It was caught by grepping for the marker before committing,
and the file was restored from `HEAD` and verified byte-identical.
**A script that edits source in place must hold a lock, and the grep for its own
marker belongs in the pre-push check.**

### TWO THINGS THAT CANNOT BE CORRECTED IN PLACE, RECORDED SO NOBODY HAS TO GUESS

**1 · The commit subject of `4bd8fb472` carries the SUPERSEDED number.** It reads
*"DEF-INT-5624, OQ-INT-12404: …"*. The renumber to `DEF-INT-5628` was applied to
the register row and to all six code and document citations, and the body of that
same message explains the move — but a commit subject cannot be rewritten without
a force-push, which CLAUDE.md law 11 forbids in a shared tree for better reasons
than this one. **`DEF-INT-5628` is the id. `DEF-INT-5624` is `DEF-MET-5624`'s**,
and the only place the old spelling survives is that one subject line.

⚠ **IT HAS A CONSEQUENCE WORTH NAMING**, because `10-scripts/allocate.py` scans
commit messages as well as registers: a future `allocate.py defect --verify 5624`
will answer **TAKEN** partly on the strength of this subject line, which is the
false-alarm shape described above wearing a second costume. The number is
genuinely taken — by `DEF-MET-5624` — so the answer is right; the reason it gives
would be half wrong.

**2 · The subject also says *"proved red before they were trusted green"*, and at
the moment it was written the sabotage run was still going.** The transcript
above is what makes it true. Stated here rather than quietly left to be assumed,
because a claim about a proof is exactly the kind of sentence hard-won law 1 is
about: *a comment claiming a guarantee is not the guarantee.*

## 2026-09-17 · `DEF-INT-5618` — what an ArcGIS query error is allowed to look like to a clerk

**The rules ran out here, so the judgment is written down rather than left in the
code to be inferred.**

**THE SITUATION.** An ArcGIS FeatureServer reports a failed query — a wrong field
name, an expired token, a layer that has moved — with **HTTP 200**, an `error`
object, and no `features` array at all. Our adapter read that as *no rows
matched*. So a connector misconfigured on the day a utility went live would have
answered **"The City has no match for that."** for every address in the city, for
ever, with nothing red anywhere in the product.

**WHAT WAS CHOSEN.** `_refuse_if_the_city_said_no` raises `ProviderTimeout`,
which reaches a clerk through `BR-INT-022` as **"the City is not answering"**.

**WHY THAT SENTENCE IS KNOWN TO BE IMPRECISE.** The city *did* answer. It
answered and refused us. The honest sentence is nearer *the City refused our
question*, and the path that would render it is **`DEF-INT-5620`**, which is OPEN
and owns exactly this rendering. Building a second refusal vocabulary here would
have put two answers to one question into the product while the first one was
still being decided.

**THE PRINCIPLE, WHICH IS THE PART WORTH KEEPING:** **a visible and slightly
wrong failure beats an invisible and totally wrong silence.** A clerk who is told
the City is not answering rings somebody. A clerk who is told the City has no
record of 500 E Washington believes it, and so does the next clerk, for months.

**THE SIDE EFFECT WAS CONSIDERED, NOT OVERLOOKED.** Repeating this raise opens
the breaker and takes the connector out of service. For what this failure usually
is — a configuration fault that will not heal itself — that is the right outcome:
calling the city again helps nobody, and a connector that says it is broken is
more useful than one that says the city is empty.

**WHAT IS EXPLICITLY NOT DECIDED HERE.** Whether a layer that states **no**
spatial reference should be assumed `EPSG:4326`. `gis_layer.walk` already treats
an absent frame as a refusal (`BR-INT-049`) and the search still assumes the
default, so the two paths now disagree about the same absence. That is
**`DEF-INT-5631`**, filed rather than half-fixed, because guessing it either way
silently changes whether a pin is written.


## 2026-09-17 · THE DO-NOT-SEND LIST — WHERE A SUPPRESSION LIVES, AND FIVE JUDGMENT CALLS MADE RATHER THAN ASKED

`DEF-NOT-5632`. `apps/notifications/models.py` has stated since the normalised
outcome vocabulary landed that *"a hard bounce SUPPRESSES the address and the
consumer keeps getting their bill on paper"*, and **nothing recorded a
suppression**, so the next bill run queued to the same dead mailbox. Runbook 22
said the same thing from the other side and put a number on it: *"No column
records a suppression, so '31 suppressed' is what this run WOULD suppress. The
KPI tile says To suppress until a writer is bound."*

This is that writer. None of what follows was put to the Product Owner: law 13's
short list is a signed rule being reversed, a ❄️ FROZEN figure, or a fact only
they hold, and none of these is one. They are ours to decide and write down.

### 1 · The suppression is keyed by ADDRESS and lives in `notifications` — not on `customers.Contact`

It was nearly the latter: the `suppress_channel` port is declared
`owning_module="customers"` and `apps/customers/runbook_ports.py` names the
missing thing as *"a contact channel marked undeliverable, dated"*. Three
reasons it is not that, and **the second is the load-bearing one**:

* a write from `notifications` into a `customers` table is a **cross-module
  write**, which DB-16 forbids outright. The port pattern lets a RUNBOOK cause
  such a write through customers' own service; it hands notifications no write
  path, and binding that port to a writer here would make `BR-RBS-022` false;
* **the two facts have different keys.** What a provider reports is about a
  MAILBOX. `OutboundMessage.recipient_address` is already the delivery key — a
  snapshot, never re-resolved (`BR-TEN-017`). And **the product sends to
  addresses that have no `Contact` row at all**: staff failures go to *"the user
  who started the action, plus all System Admins"* (`BR-NOT-021`) and *Send test
  to me* queues to the signed-in user's own address. A hard bounce on a System
  Admin's mailbox has nowhere to go in a contact-keyed store. One address also
  sits on many contacts — a landlord on forty units — and N rows for one dead
  mailbox can disagree with each other;
* **both facts are real and this closes only one.** ⚠ **`DEF-RBS-4331` IS NOT
  CLOSED.** *This person's email channel is undeliverable, dated* is a statement
  about a CUSTOMER that drives the fall-back ladder and is customers' own design
  decision — their own file says *"A column plus its rule is customers' design
  decision, not a runbook lane's."* Written here because the next lane will
  otherwise read the new table and think the port is answered.

**No seam was added.** Every input is already in this module, and a seam with
nothing to resolve is a file claiming a boundary that is not crossed (law 1).

### 2 · This table DECIDES NOTHING — the threshold stays in runbook 22

*Suppress after 2 hard bounces, or 1 returned letter* is `RB-122`'s card and is
tenant-tunable. **There is no count, window or threshold anywhere in
`suppression.py`.** Counting in both places would give one question two answers,
free to disagree, on a path where disagreeing means a consumer either keeps
getting mail at a dead address or stops getting it at a live one.

A complaint and an unsubscribe are **not** threshold questions and the runbook
never claimed them — its `HARD_KINDS` is bounces, failed texts and returned
post. A person clicking *this is spam* has given an instruction, and it is
honoured on the first one.

What this module DOES own is the invariant: **a soft bounce can never produce a
suppression**, refused at the single writer BY NAME with a sentence, so that an
adapter which drops SendGrid's bounce TYPE meets an error instead of a silent
success.

### 3 · A release keeps the row, and the unique constraint is partial because of it

Hard rule 4 names issued invoices, lines, payments and journal entries. This is
none of them and no balance moves, so a release may be a state change. **It is
still not an UPDATE that forgets:** `released_at` is stamped and the row stays,
because *why did this customer stop getting email in March* must survive
`audit_log`'s retention pruning — the cost `OQ-1340` is open about on the
payments correction path.

So `UNIQUE (tenant, channel, address) WHERE released_at IS NULL`, which does two
jobs at once: it is the rule-6 idempotency guarantee for a webhook delivered
twice, and it is what lets the release keep history. Re-suppressing writes a NEW
row, so the third time an address goes bad there are three rows and a clerk can
see the pattern.

### 4 · Email is matched case-insensitively, and the failure is asymmetric

RFC 5321 makes the local part case-SENSITIVE; every real provider treats it as
insensitive, and the address on a queue row is whatever somebody typed into a
form. **Matching too widely holds a message a clerk releases in one click.
Matching too narrowly posts to a dead mailbox for ever** and burns the sending
reputation every utility on this platform shares. Chosen on that asymmetry, not
on the RFC.

### 5 · A suppression is a money action — the precedent is two files over

No balance moves, so the question is fair. But `delivery_ops.
hold_paper_for_accounts` and `release_held_for_accounts` — the PAPER half of
exactly this idea — both write `audit.money_action`. The act is the same act:
stopping a bill reaching the customer it is addressed to, and letting it through
again. Both doors audit, under `delivery.suppressed` and
`delivery.suppression_released` — distinct from `delivery.released`, so an
auditor can tell which kind of hold was lifted.

### What was found and filed rather than built

* **`DEF-NOT-5637`** — the blocked-addresses SCREEN does not exist, so the
  Release the Product Owner asked for by name can only be performed by an
  engineer. The API for both halves is served. It was not drawn because
  `DEF-GOV-5248` is exactly the case where a lane built to `r10` while a
  blueprint it never checked for said something else, and no lane has checked
  the refs for a Notifications PDF.
* **`DEF-NOT-5639`** — ⚠ **our list is per tenant and the provider's is not.**
  Ruling 3 of the same day makes the platform hold ONE provider account for
  every utility, so the provider's own suppression list is shared. Utility A's
  hard bounce makes the provider `drop` utility B's message to the same
  consumer, while utility B's screen holds no row and truthfully reports
  **nothing blocked**. Law 7's *reporting zero over a scope it silently
  excludes*, and **no gate here could see it**: nothing crosses a tenant
  boundary in the database, the state lives at the provider. The commercial
  answer (SendGrid subusers, or a Postmark Server per utility) is already
  measured in this log and is the Product Owner's to make.
* **The `rating` migration drift** — `makemigrations --check` reports an unbuilt
  `ck_discount_versions_scope` change on `rating`. It is at the tip and is not
  this lane's; reported rather than touched.

## 2026-09-17 · `CR-115-BRC05` · The two email connectors: `email_bulk` → `sendgrid`, and `postmark` beside it

**Lane:** the two email connectors. **Version:** `2.293.0`. **Files:**
`06-backend/apps/integrations/manifests/{sendgrid,postmark,__init__}.py` ·
`registry.py` (one comment) · `seams/notifications.py` · `apps/notifications/delivery_counts.py` ·
`apps/runbooks/definitions/undeliverable_contacts.py` ·
`06-backend/tests/test_cr115_email_connectors.py` (new) and five existing suites ·
all eleven locale catalogues.

**The PO-approved plan was not re-litigated.** What follows is only the judgments
the plan did not settle, recorded because the next agent reads the repo and not
this session (law 10).

### 1 · The rename was proved free BY CONSTRUCTION, not by counting rows

A provider key lives in `integration_connection.provider_key`, so renaming after
one utility had connected would be a data migration on an RLS-FORCED table.
**No code path in this product can ever have written such a row:** the one
clerk-reachable path is `connect_with_fields`, whose step 1 refuses a
`coming_soon` card (`BR-INT-001`) and whose step 2 refuses a provider with no
adapter (`DEF-INT-4224`), **both before the write** — and this connector has
never had an adapter. `sample_data` seeds three other keys; `live_calls` seeds
two others.

⚠ **THE LOCAL DATABASE WAS ALSO CHECKED AND IT PROVES NOTHING, WHICH IS WORTH
SAYING OUT LOUD.** A freshly migrated `sbh` reports 0 connections and 0
credentials — on a database with no tenants at all, so the zero is trivial; and
`integration_credential`/`integration_connection` are RLS FORCED, so an
aggregate read with no `app.tenant_id` is exactly the blinded read
`manifests/__init__.py` already warns about. **A row count proves one
deployment; the refusals above prove every deployment.** What neither can answer
is whether some DEPLOYED tenant connected it, and the code argument is what
closes that.

### 2 · The hold was RE-AIMED rather than removed, and that was the only honest option

`test_cr110__an_unnamed_vendor_says_coming_soon` fired on the DISPLAY NAME:
*while the name is generic the card must say coming soon; the moment it changes,
this goes red.* Naming the vendor was always a PROXY for **can a utility press
this card and have it work**, and the proxy could not survive the rename in
either direction — left alone it demanded these cards go LIVE with no adapter
(`DEF-INT-4224` exactly), and satisfied by adding `{"sendgrid": "SendGrid"}` to
the placeholder map it would have recorded a real, contracted vendor as a
placeholder. **So the hold now fires on `adapter_for()`**, in
`test_cr115_email_connectors.py`, and asserts both directions. `print_vendor`
keeps the name-shaped hold, because its vendor genuinely is still unnamed.

### 3 · SendGrid ships with NO inbound verification declared — `DEF-INT-5630`

Its Event Webhook signs the body and its set-up screen calls what it issues a
*Verification Key*, which is the word for a public key. `SIGNATURE_ALGORITHMS`
is `("hmac_sha256",)` — **symmetric only, and deliberately so**: the door hands
the stored secret to `serve.resolve_caller` as *what the caller proved knowledge
of*, which is true of an HMAC and false of a public key. Adding an algorithm to
make the manifest fit would have widened a signed vocabulary from inside a
manifest file to settle a question the PO has not answered.

**So nothing is declared, and the absence is a CLOSED door rather than a quiet
one** — measured, not assumed: `inbound.verify()` was run against SendGrid's
real headers and answers `None`, which is a refusal. Declaring
`style="signature", algorithm="hmac_sha256"` would have loaded cleanly, drawn
perfectly and been a control wired to the wrong maths (law 2).

### 4 · Postmark declares `basic`, and the password it needs cannot be minted — `DEF-INT-5634`

`basic` is a true fact about Postmark and the door dispatches on it correctly
(proved: `verify()` returns the password from an `Authorization: Basic` header).
**What cannot happen is issuing that password:** `machine_auth._partner_manifest`
refuses any connection whose manifest is not `they_hold_ours`, and Postmark is
`we_hold_theirs` because we hold their server token. That is `DEF-INT-4118`'s
one-connector-two-credentials limit reached from a second direction. Declaring
the truth and filing the blocker was preferred to declaring nothing, which would
have left the door falling back to reading a header Postmark never sends.

### 5 · `Field.per_class` exists FOR Postmark's streams and cannot express them — `DEF-INT-5635`

`per_class` keys on `notification_classes()` = `CR_CATEGORIES`, five BUSINESS
AREAS. Postmark splits TRANSACTIONAL from BULK. Four of the five classes are
wholly transactional; the fifth, `service_field`, holds `service_outage_notice`
(*"Outage and broadcast messages"*) **beside** `service_appointment`,
`service_work_completed` and `service_door_hanger`, which are per-recipient
transactional mail. **No value is correct for that class** — `broadcast` would
put appointment reminders on a stream carrying unsubscribe handling and bulk
filtering. So `message_stream` ships `default="outbound"` with an EMPTY
`per_class`, and a test asserts the emptiness so a later lane cannot approximate
it quietly. The split Postmark needs is per TEMPLATE, not per CATEGORY.

### 6 · AUTH_MODES has no mode for the PO's platform-provider ruling — `DEF-INT-5636`

PO, 2026-09-17: *"our account - we will provide service to utilities as platform
provider"*. `AUTH_MODES` is `(we_hold_theirs, they_hold_ours, token_exchange,
none)`: the first is the utility's own credential, the second is a key we issue
to a partner. **Neither is *we hold OUR OWN credential and send for every
tenant*.** Nor could such a credential live in `integration_credential`, which
has RLS FORCED — a row belonging to no tenant is unreachable from a
tenant-scoped session, and a row copied per tenant is our own secret duplicated
into every utility's encrypted store. `platform_number_series` is the precedent
for a platform-level table.

**BOTH MANIFESTS THEREFORE SHIP IN THE TENANT-CREDENTIAL SHAPE THAT WORKS
TODAY** (a utility brings its own SendGrid or Postmark account), which is
honest, sellable and reversible. **What is deferred is the
platform-sends-for-you shape**, and it is a wave: a fifth auth mode, a
platform-level table, an RLS decision and a key-rotation story. Inventing it
inside a manifest file is the quiet widening law 13 forbids, so it was reported
instead.

### 7 · Postmark keeps the vendor's word *token*, and that makes `OQ-INT-12392` a different question

`test_cr110__no_connector_asks_a_clerk_for_a_token` pins an EXACT set of fields
whose label contains *token*, so a second cannot appear without a reviewer
seeing it. **The guard worked exactly as designed — it is why this lane went and
read the ruling instead of typing a label.** Postmark prints *Server API Token*
on the screen a clerk copies from, so a field labelled *Server key* would send
them hunting for a thing that does not exist — the identical reasoning that left
Twilio's `auth_token` alone. **One vendor reads as a quirk; two reads as a rule
needing a stated exception**, so the question put to the PO has been rewritten:
not *do we rename Twilio's box* but *do we adopt a standing rule — our word for
our idea is always `key`, and a field holding a VENDOR'S named credential keeps
the vendor's own label*. That closes it permanently instead of per connector.

### 8 · What was NOT added, and why the restraint is the decision

Five real wire differences have nowhere to live in manifest data (`DEF-INT-5633`):
202-vs-200 and the accepted-id field, the send batch ceiling, the payload
ceiling, and the validation call. **No vocabulary was invented for them.**
`registry.py` records that `Field.default` sat there for a day claiming a reader
it did not have (`DEF-INT-5595`) and that this is exactly what let nineteen
unusable values go unnoticed (`DEF-INT-5590`) — **a declared value nothing reads
is a fact the next lane builds on, not a harmless note.** They are in the two
manifests' closing comments and counted in a register row. Two of them turn out
to be moot or unusable anyway: the payload ceilings under this CR's
secure-links ruling, and the batch ceilings while `send_message` is keyed on
`queue_row_id`, which is one call per message by construction.

## 2026-09-17 · `DEF-INT-5622` + `DEF-INT-5623` — the partner surface learns to say *account*, and the fifth API gets a row

**Two defects the Product Owner reported from the live deployment at `2.291.0`,
fixed in one commit because they are one screen, one manifest and one route
table. Everything below is a judgment this lane made and wrote down (law 13);
nothing here was put back to the PO.**

**WHAT THEY SAID.** *"it should be account and not customer - theya re lookung
for details for accounts not customer id"* and *"this apis is not visiable in
invoice cloud"*.

### 1 · The word (`DEF-INT-5623`)

**The DATA was already right and that is why nothing went red.** PO 2026-09-16:
*"Customers = accounts"*. `id` and `consumer_no` are both `account.account_no`,
`customer_name` is the name on the account, both addresses are walked from the
account's premises — **there is no customer id in the payload at all.** Every
value was correct, so no assertion anywhere could fail. What was wrong was the
VOCABULARY, in three places, and nothing in this repo compares a ruling's words
against the surface that carries them.

**Three layers, three different homes:**

| layer | where | what moved |
|---|---|---|
| the row a clerk reads on S142 | the manifest's `label` **and all eleven catalogues** | *Read customers* → *Read accounts* |
| the address a partner dials | `partner_urls.PARTNER_ROUTES` + two manifests' `served_path` | `/partner/v1/customers` → `/partner/v1/accounts` |
| the keys on the wire | `shapes.INVOICE_CLOUD.resources["customers"].rename` | `consumer_no` → `account_no`, `customer_name` → `account_name` |

**THE CATALOGUE WINS OVER THE MANIFEST ON SCREEN**, so a lane that moved only the
manifest would have fixed nothing a clerk sees. Both moved in the one commit.

**THE ADDRESS MOVED FOR EVERY PARTNER AND NOT ONLY FOR INVOICE CLOUD, because
there is ONE route table.** `/partner/v1/accounts` could not be renamed for
InvoiceCloud and left as `/partner/v1/customers` for Aclarian without giving one
thing two names (`DEF-014`) or pointing a live manifest at a route that answers
nothing.

**THE OLD ADDRESS IS RETIRED RATHER THAN DELETED, AND THAT IS THE JUDGMENT.** The
decision handed to this lane was *rename now — the connector reads Not set up,
KEYS IN USE 0*. That is true of the connector the PO looked at. It is **not
verifiable of the other five**: `erp_aclarian`, `erp_sap`, `erp_workday`,
`erp_infor` and `erp_msgp` all carry `disposition=live`, they share this one
route table, and **this container has no access to the live deployment's
database**, so no lane can count their keys from here. What COULD be verified was
verified: the address is **one day old** (`DEF-INT-5546` moved it out of the
tenant path on 2026-09-16), the InvoiceCloud partner manifest landed the same day
in `6f7dabf4`, and **no automatic seed mints a partner credential** —
`seed_partner_morning` is a hand-run demo command for `brazosbend`.

On this surface `_status_for("refused")` is **404**, which is the same five words
and the same status a stolen key gets. So deleting the address outright would have
told a partner holding yesterday's document that their KEY was bad and sent their
engineer to look at their credentials. `410` names the replacement. The mechanism
already existed — `partner_api.RETIRED_FOR`, built for the phase-1 pair — and was
reused rather than re-invented, which is law 11's closing habit.

**IT IS NOT IN THE PUBLISHED SPECIFICATION AND THAT IS DELIBERATE.** The document
is built from the manifests' operations and none points at the retired address any
more. A partner reads it to learn what to call, not what used to exist.

**WHAT WAS DELIBERATELY NOT DONE, because it changes what five `live` connectors
receive:** the SEAM still composes `consumer_no` and `customer_name` in what its
own docstring calls *our words* — and our own column is `account_no`, so the seam
is holding a partner's vocabulary. Every partner but InvoiceCloud still reads
`consumer_no`. Filed, not fixed.

### 2 · The fifth API (`DEF-INT-5622`), and a deliberate design being reversed

`GET /api/partner/v1/consumer-info` was built, routed and covered by tests in
`CR-111-BRC04`, and declared by **no manifest**. The connector screen renders one
row per operation and puts `Operation.served_path` under its name, so the address
drew nothing: the PO counted **four APIs where five exist**. **Hard-won law 2's
mirror** — not dead UI, but a live capability with no door — and an absence is
invisible to every check this repo has.

**THE FIX REVERSES A CHOICE THAT WAS MADE ON PURPOSE, SO THE REASONING IS WRITTEN
OUT RATHER THAN LEFT TO BE INFERRED.** `CR-111-BRC04` hung the address on
`serve_customer` and said why, in the code: *"a second ADDRESS onto one door, not
a second door… a clerk who switched customers off has switched this off too."*
That safety property was real. **Its price was that the address could not be
SEEN**, and a capability a partner cannot discover is one nobody uses.

Two operations give the clerk the same property in a stronger form — **two rows,
two ticks, and the screen says which is which** — instead of one tick silently
governing two addresses. And they are genuinely different permissions:
`consumer-info` serves `remote_plan_id` and `opening_balance`, which the list
deliberately does not (`DEF-INT-5587`).

**THE PRICE, RECORDED RATHER THAN DISCOVERED LATER:** a key scoped
`serve_customer` alone can no longer call `consumer-info`, and the five ERP
manifests do not declare `serve_consumer_info` at all, so an ERP key cannot reach
it. That is correct — the address comes out of Invoice Cloud's document and
appears in no ERP's — and it is safe today because the address is one day old.

**THE ADDRESS KEEPS INVOICE CLOUD'S OWN WORD.** `consumer-info`,
`consumer_numbers` and `consumer_id` are names in THEIR document, the way
`bill-download/` keeps their trailing slash. `DEF-INT-5623` is about the word OUR
surface uses for OUR thing.

### 3 · What fixing the word uncovered — `DEF-INT-5642`

**The whole Invoice Cloud dialect was dead on every real call, and the fix for
`DEF-INT-5623` would have been dead with it.**

`shapes.resolve` is called from exactly one place — `partner_api._page_response`,
with `caller.connection.provider_key` — so the only keys that can arrive are the
connectors a partner can hold a key for. `shapes.BY_CONNECTOR` held two, and
**neither can ever be one of them**: `erp_invoicecloud` is a manifest that does
not exist (its sibling's own docstring records it as *considered and refused*),
and `pay_invoicecloud` is the CARD half, `we_hold_theirs`, which is never a
partner caller. Measured, not inferred:
`shapes.resolve("pay_invoicecloud_partner").key` answered **`native`**.

So InvoiceCloud received our envelope, our ISO dates, `id` instead of `invoiceNo`
and `phone` instead of `contact_number` — every rename in that Shape unreachable.

**WHY NOTHING CAUGHT IT, which is the part worth keeping.** The shape's own tests
call `apply_record(..., INVOICE_CLOUD)` with the shape already in hand. The ROUTE
tests connect with `provider_key="erp_aclarian"`, which correctly resolves to
`NATIVE`. **Both halves were right about themselves and no case put the real
connector key into the real resolver** — hard-won law 7's *looking at the wrong
thing*, and a test that asserts `resolve("pay_invoicecloud") is INVOICE_CLOUD` is
a true statement about a key no call can carry.

Fixed here because leaving it would have made this lane's own fix dead UI. The two
unreachable keys are LEFT in the map rather than swept up: removing them is a
separate judgment and would hide the evidence.

**AND IT IS NOW PROVED END TO END FOR THE FIRST TIME.** The `consumer-info` cases
in `test_cr111_invoice_cloud.py` had to move to a key that holds the new tick, and
the only connector that declares it is the InvoiceCloud one — so those cases now
read `results` / `count` / `account_no` off a live call, which is the dialect
arriving on the wire rather than in a unit test.

### 4 · What was measured and NOT done — the `serve_customer` rename

Renaming the OPERATION `serve_customer` → `serve_account` was put to this lane as
a question to measure rather than to answer. **It is not small and it is not a
rename.**

* **29 files, 61 occurrences** — six manifests, five backend test files, eleven
  locale catalogues (the operation name is the catalogue key's last segment), a
  browser walk script and three governance documents.
* **And the decisive fact is that it is STORED DATA, in three tables:**
  `IntegrationCredential.scope` names it on every issued key,
  `IntegrationRun.operation` on every recorded call, and
  `IntegrationRateLimit.operation` under a unique constraint. A rename without a
  data migration makes every existing key refuse its own permission —
  `machine_auth._validated_scope` refuses an unknown name and
  `serve.scope_permits` refuses an unrecognised one — so a live partner would
  start receiving the same five-word refusal a stolen key gets.

**Neither defect requires it.** Nothing a partner or a clerk reads carries the
operation name: the screen row reads the catalogue, the address reads
`served_path`, the payload reads the Shape. Recorded as owed in `OQ-INT-12405`.

## 2026-09-17 · THE FOUR EMAIL SCREENS WERE NOT BUILT, AND THE REASON IS THAT THE SPECIFICATION THEY WERE TO BE BUILT FROM DOES NOT EXIST

**A lane was dispatched to build four email connector screens** — a provider
list of cards, a four-step connect wizard (account · credentials · domain and
sender · test), a tabbed Manage screen, and an Activity screen — **from
*"CR-115-BRC05 §7, the PO's full email specification including the four screens
drawn out, 190 lines, their words verbatim"*. Nothing was built.** This entry is
why, so the next lane does not spend the same hours discovering the same thing,
and does not build it anyway.

### 1 · §7 is a different subject, and it is a different subject on every ref

`CR-115-BRC05` §7 is **`CUSTOM URLs ON A CONNECTOR — THE FULL SPECIFICATION`**:
the Name/Kind/URL/Key form, the six-column table, the five behaviour rules, the
URL-resolution trap. It is 186 lines and it is about ArcGIS layers.

It was checked on all four refs that carry the file —
`claude/kind-wozniak-rl0uzt`, `claude/clever-cannon-nh10tw`,
`claude/confirm-understanding-3ktufc` (33,466 bytes, identical) and
`claude/gifted-johnson-top7zn` (23,767 bytes, which has no §7 at all). **There is
no version of this file in which §7 is about email.** Filed as `DEF-GOV-5646`.

⚠ **AND THE SEARCH WAS WIDER THAN THAT SECTION.** Every file under
`12-governance/change-requests/`, the whole decision log, all fourteen module
folders, `01-open-questions.md`, and every remote ref were searched for the
distinctive strings of the brief — *Copy all*, *Email to my IT team*, *Replace
token*, *domain and sender*, `DNS`, `DKIM`, `SPF`, `DMARC`, `CNAME`. **Zero hits
outside this entry.** The email rulings of 2026-09-17 are real and are in this
file under *EMAIL AS A PLATFORM SERVICE* — five answers about whose account,
whose credentials, secure links rather than PDF attachments, and SMS later —
**and not one of them is about a screen.**

**The lesson is the one this file keeps learning:** a pointer naming a section is
a claim about that section, and every id-existence check passes over it, because
`CR-115` exists and `§7` exists. It is `DEF-GOV-5229`'s shape — a real id read
for a different real id — and the only thing that finds it is opening the file.

### 2 · Three of the four screens reverse rulings the PO made the same day

Checked against `CR-115-BRC05` itself, which is where those rulings are written:

| Briefed | Ruled 2026-09-17, verbatim | |
|---|---|---|
| Screen 1, **one card per provider** | R1 — *"we are overriding the deciion and converting it form Grid -> Table - table only"* | the card grid is the thing that ruling removed |
| Screen 3, **Manage, TABBED** | R8 — *"thi sis okay"*, of the connector view's four body panels, after R5–R7 moved the actions to the top and added the KPI tiles | a signature covers what was shown, and tabs were not |
| Screen 4, **a separate Activity screen** | the blueprint draws *Recent activity* as a panel INSIDE the connection view (p28) | a second home for it is a second place a clerk looks |

**None of these may be reversed by a lane.** `CLAUDE.md` law 13 names exactly
three things that legitimately reach the PO, and the first is *a ruling that
collides with a signed rule — the supersession must be stated, never assumed.*
So it is asked, once, in plain words, as **`OQ-INT-12406`**.

### 3 · The blueprint owns this module, and it draws none of the four

`05-prototype/05 Integration Blueprint.pdf` is **on the branch** (163 pages,
sha256 `c02e9518…`) and was read **as images**, per B14 rule 42 — the text
extraction was used only as an index to find the pages.

**Pages 28 and 30 draw the bulk email connector as the same two screens every
other connector gets:** `CFG-04 · Bulk email service — set up` at
`/:tenant/settings/connectors/email_bulk/configure`, stamped **NEEDS A VENDOR
NAME**, and `VIEW-04 · Bulk email service — the connection`, stamped
**PROPOSED**, carrying *"No connector exists yet. This is what the screen shows
once one does."* **There is no wizard, no tab strip and no DNS panel anywhere in
the document** — `DNS`, `DKIM`, `SPF`, `DMARC` and `CNAME` appear on zero of its
163 pages.

⚠ **`DEF-GOV-5248` (PO ruling 2026-09-14) makes that binding rather than
advisory:** for a module with a blueprint, the drawing owns layout, copy,
**flows** and states, and r10 drops to visual style alone. **A wizard's STEP
COUNT is a flow** — that is the precise word that cost the billing lane six
steps where its blueprint drew four, and four further lanes then built onto the
wrong shape. Building a four-step wizard here, where the drawing has a single
configure form, is the same defect wearing a different number of steps.

⚠ **What the drawing DOES give, and it should be reused rather than reinvented:**
the credential panel on p28 is already exactly the PO's *never show a stored
token* rule — `••••7Q2F`, *"Only the last four characters are ever shown. It
cannot be read back, by anyone, including us."*, and a **Replace key** button.
The pattern exists and is drawn; it does not need a new screen to live on.

### 4 · The connect wizard has nothing to connect, by a signed rule

`sendgrid` and `postmark` both ship `Disposition(kind="coming_soon", wave="v1.1",
phase=2)` with **no adapter bound**, and `services.connect_with_fields` refuses a
coming-soon provider **at the API, before any write**, raising `BR-INT-001` and
writing an audit row. Verified in
`06-backend/apps/integrations/services.py:142` and both manifests.

**So a four-step connect wizard built today would be four screens a clerk cannot
finish** — hard-won law 2's mirror, a live screen behind a dead door, which is
how the customer portal shipped with two working doors out of eight. The
manifests already hold that door correctly and hold it with a test that fires
when it expires (`test_cr115__a_connector_with_no_adapter_says_coming_soon`),
which is the discipline; adding a wizard in front of it would undo it.

### 5 · The DNS panel: the contract EXISTS and is a sibling's, and the wire does not — `DEF-INT-5645`

⚠ **THIS SECTION WAS WRITTEN ONCE AND CORRECTED BEFORE IT WAS PUSHED, AND THE
CORRECTION IS THE USEFUL PART.** The first draft said there was nowhere in the
product to put a DNS record set. **That is true of the BRANCH and false of the
TREE**, and the difference is a sibling lane's uncommitted work.

**What was checked and what it proved.** `git log` on the branch shows forty
commits since 2026-09-16 and **no domain-verification backend**; the twenty-two
integration routes were enumerated from `apps/integrations/api.py` and from
`openapi/schema.json` and **none of them is a domain route**. Both facts hold.
**But `git status` shows the adapter lane is IN FLIGHT in this shared tree** —
`adapters/esp_email.py`, `adapters/email_sendgrid.py` and
`adapters/email_postmark.py` are untracked, and `manifests/sendgrid.py` is
+104/-20 against the tip. **A lane that read only `git log`, exactly as briefed,
would have concluded the work did not exist and invented a second shape beside
it.** The habit that caught it was reading the working tree before believing a
branch.

**THE CONTRACT, READ OFF THE SIBLING'S OWN FILE, so the screen lane never
invents one.** `adapters/esp_email.py`:

    DomainAnswer  -> { domain, state, records[] }
      state       : "verified" | "partial" | "unverified" | "not_found"
    DnsRecord     -> { purpose, type, host, value, verified, source }
      purpose     : "dkim" | "spf" | "return_path" | "dmarc"
      type        : "CNAME" | "TXT" -- the vendor's own word, upper case
      verified    : true | false | null -- null is *they do not say per record*,
                    which is a different fact from *not published*
      source      : "provider" | "ours" -- DMARC is the one we compose, and it
                    is MARKED so a reader can see it is ours

**It already satisfies the rule the brief cared most about.** The SendGrid
adapter's `domain_answer` reads the three CNAMEs **out of the provider's answer
and never composes them**, because the `em1234` prefix and the DKIM selectors
are per account — so **the record count and type come from the provider, and a
screen that draws `records[]` in a loop can never be wrong about either.** The
sibling's docstring names the consumer in as many words: *"the sending-domain
panel another lane draws."*

**WHAT IS ACTUALLY MISSING IS ONE THING, AND IT IS THE WHOLE BLOCKER: NOTHING
SERVES IT.** There is no route, on the branch or in the tree, that a browser can
call to get a `DomainAnswer`. So the panel remains unbuildable today, for a
narrower and more fixable reason than the first draft claimed. `DEF-INT-5645`
stands on that narrower ground.

⚠ **AND THE ORIGINAL RULE STILL BITES, WHICH IS WHY THE FIXTURE FALLBACK WAS
DECLINED.** The sanctioned fallback was *render from a typed fixture matching
the shape and say so*. With the shape now known that is one hour's work — **but
a fixture of SendGrid's three CNAMEs living in the front end IS the hardcoded
provider fact**, sitting where `BR-INT-037` says a provider must never appear
(*adding a provider touches no screen*), waiting for the next lane to believe
it. A fixture in a TEST is fine and is where this one belongs. **The panel
should be built the day the route lands, against the route** — and with the
contract above written down, that is a short job rather than a discovery.

### 6 · What was proved by clicking, and what was not — stated plainly

**The browser walk did not run, and the reason is not the product.** The
documented database credential — `postgres://sbh:sbh@127.0.0.1:5432/sbh`, the
string `10-scripts/cr026_import_benchmark.py` carries — **worked for
`seed_demo`** (the `brazosbend` tenant was created and is in the `sbh` database,
confirmed by reading `tenants` as the `postgres` superuser) **and stopped working
minutes later**: `password authentication failed for user "sbh"`, with the role
still present and still `rolcanlogin`. A sibling lane's role work is the likely
cause. Restoring the password, and running the server as the `postgres` peer
user instead, were both refused by this environment's permission classifier, and
**neither was worked around.**

**So everything in §§1–5 above is read off documents, manifests, the route table
and the blueprint's own pages, and NOT off a running screen.** Under law 6 that
is the weaker kind of evidence and it is labelled as such. It happens not to
matter for the conclusion — *no specification exists* and *the vocabulary has no
slot for a DNS record* are both facts about files — but **a lane that picks this
up should get the stack running and look, before trusting any of it.**

### 7 · The judgment, recorded as ours

**Building the four screens would have passed every check in this repo.** `tsc`
would pass, vitest would pass, no gate reads rendered output, and the screens
would have rendered. **That is the exact signature of the failures this file
exists to prevent** — the six-step wizard, the property Overview, the portal's
two working doors. The cost of stopping is a day. The cost of building is a
module's worth of screens that reverse three same-day rulings, sit in front of a
door the product refuses by name, and carry a DNS panel whose numbers a lane
invented.

**So: nothing was built, three rows were filed, and one question was asked.**
`OQ-INT-12406` is the question, and it is written so the PO can answer it
without looking anything up.

## 2026-09-17 · BUILDING `BR-CUS-1079` — FIVE JUDGMENT CALLS THE RULING DID NOT MAKE, AND THE ARITHMETIC OF THE MIGRATION

The PO ruled *"utility can get their own account types"* and the entry above
records the ruling. **This entry records what the LANE decided**, because five
questions had to be answered to build it and none of them was put to the PO
(hard-won law 13: a judgment call recorded with its reasoning is the
deliverable; a question is the failure to make one).

### 1 · Where a row a tenant ADDS goes in a picker the PO drew

`BR-CUS-094` ratified an ORDER — Residential · Commercial · Industrial ·
Agricultural · Institutional · Municipal · Builder or developer — and
`service_request_api` preserved it by ITERATING the seven-tuple, which is
exactly why a tenant's own row was dropped. Sorting by `code` instead would put
Agricultural first and quietly re-order a screen the PO drew.

**Chosen: a stored `sort_order` column.** The ruled seven at `10..70`,
`government` (legacy) at `900`, and a tenant-added row appended at `max + 10` —
so a first addition lands at 910, **behind the drawn order, in the order the
utility created them.** Rejected: a `CASE` expression over the tuple (the same
hardcoding one layer down, and it re-orders every tenant's list the day the
tuple changes) and ordering by `created_at` (correct for new rows, silent about
the seeded ones).

⚠ **The CARD and the PICKER sort differently, deliberately.** S8's
reference-data grid sorts by `code` like every other card (IS-2, and the shared
list view is one component); `sort_order` is the picker's. Two orders for two
questions beats one order that is wrong for one of them.

### 2 · `used_by` now counts THREE tables, not one

It counted `accounts` alone, with a comment saying the PROTECTed FK enforced the
rest across all tenants anyway. True while the row was platform-wide. Now the
row is this tenant's, so **every referencing row that can block a Delete is this
tenant's too** — `accounts`, `service_requests` and the `account_subtypes`
sitting under it. Counting only accounts would have drawn a live Delete that the
database then refuses, which is the exact fault this whole change is fixing.

### 3 · A code FREEZES once used; the name never does

`BR-TEN-030` says so for every list, and the reason bites harder here than
anywhere: **`rating` stores `account_types.code` as TEXT** in charge narrowing
and in the plan/tax targeting JSON lists, and the lookup handler cannot see
those columns, let alone rewrite them. So an edit may always change the NAME
(which is what a clerk wants when "Commercial" should read "Business") and may
change the CODE only while `used_by` is 0.

### 4 · `legacy` is SERVED and not WRITABLE

The card publishes it — `DEF-421`'s complaint that a picker built on
`/lookups/account_types` would still offer `government` is closed by that — but
nothing on the card sets it. **Who may retire a code from new business has not
been ruled**, and a control for it would be answering an unasked question.
`OQ-CUS-12407`.

### 5 · The platform fixture goes 4 → 8, behind a version bump

⚠ **A FOUR-ROW DRIFT THAT HAD BEEN THERE SINCE 2026-08-24 AND WAS HARMLESS
UNTIL TODAY.** `BR-CUS-094` ratified seven and migration `customers.0019`
seeded the four new ones into the PLATFORM table; `lookup_defaults.json` and
`services.SEED_ACCOUNT_TYPES` went on listing the original four, and `0019`'s
own docstring REPORTED it and could not fix it from its lane. Nothing broke,
because the seam was insert-missing over a global table that already held all
eight. **The moment the rows go per tenant, a tenant seeded from that fixture
receives FOUR types and no Agricultural, Institutional, Municipal or Builder.**
So the fixture carries all eight at `V2.48.0.12` (`BR-TEN-077` bump + digest
`b5681a64…` registered with its reason), `SEED_ACCOUNT_TYPES` is derived from
`models.AccountType.SEVEN_CATEGORIES` so the two copies cannot drift again, and
`account_types` moves from `PLATFORM_REFERENCE_LISTS` (now empty) to
`STRUCTURAL_REFERENCE_LISTS` — `accounts.account_type_id` is NOT NULL, so a
tenant whose S111 toggle emptied this list could not create an account at all,
which is the `owner_categories` argument exactly.

### The migration, measured rather than estimated

Proved end to end on live PostgreSQL 16 (`sbh_at_proof`), **two tenants, eight
accounts, two sub-types**, seeded BEFORE the migration against the platform
rows:

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| `account_types` | **8** rows, one shared list | **16** = 8 × 2 tenants |
| Brazos accounts resolving to a Brazos type | — | **5 of 5** |
| Lone Star accounts resolving to a Lone Star type | — | **3 of 3** |
| `account_subtypes` resolving to their own tenant's parent | — | **1 of 1 per tenant** |
| unique constraint | `uq_account_types_code_ci` (global) | `uq_account_types_tenant_code_ci` |
| `tenant_id` | (no column) | NOT NULL, indexed |
| RLS | **none at all** | `ENABLE` + `FORCE`, policy on `USING` **and** `WITH CHECK` |

Read back from `pg_class`/`pg_policy` rather than trusted because the SQL ran:
`relrowsecurity=t`, `relforcerowsecurity=t`, one policy, both halves testing
`tenant_id = NULLIF(current_setting('app.tenant_id', true), '')::uuid`. With the
setting unset: **0 rows visible**, no error. With a stranger's uuid: **0 rows**.

⚠ **THREE THINGS THE MIGRATION DOES THAT ARE NOT OBVIOUS AND EACH COST A
FAILED RUN TO FIND.** (a) The global unique constraint is dropped FIRST — the
fan-out writes N copies of `residential` and cannot run underneath it. (b) The
repoint sets `app.tenant_id` per tenant, because all three referencing tables
are RLS `FORCE`-scoped and the migration role is not a superuser: an UPDATE with
the GUC unset does not match nothing, it RAISES. (c) `SET CONSTRAINTS ALL
IMMEDIATE` fires the deferred FK checks before the next `AlterField`, or
PostgreSQL refuses with *"cannot ALTER TABLE because it has pending trigger
events"* — a message that names nothing useful.

⚠ **AND IT REFUSES RATHER THAN DELETING.** If any referencing row still points
at a platform row after the repoint — which means a `tenant_id` no `tenants` row
matches, so there was no clone to move it to — the migration RAISES and names
the count per table. A `ProtectedError` would say the same thing far less
clearly and, on PostgreSQL, would poison the whole transaction (law 14). There
is **no per-tenant savepoint**, deliberately and unlike `assets.0013`: nothing
here catches a database error and carries on, and a half-finished fan-out would
leave accounts pointing at rows the next line deletes, so the correct outcome
for one bad tenant is that the whole migration rolls back.

### What is NOT done, and is filed rather than fixed

Every hardcoded consumer outside `apps/customers/` — the portal's
`code__iexact="residential"`, notification rules offering two of seven, and the
notification/billing template constants that spell the fourth category three
different ways (`govt` · `government` · `municipal`). A sibling lane is
de-hardcoding those in the same window and this lane left them alone (law 11).


## 2026-09-17 · A UTILITY MAY DEFINE ITS OWN ACCOUNT TYPES — `BR-CUS-094`'s PLATFORM SEVEN IS SUPERSEDED

**PO ruling, verbatim, asked as a straight either/or and answered in their own
words:**

> *"utility can get their own account types"*

**The question put to them, in full, so the answer is not read wider than it
was:** *do utilities get their own account types, or do the seven stay the
signed vocabulary and the screen simply stops pretending they're editable?*

### What this supersedes, stated rather than assumed

`BR-CUS-094` — the PO's own earlier ruling *"Expand the signed list to seven"* —
made `account_types` a **PLATFORM** table: one row set for every utility on the
install, `UniqueConstraint(Lower("code"))` global, **no `tenant_id` and no RLS
policy at all**, and `customers/lookups.py` refusing create, update, set_active
and delete by name through `_PLATFORM_REFUSAL`. That posture is now reversed.
Change-process step 2 requires the supersession to be quoted rather than
implied, and this is it: **the seven stop being the vocabulary and become the
SEED.**

### What made the question real, and it is a defect the PO found themselves

The Settings card for Account types has rendered **Add · Edit · Deactivate ·
Delete** over a server that refuses all four — four live controls on a door
designed never to open (hard-won law 2's mirror). Worse, the refusal's own
message key `customers.lookups.account_types_are_platform` exists **in the
backend and in no catalogue**, so the clerk got no sentence at all. The PO's
report was *"if they add entry in this table - look up it does not reflect in
these places"*, which is exactly what that combination produces.

⚠ **AND THE SCREEN'S TWIN BEHAVES THE OPPOSITE WAY.** `account_subtypes` IS
tenant-defined with RLS and adding one genuinely works. Two cards that look
identical and behave oppositely is most of why this read as a wiring fault.

### Why this is a return to the house pattern rather than an invention

`account_statuses` and `account_subtypes` — the two lookup tables that sit
either side of this one — are **both already seeded, tenant-extensible and
RLS-scoped** (B2: *"seeded, tenant-extensible lookup tables"*, `BR-TEN-030`,
`BR-TEN-034`, `BR-TEN-036`). `account_types` was the single exception. So the
shape to build is the one its two siblings already have, and the seeded rows
keep `is_system` — deactivatable, never deletable.

### What it costs, measured rather than estimated

* The **8 rows fan out per tenant**; the global unique constraint becomes
  per-tenant; **RLS `FORCE` is added where there is none today**.
* **Three ForeignKeys** point at `AccountType`, one `on_delete=PROTECT`.
* **Two rating columns store the code as TEXT** — charge narrowing (a `$45.00`
  residential connection fee beside an `$85.00` commercial one) and the
  plan/tax targeting JSON lists. They keep working; two tenants may now use one
  code for different meanings, which is what tenant scoping means.
* ⚠ **EVERY HARDCODED CONSUMER BECOMES A REAL BUG**, where before it was a
  defensible reading of a platform vocabulary: the portal's
  `code__iexact="residential"`, notification rules offering `("all",
  "residential", "commercial")` — **two of seven** — the notification and
  billing template constants, and the service-request picker ordering by
  `SEVEN_CATEGORIES` so a new row is silently dropped.
* ⚠ **AND THE TWO TEMPLATE MODULES ALREADY DISAGREE WITH EACH OTHER.** Billing
  spells the fourth category `"govt"`, notifications spells it `"government"`,
  and the ratified code is `municipal` with `government` marked legacy. **Three
  spellings of one idea in three modules**, which only a table read can settle.

### One thing that is NOT hardcoded, and is the pattern to copy

`metering._resolve_unit_type` reads **the tenant's own rows FIRST** and falls
back to its tuple only for a tenant that has none — with a deactivated row
deliberately NOT resurrected by the fallback (`BR-TEN-034`). That is the exact
shape every consumer above needs, it is already written, and it is tested.

### What is NOT decided here

Whether a tenant-added type may be **targeted by a plan, a charge or a tax** is
the same question as before and unchanged by this ruling — those columns exist
and the resolver reads them. And `account_subtype_id` on the rating tables is
still read by nothing, which is its own gap.
