## 2026-09-17 · `CR-115-BRC05` · THE TWO EMAIL CONNECTORS LEARN TO SEND, AND THE LONG POLE STARTS TICKING

**Lane:** the ESP adapters and domain verification. **Version:** `2.294.0`.
**Files:** `06-backend/apps/integrations/adapters/{esp_email,email_sendgrid,email_postmark}.py`
(new) · `adapters/base.py` (one hook) · `adapters/__init__.py` (two bindings) ·
`manifests/{sendgrid,postmark}.py` · `esp_fixtures.py` (new) ·
`sending_domain.py` (new) · `models.py` + `migrations/0013_cr115_sending_domain.py` ·
`api.py` (one route) · `tests/test_cr115_esp_adapters.py` (new, 38 cases) ·
`tests/test_cr115_email_connectors.py` (two holds expired).

**WHAT CHANGED FOR A UTILITY, IN ONE SENTENCE:** SendGrid and Postmark were
cards that could not be pressed; they can now be connected, tested with one real
message, and — on SendGrid — asked which DNS records a utility's IT team has
published. **Nothing reports a delivery yet**, and that is deliberate; see
judgment 6.

### 1 · WHY THE DNS RECORDS WENT OUT BEFORE THE REST OF THE FEATURE

PO, 2026-09-17, question 5 re-asked in plain words and answered in plain words:

> *"Even using our own SendGrid account, the emails will say they come FROM THE
> UTILITY — `billing@ottumwawater.gov`. For Gmail and Outlook to believe that
> and not file it as spam, whoever runs that utility's website must add three
> short records to their domain settings. It is a ten-minute job for them;
> getting it asked for, approved and done usually takes ONE TO THREE WEEKS. ⚠
> That wait is theirs and we cannot shorten it, and everything we build is
> finished long before those records are — which is why it is worth starting on
> day one rather than at the end."*

Three design decisions follow from that one paragraph and each would have gone
the other way without it:

* **`GET /integrations/{key}/sending-domain` NEVER DIALS.** It answers from what
  we last stored, instantly, so the panel opens on a connector nobody has
  checked and on a day the provider is unreachable. `POST` is the press that
  asks. A `GET` with a side effect would also spend a utility's rate limit on
  every screen refresh, which is `BR-INT-041` arriving through a read.
* **THE DMARC RECORD IS SERVED BEFORE ANY CHECK HAS EVER RUN.** It is the one
  line no ESP issues, so it needs no provider, no credential and no network. A
  utility can open its IT ticket with a third of the work in hand on day one.
  **Waiting until all three could be served would have held the whole clock for
  a value we already had.**
* **AN ABSENCE IS SERVED WITH ITS REASON.** `available: false` plus a machine
  word, never an empty list. An empty panel reads as a bug and generates a
  support call; *we cannot ask Postmark this with the token we hold* is a fact
  somebody can act on.

### 2 · THE JUDGMENT WITH A FIGURE: `p=none`, AND NO REPORTING ADDRESS

DMARC is the one DNS value in this product that is **composed by us** — every
other record is read out of the provider's own answer, because SendGrid's
`em1234` prefix and its DKIM selectors differ per ACCOUNT and a composed record
publishes cleanly, verifies never, and costs the one-to-three-week cycle a
second time. Composed values carry `source: "ours"` on the wire so no reader can
mistake one for a provider's.

**The value is `v=DMARC1; p=none;` and both halves of that are a judgment.**

* `p=none` satisfies what Gmail and Yahoo require of bulk senders — a record
  exists and parses — and instructs no receiver to reject anything.
  `p=quarantine` or `p=reject` on a domain whose OTHER mail streams we know
  nothing about would send a utility's own payroll and helpdesk mail to spam on
  the day they published it, and **nothing in this product can see those
  streams.** So it is a FLOOR a utility's IT team may raise, never a
  recommendation we made.
* **No `rua=`.** Asking for aggregate reports means naming an address WE would
  then have to receive at, parse and act on — an operational commitment nobody
  has taken. A value there would either point at a mailbox that does not exist
  or silently create that obligation.

**Recorded as OURS under hard-won law 13** — a judgment written down with its
reasoning is the deliverable; a question is the failure to make one — rather
than minted as an open question the Product Owner would have had to answer with
no more information than we have.

### 3 · AN UNKNOWN POSTMARK BOUNCE TYPE BECOMES `failed`, AND THAT IS ALSO OURS

Postmark documents more than twenty bounce types and adds to them. The truthful
word for one we cannot read is **`bounced`** — *a bounce of unknown kind* — and
`DEF-NOT-5626`'s first judgment call of this same day keeps that word lawful
while ruling it **may never be written again**. So it is not available.

Of the six that are (`delivered · bounced_hard · bounced_soft · complained ·
unsubscribed · failed`), **`failed` is the only one that takes no irreversible
action**: it puts the row on the clerk's attention list and suppresses nothing.
`bounced_hard` would suppress a possibly-live consumer on a word we could not
read — the *loses a real customer's bills for ever* outcome; `bounced_soft`
would retry into a possibly-dead mailbox for ever. **Neither is recoverable by a
clerk; `failed` is.** The same reasoning gives SendGrid's `dropped` and
Postmark's `ManuallyDeactivated` the word `failed`: no mailbox was reached, and
suppressing on somebody else's earlier decision is `DEF-NOT-5639`'s shared-list
problem wearing our own suppression list's clothes.

### 4 · `check_domain_verified` IS AN OPERATION, NOT A FIFTH ADAPTER METHOD

`base.Adapter` is four methods and the conformance kit refuses a fifth public
one. Checking a credential and checking a domain are **new operations** —
declared on the manifest and dispatched through `execute()` on
`work[i]["operation"]`, exactly as `meters_neptune360` dispatches its six.
`execute()`'s own docstring already says what an item of work is: *"one request
the runner has already decided to make"*.

⚠ **THE FIRST DRAFT FAILED THE KIT WITH SEVEN EXTRA PUBLIC NAMES.** The shared
`EspEmailAdapter` asks a subclass seven provider questions — the auth header,
the send shape, the accepted id, the two checks, the two domain hooks — and
written as ordinary methods they are PUBLIC. They are underscore-prefixed, which
is the device `base.TOKEN_MINT_METHOD` already established for a
`token_exchange` provider's minter, and the kit now runs over both classes
**unchanged**.

The feedback normaliser is the same device again and is new:
`base.FEEDBACK_NORMALISER_METHOD` / `feedback_normaliser()`. SendGrid's
`delivered · bounce · deferred · dropped · spamreport · unsubscribe` and
Postmark's `Delivery · Bounce(+Type) · SpamComplaint · SubscriptionChange`
become the same six words, and **neither vocabulary is on the returned
object** — the first draft of `FeedbackOutcome` carried a `provider_event` field
*for the record*, which would have put SendGrid's words on a dataclass the whole
product reads.

### 5 · THE DNS ANSWER IS A TABLE BECAUSE `connection.config` WOULD HAVE DELETED IT

The obvious home is the connection's own JSON. **It would have worked until the
first time a clerk pressed Save.** `services.update_connection` prunes the
stored config down to the names the manifest still declares — `DEF-INT-5582`'s
fix, and the right behaviour — so a server-written DNS answer parked there
vanishes on the next `PATCH`, with a correct file count and a green suite. The
records are a provider FACT with a timestamp, not connection CONFIG, and
`test_cr115__saving_a_setting_does_not_delete_the_dns_records` is the case that
proves it (red-proved by moving the answer onto `config`: that one case failed
and every other stayed green).

`integration_sending_domain` is the seventh tenant table this module owns and
its RLS policy is in the same migration that creates it. `verified_at` is
stamped once and never cleared — *when did Ottumwa finish their DNS* is a real
question asked months later, and a domain can go back to unverified.

### 6 · WHAT IS LIVE IS SENDING. DELIVERY REPORTING IS NOT, AND IS SAID OUT LOUD

Binding an adapter makes the card live — `register_adapter` refuses a
coming-soon provider, so the manifests' dispositions and the two bindings moved
in one commit or the product would not start. **That is sending only.** Neither
feedback door is open: SendGrid's webhook signature is `DEF-INT-5630`
(believed asymmetric, and `SIGNATURE_ALGORITHMS` is symmetric only, deliberately)
and Postmark's Basic password cannot be minted (`DEF-INT-5634`). **So
`delivered`, `bounced_hard`, `bounced_soft`, `complained` and `unsubscribed` are
still written by nothing in this product**, `delivery_counts`' *not reported*
sentence goes on being true, and the normalisers have no caller.

They were built anyway, and that is a decision rather than an oversight: the
mapping is the half that takes judgment, it is testable without a door, and
building it on the day the door opens is how a hard/soft distinction gets
guessed at under time pressure. `test_cr115__neither_feedback_door_is_open_and_that_is_stated`
goes RED the day either changes, which is when somebody has to wire a normaliser
to the door and to `suppression.suppress_for_outcome` — **the seam that already
exists, and the one this lane deliberately did not duplicate.**

### 7 · THREE FINDINGS FILED RATHER THAN LEFT IN A REPORT

Hard rule 4's own lesson from `DEF-GOV-5229`: a finding recorded only in the
file you happen to be in is a finding nobody can count.

* **`DEF-INT-5649`** — the platform SendGrid key was issued with `mail.send`
  alone (decision log, this same day: *"Restricted Access → Mail Send → Full
  Access, as asked"*). `GET /v3/whitelabel/domains` is gated behind
  `whitelabel.read`, so a real key answers `403` and a clerk reads *The service
  refused the key.* about a key that sends mail perfectly well. **A five-minute
  change on SendGrid's own screen, with no code in it.**
* **`DEF-INT-5650`** — **Postmark's domain records cannot be fetched at all.**
  `/domains` takes an ACCOUNT token; this connector holds a SERVER token, and a
  connector holds ONE credential (`DEF-INT-4118`, reached here from a third
  direction). The account token is also a PLATFORM credential, which
  `AUTH_MODES` cannot express (`DEF-INT-5636`). So `check_domain_verified` is
  **not declared on the postmark manifest at all** — declaring it and refusing
  every press would be `DEF-INT-4224` one operation down — and the route answers
  `available: false` with the reason plus the DMARC record.
* **`DEF-INT-5651`** — two of this CR's own hold tests asked a **manifest-only**
  `Registry` whether an adapter was bound, and it can never be:
  `manifests.register_all` registers manifests and `adapters.register_all` is a
  different function. One of them (`adapter_for(key) is None`) was therefore
  **incapable of failing** for the fortnight it was green, while the manifests'
  own comments cited it by name as proof. Both now read the registry the product
  serves from.

### 8 · WHAT NONE OF IT PROVES

⚠ **NOT ONE BYTE HAS REACHED SENDGRID OR POSTMARK.** Outbound HTTPS is proxied
and refused, the same wall `CR-115-BRC05` §7.10 records for the City of Ann
Arbor. Every one of the 38 cases runs against `esp_fixtures.py`, which is
**hand-shaped from the written wire specifications and says so in its first
paragraph**. If SendGrid returns its accepted id under a different header, or
Postmark's server endpoint is not at `/v3/server`, every test still passes and
the product still fails on the first real bill. Both paths are one constant each,
named so the fix is a line and not a search.

**`openapi/schema.json` was NOT regenerated.** It is already 175+ paths behind
the code at the tip (`DEF-GOV-5342`, `DEF-GOV-5402`), and regenerating from a
tree three lanes are adding endpoints to would publish their in-flight
docstrings with it — the same reasoning three earlier lanes recorded and the
same conclusion.

## 2026-09-17 · `DEF-NOT-5637` · THE BLOCKED-ADDRESSES SCREEN, AND THE SEVEN JUDGMENTS IT TOOK

**What a clerk can do that they could not do yesterday.** Settings → Notifications
now has a fifth tab, **Blocked addresses**, at
`/{tenant}/settings/notifications/blocked`. It lists every address this utility
must not send to, with the reason in words and the date, filterable by state and
by reason, and it carries **Release** on every row — the control the Product
Owner asked for by name. Before this commit `GET /suppressions` and
`POST /suppressions/{id}/release` were served, audited and tested, and **nothing
in the product called either**: a clerk who fixed a mistyped address on the
account had no way to let that address through again, so a hard bounce was
permanent from their point of view and only an engineer with a database console
could undo it.

**⚠ THERE IS NO NOTIFICATIONS BLUEPRINT, AND THAT WAS CHECKED RATHER THAN
ASSUMED.** B14 rules 41/42 make the drawing the scope where one exists, and
`DEF-GOV-5248` is ten days of a lane building to the wrong reference because
nobody looked. Every ref in this repository was searched: the branch carries
**eight** blueprint PDFs — Assets, Accounts, Meter Reads, Billing, Integration,
Premises & Units, Customer Portal, Plans & Rates — and **none of them is
Notifications**. The two that contain the word *suppress* mean *suppresses its
page header*. So rule 36's other half governs: r10's `UI-RULES.md` and the shared
component kit are the whole of the visual authority, and the screen is the
settings sub-tab pattern its four siblings already use.

⚠ **AND THE SEARCH COMMAND `CLAUDE.md` PRESCRIBES FINDS ONLY SEVEN OF THE
EIGHT** — `git ls-tree -r --name-only <ref> | grep -i 'pdf$'` cannot see
`05-prototype/03 SMARTBillHub — Meter Reads blueprint.pdf`, because git quotes a
path holding a non-ASCII character and the line then ends with `"` rather than
with `pdf`. `-c core.quotePath=false` returns all eight. Filed as
**`DEF-GOV-5652`**, not left in a docstring: a command in a document is a claim
nothing re-checks, and its failure mode is an absence, which is invisible to
every check this repo has.

### The seven judgments, where the rules ran out

1. **`f.reason` was added to the server, and that is the one API change.** The
   listing took `state` and `channel`; the screen needs to narrow by reason
   because `suppression_models.py` argues the three reasons are not
   interchangeable — a hard bounce is a typo a clerk can FIX, a complaint is a
   person who does not want the mail, an unsubscribe is a button we gave them.
   **A browser-side filter was refused**: the list is paginated in the database
   and grows for ever, so narrowing the page in hand would answer *no complaints*
   for a utility whose complaints are all on page two. That is hard-won law 7's
   *reporting zero over a scope it silently excludes*, wearing a filter chip, and
   no assertion about what is on screen can see it. An unknown reason narrows to
   NOTHING rather than falling back to all — unlike `state` it has no default to
   fall back to, and a filter that silently does nothing is worse than one that
   returns nothing, because nothing is visible and doing nothing is not.

2. **The toolbar's *All* chip sends `f.state=all` explicitly, never the server's
   own default.** `GET /suppressions` defaults to ACTIVE when `f.state` is
   absent, and the chip means *nothing is filtered*. Left alone the two would
   disagree, and a clerk clicking **All** would read a chip saying *no filter*
   over a list still quietly hiding every released row, with nothing on screen
   able to say why. The screen lands on `state=active` — the WORK — with that
   chip visibly applied.

3. **Release carries NO danger tier**, and that is a decision rather than an
   oversight. B14 rule 6's tier is for a destructive commit — disconnect, retire,
   reverse, write-off. A release destroys nothing: the row is kept and stamped,
   and what changes is that a customer starts receiving their bill again.
   **A hard bounce is most often a TYPO, so Release is the repair path**, and
   painting it in the colour the product uses for *this cannot be undone* would
   teach a clerk to hesitate over the one action they are meant to take. The
   friction is a dialog that names the address and states the consequence — *"Sending
   to this address resumes. Held messages go out."*, two sentences of five and
   four words (B14 rule 33) — not a colour.

4. **`released_at` renders as a CALENDAR DATE and `suppressed_at` as an INSTANT,
   and the two differ by a day for every North American tenant.** A release is
   dated by the clerk (`BR-TEN-043`) and the server anchors that day to midnight
   UTC purely to store it. Handing the whole timestamp to `DateCell` renders
   midnight UTC in the tenant's own zone — **03/04 typed in Chicago comes back
   03/03**, which `formatDate`'s own comment names as the mistake it exists to
   prevent. It was caught by a test asserting the day the clerk typed, and proved
   in the browser against a real `America/Chicago` tenant. `suppressed_at` is NOT
   sliced: that one is a real instant, the moment a provider told us, and an
   instant always displays in tenant time.

5. **The note is OPTIONAL, because the API made it optional.** It is the one
   field in the table that is a person's own words and the durable answer to *why
   did this customer stop getting email in March* after `audit_log` is pruned, so
   requiring it was tempting. Requiring it would be choosing a value on a
   question nobody has ruled, which the prime directive forbids. The helper asks
   for it — *"Why you let it through."* — and the screen shows it beside the
   released date so that leaving it blank has a visible cost.

6. **Three capabilities are deliberately NOT declared, and each would have been
   dead UI.** No search box (`GET /suppressions` has no `q`), no sortable column
   (it orders active-first, newest-first and honours no `sort`), and no way to
   block an address by hand (`REASON_MANUAL` is a lawful value with **no writer
   anywhere in the product**, so an empty state offering `+ Block address` would
   open onto nothing). The empty block therefore draws no CTA at all.

7. **The door is a sub-tab of Settings → Notifications**, which is the delivery
   home by `BR-TEN-041` #8 — *the addresses we must not send to* is a fact about
   delivery, and that is where a clerk looks for it. It uses the same reserved
   `:sub` segment mechanism as Messages, Sender and Rights rather than a second
   one, and `TAB_SUBS` stays the ONE list both the guard and the strip read.

### What was ALSO closed, and why here

**`DEF-NOT-5641` is closed by this lane**, exactly as its own prevention column
asked. The release refusal had no copy of its own and fell back to the module's
generic delivery key; its nearest existing key reads *"Enter the date the mail
came back"*, which is true of a returned envelope and false on this screen.
`notifications.suppression.release_date_required` — *"Enter the date you released
it."*, six words — now exists in all eleven catalogues. It was done here because
this lane was already in those eleven files, so the G15-parity cost was paid once
rather than twice.

### What none of it proves

⚠ **NOTHING ON THIS DEPLOYMENT WRITES A SUPPRESSION AUTOMATICALLY.**
`BR-NOT-013` holds and no provider adapter with a feedback door exists, so on a
live tenant this list is EMPTY until one lands. The four rows walked in the
browser were written by calling `suppression.suppress` directly. The READ and
RELEASE halves are wired and proved; the WRITE half is still waiting on the same
adapter `DEF-NOT-5632` recorded.

⚠ **AND THE WHOLE `NotificationsTab` — ALL FIVE SUB-TABS — IS GATED BEHIND THE
DELIVERY QUEUE'S OWN TWO READS.** `summary.isPending || queue.isPending` returns
a skeleton before the sub-tab branch is reached, and a permission denial on
`GET /outbound/summary` shows *"You do not have access to this utility's delivery
queue"* over a tab that never touches the queue. That is **pre-existing and shared
with the Rights and Sender tabs**, it is why this lane's door tests seed those two
reads, and it is deliberately NOT changed here — it would move four other tabs at
once on one screen's authority. Recorded rather than fixed.

## 2026-09-17 · THE FOUR HARDCODED CONSUMERS NOW READ THE TABLE — AND THE GUARD THAT WOULD HAVE CAUGHT THEM

**This is a BUILD lane's record, not a new ruling.** It implements the PO ruling
of this morning — *"utility can get their own account types"*, *"we have to
ensure it is not hard coded"* — recorded above under *"A UTILITY MAY DEFINE ITS
OWN ACCOUNT TYPES"*. Three judgment calls were made where the rules ran out and
they are written here rather than left to be inferred from the diff.

⚠ **NAMING, SO A GREP FINDS SOMETHING.** This lane refers to that ruling as
**`BR-CUS-094a`** in code, tests and defect rows — it AMENDS `BR-CUS-094` rather
than replacing it, which is why it is not a fresh number. **No register has
issued that id.** It is a label, recorded here so it can be looked up, and the
customers lane making `account_types` tenant-owned should mint the real
`BR-CUS-<nnnnn>` row in `04-docs/05-modules/03-customers/02-business-rules.md`
and rename these citations to it. Named because an id nobody issued is
`DEF-2804`'s shape and the way to stop it spreading is to say so in the register
rather than in one file's prose.

### 1 · THE HONEST FALLBACK FOR THE PORTAL IS `None`, NOT ANOTHER CLASS

`CWP-008` quotes a deposit to a visitor who has not said what kind of customer
they are, so it asks the seam for the utility's HOME class. The seam read one
typed literal, `code__iexact="residential"`.

**The tempting fallback — the tenant's first active row — was rejected, and the
reason is a money one.** It would quote a **COMMERCIAL** deposit to somebody
moving into a house, and on screen that is indistinguishable from a correct
figure: a number shown to a member of the public for a class they do not belong
to. `rating_seam.deposit` already returns `None` for a missing class and the
screen then shows no figure at all, so **withholding the number is a state the
product already renders and guessing it is not.** The seam returns `None` and
the screen says *"deposit on your first bill"* without an amount.

**The code itself is no longer typed either:** it is read from
`AccountType.SEVEN_CATEGORIES[0]`, BR-CUS-094's own ruling order, whose first
entry IS the home class. So the day the PO renames it, this follows instead of
silently returning `None` for every utility on the platform.

### 2 · THE VOCABULARY IS SPLIT IN TWO, DELIBERATELY, TO KEEP A GUARD ALIVE

The obvious fix — point `seams.account_type_codes()` at the rows — would have
destroyed a real property. `test_def273_the_class_vocabulary_mirrors_the_
platform_account_types` compares the SEEDED ROWS against that function; derive
it from rows and the guard compares the rows with themselves. **A check that
cannot go red is worse than none (`DEF-182`).**

So there are now two functions and the split is the deliverable:

| | reads | who uses it |
|---|---|---|
| `account_type_codes()` | the model's **declared constants** — the vocabulary **AS RULED** | the two guards, and `endpoints.ts`'s front-end mirror |
| `selectable_account_type_codes()` | the tenant's **ROWS** — the vocabulary **AS HELD** | every validator and every offer surface |

`rating.services.TAX_CUSTOMER_CLASSES` stays pointed at the first and its
docstring now says why. A second test, `test_the_seeded_rows_still_match_the_
ruling`, asks the narrowed question that survives tenant-owned rows: **do the
rows the PLATFORM SEEDS (`is_system=True`) still match the vocabulary the PO
ruled?** It goes red the day a migration seeds a code the ruling does not name.

**Reasons (b) and (c) of the old docstring were kept rather than waved away.**
(c) no database at import time: both are functions, evaluated at call time. (b)
no query in a per-row validator: the one site where the vocabulary sat INSIDE a
loop — the reference-fixture tax seeder — now reads it once above the loop, and
both validators read it once per request rather than once per element.

### 3 · `govt` WAS NEVER STORED, AND THAT WAS MEASURED BEFORE IT WAS REMOVED

`apps/billing/template_models.py` carried `CATEGORY_GOVT = "govt"` beside three
real codes. **It is a code this product has never had** — not in a row, not in a
migration, not in a ruling; the ratified fourth is `municipal` and `government`
is LEGACY. Meanwhile `apps/notifications/template_models.py` spells the same
idea `"government"`. Three spellings of one thing in three modules.

**Whether this needed a data migration was answered by looking, not by
assuming.** `bill_templates` holds **zero rows in every database on the build
machine** (`sbh`, `sbh_capis` and both test databases); no migration seeds a
category; the only production writer, `templates_service.ensure_seed_template`,
writes `category=None`; and `create_template` — the one path that could ever
have stored it — **is served by no route at all**, which
`templates_service.py`'s own refusal register states: *"STILL NOT SERVED:
create_template"*. So `govt` was unreachable as well as wrong, and this is a
constant change rather than a data migration. **That paragraph is in the source
file**, so if it ever stops being true the next reader knows the fix becomes a
migration.

### 4 · WHAT WAS FOUND AND NOT FIXED, BECAUSE ANOTHER LANE HOLDS THE FILE

Four more consumers were found and filed rather than changed —
`DEF-NOT-5662` (a notification rule can be targeted at only **two of the
seven** classes), `DEF-NOT-5663` (`"government"` hardcoded), `DEF-CUS-5664`
(`SEED_ACCOUNT_TYPES` is still the **pre-BR-CUS-094 four**, missing all four
codes August added), and `DEF-RAT-5665` (the base-to-charge-code command, whose
file is HUMAN-OWNED so editing it is a process event). Each is on the new
guard's allow list **by name, with its defect id**, and the allow list's size is
asserted — so none of them can be quietly forgotten and none can be quietly
joined.

### 5 · THE GUARD, AND WHAT IT CANNOT SEE

`tests/test_br_cus_094a_tenant_account_types.py` walks **740 production
modules** under `06-backend/apps` and fails on any that names **two or more**
account-type codes as quoted literals within three lines.

**The threshold is two and not three, and that difference is a real defect.**
The nearest existing check uses three, and at three
`notifications/rule_catalog.py`'s `PLAN_CLASSES = ("all", "residential",
"commercial")` is **invisible** — the guard written for exactly that shape
cannot see it. A threshold is a blind spot wearing a number.

**Seven files are forgiven and every one is named with its reason**: the OWNER
declaration (1), sample data (2), a DIFFERENT vocabulary that collides on two
words — metering's `UNIT_TYPES` — (1), and REAL DEFECTS deferred to other lanes
(3). Four whole trees are not walked at all — migrations, tests, the front end
and the docs — each with the reason. **Both counts are asserted**, per hard-won
law 7: *a declared blind spot with no number attached is indistinguishable from
an empty one.*

**And the guard re-proves itself RED on every run**, not once at birth: it runs
its own scanner over the four pre-fix constants kept verbatim in the test, over
the two-code shape the old threshold missed, and over a line of prose it must
NOT fire on. Law 7's 2026-09-05 addendum is why — *"a red proof at birth says
nothing about whether anyone ever reads it again."*

### 6 · WALKED AS A USER, ON SEEDED PRODUCT DATA — AND THE `govt` QUESTION IS SETTLED ON A SCREEN

PO instruction of the same day, verbatim: *"can you also do the Walks as user
from screens and ensure it is working as expected - if it break fix it"*. No
gate in this repo reads rendered output (hard-won law 6), so the two surfaces
this lane touches were opened.

**THE PORTAL, `CWP-008`, AGAINST A REAL `seed_portal_demo` TENANT (Pine Hill,
76 premises).** The address `103 Willow Bend Dr` was typed into the page in a
browser. ⚠ **The deposit rules are a FIXTURE this lane created deliberately, and
they are what make the walk decide anything:** `$150.00` against the home class
and **`$500.00` against Commercial**, on the same plan. Without the second rule
the screen looks identical whether the code is right or wrong.

  * home class ACTIVE → the page shows **`$150.00 deposit on your first bill`**.
    The residential figure, resolved from the table — not the commercial one.
  * home class RETIRED (`active=false`) → the DEPOSIT column shows **`—` on
    every service and the deposit line DISAPPEARS from *IF YOU APPLY*.**
    **It does NOT show `$500.00`.** That is the judgment in §1 proved on a
    screen: the tempting fallback would have quoted a business deposit to
    somebody moving into a house, and it would have looked completely normal.

The row was restored afterwards and the page returned to `$150.00`.

**THE BILL-TEMPLATES SCREEN, and this is the `govt` answer the walk was asked
for.** `templates_api._library_dict()` — the exact call the screen renders from
— returns **`templates: []`** for a freshly seeded tenant: the one seeded row
carries **no category at all**. So **no screen in this product has ever
displayed `govt`, and there is nothing to migrate.** The same call now offers
all eight ruled codes where it offered four, and picks up a class the moment the
utility adds one (checked by adding `Marina` and removing it again).

### 7 · THE GUARD WAS WIDENED TO A SECOND VOCABULARY, BECAUSE THE DISEASE HAS NOW BEEN FOUND THREE TIMES IN ONE DAY

The PO found it in account types. This lane found it in bill-template
categories. A sibling found the Add-units form reading a hardcoded five-string
array while the backend read the tenant's `unit_types` table
(**`DEF-MET-5656`**). Three vocabularies, three finders, one shape.

**So the guard is written for the SHAPE and not for one table** — *a seeded,
tenant-extensible lookup vocabulary written into our own source* — and it now
walks **the FRONT END as well**, which is where it bites hardest: a hardcoded
array there is what a clerk SEES, so the class the utility added is simply
missing from the dropdown with a perfectly green backend behind it.

Measured: **739 backend modules and 602 front-end sources**. Thirteen files are
forgiven, every one named with its reason and its defect id; four trees are not
walked, each with its reason; both counts are asserted. **And the guard's
permanent self-proof now includes `DEF-MET-5656`'s own array verbatim** — a
guard proved only against the bug its author already knew about is a guard
proved against nothing.

### 8 · TWO MORE THINGS FIXED ON THE WAY

**`DEF-RAT-5654`, filed by the sibling account-types lane against this lane's own
file.** `seams.account_type_id_by_code` resolved a code with NO tenant filter and
said in its own docstring that this was deliberate — true while the table was a
platform catalogue, and a cross-tenant read the day it stops being one. It now
filters where a column exists, through the same helper the rest of this lane
uses, so neither lane has to land first.

**The size-row `customer_class` was validated against NOTHING.** It is
`CR-087 A1`'s narrowing column — the one that makes a connection fee `$45.00`
residential and `$85.00` commercial — and it accepted any string up to 60
characters, while `size_class` beside it was refused unless served. A typo'd
`residental` row stored cleanly, matched no account that ever existed, and the
customer it was written for was billed the every-class amount instead. It is now
refused, against the tenant's table. **The storage did not move.**

## 2026-09-17 · The sub-type a clerk could not set, and the type filter that was there all along (`DEF-CUS-5674` · `DEF-CUS-5676` · `DEF-CUS-5677`) — 2.295.1

**Two gaps were reported. One was real, one was a NAME, and walking the second
as a different person found a third that is worse than either.**

### 1 · The sub-type — REAL, and built (`DEF-CUS-5674`)

`NewAccountWizard.tsx` and `MoveInWizard.tsx` — **the only two screens an
account is born on** — had zero mentions of sub-type. Not a refusal, not a
disabled control with a reason: no field. Yet the column is writable
(`CREATE_FIELDS` carries `account_subtype`), the edit dialog has offered one
since `CR-010`, and the seeded tenant already holds accounts carrying
`multi_family` and `light_industrial` — which can only have been set by the
create-then-edit round trip the PO described.

Built as a **dependent picker**: the child list is the tenant's own rows
filtered by the chosen category (`BR-CUS-067`, `parent_required` — *"a floating
sub-type is a sub-type of nothing"*), and changing the category **clears an
incompatible child**. It **fails closed**: an unknown code, which is also what
an unloaded list looks like, clears. Nothing downstream would refuse the pair —
`_resolve_account_subtype` resolves a code against the tenant and never asks
which category it hangs off — so this is the only place the pair is known to be
wrong. It is **OPTIONAL and unmarked**: `accounts.account_subtype_id` is
nullable by design.

**Proved by clicking, then read back out of PostgreSQL.** Four accounts created
end to end through the wizard on the seeded tenant, every one of them
`account_type=commercial`, `account_subtype_id` SET, `subtype_code =
small_commercial`. `10-scripts/def_cus_5674_subtype_walkthrough.mjs`.

### 2 · The account-TYPE filter — NOT a gap. It is called *Category* (`DEF-CUS-5676`)

The brief cited `selectors.py:~259` as declaring `account_type` a filter. **That
line is a `select_related`, not a filter declaration.** `ACCOUNT_FILTERS` is
`status · category · autopay · balance_gt · unit_id · premises_id · kind ·
ageing`, and `category` is applied as `account_type__code__iexact` — the file
says so in as many words: *"BR-CUS-053 `category` = account type"*.

**MEASURED rather than assumed: `f.category=commercial` returns 14 of 76, the
rows drawn equal the count served, and PostgreSQL agrees exactly.** So the
capability is complete and correct.

**No second control was added**, because two controls for one fact is a defect
this repo has filed before. What IS wrong is the vocabulary: the list, both
wizards and the account detail say **Category**; the Settings card over the same
table says **Account types**. That is why a working filter was reported missing.
**Not renamed by this lane** — the Accounts blueprint p60 draws `Category *`, so
renaming would put the product against the drawing, which B14 rule 41 makes the
one thing that reaches the PO. **One sentence to put to them:** *Category* and
*Account type* are the same list of eight — which word should a clerk see?

### 3 · ⚠ THE ONE THAT MATTERS MOST, AND ONLY A SECOND ROLE FOUND IT (`DEF-CUS-5677`)

The whole walk above passed as a **System Admin**. Signed in as the seeded
**Billing Clerk** — the role that opens accounts all day —
`GET /lookups/account_subtypes` answers **403** and the dropdown holds exactly
one option: its own placeholder.

**The refusal is CORRECT and SIGNED.** `SettingsReadAnyWriteSystemAdmin`
allows `{SYSTEM_ADMIN, EXECUTIVE}` because A4's `settings_lookups` row gives a
Billing Clerk **no cell at all**, which `DEF-196` established means no access;
`US-TEN-009 TC-5` has asserted *"clerk denied at the reference-data surface"*
since the surface was built. **What is wrong is the door, not the gate:** three
clerk-facing pickers read their vocabulary through a SETTINGS endpoint.

So the PO's report is **worse than it reads**. It is not only that the create
wizards had no sub-type field — **the edit dialog they were being sent to
instead has an empty one too** (`AccountPanelEdits.tsx`), as does service-request
capture. A Billing Clerk cannot set an account sub-type anywhere in the product.

**The fix is a tenant-role endpoint, and this repo has already done it once for
this exact problem.** `GET /reads/read-methods` is `AnyTenantRole` and its
docstring is this defect written in advance: *"S28 is the Billing Clerk's screen
and `/lookups/read_methods` is System-Admin-only (DEF-196), so the wizard could
not read the list through Settings — a clerk would have got an empty control"*.
The natural home is beside `GET /service-requests/categories`, which is already
`AnyTenantRole` and already serves the PARENT list. **NOT BUILT HERE** —
`apps/customers/` belongs to the lane making `account_types` tenant-owned;
REPORTED.

Meanwhile both wizards **STATE the refusal** rather than drawing an empty
control (`BR-SHL-025`, A18 §1), and the two facts are kept apart on purpose: *the
read was refused* and *this category has no children* are different, and a clerk
acts differently on each.

### What this cost, generalised

**A walk signed in as an admin certifies nothing about the person who uses the
screen.** Every gate, `tsc` and 14 new vitest cases were green over a control
that is dead for its actual user. That is hard-won law 2's mirror, and the only
thing that found it was changing WHO was looking.

**And the refusal frame cannot be asserted from the node-tier suite at all** —
this repo already measured that a query cached as `status:"error"` renders as
*pending* under `renderToStaticMarkup` (`AccountUsageTab.test.tsx`). Writing a
case there would have asserted the opposite of what a browser does. It is proved
in the browser instead, which is the only tier that can answer it.

## 2026-09-17 · THE FORCED PASSWORD CHANGE: FOUR THINGS THE SERVER ALREADY DECIDED, AND ONE OF THEM WAS THE OPPOSITE OF WHAT THE BRIEF ASSUMED

**`DEF-IDN-5653` — every invited user was locked out.** The screen at
`/{tenant}/change-password` is built and the route is registered OUTSIDE the app
shell. Shipped as **`2.295.4`**. What follows is the part a rule did not answer.

### The symptom was NOT a blank page, and that matters for how it was proved

The PO photographed *"We couldn't load your regional settings."* with a Retry
button. That is the APP SHELL failing to boot, not a missing screen — the
catch-all lives inside the shell, the shell boots by reading the tenant's
settings, and `identity/auth.py`'s `_FORCED_CHANGE_EXEMPT` refuses every
authenticated read to a user who owes a password change. So the user got a
frame around an error, and the frame is what made it look like a settings bug.

⚠ **This is why two of the four cases in the defect's own red proof were GREEN
on the broken screen.** The catch-all rendered a LOADING SKELETON: it is longer
than 200 characters, it does not say *"not built"*, and it has no `<nav>`. Three
obvious assertions all pass on it. The cases now assert the screen's own
`data-page="change-password"` handle and a count of exactly two password boxes,
and each was shown RED against the unregistered route before being trusted.

### Four judgments, each read out of the server rather than assumed

1. **No current-password field.** `services.change_password` reads
   `forced = actor.must_change_password` and skips the current-password check
   entirely when it is set. Measured: `POST /me/password` with only
   `new_password`/`confirm_password` answers **204**.

2. **The screen does NOT list the tenant's password rules, and it is not allowed
   to.** `GET /settings/security-policy` exists and has a client, and it answers
   **403** to exactly this user — measured, with the same cookie, before and
   after the change. Hardcoding a copy of a per-tenant policy would drift the
   first time a utility raises its minimum length. So the rules arrive from the
   server's own refusal: `validate_new_password` returns one `field_error` per
   broken rule and they render on the field. Walked: typing `abc` puts **"Use at
   least 8 characters. Use upper case, lower case and a digit."** under the box,
   which is this tenant's real policy and no part of it is written in the client.

3. ⚠ **THE SESSION SURVIVES THE CHANGE, WHICH IS THE OPPOSITE OF WHAT THE TASK
   ASSUMED, SO THE SCREEN LANDS ON THE DASHBOARD AND NOT ON SIGN-IN.**
   `BR-IDN-005` says a forced change revokes all PRIOR sessions and it is natural
   to read that as *"you are signed out"*. It is not: `MePasswordView` passes
   `current_session=request.auth` and `revoke_sessions(except_session=…)`
   EXCLUDES it. Measured decisively — `GET /me` answers **403** before the change
   and **200 on the same cookie** after it. Sending this user back to a sign-in
   form would have made them retype the password they had just chosen, for no
   reason the server asked for.

4. **A user who owes no change is sent to the dashboard rather than shown the
   form**, because without the flag the server requires `current_password`, which
   this screen deliberately does not collect. Only a POSITIVE answer moves
   anybody — see the next section for why absence must not.

### ⚠ THE FIX HAD A SECOND DEFECT INSIDE IT, AND THE FIXTURE HID IT COMPLETELY

The first build of this screen read the session from `queryKeys.me` and treated
**absence as "not signed in"**, redirecting to `/signin`. Every unit test passed,
because the test harness SEEDS that key. **The product never does.**
`SignInPage` called `POST /auth/session`, threw the answer away and navigated —
so on the one path that matters the cache was empty, and the invited user was
bounced straight back to the door they had just come through. **The same lockout
with a tidier bounce**, and it was caught only by walking it in a browser.

Two changes, and both are the rule rather than a patch:

* **`SignInPage` now writes the sign-in response into `queryKeys.me`.**
  `POST /auth/session` answers with exactly the payload `GET /me` serves, and
  this is the ONLY moment the app is allowed to learn it for a user who owes a
  change — every later read of `/me` is refused 403.
* **The screen renders the form when there is no session in cache.** A reload on
  that address, a cold tab: the person standing there has a temporary password
  and nothing else to try, so absence is not an answer and must not be treated as
  one. The *"Signed in as …"* line is DROPPED rather than faked.

**The general lesson, and it is this repo's own in a new place: a fixture that
seeds state the product never produces will make a broken screen look correct,
and no amount of test-writing discipline finds it.** Hard-won law 6 is the only
thing that did.

### The route path is `SignInPage`'s own constant

`App.tsx` mounts `FORCED_PASSWORD_CHANGE_ROUTE.slice(1)` rather than a second
spelling of `"change-password"`. The defect was a door and a destination held as
two separate strings that could disagree, and for eight days they did; one
constant makes that impossible. The durable test asserts every destination
`routeAfterSignIn` can CHOOSE is a registered route — written over the function,
so a third branch added later arrives with no test until the case is updated.

### Proved end to end, on a real tenant, twice over

Real `seed_demo` tenant, real PostgreSQL, the deployed join (`server.mjs` +
Django). A user was created through the real Add-user screen, its one-time
temporary password taken off the panel, and that person signed in, was refused
once by the policy, set a password and **reached the dashboard with the shell
booted**. Signing out and in again went **straight to the dashboard**.
**20/20 browser checks passed** —
`10-scripts/def_idn_5653_forced_password_walkthrough.mjs`.

**The membership was read back from PostgreSQL, not taken from the screen**, and
the two runs make a controlled pair in one table: the user from the FAILED run
is still `must_change_password = t`, temp expiry set, `invited`; the user from
the fixed run is `must_change_password = f`, expiry NULL, password changed,
**`active`** — `BR-IDN-011`'s activation, confirmed in the database.

### And the roles grid became an address (PO ruling the same day)

*"View roles & permissions"* was a button toggling `matrixOpen`, so the
`BR-IDN-014` grid was one of two surfaces at one address: it could not be linked,
could not be bookmarked, and vanished on navigating away. It is now
`/{tenant}/settings/users/roles`, built on the SAME `SettingsSubTab` mechanism as
Company's and Configure's strips rather than a second one. **Nothing bookmarked
broke, because nothing COULD be bookmarked** — the panel was `useState`, not a
route — and `/settings/users` still opens the user table. The blast radius was
checked first: nothing else in the product links to the matrix. It stays
read-only; there is no tenant-facing mutation route for it to gain.

### What is filed rather than fixed

⚠ **The shell's user menu still offers a dead *"Change password"* item**, whose
copy reads *"Not ready yet — password changes work, but the screen for it is
still being built."* **That sentence is now half false and this screen does not
make it true.** This is the FORCED change: it collects no current password, and
the server requires one for a voluntary change. The VOLUNTARY screen is still
unbuilt, so the hold stands and the copy is the thing that is wrong.
Filed as **`DEF-IDN-5678`** rather than silently flipped — releasing a control
onto a screen that would refuse its user is hard-won law 2's mirror, which is the
defect this lane was sent to fix.

## 2026-09-17 — `DEF-INT-5629` and `DEF-INT-5601`: what a refused row costs, and whose order a clerk is reading (`2.295.4`)

**Two defects, one story from both ends.** `DEF-INT-5629` said the parcel
reconciliation's apply path could not write a row; `DEF-INT-5601` said CR-112's
four modules had no caller. The second is why the first could exist: **no
caller, no proof.**

### The picture had already moved, and measuring it first is most of this entry

`DEF-INT-5601` was filed against four modules. Re-measured at `668a8507a` by
grepping every non-test importer:

| module | importers outside `tests/` | |
|---|---|---|
| `gis_parcels` | `gis.py::reconcile`, `api.py`'s `POST …/reconcile` | LIVE since `2836c242a` |
| `gis_layer` | `gis_parcels`, `gis_match`, `gis_search`, **and `adapters/gis_city.py`** | LIVE since `DEF-INT-5618` |
| `gis_match` | `gis_parcels`, which is now reachable | LIVE |
| `gis_search` | **none** | the genuinely dark one |

So the defect's headline count of four was two days stale, and the flat-list
line it warns about — *"the backend groups and the front end has not caught
up"* — was still true in the direction it complained of: `gis.py::search`
returned a flat list and never called `gis_search`.

### The half of `DEF-INT-5629` that was still open

`2836c242a` fixed the first half: metering's known-field sets now accept the
four columns the run patches. What it left is the savepoint's catch list.
`_persist` caught **`DatabaseError` and nothing else**, and the writer it calls —
`metering.services.update_premises` — raises a PRODUCT refusal for everything a
40,000-row apply legitimately meets: a value the validator will not take
(`ValidationError`), a rule that stopped the row (`BizError`), and **a premises
deleted between the read and the write** (`NotFoundError`, via
`deny_as_not_found`) — which is the case the PostgreSQL test file's own
docstring names and could not survive. Each of those ended the run on the row it
met, and `rows_refused` could never reach 1 by any of them.

**The fix is a NAMED list and not `except Exception`, and the distinction is the
decision.** `AuthError` and `SysError` are deliberately absent: a role refusal
is a property of the ACTOR, not of a row, so swallowing it would report *40,000
rows refused* for a run that was never allowed to start. A test holds that line
and goes red the day somebody widens the tuple.

**A count of 37 over 40,000 rows tells nobody which 37**, so the report now
names them — `BR-RBS-035`'s shape, a row for what it acted on and a count for
the rest, capped at 50, labelled by premises NUMBER and never by database id
(B14 rule 31).

### Law 14, proved on PostgreSQL for the first time in this repo

`tests/test_cr112_gis_parcels_pg.py` had **never been run**. Its own docstring
said so honestly — *"WRITTEN, REASONED, AND UNPROVEN ON THE DATABASE THAT
MATTERS"* — because every earlier attempt to build a PostgreSQL test database
failed. A role with `CREATEDB` is what let it run. **9 passed.**

⚠ **AND RUNNING IT FOUND THAT ITS HEADLINE CASE COULD NOT FAIL (`DEF-INT-5669`).**
With the savepoint removed by sabotage, `test_one_refused_row_does_not_lose_the_others`
**PASSED** — its fixture recorded the good rows by appending to a Python list and
issuing no statement, so the assertion never asked the poisoned connection
anything. The fixture now issues a real `SELECT 1` per row; with the savepoint
removed, **4 of 9 fail**, including the headline. **The savepoint is now a
measurement rather than an argument.**

### Whose order a clerk is reading — and the judgment this lane made

`gis.py::search` served the City's rows **unsorted**: a FeatureServer answers in
the layer's own order, so *"8 matches from the City's records"* was eight
arbitrary rows and typing `100 N Maple` could show eight addresses without
`100 N Maple` among them. It now ranks through `gis_search`.

⚠ **THE JUDGMENT, RECORDED AS OURS (law 13) AND NOT PUT TO THE PO.**
`gis_search`'s premise is *"the City publishes no relevance score for a `like`
query"*. That is true of an ArcGIS layer and **false of a geocoder**, which is
the other shape `candidate_from` accepts — it returns a `score`, and its index
knows things four tie-breaks over a street name cannot. So **theirs wins where
they published one, and the note is then NOT SHOWN**: saying *"Ordered by us,
not the city."* over the City's own order would be the claim that module exists
to avoid making. All or nothing, never row by row — a scored row and an unscored
one cannot be compared. Measured in a browser: the shipped geocoder recording
gives `ranking_note_key: null` and the City's order; the same four rows with
their scores stripped give `integrations.gis.our_ranking` and put the typed
address first.

**A forty-word paragraph left the screen for it.**
`metering.premises.find.noScore` explained *why* no number is shown — and B14
rule 33 is that RATIONALE is **zero words on screen**. It is in
`gis.match_word`'s docstring and `US-INT-042` §1, which is where the rule says
to put it. The key is still in all eleven catalogues with no reader.

### What was NOT done, and why each is a row rather than a silence

* **The grouping** (`DEF-INT-5671`) — `group_by_building` needs the City's
  `Unit` column to tell a building from its units, and
  `adapters/gis_city.candidate_from` does not put it on the wire. Grouping
  without it would collapse a four-flat's five address points into ONE row and
  take four `FULLPIN`s off the screen — the key `DEF-INT-5600` exists to
  deliver. **A worse screen is not a smaller gap.** `adapters/` is another
  lane's this session.
* **The ArcGIS query shape** (`DEF-INT-5670`) — the live search sends `q=` and
  `limit=` to a service that requires `where=`, so against Ann Arbor it is
  refused on every keystroke. `gis_layer._query_url`, `gis_layer.layer_base` and
  `gis_search.where_clause` are the three uncalled functions that already do it
  right. This is `DEF-INT-5618` one step upstream: **the module that understands
  the City is unreachable from the screen, and the module the screen reaches
  does not understand the City.**
* **The scheduled run** (`DEF-INT-5672`) — `OQ-INT-1728` asks for three ways to
  do one job and two exist. `BY_SCHEDULE` is a default no caller passes. The
  split is correct and is not the gap: `BR-INT-054` puts the scheduler in
  Runbooks, and integrations must not grow a second one.

### ⚠ Nothing here is evidence about Ann Arbor

The egress proxy refuses `a2mapseg.a2gov.org` — `curl` returns `000`, and inside
Django the same refusal is *"Tunnel connection failed: 403 Forbidden"*. Every
candidate and every parcel read in this work came from
`apps/integrations/gis_fixtures.py` and `gis_esri_fixtures.py`, whose own
docstrings say they are hand-shaped from documented field names and are **not
recordings**. A green walk means our search, our ranking and our run behave.

## 2026-09-17 · CR-115-BRC05 §7 — CUSTOM APIs ON A CONNECTOR, AND THE FIVE JUDGMENTS THE RULING DID NOT MAKE FOR US

**Built in `2.296.0`.** The ruling itself is `BR-INT-078` and `CR-115-BRC05` §7,
which hold every PO quote verbatim. What follows is only what the ruling left to
us — recorded here because law 10's test is *"would the next agent, with only the
repo, build the same thing?"*, and for four of these five the answer was no.

### 1 · THE BLUEPRINT'S 14-SEPTEMBER RULING IS SUPERSEDED, AND THE SCHEMA CHANGE IT AVOIDED IS NOW PAID

The Integration Blueprint (`05-prototype/05 Integration Blueprint.pdf`, p15
`CR-3`, p164) ruled: *"Can a clerk rename an API we declared? **No.** … The
disabled + Add an API control is removed."* **§7.2 records the PO calling that
too broad on 17 September**, so the later ruling wins and both are kept.

⚠ **THE BLUEPRINT'S OWN REASONING IS WHY THIS COSTS A MIGRATION.** It banked the
saving in as many words — *"If the name were the clerk's, it would need a
per-connection field that does not exist … this whole item becomes drawing work
rather than migration work."* The name IS the clerk's now, so the field exists:
`integration_api`, migration `integrations/0014`. **Worth stating because the
blueprint reads as authority on this screen and a lane checking it would find the
opposite of what was built.**

### 2 · WHERE THE ROWS LIVE — A TABLE, AND THE REASON IS A SHIPPED DEFECT

The obvious home is `integration_connection.config`. **It would be silently
destroyed.** `services.update_connection` prunes the stored config to the names
the manifest still declares (`DEF-INT-5582`), so the first time a clerk pressed
**Edit → Save and test** on the connector, every custom API would vanish — with a
correct file count, a green suite and nothing raised. A table cannot be pruned by
a field validator. *(A sibling lane reached the same conclusion for
`integration_sending_domain` the same day, independently, from the same defect.)*

⚠ **PROVED IN A BROWSER, BECAUSE §7.6 SAYS A PASSING TEST IS NOT THE PROOF FOR
THIS ONE.** Step 7 of `10-scripts/cr115_custom_apis_walkthrough.mjs` saves the
connector through the real form and then re-reads the page: the custom row and
the switch a clerk set are both still there.

### 3 · A CUSTOM ROW STORES AN OPERATION, NOT A KIND — SO THE CLOSED LIST CANNOT DRIFT OPEN

The Kind and the operation that runs it are ONE fact. Storing both would be one
fact in two columns and the copy nobody reads is the one that drifts. So
`integration_api.operation` names one of OUR operations and
`custom_apis.KIND_OF_OPERATION` maps between them — **data keyed by provider,
which `G77` allows and `gis.RUN_NOW_OPERATIONS` already set the precedent for.**

⚠ **INFERENCE WAS CONSIDERED AND REJECTED, AND THE REASON IS THE DIRECTION IT
FAILS IN.** `trigger == "scheduled"` → a sync, `executor == "browser"` → tiles,
`result_disposition == "offer"` → a lookup: it reads plausibly and fails **OPEN**
— every future connector declaring a scheduled inbound fetch would silently
acquire a *Scheduled sync* a clerk could point anywhere, on the day its manifest
landed, with every test green. A map fails **CLOSED**: a connector nobody has
thought about offers nothing (hard-won law 3 — the permissive answer is the one
you type).

### 4 · RULE 1 COUNTS OURS AND THEIRS TOGETHER, AND RULE 4's STATE HALF NEEDS NOTHING

**Rule 1.** §7.5 says *ONE Scheduled sync per connector*. `gis_esri` already
ships one, so a custom one is the SECOND and is refused — and the way through it
is to switch the shipped one off, which is why the Kind stays in the dropdown
carrying a sentence rather than vanishing. ⚠ Counting only the CUSTOM ones would
let exactly the harm the rule exists to prevent through the front door **while
reading as a correctly implemented rule**. The refusal is asked again when a sync
is switched back ON, because a rule enforced only where it was first written is a
rule with a hole in it.

**Rule 4.** *"…and the State word count only ENABLED APIs"* reads like work.
**It is already true and the only way to get it wrong is to add something.**
Since `DEF-INT-5597` the State word is `connection.status` and counts no APIs at
all, so a lane "implementing" rule 4 by filtering operation states into
`display_state` would rebuild the aggregate that defect removed and **break rule
5 in the act of obeying rule 4**. Recorded in `selectors.display_state`'s own
docstring, where the next lane will be standing.

### 5 · THE MERGE RANKS TWO LAYERS AND LEAVES ONE ALONE

Rule 2 asks that two layers be *"ranked together"*. The first build ranked
unconditionally — and turned `test_us_int_042_gis.py`'s TC-1 red: the City's
first candidate went from `88214` to `88301`. **A sibling suite's red was the
finding** (law 7 habit 1). With ONE layer there is nothing to merge, and
re-sorting changes what every existing tenant already sees on a screen that
shipped weeks ago. So the ranking applies from the second source onward, which
keeps the posture lane 1 took for the address ladder: **where the new feature is
not in play, the answers do not move.**

### AND TWO THINGS FOUND BY CLICKING, WHICH NO CHECK IN THIS REPO COULD SEE

* `DEF-INT-5683` — the closed Kind list was served on the provider card and not
  on the payload S142 actually fetches, so **`+ API` was never drawn and the
  whole feature was unreachable**, with every test green. The field is optional
  and `[]` is legal, so nothing could tell *offers no kinds* from *never plumbed
  through*. `G13` asks whether a PROP has a caller; **nothing asks whether a
  SERVED FIELD has a reader.**
* `DEF-INT-5681` — the set-up screen went on claiming *"All use the address
  above"* after a clerk gave one API its own URL, with the rows above it printing
  two different addresses. Hard-won law 1 in one line of copy.

**Both are the reason §7.10 asks for a browser walk rather than a green run, and
neither would have been found any other way** (law 6 — no gate in this repo reads
rendered output).

### DEFERRED, NOT FORGOTTEN

* **Per-API keys** — `DEF-INT-5680`, on §7.6's own instruction. A connection
  holds ONE credential; several touches the credential store, *Keys in use*,
  rotation and expiry. The blueprint's `VIEW-25` frame says the same under this
  table: *"One key. All 3 APIs use it."* Ann Arbor needs no key at all, so one
  built now would ship untested against any real vendor.
* **The known limit** — a customer with TWO custom address layers cannot add the
  second themselves. The honest answers are a manifest line from us or a
  Runbook. **There is no third, and it must not be invented** (`BR-INT-078`).
* **`DEF-GOV-5682`** — the tenant-isolation probe cannot `SET ROLE` on
  PostgreSQL 16 (`GRANT … TO CURRENT_USER` needs `WITH SET TRUE` since the
  membership options were split), so every RLS proof in the repo skips or errors.
  Granting it by hand took `tests/test_us_int_014_pg.py` from *4 passed, 2
  errors* to **5 passed** and this lane's own probe from *1 passed, 3 skipped* to
  **4 passed**. Filed rather than fixed: `isolation_helpers.py` is shared test
  infrastructure outside this lane's scope.

**⚠ NOTHING HERE WAS PUT BACK TO THE PRODUCT OWNER** (hard-won law 13). Every one
is a judgment the rules left to us, recorded with its reasoning, which is the
deliverable; a question would have been the failure to make one.

## 2026-09-17 · The two Routes & Cycles wizards: the copy cut and the shared table (`DEF-TEN-5706`, `DEF-TEN-5707`)

**What the Product Owner said**, verbatim, walking the deployed build with
screenshots: *"too much text - please reduce it"*, *"this ui is not as per our ui
guideline"*, and on step 2 of both wizards *"we are not using table component
toolkit - search, filter, colume selector - too much text"*.

Both are `SET-06.1` (`/settings/reference-data/routes-cycles/routes/new`) and
`SET-07.1` (`…/cycles/new`). Neither is a new capability: a user can do this task
in the product today, so this is **MAINTENANCE** (`22-product-maintenance-process.md`),
not a build wave, and it is a DEFECT rather than a change — the product does not
do what our own signed rules say it should.

### Is there a blueprint? Yes, and it nearly went unread

`DEF-GOV-5248` requires a blueprint check before reading `r10` for any screen.
**There are EIGHT blueprint PDFs on this branch, not seven**, and the eighth is
`05-prototype/03 SMARTBillHub — Meter Reads blueprint.pdf` — the module that owns
routes. The command CLAUDE.md prescribes cannot see it: git quotes a path with a
non-ASCII byte, so the em dash in that filename makes `grep -i 'pdf$'` miss it,
and a lane that runs the prescribed command finds seven drawings and concludes
there are seven.

⚠ **THIS LANE FOUND IT INDEPENDENTLY AND IT WAS ALREADY FILED — `DEF-GOV-5656`,
the same day, by the lane building `BlockedAddresses`.** A duplicate row was
written here and then withdrawn on noticing theirs. Recorded because the
near-miss is the lesson: **two lanes hit the same governance defect within hours
of each other**, which is what a command written into prose costs when nothing
re-checks it. `-c core.quotePath=false` is the fix in both their diagnosis and
this one.

**It does NOT draw these two wizards.** The only wizard it draws is the reads
UPLOAD wizard. So `r10` keeps layout, copy, flows and states for `SET-06`/`SET-07`
and the blueprint is not an authority over them — **but three of its findings bear
directly on this work and were followed:**

* **`MR-12`** — *"Routes and Cycles get the toolbar every other list has… a search
  box over a client-side array is the defect, not the fix"*, and it draws
  `[Search] [All + chips] [+ Filter] [▦ Columns]`. That is this defect one screen
  over, already written down.
* **`MR-14`** — the estimate dialog: *"The 25-word lede is gone; its content lives
  in the code comment and the register, which is where B14 rule 33 puts
  rationale."* The same remedy, on the same rule, ruled for a neighbouring screen.
* **The stage-3 note** — *"Exempt as a wizard table — but the rows behind it are
  the whole batch, which is the finding."* This is what settles rule 16 below.

### Ruling 1 · B14 rule 16 does NOT exempt these two tables

Rule 16 exempts a *wizard **summary** table*. Step 2 of each wizard is a **picker
over everything the filters match** — 79 premises on the demo tenant, and a real
utility builds a route from hundreds. It is a list table that happens to live in a
wizard, and the blueprint draws exactly that distinction on its own stage-3 grid.
So both step 2s move onto `DataTable`, and the exemption still covers the genuine
summary on step 4, which is untouched.

### Ruling 2 · The area filter does NOT move into `TableConfig.filters`

`BR-MET-072` is **CONFIRMED**, in the PO's own words — *"all option 1 to many
options will be required"* — and reads *"MULTI-SELECT with an All option … never
single-select"*, selections OR-ing together, with a backend test holding the
server to it. `TableRequestState.filters` is `Record<string, string>`: **one value
per dimension**. Declaring the areas there would have cut a ratified capability
down to fit the kit — the mistake `UnitsListPage` records against itself one rule
further on, and the kit's own note already says widening `filters` is an API
change (`OQ-306`, filed and not chosen).

**So the chips are composed from the kit's own `Chip`/`ChipRow`/`ChipToggle` —
the same three `FilterBar` renders — inside `DataTable`'s `filterBarSlot`, in ONE
shared component (`PickerFilterChips` in `routesCyclesShared.tsx`) used by both
wizards.** B14 rule 36's instruction is *compose the kit*; what is local is only
the multi-select semantics the signed rule requires. **Measured in the browser:
area `Downtown` → 16 rows, then ADDING `Industrial corridor` → 30. The OR holds.**

### Ruling 3 · Rationale is DELETED, consequence is KEPT

Rule 33 is five caps, not one, and the kind decides the remedy. Of 47 strings over
the caps (measured, not estimated), **15 keys were deleted and 28 reworded.**

Deleted because they are RATIONALE, which the rule puts at **zero words on
screen**: what a route IS, what a cycle IS, that a premises can be on one route
per service, that every save is audited — each explains the product to somebody
already doing the thing. Also deleted: **the step kicker on all eight steps**, under
rule 32 — the numbered step rail sits directly above it and offers the same number
and the same name, so `STEP 3 OF 4 · SCHEDULE` was the third statement of one fact.

**Kept and merely shortened, because rule 33 protects them:** `moveNote` is a
CONSEQUENCE — picking a premises MOVES it off another route — and is now *"They
move here when you confirm. No bills change."* (six words, then three).
`uncoveredBody` is a **count qualifier**, which rule 33 names as a FACT, so the
qualifier is what survived: *"Routes you picked are already counted."*

### Ruling 4 · Two signed rulings changed their home, and neither changed

* **CR-006 ruling 2** (*a cycle is a DEFINITION, not a schedule*) had been carried
  by a 32-word step-1 lede, asserted verbatim by a test. **The lede is deleted.**
  Rule 33 was ratified 2026-08-30 — **two weeks AFTER that ruling** — and the
  ruling is a statement about what the wizard STORES, not an instruction to print
  an essay. It is now asserted against the BUILD: step 2 picks ROUTES, and nothing
  on the surface states a date on which money moves (`BR-MET-078`). **A sentence
  can be reworded by any lane; a stored column and a step's subject cannot.**
* **`DEF-607`** had made the cycle step-3 lede spell out, in 44 words, that two
  boxes are days-of-the-month and two are counts. **The reason that paragraph was
  needed is the defect underneath it: `Days to complete` had NO HINT** — three of
  the four boxes explained themselves and the fourth did not. It has one now
  (*"A number of days."*), which is where rule 32 puts a control's own fact, and
  the lede is six words: *"Defaults only. Each run can change them."* — which is
  CR-006 ruling 3 intact.

**Both tests moved with their subject rather than being deleted, and each is now
harder to break by accident:** a lane rewording a lede cannot silently take a
field's hint with it.

### What was NOT changed, deliberately

* **`previewBody`** — reverted to its original wording. It is a **value strip**
  (`Read 1–3 · exceptions cleared by 4th · bills out 5th · due 26th`), not prose;
  `BR-MET-078`'s test reads it, and the CR-006 ruling names its clauses.
* **Option labels** (`Network — AMI, no visit`, the frequency words) — shared
  vocabulary beyond these two screens.
* **Step 3's meter list on `SET-06`** keeps its own `ListPager`. The PO's report
  named step 2; converting step 3 is the same argument and is worth doing, but on
  its own evidence rather than smuggled in here.

### The catalogues, and an honest measurement

All eleven, through `10-scripts/i18n_fanin.py`. **`NATIVE-REVIEW-OWED` for ten of
them** — rule 35's own honesty clause, said out loud rather than implied.

⚠ **Measured while doing it: of the 174 keys on these two screens, 159 were the
ENGLISH STRING VERBATIM in five catalogues** — `es-MX`, `hi`, `id-ID`, `ja-JP`,
`ko-KR` — i.e. 91% untranslated, passing `G15` because parity asks whether a KEY
exists, not whether it was translated. This lane's work took the product's
identical-to-English count from **6107 to 5857**; the rest is `G15`'s existing
baseline (`DEF-2603`) and is not this lane's to close.

## 2026-09-17 · Plans & Rates · A LIVE RATE SCHEDULE CAN NOW HOLD AN UNFINISHED EDIT, AND BR-RAT-037 DID NOT MOVE

**`DEF-RAT-5680` · `DEF-RAT-5681` · `DEF-055` · amends `US-RAT-010 TC-7`**

### The report, verbatim

The PO, in the beta: *"when user want to save draft version you are refusing it -
we need to solve this deadlock. - we need to save edits"*.

### What it actually was, because it was not what the report sounds like

**The Save draft button was NOT being refused. It was not on the screen at all.**
`RateScheduleWizard.tsx` rendered it inside `{!activated && …}`, so the moment
anything on a schedule went live the control disappeared. A clerk part-way through
a rate case had exactly two options: finish it and put it in front of customers,
or throw the work away and start again tomorrow. Reproduced in a browser on the
seeded tenant before a line was read: four ACTIVE schedules, **zero** of them
offering it.

⚠ **AND THE BLUEPRINT HAD ALREADY DRAWN IT.** `05-prototype/SMARTBillHub Plans &
Rates Blueprint.pdf` p048 — *"New version of Sample — Residential water"*, a
schedule that is in force — carries `Cancel` and **`Save draft & exit`** in the
wizard bar, in those words. The button was specified, the catalogue key
`rating.rate.saveDraft` already read *"Save draft & exit"*, and the component hid
it. **This is a screen not matching its drawing, which is nearly half of
everything that goes wrong on a screen in this repository.**

### The rule question, put plainly, because it looks like a collision and is not

`BR-RAT-037` is CONFIRMED (PO R5-9) and reads: *"In-force plan/tariff versions are
never edited in place: every change = new version row … + append-only
`rate_change_log` row with before/after jsonb, actor, and required reason"*.

**The guard in the code asked a different question from the rule.** It asked
`selectors.latest_version(tariff) is not None` — *has anything on this schedule
ever gone live* — which is a property of the **schedule**. The rule is about the
**row being written**. A dateless draft has never been in force: `in_force_version`
excludes it by name (*"a dateless row has no window and must never price
anything"*), `latest_version` and `tariff_versions` exclude it, and
`schedule_state` derives the status pill from what is in force, so a parked draft
cannot even make a live schedule read as a draft.

**So the guard was refusing a write that touches no activated version at all**,
and BR-RAT-037 is untouched by allowing it. Nothing about changing a live rate
moved: it is still `POST /rate-schedules/{id}/versions`, still a new row, still a
required reason, still a `rate_change_log` entry. **A DATE is the only content
write that can reach an activated version**, so the date check moved above the
immutability check and now carries both refusals.

**This is recorded at length so that nobody "fixes" it back.** The next lane to
read `update_rate_schedule` will see a guard that looks weaker than the rule it
cites. It is not weaker; it is aimed at the right object.

### The storage never needed changing, and that is the surprising part

`uq_tariff_versions_one_draft` is a **partial** unique index on
`effective_from IS NULL`. Its rule is **one draft**, never **no draft once live**.
`schedule_card` has served `draft_version` and `current_version` side by side
since `DEF-368`, whose own comment calls a rate case beside an active version
*"what CR-013 part 1 calls the whole point of the object"*. Every read path was
already built for this. **The restriction lived in one `if` and in a docstring.**

### `US-RAT-010 TC-7`, amended rather than deleted

TC-7 was *"editing a version in place is refused and the attempt is audited"* and
it posted a **dateless** `{"structure": …}` expecting `409 BIZ_IMMUTABLE`. That
froze the over-broad reading. **Its substance is intact and still asserted**: the
live tier is still `3.200000` after the post, which is the only assertion in it
that was ever about BR-RAT-037. What changed is the mechanism — the dateless form
now parks a draft, and the **dated** form is still `409` and still writes
`security.attempt_refused` under BR-AUD-018. The amendment is written into the
test's own docstring with this reasoning, not just into this log.

### The resume half, which would have made the whole fix dead work

`draftFromSchedule` read `detail.current_version ?? detail.draft_version`. Correct
only while a schedule could not hold both — which stopped being true the moment
the fix landed. A clerk would have saved their draft, reopened, and been handed
the rate that is in force, **their work stored, served in the same payload, and
ignored on screen**. That is `DEF-RAT-5681`, hard-won law 2 in its second form,
and it was latent and unreachable until now, which is why 1,505 lines of unit
tests could not have found it. The order is reversed and the screen says which of
the two rows it is showing.

### Discard, and why it is not a nicety

One draft per schedule. Without a way out, a half-finished rate case from three
months ago blocks the next one for ever — the clerk can neither see past it nor be
rid of it. `POST /rate-schedules/{id}/discard-draft`, behind `ConfirmDialog` with
B14 rule 6's danger tier because typed work is destroyed.

### Three things found on the way, each filed rather than fixed in silence

* **`DEF-055` — CLOSED HERE, after 37 days.** `rating.rate.toast.draft` and
  `rating.rate.toast.activated` were in **no catalogue at all**, parked on
  `10-scripts/gates/i18n_known_gaps.txt` whose own line says *"Closes when the key
  lands in en.json; DELETE this line then."* Fixed because this change makes the
  draft path reachable on a live schedule, which is exactly where the PO was
  working; the two baseline lines are deleted, so that list only shrank.
* **`DEF-RAT-5708`** — `US-RAT-004 TC-3` has been red since **2026-09-02**. It
  asserts a version dated `2026-09-01` is a FUTURE change, and the calendar passed
  it. Law 7's *incapable of passing*, on a clock instead of a fixture.
* **`DEF-RAT-5696`** — **thirteen** ratified `US-RAT` TCs have been red since
  **2026-09-11** (`8e7a34fca`) on `rating.schedules.no_base_charge_code`: the
  BR-RAT-088 activation guard moved and the shared fixture helper was never taught
  about it. Fourteen reds in one file is where a fourteenth goes to hide.

### What was NOT done, and why

* **`1.5` as briefed — "the two buttons say what they do" — WAS NOT BUILT, on
  purpose.** The labels are already the blueprint's own (`Save draft & exit`,
  `Create new version ✓`) and adding a sentence explaining what each one does to
  the money is **rationale**, which B14 rule 33 caps at **zero words on screen**.
  What was missing was the button's PRESENCE, not its wording. One FACT pair went
  on instead, three words each: *"You are seeing your draft. The live rate has not
  moved."*
* **`1.3` as briefed — `schedule_detail` also serving the parked draft — WAS
  ALREADY DONE** by `DEF-368` and needed no change. Asserted anyway, because a
  thing that is true by accident and a thing that is true by test look identical.
* **The version bump is the INTEGRATOR's**, per §7 as amended 2026-08-26 — *"a
  wave bumps at merge time, in the order waves land — NEVER IN ITS OWN BRANCH"*.
  `G35` is green at `2.295.5`. Recorded rather than silently skipped, because a
  step that is somebody else's and a step that was forgotten look the same
  afterwards.

### Rollback

Code only: revert the commit. **The migration half does not exist** — nothing was
migrated, because the storage already allowed this. Any draft a clerk parks
between shipping and a revert would survive the revert as an unreachable dateless
row, priced by nothing; that is the one non-reversible edge and it changes no
money.

### Proof

Backend `tests/test_def_rat_5680_park_a_draft.py`, **11 cases**, every one shown
RED first (`409 BIZ-IMMUTABLE`, `rating.schedules.version_immutable`,
`BR-RAT-037`) and then green. The two cases that were green BEFORE the fix are
named as regression guards rather than claimed as proof. Frontend: the resume
precedence proved red by restoring the old order —
`expected ['3.200000','4.800000','7.200000'] to deeply equal ['9.990000','11.110000']`.

⚠ **AND THE RENDERED BAR IS PROVED IN A BROWSER, WHICH IS A FINDING.**
`RateScheduleWizard` is **never mounted whole** anywhere in its own 1,505-line
suite — it gates on `detailQuery.isPending`, so under `renderToStaticMarkup` it
renders the loading skeleton and nothing else. **No unit test in this repository
can see this component's own action bar**, which is precisely how a drawn button
came to be absent with 58 cases green.
`10-scripts/def_rat_5680_park_a_draft_walkthrough.mjs` walks it, and it **found a
real defect nothing else could**: the Discard control survived its own commit,
because the mutation answered the schedule and nothing wrote that answer back into
the query cache. The draft was gone from the database and the button that deletes
it was still on screen.

**Gates: 49 FAIL at the tip and 49 FAIL with this change — the identical set.**
Nothing here made anything worse, and the branch was already merge-blocked before
this lane started.
