## 2026-09-18 — five list endpoints measured against `NFR-3`: one fixed, one deleted, three written down instead

The Product Owner reports lists becoming unusable as a tenant grows from 3,000
rows towards 40,000. The mechanism is one line: a list that hands
`paginator.paginate_queryset` a **built list** constructs every row in Python and
throws away all but fifty; one that hands it a **queryset** lets DRF put the page
in the SQL. `customers.api._prepaged` has documented this in its own words for
weeks — *"40,000 accounts built to draw fifty"*.

**This lane took the CHEAP half on purpose: five endpoints, each CHECKED before
anything was changed.** The answer was different for every one of them, and only
one turned out to be the cheap edit the sweep was named for. That is the finding
worth keeping.

**WHY NO TEST COULD EVER HAVE CAUGHT ANY OF THIS.** `StandardPagination` serves
the identical envelope either way — the same `count`, the same fifty rows, the
same `next` link. So a test that counts returned rows passes on both spellings,
and every one of these endpoints passed every check it had. The discriminator is
the **SQL**, so the new cases assert `LIMIT` and the statements issued, never a
row count (hard-won law 7's second habit: *what would make this check pass
wrongly?*).

⚠ **AND A QUERY COUNT IS THE WRONG INSTRUMENT HERE, WHICH IS WORTH SAYING
BECAUSE IT IS THE OBVIOUS ONE.** Paging in SQL makes the number of statements go
**UP**, from one to two — an unbounded `SELECT` becomes a `COUNT(*)` plus a
bounded page. A ceiling on the number of queries would have been satisfied by
the defect and broken by the fix. What moved is how many ROWS a statement
fetches, which is a property of the statement.

### What each of the five turned out to be

**`GET /wizard-parks` (`DEF-SHL-5748`) — the only cheap one, and it is FIXED.**
`wizard_parks.list_parks` ended in `return list(qs.select_related…)`, and the
view then built a dict for every parked draft before the paginator sliced. The
lazy queryset is now `parks_queryset` and `row_dict` runs over the PAGE.

**MEASURED, on the same fixture at two populations, before and after:**

| | statements on `wizard_parks` | bound in the SQL | rows the database returned |
|---|---|---|---|
| before, 60 drafts | 1 (no `COUNT`) | none | **60** |
| before, 1,000 drafts | 1 (no `COUNT`) | none | **1,000** |
| after, 60 drafts | 2 (`COUNT` + page) | `LIMIT 50` | **50** |
| after, 1,000 drafts | 2 (`COUNT` + page) | `LIMIT 50` | **50** |

The whole request went from **8 queries to 9** — it got *more* expensive by the
measure everybody reaches for first, and the rows fetched stopped growing. The
wire was **50 rows and `count` 60 / 1,000 in all four runs**, which is the
defect's entire disguise.

**`list_parks` is KEPT, and kept materialised** — its remaining caller
(`customers.seams.wizard_park_rows` → `sample_data`) **deletes rows while
iterating what it is handed**, which is safe over a list and safe over a queryset
only by accident of the result cache. Splitting the two costs four lines and
leaves a seam contract in another module untouched; folding them into one would
have put a subtle iteration hazard on a fixture path to save those four lines.

**`GET /finance/journal` (`DEF-LED-5749`) — NOT cheap, and not attempted.**
`ledger.reporting.journal_entry_list` genuinely builds its rows in Python: it
sums every entry's lines in one pass and returns dataclasses, so there is no
queryset to slice. The `list(...)` at the call site is a redundant copy of an
already-built list, and **removing it would have changed nothing while looking
exactly like a fix** — which is why it was left alone rather than tidied.
`reporting.py` is on `10-scripts/gates/human_owned.txt`, so paginating inside it
is a 🔒 change needing a human-review-ledger row. Filed and left.

**`GET /notices` (`DEF-NOT-5750`) — a hard cap, and it is LEFT ALONE
DELIBERATELY.** `NOTICE_READ_CAP = 2000` is passed as `limit=` through
`payments_seam.notice_history` into payments' published read, so **the 2,001st
notice is unreachable on every page of the list**. `NFR-5` says no code path may
impose a maximum. It was NOT removed, and the reason is the whole judgment:
removing the cap alone converts a bounded 2,000-row Python build into an
UNBOUNDED one, which is a worse defect than the one it fixes. The cap and the
cross-module seam have to move together, and that seam is payments'.

⚠ **ONE CORRECTION TO HOW THAT CAP HAS BEEN DESCRIBED, RECORDED BECAUSE IT
CHANGES THE SEVERITY:** it does **not** truncate silently. When it bites, the
response carries a `notice_history_truncated` entry in `problems` naming the
figure. That is the honest posture this repo asks for — and it is also why the
breach read as a considered choice for so long, which is worth knowing the next
time a stated absence is mistaken for a resolved one.

**`GET /lookups/{list}` (`DEF-TEN-5751`) — the materialisation is LOAD-BEARING.
Left alone, with the reason.** `selectors.etag_for(rows)` hashes the whole
serialized list and `_maybe_304` compares that hash to `If-None-Match`. A page
cannot produce the same tag, so removing the materialisation would silently stop
conditional requests matching — a worse defect than the one being fixed. It is
also the weakest `NFR-3` case in the product: these are catalogue lists (payment
methods, size classes, UOMs) whose length is set by the reference data and does
not grow with the account count, so the 3,000 → 40,000 move does not touch it.
If it is ever fixed, the ETag must move to something the database can produce
cheaply (a count plus a max `updated_at`) and **that changes the tag for every
existing client**, so it is a versioned change rather than a refactor.

**`service_request_api._paginated` (`DEF-CUS-5752`) — dead, and REMOVED.**
Nothing has ever called it; `GET /service-requests` has always paged
`reads.list_queryset` in SQL. It is worth more than a shrug because
`apps/metering/api.py` names it by hand as the pattern to copy for riding `kpis`
alongside the envelope — so the next lane looking for that pattern would have
been sent to the one helper in the file that pages in Python. The live example is
the endpoint itself; re-pointing metering's citation is left to that lane,
because that file belongs to another one.

### Two endpoints in the sweep needed nothing, and that is a finding too

`GET /suppressions` already pages `suppression.listing`'s queryset, and
`GET /service-requests` already pages `reads.list_queryset`. Both say so in their
own docstrings and both are true. **Checking each endpoint instead of
pattern-matching on `paginate_queryset(rows, …)` is what separated these from
the three that look identical at the call site** — the argument's NAME tells you
nothing, and `rows` is what all five call it.

### The red-first run found a bug in the TEST, and that is the part to keep

⚠ **THE FIRST DRAFT OF THE NEW CASES PAGED WITH `?per=5`, AND `per` CLAMPS TO
THE RATIFIED VOCABULARY `(50, 100, 200, 500, 1000)`.** So `5` became `50`, twelve
fixture rows all came back on one page, and the envelope cases **failed against
the FIXED tree and the BROKEN one alike**. A test written below the smallest real
page size cannot observe paging on any tree — it is law 7's *incapable of
passing* shape, and the only thing that surfaced it was running the file red
first instead of trusting a green. The populations are sixty now, which is the
smallest one with a second page.

**What the red run then said, and it is the whole argument for the file's shape:
4 failed, 5 passed.** The four are the `NFR-3` cases. **The five that passed are
the envelope, the clamp, the row shape, the filters and the seam contract —
every one of them correct on the broken code**, which is the demonstration, in a
single run, that no envelope assertion can tell a Python page from a SQL one.

### A note on where an explanation may be written

The `NFR-3` note on `GET /wizard-parks` is an inline COMMENT and not part of the
view's docstring, on purpose: `drf-spectacular` publishes a view docstring as the
operation `description`, so a paragraph added there also edits
`06-backend/openapi/schema.json` — the one committed generated file (hard-won
law 5) — which `test_be11_tc05` diffs and which three lanes were editing the same
afternoon. A note about how a page is taken is for whoever reads the code, not
for a generated client. Proved rather than assumed: every docstring in the file
was compared against `HEAD` by parsing both, and none moved.

### The ids in this work are the SECOND set it allocated

`file_defect.py` correctly returned 5744–5748 against the remote. A sibling lane
pushed `DEF-5744`, `DEF-5745`, `DEF-NOT-5746` and `DEF-CWP-5747` while this lane
worked — **`DEF-NOT-5746` would have been a true duplicate, same number and same
module segment**. Law 11's unconditional push-time re-derivation caught it: the
register was rebuilt as the tip's bytes with five raw rows appended (prefix
proved byte-identical) and the rows renumbered to 5748–5752 before anything was
pushed. The allocator did its job — it removes the stale read and cannot reserve,
exactly as its own docstring says.

## 2026-09-18 — the customers list takes its page in the database, and the helper that built every row is DELETED (`DEF-CUS-5753`)

**WHAT WAS WRONG, IN ONE SENTENCE A PERSON CAN READ.** Opening the Customers
screen made the server build a row for **every customer the utility holds**,
throw all but fifty away, and ask the database a separate question about each
one of those people's accounts on the way. At three thousand customers nobody
notices. At forty thousand — the top of our own ICP — it is of the order of
forty thousand separate questions to draw one screen.

**THE FIGURE, MEASURED RATHER THAN ESTIMATED.** On this suite's fixtures
`GET /customers` cost **5 database statements for 4 customers and 17 for 16** —
one extra for every person added — and **61 statements to draw fifty rows out of
sixty**. After the fix it is **3 and 3**, and it stays 3 when the page size
doubles from fifty to a hundred.

**WHY IT WAS INVISIBLE, WHICH IS THE PART WORTH KEEPING.** Nothing about the
ANSWER was wrong. The count was right, the page held fifty, `?page=2` served the
second fifty. Eight existing cases cover this list and every one of them passed
throughout, because **a test that counts returned rows cannot tell SQL paging
from Python paging.** The defect lived only in the statement log, and the
fixtures could not have shown it either: the largest tenant any customers case
builds holds three customers, where one-query-per-row and a constant are the
same size.

**THE JUDGMENT: EXTEND THE PATTERN, DO NOT INVENT ONE.** `selectors.account_page`
already did this exact job for the accounts list (`BR-CUS-1046`), and
`api._prepaged` already served the page it returns. So the customers list got
`customer_list_queryset` (the same five search legs and the same order, with
nothing evaluated), `customer_page` (the slice and a `COUNT(*)`, both in SQL) and
`customer_rows` (the page's `customer_accounts` links in ONE query, which is what
`account_rows` has done for seven page-wide reads since `DEF-2723`). The envelope
is the shared one, unchanged: `count` / `next` / `previous` / `results`, with
DRF's own link grammar, because a second envelope shape on one screen is a
client-side special case for ever.

**`_paginated` IS DELETED, AND THAT IS A DELIBERATE CALL RATHER THAN TIDYING.**
It was the file's original list helper. `GET /accounts` left it on 2026-09-12
(`BR-CUS-1046` / `DEF-CUS-5060`) and for six days it sat beside `_prepaged` with
`GET /customers` still on it. A helper that builds every row is a **trap the next
list endpoint in the file falls into**, exactly as this one did — and hard-won
law 1 says a comment warning you off is not a guarantee. Nothing else imports it;
`apps/customers/service_request_api.py` has its own copy, which belongs to
another lane and was not touched.

**NO FIGURE MOVED AND NO CAP WAS ADDED.** The customers row carries no money at
all, so hard rule 2 has nothing to bite on here; `NFR-5` is honoured by there
being no ceiling anywhere in the new path — `per` clamps to the IS-2 vocabulary
and `page` clamps into range (`BR-SHL-011`, re-clamped by `_prepaged` and proved
by `?page=999` serving the LAST page rather than a blank table).

### ⚠ WHAT THE REST OF THIS MODULE DOES, COUNTED RATHER THAN ASSUMED

Every list read in `apps/customers` was checked against the same question, and
the answers differ enough to be worth writing down:

| endpoint | where the page is taken | verdict |
|---|---|---|
| `GET /customers` | **was Python** → now SQL | fixed here |
| `GET /accounts` | SQL, with a named `O(tenant)` fallback | already fixed 2026-09-12 |
| `GET /accounts/{id}/documents` | SQL from birth | correct |
| `GET /transfers` | `.count()` + queryset slice | correct |
| `GET /move-ins` · `GET /move-outs` | `.count()` + queryset slice | correct |
| `GET /disconnects` | **Python** — `len(pairs)` and `pairs[start:start+per]` | **`DEF-CUS-5755`, filed, NOT fixed** |
| `GET /accounts/{id}/notes` | unpaginated, ruled | a card list, deliberately |

`GET /accounts`'s fallback is correct and stays: two of its sorts and two of its
filters are over money that lives in the LEDGER, so a row has to exist before the
figure can be read, and `account_list_is_sql_pageable` names the four rather than
hiding them. The customers list has no equivalent — every `CUSTOMER_SORTS` name
and its one filter is a COLUMN — so it is `O(page)` for every request that can be
made of it, and no fallback was built for symmetry's sake.

`GET /disconnects` is the real remaining breach and it is **reported, not
touched**: `disconnect_reads.py` belongs to another lane, and a silent reach into
another lane's file is how a shared tree loses work (law 11). The row is
`DEF-CUS-5755` so that the finding is COUNTED rather than left in a lane report
nobody greps.

## 2026-09-18 — three screens were reported as "slicing a full array in the browser"; only one was, and the other two are written down here rather than "fixed"

The Product Owner reported list tables becoming unusable as a tenant grows from
3,000 towards 40,000 rows. `pageSlice()` in `07-frontend/src/components/ListPager.tsx`
slices an array the browser is already holding, and five screens call it. Three
were given to this lane. **They turned out to be three different things, and the
useful part of this entry is the difference** — a defect, a deliberate handoff,
and a screen that was already fixed a month ago.

### 1 · Settings → Notifications → Messages — A REAL DEFECT, AND FIXED (`DEF-NOT-5746`)

The tab asked `GET /outbound` for **one page of fifty and nothing else**, then
sliced those fifty again in the browser and counted them for its own footer. So
a utility with four thousand queued messages read **"1–50 of 50"**, and pressing
the next-page arrow reached nothing, because there was no second page in the
browser to reach. `GET /outbound` has paged **in the database** since it was
written — `StandardPagination`, a real `count`, `page` and `per` honoured — so
the whole fix was on this side of the wire: the page number and the size are the
tab's state, both travel on the request, and the footer's total is the server's
`count`.

**Fetches per screen: 1 before, 1 after.** The number did not move and was never
the point — what moved is WHICH page the one fetch asks for, and that the footer
now tells the truth about the 3,950 rows it is not showing.

⚠ **`queryClient.ts`'s key factory gained a `page` argument with a DEFAULT of 1**,
so `outboundQueue(50)` still spells the key the queue opens on and the two suites
that prime or invalidate that key did not have to be rewritten. `outboundQueueAll`
is the prefix a re-queue invalidates, because a re-queue changes the COUNT and
changes which rows sit on every later page, not only the one on screen.

### 2 · The customer portal's six lists — HANDED OFF, NOT HALF-FIXED (`DEF-CWP-5747`)

`portal/components/listTable.tsx` is one shared component behind CWP-023, 027,
031, 034, 037 and 041, and it holds every row: the six portal edge endpoints
(`GET portal/bills`, `my_accounts`, `accounts/{id}/documents`, `payments`,
`accounts/{id}/readings`, equipment) each serve an unbounded array.
`apps/metering/portal_reads.readings_for_account` is handed `limit=None` by its
view, so on an AMI deployment — an interval reading per meter per hour — that one
is unbounded in the place it actually bites.

**WHY IT WAS NOT CHANGED, AND THIS IS THE JUDGMENT WORTH RECORDING.** The component
does its **search, its chips and its sort in the browser, over the whole array**.
Ask the server for one page without moving those three and every one of them
silently searches one page of N — a customer typing a bill number that is on page
7 is told they have no such bill. That is a correctness defect manufactured in the
name of fixing a payload defect, and it would pass every test in the repo, because
a search test with twelve fixture rows never crosses a page boundary.

**What the follow-up lane needs, precisely:** page, search and sort move to the six
portal endpoints; `portal/api/portalClient.ts` wrappers carry `page`/`per` and
return the server's `count`; `PortalListTable` takes a server window the way
`RejectList` already does and stops owning `query`, `chip` and `sort` state. One
wave, all three together. It is a **customer-facing** surface, so the eight
accessibility questions of `12-governance/22-product-maintenance-process.md` §6
apply to whoever touches it — they did not apply here, because nothing was touched.

⚠ **AND THAT SAME FILE IS CARRYING A DEAD PROP, WHICH `G13` HAS BEEN SAYING OUT
LOUD SINCE 2026-09-09 AND NOBODY HAS READ.** `PortalListTable.toolbarLead` arrived
in `a54389bd6` for `CWP-041`'s *All | This year* and **no caller has ever passed
it** — dated with `git log -S`, not assumed. Hard-won law 2 exactly, and law 7's
*proved red, then never read* on top of it. Whoever opens this file for the
pagination wave should close that in the same pass: either `Payments.tsx` passes
the control the prop was built for, or the prop goes.

### 3 · `components/workflow/RejectList.tsx` — NOT DEFECTIVE, AND DELIBERATELY LEFT ALONE

**The premise of the report is false for this one, and it was checked rather than
assumed.** The server does not send the whole list: `DEF-766` (2026-08-26) made the
reject list travel as a **window**, and `apps/metering/import_runs.run_dict` sets
`rejects_window` **in the same block that sets `rejects`**, so a payload carrying
rejects always carries the window. Both production call sites — stage 3 and the
stage-4 receipt, in `ImportWorkflowPage.tsx` — pass `serverPage`, and turning a page
issues `GET /imports/{id}?reject_offset=50&reject_limit=50`. That is already
asserted **as a request** and not as a row count, in
`ImportRejectFix.dom.test.tsx`.

So the `pageSlice` call in that file is the `serverPage === undefined` branch — a
fallback for a server this product does not have.

**Removing it would mean making `serverPage` a required prop**, which rewrites
~25 render sites across two shared test files and three cases that pin the
9,881-rows-draw-50 behaviour, in a tree with seven lanes in it, to delete a branch
no user can reach. **The cost is real and the benefit is zero**, so it stands, and
this paragraph is the record of why — a future lane finding `pageSlice` there
should read this before assuming it was missed.

⚠ **COORDINATION, FOR WHOEVER REWORKS THE PAGER:** `pageSlice` still has four
callers today. `RoutesCyclesPage.tsx` and `RoutesCyclesWizards.tsx` are a sibling
lane's (`DEF-MET-5743`); `RejectList.tsx` keeps its by the paragraph above; and
`portal/components/listTable.tsx` keeps its until `DEF-CWP-5747` is built. **It
cannot be deleted yet.**

### What was proved, and what was NOT — stated rather than implied

**Proved RED first, in the harness that runs it** (hard-won law 7): all four new
cases in `queuePagination.dom.test.tsx` were run against the pre-fix commit and
failed with exactly the predicted faults — `query.page` came back **undefined**,
the footer read `1–50 of 50` so `1–50 of 4000` was *"unable to find"*, and the
next-page click produced **one** recorded request where two were expected, twice.
Then green: 4 passed, and **308 passed across all 23 notifications test files**.
`tsc --noEmit` clean with the LOCAL TypeScript 5.5.4 and re-run after the last
`.ts`/`.tsx` edit; `eslint --max-warnings 0` clean; `routeBUtilities` 11 passed;
`G31` PASS at its baseline of 0.

⚠ **NOT SEEN IN A BROWSER, AND THAT IS A REAL GAP RATHER THAN A FORMALITY**
(hard-won law 6). The shared `sbh` database holds **one tenant, zero users and
zero `outbound_messages` rows**, so there is no queue to page through; showing
one would mean seeding a few thousand messages into a database seven lanes are
working against. jsdom does no layout, so what is proved here is which request
goes out and what the footer SAYS — never how the footer looks. The layout is
unchanged (same shared `ListPager`, same classes, no new class anywhere), which
is the only reason that gap is acceptable to leave open.

### Amendment, same day — two of the three endpoints left alone are N+1s as well, and their rows say only half of it

Recorded because it changes what the follow-up lanes are being asked to do.
Neither was touched; both facts were found by reading the code after the rows
were filed, and a defect row that names one cause invites a fix that addresses
one cause.

**`GET /finance/journal` (`DEF-LED-5749`) costs `2 + N` statements, not one.**
`reporting.journal_entry_list` does not merely build every row in Python. Inside
its row loop it calls **`entry.reversed_by.first()`**, and `reversed_by` is the
REVERSE side of `journal_entries.reversal_of` — one query per entry, issued
after a `select_related(None)` that explicitly clears any join. So the read is
one statement for the entries, one for the line totals, and **one per entry** to
ask whether a reversal points at it. Paginating inside `reporting.py` would cut
that to `2 + 50`; reaching a constant also wants the reversal link folded into
the entries query (a subquery, or a second pass over the PAGE's ids, the way the
line totals already work). Both halves are in a file on
`10-scripts/gates/human_owned.txt`, so both belong to one 🔒 lane and one
human-review-ledger row.

**`GET /lookups/{list}` (`DEF-TEN-5751`) is `1 + kN`, and `k` is 2 on the UOM
list.** `lookup_page` serializes every row, and each handler's `serialize` calls
`used_by(row)` — a LIVE count, which on `UomLookupHandler` is a
`TenantService` count **plus** a metering-seam count. A sixty-row reference list
is therefore of the order of 120 extra statements on a Settings screen a clerk
opens all day, at T7 as much as at T5.

⚠ **THIS DOES NOT REOPEN THE DECISION NOT TO TOUCH IT, AND IT IS WORTH SAYING
WHY.** The reason that endpoint was left alone was never that it is cheap — it
was that `etag_for` hashes the whole serialized list, so paging it silently
breaks conditional requests. That is still true. What changes is the SIZE of the
prize for whoever takes it: the `used_by` counts want folding into the queryset
as annotations, which would make both the page and the ETag affordable, and
that is a different and larger job than the one this sweep was scoped for.

## 2026-09-18 — IMPORTS AT 60–80,000 ROWS: WHAT IT ACTUALLY COSTS, WHICH CAPS MOVED, AND HOW BIG THE WORKER HAS TO BE (`DEF-MET-5756`)

**What was asked.** The product was designed for utilities of about 3,000
accounts. The assumption is now 40,000–80,000, and the Product Owner asked for
**60,000–80,000 row uploads to work**.

**What was ruled, and it narrowed the job.** Two shapes were on the table:
**(A)** raise the limits and give the worker more memory, **(B)** rebuild the
upload so the file is never held whole. The PO chose A first, verbatim:

> *"what if we test with option a first instead increase worker ram to start
> with test whether is it okay for 80k - if it does not work we can later go for
> option b"*

So what follows raises caps and measures the cost. **Nothing was re-architected,
the parse still holds the whole file, and the upload is still a JSON field.**

### THE MEASUREMENT, BEFORE ANYTHING WAS CHANGED

Live PostgreSQL 16, this dev container, one 80,000-row premises file of 8,205,757
bytes (7.83 MB, 102.6 B/row), every stage in process. Re-derivable with
`06-backend/tests/test_import_scale_benchmark.py` (skipped unless `SCALE_ROWS`
is set).

| stage | wall | per row | queries | RSS before → peak | added |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 extract (parse + stage) | **27.2s** | 0.339 ms | **93** | 187 → 411 MB | **+224 MB** | | | | |
| 2 transform | **48.0s** | 0.600 ms | **29** | 300 → 570 MB | **+269 MB** | | | | |
| 3 validate | **62.9s** | 0.786 ms | **51** | 384 → 642 MB | **+258 MB** | | | | |
| 3b dry run | **15.6s** | 0.195 ms | **8** | 502 → 697 MB | **+195 MB** | | | | |
| 4 load | no trustworthy figure — see below | | **4.45 q/row** | |  | | | | |

**Stages 1 to 3b took 153.6 seconds and the process peaked at 697 MB** — for a
file of 7.83 MB.

⚠ **THE LOAD STAGE HAS NO TRUSTWORTHY WALL-CLOCK FIGURE HERE, AND THAT IS SAID
RATHER THAN ESTIMATED.** Two attempts to time it at 80,000 rows ran on a box
carrying seven other lanes' suites against the same PostgreSQL, and a contended
number is not a per-row cost. What those runs DID establish, because a query
count does not care how busy the box is, is that **the premises load issues 4.45
queries per row** — 8,897 of them for 2,000 rows — so its wall time is round
trips, and it moves with the database rather than with the code. CR-026's own
uncontended figure therefore stands as the only one we have: **101.5s for 50,000
rows, 2.03 ms/row**. It wants re-measuring on a quiet box with
`10-scripts/cr026_import_benchmark.py --rows 80000 --pass sync`; until then the
premises load bar is deliberately the conservative one.

⚠ **THE FIRST FIGURE THIS LANE PUBLISHED WAS WRONG AND THE REASON IS WORTH MORE
THAN THE NUMBER.** The same run measured with `tracemalloc` on reported the
extract at **117.0s and +398 MB**; with it off, **27.2s and +224 MB** — 4.3x the
time and 1.8x the memory, *of the tracer*. A per-row cost taken from the traced
run had already been written into a code comment and a test before the clean run
contradicted it. **Measure with the tracer off for any number anybody will
quote; turn it on only to ask WHICH objects a stage is holding.**

### THE DATABASE WAS NEVER THE PROBLEM

**93 queries for stage 1, 29 for stage 2, 51 for stage 3 — at eighty thousand
rows.** `bulk_create(batch_size=1000)` and `bulk_write.update_import_rows` are
doing exactly what they were built to do, and there is no N+1 anywhere in stages
1–3. **The entire cost is Python memory and Python time.** Anyone reaching for an
index or a query plan here is looking in the wrong place.

### WHAT IS HELD IN MEMORY, AND WHERE

**The parse holds the whole file, several times over.** `extract` at
`import_runs.py` does `_file_bytes(data)` → the whole file as `bytes`, `_decode`
→ the whole file again as `str`, then builds `rows`, a complete list of dicts,
and then a complete list of `ImportRunRow` instances, before `bulk_create`
batches the INSERT. Four full copies of an 8 MB file, for +224 MB of resident
memory — **a 29x multiple over the file itself.**

**And every later stage holds its own full copy of the STAGED TABLE**, which is
the half that is easy to miss because the file is long gone by then:

* `_transform_locked` — `rows = list(ImportRunRow.objects.filter(...))`
* `_validate_locked` — the same `list(...)`, **and then `payloads`, a second
  full copy as dicts**
* `_loadable_rows` — the same `list(...)` again

`.iterator()` appears **twice in the whole 10,000-line module**, and both are in
the results-CSV download.

⚠ **AND THIS SETTLES THE OBJECTION THAT WILL BE RAISED AGAINST OPTION B, SO IT
IS WRITTEN DOWN ONCE RATHER THAN RE-ARGUED.** The objection is that streaming
cannot work because the validations need the whole file at once. **They do not
read the file.** Validation reads `ImportRunRow` — the staged table, in
PostgreSQL — at `_validate_locked`, `_reject_rows`, `_loadable_rows`, the
changeover scan, `_result_rows`, `_source_headers` and the three rollback walks.
The complete dataset is available for every cross-row check either way, because
it lives in the database rather than in the parser. **Streaming the parse would
cost no validation coverage at all.** That is a fact about the architecture, not
a proposal, and it stands whenever option B is picked up.

### WHY VALIDATE WAS *NOT* CONVERTED TO `.iterator()`

It was considered, measured, and left alone — deliberately, and this records the
reasoning so the next lane does not redo the thinking.

**It does not dominate.** Every stage adds roughly the same: **+224 MB, +269 MB, +258 MB and +195 MB**. There is
no single stage whose fixing would change the machine's size.

**And the two copies are both live.** `payloads` is what the rules iterate;
`rows` is the ORM instances, which are **mutated in place and written back**
through `bulk_write.update_import_rows(rows, ["outcome", "problem", "fix_hint",
"updated_at"], ...)`. Streaming the queryset would mean a second full pass to
write the verdicts back — trading memory for another 80,000 rows of round trips.
The contained change that WOULD help is `.defer("raw")`, since validate never
reads the source cells; it is not made here because a deferred field that any
path does touch becomes an 80,000-query N+1, and that risk is not worth taking
inside a change the PO scoped to "raise the caps".

### THE CAPS THAT MOVED

| | was | is | why |
|---|---|---|---|
| `import_runs.CSV_BYTE_CAP` | 10 MB, written flat | `CSV_ROW_CAP × 512 B` = 48.8 MB, **derived** | see below |
| `import_runs.CSV_ROW_CAP` | 100,000 | 100,000 — **unchanged** | it was never the binding limit |
| `read_import.CSV_ROW_CAP` | 50,000 | 100,000 | a meter file was refused at a size a premises file was accepted at |
| `read_import.CSV_BYTE_CAP` | 10 MB | `100,000 × 128 B` = 12.2 MB | a reads row is 54.5 B — the narrowest file we take |
| `exports.EXPORT_ROW_CAP` | 50,000 | 100,000 | data could go in and not come back out |

**The byte cap is now DERIVED from the row cap, and that is the actual fix.**
Two caps for one idea is the whole defect: `CR-026` raised the row cap to
100,000 in August and the byte cap stayed at the 10 MB `US-MET-004` §5 wrote when
a file was 3,000 rows. **Measured at 80,000 rows, five of the seven targets were
refused before a single row was staged** — premises 26.9 MB, units 15.9,
accounts 15.2, assets_meters 10.2, assets_submeters 10.1, all against 10.

The operator never saw a row count. They were told the file was too large, in
megabytes, while every sentence this product writes about upload size — and the
number the PO said out loud — counts **rows**. The allowance of 512 B/row comes
from measuring `sample_csv(target)` for all seven targets: **premises 353 B/row,
units 208, accounts 199, assets_meters 133, assets_submeters 132, assets_devices
126, parts 53**, and the shipped template is the *narrowest* realistic file, not
the widest. `tests/test_import_scale_80k.py` now fails if the byte cap can ever
refuse a file the row cap accepts.

### THE ASYNC BARS — DEF-2487 WAS STILL LIVE ON SIX OF THE SEVEN TARGETS

`DEF-2487` fixed the accounts load bar and asserted exactly that one pair. The
**default** of 5,000 went on being spent on every other target's load, and its
own justification — CR-026's premises load at 2.03 ms/row — was a PREMISES figure (2.03 ms/row) being spent on six
other targets' loads that **nobody has ever timed**. `DEF-2487` is exactly what
that costs when the assumption is wrong: accounts turned out to be **94 ms/row**,
and 5,000 of them would be **470 seconds inside a request gunicorn kills at 60**.
Its guard then asserted the one pair it had measured and never the rule, so
units, the three assets targets and parts kept the assumption that had just
broken accounts.

Three things changed, all in `async_row_bar`'s table and none in its callers:

* **`(premises, load)` = 500.** CR-026's 2.03 ms/row makes 500 rows about a second. It is
  deliberately below the 5,000 that figure would allow, because the 4.45 queries
  per row above mean the cost moves with the database; 500 holds better than
  four times' margin even if it has grown fourfold, and it is still above the
  431-row file the CR-023 suites use, so the common case answers synchronously.
* **A per-STAGE fallback, `ASYNC_ROW_BAR_BY_STAGE = {"load": 200}`.** Every load
  measured in this repo costs one to two orders of magnitude more per row than
  its own transform or validate — premises 2.03 against 0.9 and 0.5,
  accounts 94 against 1.9 and 1.1 — so the cost belongs to the **stage** far more
  than to the target, and one number for all three will always be wrong for one
  of them. 200 is the **worst** measured load's bar, not the best: it fails
  closed (hard-won law 3), so an unmeasured target that turns out to be
  accounts-shaped is safe on the day it is written rather than on the day someone
  remembers to measure it.
* Transform and validate keep 5,000. At the worst measured 1.9 ms/row that is
  9.5s, inside the wall.

At 60–80,000 rows every stage of every target now leaves the request, which is
what was asked for — and `tests/test_import_scale_80k.py` asserts it of **all
twenty-one (target, stage) pairs** rather than of the one that broke.

### HOW BIG THE WORKER HAS TO BE — THE NUMBER THAT SIZES THE MACHINE

**One 80,000-row premises import peaked at 697 MB of resident memory**, on a
process that started at 187 MB — so **about 510 MB is the import itself**, and
the honest figure for one import with headroom is **1 GB**.

It lands on the **Celery worker**, not on gunicorn: at 60–80,000 rows every stage
is now over its bar and leaves the request. `docker-compose.yml` runs the default
worker at **`--concurrency 2`**, which is two prefork child processes, so **two
simultaneous imports is the ordinary case and that is about 2 GB**. Three
concurrent imports — the realistic bad day — is **about 3 GB**, and that is the
number that sizes the machine. The billing worker's own `--concurrency 2` and
gunicorn's three workers sit on top of it.

⚠ **THE FIGURE IS FOR PREMISES, ON A 7.83 MB FILE.** The same 80,000 rows at the
premises template's true width is **26.9 MB** — three and a half times the file
measured — and the parse holds the file, so that stage's share grows with it.
Nothing in this lane measured that case end to end. **Treat 1 GB per import as a
floor, not a ceiling.**

⚠ **AND THE FAILURE MODE IS WORSE THAN "THE IMPORT FAILS".** An out-of-memory
kill takes the **whole worker process**, not just the import — so every other
request that worker was serving dies with it. That is the honest risk of option
A, and it is why the row cap stays where it is rather than being raised to buy
headroom nobody has measured.

### THE ONE THING THAT STILL BLOCKS 80,000 ROWS, AND IT IS NOT A CAP

⚠ **`DATA_UPLOAD_MAX_MEMORY_SIZE` IS DJANGO'S DEFAULT 2,621,440 BYTES — 2.5 MB —
AND `config/settings/base.py` NEVER OVERRIDES IT.** The import arrives as a JSON
field (`content` / `content_b64`), so the whole file is a request **body**, and
Django refuses a body over that limit before any product code runs. Measured
directly against `rest_framework.request.Request.data` with this repo's settings:

    2 MB body  → accepted
    3 MB body  → RequestDataTooBig
    8 MB body  → RequestDataTooBig
    12 MB body → RequestDataTooBig

**So the real ceiling today is about 2.5 MB — roughly 25,000 premises rows at the
template's 104 B, or 7,400 at its full 353 B — and raising `CSV_BYTE_CAP` alone
does not move it by one row.** The refusal is a Django `RequestDataTooBig`, not
one of ours, so it arrives without a `trace_id`, without a catalogue sentence and
without naming a limit the operator can act on.

`config/settings/base.py` belongs to another lane. **It needs
`DATA_UPLOAD_MAX_MEMORY_SIZE` set to at least `import_runs.CSV_BYTE_CAP`**, and
until it is, everything above is necessary and not sufficient. Handed over
rather than reached for, and stated here so it cannot be lost.

### WHAT WAS CHECKED AND FOUND ALREADY SOUND

* **The error-review screen.** `DEF-766` already made the reject list a
  server-side window — `REJECT_WINDOW_DEFAULT = 50`, `REJECT_WINDOW_MAX = 1,000`,
  `?reject_offset` / `?reject_limit` — and the payload does not grow with the
  error count (26,392 B for 60 rejects, 26,401 B for 600). Unchanged and correct
  at 80,000.
* **Can a clerk browse ALL staged rows? There is no such list.** The only
  row-level surfaces are the paged reject window, the single-row inline fix, and
  the two results CSVs — and those stream, with
  `.iterator(chunk_size=RESULT_CSV_CHUNK)`. So there is no unpaged list to fix;
  there is an absence, recorded here so the next person does not go looking.
* **The list export already streams.** `write_csv` pulls from `row_stream` →
  `selection_iter` → `.iterator(chunk_size=500)`, which is why its cap was safe
  to raise. ⚠ **True of a QuerySet and not of a list**: the derived-filter lists
  (units, assets, routes, cycles, the four rating lists) hand `selection_iter` an
  already-materialised list and hold every row whatever the cap says. That is
  `NFR-3`'s problem, not this one, and it is named so the next lane raising this
  cap knows which half of the registry it is safe for.
* **`apps/audit/services.py` still reads `EXPORT_ROW_CAP = 50_000`** — the
  BR-AUD-014 twin of the number raised here, in another lane's module. Two rules
  that meant one value now differ; stated out loud rather than left to be found.

### WHERE THE NEXT CLIFF IS

**Not where anybody would guess, and it is nearer than 80,000.**

1. **About 2.5 MB of request body — roughly 25,000 premises rows — TODAY**, and
   it is Django's `DATA_UPLOAD_MAX_MEMORY_SIZE`, not any cap in this product.
   Until `config/settings/base.py` raises it, nothing above is reachable. **This
   is the next thing to fix and it is one line in another lane's file.**
2. **Then memory, at about 1 GB per import.** The parse holds the file and every
   stage materialises the whole staged table, so the curve is linear in rows and
   there is no cliff — it simply costs what it costs, and the machine either has
   it or the worker is killed. ⚠ An out-of-memory kill takes the whole worker
   process, so other people's requests on that worker die with the import.
3. **Then the row cap at 100,000**, which is where it should be: the cap an
   operator meets is now the one the product tells them about.

**Option B — streaming the parse and moving the upload to multipart — is what
buys headroom past that**, and the note above records that it costs no validation
coverage, because the validations read the staged table and not the file. The
upload contract would become multipart rather than a JSON field, which touches
the front-end screen that posts it; that is flagged, not started.

## 2026-09-18 · `DEF-RAT-5742` — Plans & Rates takes its page in the DATABASE, and three derived predicates deliberately do not

**THE DEFECT, IN ONE SENTENCE THE PO CAN READ ALOUD.** Every list on the Plans &
Rates screens — plans, rate schedules, charge codes, taxes & fees, discounts and
the History tab — read **every row a utility has** and then threw away all but
the fifty on screen. On a utility with a thousand plans, opening the Plans tab
asked the database about **two thousand times** to draw one screenful. The PO
reported the screens getting slower as a tenant grows; this is why.

**WHAT IT WAS.** `apps/rating/api.py:110` defined
`_paginated(request, rows: list[dict], extra)` and called
`paginator.paginate_queryset(rows, request)` on a **list**. A list has to exist
in full before anything can slice it, so the fifty rows on screen cost the whole
catalogue. Six views used it. `BR-CUS-1046` / `DEF-CUS-5060` fixed exactly this
shape on `GET /accounts` on 2026-09-12 and the fix never reached rating — the
same *"a fix landed on a neighbouring endpoint"* mechanism `DEF-MET-5205`
records.

**WHAT IT IS NOW, WITH THE MEASURED FIGURES.** Each list splits into
`<x>_list_queryset(params)` — every predicate and the whole ordering, in SQL —
and `<x>_page(params) -> (rows, total)`, which takes the page with a
`LIMIT`/`OFFSET` and the count with a `COUNT(*)`. `api._prepaged` builds the same
DRF envelope over the pair. **Measured on both trees** — the same six endpoints,
page 1, on catalogues of **60, then 120, then 240 rows**, SQL statements per
request:

| endpoint | BEFORE (60 / 120 / 240) | AFTER (60 / 120 / 240) |
|---|---|---|
| `GET /plans` | 248 / 488 / 968 | **209 / 209 / 209** |
| `GET /rate-schedules` | 482 / 962 / 1922 | **403 / 403 / 403** |
| `GET /charges` | 181 / 361 / 721 | **152 / 152 / 152** |
| `GET /taxes` | 241 / 481 / 961 | **202 / 202 / 202** |
| `GET /discounts` | 301 / 601 / 1201 | **252 / 252 / 252** |
| `GET /rate-changes` | 1 / 1 / 1 | **2 / 2 / 2** |

**Every BEFORE column doubles when the catalogue doubles; every AFTER column is
FLAT.** That is the whole promise of `NFR-3`, and 240 rows is a tenth of one
percent of the T5 ceiling — the ratio has no upper bound.

⚠ **`GET /rate-changes` WENT UP, FROM ONE STATEMENT TO TWO, AND IT IS THE MOST
IMPORTANT LINE IN THE TABLE.** `history_row` reads nothing extra, so the old code
fetched the WHOLE append-only compliance trail in ONE statement — a flat statement
count over an unbounded number of ROWS ON THE WIRE. The second statement is the
`COUNT(*)`; the first now carries a `LIMIT 50`. **A statement-count check alone
would have reported this endpoint healthy while it read a whole tenant's rate
history to draw fifty lines**, which is why the suite asserts the `LIMIT` as well
as the count, and why that is the assertion that went red on all six. The absolute figures are still
high because the ROW BUILDERS read per row (`plan_row` costs two statements a
plan, `charge_row` about three a code); that is a separate, smaller defect and
is deliberately NOT fixed here, because batching a row builder changes what a row
SAYS and this change must not be able to move a figure. The cost is now `O(page)`
where it was `O(tenant)`, which is the difference `NFR-3` exists to buy.

### Judgment 1 — three DERIVED predicates keep their `O(tenant)` path, and are NOT re-implemented in SQL

A tax's **status**, a schedule's **structure** and **status**, and a discount's
**type** and **verification** are not columns. Each is derived from the version
in force and, for a tax, from the tenant's own today. `DEF-387` already recorded
the reasoning when it moved the tax status filter OUT of the queryset, and it is
kept verbatim: *"a derived value cannot be filtered in the database without
re-implementing the derivation in SQL — two implementations of one rule, which is
how a list and a detail end up disagreeing about the same row."* A pagination
change is not the place to overturn that.

So `f.status`/`f.service` on taxes, `f.type`/`f.verification` on discounts, and
`f.structure`/`f.status` plus the seven derived sorts on schedules still build
every matching row and then slice. **The judgment is that this is acceptable
because it is NAMED**: `tax_list_is_sql_pageable`, `discount_list_is_sql_pageable`
and `schedule_list_is_sql_pageable` each say, in one readable predicate, exactly
which requests land on the slow path — so the exception can be counted rather
than discovered. It is the shape `customers.account_list_is_sql_pageable` already
takes, and its own sentence applies here unchanged: **the answer is *yes* for
every request a clerk makes by opening the screen, and *no* only for one they
make deliberately.**

### Judgment 2 — `_prepaged` is a SECOND COPY, and that is a cost recorded rather than hidden

Its home is `core/pagination.py`, beside `StandardPagination` and `order_terms` —
exactly the reasoning `order_terms`' own docstring gives for existing at all, and
the PO's standing instruction of 2026-09-12 (*"dont create duplcate code"*).
**This lane owned `apps/rating/` and not `core/`**, and moving shared plumbing
from inside a module lane is how two lanes collide on one file. So it is copied,
the copy says so in its docstring and names its real home, and **a third copy
should trigger the move instead of being written.**

### Judgment 3 — the `<x>_list` functions are KEPT, unchanged

They are not dead. `apps/rating/exports.py` builds four CSVs from them,
`seed_demo` and `sample_data` index catalogues with `per=1000`, and
`customers.seams` publishes `plan_list` and `discount_list` by name across a
module boundary. All of those genuinely want the whole ordered set. Each now
carries a docstring saying it is `O(tenant)` and that a SCREEN wants `<x>_page`.

### Judgment 4 — the brief said SEVEN endpoints; there are SIX, and the seventh was filed

`grep -n "_paginated(" apps/rating/api.py` returns **six** call sites, not seven.
Rather than stop there, every list-shaped read in the file was enumerated: the
seventh is **`GET /tax-jurisdictions`**, which has no pager at all and serves a
bare `TaxJurisdiction[]` rather than the house envelope. It is **not fixed here
and the reason is the point** — paging it changes the shape on the wire, so the
backend half alone would silently break the S13 wizard's step-1 picker, and the
typed client is outside this lane's territory. Filed as **`DEF-RAT-5754`**, so
it is counted rather than mentioned in a paragraph nobody can grep.

### The law-7 proof, and the false pass that had to be designed out

The 38 new cases in `tests/test_def_rat_5742_rating_lists_page_in_sql.py` assert
**the SQL that was sent** or **the number of statements it took** — never a
returned row count. ⚠ **A case counting returned rows would have been green
throughout the entire life of this defect**: DRF sliced the built list to exactly
fifty, served a correct `count`, a correct `next` and correct rows. Everything
about the ANSWER was right; only the work behind it was wrong.

⚠ **AND THE FIRST DRAFT OF THE SQL ASSERTION COULD HAVE PASSED WRONGLY ON THE
WORST ENDPOINT.** Checking the captured statements for the word `LIMIT` looks
sufficient and is not: `plan_queryset` annotates two `Subquery(...[:1])`
expressions, which Django renders as `LIMIT 1` inside the SELECT list. A `LIMIT`
check would therefore have reported success for `GET /plans` on the unfixed code
— the endpoint with the worst breach in it. The assertion is `LIMIT 50`, over the
list's own table, and `_limit_50`'s docstring says why.

---

## 2026-09-18 · `DEF-MET-5743` — ROUTE SETUP PAGES ON THE SERVER AT BOTH ENDS, AND THE SIXTEEN CALLERS OF `listAll` ARE WRITTEN DOWN

**PO report, verbatim:** *"Route setup becomes unusable at 5,000–10,000
premises"*, and the same shape across tables at 30–40,000 rows.

**The relayed ruling this lane worked to:** *fix it, and do NOT reintroduce
silent truncation* — *"a picker that silently shows the first 50 of 4,000 routes
is a worse defect than a slow one"*.

### What was actually wrong — three things, and the biggest was not in the brief

1. **`GET /routes/premises-picker` served every matching premises in the tenant
   as a bare array, built with a query per row.** `selectors.route_premises_
   picker` ran one `Unit` query per premises and one `assets_on_unit` call per
   unit. **Measured on `caf716c13`: 18 queries for 4 premises, 82 for 20** —
   four per row. Extrapolated to the top of T5 that is about **160,000 queries
   and 40,000 rows on the wire to draw fifty**. This is SET-06 step 2, the
   screen the PO was describing, and it was found while tracing the two things
   the brief did name.
2. **`listAll` walked every page** of `/routes` and `/cycles` before a row was
   drawn.
3. **`pageSlice` then sliced the result in the browser** on four tables.

### The fix, and the property it had to keep

`route_premises_picker_page` filters, orders and **slices in SQL**, then builds
the page's rows from **three batched reads** — the units, `seams.asset_counts_
for_units` (the batched seam `CR-029` D7 added for exactly this), and the
memberships. **Measured after: 5 queries, flat at 4 premises and at 20.**

⚠ **IT WAS NOT FIXED BY WIDENING THE ROW, WHICH IS THE TRAP `DEF-650` AND
`DEF-324` LEFT.** Those two REMOVED a per-row owner-account expansion from the
premises list because it cost an account read and a ledger derivation per row.
The row here holds exactly the thirteen keys it held before, and
`test_the_row_shape_is_exactly_what_it_was` pins them so a later batch cannot
quietly widen them.

⚠ **THE `unassigned` CHIP HAD TO MOVE INTO THE QUERYSET BEFORE ANY OF THIS WAS
POSSIBLE.** It dropped rows *while building them*, so it could only be applied
after the whole list existed — which is why this endpoint could not be paged at
all. As a `NOT IN` subquery it narrows before the slice, and the `count` beside
the page is therefore true.

### The honest cost: two sort controls are GONE

`meters` and `current_route` are derived through the assets seam and the
membership table. Ordering by either means building every row in the tenant
before the slice — the defect again. They are **not sortable** now, which is the
refusal `ACCOUNT_SORTS` already carries for `last_bill`: a header offering an
ordering the request cannot ask for is worse than no header. **Five orderings
that are true at 40,000 premises beat seven that are only true at 3,000.**

### `listAll` IS DEPRECATED AND DELIBERATELY NOT CAPPED

A ceiling on it would be **a hard cap that has to be removed when T4 arrives**,
which `NFR-5` forbids by name, and a **truncating** ceiling would be worse than
the slowness it cured. So it keeps its one honest property — it never truncates
— and the fix is to stop calling it. A test now asserts that it still walks
every page, so the day somebody "simplifies" it by stopping early, 3,000 routes
do not silently vanish.

### THE CALLERS, TRACED — and there are SIXTEEN, not eight

The note in `endpoints.ts` said *"eight shipped callers"*. That was true on
2026-08-23 and has not been true for some time; the count today is **16 call
sites in 12 files**. That is worth its own line: **a number written in a comment
is a claim nothing re-checks**, and this one was cited by the brief that
commissioned the work.

⚠ **AND THE COUNT IN THE TABLE BELOW NEEDED CORRECTING BEFORE IT WAS EVEN A
DAY OLD, WHICH IS THIS DEFECT'S OWN LESSON POINTED AT ITS OWN RECORD.** The
first draft of this entry said *"six moved, ten left"*, counting SURFACES.
Counted as `listAll` CALL SITES — which is what a reader greps for — it is
**16 before and 12 after; four moved** (`RoutesCyclesPage` ×2,
`RoutesCyclesWizardPages` ×2). The other two rows in the table are surfaces
that stopped receiving a whole list by a different route: SET-06 step 2 was
served a bare array of every matching premises by `GET /routes/premises-picker`,
and SET-07 step 2 was handed `props.routes` by the page above it. Both readings
are true of something; only one of them can be checked with a grep, so both are
written out.

**Moved off it in this lane (6 surfaces, of which 4 are `listAll` call sites):**

| Caller | What it needed | What it got |
|---|---|---|
| `RoutesCyclesPage.RoutesOpsPage` (S26) | a TABLE | `getRoutesPage` + server total |
| `RoutesCyclesPage.CyclesOpsPage` (S27) | a TABLE | `getCyclesPage` + server total |
| `RoutesCyclesWizardPages.CycleWizardPage` `getCycles` | ONE ROW BY ID | `getCycleDetail` |
| `RoutesCyclesWizardPages.CycleWizardPage` `getRoutes` | a paged PICKER | the wizard asks for its own page |
| `RoutesCyclesWizards.RouteWizard` step 2 | SEARCH | server `q`/`sort`/`page`/`per` |
| `RoutesCyclesWizards.CycleWizard` step 2 | SEARCH | `getRoutesPage` + the new `f.on_cycle` |

**Left on it, each with its reason (10 call sites, 8 files — every one outside
this lane's write scope, and every one still CORRECT, only slow):**

| Caller | Verdict |
|---|---|
| `BillRunWizard` `getCycles` | **SEARCH** owed. A cycle vocabulary is bounded by the billing calendar — a dozen to a few dozen rows — so `listAll` runs ONCE for any real tenant. Lowest value of the ten. |
| `RunScopeStep` `getCycles` | as above |
| `FixABillTab` `getCycles` | as above |
| `PastBillingRunsPanel` `getCycles` | as above |
| `PrintBillsPage` `getCycles` | as above |
| `RouteReadsPage` `getCycles` | as above — and it already composes `SearchSelectField` past `LONG_LIST_THRESHOLD`, so `getCycleOptions` is a two-line change when a lane owns that file |
| `ReadsListPage` `getCycles` + `getRoutes` | **SEARCH** owed on the ROUTE half — a route filter grows with the tenant |
| `UploadReadsWizard` `getCycles` + `getRoutes` | **SEARCH** owed on the ROUTE half |
| `AddPremisesWizard` `getRoutes` | **SEARCH** owed — this is the one a clerk hits most, and `getRouteOptions` exists for it |
| `CycleDetailPage` `getRoutes` | **SEARCH** owed — it lists a cycle's routes; `getCycleRoutes` (bounded by the cycle) is the right shape |

**Nothing in that table legitimately needs the whole set.** The cycle ones are
tolerable because cycles are few, not because the pattern is right. The four
route ones are the real remainder and each is a picker that should search.
`getRouteOptions` / `getCycleOptions` are in `endpoints.ts` waiting for them.

### THREE WHOLE-SET READS SURVIVE ON PURPOSE, AND EACH IS BOUNDED BY SOMETHING THAT IS NOT THE TENANT

Written down because each one LOOKS like the defect and is not:

* **`getRoutePremisesMembers(routeId)`** — the premises already on a route, for
  re-opening an edit. ⚠ **Seeding that from the page in front of you would have
  DELETED members on save**: the commit sends `premises_ids` as the whole
  membership, so every member past row fifty would have been dropped, silently,
  on a screen that looked right. Bounded by one crew's walk (`BR-MET-055`).
* **`getCycleRoutes(cycleId)`** — the same, cycle-shaped, for SET-07's totals.
  It FOLLOWS `count` rather than trusting one page, for the same reason.
* **`Select all {n}`** — one deliberate request on an explicit act. ⚠ It read
  `rows.map(...)`; left alone, a button labelled **"Select all 9,412"** would
  have selected **fifty** and reported success. The label states the number
  first, so nobody presses it without seeing what they are asking for.

### The selection is a MAP now, and that is the half a paging change always forgets

Both pickers held a `Set` of ids and read everything else — the running count,
the move badges, step 3's meter list, the conflict warnings — back out of the
array holding the whole tenant. With one page in hand, a selection made on page
1 would have vanished from every one of those on page 2, **with the row still
ticked when the clerk came back**. The row travels with the id.

### A new filter: `f.on_cycle` on `GET /routes`

SET-07 step 2's one chip asks *"is this route already on a cycle"* — **any**
cycle, which `f.cycle` (which names ONE) cannot express. It was answered in the
browser over the whole-tenant array; a chip filtering the PAGE would report *"no
routes are on a cycle"* whenever that page held none.

### Law 7 — what these tests would have to be to pass wrongly

⚠ **A test that counts rendered rows cannot see this defect at all.** Fifty rows
appear whether the browser fetched fifty or forty thousand, and `pageSlice` drew
a correct-looking footer too. So every new case asserts **the request** or
**query count**:

* `test_def_met_5743_route_setup_paging.py` (12 cases) compares the query count
  at two fixture SIZES rather than pinning a constant — the claim is *this does
  not grow with the tenant*, and a pinned number would go red on the next
  legitimate `select_related` while saying nothing about growth.
* `routeSetupRequests.def5743.dom.test.tsx` mounts S26 over a 4,000-route stub
  and counts requests. **PROVED RED at `caf716c13`: `expected [1,2,3,4] to
  deeply equal [1]`.**
* `routeSetupPaging.def5743.test.ts` (8 cases) — **6 RED at `caf716c13`**.
* The N+1 case — **RED at `caf716c13`: *"the picker grew from 18 to 82 queries
  when the tenant grew from 4 premises to 20"*.**

⚠ **THE STUB HAD TO BE BUILT TO PAGE.** A fixture that returned its whole array
whatever it was asked would pass over a screen that had gone back to slicing in
the browser — a fixture that cannot tell a working page from a broken one, which
is `DEF-CWP-3925`'s shape exactly.

### What is NOT fixed, and is written down rather than mentioned

* **`selectors.routes_page` / `cycles_page` still build a `route_dict` for every
  filtered row before DRF slices.** They ARE server-paged, so `NFR-3` holds; the
  remaining cost is a Python pass bounded by the tenant's ROUTE count, not by
  its premises count. Fixing it means teaching `_page()` a limit, and `_page()`
  belongs to the follow-on lane.
* **`GET /routes/meter-picker` takes one repeated `unit_id` query parameter per
  selected unit.** A route of a few hundred premises is fine; a selection of
  thousands would build a URL no server accepts. Bounded by the ROUTE rather
  than the tenant, so it is a smaller problem than the one fixed here — but it
  is a real ceiling and it is named so the next lane does not rediscover it.
* **`sortPickerRows` in `routesCyclesShared.tsx` has no callers left.** Not
  deleted from a file this lane does not own; named here so it is retired
  knowingly rather than found later as mystery code.

## 2026-09-18 · `DEF-MET-5761` — the metering lists take their page in SQL, and the S14 roll-up stops asking the ledger once per unit

**What the PO reported:** route setup and the premises lists become unusable at
5,000–10,000 premises, and the same shape appears across the tables at 30–40,000
rows. Route setup itself is `DEF-MET-5743`, a different lane. This entry is the
rest of `apps/metering/api.py`.

### The one line that was the defect

`_page()` at `api.py:190` read `paginator.paginate_queryset(list(rows), request)`.
Every caller hands it a QuerySet or a paginator-shaped result set, so `list()`
built **every row the tenant has** and the paginator then kept fifty. Handed the
result set itself, Django counts it with one `COUNT(*)` and slices it with
`LIMIT`/`OFFSET`. That is the whole fix for four of the six endpoints.

It was not merely a wasted copy. `selectors.ReadArchiveResultSet` was built with
`count()` and `__getitem__` **precisely so the paginator could page a detached
partition**, and `list()` reached its `__iter__` instead — `self[0:None]`, a
union SELECT over every archived partition with no `LIMIT` clause at all. The
object was paginator-shaped and nothing had ever paged it.

### The measured figures (sqlite, `CaptureQueriesContext`, before → after)

| read | population | before | after |
|---|---|---|---|
| `premises_rollup()` alone | 31 premises, **0** units | 4 | 4 |
| `premises_rollup()` alone | 31 premises, **50** units | **54** | **5** |
| `GET /premises` | 10 premises, 10 units | 45 | 37 |
| `GET /premises` | 10 premises, **100** units | **135** | **37** |
| `GET /units` | 10 premises, 10 units | 32 | 33 |
| `GET /premises-owners` | 10 owners | 11 | 12 |

Read the roll-up row first: **one account query per unit in the tenant**, on the
header of a screen a utility opens all day. Extrapolated to the top of T5 —
40,000 units — that is roughly **40,004 round trips for one `GET /premises`**,
against **5** now. The `GET /premises` row is the same fact seen from the
endpoint: it was `O(units)` and is now flat at 37 whatever the tenant holds.

**`/units` and `/premises-owners` each gained ONE query, and that is the honest
price of the fix, not a regression.** The extra statement is the `COUNT(*)` that
tells a clerk the true total; what it buys is that the rows BUILT drop from the
whole tenant to fifty, which no query count can show. The `LIMIT` assertions are
what prove that half.

### The judgment calls, with their reasoning

**1 · `GET /units` could not use `_page`, so it got `customers`' shape instead.**
Three of its filters — `occupancy`, `sub_metered`, `service` — partition on
values no column on `units` holds (`BR-MET-036`: occupancy is DERIVED and there
is no column to set). A `LIMIT` applied before those run would page a different
set than the one the count claims. So `selectors.units_page(params)` returns
`(rows, total)` and `units_list_is_sql_pageable` names, in one place, which
filters force the build-then-slice path — deliberately the same shape as
`customers.account_page` / `account_list_is_sql_pageable`, which `BR-CUS-1046`
required for *"40,000 accounts built to draw fifty"*. `api._prepaged` serves the
**byte-for-byte identical DRF envelope** over it. A second envelope shape on a
list screen would be a client-side special case for ever.

**The predicate reproduces `units_list`'s three Python passes EXACTLY, including
where they are loose** — `sub_metered` is tested for truthiness there, so
`f.sub_metered=false` narrows; an unrecognised `occupancy` filters nothing and is
therefore SQL-pageable. Tidying either reading would page one set and count
another, which is worse than the cost removed.

**2 · `units_list` was SPLIT, not rewritten.** `units_queryset` is its SQL half,
extracted verbatim; `units_list` still calls it and still returns what it always
returned. A dozen callers — the exports, the seed, both sample-data builders,
the customers seam, the runbooks seam — read every row on purpose and are not
screens, so none of them moved.

**3 · The roll-up was made cheaper and counts EXACTLY what it counted.**
`seams.accounts_for_units` is `active_account_for_unit` asked about a LIST, and
`apps/customers/selectors.py` states the equivalence in its own docstring: the
same `occupying_accounts_for_unit` reading, the same `BR-CUS-055` behaviour-class
boundary, the same first-by-`created_at` tie-break. Both filter `tenant_id`,
`unit_id` and `status__behavior_class__in` and nothing else, so a unit is in the
returned map exactly when `occupancy_of` would have said *occupied*. `vacant` is
the same integer, reached by subtraction instead of by 40,000 questions.

**4 · `NFR-5` is untouched. Nothing here caps anything.** `per` still clamps to
the IS-2 vocabulary and `page` still clamps into range; no maximum row count,
no per-tenant limit, nothing a T4 migration would have to remove.

### What is NOT fixed, and is written down rather than mentioned

* **`GET /premises` and `GET /units` pay about THREE queries per SERVED row** —
  `premises_detail_dict` and `unit_list_dict` each walk their row's relations one
  at a time. Measured: premises costs **9 queries for a page of 1 row, 39 for 11,
  99 for 31**; units costs **33 for a page of 10 and 153 for a page of 50**. It
  is **bounded by the page**, so it is not an `NFR-3` breach and the paging fix
  does not touch it — but a page of fifty is ~150 round trips whatever the tenant
  size. Filed as `DEF-MET-5762` rather than fixed here, because `unit_list_dict`
  is also every single-row reader's shape and `premises_detail_dict` is the
  export's. It is `DEF-2723`'s shape on the accounts list and `DEF-5745`'s on
  `GET /assets`.
* **`selectors.routes_page` / `cycles_page` still build a row for every filtered
  route or cycle before DRF slices.** `DEF-MET-5743`'s own entry hands this to
  "the follow-on lane" as *teaching `_page()` a limit*. **It was deliberately not
  done.** Those two return LISTS because they sort on counts no column holds, and
  say so in their docstrings; a limit inside `_page` would page a different order
  than the header claims, which is the same trap `units_page` avoids by branching.
  The right fix is theirs: a `(rows, total)` selector per endpoint, as `units_page`
  now is. Removing `list()` changed nothing for them — the paginator slices a list
  exactly as it did before.
* **The roll-up still reads every unit id once.** `seams.accounts_for_units` takes
  a LIST, so there is one `SELECT id` and one `IN (…)`: four queries where there
  were `1 + N`. The durable removal is a COUNTING seam owned by `apps/customers`
  (*"how many of these units are occupied"*), which is that module's to publish
  and not metering's to reach around.
* **`GET /premises/picker` was reported as materialised and IS NOT.** It has
  handed the paginator an unevaluated queryset since `fe08a6c3c` (2026-09-16) and
  explains why in its own docstring. Two days of prose that nothing re-checked;
  `test_address_picker_slices_in_sql` is now that sentence as a check, green on
  both sides of this change and labelled as such in the test.

### Law 7 — what these tests would have to be to pass wrongly

⚠ **A TEST THAT COUNTS RETURNED ROWS CANNOT SEE THIS DEFECT.** A Python slice of
a fully-built list hands back exactly the same fifty rows as a `LIMIT`, so every
pre-existing assertion in the metering suite passes on both spellings. So each
case asserts either **the SQL** (does a non-`COUNT` SELECT from the list's own
table carry a `LIMIT`, and does `?page=2` move the `OFFSET`) or **the cost at two
population sizes**, never a pinned constant — a pinned number goes red on the next
legitimate `select_related` while saying nothing about growth.

**PROVED RED at `442799d50` in `pytest`, the harness that runs them: 7 of 14
cases failed**, including *"the roll-up followed the tenant: 12 queries over 4
units, 28 over 20"*. All 14 pass on the fix.

⚠ **ONE CASE WAS WRITTEN WRONG FIRST AND THE MISTAKE IS WORTH THE LINE.**
`test_reads_list_slices_in_sql` originally ran against an EMPTY `meter_reads`
table. It passed on the fixed code and could never have failed on the broken one:
Django's paginator collapses `top` to `self.count`, so a count of zero makes the
page slice `[0:0]`, the compiler raises `EmptyResultSet` and **no second query is
issued at all** — the assertion was reading a `COUNT(*)` and an absence. That is
hard-won law 7's *structurally incapable of failing*, met while writing a test
for law 7. It seeds a row now.

### Two lanes, one file

`apps/metering/api.py` and `selectors.py` were being edited by `DEF-MET-5743`'s
lane at the same time. This change was three-way re-derived onto `442799d50`
(which carries their `route_premises_picker_page` work) and **verified by
subtraction**: every line the merge deletes from the tip is one of this lane's
own intended edits, and `route_premises_picker_page`, `_positive_int` and
`on_cycle` are all still in `HEAD` afterwards. The shared surfaces are `_page()`
itself and `_list_params()`; `_list_params` keeps its exact signature and return
shape and now delegates to a new `_parsed()` that keeps `page`/`per` on the
params, which is what a SQL-paging selector needs and a whole-set selector does
not.

## 2026-09-18 — the Assets list was ALREADY paging in SQL; what is actually slow is two other things, and only one of them is this lane's (`DEF-5744`, `DEF-5745`)

A lane was dispatched to fix `GET /assets` on the reported scaling defect — the
PO's report that lists become unusable as a tenant grows from 3,000 to 40,000
rows, with Assets named at 30,000–40,000. The brief named
`apps/assets/api.py:127` and asked, first, whether `selectors.asset_list`
returns a built list or a lazy queryset, and said in as many words that if it
was already lazy the finding was *already correct* and should be reported
rather than turned into a change.

**It is already correct, and it was verified rather than read.** Hard-won law 1
says a comment claiming a guarantee is not the guarantee, and `asset_list`'s
docstring makes exactly such a claim — so the claim was measured:

* `asset_list(...)[:50]` issues **ONE query for 10 rows and ONE for 40**. The
  statement carries `LIMIT` and `ORDER BY`, so the page and the sort both reach
  the database.
* The endpoint's cost follows the **page**, not the match set: growing the
  match set from 20 to 140 while holding `per=50` moved the served rows from 20
  to 50 and the query count from 103 to 253 — 5.15 and 5.06 queries **per
  served row**, i.e. flat per row served.
* The other three call sites the brief named — `assignments_page`,
  `maintenance_page`, `asset_read_dates_page` at api.py lines 261, 281 and 305 —
  are lazy QuerySets too, and `tests/test_cr092_registry_paging.py` and
  `tests/test_cr092_asset_paging.py` already prove all four. Both files were
  re-run: **65 passed.**

`DEF-MET-4951`, `DEF-MET-4962` and `DEF-MET-4995` closed this in `4accdfd5e`,
`784361367` and `fe08a6c3c`. Assets needs no `_prepaged` the way
`apps/customers` does, and that is worth writing down because the brief
reasonably assumed it would: `_prepaged` exists because `account_page` returns
**dicts**, which DRF cannot slice, so customers has to take the page in SQL and
rebuild the envelope by hand. `asset_list` returns **model instances**, so
`StandardPagination.paginate_queryset` slices the queryset natively and the
envelope is DRF's own. Copying `_prepaged` here would have been a second
envelope implementation bought for nothing.

**Two things are genuinely wrong, and neither had a register row.**

`DEF-5744` (high, FIXED here). `f.status=unassigned` read every current
assignment's `asset_id` into a Python `list` and handed it to
`exclude(id__in=…)`, so the statement carried one uuid literal per assigned
asset in the tenant. Measured: the SQL grew **4,797 → 6,417 → 10,017
characters** for **5 → 50 → 150** assigned assets, about 36 characters each; in
bind parameters, **7 → 37 for 5 → 35** assets. At the top of T5 (40,000, ruled
2026-09-06) that is roughly **1.4 MB of SQL carrying 40,000 parameters** —
**past SQLite's 32,766-variable limit outright**, so the Unassigned filter would
have stopped answering rather than merely answering slowly. That makes it an
`NFR-5` hard cap as much as an `NFR-3` cost. The `q=` address arm
(`BR-AST-041`) had the identical shape: **12 → 42 parameters for 5 → 35**
assets. Both now narrow by a lazy `values("asset_id")` subselect, so the ids
never leave the database and the parameter count is a constant. The predicate
is named once, as `_current_seat_ids()`, because `f.status=unassigned` and
`f.assigned=` are the same question asked twice and two spellings of one
predicate is how the two directions of a filter drift apart — which is
literally the `CR-089` G2 fault, in reverse.

⚠ **THE REASON IT SURVIVED THE LANE THAT FIXED EVERYTHING AROUND IT IS THE
GENERALISABLE PART.** `CR-092` lane 1 moved four filters into SQL and proved it
with query counts, correctly. **An `IN` clause holding forty thousand literals
is still exactly ONE query.** So
`test_no_query_per_row_however_many_rows` is true and blind at the same time —
law 7's *ask what would make this check pass wrongly*, and the answer is *this*.
`tests/test_def5744_registry_subqueries.py` therefore counts **bind
parameters**, not queries, and it was proved red on the unchanged code at
`bfaeb4120` before it was trusted green. It also asserts the statement still
names `asset_assignments` as a subselect, because a filter DELETED outright
sends no parameters either and would have turned both cost cases green over a
registry that had quietly forgotten how to filter.

`DEF-5745` (medium, FILED AND DELIBERATELY NOT FIXED). `asset_dict` costs
**five queries per SERVED row** — the current assignment, its unit, the service
point, the service code and a sub-meter `COUNT(*)` — so `asset_page_rows` is
**51 queries for 10 rows and 201 for 40**. This is **bounded by the page, not
the match set**, so it is not the `NFR-3` breach the lane was sent for and the
list is not unusable at 40,000 because of it. It is still real: `per=1000` is a
legal page size (`core/pagination.py PAGE_SIZES`), which is about **5,000
queries in one request**.

**The judgment, recorded because it is a scope call somebody will otherwise
re-litigate:** it is filed rather than fixed. The fix is `asset_page_rows`' own
pattern — batch the four seam reads across the page the way
`latest_reads_for_assets` already is — and that changes `asset_dict`'s contract,
which every consumer of a registry row depends on. That is a wave with its own
blast radius, not a line inside a lane scoped to SQL paging, and doing it here
would have been the redesign-as-a-side-effect the maintenance process names.

⚠ **AND ITS ESCAPE REASON IS A SECOND INSTANCE OF THE SAME BLIND SPOT, ONE STEP
OVER.** The `NFR-3` test measures the **selector** and never the **view**: it
calls `list(selectors.asset_list(...)[:50])`, which does not run
`asset_page_rows` at all. And it is written as *the cost did not move with the
population* — which is TRUE here and always will be, because this cost follows
the PAGE. Two correct checks with one uncovered step between them, reporting
zero over a scope they silently exclude. **To see it you have to vary the PAGE
SIZE, not the population**, and measure the view.

**Proved on real PostgreSQL as well as on the suite, and that was not ceremony.**
The change replaces `IN (<literals>)` with `NOT IN (<subselect>)`, and **on
PostgreSQL a `NOT IN` whose subquery yields a single NULL matches nothing at
all** — the Unassigned tab would have gone silently empty on every tenant with
the default SQLite suite green, which is hard-won law 14's shape one column
over. It is safe because `AssetAssignment.asset` is a non-nullable FK, but *"the
model file says NOT NULL"* is a claim about a file and the law asks for a claim
about the database, so it was run against one: **7 passed under
`--ds=config.settings.pgtest`.**

**And the suite run surfaced something that is not this lane's work at all
(`DEF-5763`, filed).** `tests/test_br_ast_049_external_ref.py` has **17 failing
cases**, and they are not new: the same seventeen, with byte-identical names,
fail at `d04823bb3`, at its parent `8cb5e573d`, and at `fe08a6c3c` — **2026-09-16,
two days earlier**. The test file itself has not been touched since it was merged
on 2026-09-08 in `c7485bebc`, so the product moved under it. The lead failure is
*"a corrected re-run was rejected for the seats its own meters already hold"*.

⚠ **THE POINT IS NOT THE SEVENTEEN, IT IS THAT NOBODY READ THEM FOR TWO DAYS**,
which is hard-won law 7's own named shape — *proved red at birth, then never
read*. And the branch's standing expectation of *roughly 50 pre-existing
failures* is the thing that makes it possible: a lane that expects red learns to
scroll past it, so a true red acquires the protective colouring of a known one.
**The habit that found it is the one `DEF-CWP-4187` added: do not call a red
pre-existing — DATE it.** Here that meant running the same file at two earlier
commits rather than asserting. An undated *"not mine"* would have left it
standing for a third day.

## 2026-09-19 · `DEF-5745` — a page of Assets rows costs a handful of reads instead of five per row

**What was wrong.** `GET /assets` fetched its page in SQL correctly — `DEF-5744`
and `CR-092` had already seen to that — and then shaped each row one database
round trip at a time. `asset_dict` walked the asset's current assignment, that
assignment's unit, the asset's service point, the service point's service code
and, on the meters tab, a `COUNT(*)` of its sub-meters. Five reads per SERVED
row, and seven on the sub-meters tab, where the Parent/master cell walks the
MASTER's seat and the master's unit as well.

**Measured before and after, same fixture both times** — 1,000 assigned meters
spread over 200 units on `brazosbend`, sqlite, `CaptureQueriesContext`, rows
fetched counted by replaying each captured `SELECT`:

| read | page | served | queries before | after | rows fetched before | after |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `asset_page_rows` (the row shaping) | 40 | 40 | **201** | **6** | 200 | **121** |
| `asset_page_rows` | 1,000 | 1,000 | **5,001** | **9** | 5,000 | **1,401** |
| `GET /assets` (the whole endpoint) | 50 | 50 | **257** | **12** | 305 | **206** |
| `GET /assets` | 1,000 | 1,000 | **5,007** | **15** | 6,005 | **2,406** |

**The endpoint is measured as well as the selector because the register asked
for it in those words** — *"Measure the VIEW, not the selector"*. 50 rather than
40 is not a slip: `core/pagination.clamp_page_size` clamps `per` DOWN to the
vocabulary 50/100/200/500/1000, so 50 is the smallest page this endpoint can
actually serve and 1,000 is the largest. The shaping rows above are measured at
exactly 40 and 1,000 because that is what `asset_page_rows` is handed.

**Read the rows-fetched column too, because the query count alone flatters the
fix in one direction and hides half of it in the other.** At page 1,000 the
round trips fall 556-fold, and the ROWS the database hands back fall from 5,000
to 1,401 — because 1,000 rows standing on 200 units and 200 service points now
resolve 200 units and 200 points, not 1,000 of each. A query count cannot show
that, and it is the half that matters on a page whose rows share their places.

**Nine at page 1,000 rather than six is the chunking, and it is deliberate.**
The id lists are cut into runs of 900 (`_ID_CHUNK`), so a page of 1,000 issues
two statements for the seats, two for the counts and two for the reads instead
of one each. `per` clamps to 1,000 today, so nothing today needs it; what it
buys is that the fix cannot itself become an `NFR-5` cap — an `IN` clause
holding 40,000 literals is still exactly ONE query, which is `DEF-5744`'s own
lesson one function along, and it surfaces as SQLite's 32,766-variable limit
rather than as a slow page.

⚠ **AND THE FIRST ENDPOINT FIGURE THIS LANE TOOK WAS WRONG — 3,541 WHERE THE
TRUTH IS 5,007 — WHICH IS WORTH MORE THAN THE FIGURE IT CORRECTS.**
`connection.queries_log` is a `deque` capped at `queries_limit`, **9,000**.
`CaptureQueriesContext` records `len(log)` on entry and subtracts on exit, so
once that deque is SATURATED it evicts from the left and the subtraction returns
a number **smaller** than the queries that actually ran — silently, with no
warning and no error. The measuring run had already issued about 10,400 queries
before it reached the endpoint block, so it under-reported by 1,466 and the
under-report was in the direction that makes a per-row cost look CHEAPER than it
is. Clearing the log immediately before each capture makes the count exact, and
`_cost` in the committed test does that with the reason written beside it. **A
query counter that can only ever under-report is hard-won law 7's *reporting
zero over a scope it silently excludes*, wearing a measurement's clothes** — and
nothing about its output distinguishes a saturated run from an honest one.

### The risk the filing lane named, and what makes it managed

`DEF-5745` was filed with a reason not to fix it inside the paging lane: *"it
changes `asset_dict`'s contract and every consumer of a registry row"*. That was
right. `asset_dict` is also what `services.py` records as the `before` and
`after` of every audited asset write, and what `asset_detail` builds the S50
header on — sixteen single-row call sites.

**So the contract does not move.** `asset_dict(asset)` with one argument reads
and answers exactly what it read and answered before; `asset_dict(asset, page)`
answers the same row out of dictionaries the caller already holds. The page
bundle is built once by `asset_page_rows`, which is the endpoint's only caller.

Two pins hold it, and they fail on different things:

  * **the key set per tab, written as literals** — a batch that pays for itself
    by widening the row is `DEF-650`/`DEF-324` in reverse;
  * **the VALUES, key for key, against the single-row path** — both sides
    recomputed in the test, so a regression cannot be absorbed by editing an
    expected value. This is the route-setup lane's
