    `test_the_row_shape_is_exactly_what_it_was` with its second half added.

Both were GREEN before the change and after it. That is the point of writing
them first.

### The batch each per-row read was replaced by — all of them already existed

| per-row read | batched by | queries for the page |
|---|---|---|
| current assignment | one `asset_assignments` filter, chunked | 1 |
| the seat's unit | `seams.unit_refs` | 1 |
| service point + service code | `seams.service_codes_for_points` | 2 |
| sub-meter `COUNT(*)` | one grouped count, chunked | 1 |
| last read | `seams.latest_reads_for_assets` | 1 |

**THREE of the five cross the module boundary, and all three were already
published — this list was simply not using two of them.** `latest_reads_for_assets`
was already in use (`CR-089` wave C); `service_codes_for_points` has been
published since `DEF-1549` and the map was pointed at it by `DEF-MET-4962`;
metering's batched `unit_refs` has existed since `DEF-2723` and `customers.seams`
uses it. The other two — the seats and the sub-meter counts — are the assets
module's OWN tables, so they needed no seam, only a grouped query instead of a
loop. The two that had to be adopted are `DEF-MET-4962`'s shape exactly — *the
batch read already existed and assets went on paying the singular* — which is
now the third time that sentence has been written about this module.

⚠ **`apps/assets/seams.py unit_refs` WAS A LOOP WEARING A BATCH'S NAME.** Its
docstring is accurate about what it does — *"ONE lookup per DISTINCT unit"* —
and a reader takes its plural name to mean one query. It called `unit_ref` per
distinct unit, so a page whose rows stand on distinct units paid one per served
row. `metering.selectors.unit_refs` has answered the set in one query since
`DEF-2723` and `customers.seams` has used it since. The assets seam now resolves
to it, which also takes the per-row cost out of the S50 Assignment-history tab,
its only other caller.

The entry it returns narrows from the full `unit_detail_dict` to metering's
five-field list ref. That is deliberate: the detail dict also reads the
premises' whole service list, which no caller of this function draws, and the
three fields anything does read — `label`, `premise_address`, `premises_id` —
are all present.

### Law 7 — what these checks would have to be to pass wrongly

  * **a fixture whose two pages are the same size.** The sizes are asserted
    explicitly, 10 against 40 and 5 against 20.
  * **a fixture with nothing assigned**, so no unit or service read ever runs
    and the count is flat because there was no cost. The rows are asserted to
    carry a real address, a real service code, a real sub-count and a real
    parent premises.
  * **an unwired metering seam answering `{}`**, which is cheap and wrong. The
    same value assertions catch it.
  * **counting outside the work.** Every count is taken inside
    `CaptureQueriesContext` around the call being measured, and the queryset
    fetch is deliberately outside it — that cost is
    `test_cr092_registry_paging.py`'s subject and is already flat.
  * **the chunk check passing over an unchunked list.** A query count cannot see
    a bind-parameter ceiling, so that one asserts the boundary on the helper
    instead. A fixture of 32,767 assets is not a test.

### Why no existing check could see it, and both of them are correct

`test_cr092_registry_paging.py` measures `asset_list` — the QUERYSET — and
asserts *the cost did not move with the population*. True here, and always will
be: this cost follows the PAGE, so growing the tenant can never reveal it.
`test_def5744_registry_subqueries.py` counts bind parameters, which is blind to
it by construction. **Two correct checks with one uncovered step between them.**
The case that can see it varies the PAGE SIZE over one population and measures
the step between the queryset and the payload.

### What this lane did NOT do, written down rather than mentioned

  * **`GET /assets/geo`, `/stock` and `/lifecycle` were not touched.** They
    build their own rows and do not call `asset_dict`; `DEF-MET-4962` and
    `CR-092` already batched what they read. Not measured here, so not claimed.
  * **`DEF-MET-5762` — the premises and units lists pay three per served row —
    is the same shape in another module and is still open.** It is named here
    because this fix does not touch it and a reader of this entry will wonder.
  * **`_premises_of` in `apps/assets/selectors.py` has no callers at all.** It
    is left exactly as it was: removing dead code on the way past is how a
    performance lane acquires a blast radius it did not measure.
  * **Not proved on PostgreSQL, and it does not need to be.** Law 14 binds code
    that catches a database error and continues; nothing here does. The change
    is five reads becoming five batched reads, with no exception handling added
    and no `NOT IN` semantics in play — which is what made `DEF-5744` a
    PostgreSQL question and this one not.

### The eighteenth red, filed rather than mentioned (`DEF-AST-5776`)

The assets suites run for this lane came back **18 failed, 237 passed**.
Seventeen are `DEF-5763`'s `test_br_ast_049_external_ref.py` cluster, already
filed. **The eighteenth belonged to nobody:**
`test_cr028_ast_w2_detail.py::test_w2_t7__the_maintenance_api_serves_rows_and_the_lifetime_total`
asserts `response.data["rows"]` on `GET /assets/{id}/maintenance`, which has
answered `{count, next, previous, results}` since `784361367` on **2026-09-12**.
`KeyError: 'rows'`.

**It is dated rather than called pre-existing, which is `DEF-CWP-4187`'s whole
point.** The test file has not been touched since `c7485bebc` on 2026-09-08;
the envelope commit is 2026-09-12; and it fails at `a402238a2` in a worktree
holding none of this lane's work. **Seven days, and every lane ran past it.**

⚠ **THE MECHANISM IS WORTH MORE THAN THE CASE: the lane that changed the shape
brought its OWN passing test for the new shape** —
`test_cr092_asset_paging.py::test_reads_assignments_and_maintenance_answer_the_one_envelope`,
green — **so it had real evidence for what it intended and never looked at the
older file asserting the shape it had just retired.** A new green case for a new
shape is not evidence that the old shape's assertions were moved. And this
branch's standing expectation of ~50 pre-existing failures is what let it hide:
seventeen unowned reds in the same run make an eighteenth read as more of the
same.

**Filed, not fixed.** Moving somebody else's assertion is a second blast radius
this lane did not measure, and `DEF-5745` was one commitment.

## 2026-09-19 · `DEF-CUS-5755` — the Disconnects list takes its page in the DATABASE, and TWO derived reads deliberately do not

**THE DEFECT, IN ONE SENTENCE THE PO CAN READ ALOUD.** The Disconnects tab read
**every account in the utility that a disconnection could touch** — everyone on
the collections ladder and everyone held back by a medical certificate, a
payment plan or a weather moratorium — and then threw all but forty of them
away. It did that to draw one screenful, and it did most of it a second time to
print the number beside the pager. This was the last list in the Accounts area
still built that way.

**WHAT IT WAS.** `apps/customers/disconnect_reads._rows_for` returned a Python
`list` of `(account, case)` pairs and `list_disconnects` did
`total = len(pairs)` and `pairs[start : start + per]`. Both halves were
`O(tenant)`: the count was a `len()` over rows already built, and the page was a
slice of that list. `BR-CUS-1046` / `DEF-CUS-5060` fixed this shape on
`GET /accounts` on 2026-09-12, `DEF-CUS-5753` on `GET /customers` and
`DEF-RAT-5742` across Plans & Rates on 2026-09-18, and none of them reached this
file — the same *"a fix landed on a neighbouring endpoint"* mechanism
`DEF-MET-5205` records.

**WHY IT WAS A LIST AND NOT A LAZY `list()` SOMEBODY COULD DELETE — THE
INTERESTING PART.** The row set is a UNION: *open disconnect cases* ∪ *accounts
with a protection in force*. The second half is **DERIVED**.
`disconnects.STATE_ON_HOLD` exists in the state vocabulary and **nothing in this
repository ever assigns it**, so *on hold* is computed rather than stored, and a
`payment_plan` protection's liveness (`LIFETIME_DERIVED`) is read from payments
on every call. There was a real reason for the list.

**THE FIX IS TO SPLIT THE UNION RATHER THAN TO RESOLVE IT.** *Which accounts
have an open case* is a stored `state` on `disconnect_cases`, so it is now a
**subquery** and returns no row to Python at all. *Which accounts are protected*
is still computed in Python and handed to SQL as a list of ids. The page is then
a `LIMIT`/`OFFSET` over the union, the total a `COUNT(*)`, and the page's cases
one query for the forty accounts on screen instead of a dict keyed from every
open case the tenant holds.

### MEASURED, on ONE population at TWO page sizes

120 accounts on the tab — 100 with an open case, 20 with a medical hold.

| | rows on the wire | total served | **account rows built** | **case rows built** | statements | `LIMIT` in SQL | `COUNT(*)` |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| BEFORE, page size 40 | 40 | 120 | **320** | **200** | 285 | none | no |
| BEFORE, page size 1,000 | 120 | 120 | **320** | **200** | 845 | none | no |
| AFTER, page size 40 | 40 | 120 | **40** | **120** | 265 | `LIMIT 40` | yes |
| AFTER, page size 1,000 | 120 | 120 | **120** | **200** | 825 | `LIMIT 1000` | yes |

**BEFORE, the account rows do not move when the page size changes 25×.** That
flatness is what a Python pager IS, seen from outside. AFTER, the same figure
follows the page: 40 → 120.

**The 320 decomposes exactly, and the third term is the one nobody would have
looked for:** 100 accounts joined in by `open_cases`' `select_related("account")`
inside `_rows_for`, 120 from the union queryset itself, and **100 joined in AGAIN
because `kpi_strip` calls `open_cases()` a second time in the same request.**
Nothing in this module has ever read `case.account`, so that join was fetching a
whole `accounts` row per case, tenant-wide, twice, for nobody.

**The wire is byte-identical in all four runs** — the same forty rows, the same
total of 120, the same five tiles. That is the defect's entire disguise and the
reason no existing test could see it.

⚠ **TWO PAGE SIZES AND ONE POPULATION, ON PURPOSE.** A cost that does not move
when the page size changes 25× is a cost that is not about the page. A second,
larger population would have answered a different question, and the *flat*
column above is the evidence a population sweep would have buried.

⚠ **A STATEMENT COUNT IS THE WRONG INSTRUMENT AND WOULD HAVE CALLED THIS A
NON-EVENT.** 285 → 265 at page 40: a 7% move, while the rows dragged into memory
fell by 280. Paging in SQL normally ADDS statements — a `COUNT(*)` and a
page-scoped case read appear — and here they are paid for by the duplicated
derived read that is now computed once. What moved is how many ROWS a statement
fetches, which is a property of the statement and not of their number.

### Judgment 1 — the DERIVED protected half keeps its Python path and is NOT re-implemented in SQL

An account is on this tab under `ON HOLD` because a **protection is in force**,
which for a `payment_plan` is payments' answer and not a column — `protections_for`
asks `apps.payments.dunning` every time it is called. `DEF-387`'s reasoning is
kept verbatim because it is the reason this is a note and not a fix: *"a derived
value cannot be filtered in the database without re-implementing the derivation
in SQL — two implementations of one rule, which is how a list and a detail end up
disagreeing about the same row."* On a tab that authorises turning somebody's
water off, the row that disagrees is an account under a medical certificate.

**The judgment is that this is acceptable because it is NAMED and because it is
not what people assume it is.** `PROTECTED_HALF_IS_DERIVED` says it in one
sentence beside the code. It is stated as a CONSTANT rather than as a
`<x>_list_is_sql_pageable` predicate — the shape `selectors.account_page` and
`rating.tax_page` use — for a reason worth recording: **those predicates answer a
question about the REQUEST, and this is a property of the DATA.** Every request
pays it and no request can avoid it, so a predicate here would always return
`True` and be a check incapable of failing (law 7's second shape). And the cost is
`O(accounts carrying a protection)`, **not** `O(accounts)`: twenty rows on a
tenant of 40,000 with twenty holds. It is only `O(tenant)` for a utility that has
declared a moratorium over everybody, and that is `DEF-CUS-5778`.

**One thing the split did buy for free:** with `f.state` set, the filtered branch
does not compute the protected half **at all**. The old code unioned both halves
and then kept only ids whose case matched — and every surviving id had a case, so
the protected half could never contribute a row. The set algebra is identical and
the derived read is skipped.

### Judgment 2 — `kpi_strip` stays a whole-set read, and `ladder_tier_of` is why

Four of the five tiles could be `COUNT(*)` aggregates today: they read `state`
and `cut_scheduled_for`, columns nothing wraps. **The fifth cannot.** `AT NOTICE`
asks `disconnects.ladder_tier_of(case)`, and that function's own docstring says
it exists so that *"which tier is this case on"* has ONE home — *"so that folding
`disconnect_cases.tier` into payments' `account_collection_state` … is a change
to this function and not to five call sites."* Writing `tier__in=LADDER_TIERS`
into a `WHERE` clause would make a paging commit the second of those sites, on a
money-adjacent predicate, in a file whose writer is `10-scripts/gates/human_owned.txt`.

**And moving only the other four would have bought nothing**, because `AT NOTICE`
scans the same rows either way. So the whole strip stays in Python, in one pass —
a KPI is a count over the whole set by definition, which makes a whole-set read
the honest shape here rather than the leftover one — and the residue is FILED as
`DEF-CUS-5778` rather than left to be rediscovered. What did change on that path
needed no judgment at all: the `select_related("account")` that was joining an
`accounts` row per case for nobody is gone, and `_protected_account_ids` is
computed once per request and handed to both readers instead of twice.

### Judgment 3 — `_rows_for` is DELETED rather than kept beside the new pair

`DEF-CUS-5753` deleted `api._paginated` on the same reasoning and it applies
harder here: a private helper that builds every row is a trap the next reader of
this file falls into. Unlike `customer_list` and `account_list`, which stay
because exports, seeds and two published seams genuinely want the whole ordered
set, `_rows_for` was private, had exactly one caller, and its `(account, case)`
pair shape existed only to feed the slice. `_search_account_ids` went the same way
and for the same reason — it ran its own `SELECT id FROM accounts` so the caller
could intersect sets in Python. **Not one search leg moved**: the three `Q` terms
are the ones that were there, in the same order, and are now `AND`-ed onto the
list's own queryset as `_search_q`.

### Judgment 4 — a third copy of one state set was found and deliberately NOT fixed

`open_cases()` excludes `stopped` and `restored`. `disconnects.CLOSED_CASE_STATES`
holds THREE — `closed_out` joined them under `BR-CUS-430` on 2026-08-27 — and it
is what the partial unique index and `disconnects.open_case_for` both read. That
constant's own docstring says it was minted because the set had been written twice
as a literal tuple; **there was a third copy, in another file, and nothing counted
copies.** So an account whose service case was closed out and whose surviving debt
opened a `BR-CUS-082` collections case beside it has TWO rows here, and the dict
that collapses them is keyed by `account_id` over a queryset with no `ORDER BY` —
the row a clerk sees is whichever the database returned last.

**It is filed as `DEF-CUS-5777` and carried over unchanged, collapse and all.**
Widening that tuple changes WHICH ROW A CLERK SEES on the tab that authorises a
cut. That is a product decision and not a paging one, and a paging commit is the
worst possible place to make it.

### What was NOT touched, and why it is worth naming

The per-row builders. Drawing forty rows still costs about six statements a row —
`primary_contact_name`, `_premise_cell`, `protections_for` and `halt_reason` each
ask their own question per row — which is most of the 265. That is `O(page)` and
no longer `O(tenant)`, so it is a smaller, separate defect, and `DEF-RAT-5742`'s
reasoning is why it is not fixed here: **batching a row builder changes what a row
SAYS, and this change must not be able to move a figure on a disconnect list.**
`halt_reason` in particular is documented as deliberately un-batched and
un-memoised — *"a RUN cached on a row outlives the debt"*, which is the customer
who paid on Friday and got a certified letter on Monday.

## 2026-09-19 — THE LAST UNPAGED LIST IN PLANS & RATES, AND WHY THE PICKER IN FRONT OF IT DID NOT MOVE

`DEF-RAT-5754`. `GET /tax-jurisdictions` returned `selectors.jurisdiction_list()`
straight to `Response`, so the wire carried a bare `TaxJurisdiction[]`: no
`count`, no `per`, no page, nothing bounding a tenant-wide read.
`core/pagination.py` states the rule it broke in its own docstring — pagination
is on by default for every list, so *"an endpoint has to go out of its way to be
unbounded, and none may"* — and this one went out of its way by never reaching
the paginator at all.

**IT IS THE SEVENTH LIST IN THIS MODULE AND THE ONE `DEF-RAT-5742` COULD NOT
FIND, WHICH IS THE ESCAPE WORTH KEEPING.** That lane enumerated its six by
grepping for `_paginated`. A read that never called the paginator is invisible
to that grep **by construction** — the same blind spot `DEF-BIL-5234` records
for `GET /billing/pending`. A search for the thing that is present cannot find
the case where it is absent, and the absent case is the worse one.

**AND IT DOES NOT LOOK LIKE A LIST, WHICH IS WHY IT SURVIVED SIX WEEKS.** It
feeds the S13 tax wizard's step-1 picker, so it reads as a lookup vocabulary
rather than as a catalogue — and a vocabulary is the one shape a reader forgives
for being whole.

**THE HONEST SIZE OF THIS, STATED FIRST SO NOBODY READS IT AS A RESCUE.** A real
tenant holds about **53** jurisdictions — `CR-077` seeds `TX`, `ALL` and every
remaining US state code, and a tenant naming Iowa gets five. So before and after,
the tax wizard makes **one** request and receives **53** rows. **Nothing a
customer can see changed today.** What changed is that the shape is no longer
unbounded: there was no rule, index or code path stopping a utility entering five
thousand jurisdictions, and nothing would have refused to serve them all in one
response. That is `NFR-3` conformance and `NFR-5`'s *no hard caps* read forwards
rather than a performance fix, and the review row says so in those words.

**THE JUDGMENT THIS NEEDED, AND IT IS THE WHOLE REASON THE DEFECT WAS LEFT OPEN
BY THE LANE THAT FOUND IT.** Paging the endpoint CHANGES THE SHAPE ON THE WIRE.
The one consumer is `getTaxJurisdictions`, and the control behind it is
`SearchSelectField`, which **filters client-side** and **resolves the selected
option's label out of the same array**. Handing it one page breaks two things at
once and in silence:

  * the type-ahead stops finding a jurisdiction past the page size; and
  * **reopening a tax whose jurisdiction sits past the page size renders the
    picker EMPTY** — a wizard step that looks unfilled over a value that is set,
    which is worse than the truncation, because it invites a clerk to re-pick and
    overwrite a correct answer.

`tsc` sees neither. Every existing test passes over both. So the client follows
`count` until it holds every row — **the `/routes` and `/cycles` precedent from
`CR-029` RC-W5-T6, verbatim in shape** — and `getTaxJurisdictions` still returns
`TaxJurisdiction[]`. **`TaxWizard.tsx` is untouched**, which is the strongest
statement available that `BR-SHL-033` behaviour did not move.

**WHAT WAS DELIBERATELY NOT DONE, AND IT IS THE BETTER FIX.** The server now
accepts `q` and matches `name`, `authority` and `reference_no` in SQL, so a
type-ahead COULD be narrowed on the server and the client could stop holding the
set. It is not done here because `SearchSelectField` has **no remote-search
prop**, and adding one is a change to the shared component kit — which **B14 rule
38** makes a UI-rules decision affecting every dialog in the product, on one
screen's authority. `PickerOptions` in `endpoints.ts` is the shape that work
would use; it already exists for routes and cycles and is itself not yet wired to
a control. Recorded rather than half-built.

**NO FILTER WAS DECLARED.** `f.level` is the obvious candidate and is left out:
BE-05 ignores an undeclared `f.*` silently, so a filter with no caller is a
surface that can rot unwatched. Three lines to add when something asks.

**AND THE CHECK THIS DEFECT STILL DESERVES IS THE ONE THREE ROWS HAVE NOW ASKED
FOR AND NOBODY HAS BUILT** — `DEF-BIL-5234`, `DEF-CUS-5061` and `DEF-RAT-5754`'s
own row each name it: ONE gate, over every module, that walks `urlpatterns` and
asserts each list-shaped view reaches the paginator with a queryset. Written once
over every module, so it cannot report zero over a scope it silently excludes
(law 7's `G32` clause). This lane did not build it, because a gate over eleven
modules is its own commitment with its own blast radius, and writing it from
inside one module is how it acquires that module's blind spots.

## 2026-09-19 · `DEF-CWP-5747` — THE CUSTOMER PORTAL'S FIVE LISTS TAKE THEIR PAGE, THEIR SEARCH AND THEIR SORT FROM THE SERVER

**The defect, in one sentence:** every customer-portal list held ALL its rows in
the browser. Six portal edge endpoints served an unbounded array and
`portal/components/listTable.tsx` searched, chipped, sorted and sliced it —
`GET accounts/{id}/readings` was every reading an account had ever taken, and an
AMI deployment writes an interval reading per meter per HOUR.

**This is the one customer-facing scale defect of the set**, which is why it went
first, and `NFR-3` (universal server pagination) and `NFR-5` (no hard caps) are
the rules it was filed against.

### 1 · ALL FOUR MOVED TOGETHER, AND THAT IS THE WHOLE JOB

The row this lane built was filed rather than fixed on 2026-09-18 with the reason
written into it: *"asking the server for one page while search, sort and chips
stay in the browser makes every one of them silently search one page of N"*. A
customer typing a bill number that is on page 7 would be told they have no such
bill — **a correctness defect manufactured in the name of fixing a payload
defect**, and one that passes every test in this repo, because a search case with
twelve fixture rows never crosses a page boundary.

So the page, the search, the chips and the sort all moved in one commit, on five
lists: `CWP-023` my accounts · `CWP-027` bills · `CWP-031` documents · `CWP-034`
readings · `CWP-041` payments.

### 2 · THE MEASUREMENT — TWO PAGE SIZES, ONE HISTORY

`NFR-3` promises that ONE SCREEN costs what one screen costs, so the honest
comparison holds the account's history fixed and moves only `per`. A pair of
figures taken over two population sizes measures the fixture and reads as a
speed-up whichever way the code went.

**One account, 1,100 readings, `GET accounts/{id}/readings`:**

| | rows returned | statements | `count` |
|---|---|---|---|
| **before** (the tip, `limit=None`) | **1,100** | **1,106** | not served |
| **after**, `per=40` | 40 | **7** | 1,100 |
| **after**, `per=1000` | 1,000 | **7** | 1,100 |

⚠ **THE STATEMENT COUNT IS FLAT ACROSS THE TWO PAGE SIZES AND THAT IS THE
POINT.** Before, it followed the account's history — not because the read was
naive, but because `apps/portal/selectors.account_readings` asked
`billing_seam.bill_number_covering` **once per DISTINCT READING DATE** to fill
one column. On an AMI account that is one statement per day of history. It is a
`CASE` over the account's issued periods now, resolved in the same query that
takes the page, so the cell, the SEARCH and the SORT are one derivation.

The endpoint case quotes the before figure in its own failure message, measured
on a pristine worktree at the tip: *"GET readings sent no `LIMIT 50` — the page
was taken in Python, or not at all. **Statements: 74**"* — 74 to draw a screen
over sixty readings.

### 3 · WHICH LISTS PAGE IN SQL, AND WHICH PAGE IN PYTHON ON THE SERVER — NAMED, NOT IMPLIED

`apps/portal/paging.SQL_PAGED` is a dict of five names and a boolean, and
`test_the_split_is_declared_and_readings_is_the_sql_one` asserts it. **A declared
blind spot with no NUMBER attached is indistinguishable from an empty one**
(hard-won law 7), so the exception is countable rather than described.

**`readings` is the only one in SQL**, and the register row says why in one
sentence: *"a customer has a dozen bills, and an AMI deployment writes an
interval reading per meter per hour"*. It is the only portal list whose size is
not bounded by one customer's own history.

**The other four keep an `O(this customer's own history)` path**, each because it
has a predicate over a DERIVED figure that SQL cannot reach without a second
implementation of a derivation the product already has one of — which is
`DEF-387`'s lesson and `DEF-RAT-5742`'s precedent from the day before:

* `bills` — the *Unpaid* chip is `owing > 0`, and owing comes from
  `payments.open_bill_position`, never from subtraction here (`BR-CWP-043`);
* `payments` — a bounce is TWO ROWS anchored at the reversal's date
  (`BR-CWP-061`), which is a pairing pass over the whole list, and a `LIMIT` in
  the database would be free to cut between them;
* `documents` — the rows come from the notifications queue and may be `null`
  (unreachable) rather than empty, which is a different answer from a page of
  nothing;
* `my-accounts` — every row carries a live balance from the ledger.

**Both answers fix the defect and only one fixes the cost.** One page crosses the
wire on all five, and the search sees the whole set on all five; what the SQL one
adds is that the WORK is constant too. None of the four is `O(tenant)`: every one
is already intersected with the session's own flat account set in the QUERY
(`BR-CWP-010`), so a utility with 40,000 accounts costs a customer's page exactly
what a utility with thirty does.

### 4 · `CWP-037` EQUIPMENT IS THE SIXTH ENDPOINT AND IS DELIBERATELY LEFT ALONE

The register row names six lists. Five moved. **Equipment did not, and this
paragraph is the record of why** — a future lane finding `pageSlice` still in
`listTable.tsx` should read this before assuming it was missed.

`Equipment.tsx` passes `footer={false}` and the drawing is what put it there:
`08-screen-layouts.md` `CWP-037` ends *"Status (StatusChip …), no footer"*. A
list with no footer has nothing to page — there is no control a customer could
press to reach a second page, so serving one would make rows unreachable rather
than cheap. It is also **one unit's current assignments**: a household has two or
three meters, `metering.portal_reads.equipment_for_unit` is one read, and the
list is bounded by construction rather than by a cap (`NFR-5` is untouched).
Paging it would mean either contradicting the drawing or drawing a footer the
drawing does not have.

**What would reopen it:** a campus unit with dozens of assets, or a drawing that
gives `CWP-037` a footer. Neither exists today.

### 5 · FIVE THINGS THE SCREENS COULD NO LONGER COUNT FOR THEMSELVES

This is the part a page-only fix would have got wrong silently, and each one was
found by reading the screen rather than by any check:

* **`CWP-034`'s METER TABS.** `Readings.tsx` folded its tab list out of the
  payload. Over one page that reads *the services in the newest fifty readings*,
  so a meter read once a quarter would simply lose its tab and the customer
  would be told they have no water readings. The server answers the set question
  separately now (`portal_reads.reading_services`, one query over the whole
  account) and the screen keeps only the LABEL, which is a display decision.
* **`CWP-027`'s `Pay` CONTROL.** It is drawn only when something is owed, read
  off the array the screen held. Counted off a page it would VANISH for a
  customer whose only unpaid bill is on page 2 — hard-won law 2's mirror wearing
  a page number. `any_owing` is the server's now.
* **`CWP-027`'s *"Every bill since you started, Jun 2026 · 3 bills"*.** Both
  halves were page facts. `oldest_on` and `count` are served.
* **`CWP-031`'s `↓ Download a year`.** Held the moment there is nothing kept to
  send — counted off a page it would be held on page 2 for a customer whose kept
  documents are all on page 1, a refusal that is simply false. `any_kept` is
  served.
* **EVERY EMPTY STATE.** `count` is the MATCHING set, so `count: 0` under a typed
  search would render *you have no bills* at a customer with eleven months of
  them. Each list serves a `populated` fact that says whether it has any rows at
  all, and `CWP-034` gets it free from the tab list.

### 6 · THE PHONE HALF WOULD HAVE BECOME A WALL

`CWP-034`, `CWP-041` and `CWP-023` each draw a CARD STACK under `max-md:flex` and
put the table — and `PortalListTable`'s footer with it — inside `max-md:hidden`.
The stack had no pager because it had every row and a customer scrolled. **One
page and no footer leaves row 51 unreachable on the device most customers open
the portal on**: the payload defect fixed by manufacturing a worse one. All three
card stacks now carry the shared `ListPager`, on the same four `table.pager.*`
keys as the table's own, so there is still one footer in the product (B14 rule
16).

### 7 · B14 RULE 35 IN THE ONE PLACE IT BITES A SEARCH

`CWP-027` prints *Aug 2026* over a bill number and `CWP-031` prints *Bills* over
a document's kind — **catalogue words, in the reader's own language**, and both
were searchable because the browser held the rows it had just rendered. The
server stores `2026-08-26` and `bill`, and may not write those words in any of
the eleven languages, let alone all of them.

**So the SCREEN, which drew the word and knows the language, turns it back into
the code the server knows.** `portal/components/listWindow.splitNeedle` does it:
`aug 2026` becomes `f.month=08` + `f.year=2026`, *Bills* becomes `f.group=bill`,
and a token it cannot name — `BL-2608` — travels as `q`. It is a SUBSTRING match
because the predicate it replaces was one: `monthYearText(...).includes(needle)`
matched `gust` as happily as `aug`, and anything stricter would be this commit
quietly removing a search a customer already relies on.

### 8 · THE DEAD PROP THAT HAS BEEN SHOUTING SINCE 2026-09-09 IS CLOSED

`PortalListTable.toolbarLead` arrived in `a54389bd6` on 2026-09-09 for
`CWP-041`'s *All | This year* and **no caller ever passed it** — dated with
`git log -S`, not assumed. `G13` said so the whole time and the decision log of
2026-09-18 named it for whoever opened this file next. Its stated reason — that a
filter the SERVER applies could not be a `chips` option, because `chips` filtered
rows this component already held — **is now simply untrue: every chip is a server
filter**. So the prop is DELETED and the year pair is an ordinary control. Law 2
in both directions: the prop was built and never wired, and the thing it was
built for now has a real home.

### 9 · TWO SHARED FILES MOVED, AND BOTH SAY WHY IN THEIR OWN DOCSTRINGS

* **`components/searchDebounce.ts` is new** and holds IS-3's debouncer, which was
  in `DataTable.tsx`. The portal needed it and **may not import that module** —
  `BR-CWP-011`, and `listTable.tsx` already records the reason: `DataTable`'s
  module scope calls `@/api/endpoints`, the STAFF edge, which answers 403 to
  every portal session. `DataTable.tsx` re-exports both constants and the
  function, so `ShellWithSession`, `FindTheAddress` and `DataTable.test.tsx` are
  untouched and there is still exactly ONE implementation. It gained a
  `minChars` option; **the portal passes 1 and the staff side keeps IS-3's 2**,
  because a customer typing `8` to find meter `8841-C` must not silently get
  their whole list back, and the predicate this replaces had no minimum at all.
* **`portal/components/listWindow.ts` is new** and holds the five pieces of state
  every portal list needs — page, size, needle, sort, chips — because they are
  the same five on every list and each has to travel on the request. Five screens
  holding their own five would be five chances to forget that typing resets the
  page to 1.

### 10 · A BUG THIS LANE INTRODUCED AND THEN FOUND, WORTH WRITING DOWN

The hook took `resolve` — the screen's word-to-code function — as an ordinary
dependency of the `useMemo` that builds the request. **A screen writes it as an
inline arrow, so it is a NEW function on every render**: the request became a new
object every render, the screen's effect re-fetched on every render, and each
answer rendered again. An endless loop, with `tsc` clean and every type green.

**What found it: `Bills.dom.test.tsx`'s failed-read case**, which could never
settle on its own error card because the effect kept resetting `failed`. It is a
ref now, and the cost is stated where it is paid — a language change does not
re-resolve the needle until the next keystroke.

### 11 · WHAT WAS PROVED, AND WHAT WAS NOT

**RED FIRST, in the harness that runs it, on a pristine worktree at the tip**
(hard-won law 7): **20 of the 21 cases failed**, and the one that carries the
defect failed on the defect itself rather than on a missing symbol —
`test_the_readings_endpoint_asks_the_database_for_one_page` with *"GET readings
sent no `LIMIT 50` — the page was taken in Python, or not at all. **Statements:
74**"*. The ONE that passed is `BR-CWP-010`'s 404 — the guard that an account
outside the session's set answers exactly what an account that does not exist
answers — and it MUST pass on both sides, which is what makes it a regression
guard rather than evidence of anything.

⚠ **`apps.portal.paging` IS IMPORTED LAZILY IN THAT FILE AND THAT IS PART OF THE
PROOF.** A module-level import of a module this commit ADDS makes the whole file
fail to COLLECT at the tip — and a collection error proves a file was added, not
that a page reaches a database. The first attempt did exactly that and the red
proof had to be thrown away and re-taken.

**Then green: 21 passed on SQLite, and 21 passed on real PostgreSQL** (hard-won
law 14, through `config.settings.pgtest`). That was not ceremony: the readings
page casts `TruncDate(read_at)` for the date search and builds the covering bill
as a `CASE` over date ranges, and **a backend difference in either would be
invisible on the SQLite suite**. The measurement is identical on both —
`per=40` → 40 rows / 7 statements, `per=1000` → 1,000 rows / 7 statements,
`count` 1,100 either way.

⚠ **AND TWO OF THE FIXTURES WERE WRONG IN A WAY ONLY POSTGRESQL COULD SAY SO**,
which is the law earning its keep on the test rather than on the code.
`meter_reads` is RANGE-PARTITIONED there, so 1,100 readings one day apart ran to
2029 and raised *"no partition of relation meter_reads found for row"* — the
fixture now spreads across meters and stays inside 2026. And `an_issued_bill`
needs an OUTER tenant context while the read helpers open their own, so calling
them on the same side of a `with` raised *"new row violates row-level security
policy for table invoices"*. Both were silently fine on SQLite, which has
neither partitions nor RLS.

⚠ **NOT SEEN IN A BROWSER, AND THAT IS A REAL GAP RATHER THAN A FORMALITY**
(hard-won law 6). The shared `sbh` database holds one tenant and no portal
customer with 1,100 readings, so there is no list to page through; showing one
would mean seeding several thousand rows into a database seven lanes are working
against. jsdom does no layout, so what is proved here is **which request goes out
and what the footer SAYS** — never how the footer looks. The layout is unchanged
on every screen (same shared `ListPager`, same `MiniTable`, no new class
anywhere), which is the only reason that gap is acceptable to leave open.

⚠ **AND A FAILURE THAT WAS NOT A FAILURE, RECORDED BECAUSE IT WILL HAPPEN AGAIN.**
A 14-minute suite run reported `test_cpb_09_readings_next_read.py::test_cpb09_tc5`
red, on `inspect.getsource(selectors.account_readings)` returning the single line
`        point`. It is not a regression: **the file was edited WHILE the run was
in flight**, so `linecache` re-read a `selectors.py` whose line numbers no longer
matched the loaded code object. Re-run on the settled tree: **8 passed.** A
source-inspecting test cannot survive its subject moving under it, and a long run
beside a live editor is exactly where that happens.

### 12 · THE EIGHT ACCESSIBILITY QUESTIONS (`22-product-maintenance-process.md` §6)

They apply because every screen here is customer-facing. Answered against what
changed, which is the toolbar, the footer and the tab picker:

1. **Keyboard** — every new control is the shared kit's: `ListPager`'s buttons
   and select, `SegmentedChoice`, `TextInput`. No new focusable element and no
   `tabIndex` anywhere in the diff.
2. **Accessible name** — the search box keeps its `sr-only` label (a placeholder
   disappears the moment somebody types, which is exactly when a screen-reader
   user needs to know what the field is); the pager's arrows keep
   `aria-label={t("table.pager.prev|next")}`.
3. **State announced** — sortable headings keep `aria-sort`, and it now reads the
   SERVER's sort rather than a local one, so what is announced is what the rows
   are actually ordered by.
4. **Focus on change** — a page turn replaces rows under a button that stays
   mounted; focus is not moved or lost. The rows deliberately stay on screen
   while the next page is in flight rather than being replaced by a spinner,
   which would blow focus away on every page turn.
5. **Colour alone** — nothing here uses colour to carry meaning; `data-list-busy`
   is a hook, not a visual state.
6. **Contrast / target size** — unchanged: no class in the diff, and the phone
   card stacks gained the same footer the table has had.
7. **Text alternatives** — no new image or icon.
8. **Reduced motion** — nothing animates.

The one that changed a real answer is (4), and it is why `busy` exists instead of
a loading card.

### 13 · A GATE THAT COULD NOT SEE ITS OWN SUBJECT — TWO BLIND SPOTS, ONE ROOT CAUSE

`G105`'s furniture check asks *"does a list have a search box and a footer"*,
and it read ONE spelling of each. It went red on this lane, so it was looked at
rather than scrolled past — and two of the four findings were already there.
**Dated by running `furniture()` at the branch tip, not asserted** (`DEF-CWP-4187`).

* **`CWP-041 search` — WRONG, AND WRONG SINCE 2026-09-11.** `DEF-CWP-4879` moved
  that screen's search box OUT of the table, because the table lives inside
  `max-md:hidden` and a box drawn by it does not exist on a phone at all. The
  gate tested `"search=" in text`, so a real, visible, working search box has
  been reported as MISSING for eight days.
* **`CWP-037 footer` — WRONG BECAUSE OF A LINE BREAK.**
  `08-screen-layouts.md` is hand-wrapped prose, and that entry's own words are
  *"Status (StatusChip …), no footer → InfoBar"* — with the wrap falling
  between `no` and `footer`. The gate tested `"no footer" in body`, so the
  drawing said exactly what the screen does and the gate could not read it. It
  reported that screen's footer as wrong over the one part of it that is right.

**And this lane would have added two more**, because the server window carries
the placeholder as `search: { placeholder` rather than as a `search=` prop.

**Filed as `DEF-CWP-5785` before the fix was pushed, and all three are one root
cause: a check that knows one idiom reports zero over the ones it cannot see** — hard-won law 7's *reporting zero over a scope it
silently excludes*, and `G13`'s 2026-08-15 widening in another family. The gate
now knows the three spellings by name, matches the drawing's phrases over
UNWRAPPED text, and **its self-test proves each new branch BOTH ways**: every
idiom must be seen, a file with none of them must still be reported, a wrapped
`no footer` must be read, and unwrapping must not turn the footer check off. A
widening that only ever answers *yes* is a check that cannot fail, which is
worse than the blind spot it replaced.

⚠ **AND CLEARING THOSE TWO LET THE RATCHET COLLECT A DEBT IT HAD ALREADY BEEN
PAID.** `G105` reports NEW findings before PAID ones, so four baselined
divergences that were **already composed at the tip** — `CWP-011 Card`,
`CWP-060 Card`, `CWP-066 KpiRow`, `CWP-066 KpiTile`, none of them this lane's —
had been standing behind two false findings. They are deleted from
`g105_layout_baseline.txt`, which is the gate's own instruction and a shrink of
a list that may only ever shrink. `G105` now reads **PASS** through `run()`,
which is the entry point `run_gates` uses (`DEF-GOV-3733`).

### 14 · WHY THIS DOES NOT GO TO THE PRODUCT OWNER, STATED RATHER THAN ASSUMED

This is MAINTENANCE (`22-product-maintenance-process.md`): a customer can read
their bills today, so the question is whether the fix changes **what a user can
DO or was PROMISED** — and the process says that is the only thing that returns
to the PO.

**It does not.** Every row is still reachable; what changed is that a customer
presses `›` for the fifty-first instead of scrolling to it, and `NFR-3` —
universal server pagination — is signed law rather than a choice this lane made.
Nothing here touches a 🔒 sensitive path (no RLS policy, no rating math, no
idempotency key, no ledger posting, no money rounding, no migration, no webhook
key), no ❄️ FROZEN B4/B5 figure moves, and no file is flagged
`HUMAN-REVIEW-PENDING` — so there is no row owed in
`09-human-review-ledger.md`. Law 13's list of what legitimately reaches the PO
has three entries and this is none of them.

**The three judgment calls this lane made are ours to make and are recorded
above rather than asked about:** the one-character search minimum (§9), the
`data-money-card` index's new reference point (a test hook, not a customer
fact), and leaving `CWP-037` equipment unpaged (§4).

**The reporter of `DEF-CWP-5747` is an AI lane, 2026-09-18, and the build to
look in is **`2.308.3`**, visible on screen through the shared version read.
(This line said `2.307.x` for the twelve minutes between the code commit and
this correction: two siblings shipped 2.308.0 and 2.308.1 while the record was
being written, and `allocate.py` — which asks the REMOTE and not this checkout —
is the only reason the number the register carries is the number that shipped.)

### 15 · TWO PICKERS THAT ARE NOT LISTS, AND HAD TO SAY SO

A paged wrapper serves fifty by default, and **two callers are not screens with
a footer**: `AddAccountPage`'s account rail and `AskAQuestion`'s *which bill is
your question about* `SelectInput`. There is no control a customer could press
to reach a second page, so a default page would silently hide every bill older
than the fiftieth from somebody asking a question about exactly that bill.

Both now name `per: 1000` — the top of the IS-2 vocabulary — rather than
accepting a page they cannot turn, and each says so at its call site. **This is
the shape to look for when the next wrapper gains a page:** a list has a footer
and a picker does not, and the compiler cannot tell them apart.

### 16 · THE GATES, AND THE ONE NUMBER THAT MATTERS

**Tier 1: 11 PASS / 7 FAIL / 0 SKIP**, and — against this lane's own recorded
run — *"0 newly failing, 0 newly fixed, 0 still red with different findings, 18
unchanged"*. The seven are the branch's standing set and none names a file or an
id from this commit.

⚠ **A FULL RUN WAS STARTED AND THEN STOPPED, ON PURPOSE.** Three lanes were
independently computing the same 129-gate answer on a four-core box at load 77,
which is a measurement nobody needs three of. It was killed BY PID rather than
by pattern (`DEF-GOV-5758`: a `pkill -f` over a shared pattern took out sibling
lanes on 2026-09-04), and what it had already produced is in
`10-scripts/gates/last-run.json` — **72 PASS / 50 FAIL**, with every FAIL read
and only two naming this lane's files: `G105`, fixed above, and `G107`, dated to
the tip and untouched here (this diff adds ZERO min-width variants, counted).

⚠ **AND ONE FRONT-END FAILURE WAS A CLOCK, NOT A FAULT.** `Equipment.dom.test.
tsx` timed out at 18.7 s against a 5 s limit during the same load spike — a file
this lane did not touch. Re-run on a quieter box: **29 passed**. A timeout under
load is not a red until it has been re-run, which is the one piece of advice
that stops a busy machine manufacturing false findings.

### 17 · WHAT A FOLLOW-UP LANE NEEDS

`pageSlice` still has three callers and **cannot be deleted yet**:
`RoutesCyclesPage.tsx`/`RoutesCyclesWizards.tsx` are `DEF-MET-5743`'s,
`RejectList.tsx` keeps its by the 2026-09-18 paragraph above, and
`portal/components/listTable.tsx` keeps its for `CWP-037` equipment and
`CWP-046`'s open-requests panel — both of which the drawing gives no footer.

## 2026-09-19 · `DEF-RAT-5774` / `DEF-RAT-5775` — THE RATE SCHEDULE BAND SHOWS THE FIGURES, AND THE SHAPE WAS NEVER OURS TO DECIDE

**PO, 2026-09-19, verbatim:** *"here can we show actual rate prices - when rates
are tiered, seasonal, ToU etc- it is not shown"*. On the Bryant Solar plan the
Usage cell read **`seasonal`** and no price appeared anywhere on the page.

### 1 · THE DECISION, AND WHY IT IS SHORTER THAN THE DEFECT EXPECTED

The defect was filed as a real design choice: *"the blueprint draws no fifth
column, so the shape is a real decision and not an omission"*, citing
`CR-087-p101` §3 and `CR-087-p105` §8, and the code carried the same sentence
in a comment beside the cell. **That premise is false, and it is what held the
PO's ruling of 2026-09-10 half built for nine days.**

Read AS IMAGES, which is what B14 rule 42 requires — rendered from
`05-prototype/SMARTBillHub Plans & Rates Blueprint.pdf` with
`10-scripts/pdf/pdf_render.py`:

| frame | page | the Rate schedule band's columns |
|---|---|---|
| step 8 (`PLN-03`) | **102** | `SERVICE · BASE · USAGE · RATE` |
| the plan's page (`PLN-02` Overview) | **107** | `SERVICE · BASE · USAGE · RATE · CHANGE ALREADY DATED` |

p102's `RATE` column is right-aligned and monospaced and holds
`4.0000 · 6.5000 · 8.0000`, `0.1100 peak · 0.0700 off-peak` and `40%`. **The
figures have had a drawn home all along.** p105 §8's own prose says so in a
clause — *"`SERVICE · BASE · USAGE · RATE · CHANGE ALREADY DATED`"* — which is
the half of the conformance file the defect did not quote.

So there was no frame to invent and nothing to put to the PO. **What we had
built was a `Rate schedule` column NEITHER frame draws, standing in the slot the
drawn `RATE` belongs in.** The fix adds `RATE` after `USAGE` on the shared card,
so both screens gain it at once.

**⚠ THE DRAWN FIGURES WERE NOT COPIED (B14 rule 37).** Every number in those
frames is an illustration. The shape was built — a right-aligned monospaced
column of the schedule's own prices — and the figures come from the tenant's
data. That `$4.0000 · $6.5000 · $8.0000` happens to appear on the running
screen is the seed matching the illustration, not the illustration being built.

### 2 · THE SCHEDULE'S NAME STAYS, AND THAT IS THE ONE JUDGMENT CALL HERE

Matching p102 exactly would mean DELETING the `Rate schedule` column. It stays,
because that cell carries a distinction nothing else on either screen draws:
*no schedule* — the plan prices nothing for this service, which is a publishing
refusal — against *the catalogue page this screen read did not carry the tariff
the plan names*. Those are different facts and only one is a fault. Removing the
column without first deciding where the second absence goes would be tidying
that costs a clerk a real signal, so it is **`OQ-RAT-12470`, OPEN**, with the
case for both answers written out, rather than done quietly here.

The cost is stated: both screens now draw **five** columns where p102 draws four.

### 3 · WHERE THE FIGURES COME FROM, AND WHY THIS IS THE ONE LAWFUL CLIENT-SIDE FORMAT

`ScheduleCard.current_version.structure` already reaches the browser with
`tiers`, `seasons`, `windows`, `capacity`, `demand` and `percent` on it. Nothing
new is served and nothing is computed: **no sum, no scale, no total.**

**A tier or window price is a RATE and rounds like one — four places, zeros
kept** (`OQ-620(a)`, PO 2026-08-27: *"A rate is not money and not a quantity - 4
decimal places"*), and the drawing agrees (`4.0000`, `0.1100`). So this uses
`formatRate`, the formatter `RateSchedulesTab` and `RateScheduleDetail` already
render a tier with — not `formatMoney`'s two places, which would print `$0.11`
for an off-peak kWh and lose the rate. A percentage still displays at two
(`formatPercent(…, "points")`), per hard rule 2.

**⚠ `unit_price` HAS NO `*_display` SIBLING AND MUST NOT BE GIVEN ONE.** The
standing rule on this card is *render the server's string*, and `TierRow`'s own
docstring forbids serving one here, with its reason: a rate carries a CURRENCY,
and currency formatting is the tenant's number format, which lives in the
browser session. Stating this once, here, so the next lane does not read the
`formatRate` call as drift from `BR-RAT-087`.

`previewVersion` and `previewKind` are imported from `RateSchedulesTab` rather
than restated, so the card and the rate-schedules tab cannot classify one
schedule two ways — the same precedence `selectors.schedule_card` applies
server-side.

### 4 · A SECOND DEFECT WAS INSIDE THE FIRST — THE CELL NAMED A NAMESPACE NO CATALOGUE HAS

The Usage cell called `t("rating.schedule.structure." + card.structure)`.
**`rating.schedule.structure.*` does not exist in any of the eleven
catalogues** — `en.json` holds exactly three `rating.schedule.*` keys and all
three are `status.*`. i18next returns a missing key's DEFAULT, and the default
passed here WAS the stored column value, so the cell printed the raw enum, in
English, in all eleven languages, and `tsc`, every test and every gate passed.
**That is the word the PO saw.** The vocabulary the rate screens already ship is
`rating.model.*`; it is used now rather than minting a second set of words for
one fact. Exactly the shape of the `rating.taxes.level.*` miss recorded in
`bandTaxes` two bands down, in the same file, found the same way — by looking at
the screen.

### 5 · `DEF-RAT-5775` — THE BASE TOTAL DROPS *"from the server"*

Step 8 read **`Plan base charge, from the server: $0.00`**. B14 rule 33 puts
RATIONALE — *why the product works this way* — at **ZERO words on screen**. The
figure is the fact. The label is `Plan base charge:` in all eleven catalogues
(three words, rule 33's cap for a label), changed through
`10-scripts/i18n_fanin.py`, the tool that owns those files.

**The reason was true and is kept, in the docstring.** It distinguishes the
SERVER's sum from a browser-side one after `DEF-RAT-5694` and hard rule 2, and a
word count can never catch that phrase coming back because the phrase is short.
`PlanSummaryCard`'s header now carries it, naming the defect, so the next lane
meets the argument before the temptation.

⚠ **The `<p>` that renders it is in `PlanWizard.tsx`, which another lane owns
and this one did not touch.** The whole fix is in the catalogues, which is where
the words live.

### 6 · TWO MORE FINDINGS, FILED RATHER THAN LEFT IN THIS FILE

`DEF-RAT-5801` — **FIXED here.** The row footnote was appended as one more
`<td>` INSIDE the row, so a four-column band rendered five cells under four
`<th>`; `PlanSummaryRow`'s docstring has always said *"One sentence UNDER the
row, spanning it"* and the markup never did. Adding `RATE` made it a sixth cell,
landing the floor past the figures it is about. It is a `Fragment` of two `<tr>`s
now, the second spanning the table.

`DEF-RAT-5800` — **OPEN.** p107 draws the charge code on the `BASE` cell's
SECOND LINE (`8.00 / month` over `BASE-W`), not in a footnote. Left alone,
because moving it is a different change from adding a column and the per-service
floor — which no frame contradicts — shares that footnote.

### 7 · HOW IT WAS PROVED, INCLUDING THE PART THAT CANNOT BE PROVED BY A TEST

Seven vitest cases were **PROVED RED FIRST** against the unmodified file:
`cells[4]` undefined (no column), `expected 'seasonal' to be 'Seasonal'`, and
`expected 'Plan base charge, from the server:' to be 'Plan base charge:'`. The
seasonal and time-of-use cases assert the **WHOLE composed string** against a
fixture whose two seasons carry DIFFERENT ladders — `Summer $5.0000 · $7.0000 ·
Winter $3.0000 · $4.0000` — because *a price appears* passes on a screen showing
one season's prices twice.

**No gate in this repo reads rendered output (law 6), so the card was also
walked in a browser on BOTH screens it feeds.**
`10-scripts/def_rat_5774_plan_rates_walkthrough.mjs` reads each cell and
compares it, digit for digit, with what the API says that schedule holds — so it
cannot pass on a plausible wrong number. It was proved red against a second
worktree built from the tip: **9 problems, exit 1**, including
`the Usage cell still prints the raw enum: "time_of_use"` and
`Plan base charge, from the server: $20.00`. Green on this branch, exit 0.

⚠ **TWO OF ITS CHECKS PASSED ON THE RED BUILD AND WERE REWRITTEN.** One asked
whether *"from the server"* was on a NEW draft's step 8 — a screen that never
draws the label at all (`PlanWizard` draws it only when the plan is SAVED), so
it could only ever pass. It is a `note` now, and part 3 walks a published plan's
edit wizard, where the label is real and where it went red. The other prints a
tick for *"the two screens draw the same columns"*, which is an AGREEMENT check
that passes when both are wrong in the same way — it now says so.

## 2026-09-19 · THE PREMISES IMPORT MAKES AN ACCOUNT NOBODY OWNS — THREE RULINGS

**Reported by the PO, verbatim:** *"User reported when we import premsies ->
provide owner deetails -> in thos ec ases Master Account is not getting
generated - can you check what is the issue?"*

### 1 · WHAT WAS ACTUALLY HAPPENING, REPRODUCED RATHER THAN READ

Seven rows through `extract → transform → validate → load` on **real
PostgreSQL** against the beta tenant, rolled back afterwards (79 premises and 5
owners before and after, 0 import runs left behind).

A complete, correct row — name `Ada Okonkwo`, `person`, an SSN, account type
`residential` — created master account **`AC-2026-00058`** and then left
`premises.owner_id` **NULL**, wrote **no `premises_owners` row**, and put the
operator's name only in the legacy free-text `owner_manager` box. The receipt
said `premises_owner_accounts_created = 2` and was telling the truth: the
account exists. **It is attached to a building with nobody named on it.**

The same file naming an owner **already on file** — `Ridge Property LLC` —
worked completely: owner matched, `premises.owner_id` set,
`premises_owners.master_account_id` written, account created, and the row came
through `staged` rather than `flagged`.

⚠ **SO THE BRANCH THAT WORKS IS THE ONE A FIRST MIGRATION CAN NEVER TAKE.**
`ensure_master_account_for_premises` documents the split deliberately and
honestly: with a typed owner it calls `ensure_owner_master_account`, which
writes the link; with none it creates the account for the ADDRESS and leaves the
party *"for a person to settle on `PRM-04`"*. On the first upload a utility ever
sends, **no owner is on file, so every row takes the second branch** — which is
exactly when the feature is being used for the first time and exactly when
nobody is watching for it.

### 2 · WHY IT COULD NOT HAVE WORKED, AND IT IS NOT A BUG IN THE DECISION

The import will not invent the party because `premises_owners.category_id` is
NOT NULL and **`BR-MET-151` clause 3 forbids reading a category off a name** —
*Whitfield Rentals LLC* is not proof of a landlord. That reasoning is correct
and is not reversed here.

**The gap is that the import never ASKS for the category either.** The tenant
seeds five as an editable Settings lookup — `owner_occupier`, `landlord`,
`property_manager`, `hoa`, `builder` — and `target_columns("premises")` returns
**32 entries of which none is the category** (verified by printing the live
offered set, not by reading the definition). So the loader is refused a guess
and never given the chance to be told.

### 3 · THE RULINGS (PO, 2026-09-19)

**(a) Add the owner category to the shipped template.** PO verbatim: *"Yes add
owner category column in csv template"*. Asking the operator to STATE a category
is not deriving one from a name, so this sits **inside** `BR-MET-151` rather
than against it. Put to them in plain English with the worked case above and the
five category names; no ID was quoted.

**(b) A row whose owner name does not land must be COUNTED on the receipt.** PO
verbatim: *"this is correct"*, on being shown that it is warned at rehearsal and
counted nowhere afterwards. `owner_account_verdict` has five verdicts;
`OWNER_ACCOUNT_NO_OWNER` is **the only one with no counter and no receipt
tile** — the loader's `elif` chain simply has no branch for it. Measured: row 5
of the reproduction was flagged *"This row names no owner."* at stage 3 and then
left `premises_owner_blank = 0` and `premises_with_no_owner = 0`.

⚠ **THIS IS LAW 7'S *REPORTING ZERO OVER A SCOPE IT SILENTLY EXCLUDES*, IN A
RECEIPT RATHER THAN A GATE.** Four owner figures print and one cannot, so a
receipt showing four zeroes reads as a clean run.

**(c) Check the beta for accounts already in this state.** PO verbatim: *"this
is correct"*. Done the same hour — see 4.

### 4 · WHAT THE BETA ALREADY HOLDS — ONE ACCOUNT, AND A SECOND SHAPE

**1 master account exists on the tenant and it is orphaned**, but *not* in the
shape the reproduction predicted: `AC-2026-00051` sits on `P-00059`, 500 Main
St, whose owner **`Ridge Property LLC` DOES exist** — and
`premises_owners.master_account_id` is **NULL**, so the account and the owner
are on the same address and are not joined.

**0 of 5 owners on the tenant carry a master account link.** That is the
declared link `DEF-2902` / `DEF-2903` report missing from every master account
in the product, still missing, now with a number against it.

⚠ **THE BLAST RADIUS IS ONE ROW, AND THAT IS THE ONLY REASON THIS IS CHEAP.**
Found before any fix was written, which is what the maintenance process's
**REPRODUCE → LOCATE → BLAST RADIUS** exists for.

### 5 · HOW THIS SURVIVED EVERY CHECK

`tests/test_cr058_w3_premises_owner_import.py` is **24 passed, 1 skipped** and
was green throughout. It asserts `premises_owner_accounts_created == 1` — which
is TRUE — and its own docstring states *"The import still creates no PARTY"* as
**deliberate**, with a test that goes red if a lane creates one. So the suite
does not merely miss this: **it pins the half of the behaviour that is the
defect**, because when it was written the account was the deliverable and the
link did not exist yet. The 1 skip is the POSTGRES-only law-14 case.

**Nothing asked whether the account had an owner.** That is hard-won law 2's
mirror — built is not wired — one layer below the UI.

### 6 · A CORRECTION TO THIS SESSION'S OWN WORK

`DEF-MET-5803` was filed hours earlier claiming the premises template has **no
owner name column** and one should be added. **That is wrong.** The live offered
set carries `owner` (label *"Owner"*, kind `KIND_OWNER_REF`, the column that
feeds `owner_ref` and every owner rule) and `owner_manager` (*"Owner name
(legacy)"*, provenance). The error came from reading `PREMISES_OWNER_COLUMNS` —
the six VIRTUAL identity columns — and concluding the name was absent; it is
absent from that tuple because it is DERIVED, `Premises.owner` being a real FK.

⚠ **THE LANE ACTING ON IT WAS TOLD MID-FLIGHT, AND THE HABIT IS THE LESSON:**
one command printing the live offered set settled what an afternoon of reading
definitions got backwards. **Where a claim is about what a tool offers, print it
from the running code.** Same shape as the module-segment caveat in `CLAUDE.md`
that named six files and was wrong about all six.
