## 2026-09-22 · PHASE 1's SCREENS WERE WALKED IN A BROWSER FOR THE FIRST TIME, AND TWO OF THEM WERE WRONG IN WAYS NO CHECK COULD SEE (lane P1-C, `2.333.1`)

**Lane P1-B said it plainly when it handed phase 1 over:** *"no gate in this
repo reads rendered output, and I did not click these screens in a browser.
Everything above is tests, types and gates."* Five phase-1 rows had shipped by
then and none of them had been looked at. This is the walk —
`10-scripts/p1c_phase1_browser_walk.mjs`, 26 assertions in Chromium at 1440
against a seeded PostgreSQL — and what it found.

### 1 · TWO OF FOUR ROW ACTIONS WERE OFF THE SIDE OF THE SCREEN (`DEF-PAY-6214`)

`P1.6` added **Move** and **Reapply** to the payments list's actions cell, beside
the two that were already there. Measured in Chromium on `brazosbend` at the
drawing's own 1440:

| control | right edge |
|---|---|
| ✎ Correct reference | 1374 |
| 🏷 Reapply | 1410 |
| ⇄ Move | **1446** |
| ↺ Reverse | **1482** |

The table is **1,214px inside a 1,120px scroller**. So `Move` sat 6px past the
right edge of the window and `Reverse` — the action the whole bulk toolbar was
built for — sat **42px** past it, reachable only by scrolling the table
sideways. At 1280 the scroller is 960 and it is worse.

⚠ **B14 RULE 15 HAS SAID THE ANSWER SINCE IT WAS RATIFIED** — *"Max 2 visible +
`…` overflow"* — **and `G37` counts the `<RowAction`s in that cell into a
variable and never compares it to the cap.** That is hard-won law 7's shape in
a new costume: not a check that cannot fail, but a check that computes the
number and never asks the question. The rule's own status column reads
`ENFORCED`.

⚠ **AND THE BLUEPRINT PUTS THESE TWO IN THE OVERFLOW BY NAME.** §03 frames 2·3f
and 2·3g both give their door as *"The row overflow on 2·1, and 2·2. **2 doors —
there are none today**"*, and 2·1 draws the ACTIONS column as two glyphs and a
`…`. So the fix is the drawing's own: `✎ Correct reference` and `↺ Reverse` stay
on the row — the everyday clerical fix and the money act — and Move and Reapply
move into `RowActionsMore`, where both are still one press away and both keep
their reason when they cannot act (`DEF-PAY-6199`'s check applied to a move
rather than a deletion).

**Proved RED first, and the existing cases could not have caught it:** the four
`moveAndReapply` cases assert the LABEL is in the markup, and `RowMenuAction`
puts the label in the markup too, so all four were green over the broken cell.
The new block counts the buttons BEFORE the overflow marker, and on the old
shape it fails with *"B14 rule 15: max 2 visible: expected 4 to be less than or
equal to 2"*. **After the fix, measured again: the two on the row end at 1374
and 1410, and the overflow's two entries at 1439** — every control inside a
1440 window.

### 2 · THE SCAN CARD GAVE THE WRONG REASON, IN ELEVEN LANGUAGES (`DEF-PAY-6215`)

`P1.19` drew *Scan paper* as the fifth source card, held, *"present and refused,
with its reason"*. On screen it read **"Not switched on yet. Upload a file
instead."** — which is byte-for-byte what SFTP and API say, and a different
fact. SFTP is unbuilt. **The scanner is a keyboard and works today**; what is
missing is the barcode on OUR OWN PRINTED BILL, which is going into the standard
layouts under the PO's ruling of 2026-09-21.

⚠ **THE CARD HAD A KEY OF ITS OWN AND THE KEY HELD THE GENERIC SENTENCE.** Every
check passed: the card has a key, the key resolves, `G32` finds nothing
unresolved, `G15` finds parity, and the copy obeys rule 33. **Nothing asked
whether two keys held one sentence — which is the entire reason a second key
exists.** It now reads *"Our bills carry no barcode yet. Upload a file
instead."* and a case asserts, in five languages, that it is not the generic
one.

### 3 · WHAT THE WALK PROVED WORKING, BECAUSE THAT IS HALF OF WHY IT EXISTS

**The Imports tab opens and the runner runs on it.** A real store file —
`ruiz.csv`, five rows with the store's own column names — was dropped through the
one door on 4·1 and carried to stage 4, and the run came back on the list as
`IMP-260922-01 · ruiz.csv · 09/22/2026 15:56 · dana@… · 5 · 0 · 5 · Checked`,
with `🔧 Fix the rejected rows` offered and **no rollback control**, which is
`P1.5`'s rule reaching the screen.

**And `P1.8`'s outcome sentence was read off the product, on the drawn case.**
The seed has no ineligible payment, so one was made the way a clerk would make
it — by reversing a payment through its own row action — and then three rows were
ticked including the reversing one:

> `3 selected · $410.08 · 2 can be reversed · 1 cannot · Reverse 2 · Refund 2 ·
> Clear selection`

and the confirm: *Reverse 2 payments* · *2 of 3 will be reversed. 1 skipped.* ·
three rows, the reversing one marked *This row is already a reversal.* ·
**$1,069.86 goes back to 2 accounts. 2 bills re-open.** — `659.78 + 410.08`, the
two eligible rows, over the two accounts and the two bills they met.

⚠ **THE TWO MONEY FIGURES ON THAT SCREEN DIFFER AND BOTH ARE RIGHT.** The bar
says `$410.08` because `POST /payments/selection-total` applies CS-35's signed
rule — the day's CASH, which nets the reversing row's `−$659.78` — and the
consequence says `$1,069.86` because that is what goes back to customers. A
reader meeting them side by side needs that sentence, which is why it is here.

### 4 · ONE THING THE DRAWING ASKS FOR THAT THE ENDPOINT CANNOT HONOUR

4·1 draws a search box — *"Search file, label or reference…"* — on the Imports
toolbar. `GET /imports` serves no `q`, and `TableConfig.searchFields` absent is
what DRAWS no search box, which is `BR-SHL-010`'s own posture: a capability
absent here is not drawn. **All four imports tabs are the same and always have
been**, so this is recorded rather than filed — the honest fix is a `q` on the
endpoint, not a box that does nothing.

## 2026-09-23 — ONE PATH PER CAPABILITY: THE OLD PAYMENTS IMPORT PIPELINE IS RETIRED, AND THE TWO REMAINING BLOCKERS ARE WORK RATHER THAN VETOES

**PO ruling, verbatim:** *"we can not have two path for 1 capabilities wew will
confuse user"*, said on being told `P1.9` was held for three reasons — and then
*"do it"*.

**THIS IS THE THIRD TIME THE PO HAS RULED ON `P1.9`** (*"(a) Delete it if
possible"*, then *"we should not use second machine"*, now this), and the third
statement is the one that names the PRINCIPLE rather than the instance: **a
capability has one path, because two paths are a thing a clerk has to learn
twice.** That is broader than the import pipeline and should be read as such.

⚠ **THE LANE REPORTING THE BLOCKERS WAS RIGHT TO REPORT THEM AND THIS SESSION
WAS WRONG TO PRESENT THEM AS A VERDICT.** *"If possible"* asked for the obstacles
to be found, not for a decision to be taken on the strength of them. Three were
found; **one of the three was false** (see below); the other two are ordinary
work with no rule against them. Reporting *"held"* where the honest answer was
*"held pending this list"* put a lane's findings in the place of a ruling the PO
had already made.

### THE BLOCKER THAT WAS FALSE, AND WHY IT IS RECORDED RATHER THAN QUIETLY DROPPED

It was stated as: *"deleting the old pipeline would delete the only provenance
this product has, because nothing links a payment back to the run that created
it."* **Measured: `import_run_rows` carries `created_record_id` — its own comment
reads *"what it made, for rollback"* — every row carries `run_id`, and
`_load_payments_rows` SETS IT** (`apps/metering/import_runs.py:10856), exactly as
the accounts and parts loaders do. **Every payment imported through the NEW path
already records which run made it.**

**`DEF-PAY-6213` is a missing READ, not a missing link.** ⚠ **A claim of ABSENCE
needs the same evidence as a claim of presence, and it is cheaper to check.** This
one was generalised from an honest measurement of the SCREEN to a false statement
about the SCHEMA, and then repeated to the PO as a reason not to do a thing they
had ruled twice.

### WHAT REMAINS, AND IT IS ALL ORDINARY

| | |
|---|---|
| Serve the run link and the source on the payments list | `DEF-PAY-6212`, `DEF-PAY-6213` — the data is already stored |
| Repoint four server callers | two `10-scripts/render-checks` fixture seeders, a PostgreSQL runbook test, and the runbooks module's published selector with three runbook definitions naming the matcher's ladder |
| Switch on `JPAYLOCKBOX` | once the two above land |
| Delete `payment_import.py`, its six endpoints and the `include` | `payment_import_api.py:269-274`, `api.py:1766` |

⚠ **`P1.4` IS UNTOUCHED AND IS THE TRAP.** `payment_import_batches` and
`payment_import_rows` are **KEPT**. They hold what the OLD path imported, and
retiring the code that wrote them does not touch that history. **Retiring a
pipeline is not deleting a record**, and a lane reading this entry as licence to
drop those tables has misread it.

⚠ **AND THE TWO FIXTURE SEEDERS ARE HARD-WON LAW 6's OWN MACHINERY.** They seed
the money for **every rendered-output check this repository has**, and rendered
output is the only thing that has ever found nine defects in a day here — it
found five more across 2026-09-22 alone, after every test, type check and gate
had passed over them. **Repointing them is proved by RUNNING those checks, not
by reading the diff.**

## 2026-09-23 — `P1.9`: SOURCE AND BATCH ARE BUILT, AND THE DELETION IS **HELD** BECAUSE THE OLD PIPELINE CAN MATCH A BILL NUMBER AND THE NEW ONE CANNOT (lane ONEPATH)

**The ruling is not in question and is not re-asked.** PO, verbatim: *"we can not
have two path for 1 capabilities wew will confuse user"*, then *"do it"*. This row
is what the enumeration the ruling's own briefing asked for actually found.

### 1 · WHAT IS BUILT AND WORKING — `2.334.0`

**A clerk can now see where every payment came from and which batch it belongs
to.** The payments list draws the blueprint's §03 screen 2·1 **Source** column —
*Counter · Digital · Post* — with its filter, and a **Batch** column carrying the
code a clerk reads: an imported payment shows the number of the run that made it,
a banked one shows its deposit batch's `DEP-` code.

**Neither needed a schema change and both facts were already in the database.**
`payments/0030` landed `origin` on 2026-09-22 and no reader followed it
(`DEF-PAY-6212`). `import_run_rows.created_record_id` has named the payment each
imported row created since the eighth import target landed (`DEF-PAY-6213`).
metering now publishes `created_record_runs(target, ids)` — in bulk, one `IN` per
page — and payments reads it through a new `metering_seam.py` resolved by name,
which is the idiom `billing_seam` already uses. **No cross-module ORM read, in
either direction.**

⚠ **AND ONE MORE COMMENT WAS FOUND TO BE FALSE ON THE WAY THROUGH
(`DEF-PAY-6216`).** The list read hardcoded `deposit_batch_id` to null under a
comment reading *"nothing writes the column"* — and `reconciliation.
cut_deposit_batches` has written it on every member payment since bank rec
shipped. That is hard-won law 1 again, and the screen half of `DEF-2353` closes
with this commit: the Batch column serves the batch's own CODE, never its uuid
(B14 rule 31). The uuid stays unserved, deliberately.

### 2 · ⚠⚠ THE DELETION IS **HELD**, AND THIS IS THE `DEF-PAY-6199` SHAPE AGAIN

**`DEF-PAY-6217`. The old pipeline's match ladder has THREE rungs and the new
one has TWO. The rung that is missing is the BILL NUMBER.**

| | old `payment_import._match_row` | new `import_writer.match_account` |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | the account number the file names | the account number the file names |
| 2 | **the BILL number the file names → CLEAN, and it names the bill** | **— nothing** |
| 3 | the payer's name → a SUGGESTION, never a commit | the payer's name → a SUGGESTION, never a commit |

**Worked, on the old path's own tested case.** A remittance row reading
`,BL-0141,,292.87,2026-08-20,10241` — no account number, just the bill number the
customer tore off their stub — matches **CLEAN** today, finds the account, and
posts. `test_cr059_cs2_payment_import.py::test_cs2__the_invoice_number_matches_clean_and_names_the_bill`
has asserted exactly that since CR-059. **On the new path the same row has no
account number and no payer name, so it is a REVIEW and the writer refuses it** —
and the bill column is not even offered: the old parser takes seven columns
including `invoice_ref` (aliases `invoice`, `bill`, `bill no`, `bill number`) and
the new target takes **six**, with no bill column at all.

⚠ **AND THE NEW TARGET'S OWN COMMENT CLAIMS THE OPPOSITE, IN AS MANY WORDS:**
*"so a file the retiring pipeline accepted is a file this target accepts — a
migration that silently narrowed what a utility could upload would be the worst
possible way to retire a pipeline."* **For a bill-number file that sentence is
false.** Hard-won law 1: a comment claiming a guarantee is not the guarantee.

⚠ **THE JUSTIFICATION IN THE NEW CODE ANSWERS A QUESTION THE OLD PATH HAD
ALREADY ANSWERED THE SAME WAY, WHICH IS WHY THE RUNG WENT WITHOUT ANYBODY
DECIDING TO DROP IT.** `match_account` argues that a bill reference must stay
PROVENANCE and never become an allocation instruction. **The old path agrees and
says so at length** — `_record_row`'s docstring: *"THE BILL THE FILE NAMED IS NOT
PASSED AS AN ALLOCATION TARGET … `invoice_id` stays on the staged row as
PROVENANCE"*. It used the bill number to find **which customer's money this is**,
and the allocator then ran its ordinary `BR-PAY-010` course. So the two are not
in conflict about allocation at all, and the rung that was lost had nothing to do
with it.

**Is it reachable today?** Not by a clerk — nothing in the front end calls the six
endpoints, measured three times now. It is reachable through the published API
(`openapi/schema.json`), which is a contract a customer can read. **That is a
narrower loss than `P1.10`'s and it is the same class**: there, deleting an
orphan would have taken the only Reject and Reverse doors in the product with it,
and both suites were green throughout. Here both suites are green too — the old
path's bill-number case passes and the new path simply has no such case, because
nothing in this repository compares two paths' capabilities.

**So the deletion stops here and goes to the PO**, and the question is one only
they can answer because it is about what a utility's bank and stores actually
send: *does any utility we are onboarding send us a remittance file that names
the BILL and not the ACCOUNT?* Three answers and each is cheap:
**(a)** no — then the rung goes with the pipeline and `DEF-PAY-6217` closes as
*not wanted*; **(b)** yes — then the new target gains a seventh column and a
third rung before anything is deleted; **(c)** unsure — then the pipeline stays
one more cycle and the six endpoints are marked deprecated in the schema rather
than removed.

### 3 · TWO SMALLER DIFFERENCES, FILED RATHER THAN LEFT IN PROSE

⚠ **`DEF-PAY-6218` — PLACING A STUCK ROW ON AN ACCOUNT LOSES ITS REASON.** The old
`assign_row_account` REFUSES an empty reason and writes a money-audit row naming
who decided and why; CS-2's own sentence is *"it is the only record of why this
money was judged to be this customer's, since after the commit the payment itself
carries no trace of having been a guess."* The new path's equivalent is the shared
runner's `fix_row`, which patches the account cell and re-validates — the ACT
survives, the RECORD does not. A grep for the capability finds one on each side,
which is why nothing saw it.

**And `discard_batch` has no equivalent act.** The old path records *"a clerk put
this file down"* with a reason and an audit row; on the new path a clerk simply
stops, and the run sits at `extracted` for ever. **Not filed as a defect** — no
capability is lost, a person can always walk away — but it is a real difference
and the next lane should know it is a choice rather than an oversight.

### 4 · WHAT THIS LANE DID **NOT** DO, AND WHY

| | |
|---|---|
| **Repoint the four server callers** | Held with the deletion. They exist to be repointed *before* the old machine goes; repointing them while it stays is churn on hard-won law 6's own fixture seeder for no gain. ⚠ **AND THE COUNT IS THREE, NOT FOUR** — `rbs_q_seed_sync.py` names `payment_import` only in a COMMENT and calls nothing. The live callers are `rbs_p_seed_money.py:241`, `test_rbs_money_runbooks_pg.py:120` and `runbooks/seams/payments_seam.py:104` |
| **Delete `payment_import.py`, its six endpoints and the include** | Held — §2 |
| **Activate `JPAYLOCKBOX`** | Its two blockers ARE closed and the journey says so now, with two new checks (**M** Source on screen, **N** the run's number on screen). **The spec is still absent and that is deliberate**: this walk has not been RUN, it needs a booted stack and a real PostgreSQL for checks **B** and **G**, and *a journey first seen green is a journey nobody has proved* |

⚠ **`P1.4` IS UNTOUCHED THROUGHOUT.** `payment_import_batches` and
`payment_import_rows` keep every row. Nothing in this lane reads, writes or drops
them.

## 2026-09-23 · `P3.19` — "PAPER AT THE WINDOW" IS A **RENDER**, NOT A SEND, AND THE PRODUCT ALREADY FORBIDS THE OTHER READING (lane P3-BACK, `CR-137-BRC07`)
**The task, verbatim from the blueprint's phase-3 table (p020):** *"Notifications:
paper at the window — the queue is asynchronous; a counter needs a receipt in hand
now."* Outcome: *"A counter customer leaves with paper."* **The drawing does not
say how**, which is why this is a decision-log row and not a build note.
### 1 · THE OBVIOUS BUILD IS FORBIDDEN BY SIGNED LAW, AND IT IS WORTH QUOTING
`04-docs/01-spec/11-api-contracts.md` Addendum r2 §4: **"no synchronous send
endpoint anywhere (queue only, `BR-NOT-005`)"**. `apps/notifications/api.py` states
it in capitals in its own module docstring — *"THERE IS NO SEND ENDPOINT AND THERE
MUST NEVER BE ONE … minting one is a gate failure."* So a
`POST /payments/{id}/receipt/print-now` that dispatched anything was never on the
table, and no lane may quietly reinterpret that.
### 2 · SO WHAT DOES *SYNCHRONOUS* MEAN AT A COUNTER? **RENDERED, NOT SENT.**
Walked through, because the answer is in the moment rather than in the code:
1. **The customer is standing there.** There is no address to resolve, no provider
   to hand off to and no delivery to record — the delivery is a person taking a
   piece of paper. The entire apparatus a send endpoint exists to drive is
   inapplicable, which is why refusing to mint one costs nothing here.
2. **The document already exists.** `BR-NOT-024`'s print floor puts a `pdf_print`
   row on every recorded payment — the blueprint's own p050 says so: *"every
   recorded payment queues one on email and text, with a printed floor so a
   utility that switches every electronic channel off still gets paper."* The
   receipt is not missing. It is queued, PINNED to a template version, and stamped
   with its figures (`render_context`, `DEF-PAY-4409`).
3. **What is missing is a way to LOOK at it.** The queue is emptied by a job on its
   own clock and nothing dispatches in this release at all (`BR-NOT-013`). A clerk
   cannot wait for that with a customer at the window.
**So `P3.19` is `GET /payments/{id}/receipt/document`:** it renders the row that is
already there, through notifications' own `rendering.render_for_dispatch`, from the
version PINNED on it (`BR-BIL-026` — there is no "latest" path and re-rendering
against today's wording is the substitution that rule forbids). **It queues
nothing, sends nothing and dispatches nothing.** The queued row keeps its place and
the print job will still take it; a counter reprint is not a second delivery, it is
the same document read early.
⚠ **AND THE TEST ASSERTS THAT BY COUNTING, NOT BY BELIEVING IT.**
`test_the_counter_receipt_is_a_read_and_queues_nothing` counts the payment's queue
rows before and after the call and requires the number not to move — *"it is only a
read"* is a claim, and hard-won law 7 asks what would make the check pass wrongly.
### 3 · IT IS TEXT, NOT A PDF, AND THAT IS THE REPO'S STANDING POSITION
`apps/notifications/rendering.py` exception (2), unchanged since 2026-08-15:
*"NO PDF. `OQ-149` closed 2026-08-12 … no page-rendering library is in the image;
printable classes render their TEXT body here."* The browser's own print dialog is
what puts it on paper. Nothing here re-opens that.
### 4 · HARD RULE 7 APPLIES, AND THE ROW IS WRITTEN
Handing a customer a document that states what they paid is a money act in every
sense that matters six weeks later, so the read writes `payment.receipt_printed`
naming who printed it and which copy they were looking at.
`apps/notifications/unsent_preview.preview` sets the precedent: a read that
discloses a document's contents writes its own trail.
### 5 · WHAT THIS DOES **NOT** DECIDE
**It does not give the counter a printer.** Phase 2 (`CR-136-BRC07`) is building the
counter screens; this is the capability they call, and the button, the print
stylesheet and the moment it fires are theirs. Built now rather than with them
because `P3.19`'s value lands with phase 2 and its *absence* would otherwise be
discovered at a window.
## 2026-09-23 · `P3.2` — CANCEL WRITES A **REVERSING ROW** AND **NO JOURNAL LINE**, AND BOTH HALVES WERE MEASURED RATHER THAN CHOSEN (lane P3-BACK, `CR-137-BRC07`)
`POST /payments/{id}/cancel` is *"the only genuinely missing logic in the module"*.
The blueprint's act table (p050) gives Cancel four consequences — **a reversing
row; the original stands · a reversing pair · the bill re-opens · the counter total
drops**. Three are built. The second is not, and this records why, with the figure.
### 1 · WHY A REVERSING ROW AT ALL, WHEN A STATUS MOVE ALREADY SAYS IT
The cheapest build is `status: processing → cancelled` and nothing else — and the
database has expected exactly that since 2026-08-11. `payments/0002`'s own DELETE
refusal reads *"Cancel on a processing payment is a status move, not a removal"*,
and `trg_payment_immutable` already permits `status` on a processing row, so the
allow list does not move (`P3.8`, and `payments/0014` is untouched).
**But the day's cash total is netted by ROWS, not filtered by STATUS.**
`selectors.payments_totals` sums every `type='payment'` row the filter matched and
reads no status at all — deliberately, and documented there: a reversed payment
nets against its own reversing row. **Worked, on the drawing's own figure:** a
$158.10 counter payment cancelled by a status move alone would leave **$158.10**
sitting in the day's takings and the drawer would be short by exactly that. So
cancel writes the negative row, the same mechanism a bounce already uses, and
*"the counter total drops"* becomes true by arithmetic rather than by a second
rule. The original keeps its row, its number and its amount; hard rule 4 is
satisfied rather than circumvented.
### 2 · WHY NO LEDGER POSTING — AND THIS IS A MEASUREMENT, NOT A PREFERENCE
`services.record_payment` returns **before** `_allocate_and_post` when
`cleared_at is None`, and says so on every such result: *"the payment carries no
clearing date, so it is `processing`: the money has not arrived. It meets no bill
and posts nothing — US-LED-001's contract row is 'Payment CLEARED → DR cash / CR
AR'."*
**So a processing payment has no allocations and a NULL `journal_entry_id`.** There
is nothing for the ledger to mirror. Composing a compensating entry here would be
inventing a posting for money that never reached the books, and hard rule 5 puts
journal lines in the ledger posting service's hands alone. The result carries
`no_entry_to_reverse_payment_never_posted` and `no_bill_reopened_payment_met_none`
on every call, so a screen states it rather than implying a bill moved.
⚠ **AND THE SERVICE REFUSES A PROCESSING ROW THAT SOMEHOW CARRIES EITHER.**
`refusal_for` returns `cancel_refused_money_already_posted` when a `processing`
payment names a journal entry or an allocation — measured, not assumed, because
cancelling one would leave a bill closed against money nobody will receive.
### 3 · THE DRAWING CONTRADICTS ITSELF HERE, AND B14 RULE 37 IS WHAT SETTLES IT
p044 says Cancel is *"for money that never cleared"*; p043 draws the Cancel modal
over `PMT-2609-000418`, which p035 draws as **Cleared**, with a clearing date and a
bill it paid off, and whose consequence box only a cleared payment could produce.
Two frames of one blueprint drawing the same fact differently is rule 37's own
case: **build the shape they agree on.** They agree on the processing case, the
task board's `P3.13` agrees (*"refused on `cleared` and the clerk is pointed at
Reverse"*), and `US-PAY-004` §1 has said *"Cancel only while processing"* since it
was signed.
**What is NOT settled is the counter**, and that is `OQ-PAY-12603`, raised rather
than decided: a cash payment at a window is `cleared` the same minute, so
*"I just took that from the wrong person"* reaches **Reverse** — which is
`SystemAdminOnly` under `BR-PAY-1070`, so in a two-person utility the clerk who
made the mistake cannot fix it.
### 4 · IDEMPOTENCY IS THE STATUS, NOT A KEY (hard rule 6)
`reversal_api` requires an `idempotency_key`; this door requires none, and the
difference is real rather than an inconsistency. **A reversal may lawfully happen
twice in parts (`BR-PAY-884`); a cancel may not happen twice at all.** So the
STATUS is the guard: a second click finds the payment already `cancelled` and gets
a **200** with the first cancel and `created: false` — never a red 409 for a button
that worked. The lost race is closed by `SELECT … FOR UPDATE` before the status is
read and by `trg_payment_immutable` underneath it, which refuses a second UPDATE
because `OLD.status` is no longer `processing`. ⚠ The lock is a no-op on SQLite,
where the whole default suite runs (hard-won law 14), so the concurrent case is
proved on real PostgreSQL and the SQLite case is marked as what it is.
### 5 · THE CANCEL REASON HAS NO COLUMN, AND NOTHING CALLS THE TRAIL PERMANENT
The reason is required, comes from a fixed vocabulary (`wrong_account ·
wrong_amount · duplicate · not_taken`) and is deliberately **not** folded into
`models.REVERSAL_REASONS` — `ck_payments_reversal_reason` is written against the
four BOUNCE reasons and conflating the two vocabularies is the exact confusion this
phase exists to undo. The clerk's free-text note is durable on the reversing row's
`memo`; the reason CODE lives in `audit_log`, which is pruned like every other row
(PO 2026-09-23, `OQ-1340`). Whether it deserves a column is `OQ-PAY-12604`. **No
screen, document or docstring calls this path a permanent record** — that
prohibition is permanent, not provisional (`CR-137-BRC07` §1.2).
## 2026-09-23 · `git ls-tree … | grep 'pdf$'` CANNOT SEE A BLUEPRINT WITH AN EM DASH IN ITS NAME, AND IT TOLD TWO PEOPLE A FILE WAS MISSING ON ONE DAY
**CLAUDE.md prescribes this command by name** for the hazard it already records —
*"Check for a blueprint BEFORE reading r10 for any screen —
`git ls-tree -r --name-only <ref> | grep -i 'pdf$'` across the refs, not just
yours."* **It has a blind spot, and it is not a rare one.**
**git QUOTES a path containing a byte outside ASCII**, so
`05-prototype/03 SMARTBillHub — Meter Reads blueprint.pdf` is printed as
    "05-prototype/03 SMARTBillHub \342\200\224 Meter Reads blueprint.pdf"
**That line ends in a double quote, not in `pdf`,** so `grep 'pdf$'` drops it —
silently, with a zero exit status and a perfectly plausible listing of the eight
files it *can* see. **On 2026-09-23 it reported the Meter Reads blueprint absent
from `claude/laughing-thompson-kpmwih` to two readers independently**: the
`CR-137` P3-BACK lane, which then went looking for the payments blueprint on
other refs, and the coordinator, who recorded the Meter Reads file as still
missing when it has been on the branch all along — **4,779,186 bytes, readable
with `git cat-file` today.**
**THE FIX IS ONE FLAG:** `git -c core.quotePath=false ls-tree -r --name-only <ref> | grep -i 'pdf$'`.
⚠ **AND THE GENERAL SHAPE IS THIS REPOSITORY'S OWN, WHICH IS WHY IT IS WORTH A
ROW RATHER THAN A FOOTNOTE.** It is hard-won law 7's *reporting zero over a scope
it silently excludes*: the command is not lying, it is answering truthfully about
everything it can see, and **a declared blind spot with no number attached is
indistinguishable from an empty one.** The cost was real — a lane read a drawing
from a second branch and filed a defect against an absence that was half
imaginary.
**`DEF-PAY-6230`'s own subject WAS real** — `06 Payments Page Blueprint.pdf`
genuinely was not on the branch, and it is now, at `da07c7f8d`. ⚠ **That commit's
message cites the row by its PRE-RENUMBER id, `DEF-PAY-6222`, which a sibling
lane had already pushed as `DEF-LED-6222`** — so a reader following the commit
message lands on a ledger defect. The row is `DEF-PAY-6230`. ⚠ **IT TOOK FOUR NUMBERS TO GET THERE** — 6222, then 6226, then 6227/6228, each taken by a sibling while this lane worked, and every lane's arithmetic right every time. `allocate.py` reads the PUSHED world and **cannot reserve**; the gap between reading a maximum and pushing a row is where the collision lives, and nine lanes are pushing here. What finally worked is a LOOP with nothing in it: re-derive the register from the pinned tip, read the maximum out of THAT file, number from it, push immediately, and start again on a refusal. It landed first time.; this sentence is the
only thing that joins the two, which is `DEF-2804`'s shape and is why it is here
rather than left to be inferred. The Meter Reads
half of that story is this row's correction.

## 2026-09-23 — THE WRITE-OFF QUEUE'S DRAWING STATES A RULE THIS PRODUCT DOES NOT HAVE (B14 rule 41, needs a PO ruling)

`CR-138-BRC07` `P4.9`, screen **7·3b Write-offs**, blueprint p086.

**The drawing puts two sentences on the approval queue:** *"A second person
decides."* with *"You cannot approve one you asked for."* under it, and a third
row whose action cell reads *"Yours — someone else decides"* instead of the
Approve and Refuse buttons the other two rows carry.

**`BR-PAY-037` is CONFIRMED and says the opposite, in terms:** *"the SAME user
holding the approver role MAY initiate AND approve in v1 — both acts recorded
distinctly; enforced separation-of-duties = v2."* The control that exists is a
ROLE control, not a person control: approving is `@require_role(SYSTEM_ADMIN)`
**in the service**, so a Billing Clerk cannot sign their own request and an
Admin can. `P4.24` on this same CR regressed all three halves of that and put
`BR-PAY-037` in the failure message *"so nobody 'fixes' the product into
breaking a signed rule"*.

**So this is B14 rule 41's one escalation clause** — *"the only thing that
reaches the PO is a drawing that contradicts a signed rule"* — and it reached
the PO by being written here rather than by being built.

**WHAT WAS BUILT, AND WHY THAT LINE:** the queue draws *your request* beside a
row the viewer raised — a WARNING that makes a self-approval deliberate, which
is what `WriteOffQueueTable` has always done and what its own comment already
said (*"BR-PAY-037 — this is a WARNING, never a block"*). The two sentences and
the disabled third row are **not** built, because building them would put a
separation-of-duties rule on screen that neither the service nor the signed rule
enforces — and a clerk who reads *"you cannot"* and then finds that they can is
worse served than one who was never told.

**WHAT THE PO HAS TO DECIDE**, in plain words and with the figure that matters:
*today an Admin who asks for a **$1,202.40** write-off can approve it
themselves, and both acts are recorded separately. The drawing says they should
not be able to. Do we (a) keep v1 as signed and redraw the two sentences, or (b)
move enforced separation-of-duties forward from v2, which stops an Admin
approving their own request?* **It is a rule change either way**, so it is not
ours to decide (hard-won law 13's short list: a ruling that collides with a
signed rule).

**Until it is ruled, `BR-PAY-037` stands and the screen matches it.**

## 2026-09-23 — `P2.10`/`P2.11`: FINANCE → DEPOSITS WAS OVER-INCLUDING, NOT UNDER-INCLUDING; AND THE UNCLOSED-TILL NOTICE FIRES ON *STILL OPEN* RATHER THAN ON *NOT COUNTED*

**Lanes P2-WIRE and P2-WIRE-RESUME, `CR-136-BRC07`.** Two judgments, both made
where the blueprint and the rulings ran out, both recorded before the work was
reported. ⚠ **The first lane was stopped by a usage limit before it could verify
anything it had written**; the second re-derived the work onto the tip, measured
every figure again and corrected the ones that were wrong. Where a number below
differs from the draft preserved in `12-governance/recovery/2026-09-23/`, **this
row is the measured one.**

### 1 · THE MEASUREMENT THAT TURNED `P2.10` AROUND

`P2.10` reads *"a closed counter batch **IS** the deposit batch, so it appears
on Deposits ready to match"*, and the dispatching briefing expected a filter a
counter batch could never satisfy. **Measured instead, on real PostgreSQL 16
with a seeded till: `bankrec_read.batch_queryset` filtered on `tenant_id`
alone** — plus the two optional screen filters, `f.status` and `f.method`.
Nothing about a session, nothing about a close.

**So a closed till's batch already appeared, with no change at all.** The defect
is the other direction and phase 0 created it: since `P0.6` re-keyed the batch
onto the till (`UNIQUE (tenant, session, method)`), **a batch exists from the
moment the drawer OPENS** — `counters.py` opens the session and its CASH batch
in one act, which is what the blueprint's `P2.1` row means by *"the batch exists
before the money does"*.

**MEASURED 2026-09-23 on PostgreSQL 16.13, four seeded populations:**

| batch | till | recorded | verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| `DEP-260808-CHK-LEGACY` | none (`session_id IS NULL`) | `$4,400.00` | SHOWS |
| `DEP-260923-9003` | system, born closed | `$1,284.60` | SHOWS |
| `DEP-260923-9002` | Sam counted and sealed it | `$884.00` | SHOWS |
| `DEP-260923-9001` | **Dana's, still open** | `$612.50` | **HELD** |

**Before: four rows served and the In-transit tile read `$7,181.10`. After:
three rows and `$6,568.60`, with `$612.50` stated beside them.** ⚠ The draft
row this supersedes quoted `$2,781.10` and *"three batches served"*; that was
measured before the legacy population was added to the fixture and it is wrong.

**What that would have cost.** Reconciling LOCKS a batch (`BR-PAY-004`) and
`_recompute_total` then refuses the edit, so a till reconciled at 14:00 could
never account for the money taken after it — and the clerk's own close would
fail on a batch nobody could add to. An unattended statement import could reach
it through `auto_match` without anybody pressing anything.

**The ruling this follows is the blueprint's own, p059, read AS AN IMAGE (B14
rule 42):** at Close *"The batch becomes bankable. **It is the deposit batch**,
so it appears on Finance → Deposits ready to be matched"*, and at Start that
same table changes nothing on Deposits — it lists only the `Start counter`
control. So the list serves a batch **when its till is sealed**, and that is one
expression — `bankrec_models.BANKABLE`, `session_id IS NULL OR
session.closed_at IS NOT NULL` — with **EIGHT** readers: the Deposits list · its KPI strip · S38 step 2's hand-match picker · the `needs_a_look` classifier behind it · the reconciliation statement's *deposits in transit* · `auto_match`'s candidate scan · and the two human write paths.
Written once (B14 rule 43, and §3.2's identical instruction for *Not counted*).
⚠ **THE FIRST DRAFT SAID FOUR AND WIRED TWO OF THEM.** Three further reads of
the same population — S38's hand-match picker, the `needs_a_look` classifier
and CS-14's *deposits in transit* — were still filtering on `status` alone, the
field this rule exists to say cannot answer the question. The picker would have
offered a clerk a batch `match_bank_line` then refuses, which is exactly what
`bankrec_read`'s own header forbids (*"a screen never offers a control the
service refuses"*), and the statement would have counted a drawer as money we
had banked while the tile it cites as its definition did not. **Found by
grepping for the remaining `BATCH_IN_TRANSIT` filters, by nothing else**, and
each has a case in `test_cr136_p2_10_11_wire.py`.

**Three populations keep showing and that is load-bearing:** a batch with no
session (banked the old way — PO 2026-09-22 option (d)), the SYSTEM till (born
closed, so every ACH, card, wire and lockbox deposit is bankable from its first
moment) and a counter till somebody sealed. Only a drawer still taking money is
held back. A filter that took either of the first two out would empty Finance →
Deposits for a real utility.

**The held-back money is SERVED AS A NUMBER, never a silence** —
`still_open: {batch_count, recorded_total, currency}` on the body, one line on
S37 reading ***"$612.50 still at one open counter"*** (six words — B14 rule 33).
Hard-won law 7: *"a declared blind spot with no NUMBER attached is
indistinguishable from an empty one."* Without it the list would simply be short
by `$612.50` and nothing would say so.

**No second path was built.** The PO's standing instruction — *"we can not have
two path for 1 capabilities wew will confuse user"* — holds: there is one
Deposits list with one condition added to it.

**PROVED RED FIRST, IN THE BROWSER, ON THE TIP'S OWN QUERY** (hard-won law 6 and
law 7). With `batch_queryset` put back to `filter(tenant_id=…)` and the whole
stack up — Django on the seeded clone, the *built* SPA, Chromium at 1440, signed
in as Dana — `10-scripts/p2_10_11_finance_and_notice_walk.mjs` reported **11
passed · 3 failed**: the open drawer's row on the page, the In-transit tile not
tying to the rows (`$7,181.10` against `$6,568.60`), and the held-back money
inside a tile. With the fix restored: **14 passed · 0 failed.** The same two
cases go red in `pytest` without the fix. `DEF-PAY-6266`.

### 2 · `P2.11` FIRES ON *STILL OPEN*, AND WHEN

**The state.** Two exist in this phase and they are a day and a person apart:
`closed_at IS NULL` (nobody sealed it) and §3.2's *Not counted*
(`close_kind='forced' AND declared_at IS NULL` — sealed, uncounted). **The
notice is on the first.** The blueprint's task row names it — *"Notifications:
**the unclosed till**"* (p017, read as an image) — and screen 3·1 renders exactly
that state as the words *"still open"* in its CLOSED column (p051), under the
heading *"Whose till is open, and whose did not get counted?"*, which is the two
states drawn side by side. Decisive: **§3.1 struck the midnight auto-close, so a
forced close by a System Admin is now the only way an unclosed till gets sealed,
and the notice is what prompts it.** A notice on *Not counted* would be telling a
supervisor about work they had just done — and the blueprint already gives that
moment a different message to a different person: on a force close *"the owner is
told"* (p059).

**When.** ⚠ **The blueprint gives no time for the NOTICE**, only for the
auto-close it no longer has, so this is a lane judgment. **A till is "left open"
when it was opened before the banking day being swept began.** Open at 08:55 and
still open at 23:00 the same day is a clerk at work; open since yesterday is the
problem, because `uq_counter_sessions_open_owner` refuses its owner a second one
and **Dana cannot take money that morning** — the cost the PO accepted
explicitly. §3.1 struck the CLOSING at midnight, not the MOMENT, so midnight
remains the boundary for *the day is over*.

The cut-off is a **MOMENT** — midnight of the swept day in the tenant's own
timezone — and never a truncated `opened_at::date`, which would walk into
`OQ-153` (*a tenant west of UTC banking at 6pm lands on the next UTC day*). The
day is an **INPUT** (BR-TEN-043); `sweep_open_counters` resolves it per tenant
from that tenant's own clock (BR-TEN-081) and passes it down, so `counter_watch`
reads no clock at all.

**A clean night sends nothing**, and it comes out of the machinery rather than
out of an `if`: with no signed-in user and no failures `resolve_staff_recipients`
has nobody to address and `queue_bulk_summary` refuses. That is the OPPOSITE
choice from `queue_reconciliation_summary`, which reports a clean run
deliberately — and the difference is that one is a run a clerk just started,
while this runs unattended every morning of the year. `bulk_summary.py`'s own
header says what a daily message nobody needs does: *"the first thing any clerk
does is switch the whole event off, at which point the failure they needed to
see is the one they never get."* A person who runs the sweep by hand IS the actor
and does get the clean answer they asked for.

**It is a SET-12 row and not a `queue_staff_alert`.** BR-NOT-017 is signed:
*"ONE HOME: every notification rule, internal and external, lives on Settings →
Notifications"* — and the blueprint's own `P2.11` row names `rule_catalog.py` as
its reference. `queue_staff_alert` is the one documented exception (`DEF-3422`)
and its reasoning does not reach here: it exists because *"there is no SET-12 row
for the product's own setup not finishing, and inventing one would let a utility
switch off an operational failure it has no reason to know exists."* A till left
open is not the product failing; it is the utility's own shift, and it belongs
beside `reconciliation_exceptions` under the same rule.
⚠ **The accepted cost, stated rather than discovered: `source_type="bulk_action"`
carries no print floor (BR-NOT-024 puts the floor on `invoice`, `payment`,
`notice` and `plan`), so a utility CAN switch this off entirely** — the same
exposure `billing_run_completed` and `reconciliation_exceptions` already carry.

**IT TELLS AND IT NEVER CLOSES** (§3.1, *"A System Admin closes it. Dana cannot
work Tuesday until someone is free to do that"*). `counter_watch.py` contains no
write to `counter_sessions`, and **the absence of that write is the deliverable
rather than an omission** — so the till is read back field by field, because an
absence is invisible to every other check this repo has.

**PROVED ON REAL POSTGRESQL 16, 2026-09-23** (hard-won law 14 — the default
suite is in-memory SQLite, which has no aborted-transaction state, and this
sweep's per-tenant savepoint is exactly the shape that law names). Dana's till
open since Monday 20:52, swept for a later banking day with no signed-in user:
**one queue row**, `event_key=counter_left_open`, channel `in_app`, template
`staff_bulk_summary`, context `operation: "Counter check" · total_count: 1 ·
failed_count: 1`, addressed to the tenant's System Admin under BR-NOT-021(e);
**the sentence read `1 counter(s) left open across 1 tenant(s) examined`** — the
scope beside the result, so a zero is readable; **every column of the swept till
byte-identical afterwards** (`closed_at`, `closed_by`, `close_kind`,
`difference`, `counted_totals`, `note`, `declared_at`, `declared_by` all
unchanged); and a **re-run wrote nothing** — `counter_watch_summary_already_
queued`, which is CLAUDE.md rule 6 holding through a derived `uuid5` of
(tenant, day).

**AND LOOKED AT, IN A BROWSER.** Settings → Notifications draws the rule: *Counter
left open · Staff & system · Staff · In-app alert · **"When the banking day has
ended"*** · ON, among **31 events** — no event key on screen (B14 rules 31/32).

⚠ **IT IS NOT SCHEDULED, AND THAT IS STATED IN THE COMMAND'S OWN DOCSTRING.**
This repo carries no beat schedule to add it to and a schedule is a deployment
decision — the same exception `sweep_error_diagnostics` records for itself.
Until it is scheduled, `P2.11`'s outcome (*"nobody has to notice a missing count
by looking"*) is true of anyone who runs `manage.py sweep_open_counters` and not
yet true on its own.

### 3 · FOUR SUITES WERE RED AND NOBODY HAD READ THEM — `DEF-NOT-6267`

Found by running the NEIGHBOURS of this lane's own change rather than only its
new file (hard-won law 7, habit 1), and **every one dated with `git log -S`**
rather than called pre-existing on a hunch — the clause that habit gained on
2026-09-06 after two lanes reported *"a red I did not cause"* in good faith and
the second was the lane that had caused it. Eight assertions, four causes, all
re-measured 2026-09-23: a seam that returns eight names against a test asserting
seven (`d54a7f7d7`, 2026-09-20); a `pdf_print` adapter that resolves against a
test asserting it is `None` (`28dee3b8b`, 2026-09-11); **ten** seeded wordings
with no event row against a test asserting zero; and two batch-code assertions
`P0.6` superseded (`5657a71ba`, 2026-09-22). **Filed rather than fixed** — four
modules own them, and a lane guessing at another module's ratified figure is how
a count stops meaning anything. This lane moved only the two figures its own
change makes wrong (`built_event_count` 30 → 31, staff events 5 → 6).

⚠ **AND A SIXTH RED, FOUND THE SAME WAY AND DATED THE SAME WAY, THAT IS NOT
IN THAT ROW:** the five `CS-14` cases in
`06-backend/tests/test_cr059_w8_reconciliation.py` fail on
**`NOT NULL constraint failed: refunds.account_id`** — the fixture builds a
`Refund` with no account, and `payments/0018_cr059_cs7_refund_account.py` made
that column required at **`28dee3b8b`, 2026-09-11** (the same bulk commit
behind cause (b) above). **It is recorded here with a CONTROL RUN rather than
an opinion**, because those five sit directly on top of a read this lane
narrowed and *"pre-existing, not mine"* is exactly the sentence `DEF-CWP-4187`
was filed about: the same five cases were re-run against the **tip's own
`bankrec_read.py`**, swapped in byte for byte, and produced **`5 failed, 4
passed`** — identical to the run with this lane's change. A sixth case,
`test_cr059_tc6b__an_unpublished_read_still_reports_unknown_by_name`, is red in
the same suite run and **was controlled the same way, on its own**: red with
this lane's read, red with the tip's, in 12 seconds each. **Six reds, six
dated, none of them this lane's** — and the reason each one was CONTROLLED
rather than eyeballed is that all six sit on or beside code this change
touches, which is precisely the case where *"pre-existing, not mine"* is
cheapest to say and most expensive to be wrong about.

### 4 · A CASE THAT WAS GREEN ON SQLITE AND COULD NOT PASS ON POSTGRESQL

The draft's *"the legacy and system populations still show"* case built its
legacy row with `session=None`. `trg_deposit_batch_needs_session` refuses that
INSERT at the database (`payments/0033` — a `NOT NULL` would have validated
every existing row and refused to apply, so the guard is a `BEFORE INSERT`
trigger instead). The default suite is in-memory SQLite, which has no such
trigger, so the case was green everywhere anybody would have looked and **red
on the database the product runs on** — `1 failed, 16 passed` under
`config.settings.pgtest`, measured 2026-09-23. That is hard-won law 7's
*incapable of passing* shape and hard-won law 14's whole reason for existing,
and the only thing that finds it is running the file on real PostgreSQL.

⚠ **AND THE OBVIOUS REPAIR IS SHUT TOO, WHICH IS THE PART WORTH RECORDING.**
The INSERT guard is `BEFORE INSERT` and nothing else, so the natural second
attempt is to create the batch with a session and then clear `session_id` — and
**`payments_deposit_batch_lock()` refuses that BY NAME**: *"deposit batch
DEP-260808-CHK is identified by its tenant, TILL, day, method and code — none of
them may change."* Measured the same way, on the second attempt: `1 failed, 20
passed`. **Both doors into this population are shut on PostgreSQL, and that is
not an obstacle — it is the fact the case exists to describe.** The population
is HISTORICAL and FROZEN: rows banked before 2026-09-22 are in it, and after
`P0.6` nothing may enter or leave.

**So the fixture reaches it the only way anything can** — the way
`10-scripts/p2_10_11_seed_tills.py` already did: it disables the INSERT guard
for the length of the test and **never re-enables it**, because the case runs
inside a transaction, `ALTER TABLE` is transactional on PostgreSQL, and the
rollback at teardown restores the trigger without the fixture having to
remember. **And the guard it disables now has a case of its own beside it** —
`test_no_new_batch_may_join_the_legacy_population`, which SKIPS on SQLite with
a message saying the guarantee is unchecked there rather than passing silently
(hard-won law 7: a check that cannot cover its whole subject must say what it
skipped). A fixture that switches a guard off should sit next to the test that
proves the guard is on.

### 5 · A CLAIM OF THE FIRST LANE'S THAT IS NO LONGER TRUE

The draft recorded that `05-prototype/06 Payments Page Blueprint.pdf` **was not
on this branch** — the Billing anomaly `CLAUDE.md` already describes, repeating
itself on the module six lanes were building. It was true when written and it is
not true now: another lane filed it as **`DEF-PAY-6222`** and put the file on the
branch at **`da07c7f8d`, 2026-09-23 03:46**. It is recorded here only so a reader
meeting the draft does not go looking for a defect that is already closed — and
because two lanes finding the same thing independently, hours apart, is the
argument for filing a row rather than writing it in the file you happen to be in.

## 2026-09-23 — *AWAITING SETTLEMENT* IS A FACT ABOUT THE **TENDER**, AND THIS LANE DECIDED IT RATHER THAN ASKING (`CR-139-BRC07` `P5.7`)

**WHAT WAS DECIDED, IN ONE SENTENCE.** A payment is **awaiting settlement** when
a provider is the one who will pay it out — a card, an ACH debit or a tap — and
it is in no payout yet. Everything else is **never settled**, not *awaiting*.

**WHY IT WAS A DECISION AT ALL, AND NOT A LOOKUP.** The 5·1 Settlements screen
draws a tile the blueprint annotates ① *"Awaiting settlement · the third state
no requirement names · taken, not yet paid out"* (p070). The backend lane built
`settlements.awaiting_settlement_filter()` for it, and that function's own
docstring hands the rest of the question to the screen, verbatim:

> *"A counter payment, a lockbox row and a posted cheque are awaiting settlement
> **forever**, because nobody pays those out to us — which is why the screen
> that draws this state draws THREE (in a payout · awaiting one · never will be)
> and not two, and why the third one is a fact about the TENDER rather than
> about time."*

So the filter answers *"this payment is in no payout"* and something had to
answer *"and is anybody ever going to pay it out?"*. Nothing in the repository
did.

**THE WORKED FIGURE.** A utility that took **$1,204.80** on cards across **31
payments** yesterday and **$9,860.00** in cash and cheques at its counter reads
**`$1,204.80 · 31 payments`** on this tile. Counting the drawer money too would
read **$11,064.80** — and that figure would never fall, because nobody is ever
going to pay the utility out for its own till. A tile that only rises is a tile
a finance lead stops looking at.

**THE LIST, AND WHY EACH ONE IS ON THE SIDE IT IS ON.** `settlements_read.PROVIDER_SETTLED_TENDERS`
is `card`, `ach`, `tap_pay`.

* **card** and **ach** — a processor takes the money all day and pays the utility
  one bank credit for the lot. That credit is what a settlement IS.
* **tap_pay** — `CR-139-BRC07` `P5.11`, PO ruling 2026-09-23: *"user will
  manually use it and add reference # and Tap & pay options in system - we are
  not going to integrate them drectly"*. **A tap is a card** taken on somebody
  else's terminal, so the processor pays it out exactly like any other card.
  It is a seeded row on the tenant's own `payment_methods` list, not an eighth
  tender.
* **cash · check · money_order** — physical. They reach the bank in a deposit
  batch the utility cuts itself; there is no processor in the middle.
* **wire · lockbox** — credited by the BANK. Again no processor, so again no
  payout will ever arrive.

**WHY IT WAS NOT PUT TO THE PRODUCT OWNER.** CLAUDE.md hard-won law 13: *"a
judgment call recorded in the decision log with its reasoning is the
deliverable; a question is the failure to make one."* This collides with no
signed rule, moves no ❄️ FROZEN figure and needs no fact only the PO holds — it
is a reading of tenders the product already has. It is written down here, in the
module's own read file, and **asserted by a test whose control is the cash row**:
`test_cr139_p5_7_awaiting_settlement_is_a_fact_about_the_tender`. Without that
control the case would pass on either version of the code, which is why the
cash payment is in the fixture at all.

**PROVED RED BEFORE BEING TRUSTED GREEN**, in the harness that runs it: removing
the tender narrowing from `awaiting_settlement_queryset` and re-running the file
gives `AssertionError: assert '520.0000' == '120.0000'` — the drawer money back
in the tile. Restored, `7 passed`.

**IF THIS IS WRONG, IT IS WRONG IN ONE PLACE.** The list is a module constant
with this row's reasoning beside it, so a utility that starts taking money
through a rail nobody has thought of yet is one line and one test, not a hunt.

## 2026-09-23 — THE SCAN CARD STAYS HELD, AND `P5.8`'s ROW TITLE IS THE THING THAT WAS OVERRULED (`CR-139-BRC07`)

**WHAT WAS DECIDED.** `CR-139-BRC07` `P5.8` is titled *"The Scan source,
**switched on**"* and the lane that built it **did not switch it on**. The
focused input, its endpoint and the Extract stage's wiring all landed; the CARD
stays `available: false`.

**THE FACT THAT DECIDED IT, MEASURED RATHER THAN ARGUED.** The card's hold is
about OUR OWN PAPER. `P5.10` shipped the remittance **LINE** —
`ACC-1042$BL-2608-0117$14218%` — and `documents.py` prints it on the stub. Its
**BARS** are owed: `remittance.bars()` specifies the symbol in full, the PDF
writer has no filled-rectangle primitive, and `documents.py` calls
`compose_for_invoice` and **never `bars()`**. **A wedge scanner reads bars.** A
line of text is something a person keys.

**SO RELEASING THE CARD WOULD SHIP A LIVE CONTROL OVER A DOOR THAT OPENS ONTO
NOTHING** — a clerk selects *Scan paper*, points a scanner at one of our bills
and gets no characters at all. That is hard-won law 2's mirror pointing the
other way, and it is the failure `P5.15` is named for.

**AND A SIBLING LANE HAD ALREADY WRITTEN THE REFUSAL, HOURS EARLIER.**
`07-frontend/src/features/payments/scanSourceIsReachableAndHeld.dom.test.tsx`
mounts `APP_ROUTES` at the real address and asserts `data-available="false"`,
with a failure message that names the condition in terms: *"the Scan paper card
went live. If `documents.py` now draws the bars this hold has expired — release
it deliberately, with `P5.8`'s input behind it. If it does not, a clerk can now
point a scanner at one of our bills and get nothing at all."* **Overruling a
sibling's measured, red-proved hold on the strength of a task row's title is the
more damaging of the two available errors**, so it was not done.

**WHAT LANDED INSTEAD, AND WHY IT IS NOT A DEFERRAL.** Everything `P5.8` is
*except* the flag: `ScanInput.tsx`, `remittanceEndpoints.ts`,
`POST /billing/remittance/parse` (which calls `remittance.parse()` rather than
re-deriving a second Code 39 mod-43 in TypeScript), the Extract stage's wiring,
nine backend cases and four front-end cases. **Releasing the hold is now ONE
line in `kinds.ts` plus one catalogue retire** — three of the four things
`P5.15` says move together are done.

⚠ **AND THE HOLD'S OWN SENTENCE WAS CORRECTED IN ALL ELEVEN CATALOGUES —
`DEF-PAY-6274`.** It read *"Our bills carry no barcode yet"*, citing a
`documents.py` claim that `P5.10` had made false the same morning; it now reads
*"Our bills print no barcode bars."* **A refusal whose stated reason has stopped
being true is what sends the next lane to release it for the wrong reason** —
which is precisely how this lane nearly did.

## 2026-09-23 — `CR-138-BRC07` phase 4's nine test tasks, and the three defects writing them found

**LANE P4-TESTS**, `P4.15` · `P4.16` · `P4.18` · `P4.19` · `P4.20` · `P4.21` ·
`P4.22` · `P4.23` · `P4.28`. The task rows carry what each proof runs and on
which database; this row records the judgments, because a judgment written only
in the file that needed it is a judgment nobody can count (hard-won law 10).

**1 · MEASURED BEFORE WRITING, AND THE ANSWER WAS NOT *nothing is covered*.**
Two of the nine were **partly** covered and the covering cases were read one by
one rather than trusted by their names. `P4.15`'s tone→letter half is fully
proved by `test_us_not_010__firm_selects_the_regulated_disconnect_notice` and is
**not duplicated**; its day-numbers half was proved by an exclusive-or that **a
hardcoded `return (7, 14, 30)` passes** — demonstrated, by doing exactly that.
`P4.16`'s recorded half covered **one skip reason of eight**, and the other
seven share no line of code with it. `P4.19`'s *"five controls"* describe
asserts **four facts and a door, all on a config object**, with filters and
paging absent and 7·3a uncovered entirely. `P4.21`'s existing case asserts a
**string constant** and stays green with the route deleted from `App.tsx`.
`P4.28`'s BR-NOT-008 case asserts a **fixture declared in the test file** and
never mounts the wizard. **The lesson is the method, not the numbers: a
describe's NAME is not its coverage, and four of these five gaps were invisible
until the cases were read line by line.**

**2 · A CHECK THAT PASSED ON THE DEFECT IT WAS WRITTEN FOR, TWICE IN ONE HOUR.**
`P4.18`'s first two properties — *the page serves `per` rows* and *the statement
count is bounded* — are both **blind to a page sliced in Python**. Measured, not
reasoned about: `rows = list(positions)[offset:offset+per]`, which is
`DEF-PAY-4221` put back by hand, still makes **one** statement and still serves
**fifty** rows. The third property was added for it, and **its first version was
blind too**: `"LIMIT" in sql` is TRUE either way, because the page statement
carries a correlated subquery ending `GROUP BY U0."INVOICE_ID" LIMIT 1`. What
actually separates the two is an **outer `LIMIT` after the last `ORDER BY`** —
paged in SQL the tail reads `ORDER BY 7 DESC, 1 ASC LIMIT 50`, paged in Python it
reads `ORDER BY 7 DESC, 1 ASC`. **Law 7 habit 2 is the whole of this row: both
false passes were found by asking what would make the check pass wrongly and then
MEASURING the answer, not by reasoning about it.**

**3 · THE GROWTH CHECK COMPARES `grew`, NOT `differs`, AND THAT IS A RULING.**
`GET /outstandings` costs **13 statements at 2,046 debtors and 12 at 40,046** —
the SMALLER tenant costs one MORE, because the negative-credit count is chunked
at `_IN_CHUNK = 5000` and the 40k clone holds none. An equality check would
report a regression that does not exist and send a reader looking for it. The
property `NFR-3` actually needs is *the work does not grow with the tenant*, and
that is what is asserted, against every smaller run in
`10-scripts/cr138_p4_18_statement_record.jsonl`.

**4 · THREE DEFECTS, AND THE FIRST ONE STOPS A LEGAL NOTICE GOING OUT.**
`DEF-PAY-6301` (**high**): 7·3d loses its whole selection on the first press of
**Continue**, because `setNav` advances the step with `setSearchParams(params,
{replace:true})` and a partial path carries no `state`. Measured: state present
at mount, `null` at `?step=2`. The commit reads **Send 0 ✓** and POSTs
`account_ids: []`. **The screen cannot send a notice**, it landed this morning,
and `sendNoticeWizard.dom.test.tsx` cannot see it because that file never mounts
the wizard. Not fixed by this lane — `SendNoticeWizard.tsx` is LANE P4-SCREENS-B's
and that lane was still running (law 11) — and pinned by value so the fix turns
the test file red. · `DEF-PAY-6300` (medium): the collections ladder takes no
page and serves **40,030 rows** at 40,046 debtors; `P4.2` flattened its statement
count to 20 at both sizes and **`CollectionsPage`'s docstring still says
`clientPage` is what `P4.2` deletes**. · `DEF-PAY-6297`: three screens routed
this morning have no `SCREEN_ROUTES` row, so `/payments/refunds` wears **`S32 ·
PAY-summary`** and 7·2 and 7·3d wear nothing; `screenIds.test.tsx` is red on
**16** unmapped routes, **13 older than today**.

**5 · AND ONE THAT IS NOT PAYMENTS' — `DEF-GOV-6298`.**
`core.tenancy.tenant_context` **CLEARS** `app.tenant_id` in its `finally`
instead of restoring what it replaced, and `api_call` nests one around every
view. So in any test, every ORM statement after a request runs **unscoped**
inside a `with tenant_ctx(...)` that is still open in Python. **On SQLite that
is invisible.** On PostgreSQL the WRITE direction raises
(`InsufficientPrivilege: new row violates row-level security policy for table
"tenant_settings"`) and **the READ direction returns zero rows and raises
nothing** — so a case asserting an absence after a request passes for entirely
the wrong reason, for ever. Found by running a new file on PostgreSQL after it
was green on SQLite, which is hard-won law 14's own prescription. The durable
fix is a save-and-restore token in `tenant_context`; nothing counts how many
suites are affected.

**6 · TWO JOURNEYS, WRITTEN FROM A RUN.** `JPAYCHASEMORNING` and
`JPAYCREDITORCHEQUE`, every figure printed by
`10-scripts/cr138_p4_journeys_readback.py` on real PostgreSQL 16. The chase
journey is walked at **two tenant sizes** and steps 2–6 are **byte-identical**
between 2,046 and 40,046 debtors — the `NFR-3` claim stated as a journey rather
than as a number. The credit journey ends with **one door open and one refused**,
and says in terms that this is the correct answer: a goodwill credit is raised
against a bill, **0 of the 1** credit holders on the clone has an open one, and
`available: false` means *not on this account* rather than *unbuilt*. **A
journey that hid that would be `J19` again** (`DEF-112`).

## 2026-09-23 · `DEF-MET-6304` — THE PREMISES LIST COULD NOT NAME AN OWNER IT HAD ALREADY READ, AND THE NAME IS NOT WHERE EVERYONE THOUGHT IT WAS (lane OWNER-NAME)

**THE REPORT.** The Premises list's `Master a/c` column read **"No name
recorded · AC-2026-00051"** on every row that HAD an owner account — beside a
real number, for a real, named company. This is the same screen the PO reported
today asking us to *"use one volcabory"* for owner and master account, and a
column apologising beside a real number is that confusion wearing a new coat.

**IT WAS NOT A MISSING FACT, IT WAS A QUESTION NOBODY PUT.** Open the same
property's detail page and it read **Ridge Property LLC** correctly, and had
done since the day it shipped. The LIST does not expand an account — `DEF-324`
measured that at *47 of 118 profiled seconds answering one question 304 times* —
so it takes a batched answer carrying `account_no`, `status` and `kind`, and
`premisesOwnerContract.ts`'s third case built its row with `name` hardcoded to
`null`. The screen then rendered the absence sentence, which states something
about the ACCOUNT that is false. **Hard-won law 1, in copy: a sentence claiming
a cause is not the cause.**

**THE FINDING THAT CHANGED THE FIX — `accounts` HAS NO `name` COLUMN.** The
briefing this lane was given said the name was *"a plain column on the account
row that batched query already reads"*, so it *"should cost no extra query"*.
It is not and it does not. What a clerk reads is the account's **primary
CONTACT's `full_name`**, in the `contacts` table — which is exactly how
`customers.selectors.account_row` has always served it, and precisely why the
detail was right and the list was not. **Measured rather than assumed, which is
the only reason it was caught.**

**WHAT IT COSTS, MEASURED ON POSTGRESQL 16, A CLONE OF `brazosbend`.** One page
of fifty properties, counting the exact three calls `api.premises` makes:

| page | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| 5 rows | 11 statements | 11 |
| 25 rows | 51 | 51 |
| 50 rows | **107** | **108** |

**+1 for the WHOLE PAGE, and zero where no row on the page names an account** —
the pages of 5 and 25 did not move at all, because the seam returns `{}` without
asking anything when nothing is declared. Nothing is per row. The test that
holds this asserts the cost **did not follow the page**, comparing two page
sizes with a DIFFERENT owner account on every row; a count alone proves nothing,
since 51 is fine for 25 rows and a catastrophe for one.

**THE JUDGMENT, BECAUSE THE RULES RAN OUT HERE.** Two shapes were available.
A `Subquery` annotation would have folded the name into the EXISTING statement —
literally zero extra queries — and was **rejected**. `primary_contact_names_for`
already owns which contact is *"the"* name when an account has several
(`-is_primary, created_at, id`), and its own docstring records why a second
reading is dangerous: *"a batched read that sorted differently would quietly
rename customers on the list while their detail page kept the old name — a
regression no statement count can see."* One statement saved is not worth a
second answer to that question on a screen the PO is already reading for
vocabulary confusion. **The seam's docstring now says two statements, out loud,
so nobody "simplifies" the second one away.**

**WHAT WAS DELIBERATELY NOT DONE.** An account with genuinely nobody named still
answers `null` and still reads *"No name recorded"* — now TRUE, because the list
asked. The premises' free-text `owner_manager` sits on the very same row and is
**not** borrowed to fill the gap: `BR-MET-151` clause 3 forbids deriving a fact
about a real party from a typed string, the owner of a building and the party a
bill is addressed to are not always the same, and a seeder has already been
failed for exactly this. `DEF-CUS-6295`'s lesson is the mirror and was kept
apart on purpose — a row the server did not expand is still blank, and that
blank is correct.

**THE CHECK THAT COULD NOT FAIL, FOUND BY RUNNING IT AGAINST THE BROKEN BUILD.**
`def_met_6304_owner_name_walkthrough.mjs` asserts *"every owner cell reads
`<name> · <account number>`"*. Its first draft tested `/\S+.*·\s*AC-/` — and
**"No name recorded · AC-2026-00054" matches that perfectly**, because `No name
recorded` IS `\S+.*`. It printed **PASS · 3 of 3** over the exact defect it
exists to catch, on the run meant to prove it red. The primary assertion caught
the build anyway, which is the only reason it cost nothing. **It now splits the
cell and judges the name segment**, and reads `0 of 3` on the broken build.
Hard-won law 7 habit 2 — *ask what would make this check pass wrongly* — earning
its place for the second time this week.

**PROVED BOTH WAYS, IN THE HARNESS THAT RUNS EACH.** `pytest` 7 failed → 8
passed; `vitest` 1 failed → 26 passed; and the browser walk was run against a
second stack serving the same bundle over the **pre-fix backend**, where it
exits 1 and prints the apology, and against the fixed one, where all six pass
and `500 Main St` reads **"Ridge Property LLC · AC-2026-00051"**. The one check
that passed before the fix is the B14 rule 33 word-count over all eleven
catalogues — written before the words, and it must never have been red.

**TWO DEFECTS FILED WHILE MEASURING, NEITHER FIXED HERE.**
`DEF-MET-6312` — **100 of those 107 statements are two `COUNT(*)` on `units`
per row**, from `premises_detail_dict`'s `units` and `units_common` cells: a
second N+1 on the same serializer, which the batched account read beside it has
avoided since `BR-MET-1181`. `DEF-MET-5761` measured this same list and named
`_page()`'s `list(rows)` and the roll-up, so it was believed measured.
`DEF-CUS-6313` — the guard counting who reads the master-account chain
(`test_br_met_1181…two_seam_functions`) **has been red since `f40a857b8` landed
this morning**, because `BR-CUS-1094` added a FIFTH call site. Reproduced at the
tip with this fix absent. Its docstring predicted exactly this and nobody read
its output: hard-won law 7's first shape, *proved red then never read*.

Shipped in `2.346.2`.

## 2026-09-23 — THE OPENING TIME IS A DATE-AND-TIME PICKER THE CLERK CAN SEE AND CHANGE, NOT THE MOMENT THEY CLICKED (PO ruling, overruling this coordinator)

**THE DEFECT UNDERNEATH IT** is `DEF-PAY-6314`: a clerk could not open a till at
all. `StartCounterModal` sends `service_centre` and `opening_float`; `POST
/counters` reads `service_centre_id` and REQUIRES `opened_at`. The form sends no
`opened_at` and draws no field for one, so the screen refused with *"Give the
opening time."* over a form with nothing to type it into.

**WHAT I RECOMMENDED, AND IT WAS WRONG.** I briefed the lane to send
`new Date().toISOString()` — the moment the button was pressed — and explicitly
told it *"Do not add a datetime picker."* My reasoning was B14 rule 33 and that a
clerk opening a till at 08:55 should not be typing 08:55.

**THE PO RULED OTHERWISE, verbatim, 2026-09-23**, reading the three-field table
of what the form sends against what the server reads:

> *"show date and time pciker and deult should be as per date time format set by
> utility and timezone - show the detault time"*

**SO THE BUILD IS:** a DATE AND TIME picker on the Start-counter form, both
halves; PREFILLED with the current moment so a clerk sees a value rather than an
empty box; rendered in **the utility's own configured date/time format and the
utility's own timezone** — not the browser's, not ISO, not a hardcoded US format.
The clerk may change it. `service_centre` → `service_centre_id` is unchanged and
still required; it is the second break behind the first.

**WHY THE PO IS RIGHT AND I WAS NOT.** The click-moment is correct only when the
click and the opening coincide. They frequently do not: a till is opened at the
start of a shift and the software is started when someone gets to it. My version
silently recorded the wrong business fact and offered no way to correct it, and
an opening time decides which business day's takings a payment lands in. That is
a money consequence, not a UX preference, which is why it was not mine to settle
on tidiness grounds.

**WHAT THIS DOES NOT DECIDE, AND IS NOW WITH THE PO** (put to them the same hour,
in plain words with a figure):

* **May a clerk BACKDATE the opening time, and how far?** Worked case shown:
  Dana opens the counter at 09:00, forgets to start it, notices at 11:00 and sets
  it back to 09:00 — which moves the takings into a different business day.
  Options put: (a) today only, no backdating · (b) backdate within the same day ·
  (c) any date. Recommended (b). **UNRULED — do not choose a value.**
* **Does the picker apply to the other three counter writes?** Worked case
  shown: Dana closes the till at 17:05 and counts the cash at 17:20 — which is
  the closing time? Options put: (a) a picker on all four · (b) a picker on open
  only. Recommended (a). **UNRULED — the lane builds the contract correctly on
  close, force-close and declare and reports the shape rather than deciding it.**

**THE BLAST RADIUS FOUND WHILE FIXING IT — `DEF-PAY-6315`.** The lane checked the
sibling endpoints as briefed and found **the same break on close, force-close and
declare**: each omits the required moment its endpoint reads. So it was never one
button — a clerk could not have CLOSED a till either. Found only because the
briefing asked *"if this was built wrong once, was it built wrong the same way
next door?"*, which is the habit worth keeping from this entry.

**WHY NOTHING CAUGHT ANY OF IT, and this is the escape reason.**
`StartCounterBody` (`07-frontend/src/api/counterEndpoints.ts:196`) declares only
`service_centre` and `opening_float` — the interface was written to match the
CALLER rather than the ENDPOINT. So the type agreed with the form, the form
agreed with the type, and both disagreed with the server; `tsc` could only ever
confirm the frontend agrees with itself. The dom test mocks `startCounter`, so it
cannot see this class of break either — hard-won law 7's *structurally incapable
of failing*. The new test asserts the REQUEST BODY against the keys the endpoint
actually reads.
