## 2026-09-27 — **THE STATEMENT IS BUILT ON THE LEDGER AND NOW HOLDS BOTH SIDES** (lane REP-P2-LAST, `BR-REP-038`, `CR-142-BRC07` `P2.8`)

**The row above is the authority to build it. This is the build.**

**WHAT WAS BUILT.** `reports/0007_br_rep_038_statement_on_ledger.py` moves the
platform `R24 statement` row from the `invoices` dataset to `journal_lines`,
and `apps/reports/statement.py` serves it out of
`apps.ledger.reporting.account_ledger` through the existing `report_seams`
seam — the read model `P0.14` wired for exactly this and that S59 already runs
on. **This module computes no money.** It resolves the subject, hands the ledger
the window and the page, and shapes the answer through `queries._report` so
`BR-REP-001` cannot be forgotten. Hard rule 5 is untouched: it READS journal
lines and writes none.

**THE WORKED CASE, PROVED.** One account, one September bill of `$84.20` posted
on the 1st, one payment of `$84.20` posted on the 14th, written through
`posting.post` and never by an INSERT:

| | figure |
|---|---|
| opening balance | `0.000000` |
| the September bill | `84.200000` charge, running balance `84.200000` |
| the payment on the 14th | `84.200000` payment, running balance `0.000000` |
| charges / payments over the window | `84.200000` / `84.200000` |
| closing balance | `0.000000`, and it is struck as `opening + charges − payments` rather than read off the last row |

On the invoice reading there is **one row and no payment at all**, which is the
sentence the `invoices` dataset already published when it refused this
definition by name.

**THREE THINGS WERE DECIDED HERE RATHER THAN ASKED (hard-won law 13).**

**(a) THE BASIS MOVES WITH THE DATASET, `event` → `posting`.** `0003` seeded R24
at the EVENT basis labelled *Statement date*. Every figure on the ledger reading
is struck on `journal_entries.entry_date`, the BOOK date, and the read model
publishes `posting`. The `journal_lines` dataset already refuses
`regulatory_filing` over the opposite mismatch — *"serving it here would answer
a filing with a period the regulator did not ask about, and BR-REP-001 exists so
a money report cannot state the wrong one."* Leaving the stored basis at `event`
would have shipped a statement whose stated basis contradicts its own rows. It
is a consequence of the ruling, not a fifth option.

**(b) THREE OF THE FOUR SUBJECTS REFUSE BY NAME.** `P2.14` built the four-subject
vocabulary; the ledger publishes a running record for ONE of them, `account`.
`customer` has no read model that runs a balance across the accounts a person
holds — and a jointly-held account belongs IN FULL to each holder (`BR-CUS-054`),
so it is not a sum either. `premises` has `by_premises_summary`, which is three
totals and not an ordered sequence with a carry-forward. `unit` is `P2.15`, the
one subject nobody built. Each raises `DatasetCannotServe` with its own
sentence. **A fall-back to `account` would have passed every assertion about the
account grain while printing one account's money under a building's heading** —
hard-won law 2's mirror on a money screen.

**(c) NO ACCOUNT NAMED IS AN ABSENCE, NOT THE WHOLE TENANT.** A statement handed
no `subject_id` returns zero rows with a stated reason and four null tiles each
carrying it (`BR-REP-024`). The alternative is every account's postings under
one account's heading, which is the failure the `journal_lines` dataset refuses
R25 over in its own words.

**ONE DEFECT FOUND ON THE WAY AND FIXED, BECAUSE NOTHING COULD WORK WITHOUT IT —
`DEF-REP-6908`.** `runner.bind` DROPPED `subject`, `subject_id` and `account`.
Measured on real PostgreSQL before the fix:

    runner.bind(account_ledger, {subject: premises, subject_id: abc, account: x})
      -> {'basis': 'posting'}
    runner.dropped(...)  -> ('subject', 'subject_id', 'account')

`subject` and `subjects` sit in `_DEFINITION_BOOKKEEPING`, which only lets
`validate()` ACCEPT them as STORED filters; `bind` passes a name on only when
the DATASET declares it or it is a run control. **So `P2.14`'s whole vocabulary
survived validation and reached no query at any point** — a stored string
nothing honours, which is what `subject.py`'s own docstring warns about, one
layer further down than it was looking. `subject` and `subject_id` join `page`,
`per`, `sort`, `group_by` and `columns` in `_RUN_CONTROLS`, which is where they
belong: a subject is declared on the DEFINITION, it spans two definitions
sitting on two different datasets, and putting it in `journal_lines.filters`
would tell that dataset query it honours something it does not.

**THE VIEWER IS REGISTERED BY ITS OWN MODULE AND NOT IN `queries.VIEWERS`, AND
THAT IS A CONSTRAINT AS WELL AS A DESIGN.** `apps/reports/queries.py` was FENCED
for this lane — a sibling is fixing the refusal path in it — so
`statement.MODULE_VIEWERS` holds the registration and `runner.queries_for`
consults it first. It is the SAME lookup rule and not a second one: a per-REPORT
viewer wins, then the DATASET's own query. It also keeps `queries.py` from being
the one file every report lane edits at once. ⚠ **AND IT AVOIDS A KNOWN TRAP
lane REP-P2-RETIRE PROVED:** `apps/reports/api._VIEWERS` splats
`**{key: runner.run … for key in queries.VIEWERS}` AFTER its two hand-written
ledger keys, so adding a key to `queries.VIEWERS` can silently override a live
hand-written viewer.

**WHAT WAS MEASURED AND DELIBERATELY NOT MOVED — `R44 My Bills & Payments`
CANNOT SHOW A PAYMENT TODAY.** It is seeded on `invoices` at line 241 of the
same seed, its drawn name promises both sides in the same way, and **the ruling
names the statement and not R44.** Measured on real PostgreSQL 16, seeded
`brazosbend`: `runner.run("my_bills_and_payments")` raises `DatasetCannotServe`
with the invoices dataset's own sentence — *"a customer would open their
statement, see every charge, see none of what they had paid, and read a balance
that agreed with neither."* Filed as `DEF-REP-6909`, OPEN, with one question for
the Product Owner and **no dataset chosen by a lane** on a customer-facing money
screen.

**`DEF-REP-6859` VERIFIED AGAINST THE CODE AND IT IS RIGHT.** The task rows name
`by_premises` and `customer_statement` as definitions; `report_definitions`
holds `statement` (R24) and `account_ledger` (R25) and **neither of those two
keys**, at the tip, measured. Nothing was minted to match the prose — the
drawing (p069) says the two collapse into two definitions with a `Subject`
parameter, and minting two more keys would be three implementations of one
question at three grains.

**WHAT IS STILL NOT DONE, AND WHY.** `P2.8` retires THREE pages and this lane
unblocked and built **one** of them. `account_ledger` (R25), which both the
Account ledger and the By-premises addresses collapse into, is refused by an
entry in `queries.JOURNAL_LINES_DEFINITIONS_NOT_SERVED` — **inside the fenced
file** — and `queries.definition_refusal` reads that table to decide whether a
card is available, so a viewer registered anywhere else would leave the
catalogue and the viewer disagreeing, which is the exact defect that table's
docstring exists to prevent. `P2.15` (the unit grain) needs a running-record
read model in `apps/ledger`, which no seam publishes. `P2.16` deletes
`CustomerStatementPage.tsx` — and that page is **not** a running-record
statement at all: it is one customer, their accounts, each balance and a total
across them, with a `held_with` guard and an `AbsentFigure`. Its careful parts
belong to the CUSTOMER subject, which refuses. **Retiring it now would delete a
working screen and put a refusal at its address.**

| task | state after this lane |
|---|---|
| `P2.8` | **one third built** — the customer statement is a definition and serves rows; the account-ledger and by-premises third is blocked in a fenced file |
| `P2.15` | **not built** — the `unit` subject refuses by name; it needs a ledger read model, not a screen |
| `P2.16` | **not built** — the page it deletes is a different report from R24 and its subject still refuses |


### The two things only a browser and a real role could find

**(1) THE SCREEN COULD NOT CARRY A SUBJECT, AND EVERY TEST PASSED OVER IT.**
`ReportViewerPage.paramsFrom` rebuilds the request from the URL and read seven
bare names; `subject` and `subject_id` were not among them, so
`/reports/statement?subject_id=<uuid>` reached the server with **no subject at
all**. Photographed at 1440 before the fix: four tiles reading *Opening balance
— Not counted yet — Choose an account first* over a URL that named an account.
Hard-won law 2's mirror, and **the identical miss `group_by` (`P2.17`) and
`columns` (`P5.3`) each recorded one comment further up the same file** — a
screen that rebuilds its own request drops anything this function does not read,
silently, under an address that says otherwise. Both names now join the bare
set at both ends of the round trip.

**(2) `reports/0003` SEEDS 46 PLATFORM ROWS THE PRODUCTION ROLE MAY NOT WRITE —
`DEF-REP-6906`, CRITICAL, OPEN.** `0002_rls_force` gives `report_definitions`
the asymmetric policy §7.7 asks for and a human reviewed — *"`tenant_id IS NULL`
is readable by every tenant and writable by none"* — and every platform row
carries `tenant_id = NULL`. Probed on real PostgreSQL 16 as the
`NOSUPERUSER NOBYPASSRLS` application role, **twice**, with `app.tenant_id`
unset and with it set to the documented `00000000-…-0000` default:

    ERROR:  new row violates row-level security policy for table "report_definitions"

`10-scripts/13-provision-database.sh` states in its own header that with **no
BYPASSRLS and no superuser anywhere** every migration in every app applies. That
was true when it was written; `reports/0003` landed after it, and **nothing
re-checks a claim in a comment** (hard-won law 1). An already-migrated host is a
no-op, the dev database already holds the rows, and the suite's test database is
built by a path that does not hit it — so only a **fresh deployment** fails, and
nothing in the repo would have said so. Found by trying to write a platform row
from a new migration.

`0007` gets past it by taking the table out of row-level security for the length
of one UPDATE and putting it straight back **with `FORCE`**, which the table
OWNER may do and the application role is the owner. The whole migration is one
transaction and DDL is transactional in PostgreSQL, so there is no window in
which a crash leaves the table unprotected. **Proved forward, reversed to
`0006`, and forward again on real PostgreSQL 16**: the dataset and basis move
both ways, `register`, `subject` and `subjects` survive untouched, and
`pg_class.relrowsecurity` and `relforcerowsecurity` both read `t` afterwards.
`0003` itself is NOT fixed here — fixing a signed 🔒 RLS path inside a different
change is how scope stops being reviewable.

### What the screenshots show, including one thing a sibling had already fixed

Walked at 1440 and 1280 on the running product, `v2.374.0` on screen
(`10-scripts/rep_p2_statement_shots.mjs`, shots under
`scratchpad/po-shots/statement/`):

| shot | what it shows |
|---|---|
| `02-statement` | **six rows, both sides**: three bills, a credit note and two payments, `DATE · TYPE · REFERENCE · DESCRIPTION · CHARGE · PAYMENT · BALANCE`, the running balance carrying `$137.70 → $0.00 → $137.15 → $332.89 → $195.19 → $0.00`, and four tiles reading `$0.00 · $470.59 · $470.59 · $0.00` |
| `01-no-account-named` | four tiles at *Not counted yet* with the reason under them, and no rows — the stated absence, not a zero |
| `03-premises-subject-refuses` | the refusal, and see below |

⚠ **TWO THINGS THE FIRST WALK CAUGHT THAT NO TEST COULD.** **(a)** The CHARGE,
PAYMENT and BALANCE cells printed **storage width** — `137.700000`, `0`,
`195.190000` — under tiles reading a correct `$470.59`, because a cell is money
only if the report key is listed in `ReportViewerPage.MONEY_COLUMNS` and the
statement was not. Hard rule 2 says money DISPLAYS at 2. **(b)** The headers
read `ENTRY_DATE` and `RUNNING_BALANCE`, the raw column keys, because
`reports.col.<column>` defaults to the column name. Seven header keys and four
tile keys are now in all eleven catalogues.

⚠ **THE `premises` REFUSAL DREW *"The finance figures could not be loaded /
Something went wrong on our side"* IN THIS LANE'S BUILD, AND THAT IS ALREADY
FIXED ON THE TIP — it is NOT a new defect and no row was filed for it.** This
worktree was cut at `254687fbc`; lane REP-REFUSE's `6f34d0bff` landed at 11:57
and teaches `GET /reports/{key}` to catch `queries.DatasetCannotServe` by name
(`DEF-REP-6898`, *"27 reports told a clerk the product broke"*). `api.py`'s
error handling was FENCED for this lane for exactly that reason, so the three
subject refusals inherit the named sentence on merge rather than needing one
written here. **Recorded because a screenshot of a stale build is evidence
about the build it was taken from and nothing else**, and a lane reading that
picture without this paragraph would file a duplicate.

### One fault in this lane's OWN test, recorded rather than quietly fixed

`test_br_rep_038__the_statement_holds_both_sides` counted a row as a charge by
testing `row["charge"] != "0.000000"`. **`queries._money` serves the EXACT
decimal the read model struck**, so a zero arrives as `"0"` where the other
side of the same row carries `"84.200000"` — the widths differ per row, per
column. Every payment row therefore counted as a charge as well, and the case
failed on `len(charge_rows) == 1`. It is money-as-text, which
`financeShared.isZeroAmount` exists for one layer up and says so in its own
docstring. Compared as `Decimal(...) != 0` now. **It failed rather than passing
wrongly, which is the only reason it was cheap** — the mirror version of this
mistake (`row["charge"] == "0.000000"` to find the zeros) would have found none
and reported a clean statement over any data at all.

### A rollback that is two acts, and the sentence that first got it wrong

**Undoing `BR-REP-038` is NOT `manage.py migrate reports 0006` on its own.**
`runner.queries_for` asks the per-REPORT viewer **before** the dataset, so
migrating the definition back to `invoices` leaves `statement.MODULE_VIEWERS`
serving posting-dated rows under a stored row that says `event`, beside a
catalogue card that says the report cannot be produced — the viewer and the
catalogue disagreeing, which is the exact fault
`queries._DEFINITION_REFUSALS`' own docstring exists to prevent. **Revert the
registration as well.**

⚠ **THE FIRST DRAFT OF THE REVIEW-LEDGER ROW SAID THE OPPOSITE** — *"the viewer
is inert once the definition is on `invoices` again"* — which is a comment
claiming a guarantee the code does not give (hard-won law 1), on the one line a
reviewer would act on at the worst possible moment. Caught by reading
`queries_for` rather than by any check, and corrected in both the ledger row
and `statement.py` before review. **Nothing in this repository verifies a
rollback sentence**, which is why it is written out here instead of trusted.

## 2026-09-27 — FOUR REPORT RULINGS: DISCONNECT GRAIN · PLANS PAGING · READINESS BASIS · THE PROJECTION RANGE

Four questions were put to the PO in plain English, each with a worked example
and options. **All four answered (a).** Verbatim: *"1 · Disconnect & Reconnect -
a; 2 · Plans & Discounts - a; 3 · Bill Run Readiness - A; 4 · Bill Projection -
(a) Set a percentage — say ±15% — applied to the usage part only, never to
fixed charges"*.

### 1 · `BR-REP-039` — R34 Disconnect & Reconnect is ONE ROW PER ACCOUNT

**Shown to the PO:** *"Alia is cut off on 3 June for `$210` owed and restored on
11 June when she pays. She falls behind again and is cut off on 9 September for
`$185`. Under one row per account she is one line, showing where she stands
today. Under one row per case she is two lines, and the total at the bottom
reads `$395` owed — money she never owed all at once."*

**Ruled: one row per account**, showing the **latest** case, with the earlier
cases available underneath. The balance column then foots honestly, because
each account contributes its current position once.

⚠ **The spine is `customers.disconnect_cases`, NOT `work_orders`.** A sibling
lane refused this report on `work_orders` and was right about that dataset: a
list of field jobs counts an account twice when it is cut and restored in one
month. The case table holds the whole sequence — `amount_owed_at_open`,
`opened_on`, `cut_on`, `reconnected_on`, `state`, `tier` — so the drawn shape
exists. **The refusal stands for `work_orders` and is superseded as a statement
about the REPORT.**

### 2 · `BR-REP-040` — R27 Plans & Discounts stays ONE REPORT, and accepts a slower last page

**Shown to the PO:** *"318 people are enrolled — 184 on level pay, 84 on payment
plans, 50 on assistance. The three live in three separate parts of the system
and cannot be asked in one question. Paging to the end gets gradually slower.
At 318 enrolments that is unnoticeable; at 30,000 it would not be."*

**Ruled: accept it.** One row is one ENROLMENT (account × programme), served as
a k-way merge of three SQL-sorted, SQL-limited streams — each stream fetching
`offset + per` rows, which is why the last page costs more than the first.
**Splitting is refused** and the drawing forbids it in its own words.

⚠ **THIS IS A NAMED, RULED EXCEPTION TO THIS PHASE'S "the last page is not
slower than the first", AND TO NOTHING ELSE.** It does not licence a Python
slice, an unpaginated read, or a cap — `NFR-3` and `NFR-5` are untouched. The
measured cost must be published in the module's business rules, and the report
revisited if a tenant's enrolments reach the tens of thousands.
⚠ **The drawn `ENROLLED 318 / 16.3%` tile MIXES UNITS** — 318 is enrolments and
16.3% is over accounts. Label both for what they are; do not make one read as a
share of the other.

### 3 · `BR-REP-041` — R4 Bill Run Readiness reads the LATEST PREPARED RUN for the cycle

**Shown to the PO:** *"Dana opens readiness for the September residential cycle.
A run was prepared on the 28th, so she sees 14 accounts with problems. Her
colleague opens the October cycle on the 2nd, before anyone prepares a run.
There is nothing to be ready about yet."*

**Ruled: show the latest prepared run for that cycle, and when there is none,
say so plainly.** The absence is STATED, never substituted — no empty table
pretending to be a clean result, and no made-up run. *"No bill run prepared for
this cycle"* tells a clerk what to do next; a refusal tells them nothing.

⚠ **The report is opened for a CYCLE and the readiness data belongs to a RUN** —
that mismatch is the whole question, and this ruling resolves it by mapping
cycle → its latest prepared run at read time.

### 4 · `BR-REP-042` — the bill projection carries **± 15% OF THE USAGE PART ONLY**

**Shown to the PO:** *"Alia is 18 days into her cycle. We project `$84.00` using
exactly the calculation her real bill will use. The drawing shows it as `$84.00
± $12`. That ±12 exists nowhere in the product. If she reads `$84` and the bill
arrives at `$96`, she rings the office."* PO verbatim: **_"Set a percentage —
say ±15% — applied to the usage part only, never to fixed charges"_**.

**THE RULE, and the arithmetic is the ruling:**

| | |
|---|---|
| The range is | **± 15%** |
| Applied to | the **usage-driven** part of the projection ONLY |
| Never applied to | fixed charges — base, capacity, fire, any flat monthly amount |
| So the shown range is | `0.15 × (projected usage charges)`, never `0.15 × (total)` |

**Worked, and a test must assert it:** a projection of `$84.00` made of `$24.00`
base and `$60.00` usage carries **± `$9.00`**, not ± `$12.60`. The fixed `$24.00`
is known exactly and a range over it would invent doubt the product does not
have.

⚠ **THIS IS A CUSTOMER-FACING NUMBER.** Display two decimals (hard rule 2).
B14 rule 33 puts rationale at zero words on screen — the screen shows the
figure and its range and does NOT explain straight-lining.
⚠ **The sewer row's drawn *"Winter average"* basis is a SECOND tenant rule with
the same shape and is NOT ruled here.** A lane meeting it stubs and asks.

### What this changes about the count

Of the 17 multi-source reports, five were buildable today, four needed a ruling
and three refuse permanently. **These four rulings move R34, R27, R4 and R46
into buildable**, leaving R39 Regulatory Filing, R40 External Reconciliation and
R41 Migration Assurance refused for good — each names a fact nobody recorded
(no filing template, no fetched third-party totals, no legacy balances at
cutover). `R38 Adjustment Register` remains a fixable refusal: it needs an
adjustment reference number and a *raised by* column, one migration away, and
**`audit_log` may not supply *raised by*** because it is pruned on a retention
schedule with no row type exempt.

## 2026-09-27 — **A RULE SIGNED FIFTY DAYS AGO, CITED IN THREE FILES, ENFORCED BY NOTHING** (lane REP-P5-REST, Reports Phase 5 · `P5.9` · `P5.8`, **`2.375.0`**)

**THE RULE.** `BR-REP-023`, PO AR-1, 2026-08-08, CONFIRMED: *"Access-review
report (SC-2): System Admin + Executive only — Billing Clerk excluded."*
`R36 Access Review` lists every member of staff, their role, who added them,
when they last signed in and whether they can approve money.

**WHAT WAS ACTUALLY TRUE ON 2026-09-27, MEASURED.** Signed in as
`sam.reyes@sample.test`, a **Billing Clerk** on the seeded `brazosbend` tenant:
the catalogue drew **45 of 45 cards including this one**, and
`GET /reports/access_review` served it. Three files cited the rule —
`apps/reports/catalog.py`'s trace header, `apps/audit/audit_log_dataset.py`'s
`security_note`, and this log two hundred lines up — and
`tests/test_rep_audit_log_dataset.py` asserted that the string `"BR-REP-023"`
**was present in the note**. ⚠ **That is hard-won law 1 with a test on top of
it: a check that the guarantee is DESCRIBED, standing in for the guarantee.**

**WHAT IS BUILT.** `report_definitions.min_role`, nullable, set on exactly one
platform row, read in exactly one file — `apps/reports/role_gate.py` — and
asked at the **two doors a person uses**: the catalogue leaves the card out,
and `GET /reports/{key}` refuses `403`. Walked at 1440 as three real people:
System Admin **45 · present** · Billing Clerk **44 · absent** · Executive
**45 · present**.

### FIVE JUDGMENTS, EACH RECORDED BECAUSE THE RULES RAN OUT

1. **THE CARD IS ABSENT, NOT GREYED, NOT "UNAVAILABLE WITH A REASON".** B14
   rule 33 puts RATIONALE at zero words on screen, and a greyed card is also
   hard-won law 2's mirror — a live control that refuses. **It is also a list
   of which reports are restricted, published to the person refused.** The two
   neighbours in the same loop (the tenant overlay, a service the utility does
   not have) already take this posture.
2. **`min_role` IS A LADDER THE PRODUCT DOES NOT OTHERWISE HAVE, AND THE
   LADDER IS DECLARED IN ONE PLACE.** `apps/identity` holds **four** predefined
   roles as a SET — `system_admin`, `billing_clerk`, `executive`,
   `field_technician` — with no ordering anywhere. `role_gate.RANK` is an
   ordering minted for this one question; `field_technician` sits at **0**,
   which is the transcription of `A4_MATRIX` rendering "—" for it on all nine
   rows, rather than a judgment. It **fails closed**: a role added tomorrow
   sees an unrestricted report and does not see a restricted one until somebody
   states where it sits.
3. **NOT A `CHECK` CONSTRAINT, unlike `visibility` next door.** The lawful
   values are role codes owned by another module and `identity.Role` is a
   table; a CHECK here would freeze another module's vocabulary into this
   schema and make adding a role a migration in Reports.
4. **403 AND NOT 404.** `HR-1` reserves 404 for another tenant's resource. A
   404 here would make a restricted report indistinguishable from a typo for a
   clerk who bookmarked it while holding a different role.
5. **THE REFUSAL NAMES THE REPORT AND NOT THE ROLE THAT WOULD OPEN IT.**
   *"This needs Executive"* is rationale, and it is a map.

### TWO FAULTS THAT PASSED EVERY GREEN CHECK, BOTH WORTH THE SPACE

**(a) THE MIGRATION WAS REFUSED BY POSTGRESQL AND PASSED THE WHOLE SUITE.**
A plain `.update()` on the platform row met, verbatim:

    django.db.utils.ProgrammingError: new row violates row-level security
    policy for table "report_definitions"

`reports/0002`'s `WITH CHECK` has no `OR tenant_id IS NULL`, so a platform row
is readable by every tenant and **writable by nobody — the migration role
included, because `FORCE` applies to the table's owner.** SQLite has none of
this, so the broken version was green on 17 cases. Fixed the way `0003`
already does it: `NO FORCE` → `RunPython` → `SET CONSTRAINTS ALL IMMEDIATE` +
`FORCE`, all in one transaction. **Proved forward → back → forward on real
PostgreSQL 16:** column absent → present with **1** restricted row → absent
with **0** → present with **1**, `relforcerowsecurity` **true at every step**.

**(b) `tenant_id__in=(<uuid>, None)` LOST EVERY PLATFORM ROW, SILENTLY.**
Django renders it as SQL `IN (…, NULL)` and **`IN` never matches NULL**, so
`for_key("access_review")` answered `None` — *no restriction* — and the viewer
let a Billing Clerk straight through while the catalogue went on hiding the
card, because `catalogue_read` has always used the `Q(...) | Q(tenant_id=None)`
form. **A guard that answers *no restriction* is a guard that is not there,
and nothing about it looks wrong.** Caught by the copy-on-write case, which is
the only one that asks the function about a key whose answer is not `None`.

### A THIRD THING, AND IT IS A LANE COLLISION RATHER THAN A FAULT

This migration was written as `reports/0007` and **landed as `0008`**. A
sibling lane pushed `0007_br_rep_038_statement_on_ledger` while it was being
tested; two `0007`s under one app are two LEAF NODES, and Django then refuses
**every test in the process** with *"Conflicting migrations detected"* — which
names neither lane. `a47280585` fixed exactly that once already and the
sibling filed `DEF-REP-6906` for this very collision the same afternoon. It
was caught by **re-deriving at push time**, which is what law 11 prescribes
for an allocated id: **a migration NUMBER is an allocated id like any other,
and `allocate.py` does not know about them.**

### WHAT IS NOT DONE, NAMED RATHER THAN LEFT TO BE DISCOVERED

* **A SCHEDULED restricted report is not gated** — `apps/reports/schedules.py`
  runs as the tenant and not as a person, and there is no ruling on whose role
  a schedule runs under. `role_gate.py` says so in its own docstring; nobody
  has asked for it, and this lane did not invent an answer.
* **The refusal a clerk actually reads is wrong, and it is filed rather than
  fixed** — `DEF-REP-6907`. The viewer maps every 403 to one fixed sentence,
  *"Your role cannot run reports"*, which is false for a clerk who can run 44
  of them, and whose second half is rationale (rule 33). The server already
  carries the right sentence. **Not fixed here on purpose:** that file's error
  handling belonged this week to the lane fixing `DEF-REP-6898`, and two lanes
  in one error path is how a fix gets reverted.

## 2026-09-27 — A SCHEDULED REPORT NOW TELLS THE PEOPLE IT NAMES, AND IT SENDS A LINK RATHER THAN THE FILE (lane REP-P4-REST, `CR-142-BRC07` `P4.10`, `2.376.0`)

**THE GAP, MEASURED BEFORE IT WAS FILLED.** Phase 4's own DONE WHEN, from
p014 of the Reports Build Brief: *"A schedule set on Friday produces a file on
Monday, **delivered to named internal staff**."* The product did everything up
to the comma. `apps/reports/schedules.py` fired the run, the file landed on
screen `5·1`, `report_schedules.recipients` held the people the schedule names
and refused anybody who was not staff (`BR-REP-020`) — **and nothing ever read
that list again.** Grepped 2026-09-27: `recipients` appeared in the model, the
API and the picker, and in no code path after the save.

**WHY IT IS HARD-WON LAW 2'S MIRROR AND NOT AN ORDINARY GAP.** Neither half was
wrong. The picker is correct, the refusal is correct, the run is correct, and
every test of each half passes. What did not exist is the thing that joins them,
and the question *does anything consume this* belonged to nobody. That is the
same shape as a nav word over a screen that is not built, with the screen and
the word swapped.

**WHAT WAS BUILT.** One `outbound_messages` row per finished scheduled run,
`source_type='report'`, channel `email`, written on the beat entry reports
already owns. **Nothing is sent** — `BR-REP-017` is CONFIRMED and defers the
dispatch to W6 with all email — and a test asserts `status == 'queued'` and
`sent_at is None` as VALUES, so the day something does send it goes red.

**THE FIGURE THAT MATTERS, IN PLAIN ENGLISH.** Dana schedules the AR ageing for
the first of the month and picks herself. On 1 October at 06:00 it runs, and
Dana gets one email whose body says *"AR Ageing ran on … and its file is ready.
Open it here: /brazosbend/reports/history/‹the run›"*. She is not at her desk;
that is the whole reason the schedule exists.

**THE LINK, NEVER THE FILE — AND IT IS ENFORCED RATHER THAN INTENDED.** The
task line is *"the outbound queue carries the link, not the file"* and its
outcome is *"recipients get a link that respects their permissions"*. A CSV on
an envelope respects nobody's permissions once it has left the building: it is
a page of a utility's debtors, their addresses and their balances, forwardable
by anyone who receives it. So `catalogs.email_scheduled_report` declares
`{report_link}` as **mandatory content**, `rendering.validate_body` refuses a
saved body without it, and there is **no token in the palette that could carry
an attachment** — a test asserts the palette rather than the value, so a later
lane adding one fails at merge instead of in a review comment.

**THREE LANE JUDGMENTS, RECORDED RATHER THAN ASKED (hard-won law 13).**

1. **It RECONCILES; it does not hook the job.** The natural place to queue the
   message is when the export job finishes — and that point is
   `apps/tenancy/exports.run_list_export_job`, the platform's export kernel and
   the same handler a clerk's Export button runs. Reaching into it would mean
   editing another module's job body, or wrapping the platform's `list_export`
   handler from `ReportsConfig.ready()`, whose correctness depends on
   `INSTALLED_APPS` order — law 7's *structurally incapable of failing* waiting
   to happen. So the sweep looks at the run each schedule last started and
   queues the message when that run is READY. **It therefore cannot announce a
   run that failed**, which a hook at enqueue time could and would have.
2. **The message is keyed on the RUN, never on the schedule.** A monthly
   schedule keyed on its own id would queue September's message and then report
   `created=False` every month after that — a duplicate the database refuses,
   a caller told nothing is wrong, and a report that silently stops being
   delivered while it goes on being produced. `customer_events.py` records the
   same trap for move messages; this is it one table along.
3. **There is no `delivered_at` column.** The queue row IS the record of
   delivery (hard-won law 5), and a column recording the same fact is a second
   copy free to disagree with it. The cost is stated: one indexed lookup per
   enabled schedule per minute for the three days the file survives.

**THE WORDING IS LANE-AUTHORED AND IS NOT RATIFIED.** No signed document writes
this body. It is seeded anyway, because a utility cannot be asked to author the
wording for a message their own schedules already trigger — the argument the
four applicant classes won on 2026-09-15 — and the row says so in its own
`source` string. **`OQ-REP-12757` is open** for the PO to settle the words.

**WHAT MOVED IN THE REGISTERS.** `catalogs.LISTINGS` 49 → 50 and
`seed_templates.SEEDABLE` 44 → 45, **together**, which is the healthy shape the
speed bump in `test_def_210_authored_template_bodies.py` exists to enforce.
`rule_catalog.EVENTS` gains `scheduled_report_ready`, so the class is RULED from
its first commit and `seeded_wording_without_rule()` stays empty —
`BUILT_EVENT_COUNT` 31 → 32, and that file's own prose said 31 and is amended in
this commit.

**AND THE UTILITY CAN SWITCH IT OFF.** `source_type='report'` has no print floor
(`BR-NOT-024` puts the floor on customer documents), so turning *Scheduled
report ready — email* off on Settings → Notifications writes no row at all and
the reason travels back on the sweep's own answer. That exposure is the one
`billing_run_completed` and `counter_left_open` already carry, accepted here
rather than discovered later.

## 2026-09-27 — PHASE 4 OF THE REPORTS BRIEF IS FIFTEEN TASKS AND ITS OWN MIX ROW SAYS TEN (lane REP-P4-REST)

**COUNTED BY HAND OFF THE RENDERED PAGES (B14 rule 42), p014–p016.** The TASK
MIX box on p014 reads `1 DB · 2 Backend · 2 Front end · 1 Settings · 2 Test ·
1 E2E · 1 Other-module` — ten — and it describes `P4.1`–`P4.10` exactly. The
table beneath it runs to **`P4.15`**. The true mix is **`1 DB · 4 Backend ·
4 Front end · 1 Settings · 2 Test · 1 E2E · 2 Other-module`**. `CR-142-BRC07`
§7.3 is corrected in this commit; it had carried *"up to `P4.15`"* without the
count or the mix.

**AND THE BRIEF DISAGREES WITH ITS OWN DRAWINGS IN TWO ROWS.** `P4.11` and
`P4.13` name the Reports dashboard as **`4·1`** (`P4.13`'s reference reads
`4·1 → 2·1`). **`4·1` is *Scheduled*, drawn on p040.** The dashboard is
**`3·1`**, drawn on **p036** and listed as `3·1 Dashboard` in the p078 index. A
lane following the task line would have built the dashboard's four KPIs and
five panels onto the schedules screen. Build to p036.

## 2026-09-27 — lane REP-P6-JOIN: the FIRST THREE JOINING READS, and five judgments inside them (`P6.11`, `DEF-REP-6921`)

**WHAT THIS IS.** `CR-142-BRC07` `P6.11` is *"one joining read per multi-source
report"* — fifteen of them, per §9.2. This row records the first wave of three
(**R36 Access Review · R32 Read Import Log · R23 Account Activity**) and, more
importantly, **the five judgments made inside them**, because each is a place
where the drawing, the code and the rules did not agree and somebody had to
decide. Law 9: the conversation does not survive, the repo does.

⚠ **AND ONE CORRECTION TO THE CHANGE REQUEST ITSELF, FIRST.** §9.2 names
**fifteen** multi-source reports. Read against the drawings as images (B14 rule
42), **it is seventeen**: `R24 Statement` (*accounts + invoices + payments*,
p069–p071) and `R25 Ledger` (*accounts + journal lines*, p071–p073) are plainly
multi-source in their own eyebrow lines and are absent from the list. They are
drawn separately, after the six groups, which is how they were missed. Neither
is this lane's; the count is corrected so nobody re-derives it.

### 1 · `LAST SIGN-IN` IS SERVED AS `LAST ACTIVE`, AND THE DRAWN HEADER IS NOT MATCHED

**The drawing (p066) heads the column LAST SIGN-IN.** The only table holding a
literal sign-in timestamp is `sessions`, and **`sessions` is ephemeral** — a
session is capped at twelve hours (`BR-IDN-026`).

**THE WORKED CASE.** A billing clerk signs in on 25 September 2025 and not
again. On 25 September 2026 a compliance officer opens Access Review.
`MAX(sessions.created_at)` for that person is **nothing**, so a column headed
*Last sign-in* prints **Never** — beside a real returning user, on the one
report whose entire purpose is to find the account nobody uses. The report
would manufacture the failure it exists to catch.

`tenant_memberships.last_active_at` is durable and its own column comment
already reads *"null renders 'Never'"*. **Ruled by the coordinator, 2026-09-27,
verbatim:** *"Serve `last_active_at` and label it what it is. You are right not
to have changed a drawn header unilaterally, and you are right about the failure
mode… Build it as Last active, and say so in the file's own docstring with the
reason. If the PO wants the drawn wording back, that is a copy change and a
small one."*

**BUILT AS:** the field is named `last_active_at` and **no field named
`last_sign_in_at` exists**, so the drawn header cannot be printed over it by
accident; the substitution travels to the screen in `unavailable` as
`last_sign_in_is_served_as_last_active`. A test asserts the absent field name.

### 2 · `CAN APPROVE MONEY` READS THE SIGNED GRID, NOT `role_permissions`

**This one would have shipped wrong and looked right.** The obvious read is
*does this role hold the `adjustment_approval` permission*. `A4_MATRIX`'s row
for it reads **system_admin: Approve · billing_clerk: Request · executive:
Approve** — all three are non-dash cells, so **all three are seeded into
`role_permissions`**, and `models.py` says in its own words that the CELL VALUE
*"have NO B2 column"*.

**THE WORKED FIGURE.** On a four-person utility — one administrator, two
billing clerks, one executive — the permission join answers **CAN APPROVE
MONEY = 4**. The signed grid answers **2**. The drawing draws the distinction
and depends on it: Dana Whitfield, Billing clerk, reads **No**.

A security report that overstates who can approve money is worse than one that
does not exist, so the answer is read from `A4_MATRIX` — identity's own
transcription of the SIGNED grid (`BR-IDN-014`) — keyed on the role code, cell
equal to `Approve`. **The missing cell-value column on `role_permissions` is
published as a wanted read**, not worked around in silence.

### 3 · A DENORMALISED COUNT CACHE IS BYPASSED **AND COMPARED**, NEVER TRUSTED

`read_import_batches.counts` is a JSON blob whose own column comment reads
*"denormalized composition (**must reconcile**)"*, and its sibling
`ImportRun.counts` says at more length why: *"a count that cannot be checked
against the rows is a number nobody can defend."*

**Ruled by the coordinator, 2026-09-27, verbatim:** *"Aggregate the rows. Never
trust a denormalised cache whose own comment says it must reconcile — and if
you find it disagreeing with the rows on the seeded tenant, that is a defect
worth filing with both numbers in it."*

**BUILT AS:** `ROWS`, `ACCEPTED` and `REJECTED` are a `GROUP BY` over
`read_import_rows`. **And the blob is read anyway, only to be compared** — a
row whose cache disagrees carries `counts_disagree = {"stored": …, "counted":
…}` and the report publishes `the_stored_counts_blob_disagrees_with_the_rows`.
**A cache that is quietly bypassed goes on being wrong; one that is bypassed and
compared is a defect report.** A test plants a batch claiming 999 rows over 10,
and a second test plants one that agrees — so the check cannot pass by always
firing (hard-won law 7 habit 2).

### 4 · A `warning` ROW IS **ACCEPTED**, AND THAT IS A JUDGMENT

`ReadImportRow.severity` is `ok | warning | error` — the worst rule outcome on
the row (`BR-MET-032` validate-then-accept). **A warning row LOADED**: it is in
the database, it bills, and it carries a flag.

**THE CONSEQUENCE, STATED.** Counting warnings as rejections would make the
drawn `ACCEPTED 99.6%` tile disagree with what a clerk sees when they open the
batch. Counting them as accepted means the `REJECTED` tile is strictly the
`error` rows. `SEVERITY_ACCEPTED` and `SEVERITY_REJECTED` name the split in one
place, so the tile, the column and the footer are struck with one rule — the
footing failure `assets_dataset._test_due_on` already records once.

### 5 · A TRANSFER IS COUNTED IN NEITHER `opened` NOR `closed`, AND `net` IS DERIVED

R23's tiles are `OPENED 38 · CLOSED 14 · TRANSFERRED 6 · NET +24`.

**`net` is `opened − closed` and is declared NON-ADDITIVE.** It sums across a
partition only because both of its components do, which is a different
guarantee from being additive: a renderer totalling a column of group subtotals
would be right by accident and wrong the first time a group was filtered.

**A transfer is ONE JOB and ONE EVENT** (B18 §5.7: *"one job, not a move-out
followed by a move-in"*), so folding it into both `opened` and `closed` would
move `net` by zero while inflating two tiles by six each — the double-count the
`work_orders` dataset refuses R34 for, in a smaller place.

⚠ **AND A TRANSFER RECORDS NO ACTOR.** `transfers` carries no performed-by
column at all, so the drawn BY cell is `None` with `actor_absence="unknown"` —
never the account's owner, never the word *System*, and never a bare blank,
because a blank in that column reads as *nobody did this*, which is a different
and worse claim than *we did not record who*. Published as
`a_transfer_records_nobody_who_performed_it` with the wanted column named.

### 6 · THE THREE DATASET REFUSALS **STAY** WHEN THEIR VIEWER LANDS

Each of these three is seeded on a dataset whose query refuses it BY NAME —
`audit_log` cannot see a user who never signed in, `meter_reads` never holds a
rejected row, `accounts` states one account and not one event. **Every one of
those refusals is CORRECT and none is deleted.**

`runner.queries_for` checks `VIEWERS` first, so the dataset never sees the
call; `queries.definition_refusal()` asks the same map first, so the catalogue
card and the viewer cannot disagree about whether a report can be produced.
**A refusal deleted the day its read model lands is a refusal nobody can read
when the wiring rots** — which is hard-won law 2's mirror, and the reason
`rate_schedules_dataset` keeps its own.

### 7 · THE WIRING DEFECT CAUGHT IN THE SAME COMMIT — `stream_for` HAD ONE LOOKUP

`runner.queries_for` has always had TWO lookups — a per-KEY viewer, then the
DATASET query. **`runner.stream_for` had only the second.** So three per-key
streams would have been **generators nothing could call**: the export would
have fallen back to `run(whole=True)`, which returns correct rows and
materialises the whole filtered set in memory instead of streaming it. At a
top-of-ICP tenant R23 is years of moves.

`queries.KEY_STREAMS` and a first lookup in `stream_for` land in the same
commit as the viewers, mirroring `queries_for` exactly, **so there is one rule
for *which read serves this key* and not two that can disagree.** Three tests
assert the stream a caller actually reaches. This is filed as part of the work
rather than as a defect because it was created and closed inside one lane — but
it is hard-won law 2 exactly, and it is written down because the next person to
add a per-key viewer will meet it.

### 8 · WHAT WAS **NOT** DONE, AND WHY

* **`BR-REP-023`'s restriction on who may run R36 is NOT enforced.** `P5.9` is
  open and untouched. This read model does not quietly add an authorisation
  check of its own: that belongs at the endpoint, it would be the only one of
  its kind in the module, and a check in the wrong layer is how two answers to
  *who may see this* come to exist. It is published as
  `br_rep_023_restriction_is_not_enforced_anywhere` on every run.
* **No migration.** None of the three needs one; the definitions are already
  seeded and each is served by a per-key viewer on the dataset it sits on.
  `reports/migrations/` is another lane's this week.
* **R37, R38, R39, R40, R41 are untouched.** R37 needs a wave of its own (four
  component tables, four key shapes). R38 needs two columns `adjustments` does
  not have. R39, R40 and R41 refuse permanently — a filing template, an
  external system's totals and a legacy cutover manifest are each a fact this
  product does not hold.

## 2026-09-27 — THE SCHEDULE DIALOG HAD NO DOOR, AND THE TRAILER THAT SAID SO WAS BELIEVED (lane REP-DOOR, 2.377.1)

**`DEF-REP-6913` · `ScheduleReportDialog.tsx` — 227 lines, a schema, three
fields, a full dom test — WAS MOUNTED BY NOTHING.** The only file that rendered
it was its own test. A sibling counted **39 controls** on the report screen at
`2.376.0` and not one of them said *Schedule*, so **no person could schedule a
report in this product**, while the backend half was finished end to end: the
scheduler fires, the file lands, and since `aff5f079d` the named staff are told.

**THE MECHANISM IS TWO PROSE SENTENCES THAT NOBODY COMPARED.** `ReportViewer
Page.tsx`'s own exceptions trailer recorded *"Schedule is phase 5"*. The brief
says `P4.4`, **phase 4**, and p034's DOORS row is unambiguous: *"One: the
Schedule button on `2·1`."* The lane that BUILT the dialog and the lane that
OWNED the door each wrote down a different phase, in their own file, and
**nothing in this repo compares one file's prose with another's.** `G13` could
not see it either — it asks whether a declared prop is PASSED, never whether a
built component is MOUNTED. That is hard-won law 2 for a DIALOG rather than for
a prop, and it is a new shape of it.

**WHERE THE DOOR WENT, AND WHY THERE.** `ScheduleDoor.tsx`, a component and not
inline glue (B14 rule 43), mounted in `PageHeader`'s `secondaryActions` on `2·1`
— which draws it LEFT of *Edit*, matching p028's drawn action row *Schedule ·
Edit · Save as*. `4·1` deliberately has no *+ New schedule* control (p040: one
there *"would need a report picker that `2·3` gets for free"*), so this button
is the only door and its absence was total.

**IT IS DISABLED OVER A REFUSAL, NOT HIDDEN** — p034: *"you cannot schedule a
refusal"*. A refused or unproducible report still draws the control, greyed,
with **no tooltip and no sentence**: why a control is inert is RATIONALE and
B14 rule 33 puts rationale at zero words on screen.

**`DEF-REP-6907`, FIXED IN THE SAME FILE.** The viewer mapped EVERY 403 to a
fixed helper, `reports.denied` — *"Your role cannot run reports."* — which is
**false for the clerk it was shown to**: `P5.9` refuses ONE report by role
(`BR-REP-023`) and that clerk draws 44 of the 45 cards two clicks earlier. The
six-word sentence already travelled from the server, so the fix STOPS REPLACING
IT rather than authoring new copy: the module-wide refusal keeps `reports.denied`
and the per-report one now renders `reports.viewer.role_refused`.

**AND FIXING THE DOOR EXPOSED A REAL HOLE BEHIND IT — `DEF-REP-6923`.**
`POST /reports/schedules` never consulted `role_gate`. It resolved the same
definition `api.report` refuses and asked nothing, so a Billing Clerk refused
`staff-directory` at `2·1` could **schedule it and have the CSV delivered to
themselves every month**. Nothing found it because until today the endpoint was
**unreachable from the product** — no screen posted to it, so the only walk that
would have shown it was one nobody could perform. Gated in `_create`, before any
other validation, answering `role_gate.refusal` so a clerk never meets two
sentences for one fact. **A gap behind an unbuilt door is still a gap, and it
goes live the moment the door is hung** — which is the durable lesson, and the
reason the gate landed in the same commit as the button rather than after it.

## 2026-09-27 — THE SHELF TABLE GETS THE UNIT OF MEASURE, NOT THE `Service` THE BLUEPRINT DRAWS (lane MET-UOM, `DEF-MET-6911`)

**REPRODUCED AT `2.376.0`**, on `brazosbend` unit `SCW-U-001` → Assets, in a
browser at 1440 (hard-won law 6 — no gate in this repo reads rendered output).
The PO reported it from the live beta at `2.352.0`; it is **not** fixed since.

**THE SHELF TABLE IS BUILT `Asset · Type · Connection size · Meter type ·
Status · Assign`.** The blueprint (`05-prototype/Premises & Units Blueprint
2.pdf`, p68–p69, rendered as images per B14 rule 42) draws it
`Meter · Service · Size · Where it is · Status · Assign ✓`.

**THE `Service` COLUMN IS STILL NOT BUILDABLE AND IS DELIBERATELY NOT BUILT.**
`OQ-AST-12485` is **OPEN** — checked in the STATUS column, not the prose. A
shelf spare stores no service: `service_point_id` is the only place a service
lives and it exists only once the asset sits on a unit. Measured on
`brazosbend` 2026-09-27: **sixteen unassigned assets, and not one carries a
service.** A `Service` column would therefore be an em-dash on 100% of rows,
for ever — which is the PO's own third finding on this defect, arriving one
column earlier than they expected it.

**WHAT WAS BUILT INSTEAD IS THE UNIT OF MEASURE, AND CLAUDE.md HARD RULE 3 IS
THE AUTHORITY.** The shelf's four `Meter · —` rows on this tenant are
`AST-04412`, `AST-04413`, `AST-04414` (all `kgal`) and `M-5099` (`kWh`): three
water meters and one electric one, carrying **no size class at all**, rendered
identically. A clerk picking a spare for a water service had nothing on the
screen to pick by. `assets.unit` is served on every row already and is non-null
on **every one of the nine measuring spares**, so this cost no endpoint change.

**THE HEADER BECAME `Size`.** The conformance file has specified it since it
was written — *"No `Meter type` or `Connection size` columns in the inventory
panel; `Size` is one column"* — and the on-unit table above already says
`Size`. `Meter type` is KEPT: dropping a real fact is not required to close
this defect and would be a second change wearing the first one's authority.

**AND EVERY DASH ON THOSE THREE COLUMNS BECAME WORDS.** `DEF-514`'s ruling —
an em-dash cannot tell *nobody recorded it* from *the product cannot record
it* — decides the PO's third finding. `BR-AST-009` binds `MEASURING_TYPES`
only, so `CART-0099`, `BAT-0904`, `BF-0002`, `PV-0001`, `EV-0001` and
`COM-0001` correctly have no service, no size and no unit, for ever. They now
read **not measured**. A METER with a missing size or unit reads **no size
recorded** / **no unit recorded** — a gap somebody should close. One sentence
for both would have been the dash again, wearing words.

**`CART-0099` IS A SHELF SPARE HERE, NOT AN INSTALLED ROW.** The PO saw it in
the installed table on their tenant; on `brazosbend` at this branch its
`service_point_id` is null, so it stands in the assign panel. The question they
asked is answered either way: **yes, an asset can exist with no service, and
for a cart that is correct rather than missing.**

## 2026-09-27 — CAN ONE UTILITY READ ANOTHER'S REPORT SCHEDULE? NO — MEASURED ON REAL PostgreSQL 16 (lane SEC-SCHED)

**THE ANSWER FIRST: THERE IS NO LEAK.** `report_schedules` is `relrowsecurity`
AND `relforcerowsecurity` true, with one policy, `report_schedules_tenant_isolation`,
carrying BOTH halves (`USING` and `WITH CHECK`) on `polcmd = '*'`. Run as
`smartbillhub`, read out of `pg_roles` at runtime as **NOSUPERUSER,
NOBYPASSRLS**, against a `proof-db.sh` clone of the branch's migrations: a real
schedule was planted for tenant B, **tenant B's own context was proved to see
it first** (the red-first control — without it the probe measures an empty
table), and then tenant A's context asked for it three ways.

| asked from tenant A's context | answer |
|---|---|
| unfiltered `SELECT` over `report_schedules` | **0 rows**, 0 of another tenant |
| ORM `filter(pk=<tenant B's schedule>)` | **0 rows** |
| raw SQL `select count(*) … where id = …` | **0** |
| `GET /reports/schedules/{tenant B's id}` through `schedules_api.schedule_detail` | **404** |
| the same read with `app.tenant_id = ''` (no context at all) | **0 rows** — RLS denies closed |

`10-scripts/def_rep_6916_schedule_isolation_pg_proof.py` is the run, and it
REFUSES rather than passes if the role turns out to be exempt. **And the
failing case itself was then run on that same database — `1 passed, 9
deselected, in 5090s` — so the endpoint's 404 is measured twice: once by the
probe and once by the very test that reported the breach.**

**AND THE SECOND FACT MATTERS AS MUCH AS THE FIRST: THE APPLICATION LAYER DOES
NOT SCOPE THIS QUERY — IT RELIES ON RLS ALONE, DELIBERATELY.**
`schedules_api._schedules_queryset` says so in its own words: *"⚠ NO
`.filter(tenant_id=…)`, AND THAT IS NOT AN OVERSIGHT … A second enforcement in
Python would make a MISSING context look like an empty list instead of like
the bug it is."* That is lawful here (hard rule 1, RLS FORCE), and it is
written down rather than assumed **because it has a cost**: the refusal is the
database's, so **any code path that ever runs without `app.tenant_id` set is
the hole, not the query.** Measured above: with the GUC empty the read returns
zero rows rather than everything, so the failure mode is denial and not
disclosure — which is the right direction for it to fail in.

**WHAT THAT MEANS FOR THE FAILING TEST, AND IT IS THE JUDGMENT RECORDED HERE.**
`test_another_tenants_schedule_is_a_plain_404` answered `200` on the default
suite, which `config/settings/test.py` runs on in-memory SQLite — **a database
with no row-level security of any kind** (hard-won law 14). A `200` there is
consistent BOTH with a real hole AND with an application correctly relying on
RLS, so the case proved nothing in either direction: hard-won law 7's own
example, where `G5` once called 192 skips a pass.

**Two ways out were available and one of them is wrong.** Adding a
`.filter(tenant_id=…)` would turn the case green on SQLite — and would reverse
a design decision this module argued for in writing, on the authority of a red
test, without a ruling. So the case is instead marked `@pytest.mark.isolation`
and `@requires_postgres`, which is the convention `tests/isolation_helpers.py`
already owns: it now runs **where the guarantee can exist**, `G5` runs that
suite against real PostgreSQL, and `G5` half 3 FAILS on a vendor skip, so it
cannot quietly stop running. **Nothing about the product changed; what changed
is that the claim is now measured instead of asserted.**

**THREE OF THE OTHER FOUR REDS WERE THE TEST, NOT THE CODE** (`DEF-REP-6916`).
The ratified B12 r1 / 11b §3 G1 envelope is FLAT — six keys, no `error`
wrapper — so `response.data["error"]["code"]` raised `KeyError` twice;
`test_cr139_p5_8_scan_parse.py` records the identical first draft in its own
comment. And an unrendered DRF `Response` carries Python objects, so
`next_run_at` is a `datetime` and comparing it to `timezone.now().isoformat()`
raised `TypeError` — four cases earlier in the same file the same fact is
compared correctly, to `timezone.now()`.

**THE FOURTH WAS THE TEST BEING WRONG ABOUT THE MECHANISM WHILE THE CODE WAS
RIGHT ABOUT THE OUTCOME, AND IT UNCOVERED A REAL ONE.**
`test_a_schedule_whose_report_errors_keeps_its_row_and_advances` asserted
`last_job_id is None` after an unregistered resource. `core.jobs.enqueue`
ACCEPTS that payload — only the handler refuses it — so the schedule does
point at a job, and that job FAILED. ⚠ **`last_job_id is None` would have
meant the OPPOSITE**: `status_of` treats `None` as `_job()`'s *we cannot say*
and returns **`on`** — green over a report that has not run. The case now
asserts that the schedule points at a job whose status is `failed`, which is
the fact the screen reads its word from.

⚠ **AND THE FIRST REWRITE ASSERTED `status_of == failing` AND WENT RED — WHICH
IS THE USEFUL PART OF THIS ROW.** Measured: it answered **`on`**.
`tenancy.selectors.report_run` resolves a job only when its `payload.resource`
is one of the reports module's own export resources, and this fixture's
resource is deliberately `a-resource-that-is-not-registered`, so `_job()`
cannot see the failed job at all. **A real schedule always carries a resource
from a real report definition**, so the product's screen is not wrong; the
FIXTURE cannot reach the screen's question, and a case asserting `status_of`
there would fail for a reason its own name does not mention. **The
accept-RAISES path really does render `on` in the product, though, and
`fire()`'s docstring claimed the opposite: filed as `DEF-REP-6929`, not fixed
here, and that docstring is corrected in this commit.**

## 2026-09-27 — THE SERVICES CHIPS NOW SAY WHAT THEY COULD NOT SHOW (lane CUS-CHIPS, `DEF-CUS-6917`, 2.377.6)

**THE PO'S REPORT, AND THE FIRST THING THAT HAD TO BE SETTLED.** From the live
beta at 2.352.0: `AC-2026-00057` shows **two** service chips while its premises
carries **four** services. **The chips are not wrong** — they are what this
account has agreed to take (`BR-CUS-015`, `BR-CUS-672`), and the building's
list belongs to a MASTER account only (`BR-CUS-1093`). Nothing about that is
changed by this commit, deliberately; whether an ordinary account should show
its building's services is a question for the PO and not a value a lane may
choose.

**WHAT WAS ACTUALLY WRONG IS THAT THE QUESTION COULD NOT BE ANSWERED.**
`selectors.service_codes_for_accounts` dropped any open agreement whose service
point it could not resolve to a code (`if code:`) and counted nothing, so *two
chips* was the same picture whether the account took two services or took four
and the read lost two. That is CLAUDE.md hard-won law 7's fifth shape word for
word — *a declared blind spot with no number beside it is indistinguishable
from an empty one*.

**MEASURED BEFORE ANYTHING MOVED, ON REAL POSTGRESQL, AS A ROLE THAT IS NEITHER
SUPERUSER NOR BYPASSRLS** (`smartbillhub`, `rolsuper=f rolbypassrls=f`, with
`app.tenant_id` set per tenant — hard rule 1; the control is that the same role
with no setting reads 0 accounts and 75 with one). Across the two tenants in
the development database: **479 open service agreements, 479 of them resolve to
a service code, 0 drop.** So the hole is empty today — and before this change
nothing in the product could have said so.

**AND THE REPORTED CASE IS ALMOST CERTAINLY NOT A DROP AT ALL.** The same
measurement found the PO's shape reproduced honestly: `AC-2026-00001` and
`AC-2026-00003` each sit on a premises offering **six** services, on a unit
carrying **six** service points, with **three** open agreements — a move-in
that ticked half of them. That is `BR-CUS-672` behaving exactly as signed, and
it is indistinguishable on screen from a read that lost three, which is the
whole defect.

**THREE LANE JUDGMENTS, RECORDED RATHER THAN ASKED (hard-won law 13).**

1. **THE NUMBER GOES TO TWO PLACES AND NOT THREE.** A chip in the cell
   (`?2`, accessible name *2 services not shown*) tells the clerk standing in
   front of the row; a WARNING per affected account tells an operator that it
   happened at all on a page nobody opened. **A GATE WAS CONSIDERED AND
   REFUSED**: the only mechanical form it could take is a grep for `if code:`,
   which is a spelling check, and no gate in this repo reads rendered output.
   What replaces it is two suites proved RED first —
   `tests/test_def_cus_6917_service_chip_drops.py` (6 cases: 6 failed against
   the pre-fix selector, 6 passed after) and
   `07-frontend/.../AccountServiceChipsUnresolved.dom.test.tsx` (5 cases: 3
   failed with the chip suppressed, 5 passed after).
2. **THE KEY IS SERVED ON EVERY ROW, `0` INCLUDED.** A field that appeared only
   when something went wrong would be the original defect in a better coat — an
   absent field and a zero field look the same to a reader and mean opposite
   things. `_service_cells` therefore never ASSUMES zero either: handed codes
   with no drop map beside them, it asks the singular rather than claiming a
   number nobody computed.
3. **THE CELL SAYS THE FACT AND NOT THE REASON** (B14 rule 33). Four words in
   the accessible name, a `?N` glyph that carries no word of any language — the
   posture the `+N` overflow chip beside it already takes, and for the same
   G15 reason. WHY it happened lives in the docstring and the log line.

**AND THE BRIEFING'S THIRD CANDIDATE CAUSE IS NOT REACHABLE.** It supposed a
service point could carry no service code. Measured against
`information_schema` the same day: `service_points.service_id` is **NOT NULL**
with a `PROTECT` FK, `services.code` is **NOT NULL**, and
`service_agreements.service_point_id` carries a real FK — **so a service point
with no service cannot be stored and a dangling agreement cannot be stored
either.** No upstream defect was filed, because there is nothing to fix. The
PO's second screenshot — an asset with no service and no size — is a different
table and a LAWFUL state: `assets.service_point_id` is nullable on purpose for
non-measuring BTM types (`BR-AST-009`), and 13 of 188 assets on the local
six-service tenant are in it.

**ONE ASYMMETRY FOUND BY THE TEST AND WORTH MORE THAN THE TEST.** The batched
read reaches metering through `service_points_for_units` + `service_codes_for_points`;
the singular reaches it through `service_points_for` + `service_point_ref`.
**They are different doors**, so a metering outage that closes one can leave
the other open — the register and the account detail screen can disagree about
the same account without any code being wrong. Recorded here; not fixed, because
fixing it is a seam change and this is a maintenance commit.

**WHAT REMAINS OPEN.** The account DETAIL header draws its own chips through a
different component (`accountDetailHeader.AccountServiceChips`) and does not
render the count, although the server now serves it there too. That is scope
held deliberately to the reported screen, and it is stated here rather than
left to be discovered.

## 2026-09-27 — A TENANT-SETTABLE NUMBER THAT LIVES IN ANOTHER MODULE'S CONSTANT (lane REP-P5-SETTINGS, `CR-142-BRC07` `P4.6`/`P5.12`, `2.379.0`)

**The judgment, and it is the one this task was deferred on.** The Reports
Build Brief draws four Settings cards under a REPORTS heading (p047 legend ④).
One of them, *File retention*, sets a number that lives at
`apps/tenancy/exports.ARTIFACT_RETENTION_DAYS`. The previous lane read that as
a cross-module write and stopped, correctly: `B2` §2 forbids one.

**The ruling taken here: the constant was never reports'.** It governs the
PLATFORM EXPORT KERNEL — every list export in this product runs through
`apps/tenancy/exports.py`, audit's and the platform's as well as reports' — so
the tenant-settable half belongs exactly where the constant does. It is
tenancy's sixth settings family (`settings_families.REPORTS`), written and
audited by tenancy through `PUT /settings/reports`, and READ by `apps/reports`
through the seam it has had since `P3.1`. **Nothing crosses the boundary in
either direction.** The heading is presentation, and the repo already says so
in its own words: `referenceDataConfig.ts` — *"owner is not the group"* —
with `reason_codes` as the worked case, billing's and filed under Plans & Rates.

**The worked figure.** A utility keeping downloads for **3 days** moves it to
**1**. A report run **yesterday at 14:00** stops being downloadable the moment
Save is pressed — not at midnight, not on the next sweep — because retention is
evaluated against the run's timestamp and is never stored on the run. Nothing
is deleted by that write and no job re-runs; the row presents as expired and
can be run again. Moving it back to 3 makes the same file downloadable again if
it is still on disk. **That reasoning is NOT on the screen** (B14 rule 33 puts
rationale at zero words); the form states six words — *"Files are kept for 3
days"* — and the reasoning lives in `exports.artifact_retention_days`'s
docstring and in the human-review row of the same date.

**A hazard the constant did not have, found while building and fixed here.**
`JOB_ARTIFACTS_DIR` holds every tenant's files in ONE directory and
`purge_expired` swept it whole, which was harmless while retention was one
number for everybody. Per-tenant, a sweep at one utility's **1 day** would have
deleted another utility's **2-day-old** file. `purge_expired` now takes a
`prefix` — the same tenant slug `artifact_filename` already puts at the front
of every name — and the test asserts the neighbour's file SURVIVES, which is
the half that would otherwise have passed silently.

**Two of the four cards, and the other two are absent rather than promised.**
p048's TASK row splits the section on purpose: retention and the default format
land in `P4.6`, the section completes in `P5.5`. *Report groups* needs a
`report_categories` lookup handler and a `LOOKUP_LISTS` declaration that do not
exist; *Delivery* is drawn as a LIST and recipients are stored per schedule, so
a tenant-level list is a table this product does not have and Phase 5's mix says
**0 DB**. Neither is declared with `arrivesWithKey`: a "coming soon" card with
no dated owner is hard-won law 2's mirror with better manners, and there are
already two of those in that grid. `retentionDoor.dom.test.tsx` asserts both
codes resolve to NOTHING, so the day either arrives the case names itself.

**One measurement in `CR-142-BRC07` §12.4 corrected.** It reads
*"`REFERENCE_CARDS` holds **36**, so the drawing's '35 today' is one behind"*.
It holds **35** and the drawing is right. The over-count comes from grepping
`code: "` — `account_subtypes` carries a second `code:` inside its `parentList`
block, naming the list its Parent picker offers. Recorded because the next lane
would otherwise "fix" a figure in a PDF that is already correct.

**Not put to the Product Owner, deliberately (hard-won law 13).** `BR-REP-018`
has said *"3 days by default, tenant-configurable"* since 2026-08-08 and
`IS-11` names the format vocabulary; this build implements a signed rule rather
than choosing a value. The minimum of one day and the absence of a maximum are
judgments recorded here: zero days is not a shorter window but *every download
link in the product is broken*, and a maximum would be a hard cap, which
`NFR-5` forbids.

## 2026-09-27 — THE REPORTS DASHBOARD IS A NEW TAB, AND THREE THINGS ON IT ARE DELIBERATELY BLANK (lane REP-P4-DASH, `CR-142-BRC07` `P4.11`–`P4.13`, `2.380.0`)

**The PO ruling this is built to, quoted from p036 of the Reports Build Brief,
verbatim:** *"no i dont want to update existing dashboard … you can create a tab
- dont replace existing one"*. The shell's dashboard at `/{tenant}/dashboard` is
untouched by this commit: not a tile, not a label, not a column, and
`apps/reports/dashboard.py` is neither imported nor read.

**THE JUDGMENT CALLS THIS LANE MADE, each recorded here because the rules ran
out and none of them is a question that belonged to the PO (hard-won law 13).**

**1 · Three things on the screen are blank, and each is blank for its own
reason.** In plain English, with the figures:

* **Days to collect** shows *Not counted yet*. Days-sales-outstanding is the
  receivable divided by a period's billing, and no report in the catalogue of
  forty-six publishes it. This screen renders published figures and works none
  out for itself, so the tile is drawn empty with its reason rather than filled
  with a number nothing else in the product would agree with.
* **Biggest movers** shows no rows. It wants the three accounts whose usage moved
  most between two months. `Usage & Ranking` is a real, working report on this
  deployment and serves the meter reads themselves; the comparison between two
  periods is not among the figures it publishes. Its LINK stays live, because
  the report opens and is real — what is missing is the ranking.
* **Comparing against budget** is not offered, though the drawing shows it as one
  of three choices. Nothing in this product publishes a budget. The nearest
  thing is a single typed monthly revenue target the OTHER dashboard renders;
  building *budget* on that would give a real comparison on the billed tile and
  an invented one on the other three, which is a screen that is wrong in a way
  a reader cannot see.

**The alternative in all three cases was to compute the figure here, and that is
the one thing the design forbids by name** (p038: *"Nothing on this screen
computes anything. The moment a panel does its own arithmetic, the dashboard and
the report start disagreeing, and the utility stops trusting both."*).

**2 · No charting library was added, and the drawing had already ruled it.**
p038: *"there is no charting library in `07-frontend/package.json`. The bars
above are drawn in CSS … five panels do not justify a dependency, and a CSS bar
prints, scales and theme-switches for free."* Checked against `package.json`
before building: still true. Two of the three bar panels are the kit's existing
`ContributionBars`, whose denominator is already *the largest row and never the
total* — which is what the drawing asks for. The twelve-bar revenue chart is
about forty lines of CSS in its own component.

**3 · The kit's `AgeingCards` was NOT reused for the ageing panel.** It colours
the `90+` band in the danger tier by position, which is right on the Finance
ageing screen where the bands are filters a clerk presses. The drawing rules the
opposite here and argues it: colouring bands by size made *Current* — the
healthy band — come out warning-coloured because it was the biggest, and colour
that encodes magnitude reads as a judgment.

**4 · The worked figure a reviewer should check, and it is a real one.** Asking
`AR Ageing` for a DATE RANGE and asking it AS AT A DATE are not the same
question, and only one of them has an answer. Measured on this deployment's
PostgreSQL:

  * `ar_aging` over **1–30 September 2026** returns an em-dash and the words
    *"Balances do not sum across time"* for **every one of its five bands** —
    correctly, because adding one month's closing receivable to the next counts
    every account that owed money in both months twice.
  * `ar_aging` **as at 30 September 2026** returns **$8,372.06 over 26 accounts**.

A first draft of this screen asked the first way. Every ageing figure on the
dashboard, and the Outstanding tile with them, would have been a dash — with the
server answering 200, every type checking, and a test asserting *"the panel has
five bands"* passing over five dashes. Filed as `DEF-REP-6933`. The screen now
asks as-at, and the link it hands you to the full report asks as-at too, so the
panel and the report behind it cannot show different money.

**5 · Two figures shown on screen carry no reason beside them, and that is B14
rule 33 rather than an omission.** Why a figure is absent is RATIONALE, and
rationale is zero words on screen. The reason lives in the payload, in the
code's own docstrings and in this row.

## 2026-09-27 · A NAMED BASE CHARGE CODE THAT CANNOT ANSWER REFUSES, IT DOES NOT FALL BACK (`DEF-RAT-5782` · `DEF-RAT-6918`)

**THE RULING THIS IMPLEMENTS IS ALREADY SIGNED AND NOTHING NEW WAS PUT TO THE
PRODUCT OWNER** (law 13). `BR-RAT-1025` (PO 2026-09-19, verbatim: *"no this is
not correct ; So: plan → rate schedule -> charge code → base charges - this is
correct"*) says the rate schedule NAMES the charge code that owns its service's
base. What was decided here is the one thing the ruling does not state: what the
LIVE billing path does when the named code cannot answer for this account.

**THE WORKED CASE.** Three charge codes are ticked as water's base — `$8.00`,
`$19.75` and `$34.00`, all reaching every customer class. A schedule names the
`$19.75` one. Until today every bill on that schedule refused with *"3 base
charge codes for water. Scope them on Charge codes."*, because
`billing.gather._base_charge_code_for` called rating's read without the binding
and `selectors.pricing_inputs_for_version` did not publish it at all. It now
bills **`19.7500`** — a figure neither a first match (`8.00`) nor a last match
(`34.00`) produces.

**THE JUDGMENT: THE FAIL DIRECTION.** Once the binding arrives, a named code
that has been retired, un-ticked as a base, or narrowed to another customer
class can no longer answer. Two options:

* **fall back to the inferred `is_base` code.** A bill is always produced — and
  where any other base code survives, it is produced from a code the rate
  schedule's own first step does not show. `BR-RAT-088`'s failure shape exactly:
  every row individually correct, nobody able to see the total is wrong.
* **refuse that one account, naming the code.** CHOSEN.

It is chosen because it is what the RULED chain already does
(`resolution.resolve_base_charge`'s named arm raises `ChargeCodeAmountMissing`
for these same three causes) and what the ACTIVATION gate already does
(`services._guard_bound_base_charge_code`, conditions 1–4). A code broken after
activation now fails the same way as one broken before it, and `BR-BIL-055`
keeps the other accounts of the run billing.

**THE PARAGRAPH THAT SAID OTHERWISE IS CORRECTED RATHER THAN DELETED.**
`base_charge_from_charge_code` carried a comment asserting that an empty named
result *"FALLS THROUGH TO THE UNNAMED BRANCHES BELOW"* because *"that branch
already says it in the operator's own terms"*. **The branch it pointed at is
guarded by `not matches` and cannot run while other codes survive** — hard-won
law 1, and it is `DEF-RAT-6918`.

**WHAT WAS NOT DECIDED, AND IS FILED INSTEAD.** `DEF-RAT-6960` — the
rate-change impact analysis and the portal's standing charge read the same base
through `rating.seams.base_charge_for`, which takes no binding, so they now
disagree with the bill. `DEF-RAT-6961` — the activation gate admits an
ACCOUNT-LEVEL (`service_id IS NULL`) base code that the live read, which narrows
on the service, can never return. Both are real today and neither is this
lane's to answer.

**AND `DEF-RAT-6927` WAS OFFERED TO THIS LANE AND DELIBERATELY LEFT, WITH A
REASON THAT IS NOT *"no time"*.** The plan screen's *Monthly base total* reads
`$0.00` because `selectors._plan_base_subquery` sums `plan_services.base_charge`
— the column `BR-RAT-088` retired — and that file was this lane's. It is left
because **the total is not only a figure, it is a SQL SORT KEY**:
`plan_list_queryset` maps the `base_charges` sort onto the `base_total`
annotation, and `NFR-3` requires the Plans list to page and sort in SQL. Fixing
the figure honestly means resolving the base through the CHARGE CODES, narrowed
by customer class and connection size — which is a Python walk, not a subquery —
so either the sort leaves SQL or the figure and the sort start disagreeing with
each other. **That is a design decision about a paginated list, not a one-line
repair**, and taking it inside a money-path lane would have widened the blast
radius of a fix a live customer was waiting on. The row stays OPEN with this
reasoning attached to it.

## 2026-09-27 · A COLUMN SAYS WHAT KIND OF THING IT IS, AND THAT IS WHY THE DISPLAY FIX IS ONE DECISION AND NOT NINETY-FIVE

*Lane REP-WALKFIX · `DEF-REP-6899` `6900` `6901` `6902` `6903` `6891` `6925` ·
2.380.3 (`389c760ed`) and 2.380.6 (`5c4a2e911`).*

Three of the five defects the Product Owner reported — raw i18n keys, raw
database column names, six decimals and raw codes — **are one fault three
times: a value going to the screen the way the database holds it.** They were
reported as three because that is how they LOOK, and fixing them as three would
have meant thirty-three headings, then the next report's, for ever.

**THE JUDGEMENT: FIX IT WHERE THE COLUMN'S KIND IS KNOWN, WHICH IS THE
DATASET.** `apps/reports/datasets.Column` already carries `type`, `unit` and
the stored `scale` for every column of all forty-six reports. `runner._shaped`
already holds both the dataset and the served column list, and it sits on
`run()`, the one path the viewer and the export both take. So the payload
carries `column_meta` and the screen renders by KIND. The alternative on the
table was extending `MONEY_COLUMNS`, the hand-typed map that named five reports
out of forty-six — which is what the sibling fix `DEF-REP-6963` did for R34 the
same afternoon, correctly and for one report. **A map has to be extended for
every report that does not exist yet; a declaration does not.**

**WHAT IS NOT CENTRAL, AND WHY THAT IS NOT A FAILURE.** The WORDS are not
derivable from anything — 89 keys in eleven catalogues, authored by hand. A
column's KIND is a fact the dataset knows; a column's NAME in Indonesian is not.

**NOTHING ROUNDS UPSTREAM AND NOTHING MAY.** The queries return stored
decimals, the wire keeps every digit, and only the last inch before a pair of
eyes trims. That is CLAUDE.md's *round only at finalization/display*, and it is
what keeps a ❄️ FROZEN B4/B5 figure reconcilable against the report quoting it.

### TWO THINGS DELIBERATELY LEFT, EACH WITH A REASON THAT IS NOT "no time"

**THE AUDIT TRAIL'S ACTION AND RECORD NAMES (`DEF-REP-6981`, filed).** Every
other vocabulary this lane worded is CLOSED and finite — the close pack's four
tie-outs, the disconnect case's three statuses. The audit trail's is OPEN: its
codes come from whatever any module writes to `audit_log`, and the seven
`work.*` values `DEF-REP-6900` lists are a sample, not the set. **A catalogue
that words some rows and leaves others raw reads as broken DATA rather than as
a gap in the WORDS**, which is worse than the honest gap. It needs the audit
module to publish its vocabulary the way `datasets.py` publishes a column type
— a list a test can walk — and that is an owner's decision, not a patch.

**THE LEDGER `reference` STRING `opening_balance`.** It looks exactly like a
stored code and it is not one: `reference` is free text on a journal line, and
the demo book happens to hold a snake_case string there. **Translating it would
put a word on a customer's own reference.** Left as data.

### AND THIS LANE'S OWN CHECK WAS BLIND TO ONE OF THE FIVE

`rep_walkfix_display_walk.mjs` reported **0 raw i18n keys over a live one**.
`document.body.textContent` joins sibling elements with nothing between them, so
the service order's subhead reads `2026-09-30cells.basis.raised` in one string
and a `\b` anchor cannot match between `0` and `c` — both word characters. The
check was not lying; it could not see the start of the string. It was found by
photographing the screen the check had just passed, which is hard-won law 6
catching hard-won law 7's fifth shape. **The detector reads per ELEMENT now**,
and the reasoning is in its own comment so the next reader does not restore the
faster version.
