## 2026-09-28 · THE COMPARISON WORKTREE WAS AT THE WRONG COMMIT, AND THE FIRST LINT VERDICT WAS WRONG

Recorded because the mistake is the useful part. To date 111 eslint errors as
pre-existing, a second worktree was made at the base commit and linted: it
reported **100**, an 11-error difference in two files this lane never touched,
which read exactly like a real regression.

**`git worktree add --detach <path> <sha>` had landed it on a different commit**
— `d8c4bc1cb`, not `8bb17b5f2` — and the output had been sent to `/dev/null`. The
give-away was a file that **did not exist** in the comparison tree at all.
Re-checked out at the right sha, the base reports **111**, and a normalised diff
of the two findings sets is **empty in both directions**.

**The lesson is CLAUDE.md law 12's, in a tool nobody suspects:** every check that
dates a red measures against a baseline, and *a baseline is a claim about which
commit you are standing on*. Suppressing a command's output is how that claim
stops being checkable. **Do not `/dev/null` a `worktree add`, and print the sha
you actually got before trusting anything you measure in it.**

## 2026-09-28 · DEPLOYMENT, BACKEND HALF: the probe answers first, the deploy stops migrating in every task

**`CR-144-BRC07`, version `2.388.0`.** Built from the three rulings recorded
earlier the same day. **Nothing here went back to the PO** — every one of these
is ours to decide and write down (hard-won law 13); what IS going to them is the
human-review row, which asks for two judgments rather than for the mechanics.

### The 400 and the 301, measured before anything was built

`tests/test_health.py` was written first and run first. Both failures are the
production failure, reproduced:

```
AssertionError: 400 for Host: 10.0.1.23 — Django refused the balancer's own
                address before the probe could answer
AssertionError: 301 — the probe was redirected instead of answered
```

The first is `ALLOWED_HOSTS`: the balancer dials the task's **private IP**, the
app knows only `api-smart360.bynry.com`, and Django validates the host in
`HttpRequest.get_host()` **before any URL is resolved** — so a health VIEW can
never be reached, whatever it is mounted on. The second is `SECURE_SSL_REDIRECT`,
which `SecurityMiddleware` applies and which the balancer (speaking plain HTTP to
port 8000) would read as a failed check.

**So the middleware is FIRST, and that is a measured requirement rather than a
preference.** `core/health.py` · `MIDDLEWARE[0]`.

⚠ **AND IT IS A LIVENESS CHECK THAT MUST NEVER BECOME A READINESS CHECK.** A probe
that queries the database turns a slow database into a **total** outage: every
task fails, every task is replaced, and the monitoring manufactures the incident.
Rather than leave that as a comment — hard-won law 1, a comment claiming a
guarantee is not the guarantee —
`test_health_answers_with_the_database_unreachable` makes every connection
attempt raise and still demands a `200`. An edit that adds a `SELECT 1` goes red
there.

### H3, verified and NOT changed — with one thing that was wrong

`health` was already reserved in `core.tenancy.NON_TENANT_SEGMENTS` and
`apps.tenancy.selectors.RESERVED_SUBDOMAINS`, and `test_be01_tc16` already holds
the two in step. **Nothing was changed there.** What WAS wrong is the comment
beside it — *"health — the load-balancer probe (09-infra; no Django route yet)"* —
which is now amended, because there is a probe and there is still no route and
there never will be one. Left alone, it would have sent the next reader to
`config/urls.py` looking for something that is not there.

### H4 — where `migrate` went, and why the sweep went with it

`docker-entrypoint.sh` ran `migrate` in **every** web task. Three faults at once
with two tasks: a concurrent migration with no advisory lock (the loser exits and
is restarted into the same race); a health check that fails for as long as the
migration runs, so the balancer kills the task **partway through the migration it
is waiting for**; and DDL executed by an ordinary scale-out.

It is `docker-release.sh` now — a one-off ECS task the pipeline runs to
completion before the rollout.

**Two judgments recorded rather than left to be inferred:**

* **THE OQ-087 REFERENCE-DATA SWEEP MOVED WITH IT.** That ruling says *"automatic
  post-migrate, across all tenants"*. Left in the web entrypoint it would run in
  every task at once, and in a fresh environment it would run **before** the
  migrate — the one order the ruling forbids. Keeping the two adjacent is what
  keeps "post-migrate" true.
* **THE DEF-622 TENANT-GUC CHECK MOVED TOO.** It is a PRE-MIGRATE check and says
  so in its own last line (*"the migrate below will report the real connection
  error"*). There is no migrate below any more, so left behind it would have
  described a step that no longer happens — this repo's most-filed rot.

**What stayed, and the rule that decides it:** every check in the entrypoint is
about THIS process's ability to serve safely — the settings module, the hosts,
and the **RLS-enforcement check that refuses to boot**. A release task cannot
answer any of those on a web task's behalf. A task whose role bypasses row-level
security must not serve, whatever some other container was doing an hour ago.

### X2 — the guard CORS does not give you, and the blind spot it declares

Three innocent facts make one cross-site request forgery: `app-*.bynry.com` and
`api-*.bynry.com` are the same **site** (a cookie's "site" is the registrable
domain, `bynry.com`), so `SameSite=Lax` does not separate them; DRF's default
parsers accept form posts; and `IdentitySessionAuthentication` is a custom cookie
class with **no CSRF check**. **CORS does not close it** — a cross-origin
`<form method=post>` is SENT with the victim's cookie and the browser merely
hides the reply, after the write.

`core/origin_guard.py` refuses a state-changing request whose `Origin` is not
ours, in middleware, before any view runs.

⚠ **A REQUEST WITH NO `Origin` AT ALL IS LET THROUGH, AND THERE IS A TEST SAYING
SO.** `curl`, `/api/partner/v1/…` and inbound payment webhooks send none; a
browser always sends one on these methods. Refusing a missing header would break
every integration we sell and defend nothing — the attack requires a browser.
That is law 7's *say what your check does not cover*, and the test exists so the
allowance cannot drift shut by accident and take the partner surface with it.

⚠ **THE REFUSAL BODY IS UNREACHABLE BY ANY BROWSER, SO IT CARRIES NO CATALOGUE
KEY.** Only a cross-origin caller can trigger it, and the browser hides the
response from the script that provoked it. Adding `errors.cross-origin-refused`
to eleven locale catalogues would be eleven strings no clerk can ever see —
written down here rather than left as an omission somebody later "fixes".

### X1/X3 — one origin, and one setting for `Secure`

`CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS` defaults to **empty**, so a deployment that forgets it
grants nothing loudly rather than everything quietly (law 3). **`*` is not a
laxer option, it is a broken one:** `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` and
`Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true` are mutually exclusive by specification
and the session cookie IS the credential — it would present as *"signed in, and
every call is 401"*.

`AUTH_COOKIE_SECURE` defaults **True** and is read at all three cookie sites.
**Neither cookie NAME moved.** ⚠ **AND LAW 4 BITES IN THE UNUSUAL DIRECTION
HERE:** a host that already has a `.env` has no such line, so it takes the code
default `true` — right for every deployed environment and **wrong for a local
`make up` over `http://localhost`**, where sign-in will appear to succeed and the
next request will be anonymous with no error anywhere. `.env.example` says so at
the line.

### `SECURE_SSL_REDIRECT` defaults OFF, deliberately

The ALB's own HTTP listener redirects one hop earlier and cannot loop. Turned on
here with `SECURE_PROXY_SSL_HEADER` missing or a listener that strips
`X-Forwarded-Proto`, it is an infinite redirect on every page. And
`SECURE_PROXY_SSL_HEADER` is **only safe because nothing but the ALB can reach
port 8000** — that security-group rule is part of the setting, not separate from
it, and is written into the runbook beside it.

`SECURE_HSTS_SECONDS` defaults to **0 = not sent**, because HSTS is the one
header you cannot take back.

### The version literal

`07-frontend/package.json` — the one source of truth — was moved to `2.388.0` by
lane DEP-FRONTEND. `06-backend/pyproject.toml` still read `2.387.1`, which is the
derived copy drifting exactly as its own comment block predicts it will whenever
one of the two moves alone. **It was made to agree; no version was allocated
here**, because two lanes each allocating is `DEF-GOV-3756`'s collision.

## 2026-09-28 · SIX SESSION AND LOCKOUT RULES BECOME PER-UTILITY SETTINGS, WITHIN FIXED LIMITS — `CR-145-BRC08`

**PO ruling, verbatim: *"Im okay with these limit"***, accepting this table:

| Setting | Before | Admin can choose | Default |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sign-out after inactivity | 30 / 60 / 240 / 480 min | **15 / 30 / 45 / 60 min** | **60** |
| Hard limit after sign-in | 12 h, fixed | **4 to 12 hours** | **12** |
| Offer *"Keep me signed in"* at all | always offered | **on / off per utility** | **on** |
| How long *"Keep me signed in"* lasts | 30 days, fixed | **1 to 30 days** | **30** |
| Wrong passwords before lockout | 5, fixed | **3 to 10** | **5** |
| Lockout length | 15 min, fixed | **5 to 60 minutes** | **15** |

**Who may touch them is UNCHANGED from today:** only the System Admin may
change them, the Executive may view them, the Billing Clerk cannot see them.

### Ruling 2 — THE CUSTOMER PORTAL KEEPS FOLLOWING THE STAFF SETTING

**PO, verbatim: *"Yes"***, to *"keep following it. One setting is less for an
admin to get wrong."* **The portal gets NO setting of its own**, and its fixed
12-hour hard limit (`apps/portal/session.py:105`, `ABSOLUTE_LIFETIME_HOURS = 12`)
must read the utility's hard-limit setting instead. The portal's idle check
already reads the staff setting, so this makes the pair consistent rather than
introducing a new dependency.

### Ruling 3 — DEFAULTS EQUAL TODAY'S VALUES, WITH ONE DELIBERATE EXCEPTION

Nothing changes for any utility on the day this ships. ⚠ **THE EXCEPTION IS THAT
240 AND 480 MINUTES ARE WITHDRAWN**, so a utility sitting on either moves to
**60**. That is a real behaviour change for those tenants — their staff are
signed out up to seven hours earlier than before — and it is the one part of
this change that is not invisible. The migration writes **one audit row per
utility moved** and prints how many it moved, so the number is a fact somebody
can check rather than an assumption.

⚠ **THE STRICTER DEFAULTS FOR NEW UTILITIES WERE OFFERED AND NOT TAKEN UP** — a
7-day *"keep me signed in"* and a 30-minute inactivity timeout. **Do not
introduce them.** A default that was declined is not a default awaiting
implementation, and this line exists so nobody reads the proposal as the ruling.

### Ruling 4 — TWO RULES ARE DELIBERATELY NOT SETTINGS

**Cookie lifetime follows *"Keep me signed in"*** rather than becoming a seventh
setting: ticked, the cookie's `max_age` equals the utility's renewal window;
not ticked, the cookie ends when the browser closes.

⚠ **AND THAT FIXES A LIVE BUG RATHER THAN ADDING A FEATURE.** Verified in the
code: all three `set_cookie` calls — `identity/api.py:183`,
`tenancy/api.py:215`, `portal/api.py:379` — pass no expiry at all. So **today
*"Keep me signed in"* dies when the browser closes**, which is the one thing it
exists to prevent. The server-side 30-day refresh was doing its job and the
cookie carrying it was not.

**Ending sessions immediately on sign-out, password change and deactivation
stays FIXED.** It is a safety guarantee, and a guarantee an admin can switch off
is not one.

### What was verified in the code before this was written

`LOCKOUT_MAX_FAILED = 5`, `LOCKOUT_MINUTES = 15`, `ABSOLUTE_SESSION_HOURS = 12`,
`TRUSTED_DEVICE_REFRESH_DAYS = 30` and `SESSION_TIMEOUT_OPTIONS = (30, 60, 240,
480)` all sit in `apps/identity/services.py` at lines 66–76, each already
carrying the `BR-IDN-025` or `BR-IDN-026` comment that ties it to the rule this
entry amends. `SecurityPolicy` (`security_policies`, one row per tenant) already
holds `session_timeout_minutes` with `default=60`, so five of the six settings
are new columns on a table that exists.

⚠ **`TEMP_PASSWORD_VALID_DAYS = 7` AND THE PASSWORD RULES ARE NOT IN THIS
CHANGE** and stay fixed — they sit in the same block and on the same screen,
which is exactly why they are named here.

## 2026-09-28 (late) · THE TWO CR-145 QUESTIONS LEFT OPEN WITH THE PO — THE RECOMMENDATION TAKEN, NOT RE-ASKED — `CR-145-BRC08`

**Why this is a judgment and not a ruling.** Both questions were put to the PO on
2026-09-28 and the session ended (credits) before an answer. The PO's instruction to
the next session, verbatim: *"Two questions are open with the PO. Do not re-ask them —
the handover records each with a recommendation. Pick the recommendation, write down
that you did, and carry on."* Hard-won law 13 says the same thing on its own terms. So
both are decided HERE, by the coordinator, on the recommendation recorded in
`12-governance/25-handover-2026-09-28-evening.md` §1, and either is reversible by a
single PO sentence.

**1 · Switching *Keep me signed in* off, or shortening its window, does NOT end
sessions that are already open. They run out on their own.** The admin's tool for
forcing it is the existing *Sign out all devices*. **Worked:** an admin at a utility
with 40 staff shortens the window from 30 days to 7 at 10:00. A clerk who ticked the
box on day 20 of the old window keeps signing in silently until their NEXT renewal
check, which now refuses anything older than 7 days — so they are asked for a password
at their next request after 10:00 rather than on day 30. Nobody is signed out at
10:00, including the admin who made the change, which is the reason given: ending all
sessions at once signs out the person still on the Settings screen. The cookie
lifetime already set in a browser is not rewritten; the SERVER's renewal check is what
enforces the new window. This is also exactly what the release note already promises
(*"nobody is forced to sign out"*).

**2 · Utilities moved from 240 or 480 minutes to 60 are TOLD BEFORE THE RELEASE
SHIPS.** A staff member signed out four to eight times sooner with no warning reads as
a fault. **Worked:** a clerk on a 480-minute timeout who steps away for 90 minutes is
signed in when they come back today and signed out after the release. This is an
OPERATIONAL step, not code: the migration prints the count of utilities it moved and
writes one audit row per utility naming the old value, so the list of whom to tell is
a query, and the deploy runbook for this release carries the instruction to send the
notice first. **No in-product banner is built** — that would be new scope nobody
asked for.

Neither choice changes a signed figure, and neither is on a money path.

### 3 · AN ALREADY-SERVED ADDRESS: AN ERROR AND A BLOCKED CONTINUE, AND IT FIRES ONLY ON THE EXACT UNIT

**PO verbatim, in two parts.** First: *"if premises is found - then it cannot be new connect
request; it will be move in request in such case"*. Then, asked what the screen should DO about it:
*"Just display the error and show the message; next step will be blocked"*. Then, asked **which
case triggers it**, the PO chose **(a)**.

**What it settles, and the (a) matters more than the rest.** The error fires **only when the exact
unit already has that service.** A building that is served, with units that are not, **is still a
New Connect** — so all three scope choices keep working on it. The clerk is shown the error and
**Continue is blocked**; **nothing routes them anywhere automatically and nothing is carried over**
into a move-in. They are told, and they decide.

⚠ **Read the two halves together or the first one alone will build the wrong thing.** *"If premises
is found it cannot be new connect"* taken on its own would refuse every unserved unit in a served
building, which is the ordinary case at an apartment complex.

### 6 · THE EXTERNAL SYSTEM REFERENCE STAYS FREE TEXT; THE MODE BECOMES A DROPDOWN

**PO verbatim, on the reference:** *"it should free text"* — offered as *(b) Free text as today*
and taken. **Not a dropdown.** ⚠ **This was the answer to a question about what would FILL such a
dropdown, and the answer is that nothing would**, which is why it stays as it is.

**And on Mode, said in the same breath — *"and this one also"*, of Mode: yes, a dropdown.** Its
options are *Our crew did it* · *External system* · *We schedule it*, the third disabled while the
Work module's scheduling is unreleased. ⚠ **A disabled option is disabled by a real check, per
answer 16 below** — not by a value typed into the code.

### 7 · THE UTILITY'S OWN ACCOUNT FIELDS MERGE INTO THE SEARCH CUSTOMER ID SECTION, AND THE CLERK FILLS THEM

**What it settles.** *Account details* — the extra fields each utility sets up for itself in
Settings — stop being a section of their own and sit **inside the Search customer ID block**. **The
CLERK fills them.** A list field offers the utility's own list; a text field is typed. **Nothing
appears if the utility set none up, and none is required unless the utility said so.** ⚠ **The
three fields on the drawing (*Service area*, *Rate class code*, *Legacy account no.*) are an
EXAMPLE of one utility's list and are not a specification** — B14 rule 37: a figure in a drawing is
an illustration. **When the search finds an existing customer, anything already held against them
arrives filled in and can be changed.**

### 8 · DOCUMENTS MOVE DOWN, GAIN A DOCUMENT NUMBER COLUMN, AND LOSE TWO COLUMNS UNTIL THE CONNECTION EXISTS

**PO verbatim, on the two empty columns:** *"keep today's behaviour and hide the two columns until
creation"*.

**Three things at once, and the middle one is a correction of ours.**

**(a) Placement.** The Documents block moves **below Co-applicant and Mailing address**, so the
step reads Owner → Gov-ID → Communication → Co-applicant → Mailing → Documents → Search customer ID
→ Reference & Work.

**(b) A Document number column is ADDED**, showing the **last four**, for a box the form already
asks for. ⚠ **`draftDocumentRows()`'s own comment still says New Connect does not ask for a document
number, and that is STALE** — the box exists and the comment outlived it. Hard-won law 1: a comment
is a note, never a guarantee, and nothing re-reads it.

**(c) *Uploaded by* and *State* are HIDDEN on the wizard, not filled with provisional values.** The
DATA behaviour is **ratified unchanged**: nothing is filed until the connection is created, so there
is genuinely no uploader and no time, and *not_checked* prints blank by the PO's own ruling of
2026-09-22 (*verified* or *rejected*, no third word). **Only the presentation moves** — the file is
filed right after creation, and both columns then show the real uploader and time on the record.
(`DEF-CUS-7603`.)

### 9 · THE MAILING ADDRESS FOLLOWS THE US STANDARD, USING THE BLOCK THE PRODUCT ALREADY HAS

**PO verbatim:** *"this should be in line with USA addess standards"*.

**Built with the existing `UsAddressFields` block** — the one move-in and new account already use:
street address · apt/suite/other · city · state · ZIP. **Nothing is required**, and the **ZIP is
checked for five digits or ZIP+4.** ⚠ **A second copy of an address block is the failure here, not
a missing one** — the product has one and it is used.

⚠ **AND THIS IS A MAILING ADDRESS, WHICH IS THE ONE LAWFUL SECOND ADDRESS.** Hard rule 8 stores an
address on `premises` and nowhere else; `customers.addresses` `kind='mailing'` is one of its three
named exceptions, because where the BILL goes is a different fact from where the service is — for a
landlord it is another building entirely. **Nothing here puts an address on any other entity.**

### 10 · *UNIT, APT. OR SUITE* IS ENABLED ON STEP 2, AS PART OF THE POSTAL ADDRESS

**PO verbatim:** *"why have you disabled it if it is part of premise address then it should be
there"*.

**Enabled and optional.** It is part of the building's postal address. ⚠ **The units themselves are
still named on step 3** — this box is not a unit list and must not become one. Hard rule 8 holds
unchanged: **a unit refines a premises by LABEL, not by address**, and nothing here gives a unit an
address column.

### 11 · THE RECORD GAINS LATITUDE, LONGITUDE AND A VERIFIED TICK — ALL OPTIONAL

**PO verbatim:** *"you should include lat and long and verified tag - all these will be options"*.

**Three optional fields on step 2's record block**, beside the parcel/GIS reference and the read
route. **The point shown is the BUILDING's**, and hard rule 8's coordinate clause already allows a
unit to carry its own later (`BR-MET-1162`, PO 2026-09-08) — so **every screen showing a point says
which of the two it is showing.** That sentence is part of the rule, not decoration.

### 12 · SERVICES ARE ONE MULTI-SELECT, AND THE PLAN IS SHOWN IN FULL — AS LABEL/VALUE PAIRS

**PO verbatim, twice.** On the plan: *"you ahve to show more details of plan and Utility services
here"*. On **how** to show it: *"we dont display it like this at other places we will ahve to follow
UI rules"*.

**The services picker becomes ONE multi-select dropdown with no search**, replacing three controls
doing one job — chips with an x, an *Add a service…* box and a second dropdown. (`DEF-CUS-7604`.)

**The plan is shown in full**: code, status and version, effective dates, account type, budget
billing, minimum bill, description; and **each service shows how the plan prices it** — base charge,
minimum, and whether it is charged outside the city. A service the plan misses gets its own row.

⚠ **AS LABEL/VALUE PAIRS, NOT INPUT BOXES, AND THAT IS THE SECOND QUOTE ABOVE.** Facts the clerk
cannot change are not drawn as fields anywhere else in this product, and B14 rule 44 gives the UI
standard the win over a drawing on how a thing is BUILT. ⚠ **AND NO MONTHLY TOTAL IS WORKED OUT ON
THIS SCREEN** — hard rule 2: money is multiplied and rounded once, on the server. The *WON'T COVER*
warning when the plan misses a chosen service is KEPT.

### 13 · STEP 3 IS ONE COMMON SELECTION AND THEN ONE TABLE, GROUPED BY UNIT, WITH A REQUIRED APPLY TO ALL

**PO verbatim, on the grouping:** *"grouped by units"*. On whether a row stays editable after the
bulk action: *"this is correct"*. On the two buttons needing their own drawings: *"you ahve to show
screens what wil happen when user press Add row and add work order - screens are required"*.

**What it settles, in five parts.**

**(a) One common selection at the top** — units from/to, occupancy, target activation date, include
a common-area unit — then **one table**, a row per unit and service.

**(b) GROUPED BY UNIT.** The unit is named once at the head of its group.

**(c) Short column names, ruled:** **Unit · Kind · Service · Asset · Size · Qty · Work order ·
Completes · Occupancy.** ⚠ **`Qty` is DRAWN and NOT BUILT** — see the open question at the end.

**(d) *Apply to all* is REQUIRED before Continue, and rows STAY EDITABLE afterwards.** Both halves
matter: required, because a clerk could reach the next step with most rows unfilled; editable,
because three units may take a 1" meter and the fifteenth a 2". (`DEF-CUS-7606`, `7607`.)

**(e) *Add row* and *Add work order* each got their own drawn screen at the PO's request**, and
neither opens a dialog: the row is added **in place, at the bottom of the group you were in**. A
work order that belongs to the build rather than to a service point becomes its own row with
Service, Asset and Size reading *—*, and an *Applies to* choice of whole build, one unit or one
service point. Only **published** templates are offered; a draft cannot be used.

### 14 · OCCUPANCY MOVES ONTO THE UNIT ROWS, AND THE REVIEW STEP STOPS ASKING IT

**PO verbatim:** *"why dot you keep this with units itself"*.

**Occupancy sits on the unit rows on step 3**, with its four real choices — *Vacant, service off* ·
*Vacant, base charges only* · *Landlord-billed between tenants* · *Open an account now* — set once
in the common selection and editable per row. **The review step SHOWS it and no longer ASKS it**,
which also removes four explanatory lines that were a B14 rule 33 breach. (`DEF-CUS-7613`.)

### 15 · A COMMON-AREA UNIT TAKES THE PREMISE PLAN — AND THIS CLOSES `OQ-CUS-12391`

**PO verbatim:** *"simialr to unit - apply same plan that we have given to premises"*.

⚠ **THIS CLOSES A QUESTION THE CODE HAS BEEN CARRYING SINCE 2026-09-16**, minted when the PO moved
the plan question to step 2 (*"plans are not required here"*) and both step-5 pickers went with it,
leaving `planCommonArea` set by nothing. **`OQ-CUS-12391`, option (a): the build's one plan covers
every unit, the common area included.** A common area is a unit like any other for pricing.

**What it was weighed against, so nobody re-opens it:** the objection to (a) was that a common area
takes a different set of services — the blueprint's own example is electric and water and **no
sewer**, *"there is nothing to drain from a hallway and a car park"* — so a dwelling plan applied to
it prices a hallway on a tariff nobody chose. **The PO has now chosen it**, and step 2's coverage
check computes against ALL the premise's services, so the *WON'T COVER* warning still fires. The
warning warns and does not block, which is unchanged and is the honest residual.

**What it replaces in the code:** `commitPlanOf` maps `unit.isCommonArea ? draft.planCommonArea :
draft.planApartments` and `planCommonArea` is never set. It becomes the premise plan for every unit.
⚠ **Plan is therefore NOT a column on step 3's table** — every row takes the same plan, and drawing
a column for it would re-introduce the second plan question the PO removed.

**Closing it is a FAN-OUT and not a status edit.** Every surface naming it was found by grep and
walked in one commit: the register row's **status** AND its **body** (which described a world where
nothing is chosen and listed three costed options — left alone, it would tell the next lane to
stub), this entry, and `04-docs/05-modules/04-metering/02-business-rules.md`. **No epic, execution
plan or story frontmatter names it** — verified, not assumed. ⚠ **One surface is owned by another
lane and is named rather than touched:** `07-frontend/src/features/customers/`
`NewConnectPlansStep.tsx:23`, whose Trace block still reads *"`OQ-CUS-12391` … OPEN; nothing here
chooses a value for it"*. **A Trace citing a closed question as open instructs the next lane to
stub**, so it is task `T7` of `CR-150-BRC09`.

### 16 · *WHO IS BILLED* KEEPS ALL THREE OPTIONS ON SCREEN, AND A DISABLED ONE IS DISABLED BY A REAL CHECK

**PO verbatim, reversing a proposal to remove the two that cannot be chosen:** *"this is wring -
keep previous options"*. And, on which payer is offered today: *"owner account only"*.

**Both halves are the ruling.** All three — *the owner's account* · *each unit's bill* · *the
connection* — **stay on screen**; **only the owner's account can be chosen today**; and **a disabled
option is disabled by a REAL CHECK against what exists, never by a value typed into the code.**

⚠ **THE SECOND HALF IS THE DEFECT THE PO WAS ASKING ABOUT — bug 11.** `NewConnectChargesStep.tsx`
passes **`available={false}` as a hardcoded literal** at both sites, under two sentences stating
facts nobody computed: *"Those accounts do not exist."* and *"Nobody can settle this debt."* That is
hard-won law 2's mirror — a live screen behind a dead control — **and `G13` cannot see it**: G13
asks whether a prop is PASSED, and a literal `false` is passed. **Nothing anywhere asks whether a
refusal is still true.** The day those accounts do exist, nothing goes red. (`DEF-CUS-7610`.)

### 17 · COMMUNICATION AND ACCOUNT PREFERENCES ARE COLLECTED, AND THEY SPLIT ACROSS TWO STEPS

**PO verbatim:** *"youa re also not asking for coommunciation and customer preferences while
creating for this customer/account"*, and then, of the drawn block: *"Communication NEW - these are
correct"*.

**Split, deliberately, and the split is the ruling:**

* **On step 1, beside the email and phone** — language, paperless bill, SMS reminders. They belong
  with the way the product will contact the person. ⚠ *A bill is always printed* is a fact, not a
  preference, and is stated where the tick is.
* **On step 4, with the money** — autopay, tax exemption with its certificate number and expiry.
  They belong with billing.

### 18 · THE ONE-TIME CHARGES REACH THE BOOKS AT CREATION, IN THE SAME ACT — AND THE PAYMENT WITH THEM

**PO verbatim:** *"we create entries in books"*, and, asked when: *"do it at creation once
submitted"*. And on the payment fields: *"based on payment type we nedd to give all paymnet
fields"*.

**This is the largest piece of new work in the whole change and it is a money path.**

**What is ruled.** Pressing **Create connection** writes, in ONE act: the connection, **an invoice
on the owner's account for the one-time charges, due after the payment terms**, and **the payment if
one was taken**. The sentence put to the PO and accepted: *"It is one act: if the books entry cannot
be written, the connection is not created either."*

⚠ **WHAT IT SUPERSEDES, QUOTED FROM THE CODE BECAUSE IT IS A MONEY PATH.** In
`06-backend/apps/metering/connections.py`, when `_post_connection_quote` cannot post,
`commit_connection` takes `quote_total` **from the client**, saves it, sets
**`one_time_charge_invoice_no` to `None`**, appends an `absence` — **and the commit carries on.** So
a build can be created today with its money remembered as a figure on the build and **no invoice
anywhere**: nothing reaches Billing, nothing reaches Finance, and nobody is ever asked for it. On a
build the size of the drawn example that is **`$1,035.00` that exists on one screen and in no
ledger.** Five refusal codes reach that branch — `build_names_no_charge`,
`quote_has_no_chargeable_line`, the payer's own code, `quote_payment_terms_not_captured` and
`billing_quote_door_unpublished`.

⚠ **A BUILD THAT NAMES NO CHARGE HAS NOTHING TO WRITE AND IS UNAFFECTED.** The rule bites where
there IS an entry to write and it fails. **Stating that boundary is part of the ruling**, because
*"the connection is not created"* read without it would refuse every build that raises no fee.

⚠ **PAYMENT TERMS KEEP NO DEFAULT — `BR-BIL-024`, PO ruling 2026-08-23, UNCHANGED AND RESTATED
BECAUSE FOUR NEW FIELDS NOW SURROUND IT.** A guessed due date starts a late-fee clock on a real
invoice. **Payment fields by payment type:** payment option (*No payment now* · Cash · Cheque · Card
· Bank transfer), amount, payment date, and a reference whose LABEL follows the option — *Cheque
number* for a cheque. (`DEF-CUS-7611`.)

⚠ **TWO EXISTING TESTS ASSERT THE SUPERSEDED TRUTH AND ARE NAMED HERE SO THEY ARE NOT DISCOVERED
LATER:** `06-backend/tests/test_w6_connections.py:1831`
(`assert result["manifest"]["one_time_charge_invoice_no"] is None`) and
`06-backend/tests/test_po20260921_a_build_prices_itself.py:303`. **The first will go on passing over
a product that has moved**, which is the worst kind; the second is still correct for the
no-charge case and needs its REASON amended, not its figure.

### ⛔ STILL OPEN, AND NOTHING MAY ANSWER IT — `OQ-CUS-12770`

**WHICH QUANTITIES WERE 1, 2 AND 15?** The PO reported that every charge line reads **qty 3** — the
unit count — while they had entered **1, 2 and 15** on an earlier step. **The PO has not said which
numbers those were, and nobody may choose.**

**Why it cannot be inferred, though it is tempting.** Step 4's own summary prints *Units 3 · 1, 2,
15*, so 1, 2 and 15 may simply be the **unit LABELS** and the counted 3 may be right. Or they may be
**per-charge quantities** — one connection fee, two same-day visits, fifteen tamper seals — in which
case every line on the invoice is wrong. **A Qty column is drawn on step 3 and may already be the
answer; it is not built until the PO rules**, because it multiplies a price on a real invoice and a
guess in billing becomes a silent production error.

**Recorded as `OQ-CUS-12770`, OPEN**, and cited wherever the Qty column is built.

## 2026-09-28 (late) · ⛔ A BUILD GETS ITS OWN PAGE AGAIN — THE 2026-09-04 "ONE DESTINATION" RULING IS SUPERSEDED IN ITS FIRST CLAUSE AND IN NOTHING ELSE — `CR-151-BRC09`

**THE RULING.** The Product Owner was shown three ways to give a clerk the whole of a build in one
place, in plain English, with what each one costs:

* **(A)** leave it — the build's facts stay spread across the premises and the account;
* **(B)** a summary panel on the New connects list, opening under the row;
* **(C)** a full detail page per build, with tabs.

**They chose (C).** A build has its own page, at `/{tenant}/connections/{id}` — **the address the
redirect already answers**, so nothing bookmarked and nothing handed out breaks. It is built the
product's own way: the shared `PageHeader` (back link, kicker, 32px title, roll-up line, actions),
then the tab bar, then the tab's content, and **seven tabs — Overview · Units · Work · Charges ·
Documents · Messages · Audit.** The seventh is **Audit** because the account detail page and the
template detail page already call that tab Audit, and one product may not hold two words for one
thing.

Three further rulings arrived in the same review and are recorded here so nobody re-asks them
(hard-won law 13):

> *"since we have given link for them in overview"*

— said when the header's **Open premises** and **Open account** buttons were shown. **They are
removed.** The Overview table's *What this build made* rows already link the customer, the account,
the premises and the invoice; a second door to each in the header is duplication, one size smaller.

> *"you need to use 1 or 2 action words - dont use 3 words"*

— **every action label on this page is one or two words.** Raise order · Hold · Release · Waiting
on · Add service · Mark outstanding · Close outstanding · Cancel build · Take payment · Resend ·
Add document · Carry on · Re-park.

> *"all these option will anyway will be in filter - so we dont need them outside"*

— **the New connects list gets no saved-view chips.** State is a filter; the tiles SET that filter
rather than filtering around it, or the two controls disagree about what a clerk is looking at.

---

### WHAT IS SUPERSEDED, QUOTED, WITH ITS CHAIN

**The statement being reversed** is this log's own row of **2026-09-04**:

> **`CR-070` WAVE O IS BUILT AND SHIPS AS `2.141.0` — A BUILD HAS ONE DESTINATION, AND IT IS THE
> PREMISES AND THE ACCOUNT.** `/connections/<uuid>` stops being a place a person navigates to:
> `features/customers/ConnectionDetailPage.tsx` (1,464 lines) and its two test files are DELETED,
> its panels live once in `features/work/buildViews.tsx`, and the premises detail and the account
> detail compose them. **The route is KEPT** and answers a redirect … **Five links repointed** …
> and **`G93` added so the destination cannot come back.**

and the Product Owner's own words that row transcribes, from `CR-070` §W.10 / §W.11:

> *"youa re duplcaiting this - there is nothing called as conenctions; Connection = Account only -
> you cannot have two differnt screen - this is an integration problem"*

scoped the same day to:

> *"One screen too many. The objection is the duplicate destination — a person should reach the
> build's progress, its units, its work orders and its charges from the account, not from a
> parallel screen."*

| # | The 2026-09-04 statement | After 2026-09-28 |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | a build has ONE destination; `/connections/<id>` is a doorway, not a screen | **SUPERSEDED.** A build has its own page, at that same address |
| 2 | wave-O judgment **(2)** — *"money and its trail are facts about a PAYER … Building a second copy inside a Build tab is the duplicate destination the ruling is about, one level down"* | ⚠ **HOLDS, AND IT IS PART OF THIS RULING.** The Charges tab shows what THIS BUILD made and **LINKS** to the account for every bill, payment, adjustment and journal line |
| 3 | the panels live **once**, in `features/work/buildViews.tsx`; hosts **compose** them | ⚠ **HOLDS, AND IT IS PART OF THIS RULING.** B14 rule 43 has since ratified it product-wide. **No panel is copied** |

⚠ **EXACTLY ONE CLAUSE MOVES, AND THE OBJECTION UNDERNEATH IT DOES NOT MOVE AT ALL.** *A build may
not have its own screen* becomes *a build has its own screen.* **Duplication is still refused** —
and the Product Owner demonstrated that themselves in the same conversation by taking the two

places holding the same facts is wrong*, and this page holds none of the account's.

process's STOP condition does not fire.

⚠ **THE 2026-09-04 ROW IS NOT REWRITTEN.** This log's convention for a superseded decision is a
NEW, forward-pointing entry that quotes what it supersedes — as at 2026-09-15 (*"THE RULING ROW OF
THIS MORNING NAMED `1000` AND IS SUPERSEDED ON THAT ONE POINT AND ON NOTHING ELSE"*) and at
2026-09-23 (*"⛔ SUPERSEDED BY THE PO: THE NEW-CONNECTION RULE IN THE TWO ENTRIES ABOVE IS

### `G93` IS AMENDED RATHER THAN DELETED, AND IT NOW CHECKS THE RULE THAT DID NOT MOVE

`10-scripts/gates/g93_one_build_destination.py` was added on 2026-09-04 to ask *"does anything in
the front end still send a person to `/connections/<id>`?"*. **That question is now the wrong way
round** — the address is a page, so every link to it is correct and the gate would refuse the build
it is supposed to protect.

**It keeps its id and it stops being about the ADDRESS. It is now about DUPLICATION, which is what
the Product Owner objected to in the first place**, and it asks three things:

1. **COMPOSED, NOT COPIED** — a build panel may be DEFINED only in
   `07-frontend/src/features/work/buildViews.tsx` and its `buildRecord/` kit. Defined anywhere
   else, it is a copy.
2. **THE PAGE COMPOSES** — whatever `App.tsx` mounts at the build address must import from that
   home. While a doorway is mounted this check is SKIPPED, and the gate says so **in its pass
   line, by name** — a blind spot with no number beside it is indistinguishable from an empty one.
3. **MONEY LINKS** — no file the build page reaches may import the account's money reads or money
   panels, or call a money API path. The Overview table's `INV-2026-00318` is a **link**; the
   `$1,035.00` beside it is a fact.

**Deleting the gate was the other option and it was refused.** The duplication it guards is the
whole reason the last page was deleted, and a gate that cannot fail is worse than none.

---

### THE ORDER OF WORK IS PART OF THE RULING, BECAUSE BOTH WAYS ROUND ARE A KNOWN DEFECT

**The redirect keeps answering `/{tenant}/connections/{id}` until the page is on the branch**, and
then one commit flips the element, deletes `BuildRedirect.tsx` and its test, and lands a route test.
Flipping first gives a live address in front of a screen that does not exist — hard-won law 2's
mirror, which on 2026-09-05 left the customer portal's front page with two working doors out of
eight. Building first and not flipping gives dead UI — law 2 itself.

⚠ **AND THE ROUTE TEST ASSERTS THE ADDRESS BY SCREEN ID, NOT BY COMPONENT NAME**, mounted under the
real path pattern `/:tenant/connections/:connectionId`. Law 7's *looking at the wrong thing*: a
hold-expiry test once asserted a screen was REGISTERED at an address while the router mounted it
somewhere else, both opened onto *"not built yet"*, and every check passed. And the portal's own
fixture mounted a component bare in a `MemoryRouter` with no tenant route, so every address it built
came out `//portal/…` — a protocol-relative URL to another host, which reads as a perfectly good
string to `toContain`.

## 2026-09-28 (late) · THE BOOKS ENTRY AT CREATION — SEVEN JUDGMENTS `BR-MET-1187` DOES NOT MAKE, DECIDED AND WRITTEN DOWN RATHER THAN PUT BACK TO THE PO — `CR-150-BRC09` `B1`

**The ruling is already made** and is answer 18 above: *"we create entries in books"*, *"do it at
creation once submitted"*, over the sentence *"It is one act: if the books entry cannot be written,
the connection is not created either."* This entry is the other half of hard-won law 13 — **a
judgment call recorded with its reasoning is the deliverable; a question is the failure to make
one** — so the seven places building it required a decision are written here with their worked
figures, and none of them went back to the Product Owner.

**Nothing here collides with a signed rule, no ❄️ FROZEN B4/B5 figure moves, and none of the seven
is a fact only the PO holds** — which is law 13's whole test for what legitimately reaches them.

### 1 · WHICH ABSENCES MEAN *NOTHING TO WRITE*, AND THEREFORE DO NOT REFUSE

`BR-MET-1187` names the boundary but not the list: *"A BUILD THAT NAMES NO CHARGE HAS NOTHING TO
WRITE AND IS UNAFFECTED — the rule bites where there IS an entry to write and it fails."* Five
refusal codes reach the branch. **Two are exempt and three refuse.**

| Code | What it means | Decision |
|---|---|---|
| `build_names_no_charge` | nobody put a charge on this build | **exempt** — the ruling's own words |
| `quote_has_no_chargeable_line` | every line of the request's quote is WAIVED by a named person, or already carries an invoice reference from an earlier commit | **exempt.** The money has already been dealt with, so this commit owes the books nothing — the same statement as *nobody put a charge on this build*, arriving by a different route. This is the one the ruling does not spell out and it is the reason this row exists |
| the payer's four codes | a charge exists and there is nobody lawful to bill | **refuses** |
| `quote_payment_terms_not_captured` | a charge exists and nobody typed the terms | **refuses** — and `BR-BIL-024` is why it cannot be defaulted instead |
| `billing_quote_door_unpublished` | a charge exists and billing is not there | **refuses** |

The list lives in `QUOTE_ABSENCES_WITH_NOTHING_TO_WRITE` with this argument beside it, because
adding a sixth code to it would silently restore `DEF-MET-7641`.

### 2 · THE CLIENT'S `quote_total` BECOMES A REFUSAL AND IS WRITTEN NOWHERE

**Worked, and it is the figure on the defect row:** a build the size of the drawn example whose
charges could not be posted used to be created with `$1,035.00` on `connections.quote_total`,
`one_time_charge_invoice_no` NULL, and **no invoice anywhere** — nothing in Billing, nothing in
Finance, nobody ever asked for it.

Two ways to obey hard rule 2 (*never take a total from the client*): drop the figure entirely, or
keep it as a CHECK. **Kept as a check**, because the alternative throws away the one thing that can
catch a catalogue that moved between the clerk reading `$800.00` on step 4 and the bill being
raised — `rating.selectors.charge_by_code` says in its own words that *"the amount is a SEED the
tenant edits, never a constant"*. So: if the client sends a total and it disagrees with the bill,
the commit refuses and names both figures; the bill is the authority either way, and a client that
sends nothing is compared with nothing. **Written: nowhere, on any path.**

### 3 · THE PAYMENT'S IDEMPOTENCY KEY IS THE CONNECTION, NOT A CLIENT TOKEN

`payments.webhook_key`, `UNIQUE (tenant_id, webhook_key)` — B2 §2 and DB-12's second row, the one
idempotency key a payment has (hard rule 6). The string is
`entry|new-connect:<connection id>`.

**The connection's id and not the browser's token**, and payments' own idempotency module gives the
reason: a key the caller invents is *"different on the second submit and would dedupe nothing while
looking like it did"*. The connection id is stable across every retry of one build and is unique per
build. **It is the SECOND guard, not the only one** — `commit_connection` already refuses any
connection that is not `DRAFT`, so a second press cannot reach the money at all; the key covers the
case the state cannot, a request that wrote and then lost its answer.

### 4 · THE MONEY GOES TO *THIS* BILL, NOT TO THE OLDEST ONE

`record_payment` defaults to `oldest_first`. On a build tagged to an account that **already owes
money**, that default takes the developer's counter payment for the new connection and puts it
against last quarter's water bill — money applied to a debt nobody named, under a receipt that says
the connection charge was paid. So the instruction is payments' own `specific`, naming the invoice
just raised, with no amount: *this bill, up to whatever it owes*. **An overpayment carries as an
account credit and is REPORTED on the commit** (`BR-PAY-010`), never dropped.

### 5 · AN AMOUNT WITH NO TENDER REFUSES; IT IS NOT DEFAULTED TO CASH

`payments.method` is nullable, so the write would succeed — and the money would sit in the day's
takings belonging to no drawer, un-bankable and un-reconcilable. It is `BR-BIL-024`'s shape on the
other side of the receipt: **a guessed tender is a real row on a real deposit.** A tender with no
amount, and an amount of zero, refuse for the same family of reasons — a receipt for `$0.00` states
that money changed hands when none did.

### 6 · THE PAYMENT'S DATE FALLS BACK TO THE CHARGE'S POSTING DATE, NEVER TO A CLOCK

They are one event: the clerk is taking the money for the charge they are raising in the same press,
and the posting date is the one they typed on the same step. `BR-TEN-043` and gate `G6` forbid a
wall clock on a money path, and a clock here would date a Friday counter payment to Saturday on a
late commit. The DATE is turned into an instant the way `billing.fee_bill.issue_moment` already
does it — start of day, UTC, derived — because that is *"the only [instant] the date itself
determines"* and therefore the only one an idempotent retry reproduces.

### 7 · CASH AT NEW CONNECT NEEDS AN OPEN TILL, AND THAT IS THE RULING APPLIED RATHER THAN WIDENED

`OQ-PAY-12601` closed on 2026-09-23 in the PO's words: *"back office or counter - if person is
punching the payemnt in system - it is same process, they ahve to open the counter - we always
capture batch number becuase we will need that reference when we reconcile."* A clerk keying a
payment at New Connect is punching a payment into the system, so the rule covers them, and New
Connect is a **call site** of the one implementation (`payments.counters.assert_till_open_for_
tender`) rather than a copy of it. The till it answers is **kept and stamped on the payment**, which
is `DEF-PAY-6226`'s lesson — the same rule was called at another door and its answer thrown away,
so the refusal worked and no payment ever named the till it was taken at.

⚠ **AND READING THAT CLOSED QUESTION AGAINST THE CALL SITES FOUND A DOOR THAT STILL SKIPS THE
GUARD — `DEF-PAY-7642`, FILED RATHER THAN LEFT IN PROSE.** `POST /customers/{id}/payments`
(`payments/tenders_api.py::customer_payments`) takes ONE cheque across several accounts and never
asks for a till, so `$520.00` in cheques can be keyed with no counter open and every dollar banks
under the day's system till. **The gap was already written down twice, in a code comment and in the
`OQ-PAY-12601` row's own recommendation, and neither is a row anything counts** — which is
CLAUDE.md's own lesson under hard rule 4, and the reason it is a defect id now.

## 2026-09-28 · The New connects list learns the customer, the age and the accent — and is told plainly that it cannot learn the money yet

**What was asked for.** The New connects list was rebuilt from its 2026-09-28 drawing and three
drawn columns and two tiles could not be built, because `GET /connections` did not serve the
fields. The list lane refused to compute them in the browser rather than show figures the server
had not produced. This is the server half.

**What it can now show, per row.** The CUSTOMER — the owner account's customer name and its
account number, or nothing at all when a build has no owner yet. The AGE in days, counted in the
utility's own calendar. Whether that age should be shown in red, decided on the server. And,
behind the Columns menu: what was quoted, whether the work is our crew's or a contractor's, the
scope somebody typed at step 1, who raised the build, and the last thing that happened to it. On
the tiles: how many open builds are waiting on somebody — anybody, not only an inspector, which
is what the old tile counted and why that tile could not be clicked.

**What it still cannot show, and this is the part worth reading.** The drawing puts money on
this list for the first time — a DUE figure on every row and a *$4,210 owed on open builds* tile.
**Neither is served and neither is faked.** A build does name its bill, and the payments side can
already tell us in one go what has been paid against a whole page of bills. The billing side
cannot: it can answer *what does this one bill come to* and there is no way to ask it about
twenty-five bills at once, so a page of twenty-five rows would be twenty-five separate questions
and the tenant-wide tile would be one question per open build. So the DUE column is simply not
there, and the tile shows nothing with a sentence saying the bills could not be read a page at a
time. **A `$0.00` would have been the easy thing and it is the one thing we must never do** — a
zero on that tile reads as *every build is paid for*. One function in the billing module closes
it, and it is billing's to write, not metering's.

**A judgment recorded rather than a question asked.** The AGE column turns red past a threshold,
and there was no threshold for a build. On 2026-08-25 the Product Owner was shown the Requests
list and ruled that a request goes red at **seven days or more**. Rather than invent a second
number, this list asks for that same one — there is one place in the product where the figure
lives and every screen that shows an age reads it from there. **But that signature was taken on
the Requests screen and this screen was never shown**, and a build takes weeks where a request
takes days, so at seven days almost every open build on the list is red and the warning stops
meaning anything. The drawing itself hints the same way: it shows a 16-day build in plain black
and a 41-day build in red. That is filed as `OQ-CUS-12771` with three answers to pick from, and
**nothing is blocked on it** — the column, the flag and the tile are built, tested and live on the
ruled figure meanwhile.

**A defect found on the way in and fixed in the same commit.** The *oldest build* tile counted a
build's age as elapsed twenty-four-hour periods measured from a UTC clock, while the new AGE
column counts calendar days on the utility's own clock. Two arithmetics under one word. Nothing
had caught it because the test fixture backdates builds by whole days, which makes both answers
identical on every seeded row. It is the same fault `DEF-CUS-6433` fixed on the Requests list four
days earlier — fixed where it was found, and nobody swept the other lists. There is now ONE
function and both the row and the tile call it (`DEF-CUS-7620`).

**What it cost.** Nothing per row. Every new cell is answered once for the whole page — one clock
read, one grouped query for the crews' modes, one call for the customers and one for the names —
so a page of six builds costs the same fixed overhead as a page of three. A test measures that
slope rather than claiming it, and it goes red if any of the new cells starts asking per row: a
list a utility opens all day cannot grow a query per row to gain three columns.

**And the work-order rows on the build page now say who has the job, as TWO facts.** A crew and a
technician are separate columns because a crew can hold an order with nobody named on it yet, and
that unassigned case is exactly what stalls a build. One field cannot tell *the contractor has it*
from *nobody has it*.

## 2026-09-28 (late, amended the same evening) · AN EIGHTH JUDGMENT ON THE BOOKS ENTRY — THE CLEARING DATE, FOUND ONLY BY RUNNING IT ON REAL POSTGRESQL — `CR-150-BRC09` `B1`

**This is an amendment to the entry above and not a second ruling.** The seven
judgments there were made before the code ran; this one was made after, and it
is recorded separately so the order is visible.

### WHAT WAS MEASURED

The first working version of the counter payment recorded the payment, returned
its receipt number on the manifest, and **allocated nothing to the bill.** On
real PostgreSQL the build's invoice came back `$0.00` settled with a receipt on
screen — and `apps/payments/billing_seam.allocated_for_invoices` returned the
bill ABSENT from its map, which is payments' own way of saying *nothing has been
paid against it*.

**The cause is a rule, not a bug.** `BR-PAY-021` and `US-LED-001`: a payment
with **no clearing date** is `processing` — *the money has not arrived* — so
`record_payment` deliberately allocates it to no bill and posts no ledger pair,
and reports `not_cleared_so_not_allocated` by name. The first version passed no
clearing date, so every counter payment at New Connect was one.

⚠ **THAT IS `DEF-MET-7641`'s OWN DISEASE ONE LAYER DOWN** — money that exists on
a screen and in no ledger — arriving inside the fix for it. It was invisible
until the allocation was asserted through the read the SCREEN uses.

### WHAT WAS DECIDED, AND WHAT WAS NOT

**Decided: step 4 asks for the clearing date, exactly as the S22 Record-a-payment
form already asks for it.** `payment_cleared_date` is the sixth payment field on
the commit payload, it is OPTIONAL, and **it is never defaulted** — a cheque
handed over is not a cheque that cleared, and defaulting it to the posting date
would take a bill out of arrears on money that has not arrived.

**Decided: an absent clearing date is REPORTED, not hidden.** The commit now
carries payments' own coded problems out onto `unavailable[]`, so a build with a
receipt and an unsettled bill says which of the two it is. Silence there is what
made the first version look right.

⚠ **NOT DECIDED, AND DELIBERATELY NOT INVENTED: WHETHER A TENDER IMPLIES ITS OWN
CLEARING.** It is tempting to say cash in a drawer has obviously arrived and a
cheque obviously has not, and to fill the date in per tender. **Nobody has ruled
that**, `BR-PAY-021` puts the date in the clerk's hands at every other counter in
the product, and a rule invented here would be a second answer to *when did this
money arrive* living in metering. The clerk answers it, on the screen, or the
commit says the money is still on its way.

**No question is minted for it**, because none is open: the rule exists and this
is it being obeyed at a new door.

## 2026-09-28 (late) · THE BUILD DETAIL PAGE STOPS WRITING ITS OWN PANELS — `DEF-CUS-7618`, THE SECOND OF THE TWO CONDITIONS THE REVERSAL WAS GRANTED ON

**The Product Owner's reversal of 2026-09-28 gave the build its own page again on two conditions,
written into `CR-151-BRC09` §2.** Money facts LINK to the account rather than being
re-implemented, and **no panel is copied — the page composes the shared ones.** The money half
was done correctly the day the page landed. This is the other half.

**What was wrong, in one sentence a person can read.** The new page wrote its own version of
every tab: 4,422 lines of new files against the 1,464-line page the Product Owner deleted three
weeks earlier for exactly this reason. Its Work tab was a hand-written table — no search, no
filter, no way to choose columns, no paging and no way to open a job without leaving the page —
sitting beside a shared work-orders table that already does all five and that the property page
and the customer's account page both use. The page borrowed two word-lists from the shared file
and not one panel.

**What it does now.**

* **Work** uses the shared table. It is the same component the property and the account use, on a
  third host. It reads the address's own work-order list — the one the property page already asks
  for, so a clerk who has opened that tab pays for no second request — and keeps the jobs this
  build raised, because the build's own read is the only thing that says which those are.
* The page gains four things the hand-written table did not have: **who holds each job**, **the
  target date**, **the job drawer**, and the search, filter, column chooser and paging.
* **Crew and technician stay two columns**, which is the Product Owner's own ruling of this
  morning. The server sends ONE holder per job and says whether it is a person or a crew, so each
  column shows what is actually known and neither guesses the other. Before this, both columns
  said *nothing is served* on every row for ever.
* **Overview, Units, Charges, Documents, Messages and Audit** have no shared panel to compose —
  and `CR-151-BRC09` §3 already said what happens then: *"new tab content that has no shared
  panel is built as components under the same kit."* Each is now a file in that kit, and each one
  says at the top WHY no shared panel serves it. Charges, in particular, stays a summary and a
  link: the account's own bills tab is the money panel, and putting it inside a build tab is the
  duplicate screen this whole chain is about.

**The judgment we made rather than asking.** Moving those six into the kit is a relocation and
not a redesign — **not one thing a clerk sees has changed on any of them.** The alternative was
to leave them where they were and write down why, which would have left the gate red and the
route flip blocked. Nothing here needed a ruling: `CR-151-BRC09` §3 had already decided it and
this lane followed it.

**One finding was not ours and is now filed.** The gate was also refusing a component in the New
connects LIST called `BuildTiles`, from a sibling lane's commit earlier the same day. Two
different tile strips — one for a single build, one for the list — were writing the same marker
into the page, and a browser walkthrough reads that marker and expects a number. The list's strip
is renamed and has its own marker (`DEF-CUS-7622`). The duplication underneath it is real and is
**not** fixed: the list writes out the shared strip's markup by hand because the shared strip has
no way to make a tile pressable (`DEF-CUS-7623`).

**And `CR-151-BRC09` §6c said the gate named six panels. It named ten.** The failure line prints
three findings and a count of the rest, and six is what a reader who stopped at the first line
wrote down. §6d records the correction. **Read a check's whole output, not its first line.**

**The route is NOT flipped.** It is one commit and it belongs to the reversal lane's task R3:
swap the element in `App.tsx`, delete `BuildRedirect.tsx` and its test, give the address its
screen id back in `screenIds.ts` and `g29_allocated_badges.txt`, and raise `G29`'s count by one.
**Measured rather than assumed:** the gate's own checks were run over a throwaway copy of the
front end with the route already flipped, and all three pass — so the flip is safe from the
gate's side and the only work left is those five files.

## 2026-09-28 — THE CHARGES STEP TAKES THE MONEY, AND TWO THINGS THE DRAWING ASKS FOR ARE DELIBERATELY NOT BUILT

**What changed.** Step 6 of the New Connect wizard now collects the payment a clerk takes at
the counter and sends it with the commit, so pressing **Create connection** writes the
connection, the invoice **and** the payment in one act (`BR-MET-1187`, shipped on the server in
`2.391.0`). Until today the step drew a refusal — *"No payment is taken here. Record it against
the account."* — over a server that had taken six payment fields since that release. A clerk
holding a cheque had to key it twice, and the build's own Charges tab showed nothing taken.
`DEF-CUS-7611` is the Product Owner's report, from the deployed build: *"based on payment type
we nedd to give all paymnet fields"*.

**The one field that decides whether the money exists is the clearing date, and it is never
filled in for the clerk.** A payment with no clearing date is *processing* — the money has not
arrived — so it settles no bill and posts no ledger pair (`BR-PAY-021`). The first working
version of the server change recorded a payment, printed a receipt number on screen, and left
the invoice reading **`$0.00` settled**: a receipt for money that met nothing. So the box starts
empty, is never prefilled from a clock or from the tender, and goes to the server as an explicit
*nothing* when it is left blank. **No per-tender rule was invented here** — there is no "cash
clears today, cheques do not". The screen copies what the Record a payment screen already does
with this field, down to the words *Clearing date* and *The day the money arrived.*, because two
screens asking one question two ways is how they start disagreeing (B14 rule 44).

### Two judgments we made rather than asking

**1 · The drawing offers three answers to *Take payment* and the screen offers two.** p096 draws
*Yes — a deposit against the quote · No, invoice it on activation · No, the developer pays per
unit*. The third is the PAYER restated, and the payer is the radio group directly above it —
whose *Each unit's first bill* the server refuses by name. Offering it in both places lets a
clerk say two contradictory things, and the one the product declines would be a live control
that lies (hard-won law 2's mirror, the shape that cost the customer portal six doors out of
eight). The two no-payment answers are therefore one: **No payment now**, which is the default
and is what the server's own code calls *"the ordinary answer"*.

**2 · The drawn *Payment summary* has three rows and the screen shows two.** *Quoted* is the
pricing engine's own figure for these lines and *Taken now* is the clerk's own typed string;
neither is added, subtracted or rounded in the browser. **The third row, *Outstanding at
activation*, is `Quoted − Taken` — money arithmetic in a browser, which hard rule 2 forbids and
which `DEF-088` and `DEF-127` already cost us.** Nothing on the wizard's side can supply it
honestly: `/connections/quote-preview` prices lines and knows nothing about a payment. So the
screen states the absence in five words and the figure is read where the server derives it — the
build's own Charges tab, the moment the build exists. **The worked case:** a $3,030.00 quote with
$1,500.00 taken shows *Quoted $3,030.00* and *Taken now $1,500.00* on the wizard, and
*Outstanding $1,530.00* on the build. `DEF-CUS-7704` carries the row, with the two ways to close
it.

**And the browser's copy of the commit manifest was four keys behind the server's**
(`DEF-CUS-7681`): seven of twelve, missing `messages` and `one_time_charge_invoice_no` since
2026-09-16 and the two payment keys since this morning, with a comment still saying the quote was
*"posted by nothing"* — answered twelve days ago. **A TypeScript interface that declares fewer
keys than the server sends is not an error in TypeScript**: the extra keys are simply invisible,
`tsc` is green and the only symptom is a value nobody can render. All twelve are declared, the
false sentence is deleted rather than reworded, and a test now reads both definitions and fails
when they disagree.

## 2026-09-28 — A METER MAY NOT BE INSTALLED ON A SIZE-BANDED SERVICE WITH NO SIZE, AND THE RULE IS BOUND TO THE FORM THAT ASKS THE QUESTION

**`DEF-AST-7660` · `DEF-AST-7661` · `DEF-RAT-7662` · version `2.392.3` · branch
`claude/confirm-understanding-3ktufc`, lane AST-ASSIGN-SIZE.**

**What the Product Owner reported.** On a unit, **Assets → + Assign from inventory**, the clerk
cannot set the connection size, so the size column in the unit's table is blank.

**Reproduced in Chromium at 1440 on the seeded demo tenant, before anything was changed.** The
panel draws exactly two controls — a search box headed *Find one for U-00101-A* and a **Service**
picker reading *Choose a service* — and no size control of any kind. The unit's own Assets table
shows `M-7001 · Electric · no size recorded` and `W-7001 · Water · no size recorded`, and the
shelf table below shows `M-5099 · Meter · no size recorded`. Screenshot kept with the lane.

**What was actually wrong, and it was not the table.** The table has said *no size recorded* since
`DEF-MET-6926` landed the day before; the honest word was already on screen. **What was missing
was any way to answer it.** `POST /assets/{id}/reassign` never read a `size_class`, and the panel
never sent one, so a spare that came off the shelf blank was installed blank — and on a service
whose price BANDS by size the base charge cannot be resolved at all. The refusal arrives weeks
later, inside a bill run, as `SizeNotServed`.

**THE JUDGMENT, AND IT IS THE WHOLE OF THIS ENTRY: THE REQUIREMENT IS BOUND TO THE PAYLOAD THAT
DECLARES A SERVICE, NOT TO EVERY ASSIGN.** The obvious rule — *a measuring asset going onto a unit
must have a size* — would also fire on the full-page **Reassign** screen (S55) and on
**bulk assign**, and **neither of those draws a service control or a size control**. A clerk who
can assign a meter from the register today would be unable to assign one at all: a live screen
behind a refusal nobody can satisfy, which is hard-won law 2's mirror and the exact shape
`DEF-AST-5863` already filed once. So the rule reads: **if you are declaring which service this
device will be billed on, and that service's price is picked by the size, then the size must be
known.** Measured, not assumed: `bulk_assign` does forward `entry.get("service")`, and the only
screen that calls it (`AssetRegistryPage`) sends none — so the guard cannot fire there today, and
a bulk screen that ever adds a service picker must add a size one in the same commit.

**Three further boundaries, each decided rather than defaulted.**
* **METERS only.** `BR-AST-530` offers the size for meters, and `offersConnectionSize` draws the
  same line on the screen side. A backflow preventer declaring water is not refused for a fact no
  surface asks it for. A trash cart genuinely IS priced by size × count (fire's arithmetic), and
  that is a real gap — it is `DEF-AST-7661`'s territory and is filed, not decided here.
* **A service whose bands were never ruled does NOT refuse.** Refusing would be choosing *treat it
  as banded*, which is the prime directive resolved by a default, and it would put the cost of OUR
  open question on a clerk who cannot answer it either. ⚠ **AND THE OBVIOUS SENTENCE HERE IS TWO
  RULINGS OUT OF DATE, WHICH A TEST CAUGHT RATHER THAN A READER.** The first draft of this clause,
  of the seam's docstring and of the backend case all said *"`None` for thermal steam (`OQ-560`)
  and battery (`OQ-561`)"*, taken from the neighbouring docstrings. **Both of those services are
  RULED today and answer `False`** — thermal sums in tons, battery in kW, since `CR-062` gave them
  a capacity catalogue. The one unruled thing is the DIMENSION `thermal_heat_steam`, which is not
  a service code at all. **Measured over all eleven: no service answers `None`**, so the third
  list is empty on every tenant and is a guard for the twelfth service rather than a live case.
  Hard-won law 1, caught because the assertion was written before the sentence was believed.
* **Going back to inventory records no size.** A device returning to the shelf says nothing about
  the connection it has just left, so a `size_class` on that payload is a caller mistake rather
  than an instruction.

**Which services band is READ FROM THE SERVER and is never inferred in the browser.** New read
`GET /assets/size-banded-services`, over the assets seam onto
`apps.rating.resolution.service_prices_by_size_class`. The obvious client-side substitute — *this
tenant has size classes for water, so water must band* — is `DEF-3098`'s retired proxy, which
stopped being true when `CR-062` gave solar, battery, storm water and broadband a CATALOGUE of
installable equipment; a screen asking it would refuse a solar install over a size solar does not
have. The read answers **three** lists and not two, because `not_ruled` is a different fact from
`not_banded` and collapsing them would quietly claim a blank is lawful on a service nobody has
been asked about. Measured on the demo tenant: **banded** = electric, fire, gas, trash, water;
**not banded** = battery, broadband, sewer, solar, storm water, thermal heat.

**The refusal sentence is five words** — *Choose this meter's connection size.* — under B14 rule
33, and the rationale (*why this meter needs one and the last one did not*) is ZERO words on
screen and lives in `_guard_declared_size`'s docstring, exactly as G33's own failure text asks.

**What was NOT done, deliberately: no data was repaired.** `DEF-RAT-7662`'s overlapping rate
windows and `DEF-AST-7660`'s existing size-less meters were **counted and left alone** on PO
instruction — the numbers go to the Product Owner before anything moves. The counting script is
`10-scripts/def_rat_7662_def_ast_7660_counts.py`, read-only by construction, and it prints what it
skipped beside what it counted.

**⚠ THE COUNTS ARE DEMO COUNTS AND ARE LABELLED AS SUCH.** This container holds no production
database. Every database on the cluster is a demo or a sibling lane's scratch copy; the counts
were taken on `sbh_ast7617`, an isolated clone seeded with `manage.py seed_demo` and dropped
nowhere near a sibling's data. **Overlapping rate windows: 0 triples, 0 pairs, 0 live accounts.
Size-less meters: 9 on units taking a banded service, 0 on units taking none, 2 not installed on
any unit; 0 skipped in either skip bucket.** The zero for overlaps was PROVED CAPABLE OF BEING
NON-ZERO before it was believed (hard-won law 7): a throwaway clone was given one overlapping
activated version and one draft, the script reported the overlap with its dates and version ids
and correctly ignored the draft, and the clone was dropped.

**Rollback:** code only — revert the commit. Nothing was migrated and no row was repaired, so
there is nothing left behind.

## 2026-09-28 (late) · ⛔ THE DISCONNECT WIZARD SAID WHY — TO THE SERVER LOG, AND TO NOBODY ELSE — `DEF-CUS-7680`

**What the Product Owner saw**, on deployed `v2.352.0`: screen `DSC-02`,
`/{tenant}/disconnects/new?step=4`. Every step filled, `Schedule the disconnection ✓`
pressed, and the screen answered *"The disconnection was not scheduled. Nothing has
changed."* over *"This disconnect step can't be done as asked. Check the case."* —
with the diagnostic line empty. Trace reference `2FA5-0006`.

**Reproduced before a line of code was read** (the maintenance process's step 0), at
branch tip `db075389b`, against real PostgreSQL 16 on a freshly seeded `brazosbend`.
`POST /disconnects/schedule` for `AC-2026-00054` answers:

    422  BIZ-COMPLETENESS
         message_key : customers.disconnects.refused
         params.code : no_open_case
         params.detail: "there is no open disconnect case on this account
                         to schedule a cut for."

**So the server said exactly why, and the screen threw it away.**

### The finding, and it is bigger than the report

`transfer_disconnect_api._as_catalog_refusal` maps **every** `DisconnectRuleError` onto
ONE catalog code and ONE message key — deliberately, and its own docstring argues for it:
*"picking among the nine BIZ codes per refusal would be this layer INTERPRETING rules it
does not own."* It publishes the difference in `params.code`, and the same docstring says
what that is for: **"The service's `code` rides alongside so a screen can branch without
parsing English."** Nothing, anywhere, branched on it.

**The defect report named six refusals. `schedule_cut`'s call graph raises EIGHTEEN** —
five payload checks, five about the case, six ladder halts that can reach a cut, the
certified-proof channel, and the tier. Counting what was found against what should be
there is CLAUDE.md law 7's fifth shape, and the count is now written down in
`disconnect/disconnectRefusal.ts` as `DISCONNECT_SCHEDULE_REFUSAL_CODES`.

### Three judgments this lane took rather than putting back to the PO (law 13)

**1 · THE SENTENCE COMES FROM THE CATALOGUE, NOT FROM `params.detail`.** The obvious fix
is to render what the server wrote, and it is forbidden: `BR-SHL-020` r2 (PO 2026-08-19)
rules that server `detail` never reaches a customer screen, and `api/client.refusalParams`
deletes it before i18next can see it. The service's prose is written for an engineer —
*"a cut is scheduled after TIER 3 · 48-HOUR, the certified final notice (BR-CUS-039:
certified mail is REQUIRED on the final tier…)"* — and rendering it would re-open
`DEF-322`. **So the code selects a sentence we wrote, and the detail keeps going to the
server log and the `BR-AUD-018` attempt row.**

**2 · THE KEY FAMILY IS NOT FORKED, ALTHOUGH ITS NAME IS WRONG.** The disconnect RECORD
page minted `customers.disconnectRecord.refused.*` — 25 sentences in eleven languages,
keyed on exactly these codes. A wizard family of its own would be a SECOND ANSWER to one
question, which is this repository's most expensive recurring defect (`DEF-127`'s shape).
So the wizard reuses the stem and this lane added the **seven codes it was missing**
(`cut_before_final_tier`, `cut_reason_unknown`, `deposit_disposition_unknown`,
`service_treatment_unknown`, `service_code_unknown`, `restrictor_is_a_third_state`,
`ladder_floor_not_readable`) rather than writing 18 × 11 new strings. **Renaming the stem
is a real tidy-up and is deliberately NOT in this commit** — it moves 25 keys across
eleven catalogues and six call sites, which the maintenance process's *minimal fix* step
exists to keep out of a defect.

**3 · AN UNMAPPED CODE FALLS BACK TO THE OLD GENERIC LINE, NEVER TO A BLANK.** A refusal
the front end has no sentence for renders exactly what it rendered before this lane. A
blank would be worse than a generic: a clerk who reads nothing cannot even tell support
that something was refused (`DEF-320`'s shape). **The cost is that a NEW server refusal
degrades silently**, and that is stated in the module's own exceptions rather than hidden.

### And the clerk is no longer made to fill four steps for a case that can never go

Four of the eighteen are decided by the CASE, which is chosen on step 1 and does not
change while a clerk types: **no open case · the cut is already recorded · a COLLECTIONS
sequence or a closed account · the case is below TIER 3.** `disconnect_reads.
schedule_readiness` previews them read-only, **by calling `schedule_cut`'s own predicates
and guards** — `already_cut`, `assert_cut_reachable`, `ladder_tier_of` — in the commit's
own order, so the first blocker is the sentence the commit would really have given. It
rides on `GET /accounts/{id}/ladder`, where `cut_floor` already rides, for the same
reason: the ladder is the resource that owns the case.

⚠ **IT IS A PREVIEW AND `schedule_cut` IS UNCHANGED.** Days pass between a screen being
drawn and a button being pressed; the commit re-runs everything inside its transaction and
a `ready: true` is not permission. **A screen that decided eligibility for itself would be
the next defect**, and a browser case proves the two halves were not traded for each
other: a ready pre-flight, a commit that still refuses, and the clerk reading the commit's
reason.

⚠ **AND AN ABSENT `schedule_readiness` LETS THE CLERK THROUGH.** A tenant on an older
build serves no such key, and a screen reading a missing field as *not ready* would block
every disconnection in the product. Hard-won law 3 points the other way here: the unsafe
option is REFUSING.

### What it cost to prove, and one thing the proof taught

The frontend cases were run in a second `git worktree` at the pre-change tip `8f9bef45d`:
**13 failed, 7 passed of 20**, the failures being six commit sentences still reading the
generic line, seven missing catalogue keys, and five step-1 refusals that were not drawn
at all. ⚠ **The first attempt at that proof was worthless and is recorded because of it:**
run unmodified the file could not resolve its own import and vitest reported *"no tests"*
— a red that proves an import is missing and says nothing about the screen. ⚠ **And four
of the seven that passed, passed for the wrong reason** — an absent catalogue key returns
the KEY STRING, so *"the six sentences are all different"* was true of six key strings,
and *"every sentence is within six words"* measured empty strings. Both are named in the
suite's own header.

⚠ **THE BACKEND FIXTURE HIT HARD-WON LAW 14 ON THE FIRST RUN.** Its first draft mutated
ONE case through three scenarios and set `cut_on` alone; `ck_cut_records_the_price_of_
coming_back` refused the row, the failed statement aborted the PostgreSQL transaction, and
everything after it raised `InFailedSqlTransaction` — `2 failed, 7 passed, 2 errors`, the
errors being the poisoned teardown. **On SQLite it would have sailed through.** One account
per scenario now, every row lawful at INSERT.

### What is NOT fixed, and is filed rather than quietly absorbed

**The `BR-AUD-018` attempt row cannot name which refusal fired.** It records the catalog
code (`BIZ-COMPLETENESS`), the method, the path and the `br_ref` — verified against a live
refusal on the reproduction, resolved by its own short reference — and `params.code` is not
among them. `br_ref` narrows `2FA5-0006` to a group (`BR-CUS-039` covers three of the six)
and no further. The exact reason IS recorded, in `_log_refusal`'s server-log line, which is
where the 2026-08-19 ruling deliberately moved the diagnostic. **So the trace resolves; the
audit row alone does not identify the refusal, and the log does.**
